0.title: The King Has Come
0.overview:
Matthew begins where the Old Testament ends — with promises. His opening genealogy is not a genealogy at all; it is a theology compressed into names. Abraham to David to the exile to Jesus: the whole arc of Israel’s story, told in three movements, arriving at the one name toward which every other name was pointing. Matthew’s first words are biblos geneseos — the book of origins, the book of genesis. A new creation has begun.

Matthew wrote for Jewish Christians, probably in Antioch, in the decades after the destruction of Jerusalem. His readers knew the Old Testament. They had grown up with the promises of a coming King from David’s line, a new Moses who would deliver God’s people, a suffering servant who would bear the sins of many, a son of man who would receive an everlasting dominion. Matthew’s argument, sustained across twenty-eight chapters, is that all of these promises find their yes in Jesus of Nazareth (2 Cor. 1:20). The fulfillment formula — to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet — appears again and again like a refrain, stitching the Old Testament to the New until you cannot see the seam.

The great theme of Matthew is the kingdom of heaven. Where Mark asks who this man is, and Luke traces the universal reach of grace, Matthew announces the arrival of a reign. Heaven’s rule has broken into earth’s disorder in the person of the King. He teaches with authority (not as the scribes). He heals with a word. He calms the sea. He feeds the multitude. He raises the dead. And then he goes to the cross not as a victim of circumstances but as the King who lays down his life to ransom many (20:28) — the supreme act of royal authority disguised as utter weakness.

Matthew’s Jesus is the new Moses, but greater. Moses gave the law from Sinai; Jesus gives the new law from the mountain (chapters 5–7). Moses delivered Israel through the Red Sea; Jesus passes through death and comes out the other side. Moses saw the promised land from a distance and died; Jesus enters it, conquers it, and invites all nations to follow him in. “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them” (5:17). In Jesus, the Old Testament does not end — it arrives.

The name given to him in chapter 1 is the key that unlocks the whole: Emmanuel — God with us. And the Gospel ends with the same promise, spoken now in resurrection glory: I am with you always, to the end of the age (28:20). Matthew is bracketed by the presence of God. What began in a manger in Bethlehem does not end at a tomb in Jerusalem. It ends with a commission that will reach every tongue and tribe and nation — because the one who sends is the one to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given.

Read Matthew as someone meeting the King for the first time. Let the authority of his teaching arrest you. Let the tenderness of his healing move you. Let the cross unmake your comfortable religion. And let the resurrection send you — into all the world, making disciples, baptising, teaching. The Gospel of Matthew is not a story that ends; it is a commission that begins.

1.title: Emmanuel — God With Us
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. <sup>2</sup>Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, <sup>3</sup>and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, <sup>4</sup>and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon, <sup>5</sup>and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, <sup>6</sup>and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, <sup>7</sup>and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, <sup>8</sup>and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, <sup>9</sup>and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, <sup>10</sup>and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah, <sup>11</sup>and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. <sup>12</sup>And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, <sup>13</sup>and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, <sup>14</sup>and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, <sup>15</sup>and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, <sup>16</sup>and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. <sup>17</sup>So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations. <sup>18</sup>Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. <sup>19</sup>And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. <sup>20</sup>But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. <sup>21</sup>She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” <sup>22</sup>All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: <sup>23</sup>“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us). <sup>24</sup>When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, <sup>25</sup>but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
1.overview:
Matthew opens not with a manger scene but with a list of names — and the list is the point. Every name in the genealogy is a promise kept. From Abraham, through whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. 12:3), to David, whose throne would endure forever (2 Sam. 7:16), to the exile and back: the whole history of Israel’s faithfulness and failure, strung together like beads on a single cord that ends at the name Jesus. God’s covenant faithfulness spans every generation, including the dark ones. Especially the dark ones.

The genealogy contains surprises that Matthew intends. Four women appear — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and “the wife of Uriah” — each associated with scandal, foreignness, or irregularity. Matthew is signalling from the first page that this King comes not for the respectable but for the broken, not only for Israel but for the nations. Grace does not run through clean lines; it runs through history as it actually happened, mess and all.

Then the birth narrative proper, and its two names. Jesus: he will save his people from their sins (v. 21). The name carries the whole gospel in four letters — Y’shua, the LORD saves. And Emmanuel: God with us (v. 23). The fulfilment of Isaiah’s sign (Isa. 7:14) is no longer a child born in the eighth century BC as a near-term reassurance to Ahaz; it is the Son of God entering human flesh, the Creator wearing the creature’s nature, the infinite becoming finite — without ceasing to be infinite. This is the doctrine of the incarnation, announced in a single breath in a single verse, and it changes everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew opens not with a narrative but with a name-list, and in doing so announces that the gospel is rooted in real history. The genealogy traces Jesus' legal descent through Joseph from Abraham and David, grounding him in both the Abrahamic covenant (promise of blessing to all nations, Gen. 12:3) and the Davidic covenant (promise of an eternal throne, 2 Sam. 7:12–16). Three groups of fourteen generations form a theological argument, not an exhaustive record: Jesus is the divinely appointed culmination of redemptive history. Four women — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — appear unexpectedly, each associated with scandal or Gentile origin, signaling that this King's grace reaches beyond the expected. Three kings are missing at verse 8 — Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah (1 Chron. 3:11-12) — which is not an error: the phrase rendered "father of" means ancestor of throughout Scripture, and a Jewish genealogy was a legal document establishing descent rather than a birth register. Matthew wants his three fourteens and prunes to get them; all three omitted kings descended from Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. Two names look wrong — "Asaph" for king Asa and "Amos" for king Amon — and these are simply the fuller Greek forms Matthew used, which modern translations keep rather than tidy. The third group has thirteen names, not fourteen; Jeconiah is probably counted twice, standing as the hinge of the exile. And Jeconiah carries a curse: God had sworn that none of his offspring would sit on David's throne (Jer. 22:30), yet the royal line runs straight through him — which the virgin birth resolves, since Jesus receives the legal throne-right through Joseph without receiving Jeconiah's blood. Luke's genealogy, tracing physical descent, comes down through David's other son Nathan and never touches him. The dark names are the point: Ahaz burned his own son as an offering (2 Kgs. 16:3) and is the very king to whom Isaiah 7:14 was spoken — the verse Matthew quotes at v. 23. Manasseh, the worst man in the list, repented in a Babylonian prison and was heard (2 Chr. 33:12-13). And the six names after Zerubbabel appear nowhere else in Scripture, spanning the five-hundred-year silence between the return from exile and the carpenter's shop. Finally, verse 16 breaks the pattern: thirty-nine times Matthew has written "A was the father of B" with an active verb, and at the fortieth link he goes passive and feminine — "of whom Jesus was born" — asserting the virgin birth in the grammar two verses before he explains it.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy establishes Jesus as Messiah (Christ = Anointed One), Son of David (royal heir), and Son of Abraham (heir of the covenant). The 14-14-14 structure — possibly reflecting the numerical value of David's name in Hebrew — underscores divine superintendence: God has been ordering history toward this moment across centuries of faithfulness, failure, exile, and return. Providence is not the absence of scandal; it is the sovereign use of all things toward the appointed end.
verseByVerse.examples: This genealogy reminds us that salvation is not a timeless philosophy but a historical event rooted in a long chain of real covenantal faithfulness. God's promises survived murder, adultery, exile, and foreign domination to arrive at their fulfillment. What he has promised, he performs — across generations, across continents, across every human failure. The God who kept his word to Abraham keeps his word to you.

verseByVerse.quote: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew opens by naming who Jesus is before he tells a single event: he is the Messiah, the heir of David’s throne, and the heir of the promise God made to Abraham. In him, every promise God made to Israel comes to its goal.

Meaning first. Matthew opens the New Testament with a family tree, and it is not a preface to the gospel but the first proclamation of it. In seventeen verses he shows that Jesus is the Christ, the King promised to David and the blessing promised to Abraham, and that God carried that promise through two thousand years of saints, scoundrels, foreigners, exiles and forgotten men without ever once letting it drop. Then he tells how the Son of God entered that family: conceived by the Holy Spirit in the virgin Mary, named Jesus because he will save his people from their sins, and given the name the prophet foretold, Immanuel, God with us. The chapter begins with a list of the dead and ends with the living God lying in a cradle.

The setting. Matthew was one of the Twelve, a former tax collector (9:9). He writes chiefly for Jewish believers, probably in the AD 60s, to show that Jesus is the Messiah the Old Testament promised. He quotes or alludes to the Old Testament more than any other Gospel writer, often with the words “to fulfil what was spoken”. His Gospel stands first in the New Testament because it is the bridge from the Old.

The book of the genealogy. Matthew’s first two words in Greek are biblos geneseōs, the book of the genesis, and a Jewish reader with the Greek Old Testament in his ear would have caught the echo at once. The same phrase stands over the generations of the heavens and the earth (Genesis 2:4) and over the generations of Adam (Genesis 5:1). So before a single event is narrated, Matthew has made a claim of breathtaking size: the story is starting again. Something as great as creation is beginning, and it begins with a man. The phrase introduces the genealogy that follows, and perhaps the whole story of Jesus, as though the entire Gospel were the book of a new beginning for the world.

Jesus Christ. “Jesus” is his personal name (see v. 21). “Christ” is not a surname but a title: the Greek form of Messiah, meaning anointed one. In Israel, kings, priests and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil to set them apart for their office (1 Samuel 16:13). The prophets promised a final Anointed One, the King God would send to save his people. Matthew’s first claim is that Jesus is that King. Every time you say “Jesus Christ” you are confessing, whether you notice it or not, that the carpenter from Nazareth is the one on whom the hopes of Israel rested.

The son of David. God promised David that one of his descendants would reign on his throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 9:6–7; 11:1). By the time of Jesus, Son of David was a title for the Messiah. Matthew uses it more than any other Gospel: blind men cry it out (9:27), crowds wonder whether this could be he (12:23), and Jerusalem shouts it as he rides in (21:9). The heir is named here first, with a claim to a throne.

The son of Abraham. God promised Abraham that in his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). Jesus is the offspring through whom that blessing comes (Galatians 3:16). The promise was made to a childless man in Ur, and it was a promise about everybody.

The order. David comes first because Matthew’s main theme is Jesus as King. But Abraham is there to show that the King is for the nations too. The order is not decorative. Matthew gives Israel its King first and only then opens the door to everybody else, and that is the shape of the whole Gospel: it begins with the son of Abraham and ends with the command to make disciples of all nations (28:19).

Abraham … Isaac … Jacob … Judah. The genealogy begins with Abraham, the father of Israel, not Adam as Luke’s does (Luke 3:38). Matthew is tracing Jesus’ place in Israel’s history. From Jacob’s twelve sons, Judah is named, because God promised that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10): the royal tribe.

Why a genealogy? Modern readers often skip it, and skipping it costs something. For Matthew’s first readers it was essential, for three reasons. First, it anchors Jesus in real history. Myths and legends do not come with paperwork. Matthew names forty-two generations, most of them checkable against the Old Testament records his readers had on their shelves, which is the literary equivalent of putting your address at the top of the page. He is not offering a story about the human condition; he is filing a report about a man with ancestors. Second, in Israel a genealogy was a legal document: it established a person’s right to land, to the priesthood, or to a throne. Matthew is not being sentimental about family history. He enters Jesus’ legal claim to David’s crown into the record in the first breath, because everything afterwards depends on it. Third, it shows that the story of Jesus did not begin in Bethlehem. It began two thousand years earlier, with God’s promise to Abraham, and every generation in between was carrying that promise forward.

Receipts, not a register. So read the names not as a hurdle but as receipts. Each one is a generation in which God did not abandon what he had said, including the long stretches where nothing visible was happening, where the family was enslaved, or exiled, or forgotten, or faithless, and the promise was carried forward by people who never saw it land. Most of God’s work in the world has looked exactly like that. If you are in one of those stretches yourself, this is your chapter: it is the record of a God who keeps promises across centuries, at a pace that looks from underneath like nothing at all.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ importance rests on his ancestry, as if he were great because his family was. The point is the reverse: his family matters because God promised that the Saviour would come through it. Nor does it mean that salvation is inherited by birth. John the Baptist will warn the Jews not to trust in having Abraham as their father (3:9).

What does it actually mean for me that Jesus is the Christ? It means he is not only a teacher to admire but a King to whom you belong. If he is the Anointed One, then his word is law in your life, his promises are the ground of your hope, and his enemies, sin and death, are already on the losing side. In practice it means you bring your decisions to him rather than only your troubles, you read his words in this Gospel as commands and not suggestions, and you rest on the fact that the King has come to save, not to crush. Confessing “Jesus is the Christ” is the beginning of the Christian life (16:16), not an advanced doctrine for later.

In a sentence. Jesus is the Messiah, the promised King from David’s line and the promised blessing from Abraham’s line, the one in whom God keeps all his promises.

On a Tuesday. God kept a promise across two thousand years and forty-two generations. When his promises to you seem slow, remember that he does not forget what he has said. Take one promise you are leaning on today, perhaps that he will never leave you (Hebrews 13:5) or that he works all things for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28), and set it beside this list. Every name is a year, or twenty, in which it looked as though nothing was happening, and every name is proof that something was.

For worship. Blessed be the God who remembers. He spoke to a childless man under the stars and to a shepherd king in a borrowed palace, and then he let whole centuries go by, and he never once forgot a word. The promise passed through hands that were faithful and hands that were filthy, through slavery and exile and silence, and it did not lose a single syllable on the way. And when it arrived, it arrived as a Person: the Son of David who is David’s Lord, the Son of Abraham in whom every nation is blessed. The book of the genesis is open again, and the new creation has a name.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” marks Jesus as the promised king; “son of Abraham” as the one through whom the nations would be blessed.

parallels.desc: Luke’s genealogy, traced back to Adam
the promise of a son of David on the throne forever
all the families of the earth blessed in Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line runs through Judah to Perez, and Matthew does something unexpected: he names Tamar, the mother. With her name he reminds every reader of one of the most shameful stories in Genesis, and shows that God’s promise was carried through a family scarred by sin and injustice.

Women in a genealogy. Two things in these verses would have stopped a first-century reader. A woman’s name has appeared in a Jewish genealogy, which is not how they were written. And it is this woman. Jewish genealogies normally listed fathers only. Matthew names five women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, the wife of Uriah, and Mary. Each is unexpected. The first four were foreigners or connected with foreigners, and each had a story involving scandal or irregularity. Matthew had no obligation to mention any of them. He puts the first in the third verse of the New Testament.

The story of Tamar (Genesis 38). Matthew expects the story to be known, and most readers no longer know it, so it deserves telling. Tamar married Judah’s eldest son Er, who was wicked, and the Lord put him to death. By the custom later written into the law (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), the next brother, Onan, was to give her a child to carry on his dead brother’s name. He refused, and he too died. Judah, now down two sons and afraid of the woman, sent Tamar back to her father’s house, promising that she could marry his youngest son Shelah when he grew up. He never kept the promise. He simply left her there: not divorced, not free to remarry, a childless widow in a culture where that meant no standing and no future, waiting for a wedding her father-in-law had privately decided would never happen.

What she did. Years later, Tamar covered her face and sat by the road as a prostitute. Judah, now a widower and on his way to the sheepshearing, took her for one and hired her, leaving his seal, cord and staff as a pledge, which is to say she kept his identification. She became pregnant. Three months later, when word came that his daughter-in-law was pregnant by immorality, Judah ordered her to be brought out and burned. And she sent him his own seal with a message asking whose it was. His answer is the sentence on which the whole episode turns: she is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah (Genesis 38:26). She bore twins, Perez and Zerah.

Why Matthew names her. With one name, he reminds the reader of the whole story: a wronged woman, a hypocritical patriarch, a shameful act, and a line that continued anyway. Judah, the royal tribe’s father, behaved disgracefully; Tamar, probably a Canaanite, took a desperate and sinful way to what was hers by right, and was pronounced, by the man who had failed her, the more righteous of the two. The Messiah’s family tree begins its royal line with this. If you were forging a pedigree for a king, you would strike her out. Matthew writes her in.

Perez and Zerah. Perez means breach or breaking through, because he burst out ahead of his twin at birth (Genesis 38:29). The royal line runs through a boy named for pushing in where he was not expected. Ruth’s neighbours were still blessing a bride by his name generations later (Ruth 4:12), which is how they knew the story too, and the line runs through him to David (Ruth 4:18–22).

Hezron … Nahshon … Salmon. The generations in Egypt and the wilderness. Nahshon was the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7; 7:12). Through the centuries of slavery in Egypt, when nothing seemed to happen, the promise was still being carried. Bricks were being made under the whip, and the line of the King of kings was among the brickmakers.

What it does not mean. Not that God approved of Judah’s or Tamar’s sin. Scripture records it honestly and does not excuse it. The point is that God’s grace works through sinful people without making their sin less sinful. Nor does it suggest that the line of the Messiah was pure in itself: it needed the Messiah as much as anyone.

Was Tamar right to do what she did? No, and yes, and the Bible lets both stand. Her method was sinful: she deceived and committed sexual sin, and Scripture never holds it up as a pattern. But her cause was just. She had been wronged and abandoned, and she was seeking the child and the name that the law and Judah’s own promise owed her. Judah’s verdict, that she was more righteous than he, does not call her sinless; it says his sin was greater. The lesson is not that the end justifies the means. It is that God can bring his good purpose through a tangle of wrongs on every side, without approving any of them, and that he sees the wronged widow nobody else is watching.

In a sentence. God carried his promise through Judah and Tamar, a family marked by sin and injustice, showing from the first page that grace, not respectability, runs through the Messiah’s line.

On a Tuesday. If you think your family’s failures put you beyond God’s use, read Tamar’s name again. God did not tidy the Messiah’s family tree before he used it. And if you are the Judah in the story, the one who has made a promise and quietly let it lapse, the one with power who has left someone waiting, ask today whom you have left on the shelf and what you owe them.

For worship. Here is a God who is not embarrassed by his own family. The Son of God came down a line that ran through a roadside and a shameful bargain, and he did not ask for the page to be torn out. He took that flesh. He is the true Son of Judah who kept every promise Judah broke, the righteous one who was counted as a sinner so that sinners like Judah and Tamar could be counted righteous. The breach was made, and through it, grace came pushing in where nobody expected it.
verseByVerse.note: Tamar is the first of four women Matthew includes before Mary, each with an irregular story.

parallels.desc: the line from Perez to Nahshon

verseByVerse.quote: and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew names two more women, both foreigners, Rahab and Ruth, and then refers to David’s great sin by calling Bathsheba “the wife of Uriah”. The Messiah’s family needed grace, and God wrote outsiders and sinners into his story.

Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab. Two more foreign women, and then a silence. Rahab ran a brothel in Jericho, a Canaanite city under sentence of destruction. She hid two Israelite spies under the flax on her roof because she believed that the LORD was God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath, and she and her family were spared when the city fell (Joshua 2; 6:22–25). She is honoured for her faith (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). The Old Testament does not record her marriage to Salmon; Matthew does. Some have questioned whether this is the same Rahab, since Salmon lived about two centuries before David, but genealogies often skip generations (see vv. 7–8), and Matthew clearly means the famous Rahab. The woman of the scarlet cord became a great-grandmother of King David.

Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth. Ruth was a Moabitess. The Moabites descended from Lot’s incest with his daughter (Genesis 19:36–37), and the law barred Moabites from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). Yet Ruth, a widow, chose Israel’s God: your people shall be my people, and your God my God (Ruth 1:16). Boaz, a kinsman-redeemer, married her and redeemed her family’s land. Their son Obed was David’s grandfather. The woman the law kept at the door was carried over the threshold by a redeemer, and her great-grandson was the king.

Jesse the father of David the king. David is the only one in the genealogy called “king”. He is the hinge of the list (v. 17), the man to whom God promised an everlasting throne.

David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah. Matthew does not write Bathsheba’s name. He names her husband instead: Uriah the Hittite, a foreigner and one of David’s most loyal soldiers. David committed adultery with Bathsheba while Uriah was at war, then arranged for Uriah to be killed in battle to hide the pregnancy (2 Samuel 11). By naming Uriah, Matthew makes it impossible to read the line without saying the name of the man David had killed. Israel’s greatest king stands here in one breath as king and as adulterer and murderer, and the line runs straight through the sin without a break. Yet God gave David and Bathsheba Solomon, the heir, after David’s deep repentance (2 Samuel 12; Psalm 51).

The four women together. Stand back and look at them, because Matthew has done something deliberate and it is aimed at somebody. Not the honoured mothers of Israel, Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, but Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba. All four were foreigners or married to a foreigner. All four had stories involving sexual scandal, real or suspected. Three foreigners and a scandal apiece. Matthew’s reasons, held together: first, to show that the Messiah came for Gentiles as well as Jews; second, to show that God works through sinners and outsiders by grace; and third, to prepare for Mary, whose pregnancy also looked scandalous, though she was innocent (vv. 18–19).

Your own line. So consider what that means for your own family. Most families have a name that is not mentioned, or a stretch nobody talks about: the affair, the child born outside a marriage, the drinking, the violence, the prison sentence, the divorce, the parent who left. People carry that quietly and assume, without ever putting it into words, that it has disqualified them, that God works with families of a different kind. Matthew’s answer is the first page of the New Testament. The Messiah’s own family tree reads like that, and God did not tidy it before he used it. He wrote it down.

What it does not mean. Not that sin does not matter. Matthew’s refusal to name Bathsheba is there precisely so we remember a murdered man. Grace that pretends nothing happened is not grace. Nor is it a criticism of the women: Rahab and Ruth are models of faith, and Bathsheba was more sinned against than sinning. And it does not mean that a good family gives anyone standing before God, any more than a bad one removes it. What runs down this list is not merit, but God’s promise, and promises are kept by the one who makes them.

Did God approve of Rahab’s lie? Rahab told the king’s men the spies had gone, when they were on her roof (Joshua 2:4–5). Scripture praises her faith and her welcome of the spies (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25), not her lie. She was a new believer in a pagan city, acting in faith with the moral understanding she had, and God honoured the faith without endorsing every part of how she acted. Christians have long debated whether deception is ever right to protect innocent life from murderers, and sincere believers come down on different sides of that hard case. What is clear is that Rahab is not a licence for ordinary lying; she is a picture of a sinner who turned to the true God when everything around her said not to.

Was Bathsheba to blame? The text puts the guilt on David. He saw, sent, took and then killed (2 Samuel 11:2–4, 15). He was the king, she was the wife of a soldier at the front, and it is very hard to refuse a king. The prophet Nathan’s parable makes her the poor man’s lamb, taken by the rich man (2 Samuel 12:1–4), and God’s rebuke falls on David alone. That is why the commentary calls her more sinned against than sinning. Abuse of power is never tolerated by God, even in his greatest king, and Bathsheba is honoured in the end as the mother of the heir.

In a sentence. God brought the Messiah through foreigners and through a royal scandal, showing that his family, like ours, is made of people who need grace.

On a Tuesday. Is there a part of your family’s story nobody speaks about, the affair, the prison sentence, the parent who left? The Messiah’s family tree reads like that. God can write your story into his. And look round your church for the Ruths: the foreigners, the newcomers, the people with a history. They are not guests in the family of Jesus. Their kind are in his genealogy.

For worship. The King of glory did not come down a line of the respectable. He came through a Canaanite with a scarlet cord, a Moabitess gleaning in a stranger’s field, and a widow whose husband had been murdered by a king. And he came to be the Kinsman-Redeemer to whom Boaz was only a signpost: the one who takes the outsider under his wing, pays the price of her debt, and gives her a name and an inheritance. He is the greater Son of David who did not take another man’s lamb but laid down his own life as the Lamb. He made a family out of outsiders, and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and Ruth a Moabite — Gentiles in the royal line. “The wife of Uriah” is Bathsheba.

verseByVerse.quote: and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line passes through the kings of Judah, good and bad alike, listed with no comment. God’s promise did not depend on the quality of the men who carried it, but on the faithfulness of the God who made it.

The kings of Judah. After Solomon the kingdom split in two (1 Kings 12). The northern kingdom, Israel, had no kings from David’s line. The southern kingdom, Judah, was ruled by David’s descendants for nearly four centuries. These verses list them.

Good and bad together. Read the names slowly and notice what Matthew declines to do. Some were faithful: Asa removed idols (1 Kings 15:11–14); Jehoshaphat sought the LORD (2 Chronicles 17:3–6). Some were wicked: Rehoboam’s foolishness split the kingdom; Joram murdered all his brothers to make the throne safe (2 Chronicles 21:4) and married into the idolatrous house of Ahab. Uzziah was a strong king who grew proud and was struck with leprosy for burning incense in the temple, a task only priests could do (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Matthew writes them all in the same rhythm, with no verdict and not one adjective. A genealogy has no room for a verdict. What is being traced is not the quality of the men but the durability of the promise that passed through their hands, and the chain does not thicken at the good names or wear thin at the bad ones. It did not falter once in the hands of people who did.

Three kings missing. Matthew writes that Joram was the father of Uzziah, but 1 Chronicles 3:11–12 lists Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah between them. Three generations have simply gone. This is not a slip, and it is not the embarrassment it first appears. “Father of” in Hebrew and Greek can mean ancestor of, just as Jesus is called son of David a thousand years after David died. Genealogies were not birth registers; they were legal documents that traced descent, and they were often shortened to make a pattern easier to remember. Matthew omits names to arrive at his three groups of fourteen (v. 17). No first-century reader would have counted this an error.

Why these three? Perhaps because they were descendants of Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, who married into David’s line, brought Baal worship with her and murdered the royal family (2 Kings 11:1). God had pronounced judgment on Ahab’s house (1 Kings 21:21–22). Matthew may be quietly letting that judgment show. We cannot be sure, and he does not say. Omitting names from a list does not remove the men from history; the line itself was unbroken. And notice how close it came to being broken: when Athaliah killed the royal heirs, one baby, Joash, was hidden in the temple for six years (2 Kings 11:2–3). The whole promise to David lay for six years in one small boy in a storeroom, and God kept him.

Textual note: Asaph. The ESV reads “Asaph”, following the oldest manuscripts; the king was Asa. Later manuscripts and many translations read “Asa”. A reader who knows his Old Testament may object that Asaph was a psalmist, not a king. Verdict: “Asaph” is probably original, either an alternative spelling of the king’s name current in the Greek-speaking world or a deliberate echo of Asaph the psalmist. Either way, the king meant is Asa, and nothing is amiss.

What it does not mean. Not that God does not care whether his servants are faithful. The books of Kings and Chronicles judge each king carefully, and faithfulness brought blessing while sin brought judgment. But God’s promise to David did not fail because of his sons’ sins (2 Samuel 7:14–16; Psalm 89:30–37).

If the promise did not depend on them, does it matter how leaders live? Very much. God told David in advance that if his sons sinned he would discipline them with the rod of men (2 Samuel 7:14), and he did: Judah’s wicked kings brought ruin, war and finally exile on the people they ruled. What God promised was that the line would not be cut off, not that sin would be painless. The same holds for pastors, parents and elders today. Christ will build his church whatever we do (16:18), but a faithless leader still wounds real people and will answer for it. God’s faithfulness is a reason to serve humbly, never a reason to serve carelessly.

In a sentence. God carried his promise through good kings and wicked ones, because it rested on his faithfulness, not theirs.

On a Tuesday. Do you think God’s purposes depend more on your faithfulness than on his? He keeps his promises even through weak and failing people. That should make you humble and grateful, not careless. If you lead anything, a home, a class, a team, ask which kind of king your people would say you are, and then rest your weight on the God who carries the promise, not on your own record.

For worship. Every one of these kings was given a crown that was too big for him, and every one of them died. But the crown was waiting for its true wearer all along. Jesus is the King the best of them only hinted at and the worst of them betrayed: righteous where Joram was murderous, humble where Uzziah was proud, faithful all the way to a cross. And the God who hid the infant Joash in the temple and kept the line alive by a thread is the same God who will not let a single one of his promises die in the hands of sinful men. His faithfulness is the only thing in this list that never needs a verdict.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Asa for Asaph. Matthew’s list skips several kings between Joram and Uzziah; “father of” can mean ancestor.

verseByVerse.quote: and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list now includes both the best kings of Judah, Hezekiah and Josiah, and the very worst, Ahaz and Manasseh. All four are links in one chain. Even the worst of them was not beyond God’s mercy.

Ahaz. One of the worst kings in Judah’s history. He burned his own son as an offering, following the despicable practices of the nations (2 Kings 16:3): child sacrifice, by a son of David, in Jerusalem. He stripped the temple to buy Assyrian protection, had a copy made of a pagan altar he admired in Damascus to stand in the LORD’s house, and finally shut the doors of the LORD’s house altogether (2 Chronicles 28:24). Yet Ahaz is the king to whom Isaiah spoke the promise Matthew will quote at the end of this chapter: the virgin shall conceive and bear a son (Isaiah 7:14). Ahaz was terrified of an invasion, refused to ask God for a sign, and was given one anyway. The greatest promise of the Old Testament was spoken to one of its worst kings, who did not want it. That is the chapter’s own argument in miniature: the promise does not depend on the man holding it.

Hezekiah. A great reforming king who trusted the LORD, destroyed idols, and saw Jerusalem miraculously delivered from the Assyrian army (2 Kings 18–19). He spread the enemy’s threatening letter before the LORD and prayed, and in one night the besieging army was struck down.

Manasseh. Hezekiah’s son, and the worst of all. He reigned fifty-five years, the longest reign in Judah, and filled them with idolatry, sorcery, the burning of his own sons and so much innocent blood that God declared he would wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish (2 Kings 21:1–16). He set a carved image inside the temple itself. His sins were the reason God gave for the exile (2 Kings 24:3–4). By any reckoning, the worst man in this list.

Manasseh’s repentance. But 2 Chronicles 33:10–17 adds what Kings does not record. The Assyrians took Manasseh captive with hooks and bronze chains to Babylon. There, at the end of everything, in distress, he humbled himself greatly before God and prayed, and God was moved by his plea, heard him and brought him back to Jerusalem. Manasseh then spent his last years tearing out what he had spent decades building. The darkest name in the genealogy is the strongest proof in Scripture that no one is beyond God’s mercy. His sins were not the ordinary kind. He murdered children, including his own, and God heard him when he finally asked.

Amos … Josiah. Manasseh’s son Amon (the ESV reads “Amos”, following the oldest manuscripts, as with Asaph in v. 7) was wicked and was murdered after two years. His son Josiah became king at eight and led the greatest reformation in Judah’s history, after the Book of the Law was rediscovered in the temple (2 Kings 22–23).

The lesson of the four. Ahaz the faithless, Hezekiah the faithful, Manasseh the monstrous and repentant, Josiah the reformer. All four are links in one chain, and the chain does not thicken at the good names or wear thin at the bad ones. A godly father did not guarantee a godly son, and a wicked father did not prevent one. This is not a record of achievement. It is a record of a promise being kept through people who had no claim on it whatever.

What it does not mean. Not that Manasseh’s sins had no consequences: the damage he did led to the exile, even after his repentance (2 Kings 23:26). God forgives, but sin often leaves wounds in history. Nor does it mean that repentance can be safely put off until the end of a wicked life. Manasseh wasted decades, and countless people suffered for his sins.

Is it my fault that my child has turned from God, though I tried to raise him well? Hezekiah was one of the best kings Judah ever had, and his son was the worst. Scripture does not blame Hezekiah for Manasseh. Parents are responsible for faithfulness, teaching, example and love, and every parent fails in some of these and can confess it. But parents cannot give a new heart; only God can (Ezekiel 36:26). A child’s rebellion is not proof that you were a bad parent, any more than a child’s faith would prove you were a good one. Keep loving, keep the door open, keep praying, and remember that the son of Hezekiah came home from Babylon.

Could God really forgive someone who has done what I have done? If he forgave Manasseh, the answer is yes. Manasseh was guilty of idolatry, the occult, murder and the deaths of children, and God heard him. Forgiveness is not measured by the size of the sin but by the worth of the sacrifice, and the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). The only sin that cannot be forgiven is the one never brought to him. Come as Manasseh came: humbly, without excuses, asking for mercy.

In a sentence. The promised line ran through the best and worst kings of Judah, and even the worst of them found mercy when he repented.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have privately given up on, for whom you have stopped praying in any serious way because the case seems closed? Name that person. Then notice that the man who filled Jerusalem with blood is in the direct line that leads to the Christ, and that he is there because he repented in a foreign prison at the end of a wasted life. Remember Manasseh, and pray again.

For worship. Our God gave his greatest promise to a king who did not want it, and kept his line alive through a king who did not deserve it, and heard the prayer of a king who had done everything to deserve never being heard. His mercy goes down further than the worst man in Judah could fall. And the Son born of this line is the reason: he took the hooks and the chains and the judgment that Manasseh earned, so that Manasseh could go home. There is no prison too far, and no record too dark, for the arm of the Lord to reach.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Amon for Amos. Hezekiah and Josiah were reforming kings; Manasseh was the worst.

verseByVerse.quote: and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line of kings ends in disaster, the exile to Babylon, and passes through a king whom God had cursed. Yet the line continues through the exile and out the other side. God’s promise survived both the worst catastrophe and a divine curse.

Josiah the father of Jechoniah. Josiah was in fact Jechoniah’s grandfather; Jehoiakim, Josiah’s son, stands between them (1 Chronicles 3:15–16). As in verse 8, “father of” means ancestor of, and Matthew omits Jehoiakim to keep his pattern of fourteen. The omission sharpens the point: Jehoiakim cut up and burned Jeremiah’s scroll (Jeremiah 36:23), and the curse on his son is the curse this genealogy has to pass through. Jechoniah (also called Jehoiachin or Coniah) reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar took him to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8–15).

And his brothers. Perhaps Jechoniah’s uncles and relatives, including Zedekiah, the last king, who saw Jerusalem destroyed in 586 BC.

The deportation to Babylon. Here the list breaks. The great catastrophe of Israel’s history: the temple burned, Jerusalem destroyed, the king blinded and taken captive, and the people carried away (2 Kings 25). To those who lived through it, it seemed that God’s promises to David had failed: no throne, no temple, no land, and the king of Judah in a Babylonian prison. It is worth noticing that Matthew builds the spine of his genealogy around the worst thing that ever happened to his people rather than around a victory (v. 17). The exile is a turning point, not the end.

The curse on Jechoniah. A reader with an open Bible will find a shadow over this name. God had said through Jeremiah that this man was to be written down as childless, and that none of his offspring would succeed in sitting on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:24–30). Yet Matthew runs the royal line straight through him. How can the Messiah sit on David’s throne if he descends from the one man God cursed off it?

The answer. Jesus is Joseph’s son legally, not biologically (v. 16). The legal right to David’s throne passed to him through Joseph, the heir of Solomon and Jechoniah. But Jesus was not physically descended from Jechoniah, because he was born of Mary by the Holy Spirit, not fathered by Joseph. Luke’s genealogy, which most likely traces Jesus’ physical descent, runs through David’s son Nathan, and never touches Jechoniah (Luke 3:31). So the curse stands, and the promise stands. Two divine words that look as though they cannot both be true, and the virgin birth is the needle that threads them. God did not go back on his word. He found a way through it that nobody saw coming. He generally does.

After the deportation … Shealtiel … Zerubbabel. In exile, the line continued. Jechoniah was released from prison in Babylon and treated kindly, eating at the king’s table for the rest of his life (2 Kings 25:27–30). His grandson Zerubbabel led the first group of exiles home in 538 BC and governed Judah while the temple was rebuilt (Ezra 3:8; Haggai 1:1). God called Zerubbabel his signet ring (Haggai 2:23), the very image he had used when he rejected Jechoniah (Jeremiah 22:24). The ring pulled off God’s hand was put back on it. The curse was not the last word.

What it does not mean. Not that God changed his mind or broke his word. The curse on Jechoniah’s physical descendants was kept: none of them sat on David’s throne. The promise to David was kept too, through a Son who received the legal right but not the curse.

Is an adopted child a real son? In Israel, and in the eyes of God, yes. Jesus’ whole claim to David’s throne rests on his legal sonship through Joseph, which shows how seriously Scripture takes adoption: it was enough to make the Son of God the heir of a king. If you were adopted, or have adopted, you are not in a second-class family. And every Christian is adopted. We were not born God’s children by nature, but in Christ God has made us his sons and heirs (Romans 8:15–17; Galatians 4:4–7), with the full rights of the family. The pattern runs both ways: Joseph adopted the Son of God, so that the Son of God could bring us into his Father’s house.

In a sentence. God carried his promise through the exile and through a cursed king, and the virgin birth is how he kept both his curse and his promise.

On a Tuesday. Is there a loss you have treated as the end of God’s promises: a death, a divorce, a failure? The exile was not the end for Israel, and your loss is not the end of God’s purposes for you. Read 2 Kings 25:27–30, the last four verses of that book: the deposed king, in a foreign land, given a seat at the table. It is how God ends the darkest book in the history of his people.

For worship. Who but God could keep a curse and a promise at the same time without breaking either? He said Jechoniah’s seed would not sit on the throne, and none did. He said David’s Son would reign for ever, and one does. Between those two words he laid a road no human mind could have surveyed, and at the end of it stands a child conceived by the Spirit, heir by law and Lord by right. And this is the same wisdom that saved us: at the cross God kept both his justice and his mercy whole, condemning sin in the flesh of his Son and justifying the ungodly who trust in him (Romans 3:26). The exile did not have the last word. Neither does ours.
verseByVerse.note: The deportation to Babylon came in 597 and 586 BC. Zerubbabel later led the return and the rebuilding of the temple.

parallels.desc: Zerubbabel as the LORD’s signet ring

verseByVerse.quote: and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Zerubbabel come names that appear nowhere else in Scripture. For five silent centuries, God carried his promise through ordinary, unknown people, and their unrecorded lives were essential to his plan.

Unknown names. After Zerubbabel the light goes out. Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud: we know nothing about them. Search the rest of the Bible for these men and you will not find them. Matthew probably took the names from family or public records. No king, no prophet, no chronicle, no psalm, not one recorded sentence. They lived under Persian, Greek and Roman rule in a small, occupied country, and what they did with their lives was work, marry and have children. That is the entire record.

The silent centuries. Between Zerubbabel (about 520 BC) and Jesus, about five centuries passed. Persia gave way to Alexander the Great; Alexander’s generals divided his empire; the Greek king Antiochus IV desecrated the temple in 167 BC; the Maccabees led a revolt and briefly won independence; and Rome took control in 63 BC. During all this time, after Malachi, there was no prophet in Israel. Jews called it the time when prophecy had ceased. Nine or ten generations of a family living quietly through five centuries in which God appeared to say nothing at all.

Not empty. But the silence was not emptiness. The promise was moving the entire time, through men whose names survive only because Matthew wrote them down. They worked, married, raised children, buried their parents and died, without the least idea that the line they were carrying would end where it ended. Not one of them did anything the Bible thought worth recording. Every one of them was load-bearing.

What it does not mean. Not that God was absent or inactive during these centuries. He was preparing the world for Christ: the spread of the Greek language, the Roman roads and peace, the scattering of Jews and synagogues through the empire, and the translation of the Scriptures into Greek. Paul calls the moment of Christ’s coming the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4).

What do I do when God seems silent in my life? Do what these men did: keep going in ordinary faithfulness. Go on reading the Scripture God has already given, because his silence in your feelings is not silence in his Word, which speaks every time you open it. Go on praying, even when it feels like talking to a ceiling; the Psalms are full of believers who did exactly that (Psalm 13; 88). Stay among God’s people. And judge God’s activity not by what you can see this month but by what he has promised. Five hundred years of apparent silence were the final preparation for the loudest word God has ever spoken, his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2).

In a sentence. Through five silent centuries, God quietly carried his promise in ordinary lives that no one remembered but him.

On a Tuesday. Are you measuring the worth of your faithfulness by whether anyone will remember it? Consider what proportion of your own life will be visible to anybody in three hundred years. For nearly everyone the honest answer is none of it, and these men are the proof that this is not the same as insignificance. Not one of them did anything the Bible recorded, and every one was essential. Change the nappy, finish the shift, pray with the child at bedtime. The line runs through days like that.

For worship. The God of Israel is the God of the unrecorded. He knew Azor and Achim by name when no one else would ever write them down, and he wrote them into the book of the genesis of his Son. Through five centuries of foreign empires and an empty prophetic chair, his purpose did not pause for a single day. He was setting the table for the arrival of the King, and when the fullness of time came, he sent his Son. Nothing about his people is too small for his notice, and no stretch of history is too dark for his hand.
verseByVerse.note: These men after Zerubbabel are mentioned nowhere else in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the last link, Matthew changes the pattern. He does not say that Joseph was the father of Jesus, but that Joseph was the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. Jesus is Joseph’s legal son and heir, but not his natural son. He was born of Mary alone, and he is the Christ.

Eleazar … Matthan … Jacob … Joseph. Joseph’s father is Jacob. Luke calls Joseph the son of Heli (Luke 3:23); see verse 17 for how the two genealogies relate.

The broken pattern. There is something in verse 16 that is invisible in English and is the most deliberate thing in the whole list. Thirty-nine times in a row Matthew has used the same construction: A was the father of B. The Greek verb is egennēsen, an active verb, a man begetting a son. It runs like a drumbeat down the page, unbroken, from Abraham to Jacob the father of Joseph. And then, at the last link, the beat breaks. Matthew writes not Joseph the father of Jesus but Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. In Greek, “of whom” is feminine singular: it can refer to one person only, and that person is not Joseph. And the verb goes passive: Jesus was born, not was fathered. The chain reaches Joseph and does not continue through him. It goes sideways into a woman, and the child is born rather than begotten.

Said in the grammar. Matthew has not yet said the word virgin. That comes in two verses. But he has already said it in his grammar, and any careful reader in the first century would have stopped dead at that verb and gone back to check. Which is worth noticing about how Scripture works. The doctrine is not asserted first and defended afterwards. It is built into the structure of a list of names, so that the shape of the sentence is making the claim before the narrative gets round to explaining it.

The husband of Mary. Joseph and Mary were betrothed, which counted legally as married (v. 18), and Joseph took her as his wife (v. 24). As Mary’s husband who named and received Jesus, Joseph became his legal father, and passed on to him the legal rights of David’s line.

Legal descent. In Israel, adoption gave full legal rights. A son by adoption was a true heir. So Jesus is truly the son of David through Joseph, though not by blood. (He may also be David’s descendant by blood through Mary, if Luke traces her line; see v. 17.)

Who is called Christ. “Christ” means the Messiah, the Anointed One (see v. 1). The whole genealogy has been travelling toward this title. Every promise to Abraham and David arrives at this one man. Forty generations of waiting, and the last word of the list is not a name but an office: the Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that Joseph was unimportant. God chose him to be Jesus’ legal father, to protect and raise him, and to give him his place in David’s line. Nor that Mary is the source of Jesus’ divinity: he was conceived by the Holy Spirit (v. 20), and she was the human mother through whom the eternal Son took our nature.

So should I call Joseph Jesus’ father? Yes, in the sense Scripture does. Luke calls Joseph and Mary his parents and has Mary say “your father and I” to the twelve-year-old Jesus (Luke 2:41, 48), and the people of Nazareth called him the carpenter’s son (13:55). Joseph was his father in law, in the home and in daily care: he fed him, taught him a trade and took him to the feasts. But he was not his father by nature. Jesus himself gently corrected Mary that day: he must be in his Father’s house (Luke 2:49). Joseph is honoured precisely because he was willing to raise a Son who was not his, for a Father greater than he.

In a sentence. Jesus is Joseph’s legal son and David’s heir, yet born of Mary alone: the promised Christ.

On a Tuesday. Is Jesus to you simply a figure of history, or the Christ, the King God promised? The genealogy was written to bring you to that question. Answer it today, not in the abstract but in the place in your life where you have been keeping him at a polite distance.

For worship. Look at what God did with a single verb. For thirty-nine generations men begot sons, and every one of those sons was born into Adam’s ruin and needed saving. Then God broke the pattern. The Son who stands at the end of the list was not begotten by any man, because he was the eternally begotten Son of the Father before there was an Abraham to begin the list (John 8:58). He did not come out of the line as its product. He came into the line as its Saviour. The whole of Israel’s history strained toward him, and he stepped into it from above.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew breaks the pattern at the end: Jesus was born of Mary, not fathered by Joseph. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

parallels.desc: “being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph”

verseByVerse.quote: So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew sums up the genealogy in three groups of fourteen generations: Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to the Christ. History is not random. God was steering it, through promise, through apparent ruin, and through long waiting, to Jesus.

Three groups of fourteen. Matthew stops and shows his working, which no other evangelist does. The first group rises from Abraham to David: the promise given and the kingdom established. The second falls from David to the exile: the kingdom’s decline and destruction. The third waits from the exile to Christ: the long, silent preparation. Promise, ruin, fulfilment. The three panels are a shape as well as a count: a promise given, a promise apparently destroyed, a promise kept. History, in this Gospel, is not a sequence of events. It is an argument going somewhere.

Why fourteen? Probably because of David. In Hebrew, letters also served as numbers, and the consonants of David’s name (D-V-D) add up to fourteen (4 + 6 + 4). Three times fourteen says David, David, David: this is the Son of David. A list that says fourteen three times has said David three times before it has said anything else. Others point out that three fourteens make six sevens, so Jesus begins the seventh seven, the number of completion. Either way, Matthew is showing design.

Counting the names. If you count the third group you find thirteen names, not fourteen. The likely explanation is that Jechoniah is counted twice, at the end of the second group and the start of the third, standing as the hinge of the exile, since the exile divides his life. Or Matthew is counting generations rather than names. Matthew is not being careless; he is being schematic. His numbers are a teaching structure, not a census, and his first readers, who knew perfectly well that genealogies were shaped for teaching rather than kept as archives, would not have blinked.

Matthew and Luke. Luke’s genealogy (Luke 3:23–38) differs from Matthew’s. From David the two lines part company: Matthew traces the line through Solomon, Luke through Nathan; Matthew names Joseph’s father as Jacob, Luke as Heli. Christians have offered three main explanations.

Mary’s line. Luke gives Mary’s genealogy, with Joseph as Heli’s son-in-law; Matthew gives Joseph’s.

Levirate marriage. One of Joseph’s fathers was legal and the other natural, through a levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), as the early church historian Julius Africanus suggested.

Royal and physical lines. Matthew traces the legal royal succession, the line of throne-heirs through Solomon; Luke traces Joseph’s physical descent through Nathan.

Which explanation is right? Verdict: we cannot be certain, but the third best fits Matthew’s purpose: he traces the legal, royal line by which David’s throne passed to Joseph’s son (see vv. 11–12), through Solomon and Jechoniah, while Luke follows physical descent through Nathan. Each explanation is held by careful readers, and none requires an error in Scripture. Both genealogies agree on what matters: Jesus is the son of David and the son of Abraham, and every promise God ever made to either of them lands on him.

What it does not mean. Not that we should look for secret codes in the numbers of Scripture. Matthew tells us his pattern openly; it is a memory aid and a theological statement, not a puzzle.

What should I do when I meet a difficulty in the Bible I cannot solve? First, notice that the church has known about this one for eighteen hundred years, and it has never shaken anyone’s faith who looked at it honestly; Julius Africanus was writing about it around AD 220. Second, remember that there are several reasonable answers, and you do not need to know which one is right to know that the problem is not a contradiction. Third, hold the difficulty with patience rather than suspicion. A Bible that has proved true in a thousand places has earned the benefit of the doubt in the one place where you cannot yet see how the pieces fit. Ask a pastor, read a good commentary, and keep reading.

In a sentence. God guided history through promise, ruin and waiting, all the way to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Can you trust that God is steering the confusing chapters of your life toward his purpose? He steered forty-two generations to Bethlehem. Try drawing your own life in Matthew’s three panels: where the promise first came to you, where things fell apart, and where you are waiting now. The third panel of Matthew’s list was the longest and the quietest, and it ended at a manger.

For worship. History is not a wheel that turns and turns, and it is not an accident that piles up. It is a story with an Author, and he writes in shapes. Fourteen, fourteen, fourteen: up to the throne, down to the rubble, through the long night, to the Christ. Every king and captive and nobody in these lists was held inside a design that bore the name of David and was moving toward David’s Lord. The God who counted the generations has counted the hairs of your head (10:30). The pen has never once left his hand.
verseByVerse.note: Three sets of fourteen give the story its shape: rise to David, fall to exile, and the wait for the Christ. The counts are arranged, not exhaustive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Birth of Jesus Christ: God with Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew tells the nativity through Joseph's eyes. He discovers Mary's pregnancy, intends to divorce her quietly (sparing her public disgrace), and is then visited by an angel who reveals the child's supernatural origin. Joseph's response is exemplary and immediate: he did as the angel commanded. Two names define the child — Jesus (he will save his people from their sins) and Immanuel (God with us). The birth fulfills Isaiah 7:14, establishing the pattern of scriptural fulfillment that runs through Matthew's entire Gospel. Two things more. Verse 22 introduces the formula that will ring out ten times in this Gospel — "all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet" — which is not proof-texting but the claim that these events complete Israel's whole story; and the verse-by-verse handles the controversy over Isaiah's word for "virgin" (Hebrew almah), including the fact that Jewish scholars translating their own Scriptures into Greek nearly two centuries before Christ rendered it parthenos, the ordinary Greek word for a virgin. The "virgin" reading was not a Christian invention. Verse 25's "knew her not until she had given birth" is Scripture's modest way of speaking about a husband and wife (as at Gen. 4:1), and the little word "until" fixes attention on the one thing at issue — that Jesus was conceived with no human father — rather than hinting at anything else. Note also that this is the first of four times God speaks to Joseph in a dream (1:20; 2:13; 2:19; 2:22), and that he obeys immediately every time; and that Joseph never speaks a single recorded word anywhere in the New Testament.
verseByVerse.theology: The virgin birth is not incidental decoration but theological necessity. If Jesus is to be the sinless substitute for sinners, he cannot enter the world through ordinary generation under fallen Adam. The Holy Spirit's agency in the conception ensures both his full humanity (born of woman, Gal. 4:4) and his freedom from the entail of the first Adam's sin. The two names capture the whole gospel: he is God who has come to be with us (Immanuel), and in being with us he saves us from our sins (Jesus). Doctrine and salvation are inseparable from the first moment.
verseByVerse.examples: Joseph's obedience is one of Scripture's quietly great acts of faith. He received no applause, no public vindication, no explanation beyond the angel's word. He obeyed at enormous personal cost — accepting social suspicion, raising a child not his own, surrendering his right to defend his reputation. In an age that demands visible proof and public validation before any commitment, Joseph's silent, costly fidelity is a rebuke and a model. God still calls his people to act on his word before the full picture is visible.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew now tells how Jesus was born. Mary, legally pledged to Joseph, was found to be pregnant before they came together, by the Holy Spirit. Joseph, a righteous man who did not want to shame her, decided to end the betrothal quietly. His response shows that true righteousness joins justice with mercy.

The birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. “Birth” is again genesis (see v. 1): the new beginning. Matthew tells the story from Joseph’s side; Luke tells it from Mary’s (Luke 1:26–38).

Betrothed. Betrothal was not like a modern engagement. It was a legally binding marriage contract, usually made when the girl was in her early teens. The couple were called husband and wife, but did not yet live together; that came about a year later, when the husband took the bride to his home. Only a formal divorce could end a betrothal, and unfaithfulness during it was treated as adultery, punishable under the law by death (Deuteronomy 22:23–24), though in Jesus’ time this was rarely carried out.

Before they came together. Before they lived together and had sexual relations.

She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Matthew tells the reader immediately where the child came from, so that we are never in doubt. But Joseph did not yet know. What he saw was a pregnant bride, and he knew the child was not his. So Joseph is not a disappointed young man with a decision to make about a wedding. He is a husband with a legal case, a public remedy available to him, and the sympathy of everyone he knows.

Her husband Joseph, being a just man. “Just” (dikaios) means righteous: a man who kept God’s law. That righteousness pulled him two ways. The law required him not to treat an apparently adulterous marriage as if nothing had happened. But he also did not want to humiliate her.

Unwilling to put her to shame. He could have made a public accusation before the village court, exposing her to disgrace and possibly to punishment. Joseph held every card. The law was on his side, the evidence appeared conclusive, and public sympathy would have been his entirely; he could have destroyed her and been congratulated for his piety.

Resolved to divorce her quietly. Instead, he decided on a private divorce, before two or three witnesses, with as little shame for her as possible. He would take the ambiguity onto himself, let the village think whatever it liked about him too, and cost her as little as the situation allowed.

What Joseph shows. True righteousness is not harsh legalism. Joseph did not pretend that nothing had happened, and he did not waive the matter: he still intended to divorce her. What he refused was the destructive version of a legitimate act. He chose the least harmful honest course, which is nearly always available, and nearly always more expensive than the other one. He asked not only what am I entitled to do, but what does mercy allow me to do with what I am entitled to? And God met him on the road he had already begun to walk: the angel came while Joseph was considering the merciful course, not before he had begun to choose it (v. 20).

Mary’s position. Mary said nothing in these verses. She had obeyed God, and now her reputation was ruined, and she could not explain what had happened in a way anyone would believe. Whatever she said would sound like the thing a guilty girl says. She was losing her name in a village where reputation was survival, and the vindication, when it came, came privately to Joseph in a dream and never to the neighbours at all. She shows what it is to do right and pay for it in the eyes of others.

What it does not mean. Not that mercy means ignoring sin, or that wrongs must never be named or acted on. Joseph still intended to divorce her. Nor does it mean that Mary was guilty: Matthew has already told us the truth. Joseph acted rightly on what he knew.

If my spouse has been unfaithful, does Joseph’s example mean I must stay, or must I leave? Neither is commanded here. Jesus himself teaches that sexual unfaithfulness is a ground on which divorce is permitted (19:9), and Scripture also allows it for wilful desertion (1 Corinthians 7:15; Westminster 24.6), so Joseph was not wrong to plan one. But permitted is not required. Many wronged husbands and wives, with God’s help, have forgiven and rebuilt, and that is a beautiful thing when there is true repentance. What Joseph shows is the spirit in which either path should be walked: honestly, without revenge, without humiliating the other person publicly, and seeking counsel and God’s guidance. If there is violence or danger, safety comes first, and the church must stand with the one being harmed.

In a sentence. When Mary was found pregnant, Joseph, a righteous man, chose mercy over public shame, showing that true righteousness joins justice with kindness.

On a Tuesday. When you have been wronged, or think you have, are you looking for the remedy that heals, or the one that humiliates? Most of us meet a version of Joseph’s situation eventually: someone has, as far as you can tell, wronged you badly, and you hold the power to expose them and the right to use it. Before you speak, post or reply, ask Joseph’s question. And if you are doing the right thing and paying for it in the eyes of people whose opinion matters to you, you are standing where Mary stood. God knows the truth, and that is enough.

For worship. Praise the God whose Son entered the world under a cloud. Before he was born, the Holy One was whispered about. The one who would bear the shame of sinners began his human life wrapped in a scandal he had not earned, and his mother bore it with him. And Joseph’s quiet mercy is only a small reflection of the mercy of Christ himself, who had every right to expose us and the evidence to condemn us, and chose instead to cover our shame with his own. He is the truly righteous one, and his righteousness is never harsh. A bruised reed he will not break (12:20).
verseByVerse.note: Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; ending it required a divorce. The couple did not yet live together.

parallels.desc: the law on a betrothed woman

verseByVerse.quote: But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, "Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sent an angel to Joseph in a dream to explain: the child was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Joseph must take Mary as his wife and name the child Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins. Here, at the start, Matthew tells us who Jesus is and why he came.

As he considered these things. Joseph had made his decision, but he had not yet acted. God intervened while he was thinking it over.

An angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. The first of several dreams in which God guides Joseph (2:13, 19, 22). Joseph’s namesake in Genesis, Joseph son of Jacob, was also a man of dreams, who protected his family by going to Egypt. This Joseph will do the same.

Joseph, son of David. The angel calls him by his royal ancestry, a title this Gospel otherwise keeps for Jesus himself. It reminds Joseph, and us, why his role matters: the man being asked to take this child is the man through whom the child will inherit a throne (v. 16).

Do not fear to take Mary as your wife. Joseph’s fear was reasonable: of disgrace, of marrying an apparently unfaithful woman, of breaking God’s law. The angel does not argue with the fear; he answers it with the truth.

That which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. Do not pass over these words. No human father was involved. This is the virgin conception: the Holy Spirit created the child’s human life in Mary’s womb. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) is beginning a new creation. Luke records the angel’s words to Mary: the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God (Luke 1:35). Mary is the willing soil, but the life within her is the Spirit’s gift, not man’s achievement: grace from the very first breath.

Why the virgin conception matters. Every child of Adam inherits a sinful nature (Psalm 51:5; Romans 5:12). Jesus was truly human, Mary’s real son, real flesh and blood, but his conception was a fresh act of God, so that he was without sin. Only a sinless Saviour could save sinners: a Redeemer who was himself under Adam’s guilt would need redeeming. And the virgin conception shows that salvation comes from God’s side, not from human achievement. It is no decorative miracle. Pull this thread and the whole gospel unravels.

She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. The name is not chosen by either parent but issued from heaven. “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua (Yehoshua), meaning the LORD saves. It was a common name. Joshua led Israel into the promised land; this Jesus will lead his people into a greater inheritance. By naming the child, Joseph would adopt him legally as his son.

For he will save his people from their sins. The explanation of the name. Not may save, but will save: he will certainly accomplish it. And it says what he saves from. To a first-century Jew, salvation meant rescue from Rome: a throne restored, the pagan boot lifted. The angel says the real enemy is sin. The exile that truly grieves God is the exile of a sinful heart from himself. Psalm 130:8 had said that the LORD would redeem Israel from all his iniquities; now that work of the LORD is given to Jesus, which is itself a claim about who he is. At the Last Supper Jesus explains how: his blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (26:28). The manger aims straight at the cross.

What saved from their sins includes. Reach for the old threefold answer and feel its sweep. From sin’s penalty: the guilt and condemnation we had earned were laid on him at the cross, so that there is no condemnation for those in Christ (Romans 8:1). From sin’s power: sin will not rule over them (Romans 6:14); the chains are struck off and the daily war of grace begins. And finally from sin’s presence: in the new creation, nothing unclean will enter (Revelation 21:27), and we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Penalty, power, presence; past, present and future. All of that is folded into a single name: Jesus.

His people. Those who belong to him. At first this sounds like Israel, but by the end of Matthew it includes believers from all nations (28:19), the true Israel of Jew and Gentile together, everyone the Father has given him. Reformed theology sees here the definite purpose of Christ’s saving work: he came not merely to make salvation possible for everyone, but actually to save his people. This is called definite or particular atonement (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). It does not limit the offer of the gospel, which goes to all (28:19), but it assures believers that Christ’s death actually achieved their salvation.
