What it does not mean. Not that Mary was sinless or had no need of a Saviour. She called God her Saviour (Luke 1:47), as only a sinner can. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary was conceived without original sin (the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854), but Scripture never says so, and it would only move the problem back a generation. Jesus’ sinlessness comes from the Spirit’s work in his conception, not from Mary. God sanctified what he created in her womb.

Where Christians differ: the virgin birth. Since the nineteenth century, liberal theologians have denied the virgin birth as a legend added to make Jesus seem divine. But it is plainly taught by both Matthew and Luke, independently, and confessed in the earliest creeds (the Apostles’ Creed: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary). Verdict: the virgin birth is historical fact and essential Christian doctrine.

If Jesus came to save his people, how do I know I am one of them? Not by trying to look into God’s secret decrees, but by coming to Jesus. His people are known by this: they come to him, trusting him to save them from their sins. Jesus promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you are turning from your sin and resting on Christ, however weakly, that is the mark of his people, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The doctrine is not a wall to keep you out. It is a guarantee that once you are in, he will not lose you.

Does God still guide people by dreams and angels? Not ordinarily. Many Reformed Christians, this commentary among them, hold that such direct revelations belonged to the founding era of God’s saving work, when Scripture was being given, and that God now guides his people chiefly through the completed Scriptures, prayer, wise counsel and his providence (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). Brothers who see this differently are to be held in charity, God is free to do as he pleases, and many believers have testified to dreams that drew them to Christ; the test of any such experience is whether it agrees with the Bible, which it can never add to. Joseph had the dream because this was a unique moment. You have the whole of Matthew, which tells you everything the angel told him and far more.

In a sentence. Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, without sin, and named Jesus because he came to save his people from their sins.

On a Tuesday. Have you come to Jesus to be saved from your sins, or only from your troubles? He came for the first, and that is the deeper need. Many of us come to him the way Israel wanted a Messiah, to lift a particular boot off our neck: the illness, the debt, the loneliness. He cares about those. But if you name him Jesus, you are calling him the one who saves you from yourself. Tell him today the sin you most need saving from.

For worship. The name was chosen in heaven before the child was born, and it is the whole gospel in two syllables: the LORD saves. Not helps, not advises, not makes it possible: saves. He bore the penalty, he breaks the power, he will banish the presence. The Spirit who brooded over the first creation brooded over the womb of a village girl, and a new creation began in the dark. And the Son who came did not come to see who might take him up on an offer. He came for a people with names, to save them, and every one of them he will bring home. Blessed be the name above every name.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

parallels.desc: the name given to Mary too
he will redeem Israel from all its iniquities

verseByVerse.quote: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel" (which means, God with us).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew explains that all this fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah: a virgin would conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, which means “God with us”. In Jesus, God himself has come to be with his people, truly God and truly man.

All this took place to fulfil. The first of Matthew’s ten or more fulfilment formulas (2:15, 17, 23; 4:14; 8:17; 12:17; 13:35; 21:4; 27:9). “Fulfil” means more than a prediction coming true. It means filling up, completing: the events of Jesus’ life bring Israel’s whole story and Scriptures to their intended goal. It is not proof-texting. It is the claim that the whole Old Testament was a vessel waiting to be filled.

What the Lord had spoken by the prophet. God is the speaker; Isaiah is his mouthpiece. Matthew holds a high view of Scripture: the words of the prophets are the words of God.

Isaiah’s original setting. Around 734 BC, Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel marched on Jerusalem. King Ahaz was terrified, his heart shaking as the trees of the forest shake before the wind (Isaiah 7:2). Isaiah told him to trust God and offered him a sign. Ahaz refused, preferring to seek help from Assyria. So God gave a sign anyway: a young woman would conceive and bear a son, called Immanuel, and before the child knew right from wrong, the two kings Ahaz feared would be gone (Isaiah 7:14–16). In its own day the sign said: God has not abandoned his people.

Fulfilled in Jesus. But the prophecy reached beyond Ahaz. Isaiah goes on to speak of a child born, a son given, whose name is Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, who would sit on David’s throne for ever (Isaiah 9:6–7). The sign of God with us in our crisis outran its first fulfilment by seven centuries, waiting for the day God would be with his people not by sending help from afar, but by coming himself.

The virgin. Isaiah’s Hebrew word, almah, means a young woman of marriageable age, and in the Old Testament it never refers to a married woman, so a virgin is naturally in view. Critics charge that Matthew over-read it. But about two hundred years before Christ, Jewish scholars translating Isaiah into Greek (the Septuagint) rendered it parthenos, the ordinary Greek word for virgin. The reading virgin was not a Christian invention smuggled in to prop up a doctrine; it was already in the Jews’ own Greek Bible. Matthew, carried by the Spirit, simply unveils the depth that had always been sleeping in the words.

Immanuel. Hebrew for God with us. Something here surprises many careful readers: no one in the Gospels calls Jesus “Immanuel” as a name. He is named Jesus. So how is the prophecy fulfilled? Because Immanuel was never a label to be pinned on him; it is a confession of who he is. The prophecy is fulfilled not in what people called him, but in who he is: God present with his people in a human life. Matthew frames his whole Gospel with this truth: it begins with God with us (1:23) and ends with Jesus’ promise, I am with you always, to the end of the age (28:20). Everything in between is God, with us.

Truly God and truly man. The virgin conception means that Jesus is fully human, born of a woman, and fully God, the eternal Son come in the flesh (John 1:14). The Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) confessed this: one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation. The church fought a long war to keep both halves, and the old phrase is worth carrying with you: remaining what he was, he became what he was not. He is not God in a costume, nor a good man promoted upward, but the eternal Son who took a true and complete human nature. Both are necessary: a Christ who is less than God cannot save us, and a Christ who is less than man has not stood in our place. Immanuel means both at once, in one cradle.

What it does not mean. Not that the virgin birth is borrowed from pagan myths. Pagan stories told of gods having sexual relations with women, as Zeus did; some of the stories most often cited, like those of Mithras or Horus, either describe nothing of the kind or come from sources later than the Gospels. None describes a conception with no sexual union at all. And Matthew’s first readers were Jews, the people in the ancient world least likely to borrow a pagan myth and least prepared for a virgin-born Messiah. Matthew grounds the virgin birth in Isaiah, not in pagan legend.

How could a sign for Ahaz be fulfilled seven hundred years later? Prophecy often has a near horizon and a far one. There was a child in Ahaz’s day, and before he was old enough to choose good, Syria and Israel were crushed, just as Isaiah said. That near sign was real. But Isaiah himself kept speaking about the child, until the language grew too large for any ordinary boy: Mighty God, a throne without end (Isaiah 9:6–7). The first child was a signpost; Jesus is the destination. Matthew is not twisting Isaiah. He is reading Isaiah to the end.

What does God with us mean when I feel alone? It means his presence does not depend on your feelings. Jesus is with his people by his Spirit, really and constantly, whether you sense him or not (28:20; John 14:16–18). Feelings come and go with sleep, health and circumstance; his promise does not. So when you feel abandoned, speak to him as one who is present, because he is. Read a psalm aloud to him. Go to church even when you would rather not, because he meets his people there. And remember that Immanuel himself cried out on the cross, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (27:46). He knows that darkness from the inside, and he went into it so that you would never be truly forsaken.

In a sentence. In Jesus, born of a virgin as Isaiah promised, God himself has come to be with his people.

On a Tuesday. Do you live as though God is truly with you today? In Christ, he is, in the office, the hospital ward, and the empty house. Before you walk into the hardest room of your day, say it under your breath: Immanuel. Then go in.

For worship. Do not hurry past this. The God who flung the stars into space, whom the highest heaven cannot contain, drew near. He wrapped himself in our flesh, was laid in a feeding trough, and dwelt among us (John 1:14), literally pitched his tent among us. Not a note of encouragement mailed from a safe distance: God himself, with us, and he has never once left. The sign refused by a frightened king was given anyway, because the grace of God does not wait to be asked. Worship the God who did not stay distant but came to be with us, and who will be with us to the end of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph obeyed at once. He took Mary as his wife, had no sexual relations with her until Jesus was born, and named the child Jesus, receiving him as his own son into David’s line.

When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him. Immediate, complete obedience. Woke, and did. There is no interval in the sentence: no period of reflection, no consultation, no attempt to negotiate the terms. Each of the four times God speaks to Joseph, he responds the same way, at once. Take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt, and he rose and took them by night (2:14). Go back, and he went (2:21). Turn aside to Galilee, and he did (2:22). Four instructions, four immediate obediences, and not one recorded question.

He took his wife. He brought Mary into his home, completing the marriage. And what he was agreeing to was not small: marrying a visibly pregnant woman, absorbing the village’s arithmetic about the dates for the rest of his life, and raising as his own a child he had been told was not his. It cost him his reputation.

But knew her not. “Knew” is the Bible’s modest word for sexual union, and Scripture has spoken this way since the beginning: Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived (Genesis 4:1). There is real beauty in the word. The joining of husband and wife is not treated as a mere act of the body but as two people truly knowing each other, becoming one flesh. Joseph and Mary had no sexual relations before Jesus’ birth. He guarded her, so that no one could ever claim that this baby was his doing. The child was God’s alone. This guards the truth of the virgin birth.

Until she had given birth to a son. “Until” states only what did not happen before the birth. But the natural meaning is that afterwards they lived as a normal married couple.

And he called his name Jesus. By naming the child, Joseph formally acknowledged him as his son. This gave Jesus his legal standing as a son of Joseph, and so as a son of David (v. 16). It is the last we hear of Joseph acting in this chapter: quietly faithful, publicly unrecognised, essential to it all, content simply to serve.

The silent man. Joseph never speaks. Not one word of his is recorded anywhere in the New Testament. He is spoken to, he is spoken about, and he acts decisively at every turn, and the man who headed the household in which the Son of God grew up leaves not a single line of dialogue. Then he disappears. He is present when Jesus is twelve and lost in Jerusalem, and after that nothing; by the time of the ministry Jesus is called the carpenter’s son and Mary appears without a husband. The likeliest reading is that he had died, and that the boy he had adopted into David’s line had been supporting the family for years. He was given the hardest assignment of any man in the Christmas story, carried it out without complaint or explanation, received no vindication that we know of, and left no words behind.

What it does not mean. Not that sexual union in marriage is unclean or unspiritual. Joseph abstained to protect a unique sign, not because marriage is less holy. Scripture celebrates sexual union within marriage (Genesis 2:24; 1 Corinthians 7:3–5).

Where Christians differ: did Mary have other children? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that Mary remained a virgin all her life (her perpetual virginity), and explain Jesus’ brothers and sisters as cousins or as Joseph’s children from an earlier marriage. Some Reformers, including Luther, also held this view. But the natural reading of Matthew’s until, together with his naming of Jesus’ brothers James, Joseph, Simon and Judas, and his sisters (13:55–56; 12:46), is that Mary and Joseph had other children after Jesus. Nothing in the text requires either of the other explanations. Verdict: Mary was a faithful wife who bore other children after her firstborn. This takes nothing away from her honour.

How then should we think of Mary? With deep honour, and without worship. She was chosen by God’s grace, she believed when belief was costly, and she bore and raised the Son of God; all generations rightly call her blessed (Luke 1:48). Her example of humble faith, let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38), is one every believer should follow. But she is a fellow sinner saved by her Son, not a mediator between us and him. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). We do not pray to her; we thank God for her, and we share her faith.

In a sentence. Joseph obeyed immediately, protected the sign of the virgin birth, and gave Jesus his legal place in David’s line.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word is clear, how long do you take to obey it? Joseph’s quiet, costly obedience changed history, and no one recorded a single word he said. Think of one thing God has plainly told you in Scripture that you are still negotiating over: a reconciliation, a habit, a gift, a confession. Joseph woke and did. Do it today, before the reasons to delay have time to gather.

For worship. The Son of God was carried into Bethlehem under the protection of a man who never said a word we can quote. God gave his Son a father who asked no questions and spared no cost, and in Joseph’s quiet faithfulness we see a shadow of the Father in heaven, who gave his Son freely and has never failed to protect his own. And the child Joseph named is the one who, unlike every son of Adam, was obedient at once and in everything, all the way to death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). The name Joseph spoke over the cradle is the name before which every knee will bow: Jesus, the LORD saves.
verseByVerse.note: “Knew her not” means they had no sexual relations until the birth.

1.theology:
The Incarnation and the Hypostatic Union. Matthew 1:23 is the first New Testament statement of what the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) would define as the hypostatic union: Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. Emmanuel — God with us. The one born of Mary is not a divine being wearing a human costume, nor a human being elevated to divine status. He is the eternal Son of God who took to himself a true and complete human nature, remaining what he was while becoming what he was not.

Reformed theology has insisted on both sides of this confession with equal force. Against those who diminish the humanity (docetism), the reformers affirm: he was born of a woman, grew in wisdom, wept, hungered, died. Against those who diminish the divinity, the reformers affirm: he is the Lord who saves, the one who forgives sins, who raises the dead, who will judge the living and the dead. The incarnation is not a compromise between deity and humanity; it is the union of both in one Person, the only foundation on which salvation is possible.
1.examples:
Then: The women in the genealogy — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — represent the scandalous grace of God that runs through broken and foreign vessels to accomplish his purposes. The rabbis of Matthew’s day would have found their inclusion in a royal genealogy offensive. Matthew includes them precisely because the gospel offends the self-righteous and welcomes the unlikely. The same grace that wrote Rahab the harlot into the ancestry of the Messiah writes sinners into the family of God through faith.

Now: We live in a world that determines worth by background, achievement, and social position. The genealogy of Matthew 1 demolishes every such calculation. The line of the King runs through exiles, foreigners, adulterers, and the forgotten. If your story has chapters you would rather not name in public, you are in good company in this genealogy. The God who included Rahab and Ruth and Tamar in the ancestry of his Son includes broken people in his family — not despite their stories but through them, weaving even the darkest threads into the tapestry of his redeeming purpose.

2.title: The King and the Nations
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.” <sup>3</sup>When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; <sup>4</sup>and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. <sup>5</sup>They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: <sup>6</sup>‘And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’” <sup>7</sup>Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. <sup>8</sup>And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, “Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him.” <sup>9</sup>After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. <sup>10</sup>When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. <sup>11</sup>And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. <sup>12</sup>And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way. <sup>13</sup>Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him.” <sup>14</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt <sup>15</sup>and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, “Out of Egypt I called my son.” <sup>16</sup>Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men. <sup>17</sup>Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: <sup>18</sup>“A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.” <sup>19</sup>But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, <sup>20</sup>saying, “Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead.” <sup>21</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. <sup>22</sup>But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee. <sup>23</sup>And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is a chapter of contrasts. From the east, pagan Magi travel hundreds of miles to worship a Jewish king they have never met, guided by a star and driven by a longing they cannot fully name. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes know exactly where the Messiah is to be born — they can quote the prophecy from memory — and do not move a single step toward Bethlehem. Knowledge without seeking is useless; seeking without knowledge leads to Jerusalem first and then to the star. The Magi needed both, and they found the King.

The flight to Egypt is Matthew’s second great fulfilment: Out of Egypt I called my son (Hos. 11:1). What Hosea said of Israel, Matthew applies to Jesus — because Jesus is the true Israel, recapitulating the nation’s story in his own person. Israel went into Egypt to be preserved; Israel came out of Egypt to receive the law at Sinai. Jesus goes into Egypt as an infant; he comes out to receive baptism at the Jordan and give the new law on the mountain. He is not just a figure from Israel’s history; he is Israel’s history compressed and completed.

The massacre of the innocents is the chapter’s darkest moment, and Matthew does not diminish it. Rachel weeping for her children (Jer. 31:15) — the ancient lament of exile reactivated by Herod’s paranoid terror. Children died because the King had come. This is not a comfortable note, and it should not be. The incarnation provokes powers that kill to protect themselves. And yet those children are the first martyrs — the first to die because of the King who would die for all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Visit of the Magi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wise men from the East arrive in Jerusalem following a star, seeking the one born King of the Jews. Their arrival triggers the first of Matthew's great ironies: Gentiles travel from afar to worship the Jewish Messiah, while the Jewish king plots his murder and the religious establishment is unmoved. Herod's response — feigned interest concealing murderous intent — foreshadows the opposition that will culminate at Golgotha. The magi's worship, their gifts, and their Spirit-warned departure set the pattern: the nations come to the light while those who hold the Scriptures remain in darkness. Two things more. Verses 7-8: Herod's secrecy is his first tell — he does not want Jerusalem to know what he is planning — and the detail he extracts from the magi, the time the star appeared, is precisely the data that produces the age-range of the massacre at verse 16. His "that I too may come and worship him" is a lie welding devotion to murder, which is the enemy's own signature (Jn. 8:44). Verses 9-10: the star resumes only after the Scriptures have sent them to Bethlehem, and by verse 9 the light is behaving less like an object in the sky than like the pillar of fire that went before Israel (Exod. 13:21) — it goes ahead of them at walking pace and halts over one house. Matthew's Greek for their reaction piles up four words where one would do: they rejoiced with joy exceedingly great. And note what caused it — not the sight of the child, whom they had not yet reached, but a light they had followed for months finally standing still.
verseByVerse.theology: The magi's journey is the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision: the nations streaming to Zion's light (Isa. 60:1–6). Their gifts — gold for a king, incense for a priest, myrrh for one destined to die — have long been read as prophetic of Christ's three offices. Herod represents all who will acknowledge Christ's kingship only to oppose it: knowing who he is changes nothing if the heart is not transformed. The Scripture the chief priests quote from memory (Micah 5:2) but do not obey is a standing rebuke to knowledge without submission - and the loose form of their quotation, examined at vv. 5-6, only sharpens the point: they had the text near enough to recite and far enough to ignore.
verseByVerse.examples: The magi traveled perhaps a thousand miles, following light they only partially understood, to bring costly gifts to a child. Their worship was costly, inconvenient, and preceded by great uncertainty. Many who have never left their town have more theological knowledge than these men had — and far less devotion. The question the magi's story presses: what are you willing to travel, spend, and risk to find and worship Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying, "Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon after Jesus was born, Gentile scholars from the east arrived in Jerusalem looking for the newborn King of the Jews, because they had seen his star and had come to worship him. The first people in Matthew to worship Jesus are foreigners.

Meaning first. Matthew 2 shows how the world responds to the King whose identity chapter 1 has just declared. Gentile scholars travel from the East to worship him; Herod, the king of the Jews by Roman appointment, tries to kill him; the Bible experts in Jerusalem know exactly where he is to be born and do not go. Then God protects his Son: he sends the family into Egypt, brings them back when Herod is dead, and settles them in despised Nazareth. At every step Matthew shows Scripture being fulfilled. Jesus relives the story of Israel, the true Son called out of Egypt, the new Moses rescued from a murderous king, the humble Branch of David. The chapter is full of danger and grief, and over all of it God is quietly, completely in control.

The connection. Chapter 1 showed who Jesus is: the son of David and son of Abraham, Immanuel. Chapter 2 shows how the world responds to him. Gentiles come to worship; the king of Israel tries to kill him; the religious experts know where he is and do not go. The whole Gospel is foreshadowed here.

Bethlehem of Judea. A small town about six miles (ten kilometres) south of Jerusalem, the hometown of David (1 Samuel 16:1). “Of Judea” distinguishes it from another Bethlehem in Galilee. It is named not for geography but for prophecy: the city of David, the place where the Messiah must be born (Micah 5:2). Matthew does not describe the birth itself; Luke does (Luke 2:1–20).

In the days of Herod the king. Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome from 37 to 4 BC. He was not a Jew by birth but an Idumean, a descendant of Esau, handed the title King of the Jews by the Roman Senate, which made many Jews resent him as king. He was a brilliant builder, who rebuilt the Jerusalem temple on a magnificent scale, but also ruthlessly cruel and paranoid, forever clutching at his throne. He had his favourite wife, her mother, three of his own sons and many others executed because he suspected plots; the emperor Augustus is said to have joked that it was safer to be Herod’s pig than his son. Since Herod died in 4 BC, Jesus was born a little before that, probably around 6–5 BC. (Our calendar was calculated in the sixth century and is a few years out.) Two kings of the Jews now stand face to face in the story: one crowned by Rome and drenched in blood, one born of God and worshipped by strangers.

Wise men from the east. Greek magoi, magi. Originally a priestly caste in Persia, they became known as experts in astrology, dream interpretation and ancient wisdom, serving as royal counsellors. They probably came from Persia or Babylon, where many Jews had lived since the exile and where Daniel had been head of the wise men (Daniel 2:48). They may have known Jewish hopes of a coming king, and the Roman writers Tacitus and Suetonius both record that an expectation of a world ruler arising from Judea was in the air across the East in those years. Matthew does not say how many there were; the tradition of three comes from the three gifts. Nor were they kings; that idea came later from Psalm 72:10–11 and Isaiah 60:3, and the names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar are later legend. They were Gentiles, outsiders to the covenant, and yet they are the first in this whole Gospel to seek the King and bow down.

Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? Not who will become king, but who has been born king. He is King by birth. It is the right question asked in the wrong place: they come to the palace looking for a newborn King and find only Herod. The title will appear again only at the end of the Gospel, on the lips of Pilate and the soldiers, and on the sign over the cross (27:11, 29, 37). The Gentiles call him King at his birth and at his death.

For we saw his star when it rose. “When it rose” can also be translated in the east. Many explanations have been offered: a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn (which happened three times in 7 BC), a comet, or a nova. But the star in verse 9 moves ahead of them and stops over a particular house, which no natural star does. Verdict: most likely a supernatural light, a sign God gave, perhaps in a form these star-watchers would understand. Some connect it with Balaam’s prophecy: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17). God met these men inside their own trade, the reading of the skies, and used a light they could not ignore to draw them to his Son.

And have come to worship him. The Greek word (proskyneō) means to bow down, to fall prostrate in homage. It can be used of honouring a king, but in Matthew it regularly describes worship of Jesus (14:33; 28:9, 17). At the least they meant to do a king honour; but Matthew means us to see more, for at the house they fall on their faces and pour out their treasures (v. 11), rendering to this child what belongs to God alone. The magi came a long way, at great cost, to bow before a child. And here is the wonder that should jolt us awake: Gentiles travel perhaps a thousand miles to worship the King, while Jerusalem, holding the very Scriptures that name his birthplace, will not walk six miles to see him.

What it does not mean. Not that astrology is a valid way to know God’s will. Scripture forbids divination and the worship of the stars (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Isaiah 47:13–14). God met these men where they were, but he led them finally by his word (vv. 5–6) to the Christ. The star brought them to Jerusalem; Scripture brought them to Bethlehem.

Is it right to worship a baby? Worship belongs to God alone, and Scripture is fierce about it: when John fell down before an angel, he was told at once to worship God (Revelation 22:8–9). So if the magi were wrong to worship this child, Matthew would have to correct them, and he does the opposite. He records their worship with approval because of who the child is: Immanuel, God with us (1:23). The baby in Mary’s arms was the eternal Son, as fully God at a few months old as on the mountain of transfiguration. Jesus received worship throughout his life (14:33; 28:9, 17) and never refused it. To bow before him is not idolatry; it is the only right response.

In a sentence. Gentile scholars travelled far to worship the newborn King of the Jews, a first sign that Jesus came for the nations.

On a Tuesday. The magi came a long way to worship. How far are you willing to go, what inconvenience will you accept, to seek Christ? The journey for most of us is shorter and harder: the walk across the room to the Bible on the shelf, the drive to church on a wet Sunday, the half-hour taken back from the screen. Choose one inconvenience this week and accept it gladly for his sake.

For worship. Look at the grace of this God. He did not wait for the magi to find their way to the Scriptures. He went out to them in the dark of their own superstition, hung a light in their sky, and drew them across deserts to his Son. He is the God whose purpose has always been to gather the nations, and here, before the King can walk or speak, the first of them arrive. The Morning Star (Revelation 22:16) has risen, and from the ends of the earth the strangers are coming to bow. You may be one of them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “wise men” renders the Greek magi — scholars of the stars, probably from Persia or Babylon. Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC.

parallels.desc: a star shall come out of Jacob
nations bring gold and frankincense to the light

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod was alarmed by the news of a newborn king, and all Jerusalem with him. He called together the religious leaders and asked them where the Messiah was to be born.

When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled. Herod had a title, King of the Jews, given to him by the Roman Senate. Now foreigners were asking for someone born to that title. To a paranoid old king, this meant a rival. He had already killed members of his own family to protect his throne. Herod’s trouble is the trouble of threatened power.

And all Jerusalem with him. Why would the city be troubled at the news of the Messiah? Because they knew Herod. When Herod was disturbed, people died. The city feared what he might do. And perhaps many were comfortable with things as they were and did not want disruption, even from God. The city that should have erupted in joy at the arrival of its King instead trembles.

Assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people. The chief priests were the high priest and the leading priestly families who ran the temple, mostly Sadducees. The scribes were experts in the law of Moses who taught and interpreted it, mostly Pharisees. Together they formed much of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council. These were the people who knew the Scriptures best. They are summoned not for worship but for information, treated as a reference library by a man who has no intention of bowing.

He inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. Herod connects King of the Jews with the Christ, the Messiah. He understands that this is about God’s promised King. Herod knows enough theology to be afraid of Jesus, and not enough humility to worship him.

The scholars exposed. Before that lands too comfortably on someone else, notice who is most exposed by it. The men in this scene are not sceptics or pagans. They are the Bible scholars. They can produce the right chapter and verse from memory, at speed, under pressure from a king, and they will not walk six miles down a road they themselves have just identified. That is not a failure of information. It is a failure of appetite. The person most at risk of this is the person reading a commentary. If you can locate a doctrine, follow an argument about the Greek and hold an opinion on a disputed text, you have precisely the equipment these men had. Study can become a substitute for the thing it is meant to serve, and it is a comfortable substitute, because it feels like devotion and costs nothing.

What it does not mean. Not that every person in Jerusalem was hostile. Luke tells of Simeon and Anna in the temple, longing for the Messiah (Luke 2:25–38). But as a whole, the capital was troubled rather than glad.

How does Jesus disturb the throne in my own heart? Every heart has a Herod in it: the part of us that wants to rule our own life and resents anyone who claims the right to. Jesus disturbs it whenever his word touches something we have kept for ourselves: our money, our time, our sexuality, our grudges, our plans. You can tell the throne is being disturbed when you feel that reluctance to read a particular passage, or the urge to change the subject when a sermon comes close. Herod’s answer was to get rid of the rival. The Christian’s answer is to step down and let the true King reign, and to discover that he rules for our good and not to crush us.

In a sentence. News of the true King filled Herod, and the city that feared him, with alarm.

On a Tuesday. Jesus disturbs every throne, including the one in your own heart. Does the thought of his rule trouble you, or gladden you? Put the honest question to yourself now rather than at the end of your life: over the last month, what has knowing about Christ moved you to do? If the answer is that it moved you to know more, you are standing with the scribes, and Bethlehem is still six miles away.

For worship. The King who troubled Herod’s palace was too small to lift his head. He had no army and no title from Rome, and the most powerful man in the land shook at the rumour of him. That is what it is to be the true King: his very existence is a threat to every false throne, and every false throne knows it. Psalm 2 saw it long ago. The kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens laughs. Herod is dust. The child he feared reigns.
verseByVerse.note: Herod was notoriously jealous of rivals; he had members of his own family killed. The chief priests and scribes were the experts in the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: They told him, "In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: 'And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The experts answered at once: the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem, as the prophet Micah wrote, for from there would come a ruler who would shepherd God’s people Israel.

In Bethlehem of Judea. They did not hesitate. It was common knowledge among the scholars that the Messiah would come from David’s town (John 7:42). Micah 5:2 comes to their lips at once and is obeyed not at all.

For so it is written by the prophet. Micah 5:2, written about seven hundred years earlier, combined with 2 Samuel 5:2.

And you, O Bethlehem … are by no means least. Look the prophecy up and something will stop you. Micah’s Hebrew says that Bethlehem is too little to be among the clans of Judah. Matthew’s quotation says it is by no means least. The words have been turned around, and it is not carelessness. The two are not in conflict: Bethlehem was small in size, but because the Messiah would come from it, it is by no means least in importance. Matthew draws out the meaning in the light of the fulfilment. Micah’s point was that God delights to choose what the world overlooks; the point here is what that smallness has now become. Both are true, and the second is what the first was always going to produce. Read that way, the apparent misquotation is the gospel in miniature: grace does not leave little things little. God chooses small places, as he chooses small people (1 Corinthians 1:27–28).

For from you shall come a ruler. Micah goes on to say that this ruler’s coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2): a hint that the ruler’s origin is older than Bethlehem. He was born in a town, but he did not begin there.

Who will shepherd my people Israel. These words come from 2 Samuel 5:2, where God told David that he would shepherd Israel. In the ancient world kings were often called shepherds, and in Israel the image meant caring for, feeding, guiding and protecting the people (Ezekiel 34). The prophets condemned the false shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock, and promised that God himself would shepherd his people through a new David (Ezekiel 34:11–24). Herod was a wolf-king; Jesus is the Shepherd-King (John 10:11). The shepherds of his people refused to go and find the Shepherd.

The irony. The scholars knew exactly where the Messiah would be born, quoted the right verse, and did not walk six miles to see. The magi, who knew far less, made the journey. This is the deepest irony of the infancy narrative: pagan foreigners travel a thousand miles to worship; Israel’s own scholars travel none to investigate. Knowing the Bible is not the same as following its Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that knowledge of Scripture is unimportant: it was Scripture that pointed the way to Bethlehem. But knowledge without response hardens. James says that even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19).

What should I do when I know a lot about the Bible but my heart feels cold? Do not stop reading; that would only make it worse. But change how you read. Read less at a time and more slowly, asking at each passage what it shows you of Christ and what it asks of you today. Turn what you read straight into prayer, speaking it back to God. Then do one concrete thing it says, the same day, however small. Coldness is often the result of knowledge that has never been allowed to become obedience. And ask God plainly to warm you; it is a prayer he loves to answer (Psalm 119:36–37). The magi did not have more information than the scribes. They had more desire, and desire is something God gives.

In a sentence. Scripture had foretold that the Shepherd-King would come from small Bethlehem, and the experts knew it but did not go.

On a Tuesday. Do you know your Bible better than you obey it? The scribes had the address and stayed at home. Think of one thing you have known for years that Christ asks of you and have not yet done. That is your six miles.

For worship. The God who made the stars chose a village too little to be counted, and made it the birthplace of the one whose goings forth are from of old. That is how he works, and it is good news for small people. The everlasting Son came to be a Shepherd, not a tyrant: to feed and carry and seek the lost, and in the end to lay down his life for the sheep. The scribes would not go to him. He came all the way to them, and to us.
verseByVerse.note: Bethlehem, David’s hometown, lies about six miles south of Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel”

verseByVerse.quote: Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, "Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod met the magi secretly, found out exactly when the star had appeared, and sent them to Bethlehem with instructions to report back, pretending he wanted to worship the child too.

Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly. He did not want public attention, or his plan to be known. Herod’s secrecy is the first mark of his murderous intent.

Ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. He asked carefully, because he wanted to calculate the child’s age. This explains why he later killed boys up to two years old (v. 16): the star had probably appeared some time before, perhaps a year or more. The magi’s honest answer becomes the data for a massacre.

The star and the stargazers. In the ancient world, and above all in the East, it was taken for granted that the heavens spoke: that the birth and death of kings were written in the sky for those trained to read them. Astrology was the respected science of the day, and the magi were its scholars. Yet the Bible forbids God’s people to steer their lives by the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19; Isaiah 47:13). How then does God use one? In sheer grace he stooped to meet these outsiders in the one language they knew, not to bless astrology, but to draw them up out of it and onto the road to Bethlehem. God will often call a man through the dim light he already has, but he never leaves him there; he leads him on to his Word. We are not to scan the heavens for messages. We have the prophetic word more fully confirmed (2 Peter 1:19), and the true Morning Star has already risen.

Go and search diligently for the child. Herod uses the magi as unknowing spies.

That I too may come and worship him. A lie. He wanted to kill the child. Herod wraps the murder of a child in the language of worship, and it is hard to imagine a fouler use of words. Scripture helps us name what we are looking at. To weld lying and murder together in one breath is the devil’s own signature: Jesus said he was a murderer from the beginning and the father of lies (John 8:44). Herod is doing the serpent’s work, and Revelation shows us the picture behind the picture: a great dragon crouching before the woman, so that when she bore her child he might devour it (Revelation 12:4).

Dressed as devotion. The deadliest hatred of Christ rarely comes snarling; it comes dressed in the clothes of devotion. The same evil that here says I will worship will later kiss him in a garden and quote Scripture at his trial. Herod’s claim to want to worship has been repeated by every power that has ever tried to use Christ for its own purposes. True worship dethrones the worshipper; Herod wanted information to eliminate a rival.

What it does not mean. Not that the magi were foolish to trust him at first. They had no reason to suspect a king. God protected them by warning them later (v. 12).

How can I tell whether my own worship is real or for show? Herod is an extreme case, but the question is fair for everyone. Real worship bows; false worship uses. Ask what you want from God when you worship: is it God himself, or something he can get you, such as standing, comfort or a good name? Ask whether your worship changes anything you do on Monday. Ask whether you would still praise him if no one saw. No one’s motives are perfectly pure, and that is no reason to stop worshipping; it is a reason to come as a sinner, asking him to make your heart true. Herod never asked. The tax collector who beat his breast did (Luke 18:13), and he went home justified.

In a sentence. Herod hid a murderous plan behind a pretence of worship, using the magi to find the child.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of anyone, including yourself, who uses pious words to cover selfish aims. God sees the heart. Notice when you reach for spiritual language to win an argument, to get your way in a church meeting, or to make a decision you have already made sound like God’s will.

For worship. Mark how the lie ends. God need only warn the wise men in a dream, and Joseph in another, and the child is gone before the swords arrive. The cradle the tyrant meant to empty, God himself was guarding. The dragon crouched, and the child was caught up to safety. And the King whom Herod could not kill would one day lay down his life of his own accord, and take it up again (John 10:18). No one takes his life from him. He gives it.

parallels.desc: rulers take counsel against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The magi set out, and the star they had seen went ahead of them and stopped over the place where the child was. When they saw it, they were overwhelmed with joy.

After listening to the king, they went on their way. They went alone. No one from Jerusalem, not even the scholars, came with them.

The star … went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. The text is precise. No ordinary star or planet moves before travellers at walking pace down the Bethlehem road and stops over a single house. Whatever may have stood in the sky at its rising (v. 2), by verse 9 this light is behaving less like an object in the heavens than like the pillar of cloud and fire that went before Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21): a light God set in front of his people to bring them precisely where he wanted them. He does not lose the people he is calling. If it takes hanging a light in the sky and walking it down a road to bring a Persian stargazer to Bethlehem, he will do it.

They rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. Matthew piles up words: literally they rejoiced a great joy exceedingly, a verb, its own noun, an adverb and an adjective, all heaped on one another. It is not elegant Greek. It is the sentence of a man reaching for four words because one will not do, and it is the strongest expression of gladness anywhere in this Gospel. After a long journey, and the disappointment of Jerusalem, they find God guiding them again. Their joy contrasts with the fear of Herod and Jerusalem (v. 3). The same news brings fear to some and joy to others, depending on whether they want the King.

The joy of the right road. And notice what produced it. Not the sight of the child: they have not reached the house yet. They rejoiced because a light they had been following stopped moving. What they had at that moment was confirmation that the journey had not been foolish. Months on the road, a wrong turn into a hostile palace, an audience with a man they would shortly be warned to avoid, and then the thing they had set out after was standing still over a roof in front of them. Most Christians have felt some version of it: not the arrival itself, but the moment it becomes clear the road was the right one after all.

What it does not mean. Not that God usually guides by signs in the sky. Here he gave a unique sign for a unique event. He guides his people today chiefly through his word (Psalm 119:105).

What if I have never felt that kind of joy about Christ? Feelings vary greatly from person to person and from season to season, and joy is not always a flood; often it is a quiet gladness that he is there, or a settled peace under trouble. Do not measure your faith by the strength of your emotions. But do not settle for coldness either. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), and it grows as we look at Christ: read the Gospels, sing his praises with his people, remember what he has saved you from. Ask God for joy; David did (Psalm 51:12). And remember that the magi’s joy came after a long and uncertain road. Some joys are given at the end of the journey.

In a sentence. God led the magi to the child, and finding him filled them with overwhelming joy.

On a Tuesday. Think back to a time when it became clear that God had been leading you all along, the job that fell through, the church you nearly did not visit, the friend who spoke at the right moment. Thank him for it today, out loud. And if you are still on the road, keep walking. The light has not gone out.

For worship. Thank God for the ways he has led you to Christ, and ask for the magi’s joy in finding him. He is the God who goes before. He went before Israel in fire and cloud, he went before the magi in a moving star, and he went before all of us into death and out again, the Shepherd walking ahead of his flock. There is no joy on earth like the joy of finding that the road ends at Christ, and that he was the one leading us there the whole time.

verseByVerse.quote: And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Entering the house, the magi saw the child with his mother, fell down and worshipped him, and offered him costly gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home another way.

Going into the house. Not a stable. By now, perhaps months later, the family was living in a house in Bethlehem. Luke’s shepherds came on the night of the birth and found the baby lying in a manger (Luke 2:16); the magi come to a child (paidion) in a house. Herod’s calculation of two years old or under (v. 16) suggests the visit came some time after the birth. Nativity scenes that put the magi at the manger with the shepherds combine two separate events. The truth is better than the tidy version: this is not a crowd gathered round a cradle on one magical evening. It is the slow, patient, sovereign gathering of the nations to Christ, begun here with a handful of foreign astrologers, and still going on.

They saw the child with Mary his mother. Matthew always mentions the child first (vv. 13, 14, 20, 21). Mary is honoured, but the child is the centre.

And they fell down and worshipped him. They worshipped the child, not Mary. Wealthy, learned foreigners lay face down on the floor before a child of an ordinary family. They found not a palace but a house; not a king enthroned but a child with his mother. This is authentic worship: it does not require the trappings of majesty to recognise the reality. Worship is the right response to Jesus, even as an infant, because of who he is (1:23).

Opening their treasures. Their treasure chests: gifts fit for a king. In the ancient world one did not approach a king empty-handed.

Gold. The gift for a king.

Frankincense. A fragrant resin from trees in Arabia and Somalia, burned as incense in worship, including in the temple (Exodus 30:34–38). A gift associated with God and worship.

Myrrh. Another fragrant resin, used in perfume, medicine and for preparing bodies for burial (John 19:39). It was offered to Jesus again on the cross, mixed with wine (Mark 15:23).

The meaning of the gifts. From early times, Christians have seen the gifts as pointing to who Jesus is: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for one who would die. Matthew does not say this, and the magi probably intended simply to give the most precious gifts they had. But the gifts fit, and Isaiah had spoken of the nations bringing gold and frankincense to the Lord (Isaiah 60:6; Psalm 72:10–11). The old reading is genuinely ancient and may well be right; myrrh in particular reappears at his burial.

God funded the exile. Take the gifts also as what they plainly were: portable wealth. Frankincense and myrrh were resins traded up from southern Arabia at enormous cost, the kind of goods that moved by caravan under guard. This is a fortune arriving in a working family’s house, and it arrives immediately before a flight into a foreign country. Joseph is about to be told to leave in the night, with no notice, no destination arranged and no means of support in Egypt. Then the funds turn up, carried perhaps a thousand miles by strangers who had no idea what they were for. God funded the exile before he announced it. Sometimes a provision that seems out of proportion to anything currently going on is not for now.

Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod. God protected the child and the magi. God speaks in dreams five times in Matthew 1–2, always to guide and protect.

They departed to their own country by another way. They avoided Jerusalem. Matthew says no more about them. They returned home, having worshipped the King. Everyone who truly meets Christ goes home by another way.

What it does not mean. Not that worship is measured by the size of the gift. The widow’s two small coins were worth more than the gifts of the rich (Mark 12:41–44). The magi gave their best; so should we, whatever it is.

What can I give Jesus, since he needs nothing? Nothing he needs, and everything he asks. God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25). But he delights to receive from his children what love offers, as a father treasures a child’s drawing. Give him first yourself (Romans 12:1; 2 Corinthians 8:5). Then give him your worship, your obedience, your time in prayer and his Word, and your money given gladly to his church and to the poor; Jesus counts what is done for the least of his brothers as done for him (25:40). And give your gifts and skills in serving his people. The magi brought what they had. So can you.

In a sentence. The magi bowed in worship before the child King and gave him their most precious treasures.

On a Tuesday. What is your best that you could give to Christ this week: your time, your money, your skill, your attention? Not the leftovers of the week, but the first and the best. Decide it now, before the week decides it for you.

For worship. Bow before Christ as the magi did, and give him your best. He is worth every treasure the East could carry: gold, because he is King of kings; incense, because he is God with us; myrrh, because he came to die. And the wonder is that the true exchange runs the other way. The magi opened their treasures to him, but he opened heaven’s treasures to us, and became poor so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He is the gift the whole world was waiting for.
verseByVerse.note: By now the family is in a house, not a stable. Frankincense was a resin burned in worship; myrrh a fragrant resin also used in burial.

parallels.desc: kings bring gifts to the king

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Flight to Egypt and the Return to Nazareth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy family flees to Egypt to escape Herod's massacre of Bethlehem's infant boys, returns after Herod's death, and settles in Nazareth — each movement fulfilling a specific Old Testament text. Matthew sees in these events not merely historical geography but the recapitulation of Israel's story: Jesus relives the Exodus (out of Egypt), the Exile (the weeping of Rachel), and Israel's wilderness sojourn (settling in a despised region). The Son of God is doing in himself what Israel failed to do: he is the true Israel, perfectly faithful where the nation was not. Three items the summary passes over. Verses 19-20 contain a quiet oddity: "those who sought the child's life are dead" is plural, though only Herod had died — because Matthew is quoting Exodus 4:19 almost word for word, God's word to Moses in Midian, with the direction of travel reversed. Herod died at Jericho in the spring of 4 BC, which is why Jesus was born several years before the year we number 1 — an error not in Scripture but in the sixth-century monk who built the calendar. Verses 21-22 are the fifth dream in two chapters (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), and the verse-by-verse takes up the question readers actually carry: whether God still guides this way, and what to do with a vivid dream. Note that Joseph's fear of Archelaus was reasonable on its own terms and the dream confirmed his ordinary judgement rather than overruling it. Verse 23 is the hardest fulfilment quotation in the Gospel, because no Old Testament verse says the Messiah will be called a Nazarene — and Matthew signals as much by writing "prophets" in the plural, naming nobody and quoting nothing. The strongest reading is Isaiah 11:1, where the shoot from Jesse's stump is a netser; the theme of the despised one (Isa. 53:2-3) very likely stands behind it too. And the name stuck: it is what Pilate wrote over his head, how the angel identified him at the tomb, and what the risen Christ called himself from heaven on the Damascus road (Acts 22:8).
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew's three fulfillment quotations here (Hos. 11:1; Jer. 31:15; and possibly Isa. 11:1 or Judg. 13:5 for "Nazarene") reveal his typological reading of history: Israel's great narrative events were not merely past occurrences but prophetic templates waiting for their ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Jesus does not merely happen to visit Egypt; he is the true Son whom God calls out of Egypt. The slaughter of the innocents does not merely echo Rachel's weeping; it is the event that makes the older weeping fully intelligible. This is not proof-texting but fulfillment theology.
verseByVerse.examples: The massacre of Bethlehem's infants is the event that silences easy answers about suffering. Matthew does not explain it; he quotes Jeremiah's lament and moves on. Rachel weeping for her children who are no more: there are moments when the only honest response to evil is grief, not explanation. The Messiah's birth caused suffering for the innocent. His death would be the answer to that suffering — not by explaining it away, but by entering it and overcoming it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, "Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him." And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the magi left, an angel warned Joseph in a dream to take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt, because Herod was about to search for the child to kill him. Joseph obeyed that very night.

An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream. The second of four dreams (1:20; 2:13, 19, 22). Each time God guides Joseph, he obeys at once.

Rise, take the child and his mother. Joseph is responsible for protecting the family. His role in these chapters is entirely responsive to divine commands: he is told, he does. His is the faith that acts without arguing, that obeys without understanding the full plan, and it is a form of faith harder than heroism: the faith of silent, sustained obedience to a voice only he has heard.

And flee to Egypt. Egypt was outside Herod’s territory, under direct Roman rule, about eighty miles (130 kilometres) from Bethlehem to the border, perhaps a week or more of travel. Large Jewish communities lived there, especially in Alexandria. Egypt had long been a refuge for God’s people: Abraham went there in famine (Genesis 12:10), and Jacob’s family went there under Joseph (Genesis 46). It was also the land of Israel’s slavery, from which God rescued them. The land of Israel’s ancient bondage now becomes the Messiah’s refuge.

For Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him. The first attempt on Jesus’ life. From the beginning, the world’s powers set themselves against God’s King (Psalm 2:1–2; Revelation 12:4).

And he rose and took the child and his mother by night. Immediate obedience, the same night, without waiting for morning’s reassurance. No questions recorded, no delay.

Refugees. Say plainly what is happening in this verse, because familiarity has smoothed it over. A family wakes in the dark, takes what it can carry, and crosses a border to escape a ruler who wants their child dead. They arrive in a foreign country with no standing, no relatives named in the text, and no idea how long they will be there. There is a word for people in that position, and the word is refugees. The Son of God spent part of his childhood as one. God could have protected the child in Bethlehem; he had already redirected a caravan of Persians with a dream. Instead he sent him down the road every displaced family has walked.

The pattern. Jesus relives Israel’s story. Like Israel, he goes down into Egypt; like Israel, he will be called out of Egypt (v. 15); like Israel, he will pass through water (3:16) and be tested in the wilderness (4:1–11). But where Israel failed, he will be faithful. He is the true Israel, God’s faithful Son. The one who will lead the new exodus first goes down into Egypt himself.

What it does not mean. Not that fleeing danger shows a lack of faith. God himself commanded it. Trusting God includes using the means of safety he provides. Jesus later told his disciples to flee persecution when they could (10:23).

So how should a Christian think about refugees and migrants? With compassion first, because our Lord was one. Scripture commands God’s people again and again to love the sojourner, remembering that they were strangers in Egypt themselves (Leviticus 19:33–34; Deuteronomy 10:19), and that command now has a face. Christians in good conscience differ on questions of borders and government policy, and Scripture gives governments a real duty to keep order (Romans 13:1–4). But no follower of this King is at liberty to speak of people fleeing violence with contempt. In practice that might mean befriending a refugee family in your town, supporting churches that serve them, and praying for persecuted believers who have had to run.

In a sentence. God warned Joseph to flee to Egypt to protect the child from Herod, and Joseph obeyed at once.

On a Tuesday. Refugees fleeing violence are not strangers to the story of Jesus: he was one. Pray for refugees, and welcome them as you would welcome him. And if your own life has been marked by upheaval you did not choose, moved on, uprooted, made to start again somewhere that was not home, you are not outside the experience of Christ, and you are not outside the plan of God. Those years in Egypt were not an interruption of his mission. They were part of it.

For worship. The Lord of heaven and earth had nowhere safe to lay his head before he could even walk. He was carried by night across a desert in his mother’s arms, a hunted child in a foreign land. He did not stand apart from the misery of this world; he went into it from his first year. And all the while his Father was watching over him, and over the promise. The one who fled from Herod will one day sit on the throne before which every Herod must stand, and he will remember every stranger who was welcomed in his name.
verseByVerse.note: Egypt had long been a refuge; large Jewish communities lived there.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s family goes down to Egypt

verseByVerse.quote: and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, "Out of Egypt I called my son." Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The family stayed in Egypt until Herod died, fulfilling God’s word through Hosea, “Out of Egypt I called my son”. Meanwhile Herod, furious at being tricked, ordered the killing of all the boys in and around Bethlehem aged two and under.

And remained there until the death of Herod. Herod died in 4 BC, after a painful illness. The family may have stayed in Egypt for a few months up to a year or two.

Out of Egypt I called my son. From Hosea 11:1. In Hosea, the verse looks back on the exodus: God called his son Israel out of Egypt. God had called Israel his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). How can Matthew say this is fulfilled in Jesus? It is a fair question that troubles many honest readers, since Hosea was not predicting the future at all; he was looking back.

How Matthew reads Hosea. Matthew is not saying that Hosea predicted this event directly. He is saying that Israel’s history was a pattern that Jesus completes. The word fulfil does not always mean a prediction has come true; often it means filled full, brought at last to the completion God always intended. Israel was God’s son but was unfaithful; Hosea goes on to say that the more God called them, the more they went away and sacrificed to the Baals (Hosea 11:2). Jesus is the true and faithful Son, who lives out Israel’s story perfectly. What happened to Israel as a nation happens to Jesus as its representative. This is called typology: Old Testament people and events as patterns pointing to Christ. Matthew places the quotation here, before the return, because the point is that the child is safe in Egypt in order to be called out.

Two rules for reading this way. Matthew is not playing loose with Hosea; he is reading the Old Testament as the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it, as one story, by one Author, about one Saviour (Luke 24:27). Two rules keep this honest. First, we never erase what a text meant in its own day: Hosea truly did mean the exodus. Second, we read every text in the light of the whole Bible, whose centre is Christ. That is no licence to make a verse say whatever we please. It is learning to see the Author’s single design running from Genesis to the manger.

Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men. The magi had not returned (v. 12). Herod’s fury reveals that he knew he was pursuing a child, not an army, and killed infants anyway.

Became furious. Herod’s rage was infamous. Shortly before he died he reportedly ordered that leading men be executed at his death so that there would be mourning in the land.

And he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under. Bethlehem was a small town of perhaps one thousand people, so the number of boys killed may have been around ten to twenty. No other ancient historian records this event, but it is exactly in character for Herod, who murdered on a much larger scale, and the killing of a few village children would have seemed minor beside his other crimes. The slaughter of the innocents is the first shadow of Golgotha: the powers of this world respond to the presence of Christ with violence against the most vulnerable.

But did it really happen? The silence of the Jewish historian Josephus is regularly produced as proof that Matthew made the story up, and it sounds stronger than it is. Begin with the scale, which Christmas art has thoroughly distorted: there is no host of martyred innocents, but a handful of families in a small town, and one terrible morning. Then set that against the reign it belongs to. This is the man who murdered his wife Mariamne, executed three of his own sons, and had his teenage brother-in-law drowned in a swimming pool for being too popular. An argument from silence is weak at the best of times, and weakest for small events far from the capital. Josephus wrote the better part of a century later, selecting from a reign crowded with atrocities. Matthew wrote within living memory, for readers in the region, which is the worst possible audience to invent a local atrocity for.

According to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men. He allowed a wide margin to be sure.

The parallel with Moses. Matthew’s readers would think of Pharaoh, who ordered the Hebrew baby boys to be killed, and of Moses, who was saved (Exodus 1:22–2:10). Jesus is the new Moses, saved from a murderous king to become his people’s deliverer. Later Jewish tradition even said that Pharaoh had been warned by his wise men of a coming deliverer.

What it does not mean. Not that God did not care about the children of Bethlehem. He did not cause Herod’s evil. Why God protected Jesus and not the others is not explained, and we should not pretend to know. But the same child who escaped would later die, innocent, at the hands of rulers, to defeat evil itself.

In a sentence. Jesus, the true Son, was sheltered in Egypt to be called out like Israel, while Herod murdered the boys of Bethlehem.

On a Tuesday. The world into which Jesus came was a world of violence against children. He did not come to a safe world; he came to save a broken one. Stand against violence toward the vulnerable: the unborn, the abused, the trafficked, the child in your street whose home is not safe. In the ledgers of power, poor children in an unimportant village do not count. God keeps a different ledger, and so should his people.

For worship. Where Israel stumbled in the wilderness, this Son would walk without a fault. Where Adam fell, he would stand. God called his son out of Egypt once, and the son went off after idols; he called his Son again, and the Son came, and never once turned aside. That is our salvation: not that we kept Israel’s story, but that Jesus kept it for us, and all who belong to him are counted sons in him. And though Herod raged, he could not touch a hair of the Son until the Father’s hour had come. Heaven has not forgotten one of the names of Bethlehem’s little ones, and the Son who escaped would one day go to the sword of his own will, to put an end to all the Herods for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Bethlehem was a small town; the number of boys killed was probably small, but the act fits Herod’s known cruelty.

parallels.desc: “Out of Egypt I called my son”
Pharaoh orders the Hebrew boys killed

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: "A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod’s massacre fulfilled the words of Jeremiah: Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted. Matthew does not hide the grief. But in Jeremiah, the weeping comes just before the promise of a new covenant, and in Jesus that hope has arrived.

Then was fulfilled. Matthew changes his usual wording. Elsewhere he says that something happened to fulfil Scripture, suggesting God’s purpose. Here he says then was fulfilled. He avoids saying that God intended the massacre. Herod’s evil was his own, though it fitted the pattern Scripture described.

What was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah. Jeremiah 31:15.

A voice was heard in Ramah. Ramah was a town about five miles (eight kilometres) north of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin. In 586 BC the Babylonians gathered the captives of Judah there before marching them into exile (Jeremiah 40:1).

Rachel weeping for her children. Rachel was Jacob’s beloved wife, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and so a mother of Israel. She died giving birth to Benjamin and was buried on the way to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:16–20). Jeremiah pictures her weeping from her tomb as her descendants are led away into exile. Matthew hears the same weeping in Bethlehem, near her tomb, as mothers mourn their murdered sons. Matthew does not soften this or provide an explanation; he simply names the grief. The gospel does not protect the innocent from all suffering. It enters human suffering and redeems it from within.

She refused to be comforted, because they are no more. Scripture does not hurry grief. It gives voice to it. There is a grief so deep that it refuses easy comfort. The Bible puts an inconsolable woman in the Christmas story and does not rebuke her. There are losses that are not to be tidied up, and God is not embarrassed by tears he has recorded on purpose.

The context in Jeremiah. Jeremiah 31 is a chapter of hope. Immediately after this verse, God tells Rachel to keep her voice from weeping, because there is hope for her future and her children will come back (Jeremiah 31:16–17). And a little later comes the promise of the new covenant, in which God will forgive his people’s sin (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Matthew’s readers would know the context. The weeping of Bethlehem marks the moment just before God’s greatest comfort: the child who escaped will establish the new covenant in his blood (26:28). Rachel weeps, but not for ever, and not without hope.

What it does not mean. Not that grief is a lack of faith. Rachel’s weeping is recorded in Scripture without rebuke. Christians grieve, though not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

Why did God warn Joseph and not the house next door? It is the sharpest form of the oldest question there is, and it is put here at the very beginning of the Gospel, where nobody can pretend the New Testament has not noticed. First, Scripture itself refuses to explain. Matthew offers no reason and no consoling remark about a better plan. Second, we must admit the limit: the secret things belong to the LORD our God (Deuteronomy 29:29), and anyone who offers a grieving parent the reason is guessing. But third, and this is not a guess: the child who was rescued that night was rescued for Golgotha. Thirty years later the sword that missed him in Bethlehem found him on a hill outside Jerusalem, and this time the Father sent no angel. God is not a God who keeps his own family clear of the grief he permits in yours. He entered it, at the deepest point, deliberately.

Are the little ones of Bethlehem with God? Scripture does not tell us about these particular children, so we speak carefully. But the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3). David, when his infant son died, said I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Samuel 12:23), and many believers have found great comfort in that hope. We may entrust such children to a God who is both just and very merciful, whose Son took little children in his arms and blessed them (19:14). The Judge of all the earth will do what is right.

In a sentence. The grief of Bethlehem echoed Rachel’s weeping over exile, a grief that Scripture honours, on the edge of the new covenant’s comfort.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving, you do not have to pretend. Bring your tears to God; the Psalms give you words for it. And sit with those who grieve, without rushing them toward comfort. You do not need an explanation to offer. You need to be there, to listen, and to remember them in a month when everyone else has moved on.

For worship. The God of Rachel is not a distant spectator of the tears of mothers. He wrote them into his Word, and then he sent his Son to weep at a friend’s grave and to die under the curse that brought all death into the world. That is not an explanation of our losses. It is the presence of someone in them with us who knows exactly what it cost. And it is why Jeremiah’s next sentence, your children shall come back, is not a poetic flourish but a promise with a cross and an empty tomb standing behind it. The day is coming when he will wipe away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 21:4), and Rachel will be comforted at last.
verseByVerse.note: Ramah lay north of Jerusalem, on the road into exile. Rachel, Jacob’s wife, was buried near Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: Rachel buried on the way to Bethlehem

verseByVerse.quote: But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying, "Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Herod died, the angel again appeared to Joseph in Egypt and told him to return to the land of Israel, because those who had tried to kill the child were dead.
