But when Herod died. The tyrant who tried to kill God’s King died, and the King lived. Every enemy of Christ passes; he remains. Josephus describes the end in some detail: a disease that produced fever, ulceration, convulsions and worms, borne with increasing rage, at Jericho in the spring of what we call 4 BC. It was during that final illness that he had the leading men of the nation shut in the stadium with orders that they be killed the moment he died. His sister quietly countermanded it.

Why our calendar is a few years out. If Herod died in 4 BC and Jesus was born before that, then Jesus was born several years before the year we number 1. The error is not in Scripture but in a sixth-century monk, Dionysius Exiguus, who was asked to construct a calendar from the incarnation and miscalculated by a few years. The date on the wall is wrong; the events are not.

An angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt. The third dream. God had promised to tell Joseph when to return (v. 13), and he did. Joseph had been told to remain there until I tell you: no duration. He waited in a foreign country with a small child and no idea whether it would be months or a decade. He was not given a date. He was given a person who promised to speak again, and the promise was kept.

Go to the land of Israel. “The land of Israel” is a phrase used only here in the New Testament. It recalls God’s promise of the land to Abraham, and the exodus journey back to it. Like Israel, Jesus is called out of Egypt into the land.

For those who sought the child’s life are dead. There is a small oddity in the wording that is easy to read past. Those who sought: plural. But only one man had sought the child’s life, and only one man had died. The reason is that the sentence is a quotation. In Midian, God told Moses to go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking his life were dead (Exodus 4:19). Matthew has reproduced it almost word for word, plural and all, and has simply reversed the direction of travel: Moses is told to go back to Egypt, Joseph to come back from it. The parallel is not a general resemblance; Matthew has left the grammar showing. Jesus is the new Moses, returning to deliver his people, and more than Moses: Moses led Israel out of Egypt, and Jesus will lead a new humanity out of bondage to sin and death.

What it does not mean. Not that every danger had passed: Herod’s son would be a new threat (v. 22). God guides one step at a time.

Is it wrong to feel relief when a wicked ruler dies? No. Scripture itself records the relief of God’s people when oppressors fall, and Israel sang when Pharaoh’s army was overthrown (Exodus 15:1). It is right to thank God when he ends a reign of cruelty and protects the vulnerable. But it is wrong to delight in any person’s death for its own sake, because God himself takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). We rejoice in God’s justice and his rescue, we leave vengeance to him (Romans 12:19), and we remember that we too deserved judgment and were shown mercy.

In a sentence. God called Joseph back from Egypt when Herod was dead, as he had once called Moses back to deliver Israel.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his word about timing: he told Joseph to wait until he spoke, and he spoke. Wait for him, and act when he makes the way clear. If you are in the middle of a wait without a date, a diagnosis, a job search, a prodigal, do the next faithful thing in the place where you are, as Joseph did in Egypt, and trust the one who has promised not to forget you.

For worship. Herod had armies, spies and swords, and he is gone. The child had nothing but his Father’s word, and he lives. That is the whole of history in one verse. Every tyrant who has raised his hand against Christ has gone down to the dust, and the King is still on his throne. And the God who said I will tell you, and then told, is the same God who has promised that his Son will come again. He has never yet failed to speak when he said he would.

parallels.desc: “all the men who were seeking your life are dead”

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph obeyed and returned. But when he heard that Herod’s son Archelaus ruled Judea, he was afraid, and, warned in another dream, he went north to Galilee instead.

And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. The same immediate obedience (vv. 14, 21).

Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod. When Herod died, Rome divided his kingdom among three of his sons. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea. He began his reign by massacring about three thousand people at the temple during Passover. He was so brutal and incompetent that Rome removed him in AD 6 and sent him into exile, putting Judea under Roman governors, of whom Pontius Pilate was later one.

He was afraid to go there. Joseph’s fear was reasonable. Bethlehem, in Judea, was under Archelaus. God does not overrule that fear or scold him for it.

Being warned in a dream. The fourth and last dream. God confirms and directs Joseph’s caution. Divine guidance does not override prudence; here the dream confirms what ordinary wisdom already suspected.

He withdrew to the district of Galilee. Galilee, the northern region, was ruled by another of Herod’s sons, Herod Antipas, who was less violent (he later executed John the Baptist, 14:1–12). Galilee had a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles and was looked down on by people in Judea. Isaiah had spoken of Galilee of the nations, where those in darkness would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16).

How does this fit Luke’s account? Luke has the family return to Nazareth after the presentation in the temple (Luke 2:39). Most likely the order was: birth in Bethlehem, where they had come for the census (Luke 2:1–5); the presentation in Jerusalem forty days later; a stay in Bethlehem, now in a house (2:11), where the magi found them; the flight to Egypt; and then Nazareth. Luke compresses the story and Matthew supplies the episode Luke leaves out. Matthew writes as if Nazareth is a new decision because from his angle it was: Joseph’s first thought was to settle in Judea.

Does God still guide by dreams? This is the fifth dream in two chapters (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), and readers genuinely carry the question. Notice first how rare this cluster is. Scripture covers thousands of years, and guidance by dream is concentrated at a handful of hinge points in redemptive history: Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in Babylon, and here at the arrival of the Messiah. Notice second that these dreams tell Joseph something he could not have worked out and needed urgently. None of them tells him what to believe or how to live; for that, God had already spoken. Some Christians believe God still guides through dreams and visions today, pointing to Joel’s promise in Acts 2:17. The more likely reading is that those revelations belonged to the founding of the church, and that God now guides his people by his finished word. That does not stop God from using a dream in his providence, for example to send someone to read the Bible. But a dream is never a word that binds the conscience, and it must always be tested by Scripture. If a dream moves you to obey Scripture, obey Scripture. If it moves you against it, or merely flatters you, put it down.

What it does not mean. Not that Joseph’s fear was faithlessness. God did not rebuke him; he confirmed his judgment and guided him. Fear can be a wise response to real danger, and God works through it.

Then how do I make a big decision without a dream? Use the means God has actually given. First, ask what Scripture commands or forbids, because many choices are settled there. Then pray, asking for wisdom, which God promises to give generously (James 1:5). Gather the facts, weigh them honestly, and notice your circumstances, as Joseph did when he heard who was ruling Judea. Seek the counsel of mature Christians who know you (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God to close doors if you are wrong. Between two good options, God does not leave you guessing at a hidden answer; you are free to choose, and he goes with you.

In a sentence. Fearing Herod’s brutal son, and guided by God, Joseph took the family to Galilee.

On a Tuesday. God often guides through ordinary prudence as well as through clear words. Use the wisdom he gives, and trust him to correct your course. He is equally sovereign in the ordinary as in the spectacular: in a news report about a new ruler, a conversation with a friend, a door that will not open.

For worship. Our God is sovereign over palaces and over the fears of a carpenter. He moved the emperor’s census, Herod’s death, Archelaus’s cruelty and Joseph’s anxious heart, and every one of them carried his Son to exactly the place the prophets had foretold. Nothing is outside his rule, not the brutality of kings nor the worries in the night. We have something steadier than dreams: the prophetic word, more fully confirmed (2 Peter 1:19), and the Shepherd who leads us by it.
verseByVerse.note: Archelaus, Herod’s son, ruled Judea so brutally that Rome removed him in AD 6. Galilee was ruled by his brother Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The family settled in Nazareth, a small and despised village in Galilee. Matthew sees in this the fulfilment of what the prophets had said, that the Messiah would be called a Nazarene: lowly, rejected, and yet the true Branch of David.

He went and lived in a city called Nazareth. Nazareth was a tiny village in the hills of lower Galilee, probably with a few hundred inhabitants. It is never mentioned in the Old Testament, in the Jewish historian Josephus, or in early rabbinic writings. When Nathanael heard that Jesus came from Nazareth, he asked whether anything good could come from there (John 1:46): the local verdict in seven words. Luke tells us that Joseph and Mary had lived there before (Luke 1:26; 2:39); Matthew focuses on God’s guidance there.

So that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled. Notice prophets, plural. Elsewhere Matthew names a specific prophet. Here he refers to a theme found in several prophets, not to one verse. No Old Testament verse says the Messiah will be called a Nazarene, and Matthew knows it. He names nobody and quotes no text; he is signalling that he is pointing at a theme running through the prophets rather than citing a line.

That he would be called a Nazarene. What did Matthew mean? There are three main suggestions, and they may work together.

The despised one. To be called a Nazarene was to be called a nobody from nowhere. Many prophets said the Messiah would be despised and rejected (Isaiah 53:3; Psalm 22:6–8). He had no form or majesty that we should look at him. Being from Nazareth fitted that pattern: the Messiah would be looked down on. Jesus was rejected before he preached a word. His address was scandal enough.

The Branch. The Hebrew word for branch is netser, which sounds like Nazareth. Isaiah 11:1 promises that a branch (netser) will grow from the stump of Jesse, David’s father: a new shoot from a fallen royal line. Other prophets also call the Messiah the Branch (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12, using a related word), which may be why Matthew says prophets in the plural. The village name echoes the messianic title: the Branch grew up in Branch-town. And note the image itself. A stump is what is left when a tree has been cut down. Isaiah describes David’s royal house reduced to a dead-looking stub, and a green shoot coming out of it. By Joseph’s day that was the literal situation: the heir to David’s throne was a carpenter in an occupied province.

A Nazirite. Some connect it with the Nazirite, a person set apart by a vow (Numbers 6), like Samson (Judges 13:5). But Jesus was not a Nazirite (he drank wine, 11:19), and the spelling is different, so this is less likely.

Which is right? Verdict: the first two together. Matthew uses a wordplay on the Branch (netser) to show that the despised village of Nazareth fits what the prophets said of the Messiah: a humble shoot from David’s line, despised by men.

What it does not mean. Not that Matthew invented a prophecy. He signals that he is summarising the prophets’ teaching, not quoting one text. And it does not mean that Jesus’ humble origin was an accident or embarrassment that had to be explained away. It was part of God’s plan: the King came in lowliness.

The name that stuck. Then the thing that makes this more than a puzzle. He is Jesus of Nazareth to the crowds, to the demons, to the blind man on the road. It is what Pilate had written over his head. It is how the angel identifies him at the empty tomb (Mark 16:6). It is what Peter preaches at Pentecost (Acts 2:22). And it is the name the risen and glorified Christ uses of himself, from heaven, to a man on the Damascus road: I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting (Acts 22:8). He was given a village that was a byword for insignificance, and he took its name and kept it. He could have dropped it at the resurrection. What he answers to instead, in glory, with the wounds still on him, is the name of the poor village nobody expected anything from.

What was Jesus doing in Nazareth all those years? Growing up, working and waiting. Luke tells us he grew in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:52), and the townspeople later called him the carpenter (Mark 6:3). For about thirty years the Son of God lived an ordinary life in a small village: learning a trade, keeping the Sabbath, obeying his parents, likely supporting his widowed mother. Those years were not wasted. He was fulfilling all righteousness as a true man, for us, in the ordinary duties where most of our lives are spent. Your hidden, ordinary days can be lived to God as well, because your Lord sanctified them first.

In a sentence. Jesus grew up in despised Nazareth, fulfilling the prophets’ picture of the Messiah as the humble Branch of David, scorned by men.

On a Tuesday. If you come from somewhere others look down on, so did your Lord. God’s greatest work often begins in places people dismiss. And if you have ever dismissed someone because of where they come from, their accent, their estate, their country, remember the question Nathanael asked, and the answer he got: come and see.

For worship. The Lord of glory chose the poorest address in Galilee and has never given it back. The stump of Jesse looked dead, and out of it grew the Branch who will fill the earth with the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea (Isaiah 11:9). He was despised so that despised people could be welcomed; he was called a nobody so that nobodies could be called the children of God. Jesus of Nazareth: the name of a slight, worn as a crown. Blessed be the King who came in lowliness and reigns for ever.
verseByVerse.note: No single prophecy says “he shall be called a Nazarene”; Matthew speaks of “the prophets” in general. Nazareth was a despised backwater, and the prophets foretold a despised Messiah.

parallels.desc: a branch from the stump of Jesse
“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

2.theology:
Typology and the Unity of Scripture. Matthew 2 demonstrates the Reformed doctrine of the unity of the two Testaments through typological fulfilment. When Matthew reads “Out of Egypt I called my son” as fulfilled in Jesus, he is not wresting Hosea from its context. He is reading with the grain of Scripture’s own logic: Israel was God’s son (Exod. 4:22), whose history was a pattern that pointed forward to the Son of God. The Old Testament is not a collection of proof texts waiting to be claimed; it is a single story moving toward a single climax.

Reformed biblical theology, developed through scholars like Geerhardus Vos and continued by Edmund Clowney, has called this “redemptive-historical” interpretation: reading every text in the light of its place in the one story of God’s redemptive purpose. Matthew 2 is a masterclass in this method. Every Old Testament quotation is not forced but organic — the story was always moving here, toward the child in Bethlehem, the flight to Egypt, the return to the land, the settlement in Galilee of the nations (Isa. 9:1–2).
2.examples:
Then: The Magi represent the first fruits of the Gentile mission that will be formally commissioned in Matthew 28. They come from outside the covenant, guided by general revelation (the star), and are brought to special revelation (the Scriptures) and to the King himself. This is the pattern of mission throughout Acts: Cornelius, the Ethiopian eunuch, the Philippian jailer — each guided by a mixture of seeking and sovereign orchestration to the one who is the answer to every longing.

Now: In our world, the contrast of chapter 2 repeats daily: people with no theological background travelling great distances (literally and metaphorically) to find Jesus, while those with full access to Scripture never move toward him. Church membership without worship, theological knowledge without seeking — this is Jerusalem troubled but not travelling. The question Matthew 2 poses is not “how much do you know?” but “are you moving toward the King?” The Magi found him because they went. That remains the condition of finding him today.

3.title: The Voice and the Voice
3.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, <sup>2</sup>“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>3</sup>For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” <sup>4</sup>Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey. <sup>5</sup>Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, <sup>6</sup>and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>7</sup>But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup>Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. <sup>9</sup>And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>10</sup>Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>11</sup>I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>12</sup>His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>13</sup>Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. <sup>14</sup>John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” <sup>15</sup>But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented. <sup>16</sup>And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; <sup>17</sup>and behold, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a chapter of two voices. The first voice is John’s: rough, wilderness-forged, prophetic, urgent. He wears the clothes of Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:8) and preaches with Elijah’s directness. Repent. The kingdom is not arriving on your terms. Your ancestry will not protect you. Bear fruit — now, because the axe is already laid to the root. John’s preaching is the sound of the law doing its proper work: exposing the bankruptcy of religious privilege and the urgency of genuine turning.

The second voice is the Father’s: tender, declarative, public. This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. It comes from heaven, over the Jordan, spoken in Matthew's account as a declaration to those watching: This is my beloved Son. The Father is not waiting to see how the ministry goes before rendering his verdict; he speaks it before the first sermon, before the first miracle, before the temptation is overcome. The approval is unconditional, grounded not in performance but in person and covenant.

Between the two voices stands the baptism — and the question it raises: why does the sinless one need a baptism of repentance? Jesus answers it: to fulfil all righteousness. He is not confessing sin; he is identifying with sinners. The one who needs no baptism submits to it on behalf of those who need it most. This is the logic of substitution, enacted in water before it is enacted in blood. The baptism of Jesus is the first act of the atonement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness preaching repentance, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a voice preparing the way. His ministry draws crowds from Jerusalem and all Judea, but he reserves his sharpest words for the Pharisees and Sadducees — those who came for baptism without repentance. Jesus then comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, and at his baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." The Trinity is present at the inauguration of the Son's public ministry. Several things the summary passes over, all treated in full below. Verse 4's clothing and diet are not a costume: camel's hair and a leather belt are Elijah's uniform (2 Kgs. 1:8), whose return was promised before the day of the LORD (Mal. 4:5); locusts were among the few insects the law permitted (Lev. 11:22) and wild honey is what the wilderness gives away, so John lives on what God provides and takes nothing from anybody — which is precisely why nobody can buy him. The Jordan itself matters: it is where Israel crossed into the land (Josh. 3), where Elijah was taken up (2 Kgs. 2), and where Naaman went down a leper and came up clean (2 Kgs. 5:14). Note the direction of travel — the crowds go out of the towns to the river, leaving the land the way their ancestors entered it and coming back in through the water. John is asking Israel to start again from the beginning. Verse 9 contains a pun English cannot show: in Aramaic, stones are abanim and children are banim — take away a letter and the rubble becomes the family of God — and he says it standing at the river where Joshua set up twelve stones from the riverbed as a memorial to the twelve tribes (Josh. 4:1-7). Verses 13-14: Nazareth to the Jordan is sixty to eighty miles, three or four days on foot; and behind that walk lie eighteen years of which Scripture says nothing at all, since Luke last showed him at twelve and now says he was about thirty. The Son of God spent roughly nine-tenths of his life on earth doing work nobody recorded — and that was not preparation for obedience, it was obedience. John's protest is an imperfect verb, "he kept trying to prevent him", and his theology in it is impeccable while his conclusion is wrong: right premises do not guarantee a right conclusion about what God will do next. Verse 15's "to fulfil all righteousness" is the answer and the hinge of the chapter — not personal repentance but substitution enacted in water before it is enacted in blood.
verseByVerse.theology: John's baptism is a baptism of repentance, anticipating the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. He is the last of the old-covenant prophets and the first herald of the new. His insistence on fruit worthy of repentance cuts against every form of religious privilege — ancestry, tradition, institutional membership. You cannot inherit faith; you must repent. Jesus's baptism is not a baptism of personal repentance (he has no sin) but an act of identification and consecration: he enters the waters of judgment on behalf of sinners and emerges declared righteous by the Father. The Spirit's descent and the Father's voice confirm him as the inaugurator of the new age.
verseByVerse.examples: John confronted the religious establishment with their false security: "Do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.'" The same temptation runs through every tradition — to substitute membership for repentance, heritage for faith, attendance for transformation. John's question to each worshiper is still the right one: is there fruit? Not feeling, not knowledge, not ancestry — fruit. The tree is known by what it produces.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About thirty years later, John the Baptist appeared in the desert of Judea with one urgent message: turn back to God, because God’s promised reign is about to arrive.

Meaning first. After nearly thirty years of silence, Matthew opens Jesus’ public story with John the Baptist, the first prophet in Israel for four centuries. John appears in the wilderness as the voice Isaiah promised, dressed like Elijah, calling the whole nation to repent because the kingdom of heaven has come near. He baptises crowds confessing their sins, warns the religious leaders that descent from Abraham will not save them, and announces one far mightier than himself, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and with fire, gathering his wheat and burning the chaff. Then that one arrives. Jesus, who has no sin, steps into the water to fulfil all righteousness for his people; the heavens open, the Spirit descends on him, and the Father declares him his beloved Son. The chapter that begins with a call to turn ends with the whole Trinity revealed, and with the One in whom the Father’s delight is given to sinners.

In those days. A loose time marker. Matthew jumps from Jesus’ childhood to the start of his ministry, about AD 27–29 (Luke 3:1–2, 23). Nearly thirty years pass in silence.

John the Baptist. “The Baptist” means the one who baptises. John was the son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, a relative of Mary, born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1). He was the first prophet in Israel for about four hundred years, since Malachi. His appearance meant that God was speaking again.

Came preaching. “Preaching” (kēryssō) means proclaiming like a herald, a royal messenger announcing the king’s decree in the town square. John is not offering ideas for discussion; he is announcing news from God.

In the wilderness of Judea. The dry, rocky land between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, falling steeply to the Jordan valley. In Israel’s history the wilderness was the place of new beginnings. Israel was formed there after the exodus; God met Moses and Elijah there; and the prophets promised that God would lead his people through the wilderness in a new exodus (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14). John’s location says: God is starting again.

Repent. Metanoeite: literally change your mind. John’s first word is not God loves you or you are enough, but a call to a complete turning of direction. In the Bible repentance is more than changing an opinion. It translates the Hebrew idea of turning (shuv): turning around, coming home to the LORD one has wandered from. The prophets had thundered it for centuries: return, O Israel, to the LORD your God (Hosea 14:1); rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:12–13). It includes a change of thinking (seeing sin as God sees it), a change of heart (sorrow for sin and hatred of it), and a change of direction (forsaking sin and turning to God in obedience). It is not merely feeling sorry, nor merely doing better, but a turning of the whole person.

For the kingdom of heaven is at hand. “The kingdom of heaven” means the kingdom of God. Matthew, writing for Jews, usually says heaven in place of God, following the Jewish habit of reverently avoiding God’s name. It is ordinary speech in the Bible: the prodigal comes home saying he has sinned against heaven (Luke 15:21), and he does not mean the sky; Daniel had said that Heaven rules (Daniel 4:26). It does not mean a place, heaven where people go when they die. A kingdom is a reign before it is a realm: “kingdom” here means rule, kingship, God exercising his royal power to save his people and to judge evil, as the prophets promised (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14; Isaiah 52:7). The Jews longed for it. “At hand” means it has come near, arriving now, in the person of the King who is about to appear. What is at hand is not a place opening up but a throne being occupied, here, on this earth, in a man about to walk down to this river.

Why repent? Because when the King comes, he comes to save and to judge. To be ready for his reign, people must turn from their rebellion and submit to him. The appropriate response to the arrival of the holy King is not first celebration but self-examination. Jesus will begin his ministry with exactly the same words (4:17).

What it does not mean. Not that repentance earns entry into the kingdom. Repentance is the turning of empty hands to God; the kingdom is his gift. It is the godly grief that produces a repentance that leads to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10), the homeward turn of a heart that grace has already begun to thaw. Nor is repentance a single moment only: the Christian life is a life of continual repentance. The first of Luther’s ninety-five theses (1517) says that when Jesus said Repent, he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance. And “kingdom of heaven” does not mean that God’s kingdom is only spiritual and future. It is God’s rule breaking into this world now, in Jesus, and it will be complete when he returns.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom. Dispensationalists distinguish the kingdom of heaven (an earthly, Jewish, millennial kingdom offered to Israel and postponed when Israel rejected it) from the kingdom of God. Those who hold this love the Scriptures and read them carefully. But most interpreters, including the Reformed tradition, hold that the two phrases mean the same thing. Matthew proves it himself: watching the rich young man walk away, Jesus says it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, and in the very next sentence, easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (19:23–24). Two consecutive verses, one subject, both names. The kingdom has come in Christ, grows now through the gospel, and will be consummated at his return (see more fully at 4:17). Verdict: one kingdom, already inaugurated and not yet consummated.

How do I know whether I have really repented? Not by the strength of your tears, but by the direction of your life. Ask: Do I now see this sin as God sees it, as an offence against him and not only a problem for me? Have I stopped excusing it and started fighting it? Have I brought it to Christ for forgiveness, trusting him rather than my own resolve? Has anything actually changed, even a little, in how I live? Real repentance often begins small and is imperfect; you will fall again. But it keeps turning back to God. If you are grieved by your sin and still running to Christ with it, that grief and that running are the Spirit’s work in you.

In a sentence. John announced that God’s promised reign was arriving, and called everyone to turn from sin to God to be ready for it.

On a Tuesday. Repentance is not only for the day you became a Christian. What do you need to turn from today? Our temptation is the old one in new dress: we lean on our churchgoing, our baptism, our decent name, our Christian family. None of that is the turning itself. Name one specific thing, bring it to God by name, and take one concrete step away from it before the day is out.

For worship. After four hundred years, God spoke again, and his first word was a summons home. That is grace, not harshness: a King who announces his coming in advance, so that rebels may lay down their arms and be received. The kingdom John proclaimed was not a programme but a Person, and he was already walking down from Galilee. We do not repent to make the King draw near. We repent because in Christ he already has, and his reign is the best news a ruined world has ever heard.
verseByVerse.note: The wilderness of Judea is the dry, barren land between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea. Matthew usually says “kingdom of heaven” where the others say “kingdom of God” — the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'" Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John was the voice Isaiah had promised, preparing the way for the Lord himself. His rough clothing and wilderness food marked him out as a prophet like Elijah.

For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah 40:3. Isaiah 40 begins the great section of comfort: God speaks tenderly to his people in exile, telling them their warfare is over and their sin is pardoned, and that he himself is coming to lead them home. Its promise is a new exodus: God coming in person to lead his people home across the desert, like a shepherd-king at the head of the march (Isaiah 40:10–11).

The voice of one crying in the wilderness. In Isaiah, a voice calls for a road to be prepared through the wilderness for God’s coming. John is that voice. He is not the main event; he is the announcer. He described himself in these words (John 1:23). By John’s day the verse had become a watchword of hope. The wilderness community at Qumran, beside the Dead Sea, took these very words and withdrew into the desert to prepare the way of the LORD, certain God was about to act. So when John appeared in that same wilderness crying Isaiah 40:3, every devout ear caught its weight: the King is coming, ready the road.

Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight. In the ancient world, before a king visited a region, workers would prepare the road: filling in potholes, levelling hills, straightening curves, so that the king’s procession could sweep through unhindered. Isaiah’s very next verse paints it: every valley lifted up, every mountain and hill made low, the rough places a plain (Isaiah 40:4). John’s preaching prepares the way by preparing hearts: repentance removes the obstacles. The proud hills of self-righteousness are brought low, the sunken valleys of despair filled with hope, the crooked dealings made straight.

Whom the road is for. The striking thing is whom the road is for. In Isaiah, “the Lord” is the LORD, Yahweh, God himself. Matthew applies it to Jesus. John prepares the way for Jesus, and in doing so prepares the way for God. It is a staggering identification: Jesus is the LORD come to his people.

Now John wore a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist. This is almost exactly how the Old Testament describes Elijah: a hairy man, with a belt of leather about his waist (2 Kings 1:8). John dressed as a prophet, and as the Elijah promised in Malachi 4:5–6, who would come before the great day of the Lord. Jesus confirms that John was that promised Elijah (11:14; 17:12–13). John is not wearing prophet’s clothes as a costume; he inhabits the prophetic calling with his whole life, refusing comfort and the establishment, living in the wilderness as a sign that the old order is passing.

And his food was locusts and wild honey. Locusts were permitted food under the law (Leviticus 11:22) and are still eaten by poor people in the region. Wild honey came from wild bees in the rocks. It was the diet of a man living off the land: simple, independent and austere. He lives on what God provides and takes nothing from anybody, which is precisely why no one can buy him. He was not part of the comfortable establishment of Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. Not that rough clothing or a strict diet makes someone more spiritual. Jesus later contrasted John’s austerity with his own eating and drinking, and said that both were rejected (11:18–19). John’s lifestyle fitted his particular calling as a prophet of repentance. Nor does it mean that John was literally Elijah returned from heaven: he denied that (John 1:21). He came in Elijah’s spirit and power (Luke 1:17).

How can I point people to Christ rather than to myself? Start by remembering what you are: a voice, not the Word. In conversation about faith, talk more about what Jesus has done than about your own experience or opinions, and open the Bible with people rather than only telling them what you think. Resist the pull to be seen as the wise one or the indispensable helper; John’s joy was to decrease so that Christ would increase (John 3:30). Invite people to come and hear Christ’s word preached, not only to come and hear you. And when you are thanked, pass the thanks upward. A signpost has done its job when people stop looking at it and walk on.

In a sentence. John was the herald Isaiah foretold, dressed like Elijah, preparing hearts for the coming of the Lord, who is Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Like John, every Christian is a voice, not the main event. Point people to Christ, not to yourself. And look for the road-work in your own heart: one proud hill to be brought low, one crooked dealing to be made straight. Repentance is simply how a sinner levels the ground for a holy King.

For worship. Isaiah saw the LORD himself coming to his ruined people in the desert, to carry the lambs in his arms and lead his flock home. And when the road was prepared and the herald had cried, the one who came walking down it was Jesus. The God of comfort did not send a message across the wilderness. He came himself. Every valley he fills, every mountain he lowers, every crooked thing he makes straight, until the glory of the LORD is revealed and all flesh sees it together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crowds from Jerusalem, all Judea and the Jordan valley went out to John, and he baptised them in the river Jordan as they confessed their sins.

Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him. A great movement. “All” is a natural exaggeration for very many. People walked a day or more into the wilderness. The Jewish historian Josephus also records John’s popularity. And notice the direction of travel. The people are not going to the temple. They are going out: out of Jerusalem, out of the towns, out to the wilderness and down to the river.

And they were baptized by him. To baptise (baptizō) means to dip, immerse or wash. Jews used ritual washings for purification, and Gentile converts to Judaism were washed as part of their conversion. John’s baptism was startling because he called Jews to be baptised, as if they needed to start again like outsiders. Being born a Jew was not enough. He is saying: you are no cleaner before God by birth than any Gentile.

In the river Jordan. The river where Israel had crossed into the promised land under Joshua (Joshua 3). The priests carrying the ark stepped in, the flow stopped upstream, and a nation walked over on dry ground into the inheritance. It is where Elijah struck the water with his cloak and was taken up (2 Kings 2:8–11), and where Naaman the Syrian went down a leper and came up clean (2 Kings 5:14). Entry, ascent and cleansing, all at the same muddy, unimpressive river. Coming through the Jordan again pictured a new entry into the land, a new beginning as God’s people. John was asking Israel to start again from the beginning, to go back outside, admit they had no more claim on the land than a Gentile convert, and come in again by grace.

Confessing their sins. Confession means agreeing with God about one’s sin, naming it openly. John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance (Mark 1:4; Acts 19:4). It did not take away sin by itself; it expressed repentance and pointed forward to the forgiveness the coming one would bring.

What did they confess? We are not left to guess, for John named some when the crowds asked him what they should do. To ordinary people: you keep two coats while your neighbour shivers (Luke 3:11). To the tax collectors: your greed and extortion (Luke 3:13). To the soldiers: your bullying, your false accusations, your discontent with your pay (Luke 3:14). Behind it all lay the sins the prophets had forever exposed: dishonest scales and withheld wages (Malachi 3:5), worship that was all lips and no heart (Isaiah 29:13), the quiet idolatry of loving money and reputation more than God. Their sins were not strange ancient relics. They were ours.

What it does not mean. Not that John’s baptism is the same as Christian baptism. Christian baptism is into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (28:19), and signifies union with Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4). Paul rebaptised disciples who had only received John’s baptism (Acts 19:1–5). Nor does confession mean that we must list every sin to a priest to be forgiven. Confession is made to God (1 John 1:9), and sometimes to those we have wronged or to fellow believers (James 5:16).

Should I confess my sins to another Christian? Not to obtain forgiveness, which comes from God alone through Christ (1 John 1:9). But often it is wise and healing. Confess to anyone you have wronged, and put it right where you can (5:23–24). And when a sin has a grip on you, telling a trusted, mature believer brings it into the light, breaks its secrecy and gives you someone to pray with and keep you accountable (James 5:16). Choose someone discreet and of the same sex for sexual matters. You do not need a priest; you need a brother or sister who will point you to Christ.

Should I be baptised now, if I was baptised as a baby? This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for those who have repented and believed, and is rightly given by immersion; so we believe a person baptised in infancy who has come to faith should be baptised as a believer. Many godly Christians, our paedobaptist brothers in Presbyterian and Anglican churches, hold sincerely that infant baptism is true baptism and should not be repeated, and we honour them. Talk it through with the elders of your church, study the passages (28:19; Acts 2:38–41; 8:36–38), and act with a clear conscience. The faith of the one baptised is what John’s riverside crowd teaches us to look for.

In a sentence. Crowds went out to John and were baptised in the Jordan as a sign of repentance, openly confessing their sins.

On a Tuesday. Is there sin you have not confessed to God by name? Name it today. Run John’s list down your own week: the coat you kept, the corner you cut, the person you bullied with words, the grumbling. Then confess it plainly, without excuses, and receive the forgiveness Christ has purchased.

For worship. The God who parted the Jordan for Israel to enter the land opened it again as a door of return for sinners. He does not ask us to climb up to him; he calls us down into the water, to start again with nothing in our hands. And the river that received the confessions of a nation would, in a few verses, receive the Son of God himself, who came not to confess his sins but to bear ours. Blessed be the God who makes a way home.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit in keeping with repentance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When John saw many of the religious leaders coming to watch or to be baptised, he denounced them as a nest of snakes and demanded proof of real repentance: a changed life.

Pharisees and Sadducees. The two leading religious parties, who normally opposed each other. The Pharisees (separated ones) were a lay movement, devoted to strict keeping of the law and of the oral traditions that interpreted it, the tradition of the elders, scrupulous about tithing, ritual purity and the Sabbath, and widely respected by ordinary people. They believed in the resurrection and in angels. They were undone by the very thing they prized, as their religion curdled into the self-righteous show Jesus would later lay bare (Matthew 23). The Sadducees were the wealthy priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple, cooperated with Rome, accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative, and denied the resurrection (22:23; Acts 23:8). When the temple fell in AD 70, they vanished with it. Here both groups come together. They will unite again against Jesus (16:1). Nothing unites enemies like a shared threat to their religion.

Coming to his baptism. Possibly to inspect it, possibly to be seen taking part. Luke 7:30 says the Pharisees rejected John’s baptism. Either way, John saw no sign of true repentance. A baptism received without repentance is just getting wet.

You brood of vipers! A brood is a family of offspring; vipers are poisonous snakes. In the desert, when a fire swept through the brush, snakes would flee in front of it. John pictures these leaders as snakes slithering away from the fire of judgment, not because they hate their sin, but because they fear the flames. It may also echo the serpent in Eden (Genesis 3): they are children of the deceiver (John 8:44), carrying poison under religious clothing. Jesus uses the same words of the Pharisees (12:34; 23:33).

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? “The wrath to come” is God’s coming judgment on sin at the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:1; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). It was not a new idea but one straight from their own Scriptures: a day of wrath, of distress and anguish (Zephaniah 1:15), the day that comes burning like an oven (Malachi 4:1), the day for which Malachi asked who could endure it (Malachi 3:2). Amos had warned that for the complacent it would be darkness and not light (Amos 5:18–20). But here lay the deadly assumption John meant to shatter: they took it for granted that this wrath was for Gentiles and sinners, and that they, as sons of Abraham, would stand safe among the spectators. John is asking sarcastically: what has suddenly made you, so confident in your righteousness, think you need to escape it? The fire is for every unrepentant heart, the religious ones first of all.

Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. Fruit is what a tree produces, the visible result of its life. A tree shows what it truly is by what hangs on its branches, not by its leaves. Repentance is invisible, in the heart; but real repentance shows itself in a changed life. Luke records examples: share your clothing and food with the poor; tax collectors, collect no more than you are authorised; soldiers, do not extort money (Luke 3:10–14). “In keeping with” means matching, worthy of, fitting. Paul would echo the phrase, calling people to perform deeds in keeping with their repentance (Acts 26:20). Do not show me your pedigree or your ceremonies, John says; show me a changed life.

What it does not mean. Not that the fruit earns forgiveness. Fruit does not make a tree good; it shows that the tree is good (7:17–18). Repentance and faith receive forgiveness as a gift; good works are the evidence that the repentance was real. And the branch bears fruit only by staying joined to the vine (John 15:5): the change John demands is one only the Coming One can work in a heart. Nor does John’s harshness license Christians to insult people. John spoke as a prophet with a unique role, and his anger was aimed at religious leaders who were misleading others, not at seekers or ordinary sinners, whom he received.

If I still struggle with the same sin, is my repentance fake? Not necessarily. Fruit grows slowly and unevenly, and every believer fights remaining sin to the end (Romans 7:15–25; 1 John 1:8). The question John presses is not whether you are perfect but whether you are a fruit-bearing tree at all: is there a real fight, a real grief, a direction of change? The man who has made peace with his sin and hides it behind religion is the viper John exposes. The man who hates his sin, confesses it again and again, and slowly sees a little ground taken back, is a tree with fruit on it, however small. Keep fighting, and keep coming to Christ.

In a sentence. John exposed religious leaders whose fear of judgment had produced no real repentance, and demanded a changed life as its proof.

On a Tuesday. What fruit in your life shows that your repentance is real? Not perfection, but a change of direction others can see. Ask someone who lives with you or works beside you whether they have noticed any change in you in the last year. The answer may humble you, or it may encourage you. Either way it is fruit-inspection, and John would approve.

For worship. The only shelter from the wrath to come is not ancestry but the Coming One himself, who would pass through the fire for his people. John cried that the wrath was near; Jesus walked into it, and it fell on him, so that all who flee to him find not flames but a refuge. He is the true Vine, and every fruit we bear is his life flowing in us. Glory to the Saviour who does not only demand fruit, but gives the life that bears it.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law; Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, who denied the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not presume to say to yourselves, "We have Abraham as our father," for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John warned them not to rely on being descendants of Abraham. God could make children of Abraham out of the desert stones. Judgment was imminent, like an axe already resting against the roots of a tree: every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and burned.

And do not presume to say to yourselves. Do not even think it, do not comfort yourselves with it.

We have Abraham as our father. Many Jews believed that being physically descended from Abraham guaranteed a place in God’s kingdom. Some rabbis taught that Abraham sat at the gate of Gehenna (hell) to turn back any Israelite. The appeal to descent from Abraham was the deepest form of Jewish religious security: covenant membership by birth. John says: your ancestry will not save you. Jesus makes the same point (John 8:33–44), and Paul explains that the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham’s faith (Romans 4:11–12; Galatians 3:7).

God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Probably a wordplay in Hebrew or Aramaic: children (banim) and stones (abanim). Take away a letter and the rubble at your feet becomes the family of God. It is a pun, and it is deadly serious. Pointing to the stones of the desert, John says: God does not need you. If he wishes, he can make Abraham’s children out of rocks. And notice where he is standing. When Israel first came into this land, Joshua had twelve men carry twelve stones up out of this very riverbed as a memorial for the twelve tribes (Joshua 4:1–7). John stands at that river, gestures at the stones, and tells the sons of Abraham that God could begin the twelve tribes again from the rocks. God has never been short of raw material: he made Adam from the ground and Abraham’s own heir from a dead womb (Romans 4:19). This anticipates the Gentiles, dead stones, being brought into Abraham’s family by faith (8:11).

Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. A woodcutter about to fell a tree first lays his axe against its base to measure the stroke. Judgment is not far off; it is about to fall. Israel was often pictured as God’s tree or vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 11:16). This is not a gentle warning but an imminent verdict.

Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. A tree that produces no fruit is useless and is cut down for firewood (Luke 13:6–9). Fire is a common biblical image of God’s judgment. The tree that produces no fruit is not warned again; it is cut down. Grace is real, but so is the axe.

Does verse 10 teach salvation by works? No. We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone; our works add nothing to the verdict (Ephesians 2:8–9). Yet the faith that justifies is never a faith that stays alone. A living faith bears fruit as surely as a living tree does; faith apart from works is dead (James 2:26). So John is not saying that fruit earns life; he is saying that fruitlessness exposes death. When Scripture speaks of judgment according to works (Romans 2:6), it means our works are the evidence brought into the court, not the price paid. We are saved by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. And even the fruit is grace, for God must first make the tree good. An axe never turned a dead tree into a living one; that making alive is the Coming One’s work.

What it does not mean. Not that God had rejected the Jewish people as a whole, or that being born into a believing family is worthless. Being in a godly family is a great privilege (Romans 3:1–2; 9:4–5). But privilege does not save. Each person must repent and believe. The same applies to people raised in Christian families or churches today: a Christian upbringing is a gift, not a guarantee.

Can I assume my children are Christians because they are growing up in a Christian home? Treat them as precious children under the sound of the gospel, with every privilege, and pray and hope for their salvation with great confidence in God’s faithfulness. But do not assume it on the basis of the family alone. Each child must come to Christ personally in repentance and faith. So teach them the gospel plainly, call them to trust Christ for themselves, rejoice at every sign of real faith, and never let them think that being your child, or attending church, makes them right with God. Many children of believers come to faith so early that they cannot remember a time without it. That is a great mercy, and it is still their own faith.

In a sentence. Religious ancestry cannot save anyone; judgment is imminent, and only a life of real repentance shows that a person is ready.

On a Tuesday. Are you relying on your Christian family, your church membership or your baptism, rather than on Christ himself? Those are gifts, but they are not faith. Finish this sentence honestly: I am right with God because… If the answer is anything other than Christ, John is speaking to you.

For worship. Bless the God who can make sons out of stones. We were stones: dead, hard, without a claim on Abraham or on heaven. And he who raised Isaac from a barren womb and Adam from the dust has raised us, by his Spirit, into the living family of faith. The axe lay at the root of every tree, and it fell on the one Tree that had borne nothing but good fruit, when Jesus was cut off from the land of the living for us. Now no child of God need fear the axe. He is the root, and we are grafted into him.

parallels.desc: every tree that does not bear good fruit

verseByVerse.quote: I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John contrasted his own ministry with that of the one coming after him. John washed people with water as a sign of repentance; the Coming One, far greater, would baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire, gathering his people like grain and burning the chaff in unquenchable fire.

I baptize you with water for repentance. John’s baptism was an outward sign of repentance. The water was a sign, no more: an outward washing that pictured the inward cleansing the people sought, and marked their turning from sin as they made ready for the King. Water can wash the body; it cannot change the heart. It pointed beyond itself to One who could. Ezekiel had long before joined the two: clean water sprinkled, and a new heart and a new Spirit given (Ezekiel 36:25–27).

He who is coming after me is mightier than I. “The coming one” was a title for the Messiah (11:3). John, the greatest prophet (11:11), says that the Messiah is far greater than he. He gives the sign; Jesus gives the substance. John can lower you into the river; only Jesus can baptise you in the Spirit.

Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. Carrying or untying a master’s sandals was a task given to the lowest slave. Some Jewish teachers said that a disciple should do anything for his teacher except handle his sandals, because that was too degrading. John says he is not worthy even of that task. John, the great prophet, knew his place.

He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. The prophets promised that in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on his people, giving them new hearts and new life (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28–29). The Messiah would do this. It happened at Pentecost, when the risen Jesus poured out the Spirit (Acts 1:5; 2:1–4, 33). To baptise with the Spirit is to immerse a person in the Spirit’s life: to bring them into the new covenant, regenerating, cleansing and indwelling them. Every believer receives this (1 Corinthians 12:13).

And fire. Fire in Scripture can mean purifying (Malachi 3:2–3; Isaiah 4:4) or judgment (vv. 10, 12). The context, with fire in verse 10 and verse 12, points to judgment, and one does not refine wheat with unquenchable fire. John speaks to a mixed crowd, and the one Messiah’s coming divides it in two. The Coming One brings a double baptism: the Spirit for those who repent, fire for those who do not. Some also see a purifying sense, fulfilled in the tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3). Verdict: chiefly judgment, though the Spirit’s work also purifies; the Messiah comes both to save and to judge.

His winnowing fork is in his hand. Picture an ancient threshing floor: a flat, hard patch of ground on a breezy hilltop. After harvest, grain was spread there and trodden to loosen the husks. Then a farmer used a winnowing fork, a large wooden pitchfork, to toss it into the wind. The heavy grain fell back to the floor; the light husks and straw, called chaff, blew to one side. Until he comes, wheat and chaff lie mingled on the one floor, and to the eye they look like a single heap: the truly repentant and the merely religious stand side by side in the crowd at the Jordan. But his coming is the wind that sorts them. And the fork is in his hand now: not a distant threat but a present summons (Psalm 1:4).

He will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn. The wheat, his true people, will be gathered and kept safe. What has real weight, a heart truly turned and a faith that bears fruit, falls safely to the floor and is gathered in.

But the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. The chaff was swept up and burned. “Unquenchable” means it cannot be put out: final, eternal judgment (Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:43–48). There is no third category between wheat and chaff: only two heaps and two destinations, the barn or the fire. John’s picture is sobering: the Messiah comes not only to bless but to separate.

What it does not mean. Not that the baptism with the Spirit is a second experience after conversion that only some Christians receive. Some Pentecostal traditions teach this, often with speaking in tongues as its sign, pointing to the disciples at Pentecost, the Samaritans (Acts 8:14–17) and the Ephesian disciples (Acts 19:1–7). But those episodes in Acts mark unrepeatable turning points as the gospel crossed from Jews to Samaritans to Gentiles, and Paul says all believers have been baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Verdict: Spirit baptism happens at conversion for every believer, though believers may be filled with the Spirit again and again (Ephesians 5:18). Nor does the warning of fire mean God delights in judgment. He is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). But the warning is real, and John speaks it because he wants people to escape.

How does John’s baptism relate to Christian baptism? John’s looked forward to the One who was coming; Christian baptism looks back to his death and resurrection and is given in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (28:19). That is why the disciples at Ephesus, who knew only John’s baptism, were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:3–5). Christian baptism rests on Jesus’ command, not on his own baptism, which was unique.

Where Christians differ: hell. Some evangelicals hold annihilationism: that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist, and that the fire is unquenchable but its victims are consumed. The traditional view holds that hell is conscious, eternal punishment (25:46; Revelation 14:11). Verdict: the traditional view. Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (25:46).

How can a loving God send people to unquenchable fire? Because his love is holy, and holy love is not indifferent to evil. A judge who shrugged at cruelty and murder would not be loving but corrupt. Sin is not a small slip against a small law; it is rebellion against an infinitely good God, and its punishment is just. But notice who is speaking these words: the herald of the Saviour. God warns before he judges, he gives his own Son to bear the fire for all who will come, and he pleads with sinners to turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). No one in hell will be there because God refused to receive them when they came. The fire is real so that the refuge would be precious.

How do I know whether I am wheat or chaff? Not by inspecting your own feelings, and not by comparing yourself with others, but by asking where you are resting. Chaff is not bad wheat; it is empty husk. The way to be found wheat is not to be impressive in oneself but to come to the Coming One in repentance and faith. If you have fled to Christ, trusting him and not yourself, and if your life is turning, however slowly, then you are his, and he gathers his wheat; he does not lose it (John 10:28). If you are not sure, come to him now. He has never yet sent away anyone who came.

In a sentence. The Coming One, far greater than John, will pour out the Spirit on those who repent and bring fiery judgment on those who do not.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is the Saviour who gives the Spirit, and the Judge who separates wheat from chaff. Do not take the first and ignore the second. Let the thought of the winnowing fork make you serious, and let the thought of the barn make you glad. Then speak to someone this week who is still standing in the crowd, looking religious and empty, as you once may have done.

For worship. Here is the wonder for all who are his: the reason the wheat need never dread the fire is that the Coming One would himself pass through it for them. He who holds the winnowing fork bore the judgment he will one day execute, so that every grain of his harvest would be gathered safe. And the one before whom John felt unfit to stoop is the one who stooped lower than any slave, knelt to wash his disciples’ feet, and poured out his own Spirit on sinners. Mighty to judge, mighty to save, and in both, mighty beyond all comparison.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back, the chaff blew away and was burned.

parallels.desc: tongues as of fire at Pentecost

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. John would have prevented him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus himself came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptised by John. John tried to stop him: he was the one who needed Jesus’ baptism, not the other way round.

Then Jesus came from Galilee. From Nazareth (2:23), about seventy miles (110 kilometres) north, the despised north, far from Jerusalem. This is Jesus’ first appearance as an adult in Matthew. He was about thirty years old (Luke 3:23). Most Galileans went the long way round through Perea to avoid Samaria: three or four days on foot, in sandals. He walked for the better part of a week to stand in a queue of sinners.

The hidden years. Matthew last showed him as a small child returning from Egypt; Luke gives us one incident at twelve. Between that and this river there are eighteen years about which Scripture says precisely nothing. Eighteen years in a workshop in a village of a few hundred people: no sermons, no miracles, no disciples, and no record. The Son of God spent most of his life on earth doing work that nobody thought worth writing down, and it was not wasted time or mere preparation for the real thing. It was obedience. Those years are part of the righteousness he is about to say he came to fulfil.

To the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. He came on purpose, for this. It is a surprise: John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance, with confession of sins. Why would the sinless Son of God (1:20–21) be baptised?

John would have prevented him. The verb is imperfect: he kept trying to stop him. This was not one polite demurral but a struggle at the water’s edge. John recognised who Jesus was. (In John’s Gospel, the Baptist says he did not know him until the Spirit descended, John 1:31–33. Perhaps John knew Jesus personally and sensed his holiness, while the sign of the Spirit confirmed that he was the Messiah. The two were relatives, but family acquaintance and messianic certainty are different things.)

I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me? John confesses his own sin and need. He has just said that the Coming One will baptise with the Spirit (v. 11); he himself needs that. Even the greatest prophet needs the Saviour. This is the man who has just called the religious leadership a brood of vipers. Of all the men on that riverbank he had least reason to think himself dirty, and he is the one who says out loud that he needs washing. The people most conscious of their own need are almost never the people you would nominate.

Right premises, wrong conclusion. John’s theology here is excellent and his conclusion is wrong. He has correctly identified who Jesus is, correctly understood what his own baptism means, correctly deduced that the sinless one does not need it, and on the strength of three correct premises he tries to stop the Son of God doing what he came to do. It is a useful warning for people who reason carefully about God. Right premises do not guarantee a right conclusion about what he should do next, because he is always working with more of the picture than we have. John’s mistake is the best kind of mistake, made for the best reasons, and Jesus corrects it in one sentence.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus came to confess his own sins. Scripture is clear that he had none (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). Verse 15 explains why he was baptised.

Do mature Christians still need Jesus as much as new believers do? More, if anything, and they know it better. John was the greatest man born of women, on Jesus’ own testimony (11:11), and his first instinct on meeting Jesus was to say: I need you. Growth in grace does not make us less dependent on Christ; it makes us more aware of how dependent we are. The longer a believer walks with him, the more clearly he sees his own sin and Christ’s sufficiency. If you find yourself feeling that you have outgrown the simple gospel, that is not maturity but drift. The mature saint’s prayer sounds very like the new convert’s: Lord, I need you.

In a sentence. Jesus came to be baptised by John, and John, knowing his own sin and Jesus’ greatness, tried to refuse.

On a Tuesday. John’s humility was the right response to Jesus: I need you. Can you say that to him today? Say it about the specific thing you have been trying to handle on your own.

For worship. The Lord of glory walked for days to stand in line with tax collectors and soldiers and the sinners of Judea. He did not wait on the bank for them to come up clean; he went down where they were. And before that, for thirty years he lived in obscurity, perfectly obedient in a carpenter’s shop, keeping every command no one would ever record, for us. The prophet tried to hold him back. Nothing could, because love had brought him to the water, and love would bring him to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered him, "Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." Then he consented. And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told John to go ahead, because it was right for them to fulfil all righteousness. So John baptised him. As Jesus came up from the water, heaven opened, and the Spirit of God came down on him like a dove.

Let it be so now. “Now”: for the present, at this stage of God’s plan. Jesus does not deny that he is greater than John; he asks John to accept this for now.

For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. The key sentence, found only in Matthew. “Righteousness” in Matthew means doing what God requires, living in line with his will (5:6, 20; 6:33). “Fulfil” is Matthew’s great word: Jesus fulfils the Scriptures and the law (5:17). He came not to bypass the law’s requirements but to meet them all on behalf of his people. Why is it right for Jesus to be baptised? Several truths fit together.

Identification. Jesus identifies himself with sinners. He stands with them in the water of repentance, though he has no sin of his own. This is the beginning of what the cross completes: he is numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12) and takes their place. He enters the waters as the representative of the people he came to save.

Obedience. John’s baptism was God’s command for Israel at that time (21:25). Jesus, as the true Israelite, obeys every command of God, so that his righteousness would be complete. Reformed theology calls this Christ’s active obedience: he kept the whole law perfectly on our behalf, so that his righteousness could be credited to us (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). It is not merely his dying in our place, but his living the life we owed and never lived, so that what is credited to a believer is not a blank record but a kept one.

Commissioning. His baptism marks the start of his public work as Messiah. As priests and kings were washed and anointed for their office (Exodus 29:4–7), Jesus is washed and anointed with the Spirit.

Then he consented. John obeyed.

And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water. Probably out of the river, after being immersed. The phrase fits immersion well, as does the word baptise itself, which means to dip or plunge, and immersion is the natural picture of a believer’s burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:4). Christians who baptise by pouring or sprinkling argue that the text describes where Jesus stood, not how the water was applied, and the phrase alone does not settle the debate. But Jesus’ baptism was unique, the anointing of the sinless Son, so it does not by itself settle who should be baptised; that rests on the command to baptise disciples (28:19).

And behold, the heavens were opened to him. Heaven opening was a sign that God was about to reveal something (Ezekiel 1:1; Acts 7:56). Isaiah had prayed that God would tear open the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Now he does. The silence between God and his people that had lasted since Malachi is broken.

He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him. The Spirit came visibly, in a form like a dove. The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), signalling a new creation; or the dove that brought Noah an olive leaf after the flood, a sign of new beginning and peace (Genesis 8:8–12). Isaiah had promised that the Spirit of the LORD would rest on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). Messiah means anointed one: here is his anointing, not with oil, but with the Spirit. And the Spirit comes to rest, to remain, not to come and go as he had with the prophets of old.

Was the Spirit not already with Jesus? Indeed he was, fully, from the very first. This child was conceived by the Holy Spirit (1:20); as the eternal Son he was never for one instant without the Spirit, never less than fully God, never touched by sin. Nothing changes in his person at the Jordan. What happens is two things at once. First, it is his anointing: the Spirit who always dwelt in him now equips the incarnate Son, in his true humanity, for the work that begins this day (Acts 10:38). Second, it is a sign for others: John tells us that the Spirit descending and remaining on him was the appointed sign by which he would know the Messiah (John 1:32–34). The dove was God’s own testimony, pointing out his Son.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus became the Son of God at his baptism. Some early heretics (called adoptionists) taught that Jesus was an ordinary man adopted as God’s Son at his baptism. But Matthew has already shown that he was conceived by the Spirit and is Immanuel, God with us (1:20–23). The baptism publicly declares and equips who he already was. Nor was the Spirit a literal dove: Matthew says like a dove.

Do I need to be baptised to follow Jesus? Yes, because he commands it, not simply because he set an example. His own baptism was unique: he was the sinless Son standing in for sinners. Ours is a sign of something he has done for us: our union with him in his death and resurrection, and our cleansing from sin (Romans 6:3–4; Acts 22:16). Baptism does not save; the thief on the cross was saved without it (Luke 23:43). But a believer who refuses it is disobeying his Lord’s clear command (28:19). If you have come to faith and have not been baptised, speak to your church’s elders this week.

In a sentence. Jesus was baptised to stand with sinners and fulfil every righteous requirement on their behalf, and he was anointed with the Spirit for his work as Messiah.

On a Tuesday. Jesus obeyed perfectly for you, including in things he did not personally need. His obedience is credited to everyone who trusts him. Rest in his righteousness, not yours. On the day you feel you have done nothing right, remember that your standing with God rests on a record Christ kept, every day of it, from the carpenter’s bench to the cross.

For worship. Behold the Lamb of God, standing waist-deep in the river of sinners’ confessions. He who had nothing to confess took his place among those who had everything to confess, and so began the exchange the cross would finish. And heaven could not stay shut. The Father tore it open, the Spirit came down to rest on him, and the Head was anointed so that the oil might run down to the whole body (Psalm 133:2). The Spirit who rests on him he now pours out on all who are his. All righteousness fulfilled: and all of it ours, by faith, in him.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records John’s protest and Jesus’ reply.

verseByVerse.quote: and behold, a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Father spoke from heaven: this is my beloved Son, in whom I delight. At the start of Jesus’ ministry, Father, Son and Spirit are all revealed together.

And behold, a voice from heaven said. God the Father speaks. Jews in Jesus’ time spoke of a daughter of the voice (bat qol), an echo of God’s voice, since prophecy had ceased. Here is not an echo but God’s own voice.

This is my beloved Son. Echoes Psalm 2:7, where God says to his anointed King, you are my Son. It declares Jesus as the royal Messiah, the Son of David (2 Samuel 7:14). But beloved Son also recalls Genesis 22:2, where God told Abraham to take his son, his only son, whom he loved, Isaac, and offer him as a sacrifice. The beloved Son will be offered. And it goes deeper still: Jesus is the Son of God not merely as a title of kingship, but by nature, the eternal Son (11:27).

With whom I am well pleased. Echoes Isaiah 42:1, about the Servant of the LORD: my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him. The Servant in Isaiah suffers and dies for the sins of the people (Isaiah 53). In one sentence, the Father declares Jesus to be both the royal Son of Psalm 2 and the suffering Servant of Isaiah: a King who will reign by suffering. “Well pleased” means delighted, entirely approving. Before Jesus has performed a single miracle or preached a single sermon in Matthew, the Father delights in him, after thirty years of hidden obedience. The Father’s delight is the fountain from which all of Jesus’ ministry flows: he acts out of a secure identity, not toward an uncertain approval.

The Trinity. Here the three persons of the Trinity appear together, each distinct: the Father speaking from heaven, the Son standing in the water, the Spirit descending. One God in three persons. The church has always seen this as one of the clearest pictures of the Trinity in Scripture. The same three names appear at the end of the Gospel in the baptismal command (28:19).

The voice everyone wants to hear. Is that word ever spoken over anyone else? Every human being alive is trying to hear it from somebody. We spend our lives auditioning: for a parent whose approval never quite arrived, for an employer, for a congregation, for an audience of strangers on a screen. And the ache underneath it all is the ache to hear a voice we trust say: you are mine, and I am pleased with you. Matthew has just recorded that sentence being said out loud over a man standing in a river. The question is whether it has anything to do with us.

For believers. It has everything to do with us, and the link is not imitation but union. Because believers are united to Christ, the Father’s love for his Son reaches them. Paul says we are blessed in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6), not accepted alongside him, or for trying to be like him, but in him, our life hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3). The Spirit of God’s Son is sent into our hearts so that we cry Abba, Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:16–17). In Christ, God says to every believer: you are my beloved child (1 John 3:1). This is the ground of our assurance, not our performance.

The great exchange. Watch how it works, because it began here in the water. At the Jordan the sinless one stepped into the place of sinners, taking a washing he did not need.
