At Golgotha he stepped into the place of sinners again, taking a judgment he did not deserve. He took what was ours: the guilt, the verdict, the abandonment, and on the cross the silence where a voice from heaven should have been. And what he gives in exchange is what was always his: the standing, the sonship, and the Father’s welcome. For our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).

What it does not mean. Not that there are three gods, or that one God appears in three different modes at different times (the error called modalism). Here all three persons are present at the same moment, distinct from one another, yet one God. And not that God approves of everyone exactly as they are and nothing more need be said. The same chapter has an axe at the root and a fire that is not quenched. The word is spoken over those who are in the Beloved, and there is a door to be walked through to get there: turn, and come.

Textual note. Matthew has This is my beloved Son, spoken about Jesus; Mark and Luke have You are my beloved Son, spoken to him (Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22). The Gospel writers often report speech by its sense rather than word for word, and both forms say the same thing. Matthew’s form stresses the public declaration to the witnesses.

How can one God be three persons? We cannot fully explain it, and should not expect to; God is greater than our minds. But we can say what Scripture says. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father is God, the Son is God (John 1:1), and the Holy Spirit is God (Acts 5:3–4). They are not three parts of God, nor three masks one God wears, but three persons who each fully possess the one divine nature, eternally loving one another. That is why God is love in himself, before there was a world to love (John 17:24). The Trinity is not a puzzle for clever people; it is the God the gospel reveals: the Father who sends, the Son who saves, the Spirit who gives life.

How can I believe God is pleased with me when I keep failing? Notice when the Father spoke: before a single sermon, before one miracle, before the cross. If the Father’s delight in his Son was not produced by performance, then the delight he has in those who are in his Son is not produced by yours either. You will not settle this by inspecting your feelings, but by looking away from yourself to the one you have come to. God is not pleased with your sin, and he will discipline you as a father does (Hebrews 12:6). But his verdict on you was announced in his Son, it was not earned, and it cannot be forfeited by a bad week. A father can be grieved by his child’s disobedience without ceasing to delight in his child.

In a sentence. The Father declared Jesus his beloved Son and delighted Servant, as the Spirit came on him: the whole Trinity revealed at the start of his ministry.

On a Tuesday. Before you face the day, its tasks and its judgments of you, remember whose verdict comes first. If you are in Christ, the most important thing anyone will say about you today has already been said, by the Father, in his Son. Work from that approval, not for it. And when someone near you is auditioning for love they never received, tell them where that voice can be heard.

For worship. Worship the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The heavens opened, and for one moment the eternal life of God was shown on earth: the Father delighting, the Son obeying, the Spirit resting in love between them. And if you are in Christ, hear the Father’s delight in his Son as spoken over you too. He is well pleased: not with your performance, but with his Son, and with you in him. The verdict on your life has already been announced, in public, by the only voice that finally matters. Glory to the Father, who loved us in his Beloved; to the Son, who took our place in the water and on the cross; and to the Spirit, who seals us as children of God.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights
the same voice at the transfiguration

3.theology:
The Trinity at the Jordan. Matthew 3:16–17 is one of the clearest Trinitarian texts in the New Testament. The Son stands in the water; the Spirit descends upon the Son; the Father speaks from heaven. Three distinct persons, one divine act. Reformed theology has always insisted that the doctrine of the Trinity is not a late addition to Christian thought but the grammar of the gospel itself — the structure of reality that makes salvation possible.

The baptism of Jesus is a Trinitarian event. The Father approves; the Spirit empowers; the Son obeys. This pattern runs through the whole New Testament: the Father sends, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies. The atonement is Trinitarian (the Father gave, the Son died, the Spirit regenerates); the church is Trinitarian (baptised in the name of Father, Son, and Spirit, Matt. 28:19); the Christian life is Trinitarian (praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit). The Jordan reveals the shape of everything that follows.
3.examples:
Then: John the Baptist stands in a long line of prophets who prepared the way for God’s action: Moses before Joshua, Elijah before Elisha, Isaiah before the return from exile. Each was a voice, not the Word; each pointed away from himself. John is the culmination of this pattern — the last and greatest of the preparers. His greatness lay precisely in his self-effacement: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Every faithful preacher, teacher, and leader stands in John’s tradition: making straight the way, getting out of the way.

Now: The Father’s declaration over Jesus at the baptism — This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased — is the word every human being is searching for. We spend our lives seeking approval: from parents, employers, social media, achievement. The gospel announces that in Christ, the deepest possible approval has already been given — not because of what we have done but because of who he is and what he has done. The restless search for significance ends not in achievement but in adoption: we are accepted in the Beloved. That is the word the Father spoke at the Jordan, and it is addressed to everyone who is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3).

4.title: The Tested King
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. <sup>2</sup>And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup>And the tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.” <sup>4</sup>But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” <sup>5</sup>Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple <sup>6</sup>and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>7</sup>Jesus said to him, “Again it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>8</sup>Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. <sup>9</sup>And he said to him, “All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.” <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>11</sup>Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him. <sup>12</sup>Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. <sup>13</sup>And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, <sup>14</sup>so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: <sup>15</sup>“The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles — <sup>16</sup>the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned.” <sup>17</sup>From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>18</sup>While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>19</sup>And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” <sup>20</sup>Immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. <sup>22</sup>Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. <sup>23</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. <sup>24</sup>So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them. <sup>25</sup>And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the axis on which the Gospel turns. The Spirit who descended at the baptism immediately drives Jesus into the wilderness — not as abandonment but as commission. The forty days echo Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, where God’s people failed at every test. Jesus succeeds at every one, and he does it using the same weapon available to Israel and to us: the written Word of God. Three times the devil attacks; three times Jesus answers with Deuteronomy. The true Israel passes where the nation failed.

Each temptation targets a specific aspect of Jesus’ identity and mission. Turn stones to bread: use divine power for personal comfort. Throw yourself from the temple: leverage God’s promises for public spectacle. Bow to me: gain the kingdoms without the cross. Every temptation is a shortcut past suffering to glory — and Jesus refuses every one. There is no crown without the cross, no glory without the grave, no kingdom without Calvary. Satan offers the destination without the path; Jesus insists on the path.

Then the ministry begins — in Galilee of the Gentiles (Isa. 9:1), the region of mixed ethnicity and questionable reputation, the last place a respectable rabbi would choose as his base. The people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light. The light does not go to the well-lit; it goes to the dark. And the first disciples he calls are working men with nets and boats — not scribes with scrolls. The kingdom of heaven is staffed from the margins, then and now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Temptation of Jesus in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. The forty days echo Israel's forty years in the wilderness; the three temptations echo Israel's great failures — bread, testing God, idolatry. But where Israel fell, Jesus stands. He defeats each temptation not by miraculous power but by the word of God alone, quoting Deuteronomy three times. The temptations are not trivial: they are the offer of the kingdom by a shortcut — bread without suffering, glory without the cross, dominion without death. And he overcomes not merely as our example but as our champion — the last Adam and true Israel, whose perfect obedience is reckoned to all who are his, so that we now resist temptation not to win God's favor but from within the victory he has already won for us. Two things the summary passes over. Verse 2's hunger is the ground of the first temptation — the devil does not waste his best offer on a man with full hands, and he waits for the sixth week. And verse 11 is not the end of the matter: Luke adds that the devil departed "until an opportune time" (Lk. 4:13), and Matthew shows where those times came. At Caesarea Philippi, when Peter says the suffering shall never happen, Jesus answers with the same words he used here — "Get behind me, Satan" (16:23) — because it is the same offer, the crown without the cross, arriving from a friend. And at Golgotha the passers-by shout "if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross" (27:40), which is the identical formula the devil used twice in this wilderness (vv. 3, 6). The temptation that opens the ministry is the temptation that closes it. Note also the quiet irony of the angels: the devil had proposed a scenario in which angels would catch him spectacularly before a temple crowd, and Jesus refused — so they come instead in an empty desert with nobody watching, and the verb is an imperfect (they kept ministering) of the ordinary word for waiting at table. What he would not seize, he was given.
verseByVerse.theology: The temptation of Jesus is not merely a test of personal willpower but a cosmic conflict at the hinge of redemptive history. The devil who succeeded in Eden now faces the second Adam in a wilderness, and loses. Jesus is revealed as the true Israel — obedient where the nation failed — and the true Adam — resisting the serpent where the first man did not. His weapon is the word of God alone: not angelic power, not divine fiat, but the Scripture he has internalized and believes. This models the Christian's resource in temptation: not mystical experience but the word of God believed and obeyed.
verseByVerse.examples: The devil's three temptations all contain a kernel of legitimate desire: food is not evil, protection is real, authority over the nations is Jesus's ultimate inheritance. The temptation is in the shortcut — get the good thing the wrong way, on the wrong timetable, from the wrong source. This is how temptation almost always works: it offers real goods through illegitimate means. Jesus refuses not because the ends are bad but because the path bypasses the Father's will and the cross's necessity.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after his baptism, the Spirit led Jesus into the desert to be tested by the devil. After forty days without food, he was hungry. Where Adam fell in a garden and Israel failed in the wilderness, Jesus, the true Son, would stand.

Meaning first. Matthew 4 shows the beloved Son proved in battle and then beginning his work. Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and faces the devil three times. Where Adam fell in a garden and Israel fell in the desert, he stands, answering every temptation with the word of God from Deuteronomy: he will not feed himself outside his Father’s will, he will not force God to prove his love, and he will not buy the kingdoms of the world with one act of false worship. The devil leaves; angels serve him. Then, when John is arrested, Jesus moves to Capernaum in despised Galilee, where Isaiah said the great light would dawn, and begins to preach that the kingdom of heaven has come. He calls four fishermen to follow him, and he goes through Galilee teaching, proclaiming the gospel and healing every disease, while crowds gather from the whole land. The King has won his first victory, and his kingdom has begun.

Then. Immediately after the Father declared him his beloved Son (3:17). The order matters: first the Father’s word of love, then the testing. Jesus faced the devil secure in the Father’s delight. And the devil’s first attack goes straight at that word: “If you are the Son of God” (v. 3).

Jesus was led up by the Spirit. The temptation was not an accident or a defeat. God the Spirit led Jesus into it, deliberately. The same Spirit who had just come upon him (3:16) now directs him, not away from God’s will but deeper into it. God’s purpose was to prove his Son faithful and to begin his victory over the devil. Notice that the wilderness was not a wrong turning. He did not wander there through carelessness or sin; he was led there, immediately after the best moment of his life, straight from the water and the voice and the open heaven. There is no rule that says the desert follows failure. Sometimes it follows blessing, and it is the appointed next thing.

Into the wilderness. The Judean desert, the barren land near the Jordan (see 3:1). Israel spent forty years in the wilderness after passing through the Red Sea (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). Jesus, having passed through the water of baptism, now goes into the wilderness. He relives Israel’s story (see 2:15).

To be tempted by the devil. “Tempt” (peirazō) means both to test and to tempt; one Greek word does the work for which English needs two. From God’s side, this was a test, to prove his Son’s faithfulness, as God tested Israel in the wilderness to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). From the devil’s side, it was a temptation, an attempt to make him sin. A test is designed to prove and strengthen what is there; a temptation is designed to break it. The same circumstance was aimed at one man from two directions. “Devil” (diabolos) means slanderer, accuser. He is a real, personal, fallen angel, the enemy of God and his people (John 8:44; Revelation 12:9). He tempted the first Adam in the garden and succeeded (Genesis 3). Now he tempts the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45).

After fasting forty days and forty nights. Forty is a significant number in Scripture: Moses fasted forty days and nights on the mountain when he received the law (Exodus 34:28); Elijah travelled forty days and nights to Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:8); Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33–34). Jesus’ fast connects him with Moses, Elijah and Israel: forty days for their forty years. Fasting means going without food for a spiritual purpose, to focus on God.

He was hungry. An understatement. After forty days a human body is near starvation. Jesus was truly human, with real hunger and real weakness. The devil attacked him at his weakest point. He is shrewd enough not to waste his best offer on someone who has everything; he waits for the moment of need.

The three temptations. The three temptations that follow correspond to three tests of Israel in the wilderness, and Jesus answers each with a verse from Deuteronomy 6–8, where Moses reminds Israel of those tests. Israel grumbled for bread, put God to the test, and worshipped idols. Jesus trusts, does not test God, and worships God alone. Where Israel failed, the true Son succeeds.

What it does not mean. Not that God tempts anyone to sin. James says that God tempts no one (James 1:13). God tested Jesus; the devil tempted him. The same event can be both: God’s purpose for good, the devil’s for evil (Genesis 50:20). Nor does it mean that being tempted is itself sinful. Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Temptation is the offer of sin; sin is accepting it. A believer who is fiercely tempted has not sinned by being tempted.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? Some say Jesus was able not to sin, but could have sinned, otherwise the temptations were not real. Most of the Reformed tradition holds that Jesus was not able to sin, because he was one person, the eternal Son of God, who cannot sin. Verdict: he could not sin, yet the temptations were entirely real. A strong army cannot be defeated, but the attack against it is still real; indeed, only one who does not give in feels the full weight of temptation to the end. The soldier who never surrenders is the one who knows the full force of the attack. Jesus knows the pressure of temptation more fully than anyone, which is why he can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

Does a hard season mean God is punishing me? Not necessarily. Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit, sinless, and straight after the Father’s word of love. If you are in a long dry stretch, prayers that seem to go nowhere, a season of loss or waiting with no visible end, take three things from these verses. It is not necessarily discipline; the Spirit sometimes leads his own into hard country on purpose. It has a limit: forty days, and Matthew tells you at the outset that it ended. And you are not alone in it, because the one who has been through this country walked out of it, and is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). The wilderness is where the enemy expects to finish you. In the hands of God it is very often where you are being made.

Should Christians fast today? Yes, as a voluntary help to prayer, not as a rule or a merit. Jesus assumes his disciples will fast (6:16–18; 9:15), and the early church fasted when seeking God’s guidance (Acts 13:2–3). Fasting is not a way to earn God’s favour or twist his arm; it is a way of saying with the body that we need God more than food. Start simply: skip one meal and use the time to pray. Anyone with a medical condition, an eating disorder, or who is pregnant should take advice and may fast from something other than food. Do it quietly, before your Father who sees in secret.

In a sentence. The Spirit led Jesus into the desert to be tempted, so that as the true Israel and the last Adam he would stand where they had fallen.

On a Tuesday. Temptation often comes right after a high point, and at your weakest moment. Expect it, and remember that facing temptation is not the same as sinning. Be most watchful when you are tired, hungry, lonely or just back from a spiritual high. Those are the hours the tempter chooses.

For worship. The Son went out into the desert alone, on our behalf, to meet the enemy who had ruined the human race. He went as the Father’s beloved and as our champion, led by the Spirit, weak with hunger, with no weapon but the word of God. The first Adam had a garden and fell; the true Israel had a wilderness and stood. Everything we lost in Eden he began to win back there, among the stones. Blessed be the Captain of our salvation, who went into the battle first and does not send us anywhere he has not been.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls Moses on the mountain and Israel’s forty years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: tempted as we are, yet without sin

verseByVerse.quote: And the tempter came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread." But he answered, "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil’s first temptation: if you are God’s Son, use your power to turn these stones into bread. Jesus answered from Scripture: people do not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from God. He would trust his Father rather than use his power for himself.

The tempter came. The devil is called the tempter: that is his work (1 Thessalonians 3:5).

If you are the Son of God. The grammar in Greek assumes that it is true: since you are the Son of God. The devil is not doubting it; he is twisting it. The Father had just said, This is my beloved Son (3:17). The devil says, in effect: if you are his Son, act like one. Use your rights. Look after yourself. Why should God’s beloved Son go hungry? It is a provocation: use your divine power for your own comfort, act as Son of God independently of the Father’s provision and timetable.

Command these stones to become loaves of bread. The desert was littered with stones the size and shape of small loaves. Was making bread wrong? Jesus later fed five thousand people (14:13–21). The poison is in the if: prove your sonship by serving yourself, snatch relief at my suggestion, step out from under your Father’s hand. The temptation was to use his divine power for his own benefit, outside his Father’s will, and to escape the path of humble dependence the Father had given him. It was a temptation to distrust: to doubt that the Father would provide, and to take matters into his own hands. Israel did the same in the wilderness, complaining that God had brought them out to starve (Exodus 16:3).

But he answered, It is written. Jesus answers with Scripture. “It is written” is a perfect tense in Greek: it stands written, and remains true and authoritative. Jesus, the Son of God, submits to the written word, and uses it as his weapon (Ephesians 6:17).

Man shall not live by bread alone. From Deuteronomy 8:3. Moses is on the plains of Moab, looking back over forty years, and explains why God led Israel the long, hard way: he humbled them, let them hunger, and fed them with manna, bread they had never seen and could not make, gathered fresh each morning in simple trust, so that they would learn that people do not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from God’s mouth. The whole aim was to wean them off the lie that life is secured by what we can provide for ourselves. Physical life depends on food, but true life depends on God’s word: his promises, his commands, his will. Bread keeps the body alive for a while; God’s word gives life now and for ever.

How we know it was a God-ordained hunger. No verse says the Father commanded him to stay hungry, but the reading is firm. The Spirit had led him here on purpose (v. 1), so the hunger was no accident of the road. There was nothing wrong with bread or with Jesus’ power; the wrong was in acting at the devil’s suggestion to prove himself. And Jesus tells us himself how he reads the moment by the text he reaches for: a verse about God deliberately letting his people hunger to teach them dependence. We are not imposing a guess on the scene; we are reading it as he read it.

But by every word that comes from the mouth of God. Jesus would rather be hungry and obedient than full and disobedient. He trusts that the Father who led him into the wilderness will sustain him. And he did: angels came and served him (v. 11). Jesus later said that his food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34). Where Israel said, in effect, give us bread or we perish, Jesus says: my life rests not on bread I can conjure but on every word from my Father’s mouth, including his word that I be here, and wait, and trust. He renders in obedience the very lesson Israel would not learn.

What it does not mean. Not that physical needs do not matter. Jesus teaches us to pray for daily bread (6:11), and he fed the hungry. The point is the order: God’s word and will come first, and we trust him for the rest (6:33). Nor does it mean that quoting Scripture is a magic formula. Jesus quoted it because he believed it and lived by it.

How do I actually use Scripture against temptation? Know your particular temptations, and prepare in advance a few verses that speak directly to them: for anxiety about money, 6:31–33; for lust, 5:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:18–20; for anger, James 1:19–20; for fear, Isaiah 41:10. Learn them by heart, because in the moment of temptation you will not have time to look them up. When the temptation comes, say the verse, aloud if you can, and turn it into a prayer. Then do what it says: walk away, close the screen, hold your tongue. Scripture is not a charm; it is the truth that exposes the lie, and the Spirit uses it to strengthen your will.

In a sentence. Jesus refused to use his power to satisfy his hunger outside God’s will, because true life comes from trusting and obeying God’s word.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to meet a real need in a wrong way, or a hurried way, instead of trusting God? The need for comfort, money, intimacy or rest is real; the shortcut is the sin. Answer the temptation with a specific word from Scripture, and then wait for the Father to provide in his way.

For worship. Adam was tempted in a garden where every tree was good, and fell; Israel was tested in the wilderness, and fell; Jesus, in a far harsher wilderness, starving and alone, was tempted, and prevailed. He is the last Adam and the true Israel, the obedient Son who keeps the covenant we all broke, and he keeps it as our representative. His victory is not merely admirable; it is counted to us, the spotless obedience that becomes our standing before God. We do not climb up to God’s acceptance by fighting temptation like Jesus. We fight temptation because in Jesus we are already accepted, and never once alone in the fight. He is the Bread of Life, who went hungry so that we might be fed for ever.

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, 'He will command his angels concerning you,' and 'On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.'" Jesus said to him, "Again it is written, 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Next, the devil took Jesus to the highest point of the temple and dared him to throw himself down, quoting a psalm that promises angels would catch him. Jesus answered with Scripture again: do not put the Lord your God to the test.

Then the devil took him to the holy city. Jerusalem, called the holy city because the temple was there (Nehemiah 11:1; Isaiah 52:1). Whether this happened physically or in a vision, the temptation was real.

How did it happen? Christians who take Scripture with equal seriousness have answered in three ways. Some hold it was bodily throughout: Scripture elsewhere records people carried from place to place (Acts 8:39; Ezekiel 8:3). Others hold that it was visionary, as prophets were shown what their eyes could not otherwise have seen. Others take it as a mixture: a real ascent to the temple, and a showing of the kingdoms no eye could take in from any mountain. Matthew does not tell us, and nothing hangs on it. A temptation presented to the imagination is not a lesser temptation; most of ours arrive that way, and they are quite strong enough to ruin a man. What Matthew wants us to know is that the devil came with real bait, and that the Son of God said no.

And set him on the pinnacle of the temple. The pinnacle (literally little wing) was probably the southeast corner of the temple courts, where the wall towered high above the Kidron Valley. The Jewish historian Josephus said that looking down from there made a person dizzy.

If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. Again the challenge to the Father’s word (3:17). The devil suggests: prove that God loves you. Force him to show his care. Perhaps also: give the crowds in the temple a spectacular sign, so that they will accept you without the cross. It would have been the ultimate public demonstration, faith demanding proof rather than faith resting in promise.

For it is written. Now the devil quotes Scripture too, imitating Jesus’ method. The devil knows the Bible and uses it. Knowing the text is not the same as submitting to its intent.

He will command his angels concerning you. From Psalm 91:11–12. The psalm promises God’s protection to those who trust him: he will send his angels to guard you, so that you will not even strike your foot against a stone. But the devil leaves out a phrase, to guard you in all your ways, meaning the paths of ordinary obedience. And he twists the meaning: the psalm promises protection for those who trust God in danger, not for those who deliberately throw themselves into danger to force God’s hand. It is a promise to the humble, not a licence for the presumptuous.

Jesus said to him, Again it is written. Jesus does not argue about the psalm. He answers Scripture with Scripture, showing that the Bible must be interpreted by the Bible. One verse must not be set against the rest.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. From Deuteronomy 6:16, which in full adds: as you tested him at Massah. At Massah, Israel, thirsty in the wilderness, instead of trusting the God who had just split the sea and rained down manna, turned on Moses and asked whether the LORD was among them or not (Exodus 17:1–7). Massah means testing, and it became a byword for the sin of cornering God (Psalm 95:8–9). To put God to the test is to demand that he prove himself on our terms, to create a crisis and dare him to act. It is not faith, but its opposite: it is refusing to trust God unless he gives a proof we have chosen.

The costume of faith. Notice the twist, for it teaches us much. Israel tested God out of open unbelief: is he even here? The devil dresses the same sin as its opposite, as daring faith: you trust your Father? Then prove it; leap, and let him catch you. Jesus sees through the costume. A faith that must have a spectacle to lean on is not faith but presumption; a trust that demands proof has already stopped trusting. The weak and starving Son trusts the promise without forcing the promise, the very thing Israel, with full bellies and water from the rock, would not do.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should never ask God for help or for guidance in danger. Faith trusts God when danger comes; presumption creates the danger and demands rescue. Nor is it wrong to quote Scripture: the problem is quoting it out of context to support what we already want. The devil can quote the Bible; we must read it whole.

But does God not invite us to test him, as in Malachi 3:10? He does, and that is the difference. Testing God is sin when we set the terms and demand proof of our own choosing; it is faith when we take God at his word where he himself has invited it. In Malachi he invites his people to bring their tithes and see whether he will not pour out blessing. That is trusting a promise, not manufacturing a crisis. Gideon’s fleece (Judges 6:36–40) was a concession to a fearful man, not a pattern for guidance.

Is it trusting God to stop taking my medicine? No. Picture a man who stops the treatment his doctor prescribed and announces he is trusting God to heal him, or who makes some rash, ruinous leap with his money and assumes God is bound to catch him. That is not the faith that rests in God; it is the presumption that dictates to him. God ordinarily works through means: food, sleep, doctors, medicine, wise planning. Using them is not a lack of faith but a way of receiving his care. Pray for healing and take the medicine. Trust God for provision and keep a budget. Real faith uses the means God provides and waits on him without demanding he prove his love on cue.

In a sentence. Jesus refused to force God to prove his love by a spectacular rescue, because true faith trusts God without testing him.

On a Tuesday. Are you taking foolish risks with your health, money or morals, and expecting God to rescue you? That is not faith but presumption. And when someone quotes a verse to justify sin, ask what the rest of the Bible says.

For worship. Where Israel failed the Massah test, and where we fail it still, the true Israel stood firm, and his unwavering trust is counted as ours. Rejoice: he passed the exam we keep failing. He would not throw himself from the temple to make angels catch him. Instead, in his Father’s hour, he would give himself to be lifted up on a cross, with twelve legions of angels at his call and not one summoned (26:53). He needed no spectacle to know the Father loved him. And now the One who walked that road perfectly lives in us and helps us walk it, our High Priest who sympathises with our weakness (Hebrews 4:15–16).
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall. The devil quotes Scripture but cuts it short.

parallels.desc: Israel tests the LORD at Massah

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." Then Jesus said to him, "Be gone, Satan! For it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their splendour, and offered them all to him in exchange for one act of worship. Jesus sent him away: worship the Lord your God and serve him only.

A very high mountain. Mountains in Matthew are places of revelation: the Sermon on the Mount (5:1), the transfiguration (17:1), and the Great Commission (28:16). This mountain is a counterfeit.

Showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. Probably a vision. Luke says it was in a moment of time (Luke 4:5). The wealth, power and splendour of every empire. The temptations escalate: from personal need (bread), to public recognition (the temple), to global dominion (all kingdoms). The devil moves toward what Jesus actually came to possess.

All these I will give you. The devil claims authority over the world’s kingdoms (Luke 4:6). Jesus calls him the ruler of this world (John 12:31), and John says the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). But his authority is borrowed and limited; it is not truly his to give. Jesus does not dispute the offer’s reality; he refuses its terms.

If you will fall down and worship me. The real offer: the crown without the cross. Jesus had come to receive all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18), but by way of suffering and death (Philippians 2:8–11). The devil offers a shortcut: power now, without the cross, global authority without Gethsemane, inheritance without suffering, if only Jesus will bow to him. It is the temptation to gain good ends by evil means, and to gain the world by compromising worship. The Father had already promised him the nations as his heritage (Psalm 2:8). The devil offers to sell him at a discount what was already his by promise.

Be gone, Satan! “Satan” is Hebrew for adversary. Jesus commands, and the devil must obey. It is the only point at which Jesus directly commands the tempter, and with a single word he binds the strong man. Later Jesus uses almost the same words to Peter when Peter tells him he must not go to the cross (16:23). The temptation to avoid the cross came again, through a friend.

For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve. From Deuteronomy 6:13, the command that follows the great confession, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). In the wilderness Israel made a golden calf and worshipped it (Exodus 32). Jesus worships God alone. The worship of God alone is not negotiable, not for any conceivable reward. He will receive the kingdoms, but from his Father, not from the devil, and by obedience, not compromise: through the cross, not around it.

The three temptations together. The first appealed to physical need, the second to spiritual pride, the third to power and ambition. John later describes the world’s temptations as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16). Eve saw that the fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desirable to make one wise (Genesis 3:6). Jesus faced the same kinds of temptation, and conquered.

What it does not mean. Not that power, wealth or influence are evil in themselves. Christ will reign over all kingdoms (Revelation 11:15). The question is how they are gained and whom they serve. Nor does Jesus’ victory mean we can conquer temptation in our own strength. We overcome in him: he was victorious for us, and we share his victory as we trust him and use the same weapon, God’s word.

The shortcut in ordinary clothes. This same temptation comes to us in a hundred ordinary disguises, and underneath it is always a question of worship: the prize you long for, offered at the price of a small bow to something other than God. The promotion is yours if you will fudge the figures. The relationship is yours if you will set aside what God says about it. The comfort, the security, the applause can be had if you will quietly serve money, or status, or self, and give God only your leftovers. Satan’s oldest trick is unchanged: he shows you the kingdoms and hides the bill.

Should I be afraid of the devil? Take him seriously, but do not fear him. He is real, cunning and hostile (1 Peter 5:8), and Christians should not be naive about him. But he is a creature, not God’s equal; he is limited, defeated at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and on a short chain. Here he must leave at one word from Jesus. Resist him, firm in your faith, and he will flee from you (James 4:7). Do not go looking for him in every misfortune, and do not dabble in anything occult. Keep close to Christ, use the armour God gives (Ephesians 6:10–18), and remember that he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

In a sentence. Jesus refused the devil’s offer of power without the cross, and worshipped God alone.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to take a shortcut to something good by compromising your loyalty to God: a promotion, a relationship, influence? The crown comes by the way of the cross; the disciple is not above his teacher (10:24). Name the shortcut you are being offered, and say your own be gone, not in raw willpower but as one joined to the Victor.

For worship. Lift your eyes and worship the Conqueror. The world had a rightful King who could not be bought. He chose Gethsemane over the easy throne and obedience over the bypass, and he won. By the long road of the cross and the empty tomb he could stand at last on another mountain and say that all authority in heaven and on earth had been given to him (28:18). He gained the very kingdoms Satan dangled, but gained them rightly, and gained them for us. In him we are more than conquerors (Romans 8:37), and every shortcut we turn down was only ever a path to a kingdom that crumbles.
verseByVerse.note: “Satan” means adversary.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Defeated, the devil left Jesus, and angels came and cared for him.

Then the devil left him. He had to: Jesus had commanded him to go (v. 10). Luke adds that he left until an opportune time (Luke 4:13). This is a withdrawal, not a surrender. The battle would continue throughout Jesus’ ministry, and reach its climax at the cross. But this first round was won.

The opportune times. Matthew shows us where they came. The first is at Caesarea Philippi, when Peter rebukes Jesus for speaking of his death, and Jesus says: get behind me, Satan (16:23), the same offer of the crown without the cross, this time out of the mouth of his closest friend. The second is at the cross itself, and it is the most exact. Twice in this wilderness the devil began: if you are the Son of God. And on the hill outside Jerusalem the passers-by say: if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross (27:40). The identical formula, the identical logic: prove it by rescuing yourself. The temptation that opened his ministry is the temptation that closes it. He refused it in the desert on an empty stomach, and he refused it on the cross with nails through his hands.

And behold, angels came and were ministering to him. “Ministering” (diakoneō) means serving, especially serving food (8:15). The verb is imperfect: they kept ministering. Jesus had refused to make bread for himself; now God provided for him. He had refused to call on angels to rescue him from a fall (v. 6); now angels came to serve him on God’s terms: quietly, in an empty wilderness, with no one watching, to a man too weak to stand. Elijah was fed by an angel in the wilderness (1 Kings 19:5–8). The Father did what Jesus trusted him to do. What he would not seize, he was given: not on the terms offered, not on the timetable suggested, and not in front of anybody, but given.

The victory. Adam, in a garden, with every tree but one available, gave in. Israel, fed with manna, grumbled and fell. Jesus, starving in a desert, stood firm. He is the true Son, the faithful Israel, the last Adam. His victory here is the beginning of his work for us. Because he resisted temptation perfectly, he is our perfect substitute and our sympathetic High Priest (Hebrews 2:18; 4:15–16).

What it does not mean. Not that believers will never feel the devil’s attacks after resisting once. The attacks return. But if we resist him, he will flee (James 4:7), and God will provide what we need.

Why does the same temptation keep coming back after I have resisted it? Because the devil does not give up after one defeat, as this verse shows; he waits for an opportune time. That is not a sign that your resistance failed, but that you are in a real war. Every time you resist, you grow stronger and the habit of obedience deepens. Notice when your opportune times come: when you are tired, alone, hurt, or bored. Plan for them. And when you fall, do not conclude that you have lost the war. Confess, receive forgiveness, and stand again. God promises that no temptation will be beyond what you can bear, and that he will always provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Do angels help Christians today? Scripture says they are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), so God does use them in caring for his people, usually unseen. But we are never told to pray to angels, seek contact with them or worship them (Colossians 2:18; Revelation 22:8–9). Our attention is to be on God, who commands them, and on Christ, who is far above them (Hebrews 1:4). You may take comfort that God has more help for you than you can see, and leave the details to him.

In a sentence. When Jesus had defeated the devil, God sent angels to care for him, providing what he had trusted the Father for.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted, run to Jesus. He has been there, he understands, and he can help you (Hebrews 2:18). And trust God to provide what you refused to grab. Think of one thing you have said no to for Christ’s sake. Ask the Father to provide for that need in his way, and watch for his answer.

For worship. Thank Christ that he stood where Adam fell, and that his victory is counted for you. The angels who had been offered as a stunt came instead as servants, laying a table in the wilderness for the King. Obedience is always vindicated, though rarely on our timetable. And the one they served that day is the one who will return with all his angels in glory (25:31), the conqueror of the tempter, the faithful Son, the Lord of hosts. The devil left him. The Father never did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — The Beginning of Ministry in Galilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After John's arrest, Jesus withdraws to Galilee and settles in Capernaum, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy about light dawning in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali. He begins preaching the same message as John — "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" — and immediately calls his first disciples: Peter, Andrew, James, and John. They leave their nets and their father without delay and follow him. Matthew concludes with a summary of Jesus's ministry: teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and affliction, drawing crowds from all of Syria and the surrounding regions. Three details more. The word for John's arrest (v. 12) is paradidomi, to be handed over — not the ordinary word for a legal arrest, but the very verb Matthew will use of Jesus again and again (17:22; 20:18; 26:2), and of what Judas, the council and Pilate each do. The forerunner goes before him in this too. And "he withdrew" is anachoreo, a favourite of Matthew's for keeping to a timetable his enemies are not setting (2:14, 22; 12:15; 14:13; 15:21) — never presented as cowardice. Capernaum has been excavated: a fishing village of perhaps 1,500 on the Via Maris, with a customs house (Matthew's own booth was there, 9:9) and a small garrison (hence the centurion of ch. 8). He based himself among tax collectors, soldiers, fishermen and foreigners passing through. And Zebulun and Naphtali were not chosen at random by Isaiah: they were the first tribes deported, carried off by Tiglath-Pileser in 733 BC (2 Kgs. 15:29), a decade before Samaria fell. They went into the dark first — which is exactly why Isaiah 9:1 promises the light dawns there first. God begins the repair at the place that broke earliest.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus's settlement in Galilee of the Gentiles fulfills Isaiah 9:1–2: the regions most despised in Israel — the northern territories given first to Assyrian darkness — receive the first light of the kingdom. This is the pattern of the kingdom: light to the edges, hope to the marginalized, the first shall be last and the last first. The calling of the disciples is not recruitment but sovereign summons: "Follow me" is a command, not an invitation to consider. Their immediate response models discipleship — not eventual obedience after weighing options, but the abandonment of everything for the one who calls.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples left their nets immediately. They left their boats. James and John left their father. The commentaries note what Matthew stresses: the immediacy and totality of their response. Jesus did not give them time to consult, calculate, or negotiate terms. He called; they followed. This is the New Testament pattern of conversion — not gradual warming to the idea of Jesus but the decisive moment of abandonment and allegiance. The question the passage presses: what are your nets? What would obedience cost you to leave behind?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard that John the Baptist had been arrested, he went back to Galilee. He left Nazareth and made his home in Capernaum, a town by the Sea of Galilee in the old tribal lands of Zebulun and Naphtali.

When he heard that John had been arrested. Literally handed over (paradidōmi), delivered up, given into someone’s power; it is not the ordinary word for a legal arrest. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, had imprisoned John because John condemned him for marrying his brother’s wife (14:3–4). John’s arrest marked the end of his ministry and the start of Jesus’ public ministry in Galilee. The word handed over is later used again and again of Jesus: the Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men (17:22), delivered up to be crucified (26:2). It is what Judas does, and the council, and Pilate. The forerunner goes before him in this too: John announced him, baptised him, and now is handed over, and the same verb will follow Jesus all the way to the cross.

He withdrew into Galilee. Not fleeing in fear, since Galilee was Herod’s territory too. Matthew uses withdrew (anachōreō) several times: of Joseph taking the child to Egypt (2:14) and turning aside to Galilee (2:22), and of Jesus moving away from opposition (12:15; 14:13). It is never presented as cowardice. It is a man whose hour has not yet come, keeping to a timetable that is not being set by his enemies. Each time, God’s plan moves forward.

And leaving Nazareth. His hometown, where he had grown up (2:23). Luke tells us that Nazareth rejected him, and even tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:16–30).

He went and lived in Capernaum by the sea. Capernaum was a prosperous fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, perhaps fifteen hundred people, on a major trade route, with a customs office (9:9) and a Roman garrison (8:5). It became the base of Jesus’ Galilean ministry, called his own city (9:1). Peter’s house was there (8:14). Archaeologists have found remains of its synagogue and of a house venerated from early times as Peter’s. That is where the Son of God based himself. Not Jerusalem, where the temple was; not even a large town. A working town on a trade road, with a customs post and a barracks, full of exactly the people the respectable would not have chosen: tax collectors, soldiers, fishermen and foreigners passing through. He made his home among the sort of people he intended to save.

In the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali. Two of the twelve tribes of Israel had been given these lands in Galilee (Joshua 19). They were among the first parts of Israel to be conquered and deported by Assyria, around 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29). After that, many Gentiles settled there, and the region was considered spiritually dark and mixed.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ move was merely practical or accidental. Matthew immediately shows it fulfilled Scripture (vv. 14–16). God placed his Son exactly where Isaiah said the light would dawn.

Why did God let John be arrested? Scripture does not give a full reason, and John himself later struggled with it in prison (11:2–3). But some things are clear. John’s work was done: he had prepared the way, and the one he announced had come. He decreased so that Christ might increase (John 3:30). His suffering for righteousness was not a sign of God’s absence; Jesus called him more than a prophet (11:9–11), and his faithfulness to death bore witness to the truth. And his being handed over pointed ahead to the greater handing over of Jesus, through which our salvation came. God does not always spare his best servants. He never wastes their suffering.

In a sentence. After John’s arrest, Jesus began his ministry from Capernaum in Galilee, in the lands that had first fallen into darkness.

On a Tuesday. God often moves his servants through events they did not choose, a closed door, an arrest, a rejection, to the places where he wants them. If you are somewhere you did not plan to be, ask not only how to get out, but whom God has placed around you there.

For worship. The Lord of glory chose a border town with a tax office and a barracks for his home. He did not set up his headquarters among the religious elite but among sinners and strangers, and he walked into the very region Assyria had first emptied. He is the Shepherd who goes where the sheep are lost. And as John was handed over, so would he be, willingly, for us: delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). Every handing over in this Gospel is moving toward that one.
verseByVerse.note: Zebulun and Naphtali were tribal territories in Galilee, among the first to fall to Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ move to Galilee fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy about the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, the region by the sea and across the Jordan, “Galilee of the Gentiles”.

So that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled. Isaiah 9:1–2. The context in Isaiah is important. Isaiah 8 ends with darkness and distress as Assyria invades. Isaiah 9 begins with hope: the lands that were first humbled will be the first made glorious. And then comes the great promise: for to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). Matthew is saying: the child of Isaiah 9 has come, and he has come first to the very region Isaiah named.

The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali. See verse 13. Zebulun and Naphtali were not chosen at random by the prophet. They were the tribes whose land lay furthest north, on the exposed frontier, and they were the first to be taken. When Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria came down, he carried off all the land of Naphtali and its people captive to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). They went into the dark first, a decade before Samaria fell and more than a century before Jerusalem.

First into the dark, first into the light. And that is the whole point of Isaiah’s sentence: in the former time God brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea (Isaiah 9:1). The reversal is deliberate and specific. The ground that was first into the darkness is the ground on which the light dawns first. Seven hundred years later, a man from Nazareth moves to that exact stretch of shoreline to begin. God’s habit is to begin the repair at the place that broke first.

The way of the sea. The ancient trade route that ran along the Sea of Galilee toward the Mediterranean coast and Damascus, the great highway from Egypt to the East. Galilee was a crossroads of nations. When God chose the spot to plant the light, he did not choose a hidden valley; he chose the roadside of the world, where the caravans of every people would see it.

Beyond the Jordan. The region east of the Jordan river, also once part of Israel.

Galilee of the Gentiles. Galilee of the nations. After the Assyrian conquest, Galilee had a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles. People in Jerusalem looked down on Galileans as half-pagan and unsophisticated, with a strong accent (26:73; John 7:52). This is the place the Messiah chose to begin. The kingdom begins at the edges of Jewish respectability and moves outward.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ ministry was mainly to Gentiles at this stage. He went first to the lost sheep of Israel (10:6; 15:24). But beginning in Galilee of the Gentiles was a sign of where the gospel was heading: to all nations (28:19).

What does Isaiah 9 tell us about who Jesus is? A great deal, because Matthew quotes the opening of a passage everyone knew continued. The light that dawns on Galilee is a child born and a son given, who will sit on David’s throne for ever, and whose names include Mighty God and Everlasting Father (Isaiah 9:6–7). The title Mighty God is used of the LORD himself in the very next chapter (Isaiah 10:21). So by pointing to this passage, Matthew is quietly saying again what he said with Immanuel (1:23): the one who walks along the shore of Galilee is God come to his people, and the Prince of Peace whose kingdom will have no end.

In a sentence. Jesus began his ministry in despised, mixed Galilee, exactly where Isaiah promised the Messiah’s light would first shine.

On a Tuesday. God’s light often reaches first the places and people others write off. Where is the Galilee near you that your church overlooks? And in your own life, the part that went wrong earliest, has been dark longest and would be nobody’s choice for a starting point, is the very place where God has a documented preference for starting. Bring that part to him first.

For worship. Who is like our God, who remembers the forgotten tribes seven hundred years after the world had stopped thinking of them? He let Zebulun and Naphtali go first into the dark, and he brought his Son to them first when the light came. He chose the highway of the nations to set his lamp on, so that every passer-by might see. And the child of Isaiah’s song walked along that road in sandals: Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end.
verseByVerse.note: “Galilee of the Gentiles”: the region had a mixed population, looked down on by Judeans.

verseByVerse.quote: "the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah’s prophecy continues: people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, light has dawned. In Jesus, that light has come.

The people dwelling in darkness. Darkness in Scripture pictures ignorance of God, sin, misery and death (Ephesians 4:18; 5:8). The people of Galilee lived in political darkness (conquered and occupied), spiritual darkness (far from the temple, mixed with pagans), and the darkness of sin that covers every human life. Darkness is not a mere metaphor for ignorance; it describes the human condition before God: estranged, condemned, without hope.

Have seen a great light. Light pictures God’s presence, truth, salvation and life (Psalm 27:1; John 8:12). The light is not a doctrine but a person: Jesus himself. The promise reaches its fulfilment not in a Jerusalem spectacle but in a Galilean teacher walking along a lakeshore.

The region and shadow of death. Literally the land and shadow of death, a phrase that echoes Psalm 23:4, the valley of the shadow of death. It describes deep darkness, where death’s power looms over life.

On them a light has dawned. Like the sunrise after a long night. The image is of sunrise: total, irreversible, making everything visible at once. Zechariah had sung of the sunrise from on high visiting those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace (Luke 1:78–79), and Malachi had promised that the sun of righteousness would rise with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:2). Light does not have to be earned; it simply comes, and darkness cannot stop it (John 1:5).

A light that saves. A lamp only shows you the room; this Light does what no lamp can. It does not merely expose the shadow of death; it breaks it. It warms the frozen and heals the wounded, and speaks life into the dead as God once spoke a world out of nothing. The God who said let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). When this Sun rises on a soul, the night does not merely become visible; it is over.

What it does not mean. Not that everyone who saw Jesus received the light. Many in Galilee, including Capernaum, rejected him (11:23). Light shining is not the same as eyes opened (John 3:19).

I still feel in the dark at times. Has the light really dawned on me? If you have trusted Christ, yes. The light is not your feeling but a Person, and he does not leave the souls he has entered (John 8:12; 10:28). Believers still pass through dark valleys: grief, depression, doubt, the hiding of God’s face for a season (Psalm 88; Isaiah 50:10). Isaiah’s counsel to the one who walks in darkness and has no light is to trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God. Feelings of darkness are real and should be brought honestly to God and to wise friends, and sometimes to a doctor. But the sunrise does not reverse. Christ’s light in you is held by his faithfulness, not by your sense of it.

In a sentence. In Jesus, the great light Isaiah promised dawned on people living in the darkness and shadow of death.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you know who is sitting in the shadow: bereaved, addicted, hopeless, far from God. Pray for them by name today, and look for one way to bring a little of Christ’s light near them, a visit, a meal, a word of hope, an invitation.

For worship. Thank God that the light has dawned on you, in Christ, and pray for those still sitting in the shadow. In Isaiah’s day the promised dawn was first the daybreak after the Assyrian night, real but partial. In Jesus the true Sun rose over a far deeper darkness, the night of sin and death itself, and not for Zebulun and Naphtali only but for the whole world. The dead man blinks, and breathes, and lives. That is what dawned on Galilee. That is what has dawned on every believer, and it will never set.

parallels.desc: “I am the light of the world”

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From then on, Jesus began to preach the same message John had preached: turn back to God, because the kingdom of heaven has come near.

From that time Jesus began. A turning point. Matthew uses this phrase twice to mark the two great sections of his Gospel: here, as Jesus begins his public ministry, and at 16:21, as he begins to tell his disciples that he must suffer and die.

To preach. To proclaim as a herald (see 3:1).

Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Word for word the message of John (3:2). But with a difference. John announced the coming King; Jesus is the King. In Jesus, the kingdom has arrived. His preaching, his healings and his casting out of demons are signs that God’s reign is breaking in: if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (12:28). The message has two parts: an announcement (the kingdom is here) and a command (repent). The announcement is good news, which is why Matthew calls it the gospel of the kingdom (v. 23). Mark adds, and believe in the gospel (Mark 1:15). Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning: turning from sin, and turning to God in trust. It is a command, and it is also a gift (Acts 11:18).

What the crowds hoped for. When an ordinary Jew heard the word kingdom, his heart leapt to a long-cherished hope: that God would at last act in power to throw off Rome, restore the throne of David, regather his scattered people, judge the wicked and reign in peace from Zion. It was a hope soaked in the prophets: your God reigns (Isaiah 52:7), the everlasting dominion given to the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13–14), the kingdom that shall never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44). But for most it was largely an earthly, national dream. Jesus takes up that ancient hope and both fulfils and transforms it. The kingdom he brings comes first not against Rome but against sin, Satan and death; not by the sword but by a cross; not in one blaze of glory but quietly, like a buried seed, before it fills the earth. It is deeper, wider and more glorious than they dreamed, and it asks not for revolution but for repentance.

Already and not yet. “At hand” means has drawn near, and it has been read as a kingdom soon to come, as one that has actually arrived, or, best, as both at once. In Christ’s first coming the kingdom has truly arrived, present now and advancing through the gospel, the Spirit and the church; it will be consummated in fullness only when the King returns.

Where Reformed and dispensational readers part company. Many dear brothers and sisters hold a dispensational understanding: Jesus offered Israel a literal, earthly, Davidic kingdom; when the nation’s leaders refused him it was postponed, the present church age came in as an interval, and the promised reign will be set up in a future thousand-year kingdom centred on Israel and Jerusalem. The Reformed reading, held in this commentary (see the verdict at 3:2), is that the kingdom was not postponed but inaugurated, that the one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, is the true Israel, and that the Old Testament promises of throne and land are fulfilled in Christ and at last in the new heavens and new earth. Christians also differ, with good arguments on several sides, about whether Scripture promises a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–27). We hold our reading clearly and humbly, remembering how much we share: Christ is King, his promises are sure, and he is coming again in glory.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ message was only moral reform: stop sinning and be good. It is first good news about what God is doing, and the call to repent is the response to that news. Nor does at hand mean that Jesus expected the end of the world within a few years and was mistaken. The kingdom came near in his person, and it continues to grow until its full arrival at his return (13:31–33).

If the kingdom has come, why is the world still so broken? Because the kingdom has come the way Jesus said it would: like a seed, like yeast, growing quietly before it fills everything (13:31–33). The King has won the decisive battle at the cross and resurrection, and he now reigns at the Father’s right hand (28:18). His rule is real in every heart he renews and every church that obeys him. But he has not yet returned to remove all evil, because he is patiently gathering his people from every nation (2 Peter 3:9). We live between D-Day and the final victory: the outcome is settled, and the fighting goes on. So we pray, your kingdom come (6:10), and we live now as citizens of the coming world.

In a sentence. Jesus began his ministry announcing that God’s kingdom had arrived in him, and calling people to turn to God.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is first news to believe, then a call to turn. Share both parts when you speak of Christ. If you only tell people to be better, you have left out the news; if you only tell them the news, you have left out the call. Jesus never separated them.

For worship. The King has come, and his first word was not a threat but an invitation dressed in a command: turn, for I am here. God’s reign, longed for by prophets and kings, broke into a Galilean afternoon in the voice of a carpenter, and it has never been pushed back since. Every heart that turns to him is a province of his kingdom reclaimed. And the day is coming when the kingdom of the world will become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ever and ever (Revelation 11:15).

verseByVerse.quote: While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers, Simon Peter and Andrew, fishing with a net. He called them to follow him, promising to make them fishers of people, and they left their nets at once and followed him.

The Sea of Galilee. A freshwater lake about thirteen miles (21 kilometres) long and eight (13 kilometres) wide, lying about seven hundred feet (210 metres) below sea level. It was full of fish, and fishing was a major industry. Fish were salted and exported across the region. The scene is deliberately ordinary: working men ankle-deep in fish and routine. The kingdom does not come through unusual people in unusual places; it breaks into the ordinary and calls it to something greater.

Simon (who is called Peter). Simon was his name; Jesus later gave him the name Peter, meaning rock (16:18; John 1:42). He would become the leader of the Twelve.

And Andrew his brother. Andrew had been a disciple of John the Baptist, and had first met Jesus at the Jordan and brought Peter to him (John 1:35–42). So this was not their first meeting with Jesus. They already knew him; now he calls them to leave everything and follow him permanently. Their obedience was costly, but it was not blind.

Casting a net into the sea. A casting net was circular, about fifteen to twenty feet across, weighted around the edge. The fisherman threw it over shallow water so that it spread out and sank over the fish.

Follow me. Literally come behind me. In Jesus’ time, students chose their rabbi and applied to study with him. Jesus reverses this: he chooses and calls his disciples (John 15:16). And he does not call them to follow a set of teachings or a law, but to follow him personally. Discipleship is attachment to a person. Follow me is the whole of the call: no exam, no conditions.

And I will make you fishers of men. “Men” means people. Jesus uses their trade as a picture of their new calling. As they had caught fish, they would now gather people into God’s kingdom. Notice I will make you: Jesus takes responsibility for training them. They do not need to be qualified; he will make them what he calls them to be. He does the making; they do the coming. And there is more in the phrase than warmth. In the prophets, to fish for men was to gather them for judgment (Jeremiah 16:16; Amos 4:2). Jesus turns that solemn image inside out. His fishermen will gather people not to drag them to judgment but to draw them out of it, hauling them up out of the waters of death into the safety of the kingdom. The old net of judgment becomes, in his hands, a rescue.

Immediately they left their nets and followed him. Their nets were their livelihood, their business, their security. They left them at once. Immediately is the word Matthew loves for true discipleship: not after I settle my affairs, but now. Following Jesus has a cost, and it comes first. A discipleship that costs nothing is not discipleship.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must leave their job to follow Christ. Peter and Andrew were called to be apostles, a special calling. Most believers follow Christ in their ordinary work (1 Corinthians 7:17–24). But every Christian must be willing to leave anything that stands in the way of following him (10:37–39), and every Christian is called to bring others to him.

What does following Jesus look like for me day to day? Following is less about which job you quit than about who now owns your life: Jesus as Lord of the very boat you are in, your work, your family, your ordinary week. In practice it means hearing his voice in his Word and obeying it; turning from sin and trusting him afresh each morning; loving him above all; taking up your cross daily (Luke 9:23), which is not bearing life’s random troubles but dying each day to self-rule for his sake; and abiding in him as a branch in the vine (John 15:5), for apart from him you can do nothing. The fruit grows from the union, not from your striving.

Am I following him well enough? Following is a direction, not a flawless performance. These first followers argued over greatness, slept when he needed them and scattered at his arrest; Peter denied him three times. Yet they were following still, and Jesus did not cast them off but restored Peter and made him a rock. If your heart is turned toward him, grieving sin, longing to obey and rising again after every fall, you are following, however stumbling it feels. Your standing rests not on the quality of your following but on the strength of the One you follow, who began a good work in you and will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Keep near him; he will keep you.

How can I be a fisher of people if I am shy or feel unqualified? Remember who does the making: I will make you. Jesus did not choose these men for their eloquence. Begin where you are, with the people already around you. Pray regularly by name for two or three who do not know Christ. Be a real friend to them. Be honest, when the moment comes, that you belong to Jesus and why. Invite them to read a Gospel with you or come to church. Andrew’s first act of fishing was simply to bring his brother to Jesus (John 1:41–42). Many of the best fishers of people are quiet. Faithfulness matters more than flair.

In a sentence. Jesus called fishermen to leave their nets and follow him, promising to make them gatherers of people for God’s kingdom.

On a Tuesday. What are your nets, the things you rely on for security? Hold them loosely enough that you could leave them if Christ asked. And ask him to make you a fisher of people where you are.

For worship. The Lord of the sea walked along its shore and called fishermen by name, and they came. That is the sovereign grace of the King: he chooses, he calls, and he makes. He did not wait for qualified men; he made fishermen into apostles, and through their nets he has drawn in a multitude no one can number. The voice that said follow me on the beach of Galilee still calls, and still makes nobodies into rescuers. Blessed be the Fisher of men, who has drawn us out of the deep.
verseByVerse.note: A casting net was a round net thrown by hand into shallow water.

parallels.desc: Luke’s account of the call by the lake
Andrew and Simon first meet Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Further along, Jesus called two more brothers, James and John, who were mending nets in their father Zebedee’s boat. They left both the boat and their father at once and followed him.

James the son of Zebedee and John his brother. Together with Peter, they became the inner circle of the Twelve, present at the transfiguration (17:1) and in Gethsemane (26:37). Jesus nicknamed them Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17). James was the first apostle to be martyred (Acts 12:2). John wrote the Gospel of John, three letters and Revelation, and lived longest.

In the boat with Zebedee their father. Zebedee ran a fishing business with hired servants (Mark 1:20), so the family was reasonably prosperous. Their mother may have been Salome, possibly the sister of Jesus’ mother Mary (27:56; John 19:25), which would make them Jesus’ cousins.

Mending their nets. Repairing torn nets after a night’s fishing. The word (katartizō) means to put right, restore to working order, make fit for use. It is the same word Paul uses for equipping the saints (Ephesians 4:12) and for restoring a brother caught in sin (Galatians 6:1), and it is what Hebrews prays God will do for us: equip you with everything good that you may do his will (Hebrews 13:21). They were making torn things fit for use when he called them to do it to people for the rest of their lives. Jesus would mend them for a new work.

And he called them. Jesus’ call is personal and authoritative.

Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. They left not only their livelihood but their family ties. In that culture, a son working in his father’s business was expected to carry it on. Leaving was a serious break. Jesus later says that loyalty to him must come before family (10:37), and that those who leave houses or family for his sake will receive a hundredfold and eternal life (19:29). The kingdom does not abolish family; it reorders it.

What it does not mean. Not that they abandoned their father callously: Zebedee had hired servants. And not that following Christ means despising family. Jesus commanded honour for parents (15:4–6). But when family and Christ pull in different directions, Christ comes first.

Christ first, for the family’s good. Here is a sweeter truth, easily missed: though Christ must come before family, in the end he comes for the family’s good as well. The son who loves Jesus first becomes a truer son; love rooted in God loves rightly, not clutching the other as an idol but receiving them as a gift. Often the Lord uses the one who follows him to draw the rest home: Zebedee’s own wife would later follow Jesus all the way to the cross (27:56), and the gospel would sweep through whole households (Acts 16:31).

One call, two roads. Two brothers: same boat, same father, same trade, called on the same morning by the same voice. James was the first of the Twelve to be killed: Herod Agrippa killed him with the sword (Acts 12:2), one sentence, no details, around AD 44. John, by every account we have, was the last of them to die, exiled to Patmos and writing in Ephesus as an old man, more than fifty years after his brother was executed. And decades later, when Peter looked at John and asked what about this man, the answer he got was: what is that to you? You follow me (John 21:22). The call is identical; the road never is. Comparing your road with another Christian’s is a question the Lord has already declined to answer.

What if my family opposes my following Christ? It is painful, and Jesus warned it would happen to some (10:34–36).
