Keep honouring your parents and loving your family in every way that does not require disobeying Christ: be kind, respectful, helpful and patient, so that any offence they take is at Christ and not at you (1 Peter 2:12; 3:1–2). Do not argue them into the kingdom; pray for them faithfully and live the gospel in front of them. Where you must say no, say it gently and firmly. Find a church family who will stand with you (Mark 10:29–30). And keep the door open. Many who opposed a believing son or daughter have later followed the same Lord.

In a sentence. James and John left their boat and father at once to follow Jesus, putting his call before work and family.

On a Tuesday. Is there a family expectation that is holding you back from wholehearted obedience to Christ? Honour your family, but follow him first. And stop measuring your road against a brother’s or a friend’s. He told you to follow him, not to follow them.

For worship. The same voice that called the brothers from their boat set one on a road of fourteen years and the other on a road of seventy, and both were the gift of his love. He is Lord of the length of our days and the shape of our roads. He mended fishermen for his purposes, and he mends us still, torn and tangled as we are, until we are fit for his use. And he promised that no one who leaves house or brothers or father for his sake will fail to receive a hundredfold, and eternal life. He is a better Father than any boat could hold.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus travelled throughout Galilee, teaching in the synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every kind of disease. His fame spread far beyond Galilee, and people brought him all kinds of sick and suffering people, and he healed them.

He went throughout all Galilee. Galilee had many towns and villages; the historian Josephus counted over two hundred. Jesus’ ministry was itinerant: he travelled on foot, from town to town.

Teaching in their synagogues. A synagogue (gathering place) was a local Jewish meeting house for prayer, the reading and explaining of Scripture, and community life. Synagogues developed during the exile. On the Sabbath, any qualified man could be invited to read and teach (Luke 4:16–21; Acts 13:15). Jesus used the synagogues, as Paul later did.

And proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom. “Gospel” (euangelion) means good news, an announcement of victory or of a new king. The good news is that God’s kingdom has come in Jesus (v. 17).

And healing every disease and every affliction among the people. Teaching, preaching and healing: the three parts of Jesus’ ministry (repeated in 9:35). These are not separate departments of his work: teaching illuminates, proclamation announces, healing demonstrates. The healings were not side-shows. They were signs of the kingdom: when God’s reign arrives, sickness, demons and death are driven back. They were, first, the King’s credentials. Isaiah had promised that in the days of salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened and the lame would leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:5–6), and when John later asked whether Jesus was the one, Jesus pointed to exactly these works (11:4–5). Second, they were a window into a deeper healing. Sickness is one of the bitter fruits of the fall, and in mending bodies Jesus showed what he had come to do for the whole person: with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). And third, they were a preview of the new creation, where there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4).

So his fame spread throughout all Syria. Syria was the large Roman province to the north, which included Galilee and Judea administratively. The news spread among Gentiles too. The kingdom could not be contained within Israel’s borders; the nations were already coming.

All the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains. Matthew lists them: the sick; those oppressed by demons; those having seizures (literally moonstruck, as people believed the moon caused epilepsy); and paralytics. Matthew distinguishes demon-possession from illness, listing them side by side. Not every illness is demonic, and this is not an ancient way of describing illness. Open demonic activity clusters around Christ’s coming, as the powers of darkness resisted the arrival of the kingdom.

And he healed them. All of them. Jesus had authority over every kind of disease and every kind of evil power.

What it does not mean. Not that God always heals today when Christians pray, or that sickness shows a lack of faith. Jesus’ healings were signs of the arrival of the kingdom and confirmed his identity (11:2–5). Christians should pray for healing, and God sometimes heals (James 5:14–15). But full healing awaits the resurrection. Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20), and Paul’s own thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

Where Christians differ: healing today. Some (continuationists, especially Pentecostals) hold that the gift of healing continues as it did in the apostolic church. Cessationists hold that the miraculous sign-gifts given to confirm the apostles’ message ceased with the apostles, though God still heals in answer to prayer. Verdict: cessationist, held charitably. God still heals when and as he wills, but no one today has the authority to heal at will, and healing is not promised to every believer in this life. We should be wary of any who guarantee it.

Healing delayed, not denied. And here is the deeper comfort. These healings were the firstfruits of a coming world, the future breaking into the present. Every blind eye Jesus opened in Galilee was a crack of that dawn. The believer’s healing is therefore never finally denied, only for a while delayed, and the empty tomb has made it certain. The King who healed the sick of Syria will one day heal the whole creation, and close the last grave for ever.

Should I go to the doctor, or just pray? Both. Medicine is one of God’s good gifts, and using it is not a lack of faith; Luke was a physician (Colossians 4:14), and Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). Pray for healing, ask the elders of your church to pray for you (James 5:14), and follow sound medical advice. Then leave the outcome with God, trusting that he is good whether he heals now or later. Be cautious of anyone who tells you to stop treatment or who blames your illness on weak faith.

Should Christians be afraid of demons? No. Demons are real, and Christians face real spiritual opposition (Ephesians 6:12). But they are defeated foes, and believers belong to the one who drove them out with a word. A Christian indwelt by the Holy Spirit cannot be owned by the devil (1 John 5:18). Stay away from occult practices, resist temptation, keep close to Christ in his Word, prayer and his church, and do not be preoccupied with the devil. Most of our spiritual battle is with ordinary temptation and the lies that come with it, and Christ is enough for all of it.

In a sentence. Jesus taught, announced the good news of the kingdom and healed every disease, showing that God’s reign had arrived.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cared for bodies as well as souls. Visit someone who is sick this week, and pray for them. Take a meal, sit with them, and if they are a believer, remind them that their healing is certain, even if it is delayed.

For worship. Behold the King at work: no sickness he could not cure, no demon he could not command, no sufferer too far gone for his touch. He healed them all, and every healing was a promise. He is the Lord who heals (Exodus 15:26), the Great Physician of body and soul, who carried our diseases to the cross (8:17) and rose to make all things new. A day is coming when there will be no hospitals, no wheelchairs and no graves in his kingdom, and every one of his people will be whole.
verseByVerse.note: Syria was the Roman province to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Huge crowds followed Jesus from every direction: from Galilee, the Greek cities of the Decapolis, Jerusalem and Judea, and the region across the Jordan.

Great crowds followed him. “Followed” here means physically going after him, not necessarily becoming disciples. It is the same word used of the disciples, though the crowds will prove less committed. Crowds come and go in Matthew; they welcome Jesus at his entry to Jerusalem (21:9) and call for his death a few days later (27:20–23). Not everyone who follows the crowd follows Christ.

From Galilee. The north.

And the Decapolis. Greek for ten cities: a league of Greek-speaking cities, mostly east of the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan, with mainly Gentile populations (Mark 5:20; 7:31).

And from Jerusalem and Judea. The south, the religious heartland.

And from beyond the Jordan. The region east of the river, called Perea.

The whole land. The list covers almost the whole territory of ancient Israel, Jewish and Gentile areas alike. Jesus is gathering a new Israel around himself. This sets the scene for the Sermon on the Mount, which he preaches to his disciples with the crowds listening (5:1; 7:28).

What it does not mean. Not that popularity proves faithfulness, or that large crowds mean God’s blessing. Jesus often withdrew from crowds, and many who followed turned back (John 6:66).

Which crowd am I in? It is worth asking plainly, because the two look identical from the outside. Both are near Jesus. Both are enthusiastic. Both would have said, that afternoon in Galilee, that they were following him, and Matthew uses the same word for both. The difference is not intensity of feeling; it is what happens when following costs something. The crowd came for what Jesus gave and went home with it. The disciples came for Jesus and left the boats behind. So ask whether he has ever cost you anything you did not want to give: an ambition set down, money given, a relationship ended, a habit surrendered, a reputation risked. If the honest answer is nothing whatever, sit with that rather than explaining it away. It is possible to enjoy Jesus enormously and never once have obeyed him.

And if that question makes me anxious? Do not read it as a demand to prove yourself. It was he who said I will make you; the making is his work and the coming is ours. If you find yourself uneasy at the question, that unease is itself a good sign: the crowds were not troubled by it at all. The remedy is not to whip up more commitment but to go back to the shoreline where the call was issued and answer it again today, in whatever the next costly thing turns out to be.

In a sentence. Crowds from every region, Jewish and Gentile, came after Jesus, a sign of the new people he was gathering.

On a Tuesday. Are you following Jesus because others are, or because you have heard his call? The crowd is not the same as discipleship. Name the next costly step of obedience in front of you, and take it this week.

For worship. From every corner of the land they came, Jew and Gentile, sick and curious, drawn to him like iron to a magnet. And he did not send them away; he sat down on the mountain and opened his mouth to teach them (5:1–2). That is our King: the one the nations gather to, who does not drive off the crowd but speaks to it, and calls out of it a people of his own. One day the crowd around him will be a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne, and all of them will be disciples (Revelation 7:9).
verseByVerse.note: The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

4.theology:
Active Obedience and the Imputed Righteousness of Christ. The temptation narrative is crucial to the Reformed doctrine of imputed righteousness. Jesus does not merely die for our sins (removing the guilt of our disobedience); he also lives in perfect obedience (providing the positive righteousness that we lack). This is called his active obedience — the life of perfect faithfulness to the Father from baptism to cross.

At each point of testing in the wilderness, Jesus does what Adam failed to do in the garden and what Israel failed to do in the desert: he trusts God’s word over his own need, refuses to demand signs, and worships God alone. This perfect obedience is credited to everyone who trusts in him. We are justified not only by the forgiveness of our sins through his death but by the clothing of his righteousness through his life. The temptation narrative is the biography of our justification — the record of the obedience that is now ours by faith.
4.examples:
Then: Israel’s forty years in the wilderness is the extended backstory of Jesus’ forty days. Every test Jesus faces has a corresponding failure in Israel’s wilderness narrative: bread (the manna crisis, Exod. 16), testing God (Massah, Exod. 17), worship (the golden calf, Exod. 32). Jesus passes where Israel failed, using the very Scriptures that Israel was given at Sinai. He is the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who finally does what the nation was always called to do.

Now: Every temptation we face follows one of Satan’s three patterns: use what you have for immediate gratification (stones to bread), demand that God prove himself (test the promise), or compromise your worship for immediate reward (kingdoms without the cross). Jesus’ answers are our weapons too: It is written. The Scripture that armed the Son of God in his temptation is the same Scripture available to every believer in theirs. The difference between victory and defeat in temptation is often simply whether we know the word well enough to wield it in the moment.

5.title: The New Law from the Mountain
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. <sup>2</sup>And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: <sup>3</sup>“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>4</sup>“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. <sup>5</sup>“Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. <sup>6</sup>“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. <sup>7</sup>“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. <sup>8</sup>“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. <sup>9</sup>“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. <sup>10</sup>“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>11</sup>“Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. <sup>12</sup>Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. <sup>13</sup>“You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people’s feet. <sup>14</sup>“You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. <sup>15</sup>Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. <sup>16</sup>In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven. <sup>17</sup>“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. <sup>18</sup>For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. <sup>19</sup>Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. <sup>20</sup>For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. <sup>21</sup>“You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ <sup>22</sup>But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be liable to the hell of fire. <sup>23</sup>So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, <sup>24</sup>leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. <sup>25</sup>Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. <sup>26</sup>Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny. <sup>27</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ <sup>28</sup>But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart. <sup>29</sup>If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. <sup>30</sup>And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell. <sup>31</sup>“It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’ <sup>32</sup>But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. <sup>33</sup>“Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn.’ <sup>34</sup>But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, <sup>35</sup>or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. <sup>36</sup>And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. <sup>37</sup>Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’; anything more than this comes from evil. <sup>38</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ <sup>39</sup>But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. <sup>40</sup>And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. <sup>41</sup>And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. <sup>42</sup>Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you. <sup>43</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ <sup>44</sup>But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, <sup>45</sup>so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. <sup>46</sup>For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? <sup>47</sup>And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? <sup>48</sup>You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
5.overview:
Jesus goes up on a mountain to teach — and every Jewish reader of Matthew’s Gospel would have heard the echo: Moses went up on Sinai. But this is not a repetition; it is a surpassing. Moses received the law and gave it; Jesus gives the law with his own authority: But I say to you. No prophet ever spoke like this. The prophets said “thus says the LORD”; Jesus says “I say.” He does not claim to relay a message from God; he speaks as God.

The Beatitudes are the charter of the kingdom — and they invert every human expectation of what blessed looks like. Poor in spirit, not rich in confidence. Mourning, not celebrating. Meek, not powerful. Persecuted, not applauded. The kingdom of heaven belongs to people the world dismisses. This is not a programme for self-improvement; it is a description of those who have been broken of self-sufficiency and have learned to receive everything from God’s hand. The Beatitudes describe Jesus perfectly — and they describe every person who has been conformed to his image.

The antitheses (“You have heard… but I say”) press the law deeper than the scribal tradition imagined. It is not enough not to murder; the anger that murders in the heart is already culpable. Not enough not to commit adultery; the lust that adultery in the imagination is already a violation. The law reaches inward. And this inward reach is not only a demand; it is a diagnosis. No one can meet the standard of verse 48 — “be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect” — by their own effort. The Sermon on the Mount is the X-ray that shows us the fracture and sends us to the only Physician who can heal it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Beatitudes and the Call to Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes up the mountain — deliberately evoking Sinai, where Moses received the law — and sits to teach, the posture of a Jewish rabbi. His first words are the Beatitudes: nine declarations of blessedness that systematically invert the world's value system. The poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the hungry — these are not character traits to develop but descriptions of those who know their need before God. The section closes with the salt and light metaphors: disciples are to be world-preserving and world-illuminating, not by withdrawal but by visible, costly presence. Two structural things govern this whole section and are set out at length in the verse-by-verse. First, "blessed" is not a wish. Makarios is a flat declaration about how things stand, not a hope that things go well — and it does not mean "happy" in the modern sense, since half the people described are mourning, starving or being driven out. It is the word the Psalter opens with (Ps. 1:1). Second, the eight are one argument, sealed at both ends. Verse 3 and verse 10 share the same six words — "theirs is the kingdom of heaven" — and the bracket is in the tense as well as the wording: v. 3 is present, vv. 4-9 are all future (shall be comforted, shall inherit, shall be satisfied, shall receive mercy, shall see God, shall be called), and v. 10 returns to the present. Present, six futures, present. And the order is not random: the first four describe a person's need (bankrupt, grieving, unassertive, starving) and the second four describe what comes out of a person met in that need (merciful, single-hearted, peacemaking, and consequently hated). Nobody arrives at the second four by trying; they are what the first four turn into. Individual notes: "poor" is ptochos, a beggar who crouches, not penes the working poor; "mourn" is pentheo, the word for grieving the dead; Moses is Scripture's own definition of meekness (Num. 12:3), which settles that it cannot mean timidity; "satisfied" is chortazo, the animal-feeding word, fed until you stop; verse 8 answers the temple question of Psalm 24:3-4 and then promises more than David dared write; and "peacemakers" is eirenopoios, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament, where the making is the point — peacekeeping arranges for a difficulty not to be mentioned, which is very often the opposite of this.
verseByVerse.theology: The Beatitudes are not a moral ladder to climb but a portrait of kingdom citizens in their native condition. They describe the same person from different angles: the one who is poor in spirit mourns their sin, is meek before God, hungers for righteousness, shows mercy, is pure in heart, makes peace, and bears persecution gladly. This is not nine different types of Christian but one Christian seen fully. Crucially, the blessings are not rewards for achieving these qualities; they are the condition of those who have already received the kingdom. Grace precedes the beatitudes; they describe those who know it. And before they are a portrait of the Christian, they are a portrait of Christ: he alone was perfectly poor in spirit, mourning over sin, meek, hungering for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, the peacemaker, the persecuted — he kept every blessing flawlessly, and that whole beatitude-life is reckoned to all who are united to him. This is the lens that keeps the Beatitudes from crushing the believer. We do not read them to measure ourselves and despair; we read them resting in the One who fulfilled them for us and who is now, by his Spirit, slowly forming them in us. So the struggler need not flee: the very ache of falling short — the grief over sin, the hunger to be made clean — is itself the first Beatitudes already at work, the early evidence of grace rather than the proof of its absence. Here law and gospel meet: the Beatitudes show us a righteousness we cannot produce, and then point us to the Christ who both gives it freely and grows it within.
verseByVerse.examples: Salt in the ancient world was a preservative — it slowed decay. Light is simply visible; it cannot be hidden without ceasing to be light. Jesus calls his disciples both: agents of preservation in a decaying world, and bearers of visible testimony that draws glory to the Father. Neither metaphor allows for invisible, privatized Christianity. The Christian life is inherently public — not in the sense of performance (that will be condemned in ch. 6) but in the sense of witness. The question is not whether your life will be seen, but what people will see when they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain, sat down as a teacher, and began to teach his disciples. This is the Sermon on the Mount: the King describing the life of his kingdom, as Moses once brought God’s law from a mountain.

Meaning first. Matthew 5 opens the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus sits down on a hillside in Galilee and tells his disciples, with the crowds listening, what the people of God’s kingdom are like. First come the Beatitudes (vv. 3–12): eight pronouncements of blessing over people the world would pity, the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the hungry, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and the persecuted. Then he tells them what they are to the world: salt and light (vv. 13–16). Then he says that he has come not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them, and that the righteousness of his people must go deeper than that of the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 17–20). Six times he takes a commandment as it was commonly taught and presses it to the heart: anger, lust, divorce, oaths, revenge, and love for enemies (vv. 21–48). The chapter ends with the Father himself as the standard. Every line of it is grace before it is demand, because it begins by blessing the bankrupt, and every line of it is first a portrait of the one who preached it.

The Sermon on the Mount. Matthew 5–7 is the first of five great blocks of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew (5–7; 10; 13; 18; 24–25), each ending with words like “when Jesus finished these sayings” (7:28). Some see a deliberate echo of the five books of Moses. The sermon describes what life looks like under God’s reign: the character (5:3–12), influence (5:13–16), righteousness (5:17–48), devotion (6:1–18), trust (6:19–34), relationships (7:1–12), and the call to decide (7:13–27) of those who belong to the kingdom.

Seeing the crowds. The crowds of 4:25, gathered from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan, many of them carrying the sick they wanted healed. Jesus teaches his disciples with the crowds listening at the edge (7:28–29).

He went up on the mountain. Probably a hillside near Capernaum; tradition places it on a slope above the northern shore of the lake. Matthew’s readers would think of Moses going up Mount Sinai to receive God’s law (Exodus 19–20). But Jesus is greater than Moses. Moses received the law from God; Jesus speaks with his own authority: “But I say to you” (vv. 22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44). The crowds were astonished that he taught as one who had authority, not as their scribes (7:29).

A new mountain. Moses went up a mountain wrapped in fire and smoke, and the people were told to keep back on pain of death; he came down with the law written on stone. Now a Galilean carpenter goes up a grassy slope, sits down, and his disciples come close. Matthew has arranged the scene so that nobody could miss what is being claimed. At Sinai the voice of God made the people beg that it stop. On this hill the same God speaks with a human voice, in the open air, to fishermen, and they are invited near. The law that thundered from a distance is now opened from the inside by the one who gave it.

And when he sat down. Jewish teachers sat to teach; listeners stood or sat at their feet (Luke 4:20). Jesus takes the position of an authoritative rabbi. It is the posture of a man about to say something with authority, not the posture of a man who is tired.

His disciples came to him. “Disciple” (mathētēs) means learner, student, apprentice. The sermon is addressed first to disciples: it describes the life of those who already follow Jesus, not a way to become his follower. These are men who have already left their nets (4:18–22). The crowds are present and will still be there at the end (7:28), but what follows is not a list of entry requirements. It is a description of what the kingdom does to people once they are inside it.

He opened his mouth and taught them. A solemn Hebrew way of introducing important speech (Job 3:1; Acts 8:35).

Not a ladder but a portrait. Before we climb into the Beatitudes one by one, take this to heart, or they will crush rather than bless. They are not eight entrance exams you must pass to earn God’s favour. Every one of the “qualifications” is a disqualification in the world’s eyes: poor, mourning, hungry, persecuted. This is grace from the first word, a blessing pronounced not over the strong and accomplished but over the empty-handed. The Beatitudes are not a ladder you climb up to God. They are a portrait of the people God has already stooped down to bless.

The face of the Saviour. And they are, before they are anything else, a portrait of Jesus himself. He was the truly poor in spirit, who said he could do nothing of himself (John 5:19). He mourned over sin and wept over Jerusalem. He was meek and lowly in heart. He hungered and thirsted for righteousness until it was his food to do his Father’s will (John 4:34). He was merciful to lepers and tax collectors, pure in heart without a single mixed motive, the peacemaker who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and the persecuted one whom the world hated first (John 15:18). He lived every line that you and I cannot keep, and his flawless life is credited to all who are his. So read the Beatitudes first as the face of your Saviour, and then as what his Spirit is slowly making you.

What it does not mean. Not a set of rules by which people can earn God’s favour. The sermon begins with grace: blessed are the poor in spirit (v. 3), those who have nothing to offer. It describes the fruit of being in the kingdom, not the price of entry. Nor is it an impossible ideal meant only to show us our sin, or a code only for a future millennial kingdom, as some have taught. It does show us our sin and drive us to Christ, but it is also the real pattern for Christian living now, lived by the Spirit’s power.

Where Christians differ: who is the sermon for? Some traditional Lutherans stress that it is chiefly law, showing our inability. Some Anabaptists and pacifists take it as a literal code for Christians, ruling out oaths, military service and courts. Classic dispensationalists applied it chiefly to the future kingdom. Verdict: it is Christ’s teaching for his disciples now: it humbles us, drives us to grace, and then shapes the life of those who have received grace. Its sayings must be read as Jesus meant them, sometimes as vivid pictures, in the light of the rest of Scripture.

Is this the same sermon as Luke’s Sermon on the Plain? Very probably the same occasion, or at least the same body of teaching. Luke 6:17–49 has Jesus come down and stand on a level place, and gives a shorter version with four blessings and four woes. A level place on a hillside is no contradiction. Matthew, who loves to gather Jesus’ teaching into large blocks, may also have included sayings Jesus gave at other times, and a travelling preacher certainly repeated his teaching in many villages. Either way, the words are the Lord’s, and each evangelist has recorded them faithfully for his own readers.

What if I do not recognise myself in the Beatitudes? If “pure in heart” stings because you are still battling your thoughts, do not despair. That sting is poverty of spirit. That grief is the mourning. That ache to be clean is the hunger for righteousness. The first Beatitudes are already at work in you. The struggler who keeps running to Christ is not shut out of these blessings; he is the very person they describe. “Blessed are” is God’s word spoken over you now, in Christ, even while he is conforming you to the picture across a lifetime, a work finished only on the day you see him face to face (1 John 3:2).

In a sentence. On the mountain, Jesus, greater than Moses, taught his disciples the life of God’s kingdom with his own authority.

On a Tuesday. Read Matthew 5–7 through in one sitting this week. It takes about fifteen minutes, and it is the King’s description of your life.

Where it applies: You sit down on Sunday afternoon and read the three chapters straight through, noticing first who Jesus calls blessed, and then praying over the one line that most exposed you. That is how the King meant his sermon to be heard: as the shape of the life he is giving you.

Where it would be wrong: You read the sermon as a scorecard and use it to grade yourself into despair, or to grade a struggling new believer at church and decide he cannot really be a Christian. The sermon begins by blessing the bankrupt. It drives us to Christ before it shapes us like him, and it is never a stick for beating the weak (12:20).

For worship. The God who once spoke from the fire so that the people trembled and begged him to stop has climbed a hill in Galilee and sat down among fishermen. The Lawgiver has come close enough to be touched. He did not come to lower the law but to open it, and before he opened it he blessed the people who could never keep it. Every beatitude he pronounced, he lived; every blessing he gave, he paid for. Glory to the King who teaches like this, and who makes those who hear him into what he describes.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach. The mountain setting recalls Moses receiving the law on Sinai.

parallels.desc: Moses goes up to God on the mountain

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first Beatitude: God’s blessing rests on those who know they are spiritually bankrupt, with nothing to offer God. The kingdom of heaven belongs to them.

The Beatitudes. Verses 3–12 are called the Beatitudes, from the Latin beatus, “blessed”. There are eight (vv. 3–10), plus an expansion of the last (vv. 11–12). They describe not eight types of Christian but eight sides of one character, found in every true disciple. The first and the eighth end with the same promise, “theirs is the kingdom of heaven”, framing the whole.

The shape of the set. These are not eight unrelated sayings but one argument, sealed at both ends, and the tense does the same work as the wording. Verse 3 is present: theirs is. Verses 4 to 9 are all future: shall be comforted, shall inherit, shall be satisfied, shall receive mercy, shall see God, shall be called. Then verse 10 returns to the present: theirs is. Present, six futures, present again. The kingdom is already yours at the front door and still yours at the back, and everything in between is on its way. The order matters too. The first four describe a person’s need: bankrupt, grieving, unassertive, starving. The second four describe what comes out of a person who has been met in that need: merciful, single-hearted, peacemaking, and consequently hated. Nobody arrives at the second four by trying. They are what the first four turn into.

Blessed. Makarios. Not “happy” in the sense of a feeling. It is God’s verdict: truly well off, favoured by God, in an enviable position, whatever one feels. It echoes the Psalms (Psalm 1:1; 32:1). The Beatitudes turn the world’s values upside down: the world calls the confident, the cheerful and the powerful blessed; Jesus calls the poor, the mourning and the meek blessed.

A verdict, not a wish. Jesus is not saying may you be happy, or I hope things go well for you; there was a perfectly good Greek way of saying that, and he does not use it. Makarios is a flat declaration about how things actually stand. Our word happiness comes from hap, chance, and it rises and falls with what has happened lately. Half the people described in these eight sentences are in circumstances nobody would envy: mourning, starving for what they have not got, slandered and driven out. To call them happy would be an insult. To call them blessed, rightly placed and on the receiving end of God’s favour whatever the week looks like, is the truth. That is the only reason these sentences are not cruel. You cannot order a mourner to be happy, but Jesus is not describing a feeling. He is announcing that God is for this person, and the verdict holds while the tears are still wet. The Psalms open with the word, Blessed is the man (Psalm 1:1), and every Jew listening knew the form. What they had never heard was this list of people attached to it.

The poor in spirit. Not the poor in material terms only, nor those who lack spirit or courage. In the Old Testament, “the poor” often meant the humble faithful who depended on God because they had nothing else, and were oppressed by the proud (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1; 66:2). To be poor in spirit is to recognise one’s spiritual poverty: to know that before God I am bankrupt, with no righteousness, no merit, nothing to bring. It is the opposite of spiritual pride. The tax collector who prayed “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” was poor in spirit; the Pharisee who thanked God he was not like others was not (Luke 18:9–14).

The beggar’s word. Greek has two words for poor. Penēs is the working man with nothing spare: he earns his bread and it is gone. The word here is the other one, ptōchos, from a verb meaning to crouch or cower. It means a beggar: not short of money but destitute, with no resources and no prospect of any, dependent entirely on what somebody puts into his hand. That is the word Jesus chose for the first sentence of his first sermon. And it lands on a floor Isaiah had laid. The Spirit of the Lord was to rest on one anointed to bring good news to the poor (Isaiah 61:1), the text Jesus read at Nazareth and said was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:21). More exactly still: “this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:2). Of everything in creation, that is what God says he looks at.

How poverty of spirit shows itself. It is not low self-esteem but theological honesty, and it shows itself in particular moments. In prayer, the poor in spirit have nothing to produce before God, only need. In success, they cannot take the credit. In conflict, they do not reach for the card of their own righteousness. In moral failure, they have no deflections left. It is the patient who admits he is ill who finally calls the doctor; the man who insists he is fine stays sick. The poor in spirit are simply those who have stopped pretending they are well before God, and so they are the only ones who let the Physician in.

For theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The present tense: it is theirs now. The kingdom is not earned by the rich in spirit, but given to those who come with empty hands. This is grace at the very start of the sermon. The first step into the kingdom is not achievement but admission of need.

Why “kingdom of heaven”? Matthew usually says kingdom of heaven where Mark and Luke say kingdom of God. They mean the same thing. Devout Jews often spoke of heaven out of reverence for God’s name, much as we might say “Heaven help us”. The phrase does not mean a place we go after death, though it includes that. It means God’s reign, his rule as King, breaking into the world in Jesus, gathering a people now and one day filling the whole earth. To have the kingdom is to belong to the King and to share in everything he is putting right.

What it does not mean. Not low self-esteem or self-hatred. The poor in spirit know their poverty before God, but they also know they are richly loved and given the kingdom. Nor does it mean that material poverty is a virtue that earns heaven. Luke’s version, “Blessed are you who are poor” (Luke 6:20), speaks of the literally poor, because they often know their need of God; but the rich can be poor in spirit, and the poor can be proud.

In a sentence. God blesses with his kingdom those who know they have nothing to bring him.

On a Tuesday. Begin your prayers today not with what you have done for God, but with what you need from him.

Where it applies: After a hard week you come to church feeling you have nothing to show God. Good: tell him so. Poverty of spirit begins your prayers with “I need you”, not “look what I did”.

Where it would be wrong: Your elders ask you to lead a home group, and you have the gifts for it, but you say, “I’m nobody, I couldn’t.” That is not poverty of spirit. Humility does not deny the gifts God gave; it uses them for others and gives him the credit (Romans 12:3–8; 1 Peter 4:10–11).

A test. Notice what you reach for when you are criticised. If the first thing that rises is a list of your good qualities, the card of your own righteousness is still in your pocket. The poor in spirit have learned to say, often with relief, that the critic does not know the half of it, and that Christ knows all of it and loves them still.

For worship. Come to God with empty hands. That is the only way into his kingdom. And see who made the way. He who was rich became poor for our sake, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The Son who owned the kingdom emptied his hands on a cross so that beggars might be made heirs. The first word of his sermon is a blessing on people with nothing, because he had already decided to give them everything. Blessed be the King who looks first at the humble and contrite, and who fills empty hands with himself.
verseByVerse.note: “Blessed” means truly well off in God’s sight, not merely happy.

parallels.desc: with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on those who grieve, above all over sin and its ruin, in themselves and in the world. God himself will comfort them.

Those who mourn. The word (penthountes) means deep grief, the kind of mourning for the dead. It follows naturally from the first Beatitude: those who see their spiritual poverty grieve over it. The mourning includes sorrow for our own sin (Psalm 51:3–4; James 4:9), grief over the sin and suffering of the world (Psalm 119:136; Ezekiel 9:4), and the sorrows of life in a fallen world, including bereavement. Jesus himself wept (John 11:35; Luke 19:41).

The heaviest word for grief. English has several words for sorrow, and so does Greek, and Jesus reached for a heavy one. Pentheō is the word for mourning the dead. It is not disappointment or low spirits; it is the grief that cannot be hidden, the kind that stops a household. Jacob mourned like this for Joseph, whom he believed torn apart by animals (Genesis 37:34). So the sorrow being called blessed is not a mild regret about one’s failings. It is grief of the sort people feel at a graveside, and the thing being grieved is what sin has done. Poverty of spirit is the sight; mourning is what a man does when he has seen it and cannot look away again.

Not a temperature. That needs a guard at once, because it is easily twisted into a demand for a certain intensity of feeling, and then people who cannot produce tears conclude they are not really Christians. Jesus is not prescribing a temperature. He is describing what happens when a person genuinely sees his own condition: he does not shrug. Whether it comes as tears or as a long quiet ache is a matter of temperament, and God does not appear to mind which.

For they shall be comforted. “Comforted” (paraklēthēsontai) is related to the word for the Holy Spirit, the Comforter or Helper (John 14:16). The passive voice means God is the one who comforts. Isaiah 61:1–3 promised that the Messiah would come to comfort all who mourn, giving them a garland instead of ashes and the oil of gladness instead of mourning. Jesus fulfils it. The comfort comes partly now, in forgiveness and the Spirit’s presence, and fully at the end, when God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

Ashes exchanged. The comfort word is the one that opens the second half of Isaiah: “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isaiah 40:1), spoken to exiles who knew exactly why they were in Babylon and that they had earned it. Ashes were what you put on your head when someone died. The promise is not that the mourning was a mistake. It is that the ashes are going to be exchanged for a crown. Picture the man who for years shrugged off his sharp tongue or his wandering eye as just how he is, and who at last truly grieves it before God. He finds to his surprise that the tears are not a pit but a doorway, for the LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18), never to the self-satisfied.

The logic. The world says, “Blessed are those who laugh; avoid sorrow.” Jesus says that those who never mourn their sin will never know the comfort of forgiveness. Only those who feel the weight of sin feel the relief of grace.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should be gloomy, or that sadness is a mark of holiness. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22). But Christian joy is not the shallow cheerfulness that ignores sin and suffering; it is the joy of the comforted. Nor does it mean that all grief is blessed. Self-pity and bitterness are not the mourning Jesus means. Godly grief leads to repentance; worldly grief leads to death (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Is depression the mourning Jesus blesses? No, and the two must not be confused. Godly sorrow moves toward God and produces life (2 Corinthians 7:10). Depression is an illness that often makes a person feel further from God and produces exhaustion rather than repentance. A Christian can have either, or both, or one mistaken for the other by well-meaning friends. Telling a depressed believer that his flatness is a spiritual failing is a cruelty this verse does not authorise. He may need a doctor as well as a pastor, and there is no shame in that. And he is not outside this blessing: Christ is near to him in the dark too, and the comfort promised here is for him as well.

In a sentence. God blesses with his comfort those who grieve over sin and its ruin.

On a Tuesday. When did you last grieve over your own sin, rather than only its consequences? And who near you is mourning, and needs you to sit with them?

Where it applies: You spoke harshly to your child this morning. Do not shrug it off. Let it grieve you, confess it to God, and apologise to your child.

Where it would be wrong: You confessed a sin years ago, turned from it, and still punish yourself for it every day, as if Christ’s blood were not enough. Mourning over sin leads to comfort; it is not meant to go on for ever. Receive the forgiveness God promises (1 John 1:9; Romans 8:1).

For worship. The comfort is certain because it was bought. The Man of Sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3), wept at a friend’s grave and over a city that would kill him, and in Gethsemane he was sorrowful even to death. He carried our griefs so that ours would have an appointed end. The God of all comfort does not stand at a distance from mourners; he came down into the grief himself, and one day he will wipe every tear from every face with his own hand. Blessed be the Comforter who turns ashes into a crown.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on the meek: those who are gentle and humble before God and others, who do not grab or retaliate, but trust God to give them what is right. They will inherit the earth.

The meek. Praeis: gentle, humble, not self-assertive. In Greek it was used of a tamed horse: strength under control (see Ephesians 4:2). Moses was called very meek, more than all people on the earth (Numbers 12:3), yet he confronted Pharaoh. Jesus called himself gentle and lowly in heart (11:29), yet he overturned the tables in the temple. Meekness is not weakness. It is the strength not to insist on one’s own rights, not to take revenge, and to accept God’s dealings without bitterness.

Scripture’s definition is a man. If meekness needs a definition, Scripture has already supplied a person. The man called very meek is Moses: the man who stood before Pharaoh and would not be moved, who came down a mountain, smashed the tablets in fury and ground the golden calf to powder. That man is Scripture’s picture of meekness. So the word cannot mean timidity, softness or an inability to act. Read Numbers 12 and see when the verse appears. His own brother and sister are attacking him behind his back over his marriage and his standing, and Moses says nothing at all. God answers for him. That is the picture: a man with every power he needs and no interest in using it on his own behalf. The broken horse has not lost its strength; its full strength now answers to another hand.

The connection. The poor in spirit see themselves truly before God; the mourning grieve their sin; the meek, having seen themselves truly, are gentle toward others. Someone who knows how much they have been forgiven does not demand their rights harshly.

For they shall inherit the earth. Jesus quotes Psalm 37:11. Psalm 37 tells God’s people not to fret over the wicked who prosper, but to trust the LORD, wait for him, and refrain from anger; the meek shall inherit the land. In the Old Testament, the inheritance was the land of Canaan. Jesus widens it to the whole earth. The meek, who do not grab, will receive everything. The proud seize the earth for a while; the meek will inherit the new earth for ever (Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1–7).

Trust made visible. The psalm sets this promise inside a longer command: trust in the LORD and do good, commit your way to him, and he will act (Psalm 37:3–5). Meekness is that trust made visible, the refusal to take God’s work of vindication into your own hands. And measure the promise against how land is usually acquired. The earth has always gone to whoever could take it and hold it; every border on every map was drawn by somebody with the means to draw it. The verdict of Jesus is that at the end of history the whole of it will belong to the people who never grabbed at any of it.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must be doormats, never speaking up for truth or justice, or never defending the vulnerable. Jesus spoke strongly against hypocrisy (chapter 23). Meekness concerns personal ambition and retaliation, not indifference to evil. Nor does it mean being shy or quiet by temperament. A bold, outgoing person can be meek; a quiet person can be proud.

What if keeping quiet means I am misjudged for years? Then you are in Moses’ company, and in your Lord’s. Meekness does not agree with a false verdict; it simply refuses to make vindication its life’s project. You may state the truth plainly once, where it matters, and correct a falsehood that harms others. What you hand over to God is the campaign: the rehearsed speeches, the need to be seen to be right. He keeps perfect records, and the day is coming when he will bring forth your righteousness as the light (Psalm 37:6).

In a sentence. God blesses the gentle, who trust him instead of grabbing, with the inheritance of the whole renewed earth.

On a Tuesday. Where are you insisting on your rights today, in traffic, in a meeting, at home? Practise meekness: let God defend you.

Better to let it go: In a meeting a colleague presents your idea as his own. Unless the work or someone else suffers by it, you do not need to correct the record or win the point. God sees it, your reputation is in his hands, and you are free of the need to be noticed.

Wrong to let it go: The care home is neglecting your elderly mother, or a manager is bullying a junior colleague who is too afraid to speak. Here keeping quiet is not meekness. Speak up calmly and firmly, through the proper channels, and keep at it. Meekness gives up its own rights for love; it does not give up the rights of the weak (Proverbs 31:8–9). Even for himself, Paul used his rights as a Roman citizen when it served the gospel and protected others (Acts 16:37; 22:25).

For worship. We learn meekness not from a rule book but from a person. The one who said he was gentle and lowly in heart held all authority in heaven and on earth, and stood silent before his accusers. He could have called twelve legions of angels (26:53), and he did not, because he was entrusting himself to him who judges justly. The Lord of the whole earth was willing to be robbed of everything, even his clothes, so that people who had grabbed at everything might be given the earth as a gift. In him the meek inherit all things, because all things were made through him and for him.
verseByVerse.note: “Meek” means gentle and humble before God, not weak.

parallels.desc: the meek shall inherit the land
“I am gentle and lowly in heart”

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on those who long for righteousness as a starving man longs for food and a parched man for water. God will satisfy them.

Those who hunger and thirst. Not a mild wish, but desperate desire. In the ancient world, many people knew real hunger and thirst. The Psalms use the image: as a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Psalm 42:1; 63:1).

Appetites that will not argue. He could have said those who value righteousness, or admire it, or work at it. He chose instead the two appetites a body cannot argue with. Hunger and thirst are not preferences to be weighed against other preferences; they are the conditions under which a man stops being able to think of anything else. Picture the gap between idly wishing you were a little fitter and the gasping thirst of a man lost in a desert. That is the pitch at which this beatitude is set, and it is worth asking honestly whether righteousness has ever registered with you at that level.

For righteousness. What righteousness? In Matthew, righteousness usually means doing God’s will, a life that is right before God (5:10, 20; 6:1, 33). So the hunger includes: longing to be made right with God (forgiveness and justification); longing to be holy, to do God’s will (sanctification); and longing for justice in the world, for God’s right order to prevail. The poor in spirit, who know they have no righteousness of their own, hunger for it.

Everything put right. Dikaiosynē covers more ground than the English word. In the Old Testament its family very often means justice, the setting right of what is crooked. So the appetite here is not only for personal holiness. It is for everything to be put right, including the things that are wrong out there. A person who aches at the state of the world, at the trafficked child and the cheated widow, is inside this verse as much as the one who aches at the state of his own heart.

For they shall be satisfied. The word (chortasthēsontai) was used of animals being fed until full (14:20). God will fill them. In part now: those who come to Christ are given his righteousness (Philippians 3:9) and are changed by his Spirit. In full at the end, when righteousness dwells in the new heavens and new earth (2 Peter 3:13). Jesus said that whoever comes to him will never hunger, and whoever believes in him will never thirst (John 6:35).

Fed like cattle in deep grass. Chortazō is not a polite word. It comes from the noun for fodder, and it means to be fed until you stop: the word for animals put out to graze and eaten full. The Gospels use it of the five thousand on the hillside, who all ate and were satisfied, with twelve baskets over. So the sentence is: those with a beggar’s hunger will be fed like cattle in deep grass. And there is a promise in it that should be stated plainly, because most appetites do not work this way. Nearly every hunger a person has can be starved, spoiled or fed with the wrong thing. This is the one appetite God guarantees to fill. Not manage. Fill.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn righteousness by hungering for it. Hunger is not food; it is the sense of need that drives us to the food. Nor is it a hunger that is satisfied once and then disappears. Christians who are being satisfied go on hungering for more of God.

What if I do not feel this hunger? Start by telling God so, honestly; that admission is itself the beginning of hunger. Then notice what is filling you. Appetite is dulled by snacking, and a soul that grazes all day on screens, news and noise rarely feels hungry for God. Make room: an unhurried time in Scripture, a psalm read slowly, the Lord’s Supper taken with attention. Spend time with Christians who are hungry; it is catching. And remember the strange test in this verse. It does not ask whether you are righteous but whether you want to be. A man who has lost his appetite is more ill than a man who is starving, and the surest sign that God is at work is not that you have arrived but that you cannot stop wanting.

In a sentence. God fully satisfies those who long desperately to be right with him and to do his will.

On a Tuesday. What do you hunger for most? Your appetites show your heart. Ask God to make you hungry for righteousness, and feed that hunger on his word.

Where it applies: You notice that you check the news a dozen times a day and have not opened your Bible since Sunday. Move the Bible to where the phone usually sits in the morning, and read a psalm before anything else. Feed the appetite you want to grow.

Where it would be wrong: You are so hungry for justice in the world that you rage at every injustice online, despise everyone on the other side, and have stopped praying for your own heart. Hunger for righteousness begins at home and is fed by God, not by outrage. Seek justice with clean hands, and remember that only God can finally put the world right (Romans 12:19).

For worship. The righteousness we hunger for is a gift before it is a task. Christ is the bread of life and the living water; he hungered in the wilderness and thirsted on the cross, crying out that he was thirsty (John 19:28), so that people starved of righteousness might be fed. His perfect obedience is reckoned to all who come to him empty, and his Spirit goes on feeding them until the day the whole creation is full of righteousness as the waters cover the sea. There is no famine at his table, and no one who comes to him hungry is sent away.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on the merciful: those who show compassion and forgiveness to others in their need and failure. They will receive God’s mercy.

The merciful. Mercy is compassion in action toward those in distress, and forgiveness toward those who have wronged us. It includes both pity for the suffering (the good Samaritan, Luke 10:33–37) and pardon for the guilty (18:21–35). God himself is merciful (Exodus 34:6), and his people reflect him.

The turn. The first four Beatitudes describe our relationship to God: poverty, mourning, meekness, hunger. The next four describe how that shows itself toward others: mercy, purity, peacemaking, and enduring persecution. Those who have received mercy become merciful.

For they shall receive mercy. From God, at the final judgment and now. James says that judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy (James 2:13).

The logic. This is not a deal: “be merciful, and God will pay you back with mercy”. It is a description of reality. Those who know God’s mercy cannot help showing it. A person who refuses to show mercy shows that they have never truly understood the mercy they need. Jesus’ parable of the unforgiving servant makes the point: a man forgiven a vast debt who refuses to forgive a small one shows he never grasped the first (18:21–35).

Jesus does not treat this one gently. That guard is right, and it must not be used to make the verse toothless. Jesus returns to it twice in this Gospel, both times with an edge. Of all the petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, this is the only one he stops to explain: if you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive you (6:14–15). And the parable of the unforgiving servant ends with a man released from ten thousand talents being handed over to the jailers because he would not release a hundred denarii. Mercy shown does not purchase mercy received; the whole New Testament forbids that reading. But mercy withheld is presented as evidence that mercy was never truly received, and Jesus states it in the strongest terms he has.

The arithmetic of the parable. Ten thousand talents was an absurd sum, more than the yearly tax of a whole province, a debt no man could clear in a hundred lifetimes. A hundred denarii was about three months’ wages: real money, a real wrong, the kind of debt a person is entitled to be angry about. The parable does not pretend the second debt was nothing. It says the first was so much larger that the comparison should have been decisive. The servant had just been let off a fortune, and minutes later he was standing in the street with his hands round a colleague’s throat.

What it does not mean. Not that our mercy earns God’s mercy. God’s mercy comes first (Ephesians 2:4). Nor does mercy mean ignoring wrongdoing, removing all consequences, or pretending justice does not matter. God is merciful and just (Romans 3:26), and the merciful still want justice for the oppressed.

What if the hurt keeps coming back after I have forgiven? Then you have not failed. Forgiveness is first a decision and then often a long road. You decide before God not to repay, not to hold the wrong over the person, and to hand the account to him. Then, when the memory returns with its sting, you make the same decision again; that is not failure but faithfulness. Peter asked how many times, and Jesus answered, in effect, without counting (18:21–22). The feelings usually follow slowly. Pray for the person by name each time it hurts. Over months you may find that the prayer has begun to change you more than the memory has.

In a sentence. Those who show mercy, because they have received it, will receive God’s mercy at the last.

On a Tuesday. To whom can you show mercy today: someone in need, or someone who has wronged you?

Where it applies: A teenager working for you breaks an expensive tool through carelessness, and is clearly sorry. You could take it out of his wages. Mercy lets it go, and tells him so.

Where it would be wrong: A volunteer at church has harmed a child, or an employee keeps stealing. Mercy does not mean covering it up or giving another chance that puts others at risk. You can forgive personally and still report it; abuse must always be reported to the authorities (Romans 13:4). Mercy that leaves the vulnerable exposed is not mercy.

A test. Bring to mind the person you have not forgiven, not the general category but the specific name, and put beside it what you are asking God to overlook in your own account this week. The parable’s whole force is that the two figures are not of the same order, and that the person who cannot see it has probably never looked properly at his own.

For worship. We do not work up mercy in order to earn God’s; we pass on what we have drunk deeply of. The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). He tore up a debt of ten thousand talents in our name, and he did not do it by pretending it was small. He paid it, in the blood of his Son, so that he could be just and the one who justifies. Every act of mercy his people show is a little stream running down from that fountain, and the fountain does not run dry.

parallels.desc: should not you have had mercy?

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on the pure in heart: those whose inner life is undivided and clean, devoted to God without hidden motives. They will see God.

The pure in heart. “Pure” (katharos) means clean, unmixed, unadulterated, like refined metal or pure water. The “heart” in the Bible is the centre of the person: mind, will, desires and feelings (see Ephesians 1:18). Purity of heart means two things. Moral cleanness, especially in thought and desire (5:28). And singleness: an undivided heart, wholly devoted to God, not double-minded (James 4:8; Psalm 86:11). The Pharisees were outwardly clean but inwardly full of greed and self-indulgence (23:25–28). Jesus wants purity at the source.

The opposite is a divided heart. Katharos is the ordinary word for washed dishes, clear water, and metal with the dross taken out. Its opposite is not so much dirty as mixed. So the opposite of a pure heart is a divided one: the person who genuinely wants God and also wants three or four other things, and could not tell you which he would give up if it came to it. Think of a man who worships on Sunday with one eye always on his money, his image or his comfort. The water is cloudy. The pure in heart is the one whose loves have been simplified, who wants God more than the gifts of God, and only such clear water can mirror the face of heaven. That is a mercy to hear, because a divided heart is the honest description of most Christians much of the time, and it is exactly what God has promised to work on: unite my heart to fear your name (Psalm 86:11).

Psalm 24. The psalm asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD and stand in his holy place. The answer: those who have clean hands and a pure heart (Psalm 24:3–4). Jesus says these people will see God himself.

More than David dared to write. That is the temple question. Who may come up? Who may go in and not be struck down? The answer given a thousand years earlier is the phrase Jesus uses here, and to it he attaches something David did not dare to write. Not merely shall stand in his holy place, but shall see God.

For they shall see God. The highest blessing. No one can see God and live (Exodus 33:20). Yet the hope of God’s people has always been to see him (Job 19:26–27; Psalm 17:15). In part, believers see God now by faith in Christ, who is the image of the invisible God (John 14:9; 2 Corinthians 4:6). In full at the end: they will see his face (Revelation 22:4; 1 John 3:2). Theologians call this the beatific vision, the blessed sight of God.

The one thing refused. Measure the promise against the Old Testament. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20); he was hidden in a cleft of the rock and shown only the back. Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up and cried out that he was lost. Nobody in the whole Old Testament sees the face of God and walks away comfortable. The tabernacle and temple, the curtain and the priesthood, existed to say in the most emphatic architecture ever built that this was the one thing not available. And a man sitting on a hillside in Galilee tells fishermen and farmers that some of them will. Within three years the curtain was torn in two, from top to bottom (27:51): torn from the top, the end nobody could reach.

How can anyone be pure in heart? No one is by nature (Jeremiah 17:9). Purity is first God’s gift: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25–26), cleanses it by faith (Acts 15:9), and through the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7). Then it is a lifelong pursuit: everyone who hopes to see him purifies himself as he is pure (1 John 3:3; Hebrews 12:14).

What it does not mean. Not sinless perfection in this life. The pure in heart still struggle with sin; what marks them is that they hate it and fight it, and that their heart is set on God. Nor is purity merely the absence of sexual sin, though it includes that. It is the whole heart turned toward God.

What will it mean to see God, since God is spirit? Scripture does not explain it fully, and we should not pretend to know more than it says. But it says enough. We shall see the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, risen in a real body (2 Corinthians 4:6; John 1:14). And we shall know God directly, face to face, as a friend is known, no longer through a mirror dimly (1 Corinthians 13:12). The seeing will change us: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Every other gift of the gospel is something from God. This one is God himself.

In a sentence. Those whose hearts are made clean and undivided toward God will see God himself.

On a Tuesday. What are you allowing into your heart through your eyes and screens? Guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it (Proverbs 4:23).

Where it applies: You realise that you have been praying on Sunday mornings while planning your week’s purchases in your head. Name the rival before God, put the list away, and ask him to unite your heart to love him first.

Where it would be wrong: You decide that purity of heart means cutting yourself off from every film, book and friend outside church, and look down on believers who do not. Purity is an undivided heart toward God, not a fortress of rules, and Jesus, the pure one, ate with sinners (9:10–13). Guard your heart, but do not mistake withdrawal or a critical spirit for cleanness.

For worship. The only man who ever had a pure heart, who never wanted anything more than his Father, was made sin for us on the cross, and in the darkness he could not see his Father’s face. He went without the sight so that people who never had a pure heart could look on God and live. Christ has become our righteousness and holiness (1 Corinthians 1:30); he washes us day by day, and on the last day he will present us spotless. They shall see God: not know about him more accurately, not sense him more strongly, but see him, as one sees a friend. Glory to the Lamb whose blood opened the eyes of the blind to the face of God.

parallels.desc: he who has clean hands and a pure heart
holiness, without which no one will see the Lord
we shall see him as he is

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on the peacemakers: those who work to bring reconciliation, between people and God and between people and each other. They will be called sons of God.

The peacemakers. Not peace-lovers, who simply like quiet, nor peace-keepers, who avoid conflict at any price, but peace-makers, who actively work to make peace where there is hostility. “Peace” here is the Hebrew shalom: not only the absence of conflict but wholeness and right relationship (see Ephesians 1:2). Making peace includes sharing the gospel, by which people are reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:18–20); reconciling people in conflict; and refusing to stir up division (Proverbs 6:19; Romans 12:18).

Makers, not keepers. The word, eirēnopoioi, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: peace plus make, and the making is the point. A peacekeeper stands between two parties and stops them hitting each other. A peacemaker walks into the quarrel and does the far more expensive work of getting them back together. Keeping the peace usually means arranging for a difficulty not to be mentioned. It is cheap and quiet and often the opposite of what this verse commends, because the thing left unsaid goes on rotting. Making peace means going into the difficulty on purpose, and it is why this beatitude sits immediately before persecution. Peacemakers get hit from both sides. That is the job. Picture the friend who, when two others fall out, refuses to take a side and walks back and forth between them, bearing the awkwardness and even the blame, until clenched fists become clasped hands.

For they shall be called sons of God. “Called” means recognised, acknowledged, by God. In Hebrew idiom, a “son of” something shares its character. God is the God of peace (Romans 15:33), who made peace through the blood of the cross (Colossians 1:20). Christ is the great peacemaker (Ephesians 2:14–17). Those who make peace show the family likeness: they act like their Father. “Sons” includes daughters; all believers are God’s children (Galatians 3:26–28).

Who does the calling. The passive, shall be called, names no speaker, and that was a reverent Jewish way of saying God will do it. It is God who gives the name. Not the two parties who were reconciled, who may well be ungrateful; not the watching church, which may take a different view. The verdict comes from the Father.

What peace cost God. That fixes what peacemaking costs. God did not make peace by overlooking anything, or by persuading the offended party to be reasonable, or by arranging for the matter not to come up. He made peace by the blood of the cross, absorbing the whole cost himself so that the wrong could be truly dealt with rather than quietly ignored. So a peacemaker is not someone with a talent for smoothing things over. It is someone willing to carry a cost that is not his so that something broken can be properly mended. There is no cheaper version, and the family likeness is the willingness to pay.

What it does not mean. Not peace at the expense of truth. Jesus later says he did not come to bring peace but a sword (10:34): the gospel divides between those who accept and reject it. Peacemaking does not mean papering over sin or pretending that wrongs do not matter. True peace deals with the cause of conflict. Nor does it mean that we become God’s children by making peace. We are made children by grace through faith (John 1:12); peacemaking shows that we are.

How do I actually help two people make peace? Pray first, and check your own motives: you are not there to win or to be the hero. Listen to each separately and let them feel heard before you say anything. Help each see the other’s view and his own part, however small. Encourage each to own his wrong specifically, without “but you”. Do not carry tales between them or take sides in gossip. Suggest a meeting where both can speak with you present, and keep the aim in view: not who was right but restored love. Some quarrels need the elders. Be patient; peace often comes slowly.

In a sentence. Those who work for reconciliation show the family likeness of God, the great peacemaker, and are recognised as his children.

On a Tuesday. Is there a conflict near you, in your family, church or workplace, where you could be a peacemaker? Take one step toward reconciliation.

Where it applies: Two friends in your home group have stopped speaking after a misunderstanding. Invite them both for coffee, let each be heard, and help them understand each other.

Where it would be wrong: A relative is mocked at every family gathering, or a teacher in your church is denying that Jesus is God, and everyone keeps quiet to keep the peace. That is not peacemaking. The false prophets cried peace when there was none (Jeremiah 6:14). Godly wisdom is first pure, then peaceable (James 3:17): true peace deals with the wrong instead of burying it.

For worship. We can only make peace because peace was first made with us. We were enemies, and God did not wait for us to become reasonable. He sent his Son into the quarrel, and the Son stood between heaven and earth and took the blows from both sides, until he had reconciled us to God in his body on the cross. For he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). He has broken down the dividing wall and made one new people out of enemies. Blessed is the Prince of Peace, and blessed are his brothers and sisters who bear his name and his likeness.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on those who suffer for doing right. The kingdom of heaven is theirs.

Those who are persecuted. The perfect tense suggests those who have been persecuted and still bear its marks. Persecution includes physical violence, imprisonment and death, but also exclusion, mockery, loss of jobs and reputation (v. 11).

For righteousness’ sake. Because they live rightly, according to God’s will. Not suffering for their own foolishness, rudeness or wrongdoing (1 Peter 2:20; 4:15), but because their lives of mercy, purity and peacemaking expose and challenge the world. A life described by the first seven Beatitudes provokes opposition, because it rebukes the world’s values (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12).

Not always a prison cell. The world does not usually persecute the harmless; it persecutes those whose righteousness exposes its darkness. And persecution need not be a prison cell. It may be the colleague quietly sidelined for refusing to fudge the figures, or the teenager frozen out for not joining the cruelty in the group chat. When obedience to Christ costs you something at others’ hands, you are not unblessed. You stand exactly where the citizens of the kingdom have always stood.

For theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The same promise as the first Beatitude (v. 3). The Beatitudes begin and end with the kingdom. The world may take everything from them, but it cannot take the kingdom.

The bracket closes. Verse 3 and verse 10 end with the same words, and only these two are in the present tense. The beggar at the front door and the hunted disciple at the back are told the identical thing, and it is the only thing in the list they do not have to wait for. Those who have lost everything for Christ are told that the one thing they cannot lose is already theirs.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should seek persecution, or interpret every criticism as persecution. Sometimes Christians are disliked because they are unpleasant.
