The blessing is for suffering that comes because of righteousness. Nor does it mean that suffering earns the kingdom. It is the mark of those to whom the kingdom already belongs.

Two distortions. In comfortable countries this verse is easily shrunk to social awkwardness, while a very large part of the church elsewhere is in real danger of prison and death. Both distortions should be avoided: manufacturing a persecution one does not have, and quietly deciding the verse belongs to history or to other people. The honest position for most Western Christians is to notice that it describes a normal condition of kingdom life (2 Timothy 3:12), to ask why it so rarely touches us, to be careful what conclusion we draw from the answer, and to stand by brothers and sisters for whom it is daily bread (Hebrews 13:3).

In a sentence. Those who suffer because they live God’s way have the kingdom of heaven as their possession.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked or disadvantaged for living as a Christian, you are not cursed but blessed. And pray today for believers who face prison or death for their faith.

Where it applies: You refuse to sign off a false expense claim, and are passed over for promotion. That is suffering for righteousness’ sake. Bear it without bitterness: you are blessed.

Where it would be wrong: Colleagues avoid you because you are preachy, rude or always late, and you tell yourself you are being persecuted. Ask honestly first whether they are offended by Christ or by you. Suffering for your own faults is not blessed (1 Peter 2:20; 4:15). And being blessed in persecution does not forbid lawful protection: Paul appealed to the courts and to Caesar (Acts 25:11).

For worship. The persecuted are blessed because they suffer with the one who was cast out for them. He was despised and rejected, hated without a cause, led outside the city gate and nailed up as a criminal, and he endured the cross for the joy set before him. Nothing done to his people is hidden from him; when Saul struck the church, the risen Lord said that Saul was persecuting him (Acts 9:4). In him the kingdom is already theirs, and no one who reviles them can touch it. Glory to the King who was hunted first, and who reigns now with the scars still in his hands.

parallels.desc: if you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns from “those who” to “you”, speaking directly to his disciples. When people insult, persecute and slander you because you belong to me, rejoice: your reward in heaven is great, and you stand in the line of the prophets.

Blessed are you. The shift to “you” makes it personal. Jesus expects his disciples to face this. Eight times he has said blessed are those, describing a category. Now he turns from describing to addressing, and he does it after the crowd has had eight sentences to work out whether they are in the list.

When others revile you. Insult, abuse to your face.

And persecute you. Hunt, harass, pursue.

And utter all kinds of evil against you falsely. Slander behind your back. The early Christians were accused of cannibalism (because they spoke of eating Christ’s body), atheism (because they refused the gods), and hatred of the human race. “Falsely” is important: the slander is untrue.

On my account. In verse 10, “for righteousness’ sake”; here, “on my account”, for Jesus’ sake. Jesus puts himself in the place of righteousness. To suffer for him is to suffer for what is right. Only God could say this.

An enormous substitution. A man on a Galilean hillside has just replaced the standard of righteousness with himself, in two consecutive sentences, without argument or explanation, in front of people who would stone a man for less. Nobody in that crowd could have missed it. It is allegiance to him, not merely being good, that draws the world’s fury, and it is allegiance to him that heaven rewards.

Rejoice and be glad. Not merely endure, but rejoice. The second word means to leap for joy. The apostles, beaten by the council, rejoiced that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

The least natural command in the sermon. The second verb, agalliaō, is not quiet contentment. It is the gladness that gets up and moves. Jesus is not telling his people to pretend the slander does not hurt. He is telling them that when it comes there is something to be glad about, and he gives two reasons, one looking forward and one looking back.

For your reward is great in heaven. God rewards faithfulness (see 6:1–6). The reward is not earned wages but God’s generous gift. “In heaven” means it is kept with God, safe, not yet visible (1 Peter 1:4).

For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. The prophets were rejected, persecuted and some killed: Elijah was hunted (1 Kings 19:2), Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned (Jeremiah 37:15), Zechariah was stoned (2 Chronicles 24:21). To be persecuted for Christ is to join the company of God’s faithful servants through history.

The company is the argument. That is a strange comfort until you feel its weight. The natural reading of being attacked for your faith is that something has gone wrong: that you handled it badly, or God has withdrawn, or the whole thing was a mistake. Jesus gives a different reading: this is what happened to Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah and every man God ever sent. It is not that suffering proves you are right; plenty of people suffer for being wrong. It is that this kind of suffering, for this reason, has a long and honourable history, and the people in it are the ones God kept sending.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should enjoy pain, or pretend it does not hurt. The joy is not in the suffering itself, but in what it means and where it leads. Nor should Christians respond to slander with slander: Jesus will tell them to pray for their persecutors (v. 44).

Should I defend myself against false accusations? Sometimes, yes. Jesus did not answer every charge, but he did ask the man who struck him why (John 18:23), and Paul defended his ministry at length when the gospel was at stake (2 Corinthians 10–12). Correct a lie calmly where it harms the gospel, your family, or others who trust you, and use proper channels if your livelihood is threatened. What you lay down is the bitterness, the counter-slander and the need to win. Say what is true once, plainly and gently, and then leave your name with God, who will vindicate his people on the last day.

In a sentence. Disciples who are insulted and persecuted for Jesus can rejoice, because they have a great reward in heaven and stand with the prophets.

On a Tuesday. When you are mocked for Christ, remember who stands with you: the prophets, the apostles, and the Lord himself.

Where it applies: A relative sneers at your faith over a family meal and everyone laughs. Do not sulk or hit back. Remember that the prophets stood where you are sitting, answer gently if there is an opening, and thank God quietly that you were counted worthy of a small share of the reproach of Christ.

Where it would be wrong: You are criticised at work for a genuine mistake, or for being harsh with a colleague, and you tell yourself it is reproach for Christ’s sake. It is not. Jesus blesses those reviled falsely and on his account. Own the fault, apologise, and keep the comfort of this verse for the times it truly fits (1 Peter 4:15–16).

For worship. Such suffering is no sign of God’s frown but a mark of union with his Son, who was reviled first and in our place. He was called a glutton, a drunkard, a friend of sinners and a servant of Beelzebul; false witnesses lined up against him, and he answered nothing. And because he bore the full reproach, the reproach that falls on his people has become a badge of belonging. The reward is not wages earned but grace upon grace, kept in heaven where nothing can spoil it. Rejoice, for the King who was slandered for us has written our names in heaven.

parallels.desc: rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings

verseByVerse.quote: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet. You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells his disciples what they are in the world: they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Like salt, they preserve and give flavour; but salt that loses its saltiness is useless.

You are. Not “you should become”, but “you are”. This is their identity. The disciples described in the Beatitudes, poor, mourning, meek and persecuted, are the very people who affect the world.

The salt of the earth. Salt had many uses in the ancient world. It preserved food from decay, especially meat and fish, in a world without refrigeration. It gave flavour. It was used in sacrifices (Leviticus 2:13). Christians in the world act like salt: holding back moral decay, and giving the world a taste of God’s goodness. The world is like meat that rots if left to itself; disciples are rubbed into it to slow the rot.

Salt by the lake. The men listening knew salt as a trade. Packing fish in coarse salt drew out the moisture and stopped the rot for weeks or months, and salted fish from the Sea of Galilee were carried to markets across the empire; the town of Magdala took its Greek name, Taricheae, from the salting of fish. Salt was valuable enough to be part of a soldier’s pay, and our word salary is often traced to the Latin for salt. Disciples work like that. A household of truthful, faithful, kind people on a street does not change it by force or by noise, but by the quiet, persistent influence of changed lives, the way salt works into meat: slowly, thoroughly, from the inside.

But if salt has lost its taste. Pure sodium chloride cannot lose its saltiness. But the salt of Palestine was often gathered from the Dead Sea marshes, mixed with other minerals. If damp, the salt could be washed out, leaving a white powder that looked like salt but was useless. The word for “lost its taste” (mōranthē) also means “become foolish”. Disciples who lose their distinctiveness become useless.

How it happens. It has not turned into something else. It has gradually lost the one property that made it worth having, while keeping the appearance entirely. And it is never a decision. Nobody wakes up resolved to become indistinguishable. It happens by a hundred small accommodations: the joke you laugh at because not laughing would be awkward, the figure you round in your favour because everyone does, the opinion you keep to yourself for so long that you stop holding it. Each is minor. The cumulative effect is a life that is, on close inspection, exactly like every other life in the office, with a religious residue on top.

How shall its saltiness be restored? It cannot. It is a warning.

It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people’s feet. Useless salt was thrown on paths, where people walked on it. A church that becomes just like the world will be despised by the world.

You are the light of the world. Jesus is the light of the world (John 8:12); his disciples reflect his light, as the moon reflects the sun. Israel was called to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6); now Jesus’ disciples are.

A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. Many towns in Galilee were built on hills, visible for miles, and their lamps could be seen at night. Perhaps Jesus also thought of Jerusalem, the city on Mount Zion, to which the nations would come (Isaiah 2:2–3). The church cannot be invisible. Light is simpler than salt: it is visible by nature. A city on a hill cannot choose to be hidden; its existence makes it seen. The Christian life is unavoidably public, not as performance but as testimony. The question is not whether to be visible but what the visible life will say about the one who lit it.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should withdraw from the world to keep pure. Salt must be in contact with meat to work; it does nothing in the shaker. Nor that they should become like the world to influence it: salt that becomes like the meat is useless. The call is to be in the world, but distinct from it (John 17:15–18). And it does not mean that salvation can be lost. The warning is that a disciple or church whose life no longer differs from the world shows that something is badly wrong.

Does this mean a Christian can lose his salvation? No. The salt that is thrown out describes those who looked like disciples and had none of the substance, the same people Jesus describes in 7:21–23, who called him Lord and were never known by him. Those who truly belong to Christ will be kept: no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work in them will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). The warning is real, and God uses it to keep his people. It is aimed at the danger of a profession without a life.

How would I know if I had lost my saltiness? Ask the diagnostic question rather than the anxious one. The anxious question, have I lost it, tends to produce either despair or a burst of forced intensity that fades by Thursday. The better question is this: if someone who knows me well were asked what difference Christ has made to how I work, spend, speak and treat people, could they name anything? Not something impressive; something different. If nothing comes to mind, that is not a verdict but information, and it is exactly what the rest of this sermon sets about changing.

In a sentence. Disciples are salt and light: preserving, flavouring and illuminating the world, as long as they remain distinct from it.

On a Tuesday. In what ways does your life at work look different from the lives of those around you? Salt is noticed by its taste.

Where it applies: The office is tearing a manager to pieces over lunch. You do not join in, and when the chance comes you say something fair and kind about her. Nobody makes a speech; the conversation simply changes, and the salt has done its work.

Where it would be wrong: You decide that being salt means correcting every colleague’s language, refusing every office social, and making sure everyone knows you disapprove. That is not salt but vinegar. Salt works by being rubbed in, not by standing apart and frowning. Be different in your goodness, not in your superiority (Colossians 4:5–6).

For worship. He does not say become salt; he says you are. The Lord tells his disciples what he has already made them, before he warns them not to waste it. The world would rot without the people he has scattered through it, and he scatters them on purpose, into offices and kitchens and classrooms, as his own preserving grace. He is the true light that gives light to everyone, and he has chosen to shine through cracked clay pots, so that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7). Glory to the Light of the world, who lights his people and sets them on a hill.
verseByVerse.note: Salt preserved and flavoured food. Impure salt, such as that from the Dead Sea, could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: “I am the light of the world”
shine as lights in the world

verseByVerse.quote: Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one lights a lamp and hides it. In the same way, disciples must let their light shine, so that people see their good works and give glory, not to them, but to their Father in heaven.

Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. A household lamp was a small clay bowl filled with olive oil, with a wick of flax, giving a small light. The “basket” (modios) was a grain measure holding about eight litres, which could be put over a lamp to put it out. Lighting a lamp to hide it would be absurd.

But on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. Ordinary homes were one room; one lamp on a stand lit the whole house. Not selected people, not only those who deserve it: all in the house.

In the same way, let your light shine before others. The light is the life of the kingdom described in the Beatitudes, and visible in good works.

So that they may see your good works. “Good works” are deeds of love, mercy, honesty and justice that flow from faith (Ephesians 2:10; Titus 2:14). The world should be able to see Christianity, not just hear it.

And give glory to your Father who is in heaven. The purpose is not our glory but God’s. The disciple’s good works are like a window, not a mirror: people look through them to God. Peter says something similar: keep your conduct honourable so that they may see your good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). “Your Father”: the first time in Matthew that Jesus calls God the disciples’ Father. It appears seventeen times in the sermon.

The tension with 6:1. Later Jesus says not to practise righteousness before others to be seen by them (6:1). Is this a contradiction? No. The difference is the motive. In 5:16, the aim is that people glorify God. In 6:1, the aim is to be praised oneself. Show your works when you are tempted to be cowardly; hide them when you are tempted to show off.

Two opposite failures. The two pictures do different jobs, and most of us fail at one or the other. Salt works by being different, quietly and from the inside, largely without announcing itself. Light works by being seen. So there are two ways to fail. The first is the salt that leached away: you are pleasant, entirely assimilated, and nobody around you could name a single thing about your life that would need explaining if there were no God. The second is the lamp under the basket: you are visibly different, honest, unusually kind, unwilling to join the pile-on, and nobody has ever been told why. Everyone thinks you are simply a nice person. The first failure has nothing to say; the second has something to say and never says it.

What does shining actually look like? Mostly it is unglamorous. It is the expense claim that is accurate when nobody checks; declining to join the character assassination without making a speech about it; how you speak to the person who can do nothing for you, the cleaner, the junior, the difficult customer, when there is no audience; being known as the one who tells the truth when it is expensive. None of it needs a platform, and none of it makes you insufferable; people notice it because it is rare. And then the light is simply being ready to say why when the question comes, and it does come to people who live like that. Not a prepared speech, but a plain answer, briefly given: this is what I believe, and this is the difference it has made. Peter adds the manner: with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

What it does not mean. Not that good works alone are enough to bring people to God. People must hear the gospel to believe (Romans 10:14–17). Good works open ears and adorn the message (Titus 2:10), but they are not a substitute for it.

In a sentence. Let your life of good works shine openly, so that people see it and glorify your Father in heaven.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith hidden at work, among neighbours, online? Do one good work today that points beyond you to God.

Where it applies: Your neighbour is in hospital. Organise meals for her family, openly, as a Christian, so that people see a church that loves.

Where it would be wrong: You photograph yourself serving at the food bank and post it so people will admire you. Jesus says let your light shine (v. 16) and also do not do good to be seen (6:1). The difference is the aim: here, that they give glory to your Father; there, that they praise you.

A test. The verse carries its own measure, and it settles the fear of showing off. If the effect of your visible life is that people admire you and never once think about God, the lamp is pointing the wrong way, however bright it is. The aim is that they give glory to your Father.

For worship. A lamp produces no light of its own. It only holds up a flame that was lit from elsewhere, and a lamp that has been dim or dark for years can be lit again this morning. The light is his: God, who said let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). And the end of it all is the Father’s praise. He is so good that when people see even a little of his goodness in his children, they are drawn to glorify him. Blessed be the Father in heaven, whose glory is the goal of every good work.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

parallels.desc: they may see your good deeds and glorify God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–48 — The Law Fulfilled: A Righteousness That Exceeds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses the relationship between his teaching and the law of Moses: he has not come to abolish but to fulfill. He then gives six antitheses — "You have heard... but I say to you" — in which he does not contradict the law but penetrates to its interior logic. Murder begins in anger; adultery begins in the look; divorce fractures the covenant; oaths corrupt speech; retaliation perpetuates violence; hatred divides what love should unite. The section climaxes with the demand: "You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." — a standard no one reaches by effort, which is exactly why it drives us to the Christ who fulfilled the law in our place and to the Spirit who reshapes us from within.
verseByVerse.theology: The antitheses reveal that the law was always concerned with the heart, not merely the external act. Jesus does not introduce a new, stricter morality; he discloses the full depth of what God always intended. The Pharisees' righteousness was wide but shallow — it covered the surface of behavior without reaching the roots of motive and desire. The righteousness Jesus requires exceeds theirs not by adding more external rules but by going deeper into the same terrain. This is why grace must precede the Sermon on the Mount: no one can produce this righteousness by effort; it must be worked in us by the Spirit of the one who fulfilled the law perfectly. To "fulfill" the law (v. 17) is not to abolish it but to bring it to its goal: by his flawless obedience Jesus meets its every demand, in himself he embodies the types and shadows that pointed forward, and at the cross he bears its curse. And the righteousness that "exceeds" the Pharisees comes in two layers — first the perfect righteousness of Christ credited to us through faith, the only righteousness that truly opens the kingdom, and then the real if imperfect righteousness the Spirit grows in a regenerate heart. So the very law that drives the unbeliever to Christ by exposing his sin becomes, for the believer, the shape of a Spirit-empowered life of love. Read this way, the towering standard of verse 48 humbles without crushing: it sends us to Christ for a righteousness we cannot produce, and then to the Spirit who produces it in us.
verseByVerse.examples: The demand for perfection (v. 48) has driven interpreters in two directions: some make it an impossible ideal that drives us to grace; others read it as a call to wholeness or completeness (the Greek teleios can mean "complete" or "mature"). Both are partially right: the standard is God's own character, which we cannot reach by effort, but which the Spirit progressively conforms us to (2 Cor. 3:18). The sermon is both a mirror that shows us our need and a map of the life the Spirit produces in those who have received the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus did not come to abolish the Old Testament law and prophets, but to fulfil them: to bring them to their goal and complete them in himself. Every part of God’s word stands until all that it points to is accomplished.

Do not think that I have come to abolish. Jesus was already being accused of disregarding the law, since he ate with sinners and healed on the Sabbath. He answers the accusation before it is fully made. “Abolish” means to tear down, destroy, set aside.

The Law or the Prophets. The Old Testament Scriptures as a whole (7:12; 22:40). “The Law” is the five books of Moses; “the Prophets” includes the historical books and the prophetic books.

I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. “Fulfil” (plēroō) means to fill up, to complete, to bring to its intended goal. Jesus fulfils the Old Testament in several ways at once. He fulfils its prophecies by bringing them to pass (1:22). He fulfils its commands by obeying them perfectly (3:15). He fulfils its ceremonies (sacrifices, priesthood, temple, purity rules) by being what they foreshadowed (Hebrews 10:1–14; Colossians 2:16–17). And he fulfils its meaning by revealing what the law truly required all along, as he does in verses 21–48. The Old Testament is not cancelled; it reaches its goal in him.

He fulfils its penalty too. There is one more dimension, and it is the deepest. The law does not only command; it curses those who break it. Jesus bore that curse on the cross: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). So he fulfils the law in every direction at once. He keeps its demands by his perfect obedience, he is the substance of its shadows, he bears its penalty in our place, and he opens its full meaning. The law prescribed a righteousness no sinner could produce. Jesus is the one who at last produced it, and he is himself its goal: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4).

For truly, I say to you. “Truly” is amēn. Others said “amen” at the end of a statement, to agree with it. Jesus says it at the start, to affirm his own authority. Only Jesus speaks this way.

Until heaven and earth pass away. As long as the present world lasts.

Not an iota, not a dot. The iota is the smallest Greek letter (corresponding to the Hebrew yod, the smallest Hebrew letter, like an apostrophe). The “dot” (literally “horn”) is a tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. Not even the smallest detail of God’s word will be lost.

Will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Until everything the law points to has happened. Christ accomplished much of it in his life, death and resurrection; the rest will be complete at his return.

Died to the law, and free for it. This is why Paul can say that the believer has died to the law (Romans 7:4–6). He does not mean the law was a mistake. He means that, because Christ has accomplished it and borne it for us, we are released from it as a covenant of works: no longer under its demand to do this and live, and no longer under its condemnation. Yet the law still has work to do. For the one not yet in Christ, it is a guardian that exposes sin, silences every excuse, and drives the sinner to the only Saviour (Galatians 3:24; Romans 3:20). For the one in Christ, it is no longer a ladder to climb, but its moral heart, love for God and neighbour (Romans 13:10; Matthew 22:37–40), remains the shape of the redeemed life. What was once a code demanding from outside, the Spirit now writes on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), so that the righteous requirement of the law is fulfilled in us who walk by the Spirit (Romans 8:3–4). Freed from the law as a way to be saved, we are freed for it as the way of love.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must keep every Old Testament law in the same way Israel did. Jesus himself declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); the sacrifices ended with his once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:18); the temple was replaced by Christ and his people. The Reformed tradition distinguishes the moral law (summed up in the Ten Commandments, reflecting God’s character, still binding), the ceremonial law (fulfilled in Christ, no longer practised), and the civil law of Israel as a nation (expired with that nation, though its general principles of justice remain useful) (Westminster Confession 19.3–5). Every part of the law is still God’s word, and still teaches us, but we read it through Christ. Nor does it mean that we are saved by keeping the law. Christ kept it for us.

Where Christians differ: the law and the Christian. Antinomians hold that the Old Testament law has no role for Christians. Theonomists hold that Israel’s civil laws, including their penalties, should still be applied by nations today. Some in “New Covenant Theology” hold that the Mosaic law as a whole has been replaced by “the law of Christ”. Verdict: the threefold distinction of the Reformed confessions. The moral law remains the rule of life for believers, not to earn salvation, but as the shape of love (Romans 13:8–10).

How dispensationalists read it. Many faithful believers read this passage through dispensational eyes, and they deserve to be heard fairly. They stress a sharper distinction between Israel and the church. On their reading, the Law of Moses was given to Israel as a single code which came to an end for the believer at the cross; the Christian now lives under the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2; 1 Corinthians 9:21), the commands of the New Testament, and so many are wary of the threefold division. Classic dispensationalists also tended to read the sermon chiefly as the ethics of the coming earthly kingdom, though progressive dispensationalists apply it directly to Christian living now. The difference is real, but narrower than it looks. Both sides confess that we are saved by grace through faith and not by law-keeping, that Christ fulfilled the law, and that the law still convicts and drives us to him. In practice both walk the same road of Spirit-empowered love; they chart it differently.

If Christ has fulfilled the law, why should I read Leviticus? Because it is still God’s word, and it is about him. Leviticus shows you how holy God is, how seriously he takes sin, and how costly it is for sinners to come near him. Every sacrifice, every priest, every washing, and the great Day of Atonement are pictures drawn in advance of what Christ would do, and the letter to the Hebrews cannot be understood without them. Its moral laws, like love your neighbour as yourself (Leviticus 19:18), still bind us. Read it asking what it shows of God’s holiness, and how Christ is the sacrifice, the priest and the way in. You will find the cross on every page.

In a sentence. Jesus came not to cancel God’s word but to fulfil it completely, and every part of it stands until all is accomplished.

On a Tuesday. Do you treat the Old Testament as out of date? Read it this week looking for how it points to Christ and how its moral teaching shapes your life.

Where it applies: You come to the tenth commandment and realise that you have been envying your brother’s house and promotion for months. The old commandment still speaks. Confess the coveting, thank God for what he has given you, and ask Christ, who kept the law for you, to make you content.

Where it would be wrong: A friend in your church starts insisting that Christians must keep the food laws and the feasts of Israel to be truly faithful, and you wonder whether he is right. He is not. Those laws were shadows, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17); Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). To bring back the shadows is not to honour the law more but to miss where it was pointing.

For worship. Not a letter of God’s word will fall to the ground, because the one who spoke it is faithful, and the one who came to fulfil it did not leave one stroke undone. Every promise found its yes in him; every shadow found its substance; every command found a man who loved it and kept it; every curse found a substitute who bore it. The law that once only condemned now stands, fulfilled, as a monument to the obedience of the Son. Glory to Christ, the end of the law, who kept it for us and writes it now on our hearts.
verseByVerse.note: The iota is the smallest Greek letter; the “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter. Nothing in the law is too small to matter.

parallels.desc: Christ is the end of the law

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God’s law stands, anyone who weakens even its smallest command and teaches others to do the same will be least in the kingdom. And unless the disciples’ righteousness goes deeper than that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will not enter the kingdom at all.

Therefore. Because the law stands (v. 18).

Whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments. “Relaxes” means loosens, sets aside, treats as not binding. The rabbis distinguished “light” and “heavy” commandments. Jesus agrees that some matter more than others (23:23), but says no command is to be treated lightly.

The great relaxers. There is an irony here, and Jesus surely has the Pharisees in view. The men who looked strictest were in truth the great relaxers. They buried the law under a mountain of extra rules, yet hollowed out its real weight, and at points their traditions cancelled God’s commands. Jesus later exposes exactly this: by the rule of Corban a man could dedicate his money to God and so leave his own aged parents without support, and so they made void the word of God by their tradition (15:3–6; Mark 7:9–13). To keep the letter while killing the heart, and to prize human tradition over God’s clear word, is the worst relaxing of all.

And teaches others to do the same. Teachers carry a special responsibility (James 3:1).

Will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Notice: still in the kingdom, but least. Jesus speaks of degrees of honour within the kingdom. Such a person is not necessarily excluded, but they are at the bottom.

But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great. Doing comes before teaching. A teacher’s life must match his words.

The doers. This is the note James will sound: be doers of the word, and not hearers only (James 1:22). But hear it through the gospel. It is about the direction of a life, not the perfection of it. The great in the kingdom are not the flawless but the sincere: those whose hearts mean to obey, who keep turning back after every stumble, and whose doing springs from grace received, not merit earned.

Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. A shock to the first hearers. The scribes and Pharisees were the most righteous people they knew. They tithed even their garden herbs (23:23), fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12), and kept the Sabbath in minute detail. How could anyone exceed that?

A thunderclap. Feel the shock. When Jesus says you must out-righteous the most righteous men alive or you will never enter the kingdom, the ordinary listener thinks: if they fall short, what hope is there for me? The Pharisee bristles: who is this to say my righteousness is not enough? Jesus means to unsettle them both, to close every road of self-confidence before he opens the only door that works.

Exceeds how? Not in quantity, more rules, but in kind. The Pharisees’ righteousness was largely external: actions, not the heart; the letter, not the spirit; and often done to be seen (6:1–18; 23:25–28). It also tended to lower the law to what could be managed, while adding human traditions (15:1–9). Jesus demands a righteousness of the heart: no anger, no lust, no deceit, no revenge, love for enemies. Verses 21–48 show what he means.

You will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Not “least” but excluded. A merely external religion does not belong to the kingdom.

How can anyone have this righteousness? Start with what Jesus means here. In the sermon itself, the greater righteousness is the righteousness of the heart that he goes on to describe in verses 21–48: no contempt, no lust, no deceit, no revenge, love for enemies. That is what his first hearers would have understood, and we should hear it too. But the standard is so high that Jesus ends the section with, be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (v. 48), and no one meets it. The sermon itself points to the answer: the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit (5:3), and disciples ask daily for forgiveness (6:12). The rest of Scripture then explains how God gives this righteousness, in two ways, held together by the Reformers. First, Christ’s righteousness is credited to those who trust him: he fulfilled the law perfectly in their place (Romans 3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). That is the only righteousness that counts before God’s judgement, and it is the answer to verse 48. Second, God gives his people a new heart and writes his law on it (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that the very righteousness of verses 21–48 really grows in them by the Spirit. This does not earn entry, but it marks those who have entered. Both are gifts. Jesus’ hearers heard the demand; after the cross, we also know the gift that meets it.

What it does not mean. Not that we must out-do the Pharisees by our own efforts to earn heaven. That would make the sermon a crushing burden. The demand drives us first to Christ, whose righteousness is perfect. Nor does it mean that all the Pharisees were hypocrites: some, like Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, came to faith.

Must I still keep the Sabbath, the food laws and the feasts? Read verse 19 with verses 17–18 in hand. Jesus upholds the law’s full authority, but he fulfils it, and its ceremonial parts, the sacrifices, clean and unclean foods and holy days, reach their goal in him. They were a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). We honour those laws not by repeating the shadows but by trusting the one they always pointed to; to rest in Christ is not to relax the law but to keep it at its deepest. On the Sabbath itself, Christians hold different views: some keep the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment, others see the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ’s rest while gladly keeping Sunday for worship. Both agree that a rhythm of rest and worship is God’s good gift.

In a sentence. God’s law must be kept and taught in full, and only a righteousness deeper than the Pharisees’, a righteousness of the heart, belongs to the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Are you content with outward religion: attending, giving, avoiding obvious sins? Ask God to search your heart, and rest your standing on Christ’s righteousness, not yours.

Where it applies: You have never missed a Sunday and you give faithfully, but you have not spoken to your sister in two years. Outward religion is not enough. Ask God to search the heart, rest your standing on Christ, and let the righteousness he grows in you reach your sister this week.

Where it would be wrong: You hear this verse and set out to beat the Pharisees at their own game, adding rules, keeping a tally, and hoping to earn your place. That is the very righteousness Jesus said falls short. The only righteousness that surpasses theirs is Christ’s, received by faith; the heart-obedience that follows is its fruit, not its price (Philippians 3:8–9).

For worship. He sets the bar impossibly high, surpass the holiest people you know, not to crush us but to drive us off our own righteousness and into his. The mountain we could never climb turns out, in Christ, to be first a gift and then a joy. We are not weighed, found wanting and sent away; we are clothed, accepted and changed from the inside out. The Lord Jesus kept every command, the least and the greatest, and taught them perfectly, and he is called great in the kingdom because he is its King. His righteousness is ours by faith, and his Spirit is making it ours in life. Blessed be the Lord our Righteousness (Jeremiah 23:6).

parallels.desc: the righteousness from God that depends on faith

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment." But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, "You fool!" will be liable to the hell of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of six examples. The law said, do not murder. Jesus says that anger and contempt in the heart, and insulting words, are murder at the root, and are just as liable to God’s judgment.

The six antitheses. Verses 21–48 contain six examples, each beginning “You have heard that it was said … But I say to you”. They show what the deeper righteousness of verse 20 looks like. Jesus is not contradicting the law of Moses. He is correcting the way it had been taught and limited, and revealing its full meaning. The issues are anger, lust, divorce, oaths, revenge and love for enemies.

You have heard that it was said to those of old. “You have heard”: most people heard the law read and explained in the synagogue, rather than reading it themselves. “Those of old” are the generations of Moses and after. What they heard included the law itself plus later interpretations.

You shall not murder. The sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13). “Murder” means unlawful killing of a human being.

And whoever murders will be liable to judgment. A summary of the law’s penalty (Exodus 21:12; Numbers 35:16–21), referring to a human court. The popular teaching stopped there: as long as you have not killed anyone, you have kept the commandment.

But I say to you. Jesus speaks on his own authority, as the lawgiver himself. The prophets said, “Thus says the LORD.” Jesus says, “I say to you.”

Everyone who is angry with his brother. Anger is the root of murder. Cain was angry before he killed Abel (Genesis 4:5–8). God sees the heart. “Brother” means a fellow believer, or more widely a fellow human being. The sinful anger Jesus means is the anger of resentment, hatred and contempt. (On righteous anger, see Ephesians 4:26.)

The image of God. Jesus is not adding a new law beside the old but showing what the old law always implied about the worth of a human life. Murder was forbidden because man is made in the image of God (Genesis 9:6). The same reason reaches behind the act to the heart and the tongue. Every contemptuous word is an assault on someone who bears the divine image. With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God (James 3:9). Jesus treats contempt not as a social failing but as a moral catastrophe.

Will be liable to judgment. The same phrase as for murder. Anger is as serious before God’s court as murder is before a human court.

Whoever insults his brother. Literally “says Raca”, an Aramaic insult meaning “empty-head”, “idiot”, a word of contempt.

Will be liable to the council. The Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court.

Whoever says You fool! Greek mōre, from which we get “moron”. In Scripture, the “fool” is a person who is morally and spiritually worthless, who says there is no God (Psalm 14:1). To call someone that is to write them off as beyond value.

Will be liable to the hell of fire. “Hell” is Gehenna, from the Valley of Hinnom, just south of Jerusalem. There, wicked kings of Judah had sacrificed their children to Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Josiah defiled it, and in later tradition it became a picture of God’s final judgment, a place of fire and destruction (Isaiah 66:24). Jesus uses it for the final punishment of the wicked.

Three courts. The first hearers would have felt the climb. Judgment was the local town court; in later Jewish practice a bench of twenty-three judges heard capital cases in a town. The council was the Great Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, seventy-one members, the supreme court of the nation, convened for the gravest cases. And then the valley. Ge-hinnom ran along the south side of the city, and its history was notorious. King Manasseh had burned his sons there as an offering (2 Chronicles 33:6). Josiah defiled it so that it could never be used again. Jeremiah renamed it the Valley of Slaughter, a place of corpses (Jeremiah 7:32), and Isaiah’s last picture of the dead whose worm does not die and whose fire is not quenched (Isaiah 66:24) became attached to it. So the escalation is from the village court, to the supreme tribunal, to the judgment seat of God himself: three courts for three degrees of contempt.

The progression. Anger, then contempt, then writing someone off: the judgment rises from a local court, to the supreme court, to hell itself. Jesus is not setting out a legal code with exact penalties; he is showing that the inner attitudes that lead to murder are themselves deadly before God.

What it does not mean. Not that all anger is sin. Jesus himself was angry at hard-hearted people (Mark 3:5), and God’s wrath is holy. The sin is the anger of personal resentment, contempt and hatred. Nor does it mean that every use of the word “fool” is forbidden: Jesus himself called the Pharisees blind fools (23:17). The issue is contempt, writing a person off, not truthful description of folly. And it does not mean that anger is as harmful to others as murder: murder is worse in its effects, and human courts rightly treat it more severely. But before God, the heart that hates is guilty (1 John 3:15).

How can I tell holy anger from sinful anger? Holy anger is real. God is a God who feels indignation every day (Psalm 7:11), and Jesus drove the traders from his Father’s house. When you hear that a child has been abused and something in you burns, that fire can be right: it is love for the good recoiling at evil. But holy anger is rarer than we like to think, and it has marks. It is stirred by God’s concerns, not by my wounded pride. It stays under control instead of flaring into contempt. It is slow, for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God (James 1:20). And it spends itself in doing good and seeking justice, never in writing a person off. Hold most of our anger up to that test and we find it is really about us: our rights, our comfort, our honour.

If I have spoken in contempt, am I in danger of hell? The warning describes the settled heart of contempt, the kind that never repents and is never broken, and it is meant to frighten us out of it. But it is also exactly the kind of sin the gospel exists to forgive. A believer who has spoken in anger is not condemned (Romans 8:1). He is to see it for what it is, confess it without excuse, and go and put it right, which is where the next verses lead. No one can say, I have never murdered, so I am safe. That is the point: Jesus closes every escape route so that everyone must come to him for mercy, and he has mercy.

What do I do the next time anger rises? First, be slow. Do not speak or type in the heat; a soft answer turns away wrath (Proverbs 15:1). Second, look underneath it. Ask what was really threatened, and you will usually find bruised pride or a cherished comfort rather than the glory of God; name it honestly to him. Third, take the anger to God before you take it to the person. Pour it out to him and leave room for his justice (Romans 12:19). Fourth, remember the gospel: you are the servant forgiven an unpayable debt (18:21–35), and that memory melts contempt into mercy. Then move toward the person: forgive, bless, and where you can, be reconciled. When you fail, do not despair. Confess it, receive fresh forgiveness, and let the Spirit go on retraining your heart.

In a sentence. God judges not only murder but the anger and contempt in the heart from which murder grows.

On a Tuesday. Whom do you secretly despise or write off? Contempt for a colleague, a politician or a family member is murder at the root. Confess it and ask God to replace it with love.

Where it applies: Your brother mocks your faith at dinner, and the word “idiot” forms in your head. Refuse it, in words and in thought. Contempt is the root of murder.

Where it would be wrong: You hear that a friend’s child is being mistreated, and you feel angry. That anger is not sin. Jesus was angry at hard hearts (Mark 3:5), and Paul says be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26). The question is whether the anger is about God’s honour and others’ good, or my wounded pride, and whether it moves me to put things right or to lash out.

For worship. The cross shows both things at once: that our anger and contempt deserved the court of God and the fire of the valley, and that Christ went into that judgment for us. He was called a fool and worse; he was spat on and struck and mocked by men whose hearts were full of murder, and he answered them with a prayer for their forgiveness. The Judge of all the earth took the sentence on himself. And the God who sees every hidden flash of contempt has not written us off. He calls us brothers, and gives us a new heart that can love those we once despised. Glory to the Lord who was despised so that we would not be lost.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “insults” renders the Aramaic term of abuse Raca. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice. “The council” is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom
everyone who hates his brother is a murderer

verseByVerse.quote: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because anger matters so much to God, reconciliation is urgent. If you are about to worship and remember that someone has a grievance against you, leave your offering and go to make peace first, then come back and offer it.

So. Because anger is so serious (vv. 21–22).

If you are offering your gift at the altar. A sacrifice brought to the temple in Jerusalem. For a Galilean, the journey to Jerusalem took about three days. Jesus imagines someone who has made the long journey, is standing in the temple court, about to hand his animal to the priest.

And there remember that your brother has something against you. Notice: not that you have something against him, but that he has something against you. You have wronged him, or he thinks you have. Your responsibility is to take the initiative.

Both directions. Put this beside 18:15 and the net is complete. If someone sins against you, you are to go to him (18:15). If you have sinned against someone, you are to go to him (here). Neither the wronged nor the wrongdoer is left an excuse to sit still. Love takes the first step from both sides.

Leave your gift there before the altar and go. Startling. Leave the sacrifice, travel home, and deal with the relationship. God values reconciliation more than ritual. The prophets taught the same: God desires mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; 1 Samuel 15:22).

The sequence. Remember, leave, go, be reconciled, return. The gift waits at the altar while the broken relationship is attended to, because the God to whom the gift is offered cares more about the brother than the offering. The animal can wait three days. The brother cannot.

First be reconciled to your brother. “First” is the key word. Worship and broken relationships do not belong together. John says that whoever does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20).

And then come and offer your gift. Worship is not cancelled; it is postponed until it can be offered with integrity.

What does being reconciled actually look like? Go, and go humbly. Name the specific wrong plainly: I was wrong to speak to you the way I did. Do not dress it up, excuse it, or smuggle in blame; no “I’m sorry if you were offended”, no “but you started it”. Own it, show real sorrow, and ask the costly little question pride hates: will you forgive me? Where damage can be repaired or repaid, repair it. And the brother, for his part, is called to forgive as God in Christ forgave him (Ephesians 4:32), and then to keep his word: not to rake it up again, hold it over you, or rehearse it to others. Forgiveness is a promise to bury the matter, as God remembers our sins no more (Jeremiah 31:34).

What it does not mean. Not that we cannot worship until every conflict is resolved, which in some cases is impossible because the other person refuses. Paul says, if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). Our part is to make the effort. Nor is the point about the temple: for Christians today, the same principle applies to prayer, the Lord’s Supper and public worship (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).

What if I go and he will not be reconciled? Then you are free. So far as it depends on you: you are answerable for your own part, an honest confession and a genuine reaching out, not for the other person’s response, which you cannot control. Having truly sought peace, you may come and worship with a clear conscience, leaving your brother in God’s hands and ready to be reconciled the moment the door opens. Another’s unforgiveness can grieve you, but it cannot hold your worship hostage.

In a sentence. Reconciliation with those you have wronged comes before worship, because God cares more about relationships than ritual.

On a Tuesday. Before you next go to church or take the Lord’s Supper, ask: is there anyone who has something against me? Make the call, write the message, or go.

Where it applies: You snapped at a friend last week, and she has gone quiet. Send the message before Sunday: “I was wrong. Will you forgive me?”

Where it would be wrong: The person you wronged has asked you not to contact them, or meeting would put you in danger, for example with a violent former partner. You are not required to force a meeting. Do what depends on you (Romans 12:18): perhaps a letter, or putting right what you can through someone else, and leave the rest with God.

For worship. God himself did not wait for us to make the first move. We were the ones in the wrong, and he was the one who came. He left the glory of heaven, travelled further than any pilgrim, and did what was needed to be reconciled to us, at the cost of his Son. Now every gift we bring him rests on that reconciliation. He wants our worship, and he wants it whole, with our brothers beside us, because he is making a family and not only a congregation. Blessed be the God who has reconciled us to himself through Christ and given us the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18).
verseByVerse.note: The gift at the altar is a sacrifice brought to the temple.

parallels.desc: forgive, so that your Father may forgive you
so far as it depends on you

verseByVerse.quote: Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settle disputes quickly, before they reach court, while you still can. If you wait, the judge will decide against you and you will pay in full. Behind the picture is a warning about God’s judgment: be reconciled now, while there is time.

Come to terms quickly with your accuser. Make friends, settle, come to an agreement. The accuser is someone suing you, perhaps for a debt.

While you are going with him to court. In the ancient world, a creditor could drag a debtor to the judge. There was still time on the way.

Lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard. The process of law: once it starts, it cannot be stopped. The guard is the court officer who carries out the sentence.

And you be put in prison. Debtors’ prison was common in the Roman world: a debtor was imprisoned until the debt was paid, often by family.

You will never get out until you have paid the last penny. The “penny” (kodrantēs, Latin quadrans) was the smallest Roman coin, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage. Every last bit must be paid.

Two levels. First, practical wisdom: settle disputes quickly, even at a cost, rather than let them escalate. Second, a deeper warning. In Matthew, a judge, prison and full payment often picture God’s final judgment (18:34–35). The point is urgency: we are all on our way to God’s court. Be reconciled with others now, and above all be reconciled with God now, while there is time (2 Corinthians 5:20; 6:2).

The window is open now. Jesus constantly frames the urgency of repentance this way: a limited time, and then a judgment from which there is no appeal. The road to the courthouse is still running. The wise person settles while settlement is still possible, with his brother and with his God, because it will not always be open.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never use courts or stand up for justice. Paul appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11). But Christians should not be quick to sue, especially fellow believers (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). Nor does “until you have paid the last penny” teach purgatory, as some Roman Catholic interpreters have argued, a place where believers pay off their sins after death before entering heaven. Christ has paid the debt of believers in full (Colossians 2:13–14); there is no purgatory in Scripture.

But does “until” not imply a release? It is a fair question, and three things answer it. First, the kind of speech: Jesus is urging two men to settle before they reach the court, with the most ordinary scene imaginable. Doctrine cannot be read off the furniture of a parable; by that method another story would teach that God helps people only to stop them pestering him (Luke 18:1–8), the opposite of its meaning. Second, the idiom: a man in a debtors’ prison could not earn. That was the whole horror of it. So “until you have paid” is not a release date but a closed door, the way we say when pigs fly. Third, what the debt of sin cost. It was never a sum to be worked off by degrees in this life or another. It was paid in one payment by someone else, who cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30). A purgatory implies that something was still outstanding when he said it.

In a sentence. Settle disputes quickly, because delay makes things worse, and we are all on our way to God’s court.

On a Tuesday. Is there a dispute you are letting drag on out of pride? Settle it, even if it costs you something.

Where it applies: Your neighbour claims your fence is a foot over the boundary. Instead of solicitors and years of bitterness, offer to share the cost of a survey and accept the result, even if you lose a little ground.

Where it would be wrong: A company is cheating many customers, or a settlement would require you to keep silent about abuse. Then settling quickly is not the godly course. You may need to see it through, for the sake of others and of justice (Proverbs 31:8–9). Settle your own quarrels quickly; do not sell out someone else’s cause to do it.

For worship. The settling Jesus wants with God is not the first instalment of a payment plan. It is the empty-handed surrender of a man who has finally understood that he cannot pay, throwing himself on the mercy of the one who already has. Our debt was not a penny but ten thousand talents, and the Judge himself paid it. He cancelled the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). No prison waits for those who are in Christ, because their account was settled in full on a hill outside Jerusalem. Glory to the Judge who became the payment.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” (Latin quadrans) was a small Roman copper coin, worth about 1/64 of a denarius.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall not commit adultery." But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second example. The law said, do not commit adultery. Jesus says that looking at a woman with the purpose of desiring her sexually is adultery already committed in the heart.

You have heard that it was said, You shall not commit adultery. The seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14). Adultery is sexual intercourse between a married person and someone other than their spouse. The popular teaching limited the command to the act itself: as long as you have not slept with another man’s wife, you are innocent.

But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent. The Greek is literally “looks at a woman in order to desire her”. It is not a passing glance or an involuntary thought, but a deliberate look aimed at sexual desire, feeding the imagination. The tenth commandment already forbade coveting your neighbour’s wife (Exodus 20:17). Job made a covenant with his eyes not to gaze at a virgin (Job 31:1).

Has already committed adultery with her in his heart. God sees the heart. What is entertained in the imagination is sin before him, even if it never becomes an act. The heart is where adultery begins (15:19).

Covenant love begins in the eyes. This demolishes every defence that stops at I have not done anything. The inner life is the domain of God’s law as much as the outward act. It also shows what adultery really is: the violation of covenant love, which begins not with the body but with the heart’s refusal to honour the exclusive claim of marriage. Faithfulness in marriage is a matter of the eyes and the heart, not only of the bedroom. And the look Jesus forbids uses another person, made in God’s image, as an object for one’s own gratification.

Why the man? In that culture, men had more freedom and power, and women were often blamed for men’s lust. Jesus puts the responsibility squarely on the one who looks. The principle applies equally to women.

What it does not mean. Not that noticing someone is attractive is sin, or that every sexual thought that comes into the mind is adultery. As with all temptation (see 4:1 and Ephesians 5:3), the first thought is not yet sin; it is entertaining it, dwelling on it, and feeding it that is sin. Luther said that you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them nesting in your hair. Nor does it condemn sexual desire itself, which God created good, for its proper place in marriage (Song of Songs; 1 Corinthians 7:3–5). Nor does it mean that lust in the heart is as harmful to others as adultery committed, or that a person who has lusted might as well commit the act. The act adds betrayal, harm to others, and often children and broken families. But before God, both are sin, and both need forgiveness.

Tempted is not the same as sinning. God made beauty, and the eye that registers it is working as he designed. The first, involuntary glance is not sin, any more than the arrival of a tempting thought. Our Lord himself in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). What Jesus condemns is the second look that becomes a lingering, the desire deliberately fed, the imagination invited to stay and feast. The bird is the temptation; the nest is the sin.

Today. In an age of pornography and sexualised advertising, this word cuts deep. Pornography is exactly what Jesus describes: looking at someone in order to desire them sexually. It is not harmless; it is adultery of the heart, and it exploits real people.

Why do I still feel guilty when I have looked away? Often the guilt is false. Suppose your eyes keep being drawn where they should not linger, and you look away, and then walk off weighed down with guilt. Hear this clearly: the looking away is not your failure but your obedience, a small daily victory, and heaven is not frowning at it. Much of that burden is false guilt, the accuser heaping condemnation on someone who actually fought and won, and there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Where you did let the gaze linger and feed, do not wallow. Confess it at once, receive the cleansing already promised (1 John 1:9), and walk on forgiven.

How do I fight it? Scripture hands you tools. Make Job’s covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1): decide in advance what you will not look at. Bounce the glance away quickly, and flee rather than negotiate (2 Timothy 2:22). Do not merely suppress the thought but replace it: turn the heart to Christ, give thanks to God, even breathe a prayer for that person as a soul you will meet at the judgment, not an object to be used. Bring it into the light with a trusted Christian friend. And deepest of all, the cure for a wandering eye is a captured heart. As Christ becomes your greater treasure and joy, purity grows less from gritted teeth and more from love.

In a sentence. Deliberately looking at someone in order to desire them sexually is adultery in the heart before God.

On a Tuesday. What do your eyes linger on, on your phone, on the street, on screens? Turn away from the second look. And if you have fallen, there is forgiveness in Christ; confess it to God, and if it is a habit, to a trusted Christian friend.

Where it applies: A suggestive image appears in your feed during the lunch break. Do not scroll back to it. Close the app, thank God for your wife or for the purity he is growing in you, and get on with your sandwich. That is the whole battle, won in three seconds.

Where it would be wrong: A young man is so frightened by this verse that he treats every woman at church as a danger, will not speak to her or look her in the eye, and calls it purity. Jesus forbids the look that feeds lust, not ordinary friendship and courtesy. Treat younger women as sisters, in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2): sisters are spoken to and cared for, not avoided.

For worship. The only man who ever lived with a perfectly pure heart looked on every person he met as his Father’s image-bearer, and he loved the woman at the well and the woman caught in adultery without one stained thought. He bore our impurity on the cross, and he gives his Spirit to make us clean from the inside. The aim is not that we never feel temptation, but that we grow more satisfied in our Saviour, until the day we see the Bridegroom face to face and need nothing else. Lift your head: he who calls you to purity has already made you his, and he is faithful.

parallels.desc: you shall not covet your neighbour’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deal with sin radically. If your eye or hand leads you into sin, cut it off. It is better to lose something precious than for your whole self to be thrown into hell.

If your right eye causes you to sin. “Causes you to sin” (skandalizei) means trips you up, makes you stumble, like the bait-stick of a trap. The right eye and right hand were considered the most valuable. The eye connects with lustful looking (v. 28); the hand with what we do.

The best faculty. Even your best faculty, your sharpest tool, the favoured eye and the working hand, must be surrendered if it has become the instrument of your fall. Jesus is not asking us to give up obvious evils only, but to part with anything, however valued, that keeps leading us into sin. Nothing is too precious to lose in this war.

Tear it out and throw it away. Jesus is using deliberate exaggeration, a vivid way of speaking common in Jewish teaching. He does not mean literal self-mutilation. Even with one eye, a person can still lust; the problem is the heart (15:19). The early church condemned Origen, a third-century scholar, for literally castrating himself on the basis of a similar verse (19:12). Jesus means: take decisive, costly action to remove whatever leads you into sin.

The price of the exchange. The decisive argument is inside the passage. Jesus has just spent six verses moving sin from the act to the desire behind it. A remedy that dealt only with the limb would contradict what he said a breath before. What the exaggeration does is set a price. If it came to a choice between a maimed life and a lost soul, the arithmetic is not close, and most of us have never once made a decision at anything like that rate of exchange. Picture a surgeon and a gangrenous limb. No one enjoys losing a hand, but no one haggles with gangrene.

For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. The logic is simple: if surgery saves your life, you accept the loss. Losing something you value is better than losing everything. Sin is that serious, and hell is that real.

What “cutting off” means today. Removing the internet from your phone, installing filters and accountability, ending a relationship that leads you into sin, changing your route home to avoid a bar, cancelling a subscription, refusing to be alone with a certain person, changing jobs if necessary. Paul calls it putting to death what is earthly in you (Colossians 3:5) and making no provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14).

Before the moment, not during it. Notice when the cutting happens. Obedience here means removing what feeds the sin at real cost, before the moment of temptation rather than in the middle of it: the account deleted, the route changed, the friendship ended, the device left downstairs, the bottle poured away. Every one of those is somebody’s right hand: genuinely useful, genuinely missed, and genuinely the thing that keeps the wound open.

What it does not mean. Not literal self-harm. Nor that we can make ourselves holy by removing temptations alone; the heart must be changed by the Spirit (Romans 8:13). But the Spirit works through our decisive obedience. Nor does it mean that a believer who struggles will certainly be lost: the warning is that a life of unrepented, cherished sin leads to hell, and true believers take such warnings seriously and fight.

Is there hope for me if I have cut things off and still fall? Yes. Notice where this paragraph sits: twenty-six verses after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to the spiritually bankrupt, in a sermon preached by the one who would shortly be cut off in the place of everyone listening. The severity is real, and it is not the last word. Keep fighting, keep confessing, and keep running to Christ. Ask whether something is still feeding the sin that you have not yet cut off, and bring a mature Christian into the fight. Some battles last years. The Christian who falls and gets up again, hating the sin, is not the person this warning describes.

In a sentence. Take drastic action against whatever leads you into sin, because losing it is better than losing yourself.

On a Tuesday. What is the “eye” or “hand” in your life, the thing that repeatedly leads you into sin? What would it cost to cut it off? Do it today.

Where it applies: If you keep falling into sin on your phone late at night, the phone goes in the kitchen at ten. If that is not enough, change to a basic phone. Cut off whatever feeds the sin.

Where it would be wrong: Someone takes these words literally and thinks of harming their body. Jesus is not asking for that. He speaks in vivid exaggeration, and sin comes from the heart, not the eye (15:19). If you find yourself thinking of hurting yourself, tell someone and seek help today.

For worship. Jesus speaks so sternly of hell because he was about to go into its darkness for us. The one who never sinned with eye or hand had his hands nailed and his eyes darkened, and he was cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of his people (Isaiah 53:8). He was thrown out so that we could be brought in whole. And now he gives the Spirit, by whom we put to death the deeds of the body and live. Glory to the Saviour who loved us too much to leave us comfortable in what was killing us.
verseByVerse.note: The right eye and hand were thought the more valuable. Jesus is using deliberate exaggeration to demand radical action against sin, not self-mutilation.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: It was also said, "Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce." But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third example. People took the law about the certificate of divorce as permission to divorce easily. Jesus says that divorce, except for sexual immorality, makes a person complicit in adultery. Marriage is meant to be permanent.

It was also said, Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce. A summary of Deuteronomy 24:1–4. That law did not command or approve divorce; it regulated it. It required a husband who sent his wife away to give her a written certificate, which protected her by freeing her to remarry, and it forbade him to take her back after she had married another. Jesus later explains that Moses allowed divorce because of the hardness of people’s hearts, but from the beginning it was not so (19:8).

The debate in Jesus’ day. Deuteronomy 24:1 allows divorce when a husband finds “some indecency” in his wife. The rabbis argued about what this meant. The school of Shammai said it meant only serious sexual sin. The school of Hillel said it could mean anything that displeased the husband, even burning his food; the later teacher Akiba said it could mean finding someone prettier. In practice, divorce was easy for men, and women were left vulnerable.

Who was hurt. Divorce had become casual and one-sided. A man could hand his wife a certificate and send her off for the flimsiest reason, and she was left shamed and often destitute, for a woman alone had almost no way to live. When Jesus speaks here he is not being harsh on the weak; he is defending them. He is taking the side of the woman sent away with a piece of paper.

But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife. Jesus returns to God’s original design: one man and one woman, becoming one flesh, for life (Genesis 2:24; 19:4–6). What God has joined, let no one separate.

A covenant, not a contract. Marriage is not a contract to be ended when it stops suiting one party; it is a covenant made before God, and its breaking is not a legal technicality but a moral rupture. It is meant to be a living picture of God’s own faithfulness to his people, and of Christ’s love for the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). That is why Jesus guards it so fiercely.

Except on the ground of sexual immorality. “Sexual immorality” (porneia) is a broad word for sexual sin, including adultery. Where one partner has broken the marriage covenant by sexual unfaithfulness, divorce is permitted, though not commanded. Forgiveness and restoration are better where possible (Hosea).

Makes her commit adultery. In that culture, a divorced woman would almost always need to remarry to survive. A husband who divorced his wife without just cause effectively pushed her into another marriage that, in God’s eyes, was adulterous, because the first marriage had not been rightly ended. The husband bears the guilt.

And whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. That is, a woman divorced without just cause. Her marriage to her first husband is, before God, still binding.

The hinge of the exception. Does this forbid every divorced person from ever remarrying? Not quite, and the hinge is the small phrase except on the ground of sexual immorality. By making an exception, Jesus shows that there is a ground on which a marriage is truly broken, where divorce is permitted and a later remarriage is not adultery. So the sweeping words about remarriage are aimed at remarriage after an unjust, groundless divorce.

What it does not mean. Not that divorced people are second-class Christians or beyond God’s forgiveness. Divorce, like every sin, can be forgiven, and many divorced people were the wronged party. Nor does it mean that a person must stay in a marriage where they or their children are in danger. Separation for safety is not the same as divorce, and the church must protect the vulnerable. Nor does Jesus’ word mean that the innocent party in a marriage broken by adultery sins by divorcing.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Roman Catholic teaching holds that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, so divorce and remarriage are not permitted (though annulments are granted). Some Protestants hold that divorce is permitted for adultery, but remarriage is not. Others allow divorce and remarriage widely. The Westminster Confession (24.5–6) holds that adultery, and wilful desertion by an unbelieving spouse that cannot be remedied (1 Corinthians 7:15), are the only grounds for divorce, and that the innocent party may remarry. Verdict: the Westminster position. Marriage is lifelong; divorce is permitted only for sexual unfaithfulness or desertion; and the innocent party is free to remarry. Each case needs careful, compassionate pastoral wisdom.

What does sexual immorality cover? The word is broad. It includes adultery and other serious sexual sins that break the marriage covenant in the same way. Some take it more narrowly, of unfaithfulness during betrothal, or of a marriage within forbidden degrees of kinship. The broader reading is the more likely. And permission is not command: where there is repentance, forgiveness and reconciliation remain the better path, as Hosea took back his unfaithful wife (Hosea 3:1).

Why do Mark and Luke leave out the exception? Most likely because they state the general rule, while Matthew, writing for Jewish readers who knew the debates about divorce, records the exception everyone assumed (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18). Those who hold that remarriage is never permitted while a former spouse lives rely on these shorter texts, on Paul’s statement that a wife is bound while her husband lives (Romans 7:2–3; 1 Corinthians 7:39), and on many early church fathers. Their view deserves respect, but it leaves Jesus’ exception without a clear meaning.

What about violence and abuse? Two things must be said plainly. First, without any hedging: an abused spouse must get to safety. God never calls anyone to remain in danger, and the church must protect, never pressure. Call the police and tell the elders. Second, whether brutal, persistent, unrepentant abuse amounts to the wilful desertion the Confession speaks of is a question for the elders to weigh carefully in each case.
