Because the man with a full bank account needs it as much as anyone, perhaps more, since wealth tempts us to forget that every loaf comes from the Father’s open hand. Money in the bank cannot make your heart beat, hold off illness or secure tomorrow; rich and poor alike live each day on mercy. That is why Proverbs prays to be kept from riches as well as poverty, lest I be full and deny the LORD (Proverbs 30:9). To ask for daily bread when the cupboard is stocked is to confess gladly that it is all a gift. And under this one word you may bring everything today requires: health and work, wisdom for the meeting, patience with the children, courage for the hard conversation.

In a sentence. Ask your Father each day for the things you need for that day, and trust him for tomorrow.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your next meal before you eat it, and remember those who will pray this prayer today with empty cupboards. How might you be God’s answer to their prayer?

Where it applies: You pray for your daily bread, then thank God for your wages when they arrive. He answered through your job.

Where it would be wrong: Someone stops looking for work and says God will provide. God gives daily bread, ordinarily through work (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). Praying for bread is not a reason to stop earning it.

For worship. The God who fed Israel in the wilderness for forty years, a fresh gift every morning, still opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing (Psalm 145:16). He feeds the ravens and clothes the fields, and he does not grow tired of his children asking. And he has given more than bread. The Son came down from heaven as the true bread, broken so that the world might live, and whoever comes to him will never hunger. Blessed be the Father who gives us this day our daily bread, and who gave us his Son.

parallels.desc: feed me with the food that is needful for me

verseByVerse.quote: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Next: forgive us our sins, which are like debts we owe God, just as we have forgiven those who have sinned against us. Those who are forgiven must forgive.

And forgive us. We need forgiveness as much as we need bread. Every believer must pray this daily. Even forgiven Christians still sin and need to come back to their Father for cleansing (1 John 1:8–9).

Our debts. Sin pictured as a debt. We owe God perfect love and obedience; every sin is a failure to pay what we owe, adding to an unpayable debt (18:24). Luke’s version says “sins” (Luke 11:4). The traditional English form “trespasses” comes from verses 14–15. To forgive a debt is to cancel it: the creditor bears the loss. God can cancel our debt because Christ paid it (Colossians 2:13–14).

Debts or trespasses? Matthew’s word is opheilēmata, the ordinary commercial term for what is owed. Behind it stands the Aramaic Jesus spoke, in which the word for a debt had long been used for a sin. The familiar trespasses reached most English speakers through Tyndale and the Book of Common Prayer, and it is a fair rendering, though something is lost. A trespass is a line crossed. A debt is a sum outstanding, and it goes on being outstanding whether or not anyone mentions it. That is the more uncomfortable picture, and the truer one. Sin is not only a series of boundary violations, each over when it is over. It is an account that accumulates.

As we also have forgiven our debtors. Not that our forgiving earns God’s forgiveness. Rather, a person who has received God’s forgiveness will forgive others. The tense in Greek suggests we have already forgiven before we ask. We cannot honestly ask God to forgive our vast debt while we hold others to their small debts against us (18:21–35). This is the only request in the prayer that Jesus explains further (vv. 14–15). It is that important.

Settle it downstairs first. The past tense settles the question: not as we promise to forgive, nor as we are willing to if pressed, but as we have forgiven. The petition assumes a person comes to God having already dealt with what he holds against others. It is the same order as 5:23–24: leave the gift, go and be reconciled, and then come and offer it.

What it does not mean. Not that forgiveness depends on our performance, as if God forgives us in exact proportion to our forgiving others. That would be salvation by works. God forgives freely, for Christ’s sake. But the unwillingness to forgive shows a heart that has not truly grasped grace. Nor does forgiving someone mean pretending they did nothing wrong, trusting them again immediately, or removing all consequences (see Ephesians 4:32).

If I am already forgiven, why ask for forgiveness every day? Because two things must be held apart. Our standing before God as forgiven children, our justification, is settled once for all by faith in Christ and cannot be lost (Romans 8:1). But our daily fellowship with the Father is like a child’s warmth with a parent: it is chilled by sin left unconfessed, and by bitterness held on to. So the child does not ask to be adopted again every morning; he comes to his Father and says sorry, and is cleansed and restored (1 John 1:9). Daily confession is not insecurity. It is how forgiven children live at home.

In a sentence. Ask God to forgive your sins, as those who have already forgiven others.

On a Tuesday. When you pray this today, name the person you find hard to forgive. Ask God for grace to cancel the debt.

Where it applies: You pray the Lord’s Prayer at church on Sunday, and at the words as we forgive our debtors your brother-in-law’s face comes to mind. Stop there. Tell God you release him from what he owes you, and ask for grace to mean it when you see him at the next family lunch.

Where it would be wrong: You are so afraid of praying this petition dishonestly that you leave it out, or stop praying the Lord’s Prayer altogether until you feel you have forgiven everyone perfectly. Do not. Pray it, and let it do its work on you; tell God honestly where you are struggling, and ask him to make you willing. The prayer is a gift for weak forgivers, not a test only the strong can pass.

For worship. So if forgiving feels impossibly hard, do not grit your teeth and try to earn heaven by it. Go back and look again at the mountain of debt God cancelled at the cross. He did not forgive by pretending the debt was small. He paid it in full, in his Son, and tore up the record. A heart melted by that mercy becomes, almost without trying, a heart that gives mercy away. Blessed be the God who forgives all our iniquity, and who removes our transgressions from us as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:3, 12).
verseByVerse.note: Sin is pictured as a debt owed to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally: do not bring us into the place of testing where we would fall, but rescue us from evil and the evil one. Believers know they are weak, and ask their Father to protect them.

And lead us not into temptation. The word (peirasmos) means both testing and temptation (see 4:1). God does not tempt anyone to sin (James 1:13). But he does lead his people into testing: he led Jesus into the wilderness (4:1), and he tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1). The request means: do not let us be brought into trials that overwhelm us; keep us from situations where we would fall. It is the prayer of someone who knows their weakness and does not trust themselves. Jesus told the disciples in Gethsemane to watch and pray that they might not enter into temptation (26:41). Peter, who boasted he would never fall, fell that same night.

No bravado. It is a striking thing for the Lord to teach. He does not tell his disciples to pray for courage under trial, or for strength to prevail. He tells them to ask not to be tried at all, and then, when it comes anyway, to ask to be got out. There is no bravado anywhere in it. The prayer owns our fragility and casts the whole burden of protection on the Father.

But deliver us from evil. “Deliver” means rescue, snatch away from danger. “Evil” can be translated “the evil one”, the devil (the ESV footnote). Both are possible. The devil is the tempter (4:3); evil is his work. Either way, we need rescuing, and only God can rescue us.

Dragged clear. Deliver is a strong verb: to drag out of, to pull somebody clear of something that has hold of them. The prayer ends where it began, in dependence on the Father, not in self-confidence.

The doxology. Many later manuscripts add “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen.” This ending is not in the earliest manuscripts, and it was probably added in early church worship, following David’s prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:11. It is a fitting, biblical ending, and the church rightly uses it in worship, but it was probably not part of what Matthew wrote.

Why does my Bible put the ending in a footnote? Because the oldest and best manuscripts of Matthew do not have it; it appears in later copies. The early church, praying this prayer aloud in worship, very probably added a fitting note of praise at the close, in words that echo David’s, yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory (1 Chronicles 29:11), and over time that response was copied into the text. So it was probably not part of what Matthew wrote, but there is nothing wrong with praying it. It is thoroughly biblical, and it ends the prayer where the prayer means to end: not on our need or the evil one’s threat, but on the Father. Pray it freely, and know why your Bible sets it in a footnote. No teaching of the faith depends on it.

What it does not mean. Not that God might lure us into sin if we do not ask him not to. He never does that. Nor does the prayer promise that believers will never face temptation or trials: James says to count it all joy when you meet trials (James 1:2), because they strengthen faith. God promises that with every temptation he will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). The prayer asks him to keep us, in and through testing.

In a sentence. Ask your Father to keep you from testing that would overwhelm you, and to rescue you from evil and the evil one.

On a Tuesday. Where do you know you are weak? Pray this request about that specific area before you enter the day, and avoid walking into the temptation you are praying against.

Where it applies: You know that business trips are where you are most tempted to drink too much and flirt. Pray this petition before you leave, then ask for a room away from the bar, and ring home every evening. Praying and avoiding go together.

Where it would be wrong: You are so afraid of trials that you refuse a hard but right calling, a difficult job or a move abroad for the gospel, and tell yourself you are praying lead us not into temptation. The prayer asks God to keep you from falling, not to excuse you from obedience. He led his own Son into the wilderness, and he will be with you in the hard place he sends you (1 Corinthians 10:13).

For worship. Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, for ever. Amen. The Son who taught this prayer went into the wilderness and into Gethsemane, faced the evil one at full strength, and did not fall. Where Peter slept, he watched and prayed; where we are tempted and give way, he was tempted and stood. And on the cross he disarmed the powers and triumphed over them. Our deliverance does not depend on how strong we are, but on how strong he is, and he is the one who keeps us from stumbling and will present us blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). The kingdom, the power and the glory are his.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “the evil one,” and that some manuscripts add “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen.”

parallels.desc: God will not let you be tempted beyond your ability
keep them from the evil one

verseByVerse.quote: For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus explains the request about forgiveness. If you forgive others, your Father will forgive you. But if you refuse to forgive others, your Father will not forgive you.

For if you forgive others their trespasses. “Trespasses” (paraptōmata) means false steps, wrongs (see Ephesians 2:1). Jesus returns to the one request that needs comment.

Your heavenly Father will also forgive you. Those who forgive show that they belong to the forgiven family.

But if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. A solemn warning. Someone who refuses to forgive cannot have truly received God’s forgiveness, because grace received makes a person gracious. The parable of the unforgiving servant (18:23–35) shows the logic: the servant who was forgiven ten thousand talents and then choked a fellow servant over a hundred denarii proved he had never understood the forgiveness he had received.

The order. God’s forgiveness comes first; ours flows from it. Paul says, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32). Our forgiveness of others is not the cause of God’s forgiveness, but its fruit and evidence.

Forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same. A command this sharp needs one thing said clearly, because confusion about it has done real damage to real people. Jesus is commanding forgiveness. Forgiveness is one-sided: you can do it whatever the other person does, and you are told to. Reconciliation takes two, and it depends on the other person’s repentance. Jesus himself puts the condition on the second: if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3). And Paul writes, with a realism worth noticing, if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). He knew it would not always be possible, and he did not lay the failure at the door of the one who tried.

What am I actually being asked to do? To forgive is to give up your right to collect: to cancel the debt, to stop rehearsing the offence, to refuse to make the person pay in the small currencies we actually use for it, the cold silence, the story retold to a friend, the reminder produced at the useful moment. That is a decision rather than a feeling, and it usually has to be made again tomorrow. You are not being asked to say it did not matter; the cross is the measure of how much it mattered. You are not asked to feel warmly, or to stop the memory hurting. You are not required to hand trust back as though nothing had happened; trust is rebuilt slowly, where there is real change. You are not obliged to stay within reach of someone who is still harming you or your children. And you are not obliged to shield an offender from lawful consequences; reporting a crime is not revenge.

What if they are not sorry and never will be? You can still release your own claim. The Lord did it in front of you from the cross, praying for men who had not repented that afternoon. What waits on their repentance is not your forgiveness but the restored relationship, and that may never come. That is a grief, and it is not your sin.

What it does not mean. Not that a Christian who struggles to forgive, or who has to forgive the same hurt many times, is unforgiven. Forgiveness of deep wounds is often a long process, and Jesus’ words are aimed at a settled refusal to forgive, not at the struggle. Nor does it mean that forgiving others earns salvation. God forgives freely, for Christ’s sake, those who come to him in repentance; and repentance includes letting go of our grudges against others. And forgiveness does not require us to deny the wrong, to trust the other person again immediately, or to stop seeking justice through proper authority.

How do I know whether I have really forgiven? The test is not that the wound has stopped aching, nor that you never think of it. It is whether you have stopped wanting the person’s ruin and stopped trying to collect. If you cannot get there yet, do not pretend otherwise to God. Tell him plainly that you are unable, and ask him to make you willing to be made willing; that prayer is honest, and he has never despised it. This command was never a demand to feel differently by Friday. It is the slow work of a heart being melted by a mercy it never deserved, and the melting is his to do.

In a sentence. Those who have truly received God’s forgiveness will forgive others; a settled refusal to forgive shows that grace has not been received.

On a Tuesday. Is there a grudge you are nursing? Bring it to God today, remembering how much he has forgiven you.

Where it applies: A friend gossiped about you, and has apologised. Forgive her, and do not bring it up again, to her, to others or to yourself.

Where it would be wrong: You forgive a business partner who embezzled, and think this means you must drop the police report and give him back the account. Forgiveness gives up your personal revenge (Romans 12:19); it does not cancel justice, which belongs to the authorities (Romans 13:4), nor does it restore trust that must be earned again. Forgiving an abuser never means letting him near children.

For worship. Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). The first words from the cross were a prayer for the men who were killing him. That is the heart of the God we pray to: he forgives first, and at his own cost, and he forgave us while we were still holding the hammer. Every time a wounded believer lets go of a grudge, the family likeness shows, and the Father is glorified. Blessed be the God of all grace, who forgives us freely and teaches us to forgive.

parallels.desc: forgive your brother from your heart

verseByVerse.quote: And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you fast, do not look miserable so that people notice how devout you are. Groom yourself as usual, so that only your Father, who sees in secret, knows you are fasting. He will reward you.

When you fast. Fasting is going without food (sometimes also drink) for a period, for a spiritual purpose. Jesus assumes his disciples will fast (9:15). In the Old Testament, the only required fast was on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31). But people fasted in times of mourning, repentance, danger, or seeking God (Judges 20:26; 2 Samuel 12:16; Esther 4:16; Daniel 9:3; Joel 2:12). Some Pharisees fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays (Luke 18:12).

Do not look gloomy like the hypocrites. Some made a show of their fasting, looking sad and pale.

For they disfigure their faces. Perhaps by not washing, leaving their hair unkempt, or putting ashes on their heads. The word means to make unrecognisable, and is a wordplay with “appear” in Greek: they make their faces disappear so that they may appear to be fasting.

That their fasting may be seen by others. The motive again (v. 1).

But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face. Anointing the head with olive oil was part of normal grooming, like combing your hair. Look normal.

The signal reversed. Fasting was normally visible; Jesus reverses the signal. Dress as if you are not fasting, so that the fast stays between you and God. The pattern of the whole section is now complete: the secret act, the seeing Father, the certain reward. And the three disciplines together shape the whole person: generosity toward others, communion with God, discipline of self.

That your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. Fasting is between you and God.

Why fast? Fasting expresses humility and dependence on God; it sharpens prayer; it expresses sorrow for sin; and it trains us to say no to the body’s appetites, which helps us say no to sin. It is not a way of forcing God to act or earning his favour, but a way of seeking him with our whole self. Isaiah 58 condemns fasting that is combined with injustice, and calls for a fast that shares bread with the hungry.

Better than bread. Above all, fasting turns the body’s hunger into a cry of the heart. Man shall not live by bread alone (4:4): it is a way of saying with the whole body, Lord, I want you more than I want food. It adds nothing to a standing already complete in Christ. We fast not to be loved but because we are loved, hungering for more of him. And there is a tender thread in it. Jesus said his disciples would fast when the bridegroom was taken away (9:15). We fast because he is away for now, and we long for the day the fast gives way to the wedding feast.

What it does not mean. Not that fasting is commanded at fixed times for Christians, or that it earns merit. The Reformers rejected compulsory fasts on set days, while encouraging voluntary fasting. Nor does it mean that a church may not call a corporate fast publicly (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). The issue is showing off. And fasting is not a way of losing weight or a health practice in this context; it is a spiritual discipline. Those with medical conditions or eating disorders should seek wise counsel; there are other ways to deny oneself.

Should I fast if I never have? Start with what Jesus says: when you fast, not if. He assumes it, as he assumes giving and praying. He fasted himself (4:2), and the early church fasted and prayed before sending out missionaries and appointing elders (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Yet nowhere is it laid down as a law with required days. So fasting is a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: no one should bind your conscience or make you feel condemned for neglecting it, and neither should you simply shrug off what your Lord assumed his people would do.

How do I actually fast? Start small and simple. Skip one meal, drink water, and let each pang of hunger send you to prayer; fasting without seeking God is merely dieting. Use the time you would have spent eating to read Scripture and pray, perhaps for one specific matter: a decision, a sin you are fighting, a person you long to see saved. Keep it hidden, as these verses urge. If you are ill, pregnant, elderly or have a history of eating difficulties, set aside some other comfort instead, for God looks at the heart, not the empty stomach. Do it as worship, free of legalism and free of guilt.

In a sentence. Fast quietly, for God alone, without letting people see, and your Father will reward you.

On a Tuesday. Consider fasting from one meal this week, using the time to pray for something specific. Tell no one.

Where it applies: Skip lunch on Thursday, and spend the hour praying for your church, without mentioning it to anyone.

Where it would be wrong: You are pregnant, diabetic, or have struggled with an eating disorder, and feel you must fast from food to be serious. You need not. Fast from something else, such as your phone or the television, and see a doctor before any fast from food. And when a church calls a fast together, that is not hypocrisy (Acts 13:2–3).

For worship. The Lord Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness, and when the tempter offered him bread he answered that man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of God. He hungered so that we might be fed, and the Father who saw him in secret raised him and gave him the name above every name. Now he is preparing a table, and one day the fasting will be over for ever, at the marriage supper of the Lamb. Blessed is the Bridegroom, for whom his people hunger, and who will satisfy them with himself.
verseByVerse.note: Anointing the head with oil was part of ordinary grooming. Some Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). A wordplay: they disfigure (aphanizousin, literally “make invisible”) their faces so that they may appear (phanōsin) to others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–34 — Treasure, Vision, and Trust: Seeking the Kingdom First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 6 addresses anxiety about material provision through three related teachings. Disciples are commanded not to store up earthly treasure (perishable, vulnerable) but heavenly treasure (imperishable, secure). The eye as the lamp of the body: a healthy eye (generous spirit) fills the whole person with light; a diseased eye (stinginess) fills it with darkness. You cannot serve both God and money. Then the great anxiety passage: do not be anxious about food or clothing, because the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies knows your needs. Seek first the kingdom and his righteousness, and everything else will be added. The three enemies of treasure are not decorative: wealth took three forms and Jesus names the destroyer of each — fine cloth eaten by moth, grain and metal by the second word (which means "eating away" and covers rust, corrosion and vermin), and coin, which neither can touch, taken by the thief, whose verb means "to dig through" (mud-brick walls were tunnelled, not forced). Every exit is closed before the point is made. The eye is a Hebrew idiom, not an optical metaphor: "a good eye" meant a generous person and "an evil eye" a stingy one (Prov. 22:9; 28:22), which is why these verses sit between the treasure and the money rather than interrupting them. And mammon is an Aramaic word Jesus leaves untranslated, whose root appears to be the one behind Hebrew "faith" and our "amen" — most likely meaning that in which one puts one's trust, which makes the sentence almost self-evident. On the anxiety passage, note that the command comes three times (vv. 25, 31, 34), that the birds are not idle (they do not sow, reap or store — that is, they do not hoard against a future they cannot see), that the "lilies" are probably the wild anemones that carpet Galilee for a few weeks and are then swept up as oven fuel, and that "O you of little faith" is a word almost unique to Matthew which he uses four times, every time to disciples and never to unbelievers. The guard on anxiety is the most important thing in the section and is given in full below: this passage has been used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is sin, and that is a cruelty the text does not authorise.
verseByVerse.theology: The teaching on anxiety is not a command to be carefree but to be properly ordered: anxiety is the symptom of inverted priorities — seeking the lesser things first and trusting God to manage them, rather than seeking God first and trusting him to manage everything else. The birds and lilies do not "seek" anything in the human sense; they simply exist in dependence on the Creator who provides. The disciple is not to live without thought for the future but without anxious preoccupation with it — trusting the Father's knowledge and provision while attending to the kingdom. Anxiety is fundamentally a theological problem: it reflects a practical unbelief in the Father's care.
verseByVerse.examples: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness" is the organizing principle of the entire Sermon on the Mount. Everything else — the beatitudes, the antitheses, the disciplines of chapter 6 — flows from this reorientation of desire. The person who is genuinely seeking God's kingdom first finds that anxiety about secondary things diminishes, not because circumstances change, but because the center of gravity of the heart has shifted. Worry is the heart occupied with what it fears it won't have; trust is the heart occupied with the One who has everything and gives freely.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not pile up wealth on earth, where it decays or is stolen, but store up treasure in heaven, where it is safe for ever. What you treasure will capture your heart. Your eye, the way you see and desire, determines whether your whole life is in light or darkness. And you cannot serve both God and money.

Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth. “Lay up” means to store, accumulate, hoard. “For yourselves”: for selfish security and enjoyment.

Two treasuries. Jesus sets two treasuries side by side, and the contrast is not now against later but secure against doomed. He is not banning savings or property; he is forbidding the heart that makes accumulation its great project. The question he presses is simply: what are you building, and will it last?

Where moth and rust destroy. In the ancient world, wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths ate, or as metal and grain, which rust or vermin destroyed. The word “rust” (brōsis) literally means “eating”: anything that consumes.

And where thieves break in and steal. Houses in Palestine were often made of mud brick. Thieves could literally “dig through” the walls (the Greek word). Earthly treasure is never secure. Today it may be inflation, market crashes, fraud, or simply death, which takes us away from everything we own (Luke 12:20).

Every exit closed. The three enemies are not decorative. Wealth in that world took three forms, and Jesus names the destroyer of each. Fine cloth was capital, and Joseph sent his brothers home with changes of clothing as gifts (Genesis 45:22): the moth ate it. Grain and metalwork were consumed by the eating word, which covers rust, corrosion and vermin alike. And coin, which neither moth nor rust can touch, was taken by the thief who tunnelled through the wall. There is no form of earthly wealth without a predator, and Jesus has closed every exit before making his point.

But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. Treasure in heaven is everything done for God and his kingdom: generosity to the poor (19:21; Luke 12:33), faithful service, people won to Christ, a life spent for God. It cannot be destroyed. And above all, treasure in heaven is God himself (Psalm 73:25–26).

Treasure in heaven is mostly ordinary. It would be easy to read this as a call to do something unusual or “churchy”: more meetings, more rotas, a radical gesture. Church service is good, but treasure in heaven is far wider and far more ordinary than that. It is an ordinary life, lived for God, by loving the people around you.

What Scripture counts as treasure. When Jesus describes the judgement, the deeds he names are everyday ones: food for the hungry, a drink, a welcome, clothes, a visit to someone sick or in prison. And the righteous do not even remember doing them (25:35–40). Even a cup of cold water given to one of his disciples will not lose its reward (10:42). Paul tells slaves doing ordinary daily work to do it heartily, as for the Lord, knowing that they will receive the inheritance as their reward (Colossians 3:23–24). Whether you eat or drink, do all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). He tells Christians to aspire to live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12). And he tells the rich to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, so storing up a good foundation for the future (1 Timothy 6:18–19). God does not forget the love you show in serving his people (Hebrews 6:10).

What it looks like this week. Patience with a toddler at six in the morning. Honest work done well when no one is checking. Sitting with an elderly neighbour who has no visitors. Listening properly to a colleague who is struggling. Paying a bill quietly for someone who cannot. Being faithful and kind in your marriage. Caring for an ageing parent. Treating the waiter, the cleaner and the call-centre worker as people made in God’s image. Giving generously and cheerfully. None of this is out of the ordinary. Done in faith and love, for Christ’s sake, all of it is treasure in heaven.

Why this matters. The Reformers recovered this truth: a maid sweeping a floor or a farmer ploughing a field, in faith, pleases God as truly as a monk at prayer. Your calling as a parent, worker, neighbour or friend is where you serve God most of the time. What makes something treasure is not its size or how religious it looks, but that it is done in faith, out of love, to please him (Hebrews 11:6). And it is never a way of earning heaven. Heaven is a gift. But our Father, in grace, delights to honour the small faithful things his children do for him (25:21).

For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The key principle. The heart follows the money. Whatever you value most will capture your thoughts, desires and loyalty. If your wealth is on earth, your heart is chained to earth. You can tell what you treasure by what you think about when your mind is free, what you worry about, and where you spend your money.

The heart moves in after the money. We assume the heart leads and the money follows. Jesus says it also runs the other way: put your money somewhere, and your heart moves in after it. Do you want to love God’s kingdom more? Invest in it, and watch your affections follow. Giving is not only the fruit of a generous heart; it is one of the ways God makes a heart generous.

The eye is the lamp of the body. In the ancient world, the eye was thought to be like a lamp, letting light into the body. A healthy eye lets you see clearly.

So, if your eye is healthy. “Healthy” (haplous) means single, sound, and also generous. A “healthy eye” is a generous, undivided focus on God.

But if your eye is bad. “Bad” (ponēros) also means evil. In Jewish idiom, an “evil eye” meant a stingy, envious, grasping attitude (20:15; Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22). So the picture is about money too: a generous heart fills your life with light; a greedy one darkens everything.

Not a change of subject. Proverbs uses the idiom exactly so: whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor (Proverbs 22:9), while the stingy man, literally the man with an evil eye, hastens after wealth (Proverbs 28:22). So these verses, set between the treasure and the money, are not a change of subject. Generosity is the light; grasping is the dark.

If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! If the very thing that should give you light is corrupted, you are in deep darkness without knowing it. Greed blinds.

The darkness that thinks it is light. That is the worst kind of all. The miser who calls his grip mere prudence cannot even see his own night. Greed is the one sin that almost nobody confesses, because it so easily wears the clothes of wisdom.

No one can serve two masters. “Serve” means to be a slave. A slave could not belong to two owners with full loyalty.

For either he will hate the one and love the other. Hebrew idiom for preferring one over the other (Genesis 29:31; Luke 14:26).

You cannot serve God and money. “Money” translates mamōnas, an Aramaic word, “mammon”, meaning wealth, property, possessions. Jesus personifies it as a rival master, almost a god. Money is not neutral: it demands loyalty, promises security, and competes with God for our trust and love. You can have money; the question is whether it has you.

The thing you rely on. Jesus leaves the Aramaic word untranslated, and many scholars think its root is the one that gives Hebrew its word for faith and lies behind our amen: that in which one puts one’s trust. If that is right, the rival god is simply the thing you rely on, and the sentence becomes almost self-evident: you cannot rely on God and on the thing you rely on instead of God. And the two masters issue opposite commands. One says hold loosely and give; the other says grip tight and keep. Both say trust me. Money is a good servant and a deadly master.

What it does not mean. Not that owning property, saving, or planning for the future is wrong. Scripture commends the ant that stores up food (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the wise person who leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren (Proverbs 13:22). Paul says a man who does not provide for his family is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). Stewardship is not covetousness. The difference: stewardship holds money as God’s, uses it for him, saves wisely, gives generously, and trusts God, not the bank balance. Covetousness hoards for its own sake, wants more for self, and trusts wealth instead of God (Luke 12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). The question is not how much you have, but what you trust, what you love, and what you do with it.

How can I tell whether money has become my master? Run three simple tests. Where do my daydreams drift when my mind is free? What would rob my peace if I lost it tomorrow? What could I not bear to part with if God asked? A poor man can worship money as surely as a rich man, and a rich man can hold his wealth open-handed for God. Then act on what you find. Give first, before you spend, and give enough that you notice it. Enjoy God’s good gifts with thanksgiving, for he richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and hold all of it as a steward, not an owner.

In a sentence. Invest in what lasts for ever, because your heart follows your treasure, and you cannot serve both God and money.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement this month. What does it say your treasure is? Make one decision this week that moves treasure from earth to heaven. It need not be dramatic: an hour with someone lonely, a generous gift, patience at home, honest work done well. That is treasure too.

Where it applies: You are offered a promotion with more money you do not need, but it would take you away from your church and your children’s evenings. Think hard before you take it.

Where it would be wrong: You feel guilty for having savings, a pension or insurance. Saving for the future and providing for your family are wise (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). Jesus warns against treasure that owns you, not against prudence. The question is not whether you have savings, but whether they have you.

For worship. Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Psalm 73:25). The treasure of heaven is not finally a reward stored up but a Person. Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, set aside the riches of heaven and was laid in a borrowed manger and a borrowed tomb, so that we might have an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for us. No moth reaches it, no rust eats it, no thief digs through to it. And the God who owns the cattle on a thousand hills notices the cup of cold water. Blessed be the Father, our treasure, and the Son, our inheritance.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing (eaten by moths). A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess. The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not be anxious about the basic needs of life: food, drink, clothing. Your Father feeds the birds and clothes the flowers; you are worth far more. Anxiety cannot add an hour to your life. Instead, seek first God’s kingdom and his righteousness, and he will provide what you need. Do not worry about tomorrow; today has enough trouble of its own.

Therefore. Because you serve God, not money (v. 24). The person who trusts money is anxious when money is short; the person who trusts God need not be.

Mammon in another dress. That therefore ties the passage straight to money. Anxiety is often Mammon-service in another form: the heart gripped by what it dreads losing. So Jesus floods the fear with reasons.

Do not be anxious about your life. “Anxious” (merimnaō) means to be pulled apart, distracted, troubled by care. The word appears six times in this passage. Jesus speaks to people for whom food and clothing were real daily worries: many in Galilee lived at subsistence level, one bad harvest from hunger.

Torn, not caring. The verb is very probably related to the word for dividing: anxiety pulls a mind in two. Yet Paul uses the same word approvingly of his concern for the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28) and of Timothy’s genuine concern for the Philippians (Philippians 2:20). So Scripture is not against caring. It is against being torn. And notice how the passage is built: the command comes three times (vv. 25, 31, 34), and between them Jesus argues, patiently, from creation and from the Father’s character.

Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? God gave you life and a body, the greater gifts. Will he not give the lesser things needed to sustain them?

Look at the birds of the air. Birds do not plant, harvest, or store food in barns. Yet God feeds them. (Jesus does not say birds do not work: they hunt and gather. He says they do not worry or hoard.)

Are you not of more value than they? An argument from lesser to greater: if God cares for birds, he cares far more for his children, made in his image.

The sparrow on the sill. Any bird works from first light to dusk, harder than most of us. What it does not do is hoard against a future it cannot see, or lie awake doing sums. Yet it is fed, and you are worth a great many sparrows (10:31).

And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? Or “a single cubit to his height” (ESV footnote). Either way: worry achieves nothing. It cannot lengthen your life; if anything, it shortens it.

A cubit or an hour. The word is pēchys, a cubit, a measure of about eighteen inches, and the noun with it can mean either height or length of life. So it is either add eighteen inches to your height or, taking life as a road, add one step to its length. Either way worry has never once altered a measurement. It drains today without mending tomorrow. Someone has said it is like a rocking chair: plenty of motion, and it gets you nowhere.

Consider the lilies of the field. Wildflowers, perhaps the red anemones that covered Galilean hillsides in spring.

They neither toil nor spin. They do not work to make clothes (spinning thread was women’s daily work).

Even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Solomon was famous for his wealth and splendour (1 Kings 10). A single wildflower, clothed by God, is more beautiful.

The grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. Dried grass and weeds were used as fuel for clay ovens. Wildflowers are worth almost nothing, yet God clothes them beautifully.

The argument at full strength. In a country with almost no timber, dried grass and wildflowers were the fuel, swept up and burned to heat an oven for a single batch of bread. So God dressed a weed more finely than Israel’s richest king, for a life of about three weeks, ending as kindling. Will your Father forget to clothe his own child?

O you of little faith. A gentle rebuke Jesus gives his disciples several times (8:26; 14:31; 16:8). Anxiety is at root a failure to trust our Father.

Said only to disciples. Oligopistos is almost unique to Matthew, and every time it is said to disciples, never to unbelievers. It is not a word for people who have no faith. It is a word for people who have some, and are frightened anyway. It is the gentlest rebuke in the Gospels.

For the Gentiles seek after all these things. Pagans, who do not know God as Father, make food and clothing the focus of life. They have nothing else to trust.

And your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. The heart of the passage. You are not an orphan in a hostile universe; you have a Father who knows exactly what you need.

But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Make God’s reign and his righteous will your first priority: before food, before clothing, before career, before comfort. “His righteousness” means living as he wills (5:6, 20). “First” does not mean only, but foremost.

What seeking the kingdom looks like in real life. This can sound like a call to something extra special: leaving your job for “full-time ministry”, or filling every evening with church. It is not. The kingdom of God is God’s rule, and seeking it means living gladly under the King, wanting his will done in your own life and around you. It is what you pray for in the Lord’s Prayer: your kingdom come, your will be done (v. 10). And his righteousness is simply his will done: to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8). That is an ordinary life, lived God’s way.

A question of what comes first. Everyone seeks something first. The pagans seek food and clothing (v. 32); others seek security, approval or comfort. Seeking the kingdom first does not usually add new activities to your week. It changes which question you ask first in the ordinary ones. Not “What will I get?” or “What am I afraid of?”, but “What does God want here?” Paul calls the whole of everyday life, offered to God, your spiritual worship (Romans 12:1–2).

Some everyday examples. Choosing a job: you weigh not only the salary, but whether you can be honest in it, keep the Lord’s Day, and care for your family. Your budget: you set aside your giving first, instead of giving from whatever is left. Your Sunday: worship with God’s people is the fixed point, and the rest of the week fits around it. At work: you tell the truth and do your work faithfully, even when cutting a corner would earn you more. At home: you forgive, apologise, and raise your children in the Lord. In a tight month: you pray and keep your integrity, instead of panicking or bending the rules. Looking for a husband or wife: you ask first whether the person loves Christ. None of this is unusual. It is walking day by day according to God’s will.

Not a way of earning. The kingdom is a gift before it is a task: it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom (Luke 12:32). We seek it because he has already given it, and because the King is good. And it is a kingdom of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17): seeking it first is the way to freedom from worry, not a new burden on top of it.

And all these things will be added to you. God will provide what you truly need. Not necessarily luxury, but provision. This is a promise to those who seek the kingdom first. David said that he had never seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread (Psalm 37:25).

Does this promise that faithful Christians will never go hungry or poor? No. Believers have starved, been imprisoned and died for Christ (Hebrews 11:35–38), and Paul knew hunger (Philippians 4:12). The promise is that the Father will not abandon his children, that he will give what he knows they need to do his will, and above all that he gives himself. It is not a guarantee of comfort or income, and it gives no support to the teaching that faith brings wealth. When God’s people do go without, the church is often the means by which he adds these things, which is why the previous verses told us to store treasure by giving.

Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Do not borrow tomorrow’s troubles. God gives grace for each day as it comes.

Tomorrow can manage. The line is nearly humorous: tomorrow is pictured as perfectly capable of doing its own worrying without help from today.

Sufficient for the day is its own trouble. Each day has enough difficulty. Deal with today’s, and trust God for tomorrow’s.

No promise that it will be small. The closing line is a proverb, and it comes with no promise that the trouble will be light. Jesus does not say tomorrow will be fine. He says today has enough in it already, and that the Father who gives grace for today will give it again tomorrow, like the manna.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should not work, plan or save. Birds work; Paul worked; Proverbs commends planning (Proverbs 21:5; 24:27). The difference is between planning and worrying. Planning thinks ahead and takes reasonable steps, then trusts God; worry runs the same fears round and round without trusting him. Nor does it mean that faithful Christians will never go hungry. Paul knew hunger and need (2 Corinthians 11:27; Philippians 4:12), and believers in persecution and famine have died. The promise is that God will provide what we need to do his will and that nothing can separate us from his love (Romans 8:35–39). Nor is anxiety always simple sin. Clinical anxiety is an illness that may need medical care as well as spiritual help, and Christians who struggle with it should not be shamed. Jesus calls us to trust, and he is gentle with the weak.

If I have an anxiety disorder, is Jesus telling me I am sinning? No. This passage has been used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is sin, and the damage has been real. Jesus is addressing a settled orientation of the heart, a life organised around what one is afraid of losing. Clinical anxiety is different: a body and mind doing what they were not designed to do, a racing heart and a mind that will not stop, arriving uninvited in people who love God. The command is not a lever to be pulled harder; a Christian who could stop by deciding to would have stopped years ago. Medical help is not a failure of faith, any more than a splint is. Read the passage for its reasons rather than as a rebuke: Jesus does not stand over frightened people. He reasons with them, gently, and so does his Spirit.

In a sentence. Do not be eaten up by worry about life’s needs; your Father knows them and will provide, so seek his kingdom first and live one day at a time.

On a Tuesday. Write down what you are anxious about today. Then pray over each item, telling your Father, and leave it with him (Philippians 4:6–7; 1 Peter 5:7). Then do the one thing you can do today. And before one decision today, large or small, ask first: what does God want here? Then trust him with the rest.

Where it applies: You are waiting for a hospital test result. Pray, tell your Father your fear, then go to bed and sleep. Tomorrow will have its own trouble.

Where it would be wrong: Someone refuses to plan a budget, take out insurance, or see a doctor about persistent anxiety or depression, because worry is a sin. Jesus forbids anxious fretting, not forethought or medicine (Proverbs 21:5; Luke 14:28). Getting help is not unbelief. God uses means.

A practice. Thank your Father for one specific way he has provided for you this week.

For worship. Your heavenly Father knows. He counts the sparrows and paints the anemones on the hills of Galilee, though they bloom for three weeks and then heat an oven. He knows the number of the hairs on your head, and he knew your needs before you were born. He did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all; how will he not also with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32)? The King whose kingdom we seek is the Father who feeds us, and the righteousness we seek has been given us in Christ. Blessed be the God of every morning’s mercy, whose faithfulness is new each day.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.” Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

parallels.desc: do not be anxious about anything
cast all your anxieties on him

6.theology:
Prayer and the Fatherhood of God. The Lord’s Prayer is the fullest Trinitarian statement about prayer in the New Testament. We pray to the Father, in the name of the Son (the one who taught us to pray this way and who intercedes for us, Rom. 8:34), in the power of the Spirit (who helps us in our weakness and intercedes with groaning too deep for words, Rom. 8:26). Reformed theology has always understood prayer as Trinitarian from beginning to end: the Father hears, the Son mediates, the Spirit enables.

The address “Our Father” is the fruit of adoption — the doctrine that those who trust in Christ are received into the family of God with all the rights and privileges of sons (Gal. 4:5–6). We do not pray as strangers petitioning a distant deity; we pray as children talking to a Father who knows us, loves us, and has already given us his Son. The confidence of Christian prayer rests entirely on the prior act of God in adoption, not on the fervency or frequency of the one praying.
6.examples:
Then: The contrast between secret devotion and public performance runs through the Old Testament. Hannah prayed so quietly that Eli thought she was drunk (1 Sam. 1:13) — and God heard. Daniel opened his window toward Jerusalem and prayed three times a day without announcement, in full view of a hostile empire (Dan. 6:10). The great saints of Israel prayed to an audience of One — and their prayers are the ones that shaped history. The hypocrites who prayed on street corners are forgotten; their reward was fully paid and fully spent.

Now: The anxiety Jesus addresses in verses 25–34 is the defining emotional experience of our age. Financial anxiety, career anxiety, health anxiety, relationship anxiety — the modern world has more to worry about (in terms of information access about possible threats) than any previous generation. Jesus’ answer is not information management but kingdom orientation: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who holds all things will hold yours. This is not naive — it is the most realistic posture available to a creature who is not God. You are not in control of tomorrow; the Father is. Trust the Father.

7.title: The Narrow Gate
7.text: <sup>1</sup>“Judge not, that you be not judged. <sup>2</sup>For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. <sup>3</sup>Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>4</sup>Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ when there is the log in your own eye? <sup>5</sup>You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye. <sup>6</sup>“Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. <sup>7</sup>“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>8</sup>For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>9</sup>Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? <sup>10</sup>Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? <sup>11</sup>If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! <sup>12</sup>“So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets. <sup>13</sup>“Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. <sup>14</sup>For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few. <sup>15</sup>“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. <sup>16</sup>You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? <sup>17</sup>So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. <sup>18</sup>A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. <sup>19</sup>Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>20</sup>Thus you will recognize them by their fruits. <sup>21</sup>“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. <sup>22</sup>On that day many will say to me, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?’ <sup>23</sup>And then will I declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.’ <sup>24</sup>“Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. <sup>25</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. <sup>26</sup>And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. <sup>27</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.” <sup>28</sup>And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, <sup>29</sup>for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 concludes the Sermon on the Mount with a series of choices, each framed as a binary: the wide gate or the narrow, the false prophet or the true, the one who hears and does or the one who hears and does not. The Sermon that began with Beatitudes ends with warnings. The kingdom is real and its entrance is narrow; the alternatives are easy and lead to destruction. This is not the comfortable conclusion of a TED talk; it is the solemn close of the greatest sermon ever preached.

The famous “Judge not” (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Bible. Jesus is not prohibiting all moral discernment — he commands it in verse 6 (discern who receives what is holy) and verses 15–16 (recognise false prophets by their fruit). He is prohibiting hypocritical judgment: condemning in others what you excuse in yourself. The log-and-speck image is both humorous and devastating — the person with a beam in their eye offering to perform eye surgery. Self-examination must precede fraternal correction.

The parable of the two builders is the Sermon’s climax and its challenge. Both builders hear the words of Jesus; both face the same storm. The difference is foundation: rock or sand. And the foundation is not intellectual agreement with Jesus’ teaching but doing it — the obedience that grows from genuine faith. The crowds are astonished at the end because Jesus teaches with authority, not as the scribes. He does not say “thus says the LORD”; he says “I say to you.” He is the rock on which the house is built.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Judgment, Prayer, and the Two Ways: Concluding the Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sermon on the Mount concludes with four warnings and a call. The warning against judging hypocritically (vv. 1–6), the invitation to persistent prayer (vv. 7–12), and the double warning about the narrow gate and false prophets (vv. 13–23) all converge on the final parable of the two builders (vv. 24–27). The Sermon does not end gently: it ends with a stark choice between two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and the crowds are astonished not by the gentleness of what they heard but by the authority of the one who said it. The verse-by-verse fills in what a 29-verse summary cannot. On "judge not": the proof that it cannot mean what the world takes it to mean is inside this same chapter — v. 6 requires the hearer to identify "dogs" and "pigs", vv. 15-20 require him to identify false prophets by their fruit, and vv. 21-23 have Jesus distinguishing those who did the Father's will from those who did not. All within twenty-two verses of the command. Elsewhere he settles it in one sentence: "Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment" (Jn. 7:24); and Paul asks, "Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?" (1 Cor. 5:12). "With the measure you use" is a rabbinic formula (measure for measure) and is an offer of a choice — a man sets the standard he will be tried by. The speck and the log are a tradesman's joke: karphos is a wood chip, dokos is a roof beam, both from the same building yard, told by a carpenter to people who had watched carpenters work. And v. 6 is a crossover (an X): it is the pigs that trample and the dogs that turn and attack. On prayer (vv. 7-11): "how much more" is the standard rabbinic argument from lesser to greater — and the premise slipped in without pause is that the audience are evil, stated as an agreed fact on the way to proving how kind God is. Bread/stone and fish/serpent are things that look alike (Galilean limestone weathers into loaf-shaped lumps; the lake held a whiskered catfish a Jew could not eat) — so the fear being answered is not malice but substitution. The golden rule (v. 12) is treated at length below. On false prophets: "sheep's clothing" may be the prophetic uniform itself (Zech. 13:4 has false prophets putting on a hairy cloak to deceive), and "ravenous" is harpax, from the verb to snatch — what defines him is that he is taking something. The fruit test cannot be run quickly, and that is not a defect: much damage has been done by men whose fruit would have been obvious in five years and who were given authority in five weeks. "I never knew you" (vv. 21-23) is likewise absent above and is given the fullest treatment in the chapter below. On the two houses: Luke supplies the detail that bites — the wise man dug deep (Lk. 6:48). In that country a dry wadi bed is the most inviting summer site there is, flat and easy to dig; digging down is slow, costly, and invisible when the house is finished. Both houses look identical. And "these words of mine" puts his own sayings where Israel's wisdom tradition put the Torah (Ps. 1:2). Note finally that this closing section is four pairs narrowing — two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and in every one the wrong option is the comfortable one and the two are hard to tell apart from outside. On the closing formula (v. 28): "when Jesus finished these sayings" occurs five times in Matthew and only five (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1), each sealing a discourse — five books of teaching from a man who came out of Egypt, through the water, and through forty days in the wilderness. Moses gave five books from a mountain. And "astonished" is ekplesso, to be struck out of position, in the imperfect: they went on being knocked sideways.
verseByVerse.theology: The command not to judge (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Sermon and one of the most misunderstood in the Bible. Jesus does not prohibit discernment (he commands it in v. 6 and vv. 15–20); he prohibits the hypocritical judgment that ignores one's own sin while scrutinizing another's. The warning about false prophets extends the theme: discernment is required, but it must begin with self-examination. The Sermon ends where it must — with the question of foundation. Hearing Jesus's words and not doing them is not neutrality; it is the choice of sand. The storm will decide what you built on.
verseByVerse.examples: The final verse — "he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes" — is Matthew's first and defining portrait of Jesus as teacher. The scribes taught by citing authorities: "Rabbi X says..." Jesus taught by assertion: "I say to you." This is either the most arrogant teaching in human history or the teaching of the one to whom all authority belongs. Matthew does not leave the reader in the middle. The crowd was astonished. The question is what they did with the astonishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge not, that you be not judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, "Let me take the speck out of your eye," when there is the log in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be harsh, fault-finding judges of others, because God will judge you by the same standard you use. Deal first with the great fault in yourself before trying to correct a small fault in someone else. Yet use discernment too: do not keep pressing holy things on those who treat them with contempt.

Meaning first. Matthew 7 brings the Sermon on the Mount to its close. Jesus first turns to how disciples treat one another: do not be a harsh judge of your brother while ignoring your own sin, yet do not be naive about those who trample holy things (vv. 1–6). He calls them to keep asking, seeking and knocking, because their Father is far more generous than the best earthly father (vv. 7–11), and he gathers the whole law about our neighbours into one sentence, the Golden Rule (v. 12). Then the sermon ends with a call to decide, in four pairs: two gates and two roads, two kinds of tree, two kinds of confession, and two builders on two foundations (vv. 13–27). The crowds are left astonished, because he spoke with his own authority (vv. 28–29). The chapter ends where everything in Matthew is heading: with Jesus himself as the way, the Judge and the rock.

Judge not. “Judge” (krinō) has a wide range: to evaluate, to decide, to condemn. Here it means the critical, condemning, fault-finding spirit that sets itself up as judge over others, looking for their faults and passing sentence on them. The Pharisees often judged in this way (Luke 18:9–11).

The verse everyone still keeps. Judge not has become the one command that almost everyone in our culture still quotes. But Jesus means something precise. He is not banning moral evaluation or the naming of wrong; he does both all through the sermon. He is banning the hypocritical tribunal of the self-righteous, who build careful cases against others while suppressing the evidence against themselves.

That you be not judged. By God. The passive is often a reverent way of saying “God will do this”.

For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged. The standard you apply to others will be applied to you. If you condemn harshly, without mercy, you will be judged without mercy (James 2:13). Paul says that in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you practise the very same things (Romans 2:1).

And with the measure you use it will be measured to you. A picture from the market: a merchant measuring grain. If you use a mean measure on others, God will use it on you.

Measure for measure. This was a rabbinic formula, the ordinary Jewish way of saying that God’s dealings answer to ours. It is not a threat of arbitrary retaliation. It is a choice laid before us: the standard a person applies to others is the standard he is choosing to be tried by, and he sets it himself every time he opens his mouth about somebody else. The harsh judge is the one most exposed to harsh judgment, from God, who sees every page of the file.

Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye. A speck (karphos) is a tiny splinter, a bit of straw or sawdust.

But do not notice the log that is in your own eye? A log (dokos) is a beam, a roof timber. Jesus, a carpenter’s son, uses a deliberately comic picture: a man with a plank sticking out of his eye trying to remove a speck of sawdust from someone else’s. We see others’ faults sharply and our own hardly at all. Often the faults that irritate us most in others are our own.

A tradesman’s joke. Both objects come from the same building yard: a wood chip and a joist. The image was told by a carpenter to people who had watched carpenters work, and it is meant to be laughed at, and the laugh is the argument. Nobody would think this reasonable if he could see it from outside. That is the whole difficulty: the man with the beam is the one person in the room who cannot see it.

You hypocrite. An actor (see 6:2). The judgmental person plays the part of a righteous judge while hiding his own sin.

First take the log out of your own eye. Begin with self-examination and repentance.

And then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye. Notice: Jesus does not say leave the speck. He says deal with yourself first, and then you will be able to help your brother. Removing a speck from an eye is delicate work. It requires clear sight, a gentle hand, and humility. Paul says, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself (Galatians 6:1).

Qualified, not excused. The speck is real; the brother does have a fault. But the log makes the would-be surgeon both blind and dangerous. Self-examination is not an excuse never to correct. It is the qualification for correcting rightly: humbly, as one patient helping another, not as a spotless judge.

Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs. Dogs here are not pets but wild scavengers; pigs were unclean animals to Jews. Both picture people who treat holy things with contempt. “What is holy” may refer to meat from sacrifices, which must never be thrown to dogs. Pearls were very precious. Pigs would not value them; they would trample them and turn on the giver. The holy things and pearls are the gospel and the truths of God’s kingdom.

Lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. Some people respond to God’s truth with mockery and violence. Do not keep pressing it on them. Jesus told his disciples to shake the dust off their feet when a town rejected them (10:14), and Paul turned from those who rejected the gospel to others (Acts 13:46; 18:6).

A carefully made saying. Read it again and the pairing crosses over: dogs, then pigs; then trampling, then attacking. It is the pigs that trample the pearls and the dogs that turn and attack. Two lines laid out as an X, a common Hebrew arrangement and a sign that the saying was carefully made, not tacked on. The picture is a man tossing the consecrated meat off the altar to the strays in the street.

The balance. Verses 1–5 warn against being too critical; verse 6 warns against being undiscerning. Disciples must not be judgmental, but they must not be naive. They must judge between holy and unholy, true and false (v. 15). The same chapter that says “judge not” also says “beware of false prophets” and “you will recognise them by their fruits” (vv. 15–20).

What it does not mean. “Judge not” is often quoted to mean that no one may ever say anything is wrong. That is not what Jesus means. He himself called the Pharisees hypocrites. Paul commands the church to judge those inside it who persist in sin (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). Jesus says to judge with right judgment (John 7:24). Courts, parents, church elders and employers must make judgments. What Jesus forbids is a self-righteous, fault-finding, condemning spirit that judges others without examining oneself, that assumes the worst, and that pronounces final verdicts that belong only to God. Nor does verse 6 permit us to write off people as “pigs” easily. The same Jesus who said this ate with sinners. It applies to those who have clearly and repeatedly treated the gospel with contempt.

The proof is in the same chapter. Verse 1 says judge not. Verse 6 requires the hearer to work out who is behaving like dogs and pigs. Verses 15–20 require him to identify false prophets by their fruit. Verses 21–23 have Jesus himself distinguishing those who did the Father’s will from those who did not. All of that is within twenty-two verses of the command. Whatever judge not forbids, it cannot forbid what Jesus requires in the next breath. The problem was never judging. It was judging badly: from the outside, on appearances, by a standard the judge exempts himself from.

When I hear someone say it is not my place to judge, how should I answer? Gently, and with the whole passage. Agree with what is true in it: none of us may condemn another’s soul, assume the worst, or set ourselves above anyone, and we must always start with our own sin. Then point out that Jesus himself tells us in the same chapter to tell good fruit from bad, and that he says elsewhere, judge with right judgment (John 7:24). Calling something wrong because God calls it wrong is not condemning a person; it is agreeing with God, and it can be done with tears and humility. The difference is between a judge with a gavel and a friend who has had the same disease and knows the cure.

In a sentence. Do not be harsh critics of others; examine yourself first, then help others humbly, while using discernment about those who scorn holy things.

On a Tuesday. Think of the fault that annoys you most in someone else. Ask honestly: is there a log of the same wood in my eye?

Where it applies: You hear that a colleague’s marriage is in trouble, and you begin assuming the worst about him. Stop. You do not know the story, and you have faults of your own.

Where it would be wrong: A friend is drifting into an affair, and you say nothing because you must not judge. Jesus does not forbid all judgement. In this same passage he tells us to recognise dogs and pigs (v. 6) and false prophets (v. 15). Warn your friend gently (Galatians 6:1). A church must exercise discipline (18:15–17), and parents must judge who is safe with their children. Take out the log first; then you will see clearly to help (v. 5).

For worship. There is one Judge who never had a log in his eye. He sees every page of every file, our own included, and he knows the whole story behind every speck. And this Judge came down from the bench and was judged in our place, condemned by men who had beams in their own eyes, so that the measure we deserved would never be measured to us. Now he takes the beam out of our eyes with his own hand, gently, and sends us to help our brothers as forgiven sinners. Blessed be the righteous Judge, who is also our Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Dogs and pigs were unclean animals, images of those who scorn what is holy.

parallels.desc: in passing judgment you condemn yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep asking, seeking and knocking in prayer, because everyone who does so receives. If human fathers, sinful as they are, give their children good things and not harmful ones, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him?

The connection. After the demands of the sermon, which we cannot meet in our own strength, Jesus points us to prayer. We need God’s help to live this way, and he gives it to those who ask.

The door that opens. The sermon has described a life impossible by human effort, and now Jesus shows where the strength for it comes from. The demands drive us to our knees, and on our knees we find that the door opens.

Ask … seek … knock. Three pictures, each stronger than the last. Asking is like a child asking a parent. Seeking is like searching for something lost. Knocking is like standing at a closed door and calling to be let in. In Greek, all three are present imperatives, meaning keep on asking, keep on seeking, keep on knocking. Jesus is teaching persistence in prayer (Luke 11:5–10; 18:1–8).

And it will be given to you … you will find … it will be opened to you. Each command has a promise. The passive “will be given” and “will be opened” point to God as the giver.

For everyone who asks receives. Not some, but everyone. This is a promise to God’s children.

Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? The round, flat loaves of Galilee looked like the smooth stones of the region (see 4:3). What father would trick his hungry child?

Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? Some fish of the Sea of Galilee, like eels or catfish, looked like snakes. No father would give a dangerous snake instead of food.

Never a counterfeit. Bread and stone, fish and serpent, are not random opposites. They are things that look alike. So the picture is not a father handing over something obviously cruel; it is a father palming off a convincing fake, something that looks right in the hand and turns out to be inedible or dangerous. That is the fear underneath much unanswered prayer. Nobody seriously suspects God of malice. What people quietly suspect is a substitution: that they asked for bread and got a stone that resembles it. Jesus says the one thing that is never in the parcel is a counterfeit.

If you then, who are evil. A remarkable phrase. Jesus assumes that all human beings, even good fathers, are evil: sinful by nature (see Ephesians 2:3). Yet even sinful parents love their children.

The sermon in miniature. He is not addressing enemies. This is his own audience, and he calls them evil in a passing clause, as an agreed fact requiring no defence, on the way to making a point about generosity. An assessment of human nature bleak enough to stop us in our tracks is used as an argument for how kind God is.

Know how to give good gifts to your children. Ordinary parental love.

How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! An argument from lesser to greater. God is not a reluctant giver. He is a good Father who delights to give.
