Luke’s version says, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13): the Spirit is the greatest of the good things.

What it does not mean. Not that God will give us anything we ask for, if only we persist. A good father does not give his child everything he asks for: not a knife to a toddler, not sweets for every meal. God gives “good things”, and he decides what is good. Sometimes the answer is “no” or “wait”, because he has something better. John says that we receive what we ask when we ask according to his will (1 John 5:14–15). Nor is persistence a way of wearing God down or forcing his hand (6:7–8). It is the persistence of trust, which keeps coming to the Father because it believes he is good.

The Father fathering. The very picture assumes that a child may reach for a serpent thinking it is a fish, and a good father will not give it. So a prayer answered differently is not the Father failing but the Father fathering. What may you bring? Anything that befits a child of this Father: daily provision, wisdom for a hard decision, the salvation of a wayward son, courage to obey the commands of this very sermon.

If I already have the Holy Spirit, why ask for him? Every believer receives the Spirit when he trusts Christ, and has him for good (Ephesians 1:13; Romans 8:9). In its first setting, Luke’s promise looked ahead to Pentecost, when the disciples waited and prayed for the promised Spirit (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:14). For us now, we do not ask for a Guest we lack. We ask the Guest who lives within to fill the whole house: to be filled afresh (Ephesians 5:18), as already Spirit-filled believers were filled again for boldness (Acts 4:31); for his comfort, his power to put sin to death and bear fruit, his help to understand Scripture. And Luke can call him the supreme good thing the Father gives, because in giving us the Spirit, God gives us himself.

In a sentence. Keep praying, because your Father in heaven is far more generous than the best earthly father and delights to give good things to his children.

On a Tuesday. What have you stopped praying for because you gave up? Start asking again, trusting your Father’s goodness and his timing.

Where it applies: Your son has walked away from the faith. Keep asking God for him, for years if need be. Your Father hears.

Where it would be wrong: Someone treats these verses as a promise to get whatever he names, a job, a healing or a spouse, if he believes hard enough. The Father gives good things (v. 11), and he alone knows what they are. Sometimes the good answer is no, as it was for Paul (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

For worship. Our boldness in prayer does not rest on our worthiness, or on persistence as a technique, but on the settled goodness of the Father. He is not a vending machine and not a reluctant judge. He is better than the best father who ever lived, and he has proved it. He did not withhold his only Son, and he does not withhold his Spirit. Every door he opens is opened by the hand that was pierced for us, and we come into his presence as children who know he is home. Blessed be the Father who gives good things to those who ask him.
verseByVerse.note: Flat loaves could look like stones, and some fish like snakes.

parallels.desc: every good gift is from above
if we ask according to his will

verseByVerse.quote: So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treat others the way you would want them to treat you. This sums up everything the Law and the Prophets teach about how to live with others.

So whatever you wish that others would do to you. Think about how you would like to be treated: with kindness, honesty, patience, respect, generosity, forgiveness.

Do also to them. Then treat them that way, first, without waiting for them to do it. This is called the Golden Rule.

The positive form. Other ancient teachers stated the rule negatively. The Jewish teacher Hillel, a generation before Jesus, said: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; that is the whole law. Confucius and others taught similar negative forms. The negative form says: do not harm. Jesus’ positive form says: actively do good. It is far more demanding. You could keep the negative form by doing nothing; you can keep the positive form only by love in action.

A fence and a road. It is often said that Jesus taught nothing new here, and the claim deserves a straight answer. Hillel, asked to sum up the law while standing on one leg, gave the negative form; so, in their own words, did Confucius, Greek moralists, and the book of Tobit. The negative rule is one of the commonest things wise men have ever said. Two things are new all the same. The first is the direction: a person may keep the negative rule perfectly while sitting still and never troubling himself over anyone. Jesus makes it impossible to obey by inaction. You must look at your neighbour, work out what you would long for in his place, and go and be that for him. The one rule is a fence; the other is a road.

Family likeness, not prudence. The second thing that is new is the ground. The so that opens the verse reaches back to what has just been said. The reason to treat others this way is not that society runs more smoothly, nor that we may hope for the same in return. It is that we have a Father who gives good gifts to those who ask (vv. 7–11), and children come to resemble their father. Reciprocity is prudence. This is family likeness.

For this is the Law and the Prophets. It summarises the Old Testament’s teaching on how to treat others. Jesus later says that the whole Law and the Prophets hang on two commandments: love God, and love your neighbour as yourself (22:37–40). The Golden Rule is a practical way of applying the second. It also forms a bracket with 5:17, where Jesus mentioned the Law and the Prophets: everything in between explains what fulfilling them means.

The whole, carried down the mountain. Jesus has spent two chapters pressing the law beyond the reach of every hearer, and he ends by handing them one sentence they can carry down the mountain. It is not a lowering of the standard but the whole of it, gathered into a form a person can actually begin on tomorrow morning.

What it does not mean. Not that we should give people whatever they want. We should treat them as we would rightly wish to be treated, by someone who truly loves us, which sometimes means telling hard truths or refusing harmful requests. Nor is the Golden Rule the whole of Christianity, or the way of salvation, as if we could earn heaven by being nice. No one keeps it perfectly. It shows us our sin, drives us to Christ, and then becomes the shape of the new life he gives.

Since people want different things, will I not just impose my tastes on others? It is a fair objection to the rule taken bare, and the second half of the verse answers it. This is the Law and the Prophets: what you may wish for another is bounded by everything God has revealed about what is good. The rule is a summary of the law, not a licence to substitute your appetites for it. And it asks you to imagine yourself in his place, with his needs and his situation, not to assume that he is you. The person who loves his introverted friend will not throw him the surprise party he himself would enjoy.

In a sentence. Actively treat others the way you would want to be treated, for that is the heart of God’s law about our neighbours.

On a Tuesday. Before your next difficult conversation, ask: how would I want to be spoken to if I were in their place?

Where it applies: You would want to hear about your mistake privately before your boss hears of it. Do that for your colleague.

Where it would be wrong: A drunk friend wants his car keys back. He wants them, but treating him as you would want to be treated means taking them away: sober, you would want to be stopped. The rule is to do what you would rightly want done, not to give people whatever they ask.

For worship. Only one man has ever kept this sentence perfectly, every day of his life, toward people who did nothing for him. He did to us what we would have longed for if we had known how lost we were: he came looking for us, carried our burdens, told us the truth, and gave his life. And the Father whose gifts lie behind this verse is the one who gives first, without waiting for us to deserve it. Glory to the God whose kindness to us is the pattern of all our kindness, and to the Son who fulfilled the Law and the Prophets in love.
verseByVerse.note: Other ancient teachers put this rule negatively (“do not do what you would hate”); Jesus puts it positively.

parallels.desc: the whole law in one word

verseByVerse.quote: Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are only two ways. Enter by the narrow gate. The gate is wide and the road easy that lead to destruction, and many take it. But the gate is narrow and the road hard that lead to life, and few find it.

The conclusion of the sermon. Verses 13–27 call for a decision through a series of contrasts: two gates, two roads, two kinds of trees, two kinds of fruit, two kinds of builder, two foundations. There is no third option, no neutral ground.

Enter by the narrow gate. A command. It is not enough to admire the sermon; one must enter.

For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction. “Easy” literally means broad, spacious. The wide gate admits anyone, with any baggage, any belief, any way of life. The broad road has room for everything: no self-denial, no repentance, no discipline. It is the way of the crowd. It feels comfortable, but it leads to destruction, eternal ruin.

Broad-minded and narrow. Our culture prizes being broad-minded and suspects anything narrow, and Jesus reverses the valuation. The broad gate looks free, open and welcoming, with room for everyone and everything, yet it ends in destruction. The narrow gate looks cramped and costly, yet it opens onto life. And the broad road is not crowded only with the obviously wicked. It is thronged with respectable, moral, religious people too, even some who will cry Lord, Lord (vv. 21–23). You can be very devout and still be drifting the easy way, which is exactly what makes the warning so searching.

And those who enter by it are many. Popularity is no proof of truth.

For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life. “Hard” (tethlimmenē) means pressed, constricted, and is related to the word for affliction and persecution. The narrow gate is the way into the kingdom that Jesus has just taught: becoming his disciple and living by his words (see below on whether the gate is Christ himself). It is narrow because it admits only those who come on his terms, by repentance and faith, leaving behind their self-righteousness and their sin. The way is hard because following Christ involves self-denial, opposition and suffering (16:24; Acts 14:22). But it leads to life, eternal life with God.

You enter low and empty-handed. The word pictures a passage one must squeeze through. You cannot carry your self-righteousness, your sins or your idols through it. Nobody gets through with baggage, and nobody gets through by pushing others aside. It is narrow, but it is not exclusive in the sense of keeping out the wrong kind of person: the beggar, the prostitute and the tax collector go through it, and the proud do not.

And those who find it are few. “Find” suggests that it must be sought. Jesus does not give numbers; he gives a warning. When asked whether those being saved are few, he answered: strive to enter through the narrow door (Luke 13:23–24). The point is not to calculate others’ fate, but to make sure of your own.

Not with pleasure. The many and the few are not presented with satisfaction. Jesus is not glad that many go the wide way; he wept over Jerusalem. But he refuses to soften the reality, because a doctor who will not name the disease cannot be trusted with the cure.

Is the narrow gate Christ himself? A fair question. Matthew 7 does not have Jesus calling himself the gate or door: that is John’s picture (John 10:9). Read on its own, the sermon could sound as if the gate were simply a better way of behaving. How can we be sure what Jesus meant? Read in widening circles, starting with the closest.

1. The immediate context. The picture of two ways is old. Moses set before Israel life and death, blessing and curse (Deuteronomy 30:15–19); Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked; Jeremiah set before the people the way of life and the way of death (Jeremiah 21:8). So the first meaning is two ways of life, with two destinies. And a few verses later Jesus explains his own picture: the wise builder is the one who hears these words of mine and does them (v. 24). The narrow way is the life of a disciple of Jesus, lived by his words.

2. The sermon itself points to Jesus, not to self-improvement. It begins with the poor in spirit, people with nothing to offer, to whom the kingdom is given (5:3). It demands a righteousness greater than that of the scribes (5:20), and even perfection (5:48), which no one can produce, and it teaches us to ask our Father daily for forgiveness (6:12). The sermon is not a ladder we climb, but a mirror that sends us to God for mercy. Jesus also puts himself at the centre. His people are persecuted on his account (5:11). He has come to fulfil the Law and the Prophets (5:17). He sets his own word beside Moses’ (But I say to you), and the crowds notice that he teaches with authority (7:28–29). Most striking of all, the judgement that follows the two gates turns on him. Many will call him Lord on that day, and the decisive thing is not what they did, but whether he knew them (7:21–23). The narrow road ends at Jesus.

3. The rest of Matthew. The same Gospel goes on to fill this in. Jesus calls the weary to come to him (11:28) and his disciples to deny themselves and follow him (16:24). He came to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28), and his blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28).

4. The whole Bible. Only then do we bring in John and the letters. Jesus says, I am the door; if anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9), and I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). These do not give Matthew 7 a new meaning; they say openly what the sermon already implies. Scripture interprets Scripture, but it does so by letting the plainer passages explain the less explicit ones, not by reading one writer’s picture into another’s words.

Verdict: in Matthew 7 the narrow gate is entering the kingdom as Jesus’ disciple, and the narrow road is the life he has just described. But that life begins with poverty of spirit, lives on God’s mercy, and ends before Jesus as judge, so the gate cannot be anything other than coming to Jesus himself in faith. It is not good behaviour instead of Christ, nor Christ without changed behaviour. It is coming to Christ and following him: the gate is entered by faith, and the road is walked in obedience.

How to read any passage this way. Ask four questions, in this order. What does the immediate context say? What Old Testament background is it drawing on? How does the rest of this book develop it? How does the whole Bible fit with it? Then check that your reading does not contradict what Scripture says plainly elsewhere. Here, a reading that made the gate good behaviour alone would contradict both the beginning of the sermon (5:3) and the gospel of grace (Ephesians 2:8–9).

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by a hard, difficult life, or that Christians must make life as hard as possible for themselves. The gate is entered by grace through faith; the hardness of the road is the cost of following Christ in a hostile world. Jesus also says his yoke is easy and his burden is light (11:30): the road is hard from the world’s side, but sweet in his company. Nor does “few” mean that heaven will be thinly populated: Revelation sees a great multitude that no one can number from every nation (Revelation 7:9). In any generation, compared with the crowd, true disciples are few; across history, they are a vast multitude.

Two more misreadings to avoid. Narrow does not mean the sour, censorious narrowness of the Pharisees that Jesus has just condemned (vv. 1–5); it describes the single way of salvation, not a cramped or unkind spirit. And few is no excuse for either despair or smugness. The gate stands open and the invitation goes to all: enter is a command anyone may obey. Those who do enter go in only by grace, with nothing to boast of.

Where Christians differ: exclusivism. Pluralists hold that all religions are equally valid paths to God. Inclusivists hold that people may be saved through Christ without knowing him explicitly. Verdict: exclusivism. There is one way in, through Christ, and salvation is found in no one else (Acts 4:12). This is why the gospel must be preached to all nations.

What about those who have never heard? Scripture gives no second way in. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Romans 10:13–15), which is exactly why Paul asks how they will hear without a preacher, and why the church sends missionaries. Those who have never heard are not condemned for rejecting a Christ they never knew, but for sin against the light they had, the witness of creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16), and God will judge with perfect justice. Infants who die before they can believe are in a different case, and Reformed Christians have long held that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit (Westminster 10.3). The right response is not speculation but going and telling.

In a sentence. There are only two roads: the easy, popular one to destruction, and the narrow one through Christ to life.

On a Tuesday. Are you on the narrow road, or only near it, admiring it? And are you willing to be different from the crowd for Christ’s sake?

Where it applies: Your colleagues all fiddle their timesheets. You do not. You are on the narrow road, and it may cost you their goodwill.

Where it would be wrong: Someone thinks being odd, harsh or rule-bound proves he is on the narrow road. The narrow way is coming to Christ in faith and following him in love, not a pose of being different.

For worship. The narrow gate is never locked. The one who is the door stretched out his arms on a cross so that whoever will may come in, and he stands at the entrance still, calling the weary and heavy-laden. The road beyond is hard, but he walks it with his people, and it ends in life: the city whose gates are never shut, where a great multitude from every nation will praise him for ever. The easy way asks nothing now and costs everything at the end; his way costs us ourselves now and gives us himself for ever. Blessed be Christ, the way, the truth and the life.

parallels.desc: life and death set before you
the way of the wicked will perish

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Thus you will recognize them by their fruits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch out for false prophets. They look like sheep, harmless members of the flock, but inside they are ravenous wolves. You will recognise them by their fruit: what their teaching and lives produce. Every bad tree will be cut down and burned.

Beware of false prophets. On the narrow road there will be people pointing the wrong way. A prophet claims to speak for God. A false prophet claims to, but does not. The Old Testament warned of them repeatedly (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:16–22). Jesus warns that they will multiply (24:11, 24).

Who come to you in sheep’s clothing. They look like believers. They use Christian words, attend church, may even be leaders. Prophets sometimes wore a rough cloak of animal skin (Zechariah 13:4; 3:4), so the picture may also suggest the costume of a prophet.

Dressed for the job. A prophet in Israel was known by his garment: Elijah’s hairy mantle, passed to Elisha, was practically the badge of the office, and Zechariah describes false prophets who put on a hairy cloak in order to deceive (Zechariah 13:4). So the disguise may be not just a general harmlessness but the prophetic uniform itself. And the danger is precisely that they do not look like wolves. This is a threat from inside the flock, not from outside it.

But inwardly are ravenous wolves. Their real aim is to devour: to exploit, deceive and destroy the flock for their own gain, whether money, power, sex or fame. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in among them, not sparing the flock (Acts 20:29–30).

A word about grabbing. Ravenous is harpax, from the verb to seize or snatch, the same root as the wolf that snatches the sheep in John 10:12. What defines the false teacher in this image is not only that he is mistaken but that he is taking something, and the flock is what he takes it from.

You will recognize them by their fruits. “Fruit” is what a tree produces. For a false prophet, the fruit includes their character and conduct (greed, sexual immorality, pride, love of power: 2 Peter 2:1–3, 14), their teaching (does it agree with Scripture and exalt Christ? 1 John 4:1–3; Galatians 1:8–9), and the effect on their followers (do they become more like Christ, or more proud, divided, and worldly?).

What good and bad fruit look like. Look in three places. The teaching: good fruit is teaching faithful to Scripture, which exalts Christ and his cross and calls people to repentance and grace; bad fruit twists the Bible, makes light of sin, sells a gospel of self, money or works, and draws disciples after the teacher rather than the Lord (Acts 20:30). The character: good fruit is the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), shown in humility, honesty, sexual purity, integrity with money and kept promises; bad fruit is pride, greed, immorality, manipulation, deceit, and a trail of wounded people (Galatians 5:19–21). The effect: good fruit leaves people loving Christ more and leaning harder on God; bad fruit leaves them puffed up, crushed or fleeced, with the leader exalted and God’s name dragged down.

Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? Obviously not. A plant produces according to its nature. Some thornbushes had small black berries that might look like grapes from a distance; some thistles had heads that might look like figs. But up close, the difference was clear.

So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. Character produces conduct. The heart shows itself in time.

The root decides the fruit. This is a Reformation truth before the Reformation. No amount of outward religious performance can squeeze good fruit from a corrupt root; in the end it will show its true nature. Good fruit grows only from a heart made healthy by the grace of God. False teachers may mimic the language of the kingdom and produce impressive-looking fruit for a season, but it will not survive the test of time, nor the eye of the one who sees the roots as well as the branches.

Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. The same words John the Baptist used (3:10). False prophets face God’s judgment.

Thus you will recognize them by their fruits. Jesus repeats it for emphasis. The test takes time. Fruit is not visible in the first season.

Judged in autumn. Nobody can inspect a tree in March and pronounce on it. An orchard is judged in autumn, and a bad tree can look identical to a good one for most of the year. So the test Jesus gives cannot be run quickly, and that is not a defect in it. A great deal of the damage done in churches has been done by men whose fruit would have been obvious in five years and who were given authority in five weeks (1 Timothy 3:6; 5:22). The instruction is not be suspicious. It is wait, and watch what actually grows.

What it does not mean. Not that we should be suspicious of every Christian leader, or treat every mistake or weakness as proof of false prophecy. All teachers sin and make mistakes (James 3:1–2). The test is the pattern of life and the substance of teaching over time. Nor are impressive results proof of a true prophet: large crowds, miracles and charisma can accompany false teaching (24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9). The next verses make this clear.

Are there prophets today, true or false? The prophets and apostles laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and with the completion of Scripture the canon is closed; this app holds, charitably, that the revelatory gift of prophecy has ceased. So anyone today who claims a new word from God that adds to Scripture or binds the church is to be tested with great care. But the warning reaches wider than titles. Any preacher, author, podcaster or teacher who claims to tell you what God says is to be weighed by Scripture and by his fruit (1 John 4:1; Acts 17:11).

In a sentence. Beware of teachers who look like believers but are wolves; you will recognise them by the fruit of their lives and teaching.

On a Tuesday. Whose teaching are you following: online preachers, popular authors, podcasters? Test them by Scripture, and by the fruit of their lives over time, not by their popularity.

Where it applies: A popular online preacher says God wants you rich, and his own life is marked by luxury and pride. Test him by Scripture and by his fruit, and stop listening.

Where it would be wrong: You treat your own pastor as a false prophet because he differs from you on a secondary matter, such as baptism or the end times, or because his style annoys you. False prophets deny the gospel, or live in persistent sin. A brother you disagree with is not a wolf.

For worship. The Good Shepherd does not leave his sheep to the wolves. He warns them because he loves them, and he laid down his life for them when the wolf came. He knows his own, and no one will snatch them out of his hand. And he is the true vine, the healthy tree, whose fruit never fails; every good thing that grows in his people grows from his life in them. Blessed be the Shepherd and Overseer of our souls, who sees every root and keeps his flock.

parallels.desc: the axe laid to the root

verseByVerse.quote: Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. On that day many will say to me, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?" And then will I declare to them, "I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not everyone who calls Jesus “Lord” will enter the kingdom, but only those who do his Father’s will. On the last day, many will point to their prophesying, exorcisms and miracles done in his name. He will say: I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.

Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord. The double “Lord, Lord” expresses fervour or familiarity. These people use the right words, the right confession. But words are not enough.

The most startling warning in the sermon. These are not pagans or casual churchgoers. They have a strong claim to spiritual experience and to success in ministry. The gifts and the activity can all be present where the relationship is absent.

Will enter the kingdom of heaven. Jesus speaks of the final judgment.

But the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Doing God’s will is the mark of a true disciple (12:50). Not perfect obedience, but a life of genuine submission to God, shown in repentance and in obedience to Christ’s words (v. 24).

On that day. A standard phrase for the day of judgment (Isaiah 2:11; Malachi 3:17; 2 Timothy 1:12).

Many will say to me. Jesus is the Judge. Only God judges the world (Genesis 18:25). Jesus quietly claims to be the one before whom everyone will stand (25:31–46; John 5:22).

Did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? Impressive religious activity, done in Jesus’ name, with apparent power. Yet it is not enough. Judas was among the Twelve who were sent to heal and cast out demons (10:1–8). Spiritual gifts and results are not proof of saving faith.

A résumé at the bar of God. Look at what is missing from their defence, because Jesus records it in full. Every word of it is about them: we prophesied, we cast out, we did. Three achievements offered as a record. What is entirely absent is any mention of mercy, of the cross, of needing to be forgiven. Nobody who has grasped the first line of this sermon arrives holding up a record; the poor in spirit come with empty hands (5:3). These men are not failed disciples. They are strangers who were extremely busy.

I never knew you. In the Bible, “to know” often means a personal, covenant relationship (Amos 3:2; John 10:14, 27; 2 Timothy 2:19). Jesus does not say “I used to know you” or “you lost your salvation”, but “I never knew you”. They were never his. Their religion was a performance, without a relationship.

Not too little, but never known. He does not say you did too little, or your works were not good enough. The issue is not the volume of the service but the absence of the relationship. So the anxious question people usually bring to this passage, have I done enough, is exactly the wrong question. It is the question these men were asking, and it is the reason they are outside.

Depart from me. From Psalm 6:8. The most terrible words in the Bible: banishment from Christ’s presence (25:41; 2 Thessalonians 1:9).

The Judge on the throne. In Psalm 6 David says these words to his enemies, confident that the LORD, who alone judges the earth, has heard his weeping. Jesus takes them on his own lips as the Judge who pronounces them. The carpenter from Nazareth stands in the place of God on the last day and gives the eternal verdict. The same Jesus who is so tender with the poor in spirit is the one before whose face heaven and earth will stand or fall. He is not only the teacher of the sermon; he is its Judge.

You workers of lawlessness. “Lawlessness” (anomia) means living without regard to God’s law. Their impressive works covered lives that did not submit to God’s will.

What it does not mean. Not that we are saved by doing God’s will, as if our obedience earns heaven. Jesus has opened the sermon with grace (5:3). Doing God’s will is the fruit and evidence of true faith, not its root (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17–18). Nor does it mean that true believers must live in constant fear of being rejected. The warning is for those who are religious but not truly converted. Those who trust Christ and love his will can be assured that he knows them (John 10:27–29; 1 John 3:18–24). And it does not mean that a believer can lose their salvation: “I never knew you” shows these people were never saved.

How do I know I am not one of them? Notice first that these men are surprised. Nobody in this scene was worried on the way in. The person lying awake frightened by this verse is showing the opposite of what it describes; fear of self-deception is not the mark of the self-deceived, who are perfectly comfortable. Then examine yourself honestly with the tests John gives (1 John 5:13): do you believe that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh; do you love other Christians in practice; is there real obedience, a turning from sin, however slow? Does your sin grieve you? Do you want Christ, or only his benefits? Then look away from yourself. Your grip on Christ will be unsteady all your life; his grip on you is not (John 10:28–29). And if you still cannot be sure, come again today with nothing, for whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). The one thing you must not do with this passage is assume.

In a sentence. Calling Jesus “Lord” and doing impressive works in his name are not enough; only those who truly belong to him and do his Father’s will enter the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Do you know Christ, or only about him? Is your religion a relationship that shows itself in obedience, or a performance?

Where it applies: You attend church, but have never personally trusted Christ or turned from sin. These verses are a mercy to you: come to him today.

Where it would be wrong: A believer who loves Christ and is fighting sin reads these verses and fears that every failure means he never knew Christ. The people here are those who boast of their works and practise lawlessness (vv. 22–23). The struggling believer who trusts Christ and confesses sin is not among them (1 John 1:9; John 6:37).

For worship. The Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19). That is the most frightening sentence in the world to the busy stranger and the sweetest to the weakest child of God. To be known by Christ is to be loved before the foundation of the world, called by name, washed in his blood and held in his hand. The Judge who will say depart to those he never knew is the Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep he knows, and who will say to them, come, you who are blessed by my Father. Blessed be the Lord Jesus, Judge of all, who knows his own and will never let them go.

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus ends the sermon with a parable of two builders. The one who hears his words and does them builds on rock, and his house stands through the storm. The one who hears and does not do them builds on sand, and his house falls with a great crash.

Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them. “These words of mine”: the whole Sermon on the Mount. Jesus claims that our eternal destiny depends on how we respond to his words. Only God’s word carries that weight (Isaiah 40:8). Both builders hear; the difference is doing.

Will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. In Galilee, the wise builder dug down through the soil to the bedrock and built his foundations there (Luke 6:48). It took more time and effort, and the work was hidden underground.

The landscape behind it. Much of that country is cut by wadis, watercourses that are bone dry most of the year. In summer a wadi bed is the most inviting building site imaginable: flat, level, cleared by the water, the sand easy to dig. A man could get a house up quickly and cheaply, and in July he would look like the sensible one. Luke names what the wise man did differently: he dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock (Luke 6:48). Not necessarily a different site; the same ground, and he went down through it until he hit something that would not move.

And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house. In the dry season, the beds of wadis (seasonal streams) looked like flat, sandy, convenient building sites. But in the rainy season, sudden torrential storms turned them into raging torrents in minutes. The storm pictures all the trials of life, and above all the final judgment of God (Isaiah 28:16–17; Ezekiel 13:10–14).

But it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. The foundation made the difference. In the parable itself, the rock is hearing Jesus’ words and doing them (v. 24). On whether the rock is also Christ himself, see below.

Underground work. Notice what kind of work digging is. It is slow, it costs money, it delays the house, and when the building is finished nobody can see it. The foundation is the one part of a house that is never admired, and in fair weather it makes no visible difference at all. That is exactly the point about obedience. Most of what this sermon has asked for, dealing with anger before it becomes murder, cutting off what feeds lust, loving an enemy, giving in secret, forgiving a debt, refusing to serve money, is invisible. It is done underground. Nobody applauds it. It is also the only thing that makes any difference on the day the water comes down.

And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. Easier, quicker, and from the outside the house looked the same. The foolish builder’s problem was not ignorance; he heard. It was not hostility; he was building a house too, perhaps a religious one. His problem was that he heard and did not do.

The houses look identical. Matthew does not say the foolish man’s house was shoddy or small. Both men built, both finished, both slept under a roof. Nothing suggests you could tell them apart by walking past. The sand of easy religion, respectable morality or a Christianity that costs nothing can hold up a comfortable house for years. To build on sand is to sit under good preaching and nod along, to know your Bible and enjoy discussing it, to be baptised and decent, while the words never change how you live on Monday morning.

And it fell, and great was the fall of it. The sermon ends not with comfort but with a crash. Jesus leaves his hearers with the urgency of a decision.

The sound of a house going down. The greatest sermon ever preached simply stops with the noise of a collapse, with no summary, no invitation and no softening. It is the fourth pair in a row, and they have narrowed all the way: two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations. In every pair the wrong option is the comfortable one, and in every pair the two are hard to tell apart from outside. A broad road looks like freedom, a wolf looks like a sheep, Lord, Lord sounds like faith, and a house on sand looks like a house.

Is the rock Christ, or obedience? Read plainly, the parable says the wise man is the one who hears Jesus’ words and does them. Jesus does not say here, I am the rock. And the crowd on the hillside did not yet know that he would die for sins and rise again; even his disciples did not grasp that until much later (16:21–23). So we must not hurry past what the text says. How do we know what it means? As with the narrow gate (vv. 13–14), read in widening circles.

1. What the first hearers would have heard. In the Old Testament, God himself is the Rock of his people (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 18:2), and the righteous are established for ever when the storm has swept the wicked away (Proverbs 10:25). Isaiah spoke of a foundation stone laid by God, a sure foundation for whoever believes, and of a storm of judgement that sweeps away every refuge of lies (Isaiah 28:16–17). Now Jesus says that the one secure foundation for the day of judgement is his own words. Not Moses’ words, not the scribes’ traditions, but these words of mine. That is why the crowds were astonished: he taught as one who had authority (vv. 28–29). Even before the cross, the parable confronts them with Jesus himself.

2. What “these words” actually ask. Doing Jesus’ words cannot mean keeping the sermon perfectly, because the sermon itself rules that out. It demands perfection (5:48), and it teaches disciples to ask daily for forgiveness (6:12). Its words begin with the poor in spirit, who bring nothing (5:3), and with those who mourn over sin and hunger for a righteousness they do not have (5:4, 6). It tells us to ask our Father, who gives good things to those who ask (7:7–11). So the wise builder is not the person who never fails. He is the one who takes Jesus’ words to heart and acts on them, coming as a beggar for mercy and then living as Jesus teaches. The foolish builder hears, perhaps admires, and carries on as before.

3. The verses just before. The judgement in verses 21–23 turns on whether Jesus knew them. People who did impressive things in his name are turned away; what they lacked was a real relationship with him, shown in doing the Father’s will. So hearing and doing Jesus’ words is not a substitute for knowing him. It is what knowing him looks like.

4. What the rest of Scripture makes explicit. Later, Jesus explains that he will give his life as a ransom (20:28) and that his blood is poured out for forgiveness (26:28). Peter applies Isaiah’s foundation stone directly to Christ: whoever believes in him will not be put to shame (1 Peter 2:4–7). Paul says no one can lay a foundation other than Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11). These passages do not change the parable; they show what was in it all along. Jesus’ first hearers understood less than we do, but they were asked for the same response in kind: trust him and do what he says. After the cross we know more fully who it is we are trusting, and what he did for us.

Verdict: in the parable, the rock is hearing and doing Jesus’ words, and we should let it say that, as a sharp warning against hearing without obeying. But because those words begin with mercy for the poor in spirit, and because the one who speaks them is the Lord who will judge, building on them means building on Jesus himself: trusting him and following him. Obedience does not earn the foundation. It is what building on it looks like.

He puts his words in the place of the law. Consider what has just been claimed. Israel’s wisdom had one foundation, and it was not negotiable: the blessed man is the one whose delight is in the law of the LORD (Psalm 1:2). A carpenter from Nazareth ends his sermon by putting his own sayings in that place: build on my words, and you will stand. He does not say his teaching agrees with the rock. He says it is the rock.

What it does not mean. Not that we build our own salvation by obeying Jesus’ teaching perfectly. We build on Jesus by trusting him and following him. Obedience is the evidence that we have dug down to the rock. James says that whoever hears the word and does not do it deceives himself (James 1:22–25). Nor does it mean that wise builders escape storms. Both houses face the same storm. Faith in Christ does not exempt us from trouble; it keeps us standing through it.

What if I have heard sermons for years and done little? Then this parable is God’s kindness to you today, because the storm has not yet come and the digging can begin now. Do not try to rebuild everything at once. Take one thing from this sermon you have heard many times and not done, perhaps forgiving someone, giving in secret, or praying in your room, and do it this week, trusting Christ for strength and mercy. Tell a Christian friend so that he can ask you about it. Build on the rock one shovelful at a time. The Lord who calls you to dig is the rock you are digging toward, and he does not despise small beginnings.

In a sentence. Those who hear Jesus’ words and do them build on rock and stand through every storm; those who hear and do not do them build on sand and fall.

On a Tuesday. Which part of the Sermon on the Mount have you heard but not done: forgiving, giving in secret, refusing to worry, loving an enemy? Act on it this week.

Where it applies: Your home group has studied the Sermon on the Mount for ten weeks, and every week you have nodded at the passage on worry while lying awake over money. This week, take your fears to your Father in prayer each night, set your giving aside first, and leave tomorrow with him. That is digging down to the rock.

Where it would be wrong: A believer whose life has fallen apart, through illness, redundancy or bereavement, concludes that his house must have been built on sand. Both houses faced the same storm. The wise man’s house was battered too; it simply did not fall. Trouble is not proof of a bad foundation. Standing through it, still clinging to Christ, is proof of a good one (Romans 8:35–39).

For worship. The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer (Psalm 18:2). The rock under the wise man’s house is the Lord himself, the stone the builders rejected, laid by God in Zion as a tested and precious cornerstone. The storm of judgment that will sweep every refuge of lies away broke once in full on him, at the cross, and he did not fall; he rose. Those who build on him will stand when the rain falls and the floods come and the last wind blows, not because they were strong builders but because he is an unmoving foundation. Blessed be Christ, our Rock, who cannot be shaken.
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season; a house on sand could be swept away overnight.

parallels.desc: a wall smeared with whitewash falls

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus finished, the crowds were amazed at his teaching, because he taught with his own authority, not like their scribes.

And when Jesus finished these sayings. A formula Matthew uses to end each of the five great teaching sections (11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1).

Five books from a greater Moses. The formula occurs five times and only five, each closing a block of teaching, until at 26:1 it appears for the last time with a small addition, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, and the passion begins. So Matthew has built his Gospel around five great discourses: the Sermon on the Mount (5–7), the mission charge (10), the parables of the kingdom (13), the teaching on the church (18), and the discourse on the end (24–25). Five books of teaching, beginning on a mountain, given by one Matthew has already shown coming out of Egypt (2:15), passing through the water and being tested forty days in the wilderness. Anyone raised on the Scriptures would feel where that was going. A greater than Moses has come and is giving the law its full meaning.

The crowds were astonished at his teaching. “Astonished” means struck, overwhelmed, amazed. The crowds who had gathered around the disciples (5:1) had been listening throughout.

Knocked sideways, and it did not wear off. The verb, ekplēssō, means to be struck out of position, the word for a blow that knocks somebody sideways. The tense suggests that it went on: the astonishment did not wear off when he stopped talking. And what struck them was not first the content, the demands or the beauty of it. Matthew is specific: it was his authority.

For he was teaching them as one who had authority. His own authority: “But I say to you” (5:22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44). He did not quote earlier rabbis; he did not say “Thus says the LORD” like a prophet. He spoke as the one whose word is final: who fulfils the law (5:17), who will judge the world (7:22–23), and whose words are the rock on which life stands (7:24).

And not as their scribes. The scribes taught by quoting traditions and earlier authorities: “Rabbi so-and-so said, and Rabbi so-and-so replied.” Their authority was borrowed. Jesus’ authority was his own.

There is no modest reading. The scribes were not frauds or fools; they were careful men doing careful work, and their method was how a tradition is faithfully handed on. What the crowd had never heard was a man who cited nobody. Six times in one sermon he said, you have heard that it was said, but I say to you. He opened Moses on his own word, in public, without a single supporting authority, and then told them that their eternal safety depended on doing what he had just said. This is either breathtaking arrogance or the voice of the one to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given (28:18). A man either has that standing or he does not, and the rest of Matthew’s Gospel is the working out of which.

What it does not mean. Not that astonishment is the same as faith. The crowds were amazed, but amazement does not save. Many who were astonished later turned away. The right response to Jesus’ authority is not admiration, but obedience (v. 24).

How should I respond, having read the whole sermon? Not by feeling impressed and moving on, which is what most of that crowd did. Come to him first as the poor in spirit, admitting that you have not kept these words and cannot in your own strength, and receive the mercy and righteousness he gives. Then take him at his word as your King: his words are now the final authority over your money, your eyes, your tongue, your enemies and your worries. Read the sermon again, slowly, over the coming weeks. Ask your Father daily for the Spirit to make it true in you. And expect him to do it, because the one who taught it is also the one who lives it in his people.

In a sentence. The crowds were amazed that Jesus taught with his own divine authority, not borrowed authority like the scribes.

On a Tuesday. Do you treat Jesus’ words as interesting advice, or as the final authority over your life?

Where it applies: A colleague asks what you think about revenge, or money, or lust, and you begin to say what most people think. Stop, and tell him plainly what Jesus says, as the word that settles it for you, gently and without apology.

Where it would be wrong: You decide that because Jesus’ words carry final authority, the rest of Scripture, Moses, the prophets and Paul, matters less, and you read only the red letters. Jesus came to fulfil the Law and the Prophets, not to set them aside (5:17), and he sent his apostles to speak with his authority. All Scripture is his word (2 Timothy 3:16).

For worship. Bow before the one whose word is final, and whose word is the rock you stand on. He spoke, and the crowds were struck dumb; he will speak again, and the dead will rise. The Word who was with God in the beginning sat on a Galilean hillside and opened his mouth, and blessed the poor, and taught the law its depths, and called us to his narrow gate. All authority in heaven and on earth is his, and he uses it to bless beggars and build them on himself. Glory to Christ, our Teacher, our King and our Judge, whose words will never pass away.
verseByVerse.note: Scribes taught by citing earlier authorities; Jesus spoke on his own authority (“But I say to you”).

7.theology:
Hearing and Doing: Faith and Works in Reformed Theology. Matthew 7:24–27 has sometimes been read as teaching salvation by works: do the words of Jesus and be saved. Reformed theology reads it more carefully. The doing is not the foundation; the rock is. The foundation is Christ himself, received by faith. The doing is the evidence and expression of genuine faith — what James calls the faith that works (Jas. 2:17).

Calvin wrote that we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. The wise builder who hears and does is the person who has been genuinely changed by the words of Jesus — not merely intellectually persuaded but existentially transformed. The doing of the Sermon on the Mount is not the cause of salvation but its fruit; not the foundation but the superstructure. And the foundation, as Paul will make clear (1 Cor. 3:11), is Jesus Christ himself — the one whose words these are.
7.examples:
Then: The two builders have their Old Testament counterparts in the wise and foolish in Proverbs: the one who builds their house on wisdom (Prov. 9:1) and the one who builds on folly (Prov. 9:13–18). Israel’s history is the extended parable of a nation that heard God’s word at Sinai and alternately built on it (David, Hezekiah, Josiah) and ignored it (the cycle of judges, the divided monarchy, the exile). The storm that came on the sandbuilders in Israel’s history was Babylon — and Jeremiah watched the great fall of it (Jer. 7:1–15, which echoes this passage).

Now: The Sermon on the Mount ends with the most personal challenge of the entire Gospel so far: what are you building on? The storm is coming — the storms of suffering, of loss, of death — and the question that will matter then is being answered now by what you build with your ordinary days. The person who reads the Sermon and is intellectually impressed but does nothing with it is the sand builder. The person who allows its demands to drive them to the Christ who fulfils them, and who in the Spirit begins to do what the Sermon commands — that person is building on rock. The flood will reveal the foundation. Build now while the weather is good.

8.title: The King’s Authority Over All
8.text: <sup>1</sup>When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. <sup>2</sup>And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>3</sup>And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>5</sup>When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, <sup>6</sup>“Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly.” <sup>7</sup>And he said to him, “I will come and heal him.” <sup>8</sup>But the centurion replied, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. <sup>9</sup>For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>10</sup>When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, “Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. <sup>11</sup>I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, <sup>12</sup>while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” <sup>13</sup>And to the centurion Jesus said, “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” And the servant was healed at that very moment. <sup>14</sup>And when Jesus entered Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. <sup>15</sup>He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him. <sup>16</sup>That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.” <sup>18</sup>Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. <sup>19</sup>And a scribe came up and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>20</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>21</sup>Another of the disciples said to him, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” <sup>23</sup>And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. <sup>24</sup>And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. <sup>25</sup>And they went and woke him, saying, “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.” <sup>26</sup>And he said to them, “Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?” Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. <sup>27</sup>And the men marveled, saying, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” <sup>28</sup>And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. <sup>29</sup>And behold, they cried out, “What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” <sup>30</sup>Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. <sup>31</sup>And the demons begged him, saying, “If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs.” <sup>32</sup>And he said to them, “Go.” So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. <sup>33</sup>The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men. <sup>34</sup>And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
8.overview:
Matthew 8 is a gallery of authority. Coming down from the mountain where he gave the law of the kingdom, the King now demonstrates the power of the kingdom. In rapid succession Jesus heals a leper with a touch, a Gentile servant with a word, a feverish woman with a hand, and a raging sea with a rebuke. The crowds ask the right question: “What sort of man is this?” Matthew intends the reader to answer: the Son of God, in whom all authority in heaven and on earth is vested.

The chapter also sounds the notes of grace toward outsiders. A leper — ritually unclean, excluded from community — is touched rather than avoided. A Roman centurion — a Gentile, an occupier — displays faith that shames Israel. Jesus announces that many from east and west will recline at the messianic banquet while presumptuous insiders face exclusion. The kingdom breaks every boundary of ethnic privilege. The centurion’s faith is the model: he grasps that Jesus’ authority is absolute, that his word accomplishes what he speaks. This is saving faith — resting wholly on the word of the King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Messiah Heals: Authority over Leprosy, Paralysis, and Fever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew groups ten miracles in chapters 8-9, presenting Jesus as the one Isaiah promised: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases" (v. 17, citing Isa. 53:4). The leper, the centurion's servant, and Peter's mother-in-law are the first three — representing the ritually unclean, the Gentile, and the woman. Jesus heals all with equal authority and without discrimination. The verse-by-verse fills in what these three lines cannot. On the leper: Leviticus prescribes torn clothes, loose hair, a covered lip and a shouted "Unclean, unclean", and dwelling alone outside the camp (Lev. 13:45-46) — so this man had not been touched by anyone for as long as the disease had lasted. Note that he broke the law to approach, and that his prayer is the reverse of ours: he is certain of the power and unsure of the willingness. And Jesus did not need to touch him — the very next healing in this chapter is done at a distance, by a spoken word — so the contact was gained for its own sake. He touched him first and said "be clean" second. The command to show himself to the priest handed the priesthood a ceremony (Lev. 14: two birds, cedar, scarlet, hyssop, running water) that they had learned and almost certainly never performed — in the whole Old Testament only Miriam and Naaman were cleansed of this. On the centurion: Matthew has him speak to Jesus directly while Luke has him send Jewish elders and then friends (Lk. 7:3-8); this is the ordinary convention by which a man does what he does through agents, and Luke supplies the reason the elders would carry his message — he had built their synagogue. His "I am not worthy" is not self-disparagement but consideration: a Jew entering a Gentile house contracted defilement, and he is protecting Jesus from a cost he judges unnecessary. His sentence has stood in the liturgy for centuries. And Jesus marvels exactly twice in the Gospels — here at faith, and at Nazareth's unbelief (Mk. 6:6) — so faith in its presence and its absence is the only thing recorded as astonishing him.
verseByVerse.theology: Each healing is an enacted parable of salvation: Jesus touches what is untouchable (the leper), heals at a distance by his word alone (the centurion's servant), and raises up those laid low by sickness. The healing of disease and the forgiveness of sins are not unrelated — both are expressions of the same redemptive authority. Isaiah 53:4 locates these healings within the atonement: Jesus bore our diseases not merely by healing them but ultimately by carrying them on the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The centurion's faith astonishes Jesus and becomes the template for Gentile inclusion: "not even in Israel have I found such faith." Faith is not a Jewish property or a product of religious background; it is the trust that recognizes authority and rests in it. The centurion understood command-and-response because he lived under authority. His insight: if Jesus commands, it is done.

verseByVerse.quote: When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus came down from the mountain, a man with leprosy, an outcast who was forbidden to approach people, came and knelt before him: Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean. He had no doubt of Jesus’ power; his only question was whether Jesus would want to.

Meaning first. Matthew 8 is the chapter in which the King who has just finished speaking begins to act. The Sermon on the Mount ended with the crowds astonished, because he taught as one who had authority (7:29). Now Matthew shows what that authority does when it meets the world as it actually is. It touches a leper, heals a Gentile’s servant by a word spoken at a distance, lifts a fevered woman from her bed, and empties a town of its sickness in a single evening. Then it is tested by the cost of following him, by a storm that terrifies men who had fished that lake all their lives, and by two men so possessed that nobody dared pass their tombs. Disease, the sea and the demonic each meet him, and each obeys at a word. In every scene the question is turned back on the watchers: a Gentile soldier believes, the disciples have little faith, and a whole town asks him to go away. The chapter asks its own question halfway through, what sort of man is this, and spends the rest of its length answering it: the Lord himself, come near enough to touch.

The connection. Chapters 5–7 showed Jesus’ authority in word. Chapters 8–9 show his authority in deed: ten miracles, in three groups, over disease, nature, demons and death. Matthew sums up both in 4:23 and 9:35: teaching, preaching and healing. The King who taught with authority (7:29) now acts with authority. The words and the works belong together. A sermon with no power behind it would be only advice, and a miracle with no word to interpret it would be only a marvel. Here the one who said blessed are the poor in spirit goes down the hill and shows what he meant.

When he came down from the mountain. Like Moses coming down from Sinai (Exodus 34:29). Moses came down with the law on tablets of stone and a face so bright that the people were afraid to come near him. The greater Moses comes down from his mountain, great crowds follow him, and the first person to come near him is the one man in Galilee whom the law of Moses forbade to come near anyone. The law could diagnose a leper and exclude him. It could not cleanse him. What the law could not do, the Lord of the law is about to do with his hand.

A leper. “Leprosy” in the Bible (Hebrew tsara’at, Greek lepra) covers a range of skin diseases, not only what is now called Hansen’s disease. Leviticus 13–14 gave detailed laws. A person with such a disease was ritually unclean: he had to live outside the camp or town, wear torn clothes, leave his hair loose, cover his upper lip, and cry out that he was unclean to warn others away (Leviticus 13:45–46). Anyone who touched him became unclean too. He was cut off from worship at the temple, from family, from work and from all human touch. Rabbis regarded curing leprosy as being as difficult as raising the dead, and the king of Israel said as much when Naaman came to him: am I God, to kill and to make alive (2 Kings 5:7)? In the Bible, leprosy also became a vivid picture of sin: a defilement that separates us from God and others, which we cannot cleanse ourselves.

A man at his own funeral. To feel this scene you need to know what his days had been. Torn clothes were the dress of a mourner, so he attended his own funeral every morning. Loose hair was a sign of mourning too. His mouth was covered. And he was required to shout, so that nobody came near him by accident. Later Jewish tradition fixed the distance at four cubits, about six feet, and at a hundred cubits if the wind was blowing from him towards you. He lived as a walking warning.

He had not been touched. Not by his wife, if he had one; not by his children; not by a friend’s hand on his shoulder. However long the disease had been on him, that is how long it had been since another human hand had rested on him. Loneliness of that kind does something to a person’s sense of whether anybody could want him near, and it explains the exact shape of the prayer he is about to make.

An honest note on the word. The Hebrew and Greek terms cover a good deal more than the disease we now call leprosy. Leviticus applies the same word to marks in fabric and in the walls of a house, which no bacterium produces. It was a category of ritual defilement that covered a range of visible skin diseases. That does not soften the picture; it widens it. Whatever this man had, it had put him outside.

Came to him. He should not have. The law required him to keep his distance, and every step towards that crowd was a breach of the rule he had lived under for years. The correct thing was to stand far off and shout a warning. Desperation drove him past the rules, and so did something more than desperation: he had heard enough about this man to think the rules might not be the last word.

And knelt before him. The word (prosekynei) is the same as “worship” (2:11), the word used of the wise men before the child in Bethlehem. He bowed low in reverence. He knelt before he had received anything. The worship came first and the healing second, which is the right order, and it is the order of every true approach to Christ.

Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. “Lord” may simply mean “sir”, but in Matthew it carries more. His faith is clear: you can. He does not doubt Jesus’ power. His question is Jesus’ will: does Jesus want to touch someone like me? Read the sentence twice, because most of us have it the other way round. We tend to be sure that God is kind in general and unsure that he will act in particular; we doubt his power over our situation and assume his good will. This man is certain of the ability and uncertain of the willingness, which is exactly what years of being untouchable will do to a person. And he asks to be made “clean”, not just “healed”: he wants restoration to God’s people and to worship. He is asking not only to be well but to be allowed back in.

What it does not mean. Not that “if you will” shows weak faith. It is humble faith, which leaves the outcome to Christ. Jesus does not rebuke him for it. Nor is it a model for doubting God’s willingness to forgive. When we come to him for cleansing from sin, he is always willing (John 6:37; 1 John 1:9). We may pray “if you will” about healing or circumstances, because God has not promised them; we need not pray it about forgiveness, because he has.

Is leprosy in the Bible a punishment for sin? Not as a rule. Occasionally God struck a person with it as a direct judgement: Miriam for opposing Moses (Numbers 12:10), Gehazi for his greed (2 Kings 5:27), King Uzziah for forcing his way into the priest’s work (2 Chronicles 26:19–21). But the law of Leviticus treats it as a condition, not a crime, and nobody in the Gospels suggests this man had brought it on himself. Its uncleanness was a picture of what sin does to all of us, not a verdict on the particular person who had it. So if you are ill, do not conclude that God is punishing you. Sickness belongs to a fallen world, and Jesus treats the sick with compassion, never with accusation.

In a sentence. An outcast leper came to Jesus in humble faith, certain he could heal him, and asking only whether he would.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you feel makes you untouchable to God: a sin, a shame, an illness, a history you would rather nobody knew? Notice what you actually doubt. Most of us do not doubt that Christ is able; we doubt that he would want to, for someone like us. Then do what the leper did. Do not wait at a distance until you are presentable. Come to Jesus as you are, kneel, and say the honest sentence: Lord, you can. And if you know someone who lives at a distance from everybody, the one nobody sits next to, remember who walked towards this man.

For worship. The law of God was holy, and it could only keep the leper out. The Son of God is holy, and he lets the leper in. Moses came down from the mountain and the people were afraid of his face; Christ came down from his mountain and an outcast ran to his feet. There is no defilement that sends him further away, and no man so far outside that he cannot be reached. The holy one of Israel is willing, and he has never once been unwilling to anyone who came to him for cleansing.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, "I will; be clean." And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus reached out and touched the leper: I am willing; be clean. At once he was healed. Jesus told him to tell no one, but to show himself to the priest and offer the sacrifice Moses commanded, as evidence to them.

And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him. This is astonishing. Jesus could have healed with a word, as he does a few verses later, at a distance, for the centurion’s servant (v. 13). The power did not require contact. Nothing was gained by the contact except the contact itself, and that was the point. He touched the untouchable. This man may not have been touched by anyone for years. By the law, touching a leper made a person unclean (Leviticus 5:3). But when Jesus touches the leper, Jesus does not become unclean; the leper becomes clean. Holiness flows outward from Jesus, instead of uncleanness flowing in. He is greater than the law’s categories.

The outstretched hand. The phrase is the language of the exodus. God told Moses that he would stretch out his hand and strike Egypt, and redeem his people with an outstretched arm (Exodus 3:20; 6:6). The hand that once stretched out over Egypt in judgement and rescue now stretches out across the six feet the law had put between this man and everyone else, and rests on skin that nobody had willingly touched in years. It is the same God, doing the same thing: coming down to deliver.

The order of it. He touched him first, and then said be clean. For the length of one sentence the Lord of glory was in physical contact with an unclean man who had not yet been healed. Under the law that made him unclean until evening. It did not. The flow ran the other way, and that is the whole gospel acted out in a single gesture: a holiness that is not defiled by contact with the defiled, but destroys the defilement. Christ takes our uncleanness into his hands and gives his cleanness back.

Saying, I will; be clean. The direct answer to the man’s question. Jesus is willing. And his word has power: he speaks, and it happens, as God spoke at creation (Psalm 33:9). No formula, no process, no prayer to someone higher: simply the will of the Creator restoring what disease had destroyed. The man had asked about the will, and the first word of the answer is the will: I will. Of all the questions anyone has ever put to Christ, that is the one he has answered most plainly.

And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. Instantly and completely. Skin that had been rotting for years was made whole in a moment, without a period of recovery.

See that you say nothing to anyone. Jesus often told people not to spread news of his miracles (9:30; 12:16). This is sometimes called the “messianic secret”. Reasons: to avoid crowds who wanted only miracles, which hindered his teaching; to avoid the political misunderstanding that he was a military Messiah who would overthrow Rome; and so that his identity would be revealed in God’s time, through the cross. Mark tells us how this particular command went: the man went out and talked about it freely, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town (Mark 1:45). The instruction was not arbitrary. A reputation as a healer would bury the preaching under a queue of patients, and it did.

But go, show yourself to the priest. The law required a cleansed leper to be examined by a priest, who would declare him clean (Leviticus 14:1–32). Only then could he return to society and worship. Jesus respects the law of Moses (5:17). He wants the man fully restored, not just healed: back in his home, back at the table, back in the house of God.

And offer the gift that Moses commanded. The ritual of Leviticus 14 is elaborate and worth knowing. Two living birds; one killed over fresh water in an earthen vessel; cedarwood, scarlet yarn and hyssop; the living bird dipped in the blood and released into the open field. Then washing, shaving, seven days of waiting, and on the eighth day lambs, flour and oil. It was a sacrifice of thanksgiving and cleansing. And it had almost certainly never been performed. In the whole Old Testament only Miriam and Naaman are recorded as cleansed of this disease, and neither went through the rite in Jerusalem. Every priest had learned a ceremony that no priest expected to use: the book of the law contained a full procedure for an event that did not happen.

For a proof to them. A testimony to the priests: evidence that something extraordinary had happened, and that the one who cleanses lepers had come. When a man walked into the temple courts and asked for the rite for a cleansed leper, he was not merely keeping a rule. He was handing the priesthood a page they had never had cause to open, and somebody had to ask why. When John the Baptist later asks whether Jesus is the Messiah, Jesus points to this: lepers are cleansed (11:5).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus disregarded the law: he sends the man to keep it. Nor that his touch was necessary for the healing: it was an act of compassion. And the command to silence does not mean we should keep quiet about Jesus today. After the resurrection, the command is to tell everyone (28:19–20).

How does Jesus touch people now that he is not here in the body? Through his word and his Spirit first of all: the same voice that said I will, be clean, speaks in the gospel and makes guilty people clean before God (John 15:3). He also touches people through his body, the church. When a believer sits with the dying, visits the prisoner, holds the hand of someone everyone else avoids, Christ is at work through his members (25:40). And in the Lord’s Supper he gives visible, tangible signs that his body was given for us. So if you have felt untouched for years, go where his word is preached and his people gather. That is where his hand is most often felt.

In a sentence. Jesus willingly touched and cleansed the leper, and sent him to be restored to God’s people according to the law.

On a Tuesday. Who are the “untouchables” in your community: the lonely, the stigmatised, the sick, the person with the prison record, the one with the smell? Jesus touched them, and he did not have to. Think of one person whose company you avoid because it costs you something, and make one concrete approach this week: a visit, a meal, a hand on the shoulder. And when your own sin makes you feel unclean, remember the order: he touched first, and cleansed second. You do not have to be clean before he will come near.

For worship. Here is holiness that is not afraid of us. The Holy One of Israel, before whom the seraphim cover their faces, stretched out his hand and laid it on a leper, and the leper was clean. On the cross that same hand was stretched out and nailed, and there he did not merely touch our uncleanness; he took it, and bore it outside the camp, so that we might be declared clean before God and brought back in. I will; be clean: it was the first answer he gave to a sinner’s question, and he has never changed it.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, "Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Capernaum, a Roman centurion, a Gentile soldier, came to Jesus and appealed for his servant, who lay paralysed at home in terrible pain.

When he had entered Capernaum. Jesus’ home base (4:13), the lakeside town where Peter lived and where most of the chapter happens.

A centurion. A Roman army officer commanding about a hundred soldiers (a “century”). Centurions were the backbone of the Roman army: career officers promoted from the ranks, experienced, disciplined, responsible men, paid many times a common soldier’s wage. This one was probably serving Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, whose troops were organised on the Roman pattern, since Capernaum lay in Herod’s territory rather than under direct Roman rule. Either way he was a Gentile soldier in an army the locals resented, the visible face of foreign power. Luke adds that he loved the Jewish nation and had built their synagogue, and that Jewish elders came to Jesus on his behalf (Luke 7:3–5). In the New Testament, centurions are presented positively every time (27:54; Acts 10), which is a small and striking fact in an occupied country.

His synagogue. The synagogue whose white limestone ruins visitors see in Capernaum today is a later building. But it stands on a foundation of black basalt from the first century, which is very probably the floor of the synagogue this man built. Jesus taught in it (Mark 1:21). A Gentile soldier paid for the room in which the Son of God first preached in Capernaum.

Did the centurion come himself, or send others? Matthew has the centurion come to Jesus and speak with him directly. Luke says he sent Jewish elders first, and then friends with the message about not being worthy, and does not have the two men meet at all (Luke 7:3–8). This is a difference of reporting, not a contradiction. In the ancient world, as in ours, a man is said to do what he does through his agents: we say a king built a palace or a company wrote a letter without supposing that either held the trowel or the pen.
