Matthew shortens the story and presents the request as the centurion’s own, as a message sent through others is the sender’s message, because his point is the centurion’s faith. Luke, who is interested throughout his Gospel in how Jews and Gentiles actually dealt with each other, keeps the messengers in.

Came forward to him, appealing to him. A Roman officer, a man of power, coming to a Jewish teacher with a request. A reversal of normal social order. The word (parakalōn) is the language of urgent entreaty. He does not command; he pleads. The man used to giving orders has met someone he cannot order.

Lord, my servant. The word (pais) can mean “boy”, “child” or “servant”; Luke uses the word for slave, and adds that the man was highly valued by him (Luke 7:2). The centurion cared deeply for a slave, someone his society regarded as property. That itself was unusual. Roman law allowed a master to do as he liked with a slave, and the agricultural writers advised selling off old and sick ones like worn-out tools. This man, who had every right to replace his servant, goes out to plead for him. (Some have suggested in recent years that the relationship was sexual. Nothing in either Gospel supports it: pais was a common word for a servant, and Luke’s plain word for a slave removes the ambiguity.)

Is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly. In great pain, perhaps near death (Luke 7:2). He does not tell Jesus what to do. He describes the need and lays it before him, which is what prayer often is.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ mission at this stage was to Gentiles in general: he came first to Israel (15:24). But this encounter is a preview of the Gentiles coming to Christ (v. 11).

Can I come to Christ on behalf of someone else? Yes, and this man shows how. He came for his servant, and Jesus healed the servant without ever meeting him. Praying for others is not a lesser kind of prayer; it is one of the most Christlike things a believer does, because it is what Christ himself does for us at the Father’s right hand (Romans 8:34). Bring the names of your unbelieving family, your sick friend, your colleague in trouble. But notice the limit too. Your faith can bring someone to Christ in prayer; it cannot believe for them. Every person must in the end trust him for himself. So pray for them, and pray that they will come.

In a sentence. A Gentile officer came humbly to Jesus to ask help for his suffering servant.

On a Tuesday. The centurion used his position to help someone below him. If you have authority, at work or at home, use it to care for those under you. Ask who depends on you and has no power to demand anything: the junior colleague, the cleaner, the child, the elderly parent. When did you last spend your influence on them rather than on yourself? A man’s faith is often first seen in how he treats the people who cannot repay him.

For worship. The Lord whom this soldier approached is the master who does what the Roman law never required of any master: he cares for slaves. He took the form of a servant himself (Philippians 2:7), and he died for people who had nothing to bring him and could not have commanded his attention. No one is beneath his notice, no request too humble for his hearing, and no one is kept away from him by race or rank. A foreign officer pleading for a sick slave was heard, and so is every sinner who comes in his name.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I will come and heal him." But the centurion replied, "Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus offered to come and heal the servant. But the centurion said he was not worthy to have Jesus enter his house. Jesus did not need to come: he only needed to say the word, and the servant would be healed.

I will come and heal him. Jesus is willing to go, even to a Gentile’s house. Some translate it as a question: Shall I come and heal him? The Greek can bear it. On that reading Jesus is probing, raising the very issue of a Jew entering a Gentile house so that the centurion can answer it, which is exactly what he does. It cannot be settled, and the sense of the passage is much the same either way: Jesus responds to the request, and the centurion’s reply shows what kind of faith he has.

Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. A devout Jew who entered a Gentile’s house became ritually unclean (Acts 10:28; 11:12). It is why Peter needed a vision before he would go to Cornelius, and why the men who brought Jesus to Pilate would not enter the governor’s headquarters, so as not to be defiled before the Passover (John 18:28). The centurion knows this, and does not want to put Jesus in that position. He is protecting Jesus, not only humbling himself. It is the courtesy of a man who has taken the trouble to learn what his neighbours believe, offered at the very moment when his servant is dying and he has every excuse to think of nobody else. But his words go deeper than ritual. “Not worthy” expresses real humility. The Jewish elders said he was worthy (Luke 7:4); he says he is not. True greatness knows its unworthiness before Christ.

But only say the word, and my servant will be healed. He believes that Jesus’ word alone has power, even at a distance. Jesus does not need to be present, see the patient, touch, or perform a ritual. His word is enough. What makes this faith rather than respect is what it assumes about the way things work. He has grasped that the word alone is what acts, and that is precisely what Genesis says about how the world came to be: God said, and it was so. The centurion is ascribing to Jesus the creative word of God, and he is doing it before anyone in Israel has.

The prayer the church kept. His sentence has never been forgotten. In an adapted form it has stood in the liturgy for centuries, said before communion: Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. Millions of Christians who have never thought about a Roman officer have prayed his words. And it is fitting, because this is how every believer approaches the ascended Christ: we cannot see him or touch him, and we do not need to. He is in heaven, and his word reaches as far as he sends it.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ presence is unimportant, or that touch and physical means do not matter. Jesus touched the leper (v. 3), and God works through physical means such as baptism, the Lord’s Supper, and the laying on of hands. But the centurion grasped that the power is in Jesus himself and in his word. The Roman Catholic Mass uses a version of his words before Communion: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. The words express true humility.

If I feel unworthy, should I stay away from the Lord’s Supper? No. The Supper is for people who know they are unworthy and trust Christ, and the centurion’s words are exactly the right frame of mind for it. Paul warns against eating in an unworthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27–29), which means coming carelessly, with unconfessed sin you mean to keep, or with contempt for the body of believers. It does not mean coming while feeling unworthy. If you waited until you felt worthy you would never come, and if you ever did feel worthy you would be coming wrongly. Examine yourself, confess your sin, put things right with anyone you have wronged, and then come, resting on his word and not on your worthiness.

In a sentence. The Gentile centurion confessed his unworthiness and trusted that Jesus’ word alone could heal at a distance.

On a Tuesday. Do you believe that Jesus’ word is enough, even when you cannot see him act? Much of the Christian life is lived exactly where this man stood: the need is in another place, the Lord seems far off, and all you have is what he has said. Take one promise that fits your situation today (for example, that he will never leave you nor forsake you, Hebrews 13:5) and rest on it as though he had spoken it into your room. He has.

For worship. The word that made the heavens is the word this soldier asked for, and it was given. Christ does not have to travel to his people to help them; he speaks, and distance disappears. He sits now at the right hand of the Father, upholding the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), and that same word is near us, in our mouth and in our heart (Romans 10:8). Lord, we are not worthy that you should come under our roof. And yet you have come, and made your home with us (John 14:23).
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house; the centurion spares Jesus the problem.

parallels.desc: unlawful for a Jew to visit a foreigner
he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, "Go," and he goes, and to another, "Come," and he comes, and to my servant, "Do this," and he does it." When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, "Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion explained his faith from his own experience: he knew how authority works. He obeyed his superiors, and his soldiers obeyed him. Jesus has that kind of authority over sickness. Jesus was amazed and said he had not found such faith in all Israel.

For I too am a man under authority. He is part of a chain of command: he obeys his superiors (a tribune, the governor, ultimately the emperor), and his authority comes from them. When he speaks, he does not speak as a private man; the whole weight of Rome stands behind his word.

With soldiers under me. He also has authority over others.

And I say to one, Go, and he goes. He does not have to do things himself; he speaks, and his orders are carried out. Go, come, do this: three short commands, and three men move.

The logic. The centurion reasons: just as I can give orders and they are obeyed, because I carry the authority of Rome, so Jesus carries the authority of God. Sickness and disease are under his command. He speaks, and they obey. The centurion has understood something many in Israel had not: Jesus’ authority is divine. This is the heart of faith: not confidence in the one praying, but confidence in the authority of the one addressed.

Further than he could see. Press his analogy one step further than he could, because otherwise it may mislead. He pictures Jesus as he pictures himself, a man set under authority whose word carries weight because a greater power stands behind it. That is true so far as the Son is sent by the Father and does nothing of his own accord (John 5:19). But it is not the whole truth. Jesus is not a prophet holding God’s power on loan, as Elijah and Elisha held it. He is the eternal Son, in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). When Elisha raised the dead, he prayed and stretched himself on the child (2 Kings 4:33–35); when Jesus heals, he simply speaks, and the thing is done. The authority is not borrowed. It is his own. The centurion had hold of the right end of the truth and did not yet know how far down it went.

When Jesus heard this, he marveled. “Marvelled” means amazed, astonished. Only twice in the Gospels is Jesus said to marvel: here, at faith, and in Nazareth, at unbelief (Mark 6:6). Two occasions, and both are about faith: its presence where it had no business being, and its absence where it should have been guaranteed. Nothing else in the record is said to have surprised him. Not the storms, not the demons, not the crowds, not his own betrayal. Faith is the one thing that could still astonish the Son of God, and it astonished him in both directions. Jesus was truly human: he could be surprised and moved.

And said to those who followed him, Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. Israel had the Scriptures, the covenants and the promises (Romans 9:4–5). Yet a Gentile soldier, with none of these advantages, showed greater faith than anyone in Israel. Faith here means trusting Jesus’ authority and power, and relying on his word alone. And Jesus says it to those who followed him, which means he says it to his own disciples. They needed to hear that the outsider had seen further than they had.

What it does not mean. Not that no one in Israel had faith: the disciples had followed him. But none had yet grasped his authority so clearly. Nor is faith a force or a technique that makes miracles happen. Its power lies in its object. The centurion’s faith was great because he saw how great Jesus is.

How can Jesus be amazed if he is God and knows everything? Because he is truly man as well as truly God, one person with two natures. As God the Son he knows all things. But in taking our nature he took a real human mind, which learned and grew: Luke says he increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), and he said that he did not know the day of his return (24:36). His human mind received knowledge, perceived, and responded, as ours do, and the marvel is a real human response to something wonderful. It does not mean God was caught off guard. It means the Son of God became human enough to be moved by a soldier’s trust, and that is part of the wonder of the incarnation.

In a sentence. The centurion understood that Jesus commands sickness as he commanded his soldiers, and Jesus marvelled at faith greater than he had found in Israel.

On a Tuesday. Faith grows by seeing how great Jesus is. Read a Gospel passage today that shows his authority, and let it enlarge your trust. Notice also where your prayers start. Most of us begin with how strongly we believe, and then grow anxious about whether it is enough. The centurion began with how great Jesus is, and forgot to think about the size of his faith at all. Start there. And let this verse humble anyone raised with every privilege: the outsider who has heard little may be trusting Christ more simply than you are.

For worship. Here is a Lord whose word sickness obeys as a soldier obeys his officer, and who marvels at the faith of a sinner. He holds all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18), and he does not hold it at a distance from us. The one whose command the whole creation keeps is the one who stopped on a Capernaum street, astonished and delighted, because a Gentile trusted him. He made us, he commands all things, and he rejoices when we believe him.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. And to the centurion Jesus said, "Go; let it be done for you as you have believed." And the servant was healed at that very moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declared that many Gentiles from east and west would sit at the great feast of the kingdom with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, while many of Israel, who seemed to be heirs, would be thrown out into the darkness. Then he told the centurion to go: it would be done as he believed. The servant was healed at that moment.

Many will come from east and west. From the ends of the earth: the Gentile nations (Isaiah 49:12; 59:19; Malachi 1:11). The centurion is the first of a great multitude. The picture is drawn from the prophets’ promises of gathering: God would bring his people from the east and gather them from the west (Isaiah 43:5), gathering them in from the lands, from east and west, from north and south (Psalm 107:3). The imagery is entirely Jewish and entirely familiar. What is unfamiliar is who is being gathered.

And recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. At formal banquets, guests reclined on couches around a low table. The prophets pictured the age to come as a great feast that God would prepare for all peoples, with rich food and fine wine (Isaiah 25:6–9). The patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the founders of Israel, will be there. And Gentiles will sit beside them, as members of the family, not as servants. Abraham’s blessing reaches the nations (Genesis 12:3).

The surprise at the table. To recline at a man’s table was to share his life. A Jew of that day would not eat with Gentiles at all; and here the Gentiles lie down beside Abraham himself, the father of the nation, at the most honoured meal there will ever be. The prophets had spoken of the nations coming to Zion. Jesus shows the nations at the table while some of Abraham’s own descendants stand outside. That was always where the promise to Abraham was heading: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed. A Roman soldier in Capernaum is its first instalment.

When and where is this feast? Jesus does not give a date, but the passage itself gives strong clues, and the rest of Scripture fills them in.

1. In the verse itself. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had been dead for nearly two thousand years. For them to sit at a table, they must be raised from the dead. So the feast lies on the far side of the resurrection (22:31–32). And the other side of the picture is final judgement: the outer darkness, with weeping and gnashing of teeth, is the language Matthew uses for the end of the age (13:40–43, 49–50; 25:30, 46). The feast and the exclusion happen at the same moment, at the end.

2. In the Old Testament background. Jesus is drawing on Isaiah’s feast for all peoples on God’s mountain (Isaiah 25:6–9). At that feast God swallows up death for ever and wipes away tears from all faces. Paul says that this happens at the resurrection, when Christ returns (1 Corinthians 15:51–54). So the feast belongs to a world where death is gone.

3. In the rest of Matthew and the New Testament. At the Last Supper Jesus says he will drink the cup new with his disciples in his Father’s kingdom (26:29). His parables picture the end as a wedding feast (22:1–14; 25:10). Revelation calls it the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), followed by the new heaven and new earth, where there is no more death (Revelation 21:1–4).

4. Already, and not yet. The kingdom is already present in Jesus (12:28), and the centurion is the first of the many from east and west. Gentiles are coming in now, through the preaching of the gospel to all nations (28:19), and every Lord’s Supper is a foretaste of the feast (1 Corinthians 11:26). But the feast itself, in full, comes when Christ returns, the dead are raised, and the new creation begins.

Where Christians differ: the feast and the thousand years. Revelation 20:1–6 speaks of a thousand-year reign, and Christians read it in different ways, which affects how they read this verse. Premillennialists believe that Christ will return before (pre-) a literal thousand-year reign on earth, centred in Jerusalem. Many of them, especially dispensationalists, see this verse as describing that earthly kingdom: the patriarchs raised and sharing in Christ’s reign, with believing Gentiles, before the final state. Dispensationalists also tend to see the kingdom of heaven in Matthew as a kingdom first offered to Israel and then postponed. Historic premillennialists also expect an earthly thousand-year reign after Christ returns, but without a sharp division between Israel and the church. Postmillennialists see the coming of many from east and west being fulfilled as the gospel gradually wins the nations before Christ returns, with the feast itself in the final state. Amillennialists take the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a symbolic picture of the present age, between Christ’s first and second comings, in which Christ already reigns; at his one return come the resurrection, the judgement and the new creation, and that is where the feast belongs.

Verdict: the amillennial reading fits this verse best. (1) The verse places the feast at the resurrection and the final judgement, which Jesus elsewhere teaches happen together, at one return (25:31–46; John 5:28–29); it leaves no room for a thousand-year stage in between. (2) Isaiah’s feast comes when death is swallowed up for ever, but in premillennial views death still continues during the thousand years. (3) Nothing in the verse mentions a thousand years. That idea comes from Revelation 20, a book full of symbols, and it is not wise to read it into a plain saying of Jesus. To be fair to premillennialists, they are right that this is an earthly hope: the patriarchs will be raised bodily, and the meek will inherit the earth (5:5). Amillennialists agree. The feast is not in a ghostly heaven, but in the renewed creation, the new world (19:28; 2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1–3). This is a difference among faithful Christians, to be held charitably. What all agree on is the heart of the verse: people from every nation will sit with Abraham at God’s table, by faith in Christ.

While the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. “Sons of the kingdom” means those who seemed to be its natural heirs: Jews who relied on their descent from Abraham (3:9). Many will be excluded. The bitterness of the title is the point. To be a son of the kingdom was to be an insider by birth, and Jesus takes the phrase people would have used of themselves with satisfaction and attaches it to the ones being put out. The banquet hall is pictured as brightly lit at night, and “outer darkness” is the darkness outside, away from the light, warmth and joy.

In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. A phrase Matthew uses six times for final judgment (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30), and which appears only once more in the New Testament (Luke 13:28). Weeping is grief and regret; gnashing of teeth is anguish, and perhaps anger. It is a picture of hell: exclusion from God’s presence and joy. The evangelist most concerned with Israel’s Scriptures and Israel’s Messiah is the one who reaches most often for the language of final loss, and the first time he uses it the people in view are the sons of the kingdom.

And to the centurion Jesus said, Go; let it be done for you as you have believed. He received what he trusted Jesus for. Faith is the hand through which the healing came, but it is not the source of it. The centurion’s faith did not heal his servant; Jesus’ word did. Faith simply put him in the place to receive what only Jesus could give.

And the servant was healed at that very moment. At a distance, by a word. The centurion’s faith was proved right. Luke tells us the messengers went back to the house and found the servant well (Luke 7:10). The distance between a street in Capernaum and a sickbed somewhere across town made no difference at all.

What it does not mean. Not that God has rejected the Jewish people as a whole, or that all Jews will be excluded. The apostles, and the earliest church, were Jews; Paul expects many Jews to come to faith (Romans 11:25–26). Jesus is warning against relying on privilege, and declaring that faith, not ancestry, determines who sits at the feast. Nor does “as you have believed” mean that we get whatever we believe hard enough for. The centurion trusted Christ’s authority, and Christ honoured it. Faith receives; it does not command.

A warning transferred, not retired. This verse has sometimes been used to say that God has finished with Israel and replaced her with the church. The apostle who wrestled hardest with that question asked it outright, whether God had rejected his people, answered it with an emphatic no, and pointed to himself as evidence (Romans 11:1). Then he warned Gentile believers in the strongest terms against arrogance towards the branches that were broken off (Romans 11:18–21). What Jesus is dismantling is not Israel but presumption: the assumption that descent secures anything. John the Baptist had said the same about stones and children of Abraham (3:9). And it is exactly as false when a Gentile assumes that a Christian upbringing or church membership secures it.

Is the outer darkness the same as hell, and is it for ever? Yes. Jesus uses several pictures for the final judgement of the unrepentant: darkness outside the feast, fire that is not quenched (Mark 9:48), a furnace (13:42). The pictures differ, because no single image can hold it, but they agree on what matters. It is real, it is conscious (people weep), it is exclusion from the presence and joy of God, and Jesus says it is eternal, just as eternal life is (25:46). He speaks of it more than anyone in the Bible, and he does so not to frighten us for its own sake but to warn us while the door is still open. The same verse that speaks of the darkness speaks first of the feast and of many who come in.

In a sentence. Gentiles who trust Christ will feast with the patriarchs in the kingdom, while those who rely on privilege without faith will be shut out.

On a Tuesday. Are you relying on your Christian background or church membership, or on Christ? Faith, not privilege, brings us to the table. Ask yourself honestly what you would say if asked why God should let you in. If the answer begins with anything you have done or anywhere you were born, it is the answer of a son of the kingdom. If it begins and ends with Christ, you are with the man from east and west. And when you take the Lord’s Supper, remember that you are eating a foretaste of the great feast, beside believers from every nation, and pray for the nations still far off.

For worship. The table is set, and the guest list is longer than anyone in Capernaum imagined. People from every tribe and language will recline beside Abraham, not because they were born near him but because they believed the promise he believed, and the promise was Christ. The Son of God ate with sinners and was thrown out of the city for it, cast into the darkness at noon on the cross, so that strangers might be brought into the light of his Father’s house. Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Glory to the host who paid for the feast with his own blood.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew’s recurring picture of final judgment.

parallels.desc: from the north and from the west

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus entered Peter's house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Peter’s house, Jesus found Peter’s mother-in-law in bed with a fever. He touched her hand, the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him.

When Jesus entered Peter’s house. In Capernaum. Archaeologists have found a house there that was venerated by Christians from the first century as Peter’s, later built over by a church. The miracles are not separated by long reflection; they flow one into the next. From a leper on the road and a soldier in the street, Jesus walks into a fisherman’s kitchen.

His mother-in-law. Peter was married. Paul mentions that Peter took his wife with him on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5). Matthew mentions her in passing, without comment, and in doing so records one of the plainest facts in the New Testament: a man does not acquire a mother-in-law any other way.

A married apostle. The detail is worth pausing on, because a great deal has been built on Peter that it quietly complicates. The Roman Catholic Church regards him as the first pope and requires its priests in the West to be celibate. Yet here is Peter with his wife’s mother living in his house, and Jesus in the house too, healing her. Years later Paul, arguing for his rights as an apostle, asks whether he too may take a believing wife with him, as the other apostles do, and Cephas, which is Peter (1 Corinthians 9:5). He was still married, and his wife was still travelling with him, decades after this morning in Capernaum. None of this is an argument against celibacy freely chosen. Paul was unmarried and commended singleness to those given that gift (1 Corinthians 7:7), and Jesus spoke of those who give up marriage for the kingdom (19:12). The point is narrower: whatever office Peter held, it was one a married man could hold, and a rule requiring otherwise cannot appeal to him. Paul will later say that an elder should be the husband of one wife (1 Timothy 3:2).

Lying sick with a fever. In the ancient world, a fever could be serious and even fatal, with no effective medicine. Luke, the physician, calls it a high fever (Luke 4:38).

He touched her hand. Another touch (v. 3). A rabbi would not normally touch a woman who was not his relative. Jesus is not bound by such customs when compassion calls. There is something very homely in it: the first thing we learn about the leading apostle’s household is that Jesus was in it, sitting with a sick old woman and taking her by the hand.

And the fever left her. Completely and at once. Luke says he rebuked the fever (Luke 4:39), speaking to it as to something that had no right to be there.

And she rose and began to serve him. Normally, after a fever, a person needs days to recover strength. She got up immediately, fully restored. “Serve” (diakoneō) means to wait on, to provide a meal. Her response to being healed was service. This is the pattern of the Christian life: those whom Christ restores serve him (20:28). She does not make a speech of thanks. She gets up and puts food in front of him, which is the most natural form gratitude takes.

The three healings. The first group of miracles (vv. 1–15) shows Jesus healing three kinds of people who were on the margins of Jewish religious life: a leper (ritually unclean), a Gentile’s servant (an outsider), and a woman (who had a lesser place in religious life). Jesus’ kingdom welcomes those whom others keep at a distance. And there is no threshold of seriousness below which he loses interest. He heals the dramatic case and the ordinary one with the same attention: leprosy on the road, a fever in the back room.

What it does not mean. Not that women’s calling is only domestic service. “Serve” is the same word used of the angels serving Jesus (4:11) and of Jesus’ own mission (20:28). Service is the highest calling of every disciple.

Does Jesus care about ordinary illnesses and small troubles? Yes. This is a fever, the kind of thing every household in Capernaum had seen many times, and Matthew sets it beside a leper and a dying servant as though it were just as much his concern. Peter, who was in that house, later wrote that we should cast all our anxieties on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). All of them, not only the large ones. Do not save your prayers for emergencies. The child’s temperature, the sleepless night, the worry that seems too small to mention: bring them. The Lord who walked into Peter’s kitchen is not too grand for yours.

In a sentence. Jesus healed Peter’s mother-in-law with a touch, and she rose at once to serve him.

On a Tuesday. How can you serve Christ today out of gratitude for what he has done for you? It need not be dramatic. She served a meal. Find the ordinary, unseen service in front of you, a meal cooked, a lift given, a sick neighbour looked in on, and do it for him. And if you are the one recovering, from illness or from a hard season, ask what you can do with the strength he has given back.

For worship. The Lord of glory came into a fisherman’s house and took a feverish woman by the hand. He is not only the Christ of crowds and miracles but the Christ of kitchens and sickrooms, who notices the person lying in the back room. He came not to be served but to serve and to give his life (20:28), and the first thing the healed woman did was serve him, which is how all his healed people answer him. He raised her up, and he will raise us up, and we shall serve him for ever (Revelation 22:3).

parallels.desc: Peter was married, and his wife travelled with him

verseByVerse.quote: That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick, This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening, crowds brought to Jesus many who were demon-possessed and sick. He drove out the spirits with a word and healed everyone, fulfilling Isaiah: he took our weaknesses and carried our diseases.

That evening. Mark tells us it was the Sabbath (Mark 1:21, 32). When the Sabbath ended at sunset, people could carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules. Mark adds that the whole town gathered at the door (Mark 1:33). It is one of the most moving scenes in the Gospels: the sun going down over the lake, and up every street the stretchers and the supporting arms, until the doorway of Peter’s house is surrounded.

They brought to him many who were oppressed by demons. Demon-possession is a condition in which an evil spirit controls or severely afflicts a person. The Gospels distinguish it from illness, though they sometimes overlap. Jesus’ casting out of demons shows that he has come to defeat Satan’s kingdom (12:28–29).

And he cast out the spirits with a word. No rituals, incantations or long prayers, as exorcists of the time used. Just a command. His word has authority over the spiritual world.

And healed all who were sick. All, not some. Not the most deserving, not the most faithful, not the most urgent. All. The breadth of his healing anticipates the breadth of the gospel: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah 53:4. The fourth Servant Song, the chapter of the suffering Servant who is wounded for our transgressions.

He took our illnesses and bore our diseases. Isaiah 53 describes the Servant of the LORD who suffers for his people. The verse in Hebrew speaks of him bearing our griefs and carrying our sorrows; the next verse says he was pierced for our transgressions. Matthew applies the first part to Jesus’ healing ministry. Jesus does not catch our diseases; he takes them away. But Matthew’s choice of Isaiah 53 points ahead: the healings are possible because of the cross, where the Servant bore the root of all disease, which is sin (1 Peter 2:24). Every healing in Jesus’ ministry was a down payment on the full healing that his death and resurrection would secure: a new body, in a new creation, without sickness or death (Revelation 21:4).

A shadow of Calvary. It is a remarkable move. Matthew takes Isaiah’s great sin-bearing chapter and applies it, not yet to the cross, but to an evening of healings in Galilee. The healings are not separate from the atonement; they are its advance expression. Jesus was carrying the weight of human brokenness throughout his ministry, not only at Calvary. The cross is the once-for-all bearing of sin and all its consequences; the healings are acted promises that the one who would bear it all was already present and already at work. Every healing was a shadow of Calvary, and every restoration a foretaste of the resurrection.

What it does not mean. Not that physical healing is guaranteed to every believer now, as part of the atonement, so that sickness shows a lack of faith. This is taught by some in the “health and wealth” movement. The atonement does secure our complete healing, but at the resurrection, not necessarily now. Believers in the New Testament were sick and not healed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9; 1 Timothy 5:23; 2 Timothy 4:20). Jesus’ healings were signs of the kingdom’s arrival, not a promise that every Christian will be healed before death.

Does God still heal like this today? Two things must be held together. First, yes: God is sovereign and good, he still hears prayer, and we are plainly told to pray for the sick (James 5:14–15). He has never stopped healing in answer to the cries of his people. But second, these Gospel healings must be read in their place. They came in a cluster, and the clusters of miracles in Scripture gather around the great moments of fresh revelation, Moses and the exodus, Elijah and Elisha, and now Christ and his apostles, not evenly across every age. Their purpose was largely to authenticate: to mark Jesus out as the Messiah and his apostles as his accredited messengers (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). They were signs of a unique hour, not a promise of constant healing on demand. Even in the apostolic age healing was never automatic: Paul’s thorn was left in place (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), he left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20), he prescribed wine for Timothy’s stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Epaphroditus nearly died (Philippians 2:27).

Where Christians differ: does the gift of healing continue, and is healing promised now? Continuationist Christians point out that no text says the gifts will end, that Paul lists gifts of healing among the gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9), and that James tells the sick to call for the elders to pray (James 5:14–16); some also read Isaiah 53:4 as promising healing in this life to all who have faith. Cessationist Christians hold that the miraculous gifts, healing among them, belonged to the apostolic age and confirmed the apostolic message, while God continues to heal in answer to the prayers of his people. Verdict: the cessationist reading is the more likely. The healing gifts were signs of the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12), and even Paul did not heal his own friends (2 Timothy 4:20). God still heals in answer to prayer, but Isaiah 53:4 does not guarantee healing in this life. Its final fulfilment is the resurrection, and Peter applies the same chapter to sin-bearing (1 Peter 2:24). This is a difference among godly Christians, to be held charitably, and all agree that God hears and answers prayer for the sick.

So what should I do when I or someone I love is ill? Pray boldly, and trust God to answer as he wills. Ask the elders of your church to pray, as James directs (James 5:14). Use doctors and medicine thankfully: Luke was a physician, and Paul recommended a remedy to Timothy. And beware the cruel teaching that healing is guaranteed if only your faith is strong enough. It was not promised even to apostles, and it heaps guilt on the suffering for their own pain. Sometimes grace is given to carry us through the sickness rather than to remove it (2 Corinthians 12:9). And every believer will be perfectly and finally healed at the resurrection, if not before.

Why are demons everywhere in the Gospels and so rare elsewhere? The dark powers are real throughout Scripture, but the spotlight moves. In the Old Testament they stay mostly in the background: behind idolatry, which Scripture calls sacrificing to demons (Deuteronomy 32:17; Psalm 106:37), in the occasional evil spirit (1 Samuel 16:14), in Satan the accuser (Job 1; Zechariah 3). Open possession and exorcism are almost absent. Then in the Gospels it erupts, because the King has come. The arrival of God’s kingdom in Jesus forces the kingdom of darkness into the open; the demons show themselves, scream, and are routed with a word. If it is by the Spirit of God that Jesus casts out demons, the kingdom of God has come (12:28); the strong man is being bound and his house plundered (12:29). The eruption is less a new activity than the enemy’s panic before the invading King.

And why does it fade in the rest of the New Testament? Not because the demonic vanished, but because the decisive battle was won. At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The letters still take the unseen war with deadly seriousness, but they reframe it: less the spectacular seizing of individuals, more the believer’s daily, sober resistance to the spiritual forces of evil, clothed in the whole armour of God (Ephesians 6:11–12), resisting the devil so that he flees (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9), and giving him no foothold (Ephesians 4:27). The defeated enemy still prowls, but he now meets a people covered by Christ’s victory.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. The word “oppressed” covers a range, from outward affliction to inward control. A believer can be tempted, deceived, attacked and harassed by the devil, and the New Testament warns us to be alert. But one who is indwelt by the Holy Spirit belongs to Christ and is not owned by any other power. You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). The Christian fights from within Christ’s triumph, never under the enemy’s ownership. If you are troubled by dark thoughts or fears, do not conclude you are possessed; bring them to Christ, to Scripture, and to a wise pastor.

In a sentence. Jesus drove out demons and healed every sickness, fulfilling Isaiah’s picture of the Servant who carries our weaknesses, as a preview of the full healing his cross secures.

On a Tuesday. If you are living with illness, bring it to Christ in prayer. He may heal; and if not now, he will at the resurrection, and he carries you through it. Think of the townspeople bringing the sick to the door that evening, and do the same in prayer: bring the names one by one. If you are well, ask whom you could carry, by a visit, a meal, a lift to an appointment, or simply by naming them before God.

For worship. The Servant of Isaiah stood at Peter’s door at sunset and took the town’s sicknesses away, and then he went on to Jerusalem and took the town’s sins on himself. What he did that evening for a few streets in Capernaum he will do in the end for the whole creation: no more death, no more mourning, no more pain. He bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, and by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:4–5). Blessed be the Physician who became the patient, and the Servant who carried what we could not.

parallels.desc: by his wounds you have been healed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–34 — The Cost of Following and the Lord of Storm and Demons
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 8 moves from healing to the cost of discipleship and the authority of Jesus over creation and the demonic. Two would-be followers learn that Jesus offers no earthly security (no place to lay his head, no leave for burial rites). Then Jesus stills a storm with a rebuke and casts demons into pigs, and the Gadarenes ask him to leave. The sequence shows that following Jesus is neither comfortable nor universally welcomed. Four things more, all treated below. The scribe says "Teacher" and the next man says "Lord" (vv. 19, 21) — and that distinction runs through Matthew, where disciples say Lord while opponents, enquirers and the rich young man say Teacher, and Judas alone at the supper says Rabbi. The scribe files his own assessment in his first word. Note too that across the Gospels the people who volunteer are tested and the people who are called simply go. Matthew's word for the storm is not the word for a storm: he writes seismos megas, a great shaking — the standard Greek for an earthquake — where Mark has the ordinary term for a squall. And he uses it twice more, at the crucifixion (27:51-54) and at the tomb (28:2), each time as the setting for a declaration of who Jesus is. The sleeping is the only time the Gospels record it, and the scene is Jonah replayed and inverted: a man asleep below decks in a storm, woken by terrified sailors with almost these words (Jon. 1:5-6) — but Jonah slept fleeing God and was the cause of the storm and had to be thrown into the sea, while this sleeper is the end of it, and will himself be swallowed for three days (12:39-41). On the place name, the manuscripts genuinely divide between Gadarenes, Gerasenes and Gergesenes; Gerasa is thirty miles inland, Gadara six, and Gergesa (Kursi) is on the shore with the steep bank the story requires. And the pigs raise a question the passage does not answer — two thousand animals, somebody's business, destroyed — which is faced squarely below rather than tidied away.
verseByVerse.theology: The stilling of the storm is the Christological center of the chapter: "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?" The disciples' question is Matthew's question to the reader. Only the Creator can command his creation. The storm-still and the Gadarene exorcism together display authority over the two great threats of the ancient world — chaos (the sea) and the demonic (the Legion). Both submit instantly. The appropriate response is not comfort but worship — and the disciples begin to learn it.
verseByVerse.examples: The Gadarenes' request that Jesus leave their region is one of the saddest verses in the Gospels. They preferred their pigs to their Deliverer. The economy of the region mattered more than the liberation of two men in chains. This is not ancient history; every age chooses its pigs. The question Jesus poses to every community: what do you value more than the healing he brings?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. And a scribe came up and said to him, "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw the crowd, he gave orders to cross the lake. A scribe came and promised to follow him wherever he went.

The second section. Verses 18–34 move from healing to discipleship and authority. Before the next miracles, Jesus faces two would-be followers. What does following him cost? Then the disciples who do follow him get into a boat and find out.

He gave orders to go over to the other side. To the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, Gentile territory. Jesus withdraws from the crowds, who were drawn by miracles. He is not building a following by numbers. He leaves the very people who would most have liked to keep him.

And a scribe came up. An expert in the law (see 2:4). Most scribes opposed Jesus, but not all (13:52). This is the only scribe in the Gospels who offers to follow Jesus, and the offer is unlimited. It is the boldest promise anyone makes in the chapter.

Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go. An enthusiastic, impressive promise. He calls Jesus “Teacher”, the title used by outsiders in Matthew; disciples call him “Lord”. He sees Jesus as a great rabbi to join. The next man, in verse 21, says Lord.

Teacher or Lord. That distinction runs through the whole Gospel, and once you see it, it does not go away. In Matthew, disciples call Jesus Lord; outsiders, opponents and enquirers call him Teacher. The Pharisees say Teacher (12:38; 22:16). The Sadducees say Teacher (22:24). The rich young man says Teacher (19:16). At the Last Supper the eleven ask, is it I, Lord, while Judas alone says Rabbi (26:22, 25). Matthew keeps it up too consistently for coincidence. So the scribe’s opening word is his own assessment, filed in advance: he has come to attach himself to a rabbi, which is a step he understands and a career he can picture.

Volunteers and the called. A pattern holds across the Gospels with striking consistency: those who volunteer are tested, and those who are called simply go. Peter and Andrew were casting a net and offered nothing; they were told to follow and they did (4:18–20). Matthew was sitting at a tax booth, and made no speech (9:9). Jesus does not accept the scribe’s offer and does not refuse it. He tells him one fact about the life he is proposing to join, and Matthew never tells us what the man did with it. That is very probably the point. The story is left open because the reader is meant to finish it.

What it does not mean. Not that enthusiasm is wrong. But enthusiasm without counting the cost does not last (13:20–21).

Is it wrong to make big promises to Christ? Not wrong, but dangerous if they rest on yourself. Peter promised that he would die rather than deny Jesus, and denied him that night (26:33–35, 69–75). The problem was not that he loved Jesus too much but that he trusted his own strength too much. So by all means commit yourself to Christ wholeheartedly, in baptism, in church membership, in the vows of marriage. But make the promise leaning on him, and ask him to keep you in it. Christian faithfulness is not a man keeping his word to God so much as God keeping his word to a man, and the man holding on because he is held (John 10:28).

In a sentence. A scribe made an enthusiastic promise to follow Jesus anywhere.

On a Tuesday. Promises to follow Christ are easy to make on a good day. What will it take to keep them on a hard one? Think of a commitment you made to God in a moment of warmth, at a conference, after a sermon, in a crisis. Is it still being kept? If not, do not make a bigger promise. Ask for grace to keep the one you made.

For worship. The Lord does not need our grand offers, and he is not flattered by them. He knows what is in man (John 2:25), and he tells us the truth before we start. And when we fail the promises we made, he keeps the ones he made. The disciple’s confidence is not in his own wherever you go but in the Shepherd who said he would go before his sheep and lose none of them.

parallels.desc: “Let us go across to the other side”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." Another of the disciples said to him, "Lord, let me first go and bury my father." And Jesus said to him, "Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered that foxes have holes and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Following him means giving up security. When another disciple asked first to bury his father, Jesus said: follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead. Following him comes before everything.

Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests. Even wild animals have a place to rest and shelter.

But the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Jesus had no permanent home during his ministry. He depended on others’ hospitality (Luke 8:3). Following him means sharing his homelessness, his insecurity and his rejection. The scribe had not counted that cost. He was offering to follow a famous rabbi to a lecture hall, and Jesus answers that he is going nowhere comfortable. The one through whom the world was made had no pillow of his own. The first bed he had was a manger, and the last bed he had was a borrowed tomb.

The Son of Man. The first time in Matthew that Jesus uses this title, his favourite way of referring to himself (about thirty times in Matthew). It can simply mean a human being, as in Psalm 8:4 and Ezekiel 2:1. But it comes especially from Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given everlasting dominion over all peoples. Jesus uses the title both for his humility and suffering (here, and 17:22; 20:28) and for his glory and coming as judge (24:30; 26:64). It hid and revealed his identity at once: people could not easily turn it into a political slogan.

Why use that title here? Because the contrast is the message. The one to whom Daniel saw all dominion given has, today, not even a hole in the ground. Glory and poverty in a single phrase: the King of everything chose the life of a man without a roof. That is not a failure of his kingship. It is the way his kingship comes, through humiliation to the throne.

Another of the disciples said to him, Lord, let me first go and bury my father. Burying one’s father was one of the most sacred duties in Jewish life, taking priority over almost everything, including some religious duties. Burial happened on the day of death. If the father had just died, the son would not be standing with Jesus but at home among the mourners. So the man probably meant: let me wait until my father has died (perhaps years later), fulfil my family duties, and receive my inheritance; then I will follow. “First” is the key word: he wanted something else first. It is not a plea to attend a funeral. It is a request for an indefinite postponement, dressed as duty.

And Jesus said to him, Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead. A shocking statement. “The dead” who bury are probably the spiritually dead, those who do not follow Christ (see Ephesians 2:1). Let them take care of such duties. Jesus’ call is urgent and comes before every other loyalty, even sacred family duty (10:37; Luke 9:59–62). Read in its setting, the reply stops sounding cruel and starts sounding urgent, which is what it is. Only one person in history could rightly say this, because only God can claim a loyalty above father and mother. Jesus says it without hesitation.

Two kinds of would-be disciple. The first was too quick: enthusiastic but unaware of the cost. The second was too slow: willing, but not yet. Both needed to understand that following Jesus is total and immediate.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should neglect their parents, or not attend family funerals. Jesus condemned those who used religion as an excuse to neglect parents (15:3–6), and on the cross he provided for his mother (John 19:26–27). The point is priority: when following Christ and family duty conflict, Christ comes first. Nor must every Christian literally be homeless. But every Christian must hold home and security loosely, and be willing to give them up for Christ.

Caring for family is part of following him. The saying has been misused, so the guard needs to be firm. Jesus exposed the trick of declaring money dedicated to God so that you need not support your ageing parents, and said it made void the word of God (15:3–6). Paul is blunter still: anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Looking after your family is not a rival to following Christ. It is one of the ways you follow him.

What if following Christ costs me my family? For some readers the collision is real and sharp: a family that will cut you off, a parent who forbids church, a household where becoming a Christian costs you your place in it. Jesus is telling such a person the truth in advance, and it is a hard truth kindly told. He comes first, and he knows what that will cost you. Keep honouring your parents in every way that does not mean denying him: stay courteous, stay in touch where they allow it, keep praying for them, help them when they are in need. And hold on to his promise that no one who has left house or family for his sake will fail to receive far more, now in the family of the church and in the age to come eternal life (19:29).

The quieter form. For most of us the application is closer to the bone and much less dramatic. The man in this story is not refusing Jesus. He is saying later, and he has an excellent reason that nobody could criticise. That is the shape it usually takes with us. I will get serious about this when the children are older, when work settles down, when this hard season passes, when I retire. The reasons are genuinely good, and that is exactly what makes them effective. The kingdom cannot wait for the next convenient moment, because there is never going to be one. There is only today.

So is it wrong to own a home and want security? No. Jesus stayed in Peter’s house, ate at many tables, and was glad of the home in Bethany. Scripture never despises a house, a savings account or a settled life. The question is ownership. A home held as God’s gift, opened to others and ready to be given up if he asks, is a blessing. A home that has become the thing you could not lose, the reason you will not move, give or risk anything for him, has become a rival. Ask yourself what you would refuse him if he asked, and you will know where your security is.

In a sentence. Following Jesus means giving up security and putting him before every other loyalty, even sacred family duty, without delay.

On a Tuesday. What is the “first let me” in your life, the thing you are waiting to do before you fully follow Christ? He says, follow me now. Name it specifically: the conversation you are postponing, the habit you plan to deal with later, the giving you will start when things are easier. Then take one step on it this week. Obedience delayed with good reasons is still disobedience, and the reasons rarely run out.

For worship. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head, and he chose it. He who had the glory of the Father before the world existed became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He asks for first place because he deserves it: no father, no mother, no house has ever loved us as he has, or given what he gave. And the homeless Christ is preparing a place for everyone who follows him (John 14:2). The one who had no pillow will give his people a home that can never be taken away.
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died. Jesus’ call outranks even that.

parallels.desc: no one who looks back is fit for the kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. And they went and woke him, saying, "Save us, Lord; we are perishing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus got into the boat and his disciples followed him. A violent storm arose and the waves swamped the boat, but Jesus was asleep. The disciples woke him in terror: Lord, save us, we are dying!

And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. Matthew uses the word “followed” deliberately after verses 18–22. This is what following Jesus looks like: getting into the boat with him, and into the storm. They were out on the water because he had told them to go; obedience put them there.

And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea. The word for storm (seismos) usually means earthquake, a great shaking, the word behind our “seismic”. Mark, describing the same night, uses the ordinary word for a squall (Mark 4:37). Matthew writes seismos megas, a great shaking, and it is a strange thing to say about water. He uses the same word twice more, at the cross and at the tomb: the earth shook when Jesus died, and the centurion, seeing the earthquake, said truly this was the Son of God (27:51–54); and on the first Easter morning there was a great earthquake, the same two words as here (28:2). Three convulsions of the created order in this Gospel, and each is the setting for a revelation of who Jesus is. Matthew has chosen his words so that the reader will feel the lake, the hill and the grave as one series.

The lake itself. The Sea of Galilee lies about seven hundred feet (210 metres) below sea level, in a basin ringed by hills, with the snows of Mount Hermon to the north. Cold air from the hills can rush down the ravines onto the warm water and create sudden, violent storms, and the surface can go from flat to dangerous in a quarter of an hour. Several of the disciples were experienced fishermen, at least four of them professionals who had fished that water all their lives, and they concluded they were going to drown. So this was no ordinary storm.

So that the boat was being swamped by the waves. Literally “covered” by the waves. The boat was filling with water.

But he was asleep. Jesus was truly human, and truly exhausted after a long day of ministry. It is the only time in the Gospels anyone records Jesus sleeping. Of all the ordinary human things he must have done ten thousand times, this is the one time it is mentioned, and it is mentioned in a boat that is filling with water. His sleep also shows complete trust in his Father. The psalmist says: in peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8).

A greater than Jonah. Any Jew in that boat should have felt the echo, and Jesus will make it explicit four chapters later, when he says the only sign given will be the sign of Jonah (12:39–41). There is one other man in the Scriptures who slept through a storm at sea. Jonah went down into the ship and fell fast asleep while it threatened to break up, and the terrified captain came and woke him with almost the disciples’ words: get up, call on your god, perhaps he will spare us so that we do not perish (Jonah 1:5–6). Every element is reversed. Jonah slept because he was fleeing from God; Jesus sleeps because he is resting in him. Jonah’s presence was the cause of the storm; Jesus’ presence is the end of it. The sailors had to throw Jonah into the sea to save themselves; the disciples wake a man who stands up and speaks to the water, and it stops. Jonah was swallowed by the deep for three days and came back. So, said Jesus, would the Son of Man.

And they went and woke him, saying, Save us, Lord; we are perishing. A cry of panic, but also of faith: they turned to Jesus. “Save us” is the prayer of every believer in trouble. “Lord” and “save” are words with deep meaning in Matthew: Jesus’ very name means “the LORD saves” (1:21). In Greek it is three words, and the church has prayed them across twenty centuries in every kind of crisis. The prayer is panicked, but it is prayer: they run to Jesus, not away from him. These frightened men knew where to turn.

What it does not mean. Not that following Jesus means calm seas. The disciples were in the storm precisely because they followed him. Christians are not promised freedom from trouble; they are promised his presence in it (Isaiah 43:2). Nor does Jesus’ sleep mean he does not care. Mark records that the disciples asked whether he cared that they were perishing (Mark 4:38). He did; he was with them.

If Jesus is God, how could he sleep? Because he is truly man. The eternal Son took a real human body, which grew tired, hungry and thirsty, and needed sleep like ours. His human nature slept in the stern of the boat. But his divine nature did not cease to be what it is: the one who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4). While the man lay asleep on the cushion, the Son was still upholding all things by the word of his power, including the wind and the water (Hebrews 1:3). That is the mystery of the incarnation, and it is full of comfort. The Lord who sustains the stars knows what it is to be exhausted.

In a sentence. Following Jesus into the boat led the disciples into a terrifying storm, and they cried out to him to save them.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a storm because you followed Christ, you are not out of his will. Cry out to him; he is in the boat. Notice the kind of prayer that was enough: three panicked words. You do not need to compose something fine when the water is coming in. Lord, save me, is a prayer the Bible records with approval. And if you have been praying a long time and he seems asleep, remember that he is still in the boat, and the boat is not going down with him in it.

For worship. He slept as a man, worn out by love for the crowds, and he woke as the Lord of the sea. The one Jonah ran from is the one who sleeps in the stern, and the storm that should have swallowed the disciples could not swallow him. In the end the true deep did close over him, when he went down into death for us, and he came up again on the third day. The storm of God’s judgement broke on him so that the boat carrying his people would reach the shore.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?" Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. And the men marveled, saying, "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked why they were afraid, with such little faith. Then he got up, rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm. The disciples were amazed: what kind of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?

Why are you afraid, O you of little faith? Jesus speaks to the disciples first, before the storm. The order is deliberate. Their fear was the more dangerous of the two, and it was the thing he addressed before he said a word to the wind. “Little faith” (oligopistoi) is not no faith: they did call on him. But their faith was small and mixed with panic. Jesus gently rebukes their fear. In Matthew, Jesus uses this word only of his disciples (6:30; 14:31; 16:8; 17:20). He is patient with weak faith, but he wants it to grow. And notice what he does not rebuke. He does not rebuke them for waking him, or for the panic in the prayer. The rebuke is for the fear that had crowded out trust, not for the crying out.

Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea. He spoke to the storm as one rebukes a disobedient servant, or as he rebuked demons (17:18). In the Old Testament, the raging sea often pictured chaos and evil powers opposed to God, and only God could rule it (Psalm 65:7; 89:9; 107:23–30; Job 38:8–11). God rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up (Psalm 106:9). The sea that swallowed armies and frightened Israel for centuries goes quiet at the voice of a carpenter from Nazareth.

And there was a great calm. A great storm (v. 24), and a great calm. Normally, after a storm, the waves continue for a long time. Here, the sea became calm at once. The wind did not die down gradually; the water did not settle over an hour. There was a great calm, as sudden as the great shaking had been.

And the men marveled. “The men”: perhaps Matthew stresses their humanity, in contrast to him. They had been afraid of the storm. Now they are afraid of something greater, and Mark says they feared with a great fear (Mark 4:41). It is the right fear, the fear that falls on people who realise they are in the presence of God.

What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him? The key question of the passage. Psalm 107:23–30 describes sailors in a storm who cried to the LORD, and he made the storm still and hushed the waves, and brought them to their desired haven. The disciples have just seen Jesus do what only God does. The answer to their question is that he is not merely a man. He is Immanuel, God with us (1:23). They will confess it fully later: truly you are the Son of God (14:33). It is the question Matthew’s whole Gospel is written to answer, and the psalm had answered it already: the one who stills the sea is the LORD.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus always calms the storms of our lives immediately when we ask. Sometimes he calms the storm; sometimes he calms the disciple. The story is first about who Jesus is: Lord of creation. It assures believers that no storm is outside his control.

The honest word. These verses can be preached as though every storm ends in flat calm before breakfast. Sometimes he does not still it. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be taken away, kept it, and was given grace to carry what was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). What is promised is not always a change in the weather. What is promised is that he is in the boat, that he is not indifferent though he may seem so, and that there is a far shore. He said, let us go across to the other side, and he has never yet failed to land anyone he set out with.

Is it a sin to be afraid? The feeling of fear is not itself sin. Jesus himself was in anguish in Gethsemane, and the psalmist says, when I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). Fear is what a frail creature feels in danger. What Jesus rebukes is fear that has pushed trust aside, so that we act and speak as though he were not there, or did not care, or could not help. The cure is not to pretend we are not frightened, but to take the fear to him and set beside it what we know of him. The disciples’ mistake was not that they woke him. It was that they thought, even with him in the boat, that they were going to drown.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked the disciples’ fear and then the storm, showing that he has the authority over creation that belongs to God alone.

On a Tuesday. What storm are you afraid of? Bring it to the one whom winds and sea obey, and let the question “What sort of man is this?” strengthen your faith. Write down the thing you fear most this week, and next to it write what this passage says about Jesus: that he is in the boat, that the sea obeys him, that he cares. Then pray Psalm 107:28–30 as your own. And when the storm is over, do not forget to marvel; gratitude is the soil in which bigger faith grows.

For worship. What sort of man is this? The man who is the LORD, whose voice is over the waters (Psalm 29:3), who shut in the sea with doors and told it how far it could come (Job 38:8–11), and who lay asleep on a cushion in a fishing boat. The creation knows its Maker. The wind that will not obey us obeys him at a word, and every storm that ever touches his people is on a leash in his hand. He rebuked the sea for us, and on the cross he let the waves of God’s wrath go over him (Psalm 42:7), so that there might be a great calm for ever between God and us.

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. And behold, they cried out, "What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the other side of the lake, in Gentile territory, two violently demon-possessed men came out of the tombs to meet Jesus. They were so dangerous that no one could use that road. The demons cried out: what do you want with us, Son of God? Have you come to torment us before the appointed time?

The country of the Gadarenes. The region around Gadara, a Gentile city of the Decapolis, about six miles (ten kilometres) southeast of the lake. Mark and Luke call it “the country of the Gerasenes” (Mark 5:1; Luke 8:26), after Gerasa, a larger city further away; manuscripts also vary. The place names refer to regions, not just cities; the event probably happened near a village on the eastern shore, perhaps Gergesa, now Kursi, where there are steep slopes near the water.

The place name in detail. The manuscripts of Matthew divide between Gadarenes, Gerasenes and Gergesenes, and those of Mark and Luke divide in the same way, which is why most Bibles have a footnote here. Geography explains it. Gerasa is a large city some thirty miles southeast of the lake, too far for any herd to run from into the water. Gadara is about six miles off, close enough that its lands may well have run down to the shore. Gergesa, modern Kursi on the eastern bank, is the only one of the three actually on the water, and it has a steep slope running straight into the lake. Origen noticed the problem in the third century, visited the region, and concluded for Gergesa. The likeliest account is simple: the district was known by the name of its nearest major town, as we might say something happened outside a city without meaning its centre, and different writers reached for different landmarks. What is not in doubt is that the terrain the story requires exists: a steep bank on the eastern shore, in Gentile country, with tombs cut into the hillside above it.

Two demon-possessed men. Mark and Luke mention only one, probably because he was the more prominent and later became a witness (Mark 5:18–20). Mentioning one does not deny that there were two. Matthew often mentions two where others mention one (9:27; 20:30), perhaps because two witnesses were needed for testimony under the law (Deuteronomy 19:15). At Jericho he counts two blind men where Mark names only Bartimaeus (20:30; Mark 10:46). It is the difference between a photograph that frames one face and a report that records the whole company, and the God who inspired all three Gospels was pleased to give us both.

Coming out of the tombs. Tombs were caves cut into the hillside. They were unclean places, associated with death and, people believed, with evil spirits. The men lived there, cut off from society. Uncleanness on every side: Gentile land, the tombs of the dead, unclean spirits, and in a moment a herd of unclean animals. Jesus has crossed the lake into the most defiled place Matthew could describe.

So fierce that no one could pass that way. Mark describes the man breaking chains and cutting himself with stones (Mark 5:3–5). Demonic possession destroys the person: their mind, their body, their relationships. Nobody could help them; nobody could even get near them. They were beyond every human remedy, and that is exactly where Jesus walks up the beach.

What have you to do with us, O Son of God? A Hebrew idiom meaning: what is there between us? Why are you interfering with us? The demons recognise Jesus immediately as the Son of God, before the disciples confess it (14:33; 16:16). James says even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). Recognising who Jesus is does not save; demons have the knowledge without the trust or love.

The confession made on sight. Notice who else says Son of God in this Gospel, and when. The next to say it plainly are the disciples in the boat (14:33), then Peter at Caesarea Philippi (16:16), and then a Roman officer watching him die (27:54). The confession that costs a man everything to make, the demons make instantly, and it does them no good at all. Their theology is accurate; their allegiance is catastrophically wrong. Knowing the truth about Jesus while refusing to submit to him is the condition of the lost.

Have you come here to torment us before the time? The demons know that a time of judgment is coming, when they will be punished (25:41; Revelation 20:10). They are afraid that Jesus has come to bring it early. In a sense he has: his coming means the beginning of their defeat (12:28–29). They are not disputing the outcome. They know there is a fixed date and that it goes against them; the only thing in doubt is the calendar. Nothing in the New Testament states the demonic predicament more briefly: a settled certainty about the future, and no intention whatever of changing course.

What it does not mean. Not that every mental illness is demonic. The Gospels distinguish demon-possession from other illnesses (4:24). Those who suffer from mental illness need care, medical help and love, not exorcism. Nor should Christians fear demons: they fear Jesus.

Was this really demon possession, or mental illness misunderstood? The Gospels distinguish the two (4:24), and these men’s demons speak, recognise Jesus as the Son of God and know the time of their judgement, which no illness does. But that gives no reason to treat mental illness today as demonic. Those who suffer should be given medical care and pastoral love, and every believer can know that he belongs to Christ, not to any other power.

What should I do about horoscopes, tarot cards, spiritualism or the occult? Leave them completely. Scripture forbids every attempt to consult spirits, read omens or contact the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), not because they are silly but because the powers behind them are real and hostile, and they destroy, as they were destroying these men. If you have dabbled, confess it to God, renounce it plainly, get rid of anything connected with it (as the believers in Ephesus burned their books, Acts 19:18–19), and tell a pastor you trust. You do not need special rituals. You need Christ, whom the demons themselves call the Son of God, and you need to stay close to his word and his people.

In a sentence. In Gentile territory, two violently possessed men met Jesus, and the demons in them recognised and feared him as the Son of God and their coming Judge.

On a Tuesday. The powers of evil know who Jesus is and tremble. Do you trust him as much as they fear him? It is possible to know all the right things about Jesus, as the demons did, and still keep him at arm’s length. Ask whether your knowledge of him has become trust and love. And think of the people in your town whom everyone avoids, those living among the tombs in their own way. Jesus crossed a lake in a storm to reach two of them.

For worship. The Son of God crossed the sea at night, through a storm, to reach two men nobody else would go near. He walked straight into the place of death and defilement, and the powers that terrorised a whole district fell to their knees and begged. He is the stronger man who binds the strong man (12:29), and the day the demons dread is the day his people long for. Every chain that held these men, he came to break; and he went on to the cross, where he triumphed over all the powers of darkness, and to the empty tomb, where he showed that even the grave must give up its dead.
verseByVerse.note: Gadara was a Gentile city of the Decapolis, south-east of the lake; Mark and Luke say “Gerasenes” and mention only one man. Tombs were unclean places.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. And the demons begged him, saying, "If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nearby a large herd of pigs was feeding. The demons begged Jesus: if you drive us out, send us into the pigs.

A herd of many pigs. Mark says about two thousand (Mark 5:13). Pigs were unclean animals for Jews (Leviticus 11:7). A large herd shows that this was Gentile territory. It was probably a valuable source of income for the owners. Two thousand pigs is not a smallholding; it is a substantial business, and somebody’s living, and quite possibly the living of the herdsmen and their families.

And the demons begged him. They pleaded. They have no power to resist Jesus; they can only beg. They know they must leave. They do not dispute his authority to cast them out; they bargain only about the destination. Even their request must be submitted to him. They cannot so much as enter a pig without his permission.

If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs. Why? Perhaps because demons seek to inhabit and destroy something. Luke adds that they begged not to be sent into the abyss (Luke 8:31), the place of their final confinement. They wanted to stay in the region, even in pigs. There is a dark irony in it: they would rather have the bodies of unclean animals than face what is coming.

What it does not mean. Not that demons have any authority to negotiate with Jesus. He permits their request for his own purposes. Nor does it mean that we should seek to converse with demons or learn their secrets. Jesus did not hold a discussion; he gave a command.

What about the man who owned the pigs? A thoughtful reader will ask, and deserves better than silence. In a single afternoon a herd of about two thousand animals was destroyed. Four things can be said honestly. First, the destruction is the demons’ work, not Jesus’. He does not send them into the pigs; they ask, and he permits. What follows is exactly what one would expect: the thing that had been driving two men to live among graves and cut themselves does the same to a herd of animals within a minute of getting hold of them. The pigs are a demonstration of what the demons do, not of what Jesus does. Second, this was Gentile territory, which is why there were pigs at all; the owners were almost certainly Gentiles breaking no law of their own, so this is not a judgement on Jews for keeping unclean animals.
