Third, Jesus states the valuation elsewhere in this Gospel: of how much more value is a man than a sheep (12:12)! Two men beyond anyone’s reach were given their minds back. Set against that, a herd of livestock is a real cost and a small one, and the town that made the opposite calculation is the villain of the story, not its victim. Fourth, Matthew records the loss and the reaction and moves on, neither apologising nor treating the objection as trivial. What cannot honestly be said is that the loss did not matter. It mattered to somebody, and the text lets that stand.

Why did Jesus grant the demons’ request at all? Scripture does not explain fully, and we should not pretend to know more than it says. But some things are clear. The time of their final judgement had not yet come (v. 29), and Jesus was keeping to his Father’s timetable, not theirs. The rush of the herd gave everyone visible proof that the men were truly free, so that no one could say the change was imaginary. And it showed, for anyone with eyes, what these powers had been doing to two human beings: the same thing they did to the pigs in a minute. Jesus is never at the demons’ service. Even when he grants what they ask, he is using it for his own purposes.

In a sentence. The demons, powerless before Jesus, begged to be sent into a herd of unclean pigs.

On a Tuesday. Evil has no power to bargain with Christ. Whatever has a grip on you, it must obey him. Notice that the demons tried to negotiate: not the abyss, somewhere nearby, somewhere comfortable. Sin does the same with us. It rarely asks to stay in full; it asks to be allowed to remain in a corner. Do not negotiate with what Christ has told to go.

For worship. The powers that terrified a district beg at his feet for a herd of pigs. Not one demon can move without his leave, and not one inch of creation lies outside his rule. The devil is God’s devil, held on a chain whose length is fixed in heaven (Job 1:12). And the one who will at last cast the enemy into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10) is the one who sets the captive free today. Our deliverer is the Lord of all.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a large herd shows this was Gentile country.

parallels.desc: the pig is unclean to you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go." So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said one word: Go. The demons left the men and entered the pigs, and the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. The herdsmen ran to the town and reported everything.

And he said to them, Go. One word, and the demons must obey. This is the same authority by which he calmed the storm (v. 26). It is the latest in a chapter of single words. To the leper: be clean. To the centurion: go, let it be done. To the wind and sea, a rebuke. And now to a legion of demons who had terrorised a district for years and whom no chain could hold: go. Every Jewish exorcist of the period worked with elaborate procedures: incantations, roots, rings, the names of angels. Josephus describes one at length, drawing a demon out through a man’s nose with a ring. Jesus uses one word and does not raise his voice.

So they came out and went into the pigs. The men were freed. Mark says the man was found sitting, clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15). Three phrases that tell a whole story. He had been restless; now he sits. He had been naked; now he is clothed. He had been out of his mind; now he is in his right mind, at the feet of Jesus.

And behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. The destruction of the pigs shows several things. First, the reality of the deliverance: everyone could see that the demons had left. Second, the destructive nature of demons: wherever they go, they destroy (John 10:10). What they did to the pigs they had been doing to the men. Third, the value Jesus places on people: two human beings were worth more than two thousand pigs (12:12). The rush of the herd into the sea shows what would have happened to the men if the demons had stayed.

The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything. They were frightened by what they had seen. And they are the reason the story exists. They were employees who had just watched their employer’s herd go over a cliff. They had every reason to say nothing, or to shade the account, and instead they went into town and reported the whole thing.

Especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men. The news spread quickly. Matthew is careful to say that the report included the two men. The herdsmen did not leave out the healing to make the loss look worse. So the first report of Jesus in that Gentile town came from a group of frightened pig-keepers, telling a story that was mostly about their own disaster, and telling it truthfully.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus disregarded the owners’ property carelessly. He is Lord of all creation, and he judged that freeing two people was worth more. Some ask whether it was unjust. But the pigs were destroyed by the demons, not by Jesus directly, and their loss was the price of the men’s freedom. The deeper question is the one the townspeople faced: what do you value more, your livelihood or the presence of the one who sets captives free?

Is being set free from evil the same as being saved? Not quite, and the difference matters. Jesus warned that when an unclean spirit leaves a person, it may return with others worse than itself and find the house swept and empty (12:43–45). Freedom from a bondage, whether an addiction, a dark habit or something worse, is a great mercy. But the house must not be left empty. It must be filled by Christ himself, through faith in him, his word and his Spirit. That is why the freed man in Mark’s account begged to go with Jesus (Mark 5:18). Do not be content to be rid of something. Be joined to someone.

In a sentence. At Jesus’ single word the demons left the men, entered the pigs and destroyed them, showing both Christ’s authority and the destructive nature of evil.

On a Tuesday. Jesus valued two broken men more than two thousand pigs. Do you value people above money and possessions? Look at your diary and your bank statement for the last month and ask what they say about what you value. And notice the herdsmen. They told everything, even when the story did not flatter them. When you speak of what Christ has done, tell it truthfully and include the part about the people he set free.

For worship. One word, go, and a legion obeys. The Lord does not wrestle with the powers of darkness as an equal; he dismisses them. And the men they had held are sitting, clothed and in their right minds, which is the picture of every sinner he saves: once restless, now at rest at his feet; once exposed, now clothed in his righteousness; once deranged by sin, now given a sound mind. Glory to the Christ who came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and who never loses one of those he sets free.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole town came out to Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their district.

And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus. A large crowd. Normally this phrase describes a welcome for a king.

And when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region. A tragic reversal. The demons begged Jesus not to send them away (v. 31); the townspeople begged Jesus to go away. It is the same word (parekaloun): the city begs as the demons begged. They had seen a great deliverance, two of their neighbours restored to sanity, a terror lifted from their district, but they were frightened by Jesus’ power and angry at the loss of the pigs. They preferred their pigs and their comfort to the presence of the Son of God. Luke says they were seized with great fear (Luke 8:37). The community counted its loss and not its gain. And it is not only an ancient story; it is the universal human tendency to resist a grace that costs us something.

And Jesus left. Jesus does not force himself on those who do not want him. But Mark tells us he left the freed man behind as a witness, to tell what the Lord had done for him (Mark 5:19–20), and later, when Jesus returned to the Decapolis, crowds came to him (Mark 7:31–37). The man’s testimony bore fruit.

The most sobering answer to prayer. Do not rush past this. We are rightly fond of the Jesus who seeks the lost, and the seeking Shepherd of Luke 15 is gloriously real. But here is the other side of the truth: when people settle their hearts against him and say depart, he can take them at their word. This is the judgement Paul names in Romans 1, where three times God gave them up to what they preferred (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). Scripture sounds the warning more than once. God said his Spirit would not strive with man for ever (Genesis 6:3). Of stubborn Israel he said, I gave them over to their stubborn hearts (Psalm 81:12). Of Ephraim, joined to idols: leave him alone (Hosea 4:17). Over Jerusalem Jesus wept that he had longed to gather her children and she would not, and that her house would be left desolate (23:37–38). He grieves to leave, but he leaves. The Gadarenes asked him to go, and he went.

The pattern of chapter 8. Matthew has shown Jesus’ authority over disease (vv. 1–17), nature (vv. 23–27) and demons (vv. 28–34). In each scene there is a response: faith from a Gentile soldier, little faith from the disciples, and rejection from a Gentile town. The question is not whether Jesus has authority, but how we will respond to it.

What it does not mean. Not that the town’s fear was a right fear. There is a fear of God that leads people to worship him (Luke 5:8–10), and a fear that drives people away. The Gadarenes had the wrong kind.

Could Jesus give up on me? If you are worried about it, that worry is itself a sign that he has not. The people Jesus leaves are those who want him gone and are glad to see him go, not those who fear losing him. The Gadarenes did not lie awake grieving his departure. Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37), and those the Father has given him he will lose none of (John 6:39). If you belong to Christ, he will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5). And if you are not yet sure that you belong to him, the door is still open today, and he still knocks (Revelation 3:20). Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your heart (Hebrews 3:15).

Even here, mercy. Notice that Jesus did not leave the region without a witness. He was sent away, and he left behind a man clothed and in his right mind, with orders to tell his family what the Lord had done. The rejection was real, and so was the patience. The town that begged him to go would hear about him every day from the man who had lived in its tombs, and when Jesus came back to that region crowds gathered. He is slow to give up even on those who send him away.

In a sentence. Faced with Christ’s power to free people, the town valued its pigs more and asked him to leave.

On a Tuesday. Is there any part of your life where you would rather Jesus left you alone, because his presence would cost you something you value? Invite him in instead. Name it: the business practice, the relationship, the habit, the comfortable arrangement that you have quietly fenced off. It is always cheaper in the short run to ask him to leave that region. It is always a catastrophe in the long run. Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near (Isaiah 55:6).

For worship. The Lord who commands storms and demons will not force his way into a town that begs him to leave. He is so great that nothing can resist him, and so gentle that he lets us refuse him; and that should make us tremble at the thought of refusing. Yet even as he left, he left behind a witness, a freed man telling the whole region what the Lord had done for him. That is how Christ has always come back to places that sent him away: through the testimony of sinners he has set free. Blessed be the patient Saviour, who was himself driven out of the city to die, so that all who were once outside might be welcomed in.

8.theology: The authority of Christ. Chapter 8 is a sustained meditation on the authority of the Son of God. He has authority over disease (leper, fever), over distance (servant healed at a word), over demons (v. 16), and over creation (storm). Reformed theology insists that this authority is not delegated but inherent: Jesus is not a prophet with God’s power on loan but the eternal Son in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Col 2:9). His healing word and his saving word are the same — both accomplish what they declare. The centurion’s faith grasps this: faith is resting on the word of One who has absolute authority to perform what he promises.
8.examples:
Then: A Roman officer, trained in chains of command, recognized the absolute authority of Jesus. His faith put to shame those who had grown up with the Scriptures but had domesticated their expectations of the Messiah.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that regards faith as a psychological coping mechanism. The centurion’s faith is the opposite: it is epistemically grounded in the nature of the One trusted. We trust Christ not because belief makes us feel better but because he is the Lord of heaven and earth whose word does not return void. When we pray, we address the One who stilled the Sea of Galilee.

9.title: The King’s Authority to Forgive
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. <sup>2</sup>And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” <sup>3</sup>And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.” <sup>4</sup>But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts? <sup>5</sup>For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>6</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he then said to the paralytic—“Rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>7</sup>And he rose and went home. <sup>8</sup>When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men. <sup>9</sup>As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>10</sup>And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. <sup>11</sup>And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>12</sup>But when he heard it, he said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>13</sup>Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’ For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>14</sup>Then the disciples of John came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” <sup>15</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. <sup>16</sup>No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made. <sup>17</sup>Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.” <sup>18</sup>While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” <sup>19</sup>And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. <sup>20</sup>And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, <sup>21</sup>for she said to herself, “If I only touch his garment, I will be made well.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” And instantly the woman was made well. <sup>23</sup>And when Jesus came to the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, <sup>24</sup>he said, “Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping.” And they laughed at him. <sup>25</sup>But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. <sup>26</sup>And the report of this went through all that district. <sup>27</sup>And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” <sup>28</sup>When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” <sup>29</sup>Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith let it be done to you.” <sup>30</sup>And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, “See that no one knows about it.” <sup>31</sup>But they went away and spread his fame through all that district. <sup>32</sup>As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. <sup>33</sup>And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, “Never was anything like this seen in Israel.” <sup>34</sup>But the Pharisees said, “He casts out demons by the prince of demons.” <sup>35</sup>And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. <sup>36</sup>When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. <sup>37</sup>Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; <sup>38</sup>therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
9.overview:
Chapter 9 begins with the most audacious claim in Jesus’ ministry: “Your sins are forgiven.” The scribes immediately see the implication — only God can forgive sins — and charge blasphemy. Jesus responds by healing the paralytic as evidence that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The miracle is the sign; forgiveness is the substance. This is Matthew’s thesis: Jesus has come not primarily to heal bodies but to heal souls, not primarily to liberate from Roman occupation but to liberate from the bondage of sin and guilt.

The call of Matthew himself is a microcosm of the gospel. A tax collector — a collaborator with Rome, a social and religious outcast — is called with a two-word summons. He rises and follows. The banquet that follows is a picture of the kingdom: Jesus eating with the unworthy, the Pharisees scandalized, Jesus quoting Hosea 6:6 (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice”). The chapter closes with Jesus surveying the harassed crowds with compassion and calling for labourers. The mission of the King now extends through his people.

Read straight through, the chapter reveals a second pattern woven beneath the miracles: in story after story faith stands beside unbelief, and the two are sifted apart. The paralytic comes carried by friends whose faith Jesus sees (v. 2) — while the scribes silently cry blasphemy. Matthew rises at a word — while the Pharisees mutter at the table. The ruler kneels and the unclean woman reaches, both in bold faith — while the hired mourners laugh him to scorn. The blind men confess “Yes, Lord” — while the watching Pharisees, at the chapter’s climax, sneer that he casts out demons “by the prince of demons” (v. 34). The same Jesus, the same works — and they divide every heart that meets them: some come empty-handed and receive everything, while others, certain they need nothing, receive nothing and only harden. This is the dividing line the whole Gospel will trace, and it is why the chapter closes not in triumph but in compassion for the harassed and helpless crowds (vv. 36–38) — the harvest is plentiful, and this faith must be carried to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Forgiveness, Fellowship, and Fasting: Who Has Authority?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus returns to Capernaum and heals a paralyzed man by first forgiving his sins — triggering the first direct conflict with the scribes. He then calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with sinners, outraging the Pharisees. When John's disciples ask why Jesus's disciples don't fast, Jesus answers with three images: the bridegroom, the unshrunk cloth, and the new wine. The old forms cannot contain the new reality that has arrived. The scribes never spoke — Matthew says they said it "to themselves" (v. 3), and Jesus answers the unspoken charge, which is itself a claim as large as the one being disputed (Jer. 17:10; 1 Kgs. 8:39). And their theology is correct: only the offended party can waive an offence, and no priest in Israel ever forgave anybody — he declared a forgiveness God had granted. So the alternatives really are God or blasphemer, and they could see it. Jesus does not call their conclusion mistaken but evil (poneros) — the indictment is of a heart that settled the question before weighing it. On the title: Son of Man does two contradictory things at once, which is why he chose it. In Hebrew idiom it means simply "a human being" (God calls Ezekiel that ninety times), and in Daniel 7:13-14 it is the highest title in the Old Testament — dominion, glory, an everlasting kingdom. Innocuous enough to say in public, loaded enough that anyone who had read Daniel knew. And the two decisive words in v. 6 are on earth: everyone believed sins were forgiven in heaven; the disputed point is that the transaction can be completed here, by a voice, without temple, priest or sacrifice. Note also that the crowd's "authority to men" is plural (v. 8) — Matthew alone has it, and this is the Gospel that will record the keys given to Peter (16:19) and binding and loosing given to the church (18:18). On Matthew's booth: it was a customs post on the Via Maris at the frontier between Antipas's and Philip's territory, and the point most often missed is that Peter could go back to fishing and Matthew could not — a tax franchise was a purchased concession with men queuing for it. He burned the bridge in the act of crossing it. And Hosea 6:6 is Matthew's own verse: he quotes it twice (9:13; 12:7) and no other New Testament writer quotes it at all, both times against men who are technically correct and pastorally monstrous.
verseByVerse.theology: The paralytic episode is the theological pivot: Jesus claims authority to forgive sins, which belongs to God alone. The scribes are theologically right that only God forgives sins; they are catastrophically wrong in their conclusion that Jesus is therefore blaspheming. The miracle of healing is offered as proof of the greater miracle of forgiveness — the visible confirms the invisible. Matthew's call and the meal with sinners then demonstrate what forgiveness looks like in practice: the Physician comes for the sick, not the healthy.
verseByVerse.examples: The three images of newness — bridegroom, cloth, wineskins — announce that Jesus is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfillment and transformation. The joy of the bridegroom's presence cannot be contained in old mourning forms. The new covenant is not a patch on the old but its completion. The Pharisees' question about fasting reveals that they are still thinking in terms of the old forms; Jesus is announcing that the age of the bridegroom has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back in Capernaum, people brought Jesus a paralysed man on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, he said first not “be healed” but: take heart, son, your sins are forgiven.

Meaning first. Matthew 9 carries on the story of chapter 8, and raises the stakes. In chapter 8 Jesus showed his authority over disease, storm and demons. In chapter 9 he claims an authority that belongs to God alone: the authority to forgive sins, on earth, by his own word, and he proves it by making a paralysed man walk. Then he calls a tax collector, eats with sinners, and explains that he has come as a doctor for the sick. He answers a question about fasting by calling himself the bridegroom, and warns that the new wine of the kingdom will burst the old skins. He raises a dead girl, heals a woman unclean for twelve years, opens the eyes of two blind men and the mouth of a mute one. And the chapter ends with Jesus looking at the crowds with compassion, as sheep mauled and abandoned, and telling his disciples to pray for workers for the harvest. Through it all the opposition is growing: blasphemy, says one group; he works by the prince of demons, says another. The same evidence produces worship and hatred. The question of the chapter is the question of the whole Gospel: who is this, who forgives sins, raises the dead, and pities the lost?

And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. Rejected by the Gadarenes (8:34), Jesus returns to Capernaum (4:13). He had made Capernaum his home, and Matthew calls it his own city. The town that begged him to leave got what it asked for; the town that welcomed him is about to see the greatest thing he has yet done.

Some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. A man who could not walk, carried on a mat or stretcher by his friends. Mark and Luke tell how they dug through the roof to lower him down (Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:17–26). Matthew tells the story briefly, focusing on Jesus’ words. But the effort is worth picturing. When the crowd blocked the door, the friends went up the outside stairs, broke open a roof of beams and packed earth, and lowered him into the room. It was not a polite gesture. It was a determined, undignified and expensive piece of persistence.

When Jesus saw their faith. Faith can be seen: in this case, by the effort the friends made to bring the man to Jesus. “Their” faith includes the friends’ and probably the man’s. Faith that brings others to Jesus is noticed by him. Matthew is careful: the man is carried, which means he could not come himself, and what Jesus is said to see is the faith of the people who brought him. This is the one story in the Gospels where the faith that moved Jesus belonged chiefly to the friends.

He said to the paralytic, Take heart, my son. “Take heart” means be encouraged, have courage. “My son” (literally “child”) is warm and affectionate. Before anything has been done for him, he is spoken to like a member of the family.

Your sins are forgiven. Unexpected. The man’s obvious need was physical. But Jesus addresses his deepest need first. Paralysis would end at death; unforgiven sin would last for eternity. Jesus saw that this man needed forgiveness more than he needed to walk. The present tense means the forgiveness is happening now, on Jesus’ word. The man came for his legs; Jesus goes straight to his soul.

A verdict, not a process. Weigh the grammar, because the whole gospel is folded into it. Jesus does not say: God will forgive you if you do this, or, seek God and perhaps you will find pardon. He says: your sins are forgiven. It is a verdict handed down, a thing accomplished, spoken over a man who has done nothing yet but be carried through a roof. This is what the Reformers meant by justification: not a process by which a sinner is slowly made good enough, but a declaration in which the Judge himself pronounces the guilty righteous. It is a courtroom word before it is a hospital word. The man would leave with his legs mended, which everyone could see, and with his record cleared, which no one could see and which mattered infinitely more. And the declaration is not cheap. The Judge who pronounces the pardon here will pay for it himself, outside a city wall, so that the verdict is not only merciful but just (Romans 3:26).

Sin and sickness. Was the man’s paralysis caused by a specific sin? Sometimes sickness can be connected with sin (John 5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30). But Jesus also denied that sickness is always the result of the sufferer’s own sin (John 9:1–3). All sickness belongs to a world fallen through sin, but individual illness is not usually a punishment for individual sin. Here, Jesus simply shows that forgiveness is the deeper need of every person. No one who is ill should be told that it proves some hidden sin.

What it does not mean. Not that the friends’ faith saved the man without his own trust in Christ. Each person must believe for themselves. But the faith of friends, in bringing someone to Jesus and praying for them, is precious, and Jesus responds to it. Nor does it mean that physical needs are unimportant: Jesus also healed him (v. 7).

For those doing the carrying. You may have a husband who will not come, a son who has walked away, a friend sunk in a depression too heavy to pray out of. You cannot believe on their behalf. Notice that Jesus still speaks to the man himself, pardons him personally and commands him personally to rise; nobody is saved by proxy. But you can carry them to where Jesus is, and that is a real work. It looks like praying for them by name for years without visible result; keeping the relationship intact, so that there is still a stretcher available when they finally need one; refusing to make your love conditional on their agreement; and being willing to look foolish and go through the roof. Keep carrying.

For the one who is being carried. Perhaps you suspect you are the paralytic. Your faith feels too thin to count, and you are not sure it would qualify as faith at all. Then look hard at what this man contributes to the scene, because it is nothing whatever. He does not argue his case, express his confidence or say a word. He is carried in, flat and helpless, and the first thing he hears is: take heart, my son, your sins are forgiven. That is what the church is for on the days you cannot hold yourself up. It is why we sing together when you cannot sing, and why others pray when your own praying has dried up. You are not required to arrive under your own power.

Do I need to feel forgiven to be forgiven? No. This man had no feeling to go on but the word of Jesus, and the word was enough. Forgiveness is God’s verdict, not your emotion. If you have turned from your sin and trusted Christ, your sins are forgiven because he says so, and because he died for them, whether you feel light-hearted today or heavy. Feelings follow slowly and come and go. When guilt keeps returning over a sin you have already confessed, do not confess it again as though the first time failed. Answer it with his word: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

In a sentence. Seeing the faith of the paralysed man and his friends, Jesus first met his deepest need: the forgiveness of his sins.

On a Tuesday. Whom could you carry to Jesus in prayer, or bring to hear about him? Write down one name and pray for that person every day this week, and look for one practical way to bring them nearer to where Christ is spoken of. And remember that your own deepest need is not your circumstances, but forgiveness, which Christ gives. If your prayers are all about the legs, ask whether you have thanked him today for the pardon.

For worship. He looked at a man who could not move, and the first thing he gave him was what nobody else in the room could give: take heart, my son, your sins are forgiven. Here is the Judge of all the earth speaking as a Father, pronouncing a pardon he would purchase with his own blood. The God who blots out transgressions for his own sake stood in a crowded house in Capernaum and did it in person. Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered (Psalm 32:1), and blessed be the Saviour who covered it.
verseByVerse.note: “His own city” is Capernaum, his base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, "This man is blaspheming." But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, "Why do you think evil in your hearts?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some scribes said to themselves that Jesus was blaspheming, claiming to forgive sins. Jesus knew what they were thinking and asked why they harboured such evil in their hearts.

Some of the scribes said to themselves. Silently, in their hearts. The scribes did not speak. The charge was formed in silence, in the room, and never left anybody’s mouth. And Jesus answers it out loud.

This man is blaspheming. Blasphemy means speaking against God, insulting him, or claiming for oneself what belongs to God alone. The scribes reasoned correctly that only God can forgive sins (Mark 2:7; Isaiah 43:25). A person can forgive wrongs done to himself, but sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4). For a man to declare someone’s sins forgiven was to claim to be God. If Jesus was not God, they were right: it would be blasphemy. Under the law, blasphemy was punishable by death (Leviticus 24:16). This is the first mention of the charge for which Jesus will finally be condemned (26:65).

Their theology is right. This needs saying clearly, because these men are often treated as fools. They are not being stupid. In Isaiah God says, with the pronoun doubled for emphasis, that he, he alone, is the one who blots out transgressions for his own sake (Isaiah 43:25). The point is exclusivity. A sin is an offence against God, and only the party offended can waive it. No priest in Israel ever forgave anybody; the priest declared a forgiveness God had granted through the sacrifice he prescribed. So the scribes’ logic is not merely defensible but correct. If this man is not God, he is committing blasphemy. There is no third option, and the scribes could see it.

An honest note on the grammar. Your sins are forgiven is a passive, and a passive of this kind was a common Jewish way of avoiding the divine name, so in principle Jesus might be announcing that God has forgiven rather than claiming to do it himself. The scribes plainly did not hear it that way: Mark records their reasoning in full, that no one can forgive sins but God alone (Mark 2:7). Jesus does not correct them. He goes on to prove the claim they think he has made.

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts. Jesus knew what they were thinking without being told. Only God knows the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). Solomon prayed to the one who alone knows the hearts of all the children of mankind (1 Kings 8:39). In answering their unspoken accusation that he claims to be God, he does something only God can do. So before the paralytic moves a muscle, a claim has been made that is as large as the one being disputed. The evidence for the claim is supplied by the manner of the reply.

Why do you think evil in your hearts? Their evil was not in their logic, which was right, but in their refusal to consider that Jesus might be who his words implied. They assumed the worst. The word is ponēros, the word used of wicked men and of the evil one. He does not say, why do you think this, but, why do you think evil. That would be outrageous if their reasoning were merely mistaken. It is not the conclusion he indicts but the closed heart underneath it. They had settled the question before they weighed it, and settled it against a man who had done them no harm.

What it does not mean. Not that the scribes were wrong to be concerned about blasphemy. Concern for God’s honour is good. Their error was in refusing to see the evidence of who Jesus was.

Is it wrong to have doubts or questions about Jesus? No, not if you bring them honestly. The scribes’ problem was not that they had questions but that they had already decided the answer and would not look at the evidence in front of them. Honest doubt that wants the truth is a different thing. John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus really was the one, and Jesus answered him gently with the evidence (11:2–6). Thomas said he would not believe without seeing, and Jesus showed him his hands (John 20:27). Bring your questions to him: read the Gospels, ask a mature Christian, pray as you read. Ask yourself only whether you would be willing to follow the answer if it came.

In a sentence. The scribes rightly saw that forgiving sins was God’s prerogative and accused Jesus of blasphemy, but Jesus read their hearts as only God can.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knows your thoughts. That is a warning against secret sin and a comfort in secret sorrow. The things you have never said aloud, the resentment, the lust, the private contempt for someone, are as plain to him as words spoken in the room. So are the griefs you have never told anyone and the prayers you could not put into words. Today, tell him something you have only ever said to yourself.

For worship. The one who searches the heart and tests the mind sat in a house in Capernaum and answered thoughts nobody had spoken. He knows us altogether: our sitting down and our rising up, every word before it is on our tongue (Psalm 139:1–4). And the one who knows us best is the one who forgives us most. He saw the evil in the scribes’ hearts and in ours, and he went to the cross under the very charge they were forming that day, blasphemy, so that the sins he forgave in Capernaum could be justly forgiven for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "For which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" — he then said to the paralytic — "Rise, pick up your bed and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked which is easier to say: your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk? To prove that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he told the paralysed man to get up, take his bed and go home.

For which is easier. A clever question. To say “your sins are forgiven” is easier, because no one can see whether it has happened. To say “rise and walk” is harder, because everyone will immediately see whether it works. But actually to do either is equally impossible for a mere man; both require the power of God. Any charlatan can pronounce absolution and walk away. So Jesus takes the harder, testable claim and stakes the untestable one on it, in public, with a paralysed man as the test. If the mat does not move, everything he has just said about sins is exposed within the minute. It is an argument only one kind of person can afford to make.

But that you may know. Jesus will do the visible thing to prove the invisible thing. The healing is evidence of the forgiveness. The miracle is not a distraction from the theology; it is the proof of it.

That the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. “Son of Man” (see 8:20). In Daniel 7:13–14, the Son of Man receives authority from God. “Authority” (exousia) means the right and the power to act. Here is astonishing news: God’s authority to forgive is now exercised on earth, by a man, in person. People do not have to wait for the Day of Atonement or the final judgment to know if they are forgiven; they can hear it from Jesus’ lips.

A title that hides and reveals. Son of Man is Jesus’ own preferred way of speaking about himself. Almost every one of its thirty or so uses in Matthew is on his own lips. On its face it is the most modest title available: in Hebrew idiom a son of man is simply a human being, and God addresses Ezekiel that way more than ninety times. A man could use it of himself without claiming anything. But in Daniel 7 it is one of the highest titles in the Old Testament: one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven, and to him is given dominion and glory and a kingdom that all peoples should serve him, an everlasting dominion that will not pass away. That is the paradox he wanted: a phrase modest enough to say in public without starting a riot, and loaded enough that anyone who had read Daniel would know what was being claimed. When he finally used it plainly, under oath before the high priest, they tore their robes and condemned him (26:64–65).

On earth. Two small words carry the weight. Everyone in that room believed sins were forgiven in heaven. The disputed point is the place. This man is saying that the transaction can be completed here, in a crowded house in Capernaum, by a voice: without a temple, without a priest, without a sacrifice, and without waiting. Heaven’s verdict has come down to earth in a person.

He then said to the paralytic, Rise, pick up your bed and go home. Three commands, each impossible for a paralysed man. Carrying his own bed would show the healing was complete. The stretcher that had carried him would now be carried by him.

What it does not mean. Not that priests or ministers today have the authority to forgive sins in themselves. Jesus has authority as God. The church announces his forgiveness to those who repent and believe (John 20:23; 2 Corinthians 5:18–20), but it does not create it. The Roman Catholic practice of priestly absolution in the confessional claims more than this. Reformed churches declare the gospel’s assurance of pardon to the penitent, as messengers of Christ, not as judges in his place.

How can I know my sins are forgiven when I cannot see it? In the same way as the crowd in Capernaum: by looking at what Jesus has done that can be seen. He healed the visible to prove the invisible. For us the great visible proof is greater still: he died in public, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, seen by hundreds of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The resurrection is God’s public declaration that the sacrifice for sin was accepted (Romans 4:25). So rest your assurance on his word and his finished work, not on your feelings, and look for the fruit his Spirit produces in you: a new hatred of sin, a new love for him and his people. Those are the legs moving.

In a sentence. Jesus healed the paralysed man to prove that, as the Son of Man, he has God’s authority on earth to forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. If you trust Christ, his forgiveness is as certain as that man’s walking. Hear his word: your sins are forgiven. When an old sin comes back to accuse you this week, picture the man carrying his bed through the door, and say: the one who did that has told me I am forgiven. And when you have to forgive someone else, remember how much authority was needed to forgive you.

For worship. The Son of Man, to whom Daniel saw the everlasting kingdom given, used his authority first not to judge but to forgive. He brought heaven’s pardon down to earth and spoke it over a helpless man, and then made him walk so that we would believe it. Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity (Micah 7:18)? The Lord of glory has the right to condemn, and he came to forgive.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and went home. When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man got up and went home. When the crowds saw it, they were filled with awe and praised God, who had given such authority to human beings.

And he rose and went home. Immediately, in full view of everyone. The healing proved the forgiveness. Matthew records only the rising and the going, with no comment. The man walked out through the crowd that had blocked the door on the way in, carrying the mat he had been lowered on.

When the crowds saw it, they were afraid. “Afraid” here means filled with awe, reverent fear at seeing God at work. Fear first. That is the consistent biblical response to God acting close at hand, and it is healthier than the reaction usually produced today, which is mere excitement. Something had happened in that house that made people tremble, and the fear turned into worship, not away from it.

And they glorified God. The right response. Unlike the scribes (v. 3), the crowds praised God.

Who had given such authority to men. The crowds see that a man has been given God’s authority. They do not yet grasp fully that this man is God himself. But they rightly see God’s hand. “Men” (plural) may also look ahead: the authority to declare forgiveness in Christ’s name would be given to his church (16:19; 18:18).

The plural. Only Matthew records it, and it is strange. Not to this man, which is what anyone would expect, but to human beings (anthrōpois). Two readings are possible, and they are not exclusive. The crowd may be speaking loosely, as crowds do, awed that God has entrusted such authority to someone in human form without working out who this someone is. Or Matthew has kept the plural because he can see where it goes. This is the Gospel that records Jesus giving the keys of the kingdom to Peter (16:19) and telling the church that what it binds on earth is bound in heaven (18:18), and Matthew knew that the risen Christ would breathe on his disciples and send them to declare sins forgiven (John 20:22–23). The authority to forgive sins is Christ’s alone. The announcing of it was going to be handed to men, ordinary ones of the sort standing in that room, and Matthew lets a crowd say more than it knew.

What it does not mean. Not that the crowds had faith in Jesus as Son of God: their response was praise, but not yet full understanding.

Should I be afraid of God? In one sense yes, and in another no. Believers are not to be terrified of God as an enemy, because Christ has taken away the punishment, and perfect love casts out that kind of fear (1 John 4:18). But they are to hold him in reverent awe for ever, because he is holy and great, and his love has not made him small. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). The crowd’s response is the right pattern: fear that leads to glorifying God. If your Christianity has no awe in it, you may be thinking of a smaller God than the one who forgives sins and makes the paralysed walk.

In a sentence. The man walked home, and the crowds praised God for giving such authority to a man.

On a Tuesday. When did you last stand in awe of God? Take the account of this healing and read it slowly, and let it do what it did to the crowd. Then glorify God for something specific he has done for you, aloud, to someone else. And when you speak of the gospel to others, remember that you are not the source of the forgiveness you announce, only its messenger, which makes the message both humbling and bold.

For worship. Praise God that he has given his Son authority to forgive sins, including yours. The crowd glorified God that such authority had been given to men, and they did not yet know the half of it: that the man was the eternal Son, and that his authority would one day be proclaimed in every nation by people like them. We have seen more than they saw, and we have more reason to fear and to praise. Glory to the Father who sent him, and to the Son who forgives, and to the Spirit who makes the paralysed rise and walk.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him. And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus walked on, he saw a tax collector named Matthew sitting at his tax booth and said, follow me. Matthew got up and followed him. Then Jesus ate in Matthew’s house with many tax collectors and sinners, and with his disciples.

He saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth. The author of this Gospel. Mark and Luke call him Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27); many Jews had two names. In his own Gospel, he calls himself Matthew and adds “the tax collector” to his name in the list of apostles (10:3), never forgetting where he came from. His tax booth was probably on the main road near Capernaum, collecting customs duties on goods passing between the territories of Herod Antipas and Philip.

A name and a label. Matthew means gift of God, and it may well be the name he took, or was given, when the gift of God laid hold of him at that booth. And notice a quiet grace. The other Gospels, listing the apostles, simply name him. He alone writes Matthew the tax collector (10:3), pinning the old, shameful label to his own name for good. A man truly forgiven does not hide what he was saved from. He makes it a monument to grace.

What the booth was. Not a poll-tax office. Capernaum sat on the great trade road, at the frontier between the lands of Herod Antipas and those of his brother Philip. The booth was a customs post, and Matthew’s job was to assess duty on goods crossing the border: fish, oil, produce, everything moving along the road. Collectors bought the right to collect and made their living on the margin, which is why the whole class was hated. The system paid them to overcharge, and a customs officer in a border town on the busiest road in the region was very well placed indeed.

Tax collectors. They were hated by fellow Jews for three reasons. They collaborated with the occupying powers (Rome, or Herod who served Rome). They were often dishonest, collecting more than required and keeping the profit (Luke 3:12–13; 19:8). And their frequent contact with Gentiles made them ritually unclean. They were classed with prostitutes and sinners (21:31), and were barred from serving as witnesses in Jewish courts. For a rabbi to call one as his disciple was scandalous.

And he said to him, Follow me. The same call as to the fishermen (4:19). Two words, and no conditions: no probation, no demand that he first pay everything back. The call creates what it commands.

And he rose and followed him. Immediately. Fishermen could go back to fishing (John 21:3); a tax collector who left his post could not easily get it back. Matthew gave up a lucrative career. The one who had grown rich by taking now followed the one who gave. When the fishermen left their nets, the nets were still there, and after the crucifixion Peter said he was going fishing and the trade was waiting for him. Matthew’s booth was not waiting. A tax franchise was a purchased concession and there were men queuing for it; somebody else probably had it before the end of the day. Of all the men called in the Gospels, he is the one who burned the bridge in the act of crossing it. Luke records the detail Matthew is too modest to mention: he left everything (Luke 5:28).

As Jesus reclined at table in the house. Matthew’s house (Luke 5:29). He held a great feast for Jesus and invited his friends, other tax collectors and “sinners”. His first instinct as a disciple was to introduce his friends to Jesus. And Matthew does not tell us it was his house or his feast. He simply writes, in the house, and lets the guest list speak, because the point of the story in his telling is not what it cost him but who was invited.

Many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus. “Sinners” here means people known for immoral lives, or who did not keep the law as the Pharisees did, and so were treated as outcasts. Eating together in that culture expressed friendship and acceptance. Jesus ate with them.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus approved of their sin. He calls them to repentance (Luke 5:32). But he went to them, accepted them as people, and called them, rather than waiting for them to clean up first.

Are there limits to this? Jesus went to tax collectors’ tables as a physician, not as one of the party, and his call was always: follow me. Christians are free to eat with unbelievers, to love them and reach them (1 Corinthians 5:9–10; 10:27). What Paul forbids is treating an unrepentant professing brother as if nothing were wrong (1 Corinthians 5:11). And wisdom adds a personal rule: go with a purpose, and do not walk into the places where you are weakest.

Can God use someone with a really bad past? Look at who wrote this book. The first of the four Gospels, read in every language on earth for two thousand years, was written by a man whose neighbours regarded him as a traitor and a thief. God does not merely tolerate converted sinners; he delights to use them, so that the glory goes to his grace and not to their record. Paul called himself the foremost of sinners and said that was exactly why he received mercy, as an example to others (1 Timothy 1:15–16). Your past does not disqualify you. What matters is that you rise and follow now, and make restitution where you can, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8).

In a sentence. Jesus called Matthew, a despised tax collector, who left everything to follow him and threw a feast for his fellow outcasts to meet Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When Matthew met Jesus, he invited his friends to meet him too. Who among your friends could you invite to a meal with other believers? Plan it this month: a meal at your home with a Christian friend or two and someone who does not yet know Christ. You do not need to stage a sermon. Matthew simply put Jesus and his friends at the same table and let the evening happen.

For worship. The Lord walked past every respectable man in Capernaum and stopped at the customs booth. He chose a collaborator to be an apostle and an extortioner to write his Gospel, and the man spent the rest of his life telling everyone who he had been, so that they would see what grace can do. Christ is not ashamed to call such people his own. He came to a sinners’ supper, and he is preparing a feast to which sinners will come from every nation, washed and clothed. Blessed be the God who calls the unworthy and makes them gifts.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke call this tax collector Levi. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" But when he heard it, he said, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." Go and learn what this means: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees complained to the disciples that their teacher ate with tax collectors and sinners. Jesus answered: healthy people do not need a doctor; the sick do. Go and learn what God meant when he said, I desire mercy, not sacrifice. I came to call sinners, not the righteous.

Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners? To the Pharisees, eating with such people made one unclean and showed approval of their way of life. Rabbis kept away from them. The Pharisees saw holiness as separation from sinners. The question is put to the disciples, not to Jesus: a familiar way of undermining a teacher, by unsettling his followers.

Who the sinners were. In these arguments the word was close to a technical term. It did not simply mean bad people. It meant those who did not keep the purity code: people whose trade, poverty or ignorance placed them permanently outside the observant class. Some were immoral. Many were simply poor. The Pharisees had divided the population into the clean and the unclean, and Jesus accepts the division and reverses the conclusion: yes, there are two groups, and I have come for the other one.

Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. A proverb. A doctor goes to the sick; that is his job. Jesus came as a doctor for sin-sick souls. He does not become sick by being among the sick; he heals them. This reverses the Pharisees’ view of holiness: Jesus’ holiness is not contaminated by sinners; it transforms them (see 8:3). And the Pharisees’ unspoken view of themselves as the healthy is the most dangerous misdiagnosis in the chapter. The sick who know they are sick can receive the physician. The healthy who have never admitted their need cannot. Self-righteousness is the one condition that keeps the cure out.

Go and learn what this means. A rabbinic phrase used to send students back to study a text. Jesus tells the Bible experts to go back and study their Bibles. It is a deliberate rebuke, delivered with a straight face: a formula a teacher used to a pupil who had not done the reading, used on the professional interpreters of the very text he quotes, which they could recite by heart.

I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. From Hosea 6:6. God had rebuked Israel for offering sacrifices while lacking steadfast love and faithfulness. God does not reject sacrifice altogether (he commanded it); the Hebrew idiom means “mercy more than sacrifice”. God values compassion more than ritual. The Pharisees kept rituals carefully but lacked mercy toward sinners. Jesus quotes the same verse again in 12:7.

Matthew’s verse. No other writer in the New Testament quotes Hosea 6:6. Matthew does it twice, here and at 12:7, and both times it is aimed at religious men who are technically correct and pastorally cruel. Its setting in Hosea gives it its edge. Israel was producing a great volume of religion, and God said their love was like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes away early (Hosea 6:4): it evaporated by breakfast. Then he said what he actually wanted, and the word rendered mercy is hesed, the great covenant word for steadfast, loyal love. The charge is not that the Pharisees are too religious. It is that their religion has come loose from the thing it was for.

For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners. “The righteous” are those who think they are righteous, like the Pharisees, who see no need of a doctor. In reality, no one is righteous (Romans 3:10). Jesus calls those who know they are sinners. The only qualification for being called by Jesus is to need him. The irony bites: there are no righteous ones, only sinners who know it and sinners who do not.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus overlooked sin, or that Christians should make their closest friends among those who lead them into sin (1 Corinthians 15:33). Jesus went among sinners as a doctor, to heal and call them to repentance, not as one who joins in their sin. Nor does it mean that the Pharisees were truly righteous and did not need Jesus. Jesus is speaking with irony: those who think they are healthy cannot be healed.

If Jesus came for sinners, does it matter how I live? Very much. A doctor who comes to the sick does not come to leave them sick. He comes to heal them, and the treatment changes the patient. Paul faced this exact question: shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase? and answered, by no means (Romans 6:1–2). Those Christ calls, he also cleanses and changes (1 Corinthians 6:11). The call is for sinners just as they are; it does not leave them as they are. If you find that you want his forgiveness but not his healing, ask whether you have understood what kind of physician he is.

In a sentence. Jesus ate with sinners because he came as a doctor for the sick, showing that God values mercy above religious ritual.

On a Tuesday. Are you more like the Pharisees, keeping your distance from people you disapprove of, or like Jesus, going to them with mercy? And do you know yourself to be one of the sick he came to heal? Think of the person at work or in your street whom church people tend to avoid, and treat them this week with the kindness of a friend. And when you pray, begin where the tax collectors began: not with your record, but with your need.

For worship. The Great Physician does not keep a clinic for the healthy. He sat down among the sick of Capernaum and was called a friend of sinners for it (11:19). He took our sickness so deeply into himself that he was counted among the transgressors and died with criminals on either side. Mercy is what God desires, and mercy is what God has given, in his Son. Thanks be to the doctor who came to us, and who has never yet turned away a patient who knew he was sick.

parallels.desc: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice
to seek and to save the lost

verseByVerse.quote: And then the disciples of John came to him, saying, "Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made." Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist’s disciples asked why Jesus’ disciples did not fast like them and the Pharisees. Jesus answered that wedding guests cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them; they will fast when he is taken away. And new wine needs new wineskins: the new life he brings cannot be poured into the old forms.

The disciples of John came to him. John was in prison (4:12). His disciples continued to follow his austere way of life. They ask sincerely, not with hostility, and Jesus answers them gently.

Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? Pious Jews fasted regularly, and Pharisees twice a week (Luke 18:12). Jesus’ disciples were feasting with sinners (vv. 10–11). It looked unspiritual.

Custom, not command. The law of Moses commanded only one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to afflict itself (Leviticus 16:29–31). Every other fast was added later. After the exile, four annual fasts mourned the fall of Jerusalem (Zechariah 8:19), and by Jesus’ day the devout fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays. So the frequent fasting they mention was custom, not command. Behind it lay real longing: fasting expressed grief over sin, repentance, and yearning for God to send his deliverance and his Messiah. At its best it was the posture of a people still waiting. And that is just why Jesus’ disciples were not fasting. The waiting was over.

Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? Fasting was associated with mourning and sorrow. A Jewish wedding was a week-long celebration. The wedding guests (literally “sons of the bridal chamber”, the bridegroom’s close friends) were excused from religious duties such as fasting during the festivities. Jesus is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 54:5–6; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus takes that role. His coming is a wedding feast, the time of joy that the prophets promised. John himself had called Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29). It is a staggering claim made in passing: the husband of Israel, the LORD himself, has come, and the wedding has begun.

The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. “Taken away” suggests violent removal: Jesus’ first hint in Matthew of his death. After his death and ascension, his disciples would fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). A shadow falls across the wedding. The bridegroom knows already that he will be torn from his friends, and he speaks of it at a feast.

No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. A new patch, not yet shrunk, sewn onto an old garment would shrink when washed and tear the old cloth, making the hole worse.

Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. Wineskins were made from goatskins. New wine continues to ferment and expand. A new skin is soft and stretches; an old skin has become hard and brittle, and would burst under the pressure.

But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved. The new life of the kingdom that Jesus brings cannot simply be added to the old system of Pharisaic tradition. The joy and freedom of the gospel will burst the old forms. The kingdom needs new forms: a new covenant, a new people. You cannot cram the joy of the wedding into the forms of a funeral. Jesus is the new wine; the old is the whole framework of mourning, waiting and man-made ritual that belonged to the age before the King appeared.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless or that everything old must go. Jesus came to fulfil the law and prophets (5:17). Luke adds that people who have drunk old wine say “the old is good” (Luke 5:39): people often prefer the familiar. The “old wineskins” are the human traditions and religious system of Judaism as practised by the Pharisees, not the Scriptures themselves. Nor does it mean that Christians should not fast. Jesus says they will (v. 15; 6:16–18).

So should Christians fast? Jesus plainly assumes we will: then they will fast, and, when you fast (6:16). The early church fasted at prayer and at weighty decisions (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Yet the letters lay down no command, no required days, no rule. Fasting is therefore a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: a way to humble ourselves, sharpen prayer and hunger for God, never a badge to earn his favour. (The how and why are unfolded more fully at 6:16–18.)

How would I actually begin? Simply. Choose a meal or a day, perhaps before a decision or when you are burdened for someone, and use the time you would have spent eating to pray and read Scripture. Tell no one who does not need to know (6:17–18). Drink water. If you have a medical condition, are pregnant, or have struggled with eating disorders, do not fast from food; give up something else for a time instead, and talk to your doctor and pastor. The point is not the empty stomach but the turning of the whole self towards God. A fast that leaves you proud has failed, and a fast that leaves you hungrier for Christ has done its work.

Does new wineskins mean churches should always be changing their worship? No. This is not a charter for novelty. The new wine is Christ and his gospel, and the old skins are the Pharisees’ system of human tradition that could not contain him. The gospel itself does not change, and the Scriptures are the fixed rule for what the church believes and how it worships. What the saying warns against is binding Christ’s people with man-made rules, old or new, and trying to fit his grace into a religion of earning. A church can be old-fashioned or modern in its style and fail this test either way.

In a sentence. Jesus’ presence is a wedding feast, not a time for mourning, and the new life he brings needs new forms, not the old religious system.

On a Tuesday. Is your Christian life marked by joy in Christ’s presence? And are there human traditions you are clinging to that hinder the new life of the gospel? Ask what an outsider would think, watching you, that following Jesus is like: a funeral or a wedding? Then consider whether there is a time this month to fast, not to prove anything, but because you long for the bridegroom’s return.

For worship. The bridegroom has come, and the LORD who called himself Israel’s husband sat at table with his friends. He knew that he would be taken away, and he went to be taken, so that his bride might be made clean and presented to him without spot. Now we fast as those who long for him, and feast at his table as those who know him, and wait for the wedding supper of the Lamb. His joy is new wine, and no old skin of human religion can hold it. Blessed are those who are invited.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine still ferments and expands; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–38 — The Harvest Is Plentiful: Four More Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew compresses four more miracles into a rapid sequence: a ruler's dead daughter raised, a hemorrhaging woman healed on the way, two blind men given sight, a mute demoniac freed. The chapter ends with a summary of Jesus's teaching and healing throughout all the cities and villages, and the saying about the plentiful harvest and the few laborers. The pace is breathless — Matthew is showing the sheer scope of Jesus's ministry, the range of human need he addresses, and the consistency of his compassion. Three things more. This is the tenth miracle of a set Matthew has gathered into two chapters, arranged by design rather than chronology — leper, centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, storm, demoniacs, paralytic, ruler's daughter, the woman with the flow of blood, two blind men, mute man. In a Gospel that has already drawn Jesus as the new Moses (a slaughter of infants, called out of Egypt, water, forty days, a mountain, a law), ten mighty works after a mountain of teaching is the shape of the Exodus — with the difference that Moses' ten were plagues that destroyed, and these ten fall on disease, death, storm and the demonic. Verse 34 is the first Beelzebul charge, and it is worth seeing why they had to reach for it: nobody in the New Testament ever denies the miracles, so having ruled out God there was one explanation left. Its position is what chills — the same day and the same evidence produce "never was anything like this seen in Israel" from one group and "he casts out demons by the prince of demons" from the other. (A few early manuscripts omit the verse; the evidence for keeping it is good.) and the closing summary has three words stronger than any English can afford: "harassed and helpless" is eskylmenoi (flayed, mangled — the verb for skinning) and errimmenoi (thrown down, left lying where it fell); "compassion" is splagchnizomai, the churning of the inward organs, the strongest word for pity the language had; and "send out labourers" is ekballo, the very verb Matthew has used all chapter for casting out demons — beg the owner of the field to thrust workers into it. Note too that harvest in the prophets is nearly always judgement (Joel 3:13); Jesus takes the sickle out of it.
verseByVerse.theology: The two miracles of verses 18-26 are intertwined: the ruler's daughter dies while Jesus is on the way to heal her, and the hemorrhaging woman receives healing by touching his garment. Both cases involve women (a girl and a woman), both involve twelve years (the woman's illness, the girl's age in Mark's account), and both require faith that presses past social convention. Jesus stops for the bleeding woman even while the child lies dying — he does not hurry past need in order to reach crisis. Both receive exactly what they need.
verseByVerse.examples: The harvest saying (vv. 37-38) is the theological conclusion of the two miracle chapters: the need is vast, the laborers few, and the solution is prayer — not human strategy, not program development, but asking the Lord of the harvest to send workers. The church has often responded to the harvest by increasing activity; Jesus commands increasing prayer. The two are not incompatible, but prayer is the first and foundational response.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, "My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live." And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, for she said to herself, "If I only touch his garment, I will be made well." Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, "Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well." And instantly the woman was made well. And when Jesus came to the ruler's house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, he said, "Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. And the report of this went through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was speaking, a synagogue ruler knelt before him: my daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live. On the way, a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years touched the fringe of his cloak, and Jesus healed her. At the ruler’s house, he put out the mourners, took the girl by the hand, and she rose.

A ruler came in and knelt before him. Mark and Luke tell us he was Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue (Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41), responsible for organising services. A respected leader humbled himself before Jesus. He is a man of religious rank, from the very circles that are growing suspicious of Jesus, and he kneels in public. Desperation for a child does that to a man’s dignity.

My daughter has just died. Mark and Luke say she was dying when he came, and news of her death arrived on the way. Matthew shortens the story and gives the outcome from the start.

Why the accounts differ. In Mark and Luke the father comes saying his daughter is at the point of death, and only later, while Jesus is delayed with the woman, do messengers arrive to say she has died (Mark 5:22–23, 35). Matthew has him say at the outset that she has just died. It looks like a discrepancy and is in fact a habit. Matthew is the briefest of the three here: he tells in nine verses what Mark takes twenty-three to tell, and he does it by giving the father’s request in its final form rather than walking us through the stages. It is what any of us does in summarising: we say a man came asking Jesus to raise his dead daughter, because that is what the errand turned out to be. Matthew compresses the miracle stories and expands the teaching throughout, because his Gospel is built around five great blocks of Jesus’ words. A writer’s silence is not a denial. Read the three together and you have the fuller picture; read Matthew alone and you have the point.

But come and lay your hand on her, and she will live. Remarkable faith: he believed Jesus could raise the dead. And Jesus rose at once and followed him, with his disciples (v. 19), without a question or a condition. That is how he answers a sincere cry: he goes where he is needed.

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years. Probably a chronic menstrual or uterine bleeding. Under the law, such a woman was ritually unclean, and anyone she touched became unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). For twelve years she had been excluded from worship and from normal contact, probably unable to marry or remain married. Mark adds that she had spent all she had on doctors and had only grown worse (Mark 5:26). Twelve years of being unable to embrace a friend or receive a greeting without defiling them. To press through the crowd at all was to defile everyone she brushed against: an act of sheer desperation.

Came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment. She came from behind, secretly, because she was ashamed and knew she should not touch anyone. The “fringe” (kraspedon) was one of the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garment, as God commanded, to remind them of his commandments (Numbers 15:37–41). There is something moving in that. What she touched was the sign of the very law that had shut her out. She reached past the law that condemned her to the one who keeps it perfectly, and found him kinder than any rule.

For she said to herself, If I only touch his garment, I will be made well. Her faith was real, perhaps mixed with superstition. She believed Jesus’ power was so great that even his clothes could heal. She does not announce herself; she reaches.

Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well. Jesus would not let her slip away unseen. He called her “daughter”, the only time he uses that word in the Gospels, welcoming her into God’s family. “Your faith has made you well” (literally “has saved you”): not the touch or the cloth, but her trust in Jesus. The word “saved” (sesōken) includes both physical healing and the wider salvation of the whole person. Her uncleanness did not pass to him; his power passed to her. Take heart is the same word he spoke to the paralytic (v. 2). He sees the person, not only the affliction. Faith did not heal her by itself; it joined her to the one who did.

And instantly the woman was made well. Twelve years of suffering ended in a moment.

And when Jesus came to the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion. Mourning in that culture was loud and public. Even poor families hired at least two flute players and a professional mourning woman. Wailing and lament filled the house. It is the machinery of death, already running at full volume.

Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping. Jesus does not deny that she has died physically; the mourners know she has. But for him, death is like sleep, because he is about to wake her. In the New Testament, “sleep” becomes a Christian way of speaking of the death of believers (John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14), because they will be raised. To the Lord of life, death is a sleep he can break whenever he chooses.

And they laughed at him. The mourners’ grief turned instantly to mockery. Unbelief laughs at Christ’s promises. It is the laugh of people who know a corpse when they see one, and it is the last laugh death ever had in that house.

He went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. Again Jesus touches the unclean: a dead body made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11). Again, life flows from him. Mark records his words in Aramaic: Talitha cumi, “Little girl, I say to you, arise” (Mark 5:41). The verb for arose (ēgerthē) is the word used for resurrection, the same word that will be said of him at the tomb: he has risen (28:6).

And the report of this went through all that district. News of a resurrection could not be hidden.

Twelve years. Mark notes that the girl was twelve (Mark 5:42). The woman had been suffering for as long as the girl had been alive. One was a respected man’s daughter, one an outcast woman; Jesus made both whole.

Why the two stories are woven together. They are bound by more than timing. Both are stories of uncleanness and death: the woman ceremonially unclean, the girl a corpse, which was uncleanness at its height. By every rule of the law the woman’s touch and the dead girl’s hand should have defiled him; yet the current runs the other way. His holiness is not stained; it cleanses. His life is not cancelled; it raises. And the interruption itself preaches. While Jesus stops for the woman, the girl dies, which stretches the father’s faith from heal her to raise her, and shows that Jesus is Lord not only over long disease but over death itself. A ruler of the synagogue and a nameless, penniless, unclean woman: he has time, touch and tenderness for both. He calls her daughter, and he gives the man back his.

What it does not mean. Not that touching objects associated with Jesus, or with saints, carries healing power. The power was in Jesus, and he made clear it was her faith in him that mattered.
