Nor does it mean that faith always brings physical healing. But it shows that no condition is too hopeless for Jesus, not even death.

Why does Jesus delay when I am praying for something urgent? Stand where the father is standing. His daughter is dying, he has found Jesus, Jesus has agreed to come, and then Jesus stops, for somebody else, for a woman who had lived with her illness for twelve years and could, on any reasonable calculation, have waited another hour. And in the delay the child dies. Anyone who has watched a clock while heaven said nothing knows what that pause feels like. Two things must be said. First, the delay was not neglect. It changed what the father was going to receive. He set out asking for a recovery and went home with a resurrection. God’s delays are very often the distance between what we asked for and what he intended to give. Second, not everyone gets the child back. Jairus did. Many have prayed this exact prayer and buried their child, and the passage must never be preached as though the outcome were the promise. What is promised is what Jesus said in the room: that to him the dead are sleeping, and he can break that sleep. This raising was a sign, not the destination; the girl grew up and died again in due course. I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25) is the promise. Jairus’s daughter is the preview.

For the one whose suffering has gone on for years. She is the person in the passage who waited longest and was helped last, and she is the one woman in Matthew whom Jesus is recorded calling daughter. If your affliction has outlasted your patience and everyone else’s interest, take that detail with you. He was not too busy with the emergency to stop for the long, unglamorous, chronic thing. And when he stopped, he did not only heal her. He gave her a name in his family.

Was her faith superstitious, and does Jesus accept faith that is mixed and muddled? Her idea about the clothes was imperfect, and Jesus gently corrected it by turning and speaking to her, so that she would know it was not the cloth but the person. But he did not reject her for it. He honoured the faith and fixed the theology. That is a great comfort, because all of us come to him with mixed motives and half-formed ideas. Faith does not save by being well informed or pure; it saves by reaching for the right person. Then he teaches us, as he taught her, to know him better.

Does sleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes the body, which lies still and will be woken, and it tells us that death is not the end for those in Christ. It does not mean that the soul sleeps. When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ, which Paul says is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). Jesus told the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). The body waits in the grave for the resurrection; the person is awake in the presence of the Lord. That is why Christians can call a cemetery a sleeping place and still say their loved ones are with Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus healed a woman unclean for twelve years and raised a dead girl, showing that his power overcomes both uncleanness and death.

On a Tuesday. Is there a long, hidden suffering you have carried in shame? Come to Jesus. He will not push you away; he will call you son or daughter. And if you are waiting on him in an emergency while he seems to be stopping for everyone else, keep holding on to the word he gave Jairus: do not fear, only believe (Mark 5:36). When you stand at a Christian’s grave, let the word sleeping shape how you grieve: truly, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

For worship. Praise Jesus, who calls death sleep because he will wake his people. He took a dead child by the hand and spoke to her as a father wakes his daughter in the morning, and she got up. He touched what the law called unclean and was not defiled, and he went down into death himself and was not held by it. The last enemy will be destroyed, and the one who said Talitha cumi in a little room in Capernaum will say it over every grave of his people on the last day. Then the mourners will be put out for ever, and the laughter will be ours.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke name the ruler Jairus, a synagogue leader. A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and made others unclean by touch. Hired flute players and mourners were customary at a death. The “fringe” was the tassel the law required on garments.

parallels.desc: a woman with a discharge of blood

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, "Have mercy on us, Son of David." When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" They said to him, "Yes, Lord." Then he touched their eyes, saying, "According to your faith let it be done to you." And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, "See that no one knows about it." But they went away and spread his fame through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two blind men followed Jesus, crying, have mercy on us, Son of David! In the house Jesus asked whether they believed he could do this. They said yes, and he touched their eyes: according to your faith be it done to you. Their sight was restored. Though he warned them to tell no one, they spread the news everywhere.

Two blind men followed him. Blindness was common in the ancient world, caused by disease, injury and poor hygiene. Blind people usually lived by begging. Isaiah promised that in the age of salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened (Isaiah 35:5; 42:7). The opening of blind eyes was a sign promised for the days of the Messiah.

Crying aloud, Have mercy on us, Son of David. “Have mercy” (eleēson) is the cry of those who have no claim and can only appeal to kindness. The church has prayed it for centuries: Kyrie eleison, “Lord, have mercy”. “Son of David” is a messianic title (see 1:1). Remarkably, the blind see who Jesus is when many sighted people do not. Their cry echoes the psalm of those whose eyes look to the LORD until he has mercy on them (Psalm 123:2–3). They cannot see him, yet they see him more clearly than the Pharisees do.

When he entered the house, the blind men came to him. Jesus did not respond on the road. He waited until they had followed him into the house, perhaps testing their persistence, and avoiding a public messianic demonstration.

Do you believe that I am able to do this? Jesus asks about their faith in him personally: not whether they believe in healing, but whether they trust him. The question is searching, not rhetorical. Faith is meant to come to the surface and say what it believes.

They said to him, Yes, Lord. A simple, clear confession. Two words, unhesitating and complete. They call him Lord, the disciples’ word.

Then he touched their eyes, saying, According to your faith be it done to you. Their faith in him received what he gave. “According to” does not mean “in proportion to”, as though a little faith gets a little sight. It means “in response to”: faith is the hand that receives. And he touches their eyes, in a chapter full of touching: the leper, the fevered woman, the dead girl, now the blind.

And their eyes were opened. A sign that the Messiah had come (11:5).

And Jesus sternly warned them, See that no one knows about it. “Sternly” means strongly, with deep feeling. Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a miracle-worker, or as a political “Son of David” who would lead a revolt (see 8:4).

Why the command to silence? It is often called the messianic secret, and several threads run through it. First, timing: Jesus moved on his Father’s schedule towards the cross, and a wildfire of publicity could force a premature collision with the authorities. Second, the danger of a faith built on signs: the crowds chased miracles, not the Messiah, and he told them so when they followed him for the loaves (John 6:26). Third, and deepest, the title itself could not be rightly understood until the cross defined it. To proclaim Son of David or Christ without Calvary was to broadcast a false messiah, the political deliverer the crowds once tried to make king by force (John 6:15). That is why, even after Peter’s confession, Jesus told the disciples to tell no one, and at once began to speak of his death (16:20–21). Matthew also sees in this reticence the portrait of Isaiah’s gentle Servant, who would not quarrel or cry aloud in the streets (12:18–21). And the silence was never absolute. In Gentile country, where no messianic frenzy threatened, Jesus told the freed demoniac to go and tell what the Lord had done (Mark 5:19). The secret was provisional, fitted to a work not yet finished. After the cross and the empty tomb, the command is gloriously reversed: go and make disciples of all nations (28:19). What had to be hushed before Calvary is to be shouted from the rooftops after it.

But they went away and spread his fame through all that district. They disobeyed. Understandable, but disobedience nonetheless. Gratitude does not excuse ignoring Jesus’ word. It is easy to sympathise: who could keep silent after seeing for the first time? But Jesus had a reason, and the cost of their enthusiasm fell on his ministry. Loving him means doing what he says, even when we think we know a better way to serve him (John 14:15).

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a power that produces results by itself. The two men had faith in Jesus’ ability, and Jesus healed them. Nor does it mean that people who are not healed lack faith (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

Why did Jesus ask whether they believed, when he already knew? Not to find out, but to draw it out. Faith that is spoken becomes clearer to the one who has it, and Jesus wanted them to know that their healing came through trusting him personally, not through a lucky meeting on the road. He still asks the same question, through his word, of everyone who comes: do you believe that I am able? Your answer does not need to be eloquent. Yes, Lord, is enough. It is also why Christians confess their faith openly, in baptism and before the church (Romans 10:9–10). What is believed in the heart is meant to be said with the mouth.

In a sentence. Two blind men recognised Jesus as the Son of David, trusted his power, and received their sight.

On a Tuesday. Pray “Lord, have mercy” today, for yourself and for someone you love. It is a prayer Jesus always hears. And answer his question honestly about the thing you are most anxious over: do you believe that I am able to do this? Say yes, Lord, aloud if you can. Then obey him in the small things he has told you, rather than improving on his instructions.

For worship. The Son of David has come, and the blind see. The one who made the eye (Psalm 94:9) touched two ruined pairs of eyes and opened them, and the first thing they saw was his face. He opens the eyes of the spiritually blind as well, shining into hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Lord, have mercy: the church has prayed it for two thousand years, and he has never once refused it to anyone who cried to him in faith.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah, the king of David’s line.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, "Never was anything like this seen in Israel." But the Pharisees said, "He casts out demons by the prince of demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a man who could not speak because of a demon was brought to Jesus. When the demon was driven out, the man spoke. The crowds were amazed: nothing like this had ever been seen in Israel. But the Pharisees said that he drove out demons by the prince of demons.

A demon-oppressed man who was mute. Here the inability to speak was caused by a demon. Not every disability is demonic (see 4:24), but in this case it was. He was brought to Jesus; he could not ask for himself. Others did his speaking for him, as others had done the carrying for the paralytic.

And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. Isaiah promised that the tongue of the mute would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:6). Matthew tells the healing in two clauses: cast out, spoke. He does not linger, because the accumulation of miracles is the point.

And the crowds marveled, saying, Never was anything like this seen in Israel. The crowds sum up chapters 8–9: ten miracles, unmatched in Israel’s history. Moses, Elijah and Elisha did great works, but nothing like this.

The tenth. Count them: the leper, the centurion’s servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, the storm, the Gadarene demoniacs, the paralytic, the ruler’s daughter, the woman with the flow of blood, the two blind men, and this mute man. Ten mighty works, gathered into two chapters and arranged by Matthew rather than by strict order of time; Mark and Luke place several of them elsewhere. The number is probably not accidental in a Gospel so carefully built. Matthew has already shown Jesus as the new Moses: a child escaping a slaughter of infants, called out of Egypt, passing through water, forty days in the wilderness, a mountain, a law. Ten mighty works following a mountain of teaching recalls the exodus, with one great difference. Moses’ ten were plagues that fell on Egypt. These ten fall on disease, death, the storm and the demonic. The signs of the first deliverance destroyed; the signs of this one heal.

But the Pharisees said, He casts out demons by the prince of demons. The Pharisees cannot deny the miracles, so they explain them away: Jesus is in league with Satan. This is the beginning of their charge that Jesus is demonic. Jesus will answer it fully in 12:22–32: a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and to call the Spirit’s work Satan’s is a terrible sin.

Why they had to reach for it. They could not deny the miracles. Nobody in the New Testament ever does: not the Pharisees, not the Sanhedrin, not Herod, not Pilate. The mute man was standing there talking. So there were only two possible explanations for a power that was plainly real and plainly not theirs, and having ruled out God they had one left.

A textual note. A few early manuscripts leave out verse 34, and some scholars think it was brought in from 12:24. The evidence for keeping it is good and most editions do, but a reader who finds a footnote in his Bible has met a real question rather than an invented one. Nothing in the teaching of Scripture depends on it, since the same charge is recorded beyond dispute in chapter 12.

Two responses. The same miracle produced amazement in the crowds and hostility in the leaders. Evidence alone does not produce faith. The heart that does not want to submit to Jesus will find a way to explain him away. What makes verse 34 chilling is where it stands. Immediately before it, the crowd says nothing like this was ever seen in Israel. Same day, same man, same evidence: one group concludes that God has visited his people, and the other that the devil is loose in Galilee. The difference was never the data.

What it does not mean. Not that amazement is the same as faith. The crowds marvelled, but many later turned away. Wonder needs to become trust and obedience. And though Matthew ties this man’s muteness to a demon, the Gospels also distinguish demonic oppression from ordinary illness (4:24), so this gives no reason to think that disability or illness today is demonic.

Is this the unforgivable sin, and could I have committed it? Jesus later warns that blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven (12:31–32), and he says it in answer to exactly this charge. That sin is not a careless word or a passing doubt. It is the settled, deliberate refusal to accept the Spirit’s plain witness to Christ, calling the light darkness and holding to it, so that the heart can no longer repent. Those who commit it do not care that they have. If you are troubled that you might have committed it, your very trouble shows that the Spirit is still at work in you, and the promise stands: whoever comes to Christ he will never cast out (John 6:37).

Why don’t miracles convince everyone? Because unbelief is not finally a problem of information. Jesus said that if people will not hear Moses and the Prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31), and when he raised Lazarus some went to plot his death (John 11:45–53). The heart decides how the evidence is read. That is why faith is a gift of God and not merely a conclusion (Ephesians 2:8): the Spirit must open blind eyes. It is also why we should pray for unbelieving friends and not only argue with them. Arguments matter, but only God can change a heart.

In a sentence. Jesus freed a mute man from a demon, and while the crowds marvelled, the Pharisees accused him of working by Satan’s power.

On a Tuesday. When you hear evidence for Christ, do you look for reasons to believe or for reasons to dismiss it? The heart decides how we read the evidence. Notice where you do this with lesser things: the colleague whose good work you explain away because you dislike him. Then use your tongue as the healed man did: say one thing today that you could not have said before Christ opened your mouth, a word of thanks, of witness, or of praise.

For worship. Never was anything like this seen in Israel, and never has anything like him been seen anywhere. He makes the mute speak and the dead rise, and he bears the slander of those who call his goodness evil. He was called demonic by men he had come to save, and he did not answer them with fire but went on healing. One day every mouth he opened, and every tongue in heaven and on earth, will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11).

parallels.desc: the tongue of the mute sing for joy

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few;" therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching, preaching the good news of the kingdom and healing every disease. When he saw the crowds, he was moved with compassion, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. He told his disciples: the harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers.

And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages. Almost word for word the summary of 4:23. Matthew brackets chapters 5–9 with these summaries: Jesus’ words (5–7) and works (8–9) together show the kingdom has come. And nothing the Pharisees say stops what God is doing. The accusation of verse 34 is followed not by a retreat but by a wider mission.

Teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. Teaching, preaching, healing: the three parts of Jesus’ ministry (see 4:23). They are the three inseparable expressions of the kingdom’s arrival.

When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them. “Compassion” (splanchnizomai) is a strong word, literally a movement of the inward parts: deep, gut-level pity that moves a person to act. In the Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus (14:14; 15:32; 20:34) and of characters in his parables who picture God (18:27; Luke 15:20). Jesus did not look at crowds as statistics or as an audience, but as people in need. It is the strongest word for pity the language had. It is not a decision to be sympathetic; it is what happens in the body when something goes right through you. In his parables it is the father who sees his son on the road, the Samaritan who sees the man in the ditch (Luke 10:33), the king faced with an unpayable debt.

Because they were harassed and helpless. “Harassed” means troubled, worn out, torn, as if mauled by wild animals. “Helpless” means thrown down, lying prostrate, unable to get up. The people were exhausted by life, oppressed by Rome and burdened by the religious leaders’ demands (23:4), and without anyone to care for them. The first word (eskylmenoi) comes from a verb meaning to flay or to mangle; the second (errimmenoi) means flung down and left where it fell. So the sentence is not, they looked tired. It is: mauled and dumped. That is what Jesus saw when he looked at a religious crowd in Galilee.

Like sheep without a shepherd. An Old Testament image (Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17). In Ezekiel 34, God condemns Israel’s shepherds, the leaders who fed themselves instead of the flock, so that the sheep were scattered; and he promises that he himself will shepherd his people, through his servant David. Jesus is that Shepherd (2:6; John 10:11). Ezekiel’s words are not gentle: the shepherds had not strengthened the weak, healed the sick or bound up the injured, and so the flock was scattered for lack of a shepherd (Ezekiel 34:2–5). The flock was not shepherdless because nobody held the office. It had shepherds; that was the problem. And Jesus had spent two chapters in conflict with them.

Then he said to his disciples, The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Jesus changes the picture from sheep to a harvest field. The harvest is people ready to be gathered into God’s kingdom. In the prophets, harvest often pictured the final judgment (Joel 3:13), but here it pictures the gathering of people by the gospel (John 4:35–38). There are many to be reached, and few to reach them. Jesus takes the sickle of judgement and turns it into a tool of rescue. The same fields, the same ripeness, the same urgency, and what is being gathered is people, and the workers are sent to save them, not to cut them down. Both pictures are true at once: the crowds are lost sheep, which is need, and ripe grain, which is opportunity.

Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest. God is the Lord of the harvest: he owns it and directs it. The first response to the need is not to organise but to pray. “Pray earnestly” (deēthēte) means to beg, to plead. Jesus does not say, form a committee, develop a strategy, train more preachers, though all of these have their place. He says: pray. Labourers are God’s provision, not human production.

To send out laborers into his harvest. “Send out” (ekbalē) is a strong word, the same used for casting out demons: thrust out, drive out. Workers are needed, and God must send them. The prayer often turns back on the one who prays: in the next verses, Jesus sends out the very disciples he told to pray (10:1–5). It is a strange way to describe answered prayer until you have watched how people actually come into hard work for God: rarely by strolling towards it, and very often by being moved along by something they did not choose.

What it does not mean. Not that only full-time missionaries and pastors are “labourers”. Every disciple has a part in the harvest (5:14–16; 28:19). Nor does “plentiful” mean that everyone will believe. The harvest is ready; but workers are needed to gather it.

Does Jesus still feel this compassion now that he is in heaven? Yes. He did not leave his human heart behind when he ascended. He is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses, because he was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). The same gut-wrenching pity he felt on a Galilean hillside he feels now for the harassed and helpless, including you on the day when you feel mauled and thrown aside. Come to him with confidence; you will find mercy and grace to help in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).

How can an ordinary Christian be a labourer? By living and speaking for Christ where God has put you. Most of the harvest is gathered not by professionals but by ordinary believers among their own families, neighbours and colleagues: praying for them by name, loving them practically, and being ready to explain the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15). Support those sent further afield with your giving and your prayers. Serve in your church so that its shepherds are free to shepherd. And keep praying the prayer Jesus taught here, holding yourself ready to be part of the answer.

In a sentence. Moved by compassion for weary, shepherdless crowds, Jesus told his disciples to pray for God to send workers into his plentiful harvest.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for God to send workers into the harvest: missionaries, pastors, and ordinary believers in your workplace and street. And be ready to be the answer to your own prayer. Next time you are in a crowd, a station, a shopping centre, a hospital waiting room, look at the faces and ask the Lord to let you see them as he does: not as an inconvenience but as sheep without a shepherd. Then pray for three of them silently before you leave.

For worship. Thank Jesus for his compassion toward you when you were harassed and helpless. He looked at a crowd flayed and thrown aside by the men who should have fed them, and what he felt turned him inside out. Then he told his friends to pray, and the next thing he did was answer the prayer himself, by sending the men who had prayed it. He is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), the Lord of the harvest who sends his workers into his own field, and the chief Shepherd who will come again with the reward (1 Peter 5:4). The flock that was mauled and scattered he gathers in his arms.

parallels.desc: not as sheep that have no shepherd
scattered, because there was no shepherd

9.theology: Justification and the forgiveness of sins. The healing of the paralytic is Matthew’s clearest window into the doctrine of justification. Jesus pronounces forgiveness as a judicial declaration — he does not say “God will forgive you if…” but “your sins are forgiven,” accomplished fact. This is the forensic heart of the gospel: the guilty are declared righteous by the word of the Judge himself, on the basis of the Son’s merit, through faith. The Reformers called this the article by which the church stands or falls. Matthew 9 shows it enacted in history by the King who has authority on earth to forgive sins — the same authority he will exercise from the cross, bearing the penalty that makes the declaration just.
9.examples:
Then: Matthew the tax collector was the last person anyone expected in the kingdom. His conversion was a public scandal and a public testimony. The banquet he threw was evangelism by hospitality: bring the ones who need the physician to the physician.

Now: Every church that welcomes the broken, the addicted, the socially marginal, and the morally compromised is continuing Matthew’s banquet. The temptation of respectable Christianity is the Pharisees’ error: to protect the purity of the community by excluding the sick. Jesus reverses the logic. The church is not a museum of saints but a hospital for sinners — a place where the Great Physician practices.

10.title: Sent as Sheep Among Wolves
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. <sup>2</sup>The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; <sup>3</sup>Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; <sup>4</sup>Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>5</sup>These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, “Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, <sup>6</sup>but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. <sup>7</sup>And proclaim as you go, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.’ <sup>8</sup>Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay. <sup>9</sup>Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts, <sup>10</sup>no bag for your journey, or two tunics or sandals or a staff, for the laborer deserves his food. <sup>11</sup>And whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it and stay there until you depart. <sup>12</sup>As you enter the house, greet it. <sup>13</sup>And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it, but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. <sup>14</sup>And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town. <sup>16</sup>“Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. <sup>17</sup>Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues, <sup>18</sup>and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. <sup>19</sup>When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. <sup>20</sup>For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. <sup>21</sup>Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death, <sup>22</sup>and you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>23</sup>When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. <sup>24</sup>“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. <sup>25</sup>It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household. <sup>26</sup>“So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>27</sup>What I tell you in the dark, say in the light, and what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops. <sup>28</sup>And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. <sup>29</sup>Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. <sup>30</sup>But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. <sup>31</sup>Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>32</sup>So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, <sup>33</sup>but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. <sup>34</sup>“Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. <sup>35</sup>For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. <sup>36</sup>And a person’s enemies will be those of his own household. <sup>37</sup>Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. <sup>38</sup>And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. <sup>39</sup>Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. <sup>40</sup>“Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. <sup>41</sup>The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. <sup>42</sup>And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple, truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward.”
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the mission discourse — the second of Matthew’s five great discourses. Jesus commissions the Twelve, gives them his authority, and sends them first to Israel. But the instructions quickly expand beyond a local mission trip to describe the entire missionary existence of the church until the end of the age. Persecution is not an accident but the normal condition of mission: “I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves.” The sheep do not become wolves; they remain sheep — dependent, vulnerable, and under the care of the Shepherd.

The antidote to the fear of persecution is the fear of God. Three times Jesus says “fear not” (vv. 26, 28, 31), anchoring each command in the sovereign knowledge and care of the Father. Not a sparrow falls without him; the hairs of the head are numbered. If the Father governs such small things, he governs the sufferings of his missionaries. The cross appears explicitly in verse 38: discipleship is cruciform. The disciple takes up the cross before the resurrection — only those who lose their lives for Christ’s sake will find them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Twelve Sent Out: Authority, Message, and Provision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls the Twelve, names them, and sends them out with authority over unclean spirits and disease. Their mission is confined to Israel: go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, not to the Gentiles or Samaritans. They are to preach the kingdom, heal the sick, raise the dead, and cast out demons — exactly what Jesus himself has been doing. Their provision is radical dependence: no gold, no bag, no extra tunic. Worthy households will host them; unworthy towns will receive judgment. This is the only time Matthew uses the word "apostles" — once in twenty-eight chapters, at the exact moment they stop learning and start being sent. The Twelve is a claim, not a headcount: ten tribes had been gone for seven hundred years, and Jesus says himself that these men will judge the twelve tribes (19:28), so appointing exactly twelve is the reconstituting of Israel. Note the limits of the delegation — authority over unclean spirits and disease, but not to forgive sins, which is nowhere handed over. The list is in pairs because he sent them out two by two (Mk. 6:7): Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew, James and Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas. Which sharpens the incompatibility until it draws blood: the Zealot movement existed to expel Rome by violence, and the Jews they killed first were collaborators — men like Matthew, a few names away in the same list. Nothing suggests Jesus arranged a reconciliation or that either changed his politics. On the charge: "raise the dead" is in it, and Matthew alone records that. "You received without paying, give without pay" is dorean twice — and the guard is supplied two verses later, since "the labourer deserves his food" (v. 10) is quoted by Paul to argue that preachers should be supported (1 Cor. 9:14; 1 Tim. 5:18). A worker may be supported; a gift may not be sold. "worthy" (axios) occurs four times in vv. 10-13 and the definition is purely practical — a worthy house is one that opens its door. And staying in one house forecloses the patron-shopping that itinerant teachers were notorious for; a Christian handbook of the next century, the Didache, has to legislate against exactly that. The dust-shaking was the gesture a Jew made leaving pagan soil — performed now on a Jewish town, it is a verdict delivered in mime.
verseByVerse.theology: The mission of the Twelve is an extension of Jesus's own mission: he gives them his authority (10:1) and his message (10:7). Disciples are not innovators but ambassadors — they carry the word and power of the one who sent them, not their own. The restriction to Israel (v. 5-6) is not permanent exclusion of Gentiles but the priority of the gospel going first to the lost sheep of Israel, as Paul will later articulate (Rom. 1:16). The Great Commission (28:18-20) will remove the restriction after the resurrection.
verseByVerse.examples: Radical dependence — no gold, no bag, no sandals beyond what they are wearing — is not poverty for its own sake but trust in the Lord of the harvest to provide through the households that receive them. The kingdom worker is not self-sufficient; they are wholly dependent on God's provision through his people. This dependence is not weakness but testimony: the worker who needs nothing from you has nothing to demonstrate about the kingdom's power to provide.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called his twelve disciples and gave them his own authority to drive out evil spirits and heal every disease. These twelve are named as apostles: men sent out with his authority.

Meaning first. Matthew 10 is the chapter in which Jesus, having told his disciples to pray for workers for the harvest, sends the very men who prayed. He calls twelve, gives them his own authority over demons and disease, and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel to announce that the kingdom of heaven is at hand. They are to travel light, give freely what they freely received, bless the homes that welcome them and solemnly leave the towns that refuse. Then the horizon widens far beyond that first short tour. Jesus speaks of the whole future mission of his people: sheep among wolves, councils and floggings, governors and kings, families divided, hatred for his name. Three times he says do not be afraid, and he gives three reasons: everything hidden will be revealed, God alone holds body and soul, and the Father who governs the fall of every sparrow has numbered the hairs on your head. He demands to be loved above father and mother, calls every disciple to take up a cross, and promises that whoever loses his life for him will find it. And the chapter that began with authority to raise the dead ends with a cup of cold water, which God will not forget. It is a chapter about being sent by a Lord worth everything, into a world that will not thank you, by a Father who never loses sight of you.

The connection. At the end of chapter 9, Jesus told his disciples to pray for workers for the harvest (9:38). Now he sends the very disciples who prayed. Chapter 10 is the second of Jesus’ five great teaching sections in Matthew: the mission discourse. It covers their first mission (vv. 5–15) and then looks far beyond it, to the mission of the church in a hostile world (vv. 16–42).

And he called to him his twelve disciples. Jesus had many disciples, but chose twelve to be with him and to be sent out (Mark 3:14). Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is forming a new Israel, the restored people of God, around himself. The Twelve will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (19:28), and their names are on the foundations of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:14).

A claim before it is an arrangement. The number is not a headcount. By Jesus’ day Israel had long ceased to exist as twelve tribes: ten had been carried off by Assyria seven hundred years before and never came back. So the appointing of exactly twelve men is a declaration. He is not recruiting staff. He is reconstituting the people of God, and he begins by naming a twelve, as God began Israel with twelve sons of Jacob.

And gave them authority. His own authority (see 7:29; 9:6). They do not have power of their own; it is delegated, as an ambassador carries the authority of his king. The word is exousia, the very word that has been the flashpoint of the last two chapters. The scribes disputed his authority to forgive; the crowd marvelled that God had given such authority to men; at the end of the book he will say that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (28:18). Here, one chapter after having to defend it, he gives it away.

Over unclean spirits, to cast them out. “Unclean spirits” is another name for demons: they are morally impure and defile those they possess.

And to heal every disease and every affliction. The same words used of Jesus’ ministry (4:23; 9:35). The disciples extend his work. And notice the limits, because they are exact. Authority over unclean spirits, and to heal disease. Not to forgive sins: that is nowhere delegated in this passage, and the apostles never claim it. They are given the works. The word that only God can speak stays where it belongs.

The names of the twelve apostles are these. The only time Matthew uses the word “apostles”. An apostle (apostolos) is one sent, a messenger or envoy with the authority of the sender. In Jewish law, a person’s authorised agent was regarded as the person himself (see v. 40). Once, in twenty-eight chapters, and he uses it at the precise moment they stop only learning and start being sent. It is not a title these men wore casually.

First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother. “First” does not only mean first in the list; Peter is the leader and spokesman of the Twelve throughout the Gospels (16:16–19). He always appears first in the lists of apostles (Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13), and Judas always last. The list is in pairs, perhaps because Jesus sent them out two by two (Mark 6:7). Andrew, listed straight after him, was the one who had brought Peter to Jesus in the first place (John 1:41): the first missionary brought the future leader of the apostles.

James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother. With Peter, the inner circle (see 4:21).

What it does not mean. Not that Peter was given authority over the other apostles as a pope over the church. He was first among equals, a leader and spokesman. (See 16:18.) Nor does it mean that every Christian has the same authority the Twelve had. The apostles had a unique, foundational role (Ephesians 2:20). But every Christian shares in the mission they began (28:19–20).

Are there apostles today? Not in this sense. An apostle of Christ had to have seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and Paul calls himself the last to see him (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the foundation of the church once for all, and their teaching is now in the New Testament. Missionaries and church planters are sent ones in a general sense, but nobody today carries an apostle’s authority, whatever title he gives himself. When we want to hear the apostles now, we open the Scriptures they left us.

In a sentence. Jesus gave his twelve chosen apostles his own authority over demons and disease and sent them out as the foundation of a new Israel.

On a Tuesday. The disciples who prayed for workers became the workers. Be ready for God to send you as the answer to your own prayers. If you have been praying for a neighbour, a colleague or a relative to hear the gospel, ask whether you are the person God has placed nearest to them. And remember that whatever you do for Christ is done under his authority, not your own, which is both humbling and freeing.

For worship. The Lord who rebuilds Israel begins with twelve ordinary men and gives them his own authority. He does not hoard his power; he shares his work with people who had shown no aptitude for it, and he sends them under his name. All authority in heaven and on earth is his, and he spends it on gathering lost sheep. He named his twelve, and he knows the name of every one he sends, and their names, like ours, are written in his book.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

parallels.desc: the twelve apostles on the city’s foundations

verseByVerse.quote: James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list of the twelve continues: James and John, Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew the tax collector, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.

Philip and Bartholomew. Philip came from Bethsaida, the same town as Peter and Andrew (John 1:44). Bartholomew means “son of Tolmai”; he is often identified with Nathanael, whom Philip brought to Jesus (John 1:45–49), because in John’s Gospel Philip and Nathanael are paired, and Bartholomew appears next to Philip in the lists. Bartholomew is not a first name at all, so the man must have had another, and Nathanael fits.

Thomas. Known for doubting the resurrection until he saw Jesus, and then for one of the greatest confessions in the Gospels: my Lord and my God (John 20:24–29). His name means “twin”.

And Matthew the tax collector. The author of this Gospel. Only Matthew adds “the tax collector” to his own name. He never forgot the grace that called him (9:9).

James the son of Alphaeus. Probably also called “James the less” or “the younger” (Mark 15:40).

And Thaddaeus. Probably the same person Luke calls “Judas the son of James” (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). Some manuscripts call him Lebbaeus. Many people had more than one name.

Simon the Zealot. Literally “the Cananaean”, from an Aramaic word meaning “zealous”. Luke calls him “the Zealot” (Luke 6:15). He may have belonged to the Zealots, a nationalist movement willing to use violence to overthrow Rome; or the name may simply describe his zeal for the law. Either way, it is striking that Jesus chose both Matthew, who had collaborated with Rome, and Simon, who had probably wanted to fight Rome. In Jesus’ new community, political enemies became brothers.

Six pairs. Read the list again and the pairing is unmistakable: Peter and Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew; James the son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot and Judas Iscariot. Matthew is not only listing names; he is listing teams. And it sharpens the point about the Zealot and the tax collector. Nationalists of Simon’s kind wanted Rome expelled by force (the organised Zealot party belongs to the later revolt of AD 66, so Simon’s title may mean only zeal for the law), and the men such nationalists hated most, before ever reaching a Roman soldier, were Jews who worked for the occupation. Tax collectors were at the top of that list. In the ordinary run of things, Simon’s friends existed to put a knife into men like Matthew. And they walked the same roads for three years, ate at the same fires, and are named a few names apart. Nothing suggests that Jesus arranged a reconciliation or that either man changed his politics. He simply called them both, and the calling turned out to be larger than the thing that should have made them enemies.

And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. “Iscariot” probably means “man of Kerioth”, a town in southern Judea; he may have been the only one of the Twelve not from Galilee. He always comes last, labelled by his betrayal (26:14–16, 47–50). Jesus chose him knowingly (John 6:70–71). His presence among the Twelve is a solemn warning: it is possible to be close to Jesus, to share in his ministry, even to do miracles in his name (7:22), and yet not belong to him. (A minority link Iscariot instead to the Latin word for the dagger-men of the later insurgency, which would put two revolutionaries in the last pair; the town of Kerioth is the likelier meaning.)

Remembered with care. In all four lists of the Twelve in the New Testament, here, in Mark, in Luke and in Acts, the names fall into three groups of four, with the same man heading each group: Peter, Philip, and James the son of Alphaeus. Peter is always first, and Judas, where he appears, is always last. However the memory was carried, it was carried carefully.

The kind of people. Fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot: ordinary, unremarkable, very different men. None were religious leaders, scholars or priests. Jesus chooses the weak and lowly to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:26–29). That such a group became the foundation of the church is testimony to the one who called them, not to their natural compatibility.

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was forced to betray Jesus against his will. God’s plan included the betrayal (Acts 2:23), and Scripture had foretold it (Psalm 41:9), but Judas acted freely and was fully responsible (26:24). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility are both true.

Why did Jesus choose Judas? He knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64, 70–71), and the betrayal fulfilled Scripture (John 13:18; Psalm 41:9) within God’s plan (Acts 2:23). Yet Judas was fully responsible (26:24). He was sent out with the others and did the same works, which shows that ministry and outward power are no proof of saving grace (7:21–23).

Could I be a Judas, close to Jesus but not his? The question is a healthy one to ask once, and a dangerous one to ask endlessly. Judas’s problem was not weak faith but no faith: he loved money (John 12:6), he kept up appearances, and when he was sorry he went to the priests and not to Christ (27:3–5). The test is not whether you have struggles, but where you take them. If you hate your sin, trust Christ alone for forgiveness, and keep coming back to him when you fail, you are not a Judas. You are a Peter, who also failed badly, and wept, and was restored. Judas never stops being a warning; he must never become a torment to a believer who is running to Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus chose twelve ordinary and very different men, including a tax collector, a zealot, and the one who would betray him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus puts very different people together in his church. Who is the “Simon the Zealot” to your “Matthew”? Love them as a brother or sister in Christ. Think of the person in your church whose politics, background or temperament you find hardest. This week, pray for them by name and do one kind thing for them. The calling that made the Twelve one is meant to be larger than what divides you.

For worship. Look at the list and marvel at the Lord who made it. A collaborator and a zealot, a doubter and a denier, fishermen with no education, and a traitor whom he washed and fed to the last. He was not deceived about any of them, and he called them anyway. He makes one people out of enemies, because he himself is our peace, who has broken down the dividing wall (Ephesians 2:14). And he still chooses the foolish things of the world, so that no one may boast in his presence, and all the glory goes to him.
verseByVerse.note: Bartholomew is often identified with Nathanael of John’s Gospel. Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists.

verseByVerse.quote: These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, "Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sent the Twelve out with instructions: do not go to the Gentiles or to Samaritan towns, but go to the lost sheep of Israel.

These twelve Jesus sent out. The verb is related to “apostle”: he sent them as his envoys.

Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans. A surprising restriction. The Samaritans lived in the region between Judea and Galilee. They were descendants of Israelites from the northern kingdom who intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest of 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim instead of in Jerusalem (John 4:20). Jews and Samaritans despised each other. It is one of the hardest commands in the Gospel to square with the rest of it. The same Lord will stand on a mountain in Galilee and send these same men to make disciples of all nations (28:19), and will tell them to be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8), naming the very Samaria he forbids them to enter here. The tension is real and must not be softened. But it is not a contradiction. It is a sequence.

But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. “Lost sheep” echoes 9:36: the people of Israel were like sheep without a shepherd. God had made his covenant promises to Israel, and the Messiah came first to them. Jesus said the same of his own mission (15:24). Paul’s principle was to the Jew first, and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16; Acts 13:46). And there is tenderness in it. The Twelve are sent to exactly the people over whom their Master had just been moved with compassion. This is how the mission of God always begins: not with a strategy but with a shepherd’s grief.

Why the restriction? Not because Jesus did not care about Gentiles. He has already healed a Gentile’s servant and praised his faith (8:5–13), and he will command his disciples to go to all nations (28:19). The order reflects God’s plan in history: first Israel, then the nations. The prophets pictured Israel restored first, and then the nations streaming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3; 49:6). After the resurrection, the mission goes to Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8).

Not a wall. Matthew has made sure his readers cannot mistake the restriction for a wall around God’s mercy. Gentile women stand in the Messiah’s own family tree (1:3, 5). Gentile wise men were the first to worship him while Jerusalem slept (2:1–12). He made his base in Galilee of the Gentiles (4:15). And a dozen verses later in this very chapter he tells the Twelve that they will be dragged before governors and kings to bear witness before them and the Gentiles (v. 18). The man who says go nowhere among the Gentiles in verse 5 promises a Gentile hearing in verse 18.

Three reasons for the order. First, faithfulness. The promises were made to Israel: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the patriarchs, and from them the Christ (Romans 9:4–5). God does not move his mercy to the nations before he has kept his word to the people he swore it to. The Son of David comes to David’s house first and knocks on his own door. Second, the message. The kingdom of heaven is at hand presumes a throne, a covenant, a promised son of David and centuries of prophets crying that the King is coming. Said in a Galilean village, everyone knew what was being claimed; said in a pagan market town, it would have meant nothing yet. And entering Samaritan towns would have dragged the Twelve straight into the old quarrel over Gerizim and Jerusalem. Third, and deepest, the cross. The Gentile mission cannot begin until what makes it possible has happened. At this hour the Gentiles are still strangers to the covenants of promise (Ephesians 2:12), and what tears down the dividing wall is not a change of policy but a cross. That is why the Great Commission begins: all authority has been given to me; go therefore (28:18–19). Matthew 10 stands on this side of Calvary; Matthew 28 stands on the other.

The door shut so that it could be opened. For every reader who is not a son of Abraham by birth, here is the wonder. Had the Twelve gone to the nations that summer, they would have carried a kingdom announcement with no cross in it and no atonement behind it. Instead the Lord kept them home, walked to Jerusalem, and did the work that alone could bring a Gentile near: in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). The Twelve were not sent to you that day so that a Saviour could be purchased for you on a later one. And the same Shepherd said before long that he had other sheep, not of this fold, whom he must also bring (John 10:16). He always meant to come for you. He simply had to go to the cross first.

What it does not mean. Not that this restriction applies to the church today. It was for this first mission. The Great Commission sends the church to all nations (28:19–20). Nor does “lost” here mean that every Israelite was unsaved; it describes the nation as scattered and neglected by its leaders, needing its Shepherd.

Should Christians share the gospel with Jewish people today? Yes, with love, humility and respect. The gospel is still the power of God for salvation to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16), and the apostles, all of them Jews, preached Jesus as Israel’s Messiah in synagogue after synagogue. Christians must never be arrogant towards Jewish people, and must reckon honestly with the long, shameful history of Christian hostility towards them (Romans 11:18–20). But it would be no kindness to keep from Abraham’s children the news that their Messiah has come. Christians hold different views about God’s plans for the Jewish people in the future; all agree that today, Jew and Gentile alike, salvation is found in Jesus alone (Acts 4:12).

In a sentence. On their first mission, the Twelve were sent only to Israel’s lost sheep, because God’s plan was to come to Israel first and then to the nations.

On a Tuesday. God works in order and in his time. Trust his plan when you do not yet see why one door is open and another closed. If you are not Jewish, thank God today that the door once shut was flung open for you by Christ’s blood. And ask where your own nearest lost sheep are: the people already within reach of your voice, whom God may mean you to reach before you think of anywhere further away.

For worship. The Lord keeps his promises in order. He went first to the people he had sworn to, and was rejected, and was lifted up outside their city, and by that very rejection became the Saviour of the world. The command that once kept the nations waiting is the command that secured their welcome. Glory to the faithful God, who kept his word to Abraham, and through Abraham’s Son has blessed all the families of the earth.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans lived between Judea and Galilee, a people of mixed descent who worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. The mission to the nations would come after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: the lost sheep of the house of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: And proclaim as you go, saying, "The kingdom of heaven is at hand." Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message and the work: proclaim that the kingdom of heaven has come near; heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received freely; give freely.

And proclaim as you go. The disciples were heralds (see 3:1). A herald does not invent his message or improve it. He carries it, loudly and accurately, from the king to the people.

The kingdom of heaven is at hand. The same message as John (3:2) and Jesus (4:17). God’s reign has arrived in Jesus. The disciples do not advance an agenda of their own; they extend his.

Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. Exactly what Jesus did in chapters 8–9. The disciples’ works were signs that confirmed their message: the kingdom is here, and its power is driving back sickness, death and evil. Raise the dead: it is an extraordinary thing to hand to twelve men who have shown no aptitude for anything so far, and only Matthew records it in the charge. The commission is not modest. And the list is not a general description of good works. It is a summary of the previous two chapters: a leper in 8:3, demons at Gadara, a ruler’s daughter raised in chapter 9. It is Matthew’s way of saying that the mission of the church is not an idea about Jesus but a continuation of him.

You received without paying; give without pay. They had received authority and the message freely from Jesus. They must not charge for it. In the ancient world, wandering philosophers and miracle-workers often made money from their teaching and healing. Jesus’ messengers must not. Simon the magician later tried to buy the power of the Spirit, and Peter rebuked him severely (Acts 8:18–24). Grace freely received must be freely given. The Greek word behind both halves is dōrean: as a gift, for nothing. What the messenger carries was obtained by nobody, and cost its owner everything.

A worker may be supported; a gift may not be sold. The command has sometimes been used to argue that ministers should not be paid at all. It cannot bear that, and the proof is in the very next sentence: the labourer deserves his food (v. 10). What is forbidden is not receiving bread from those you serve. It is charging admission: attaching a price to the thing itself, so that the sick are healed and the good news is preached in proportion to what somebody can pay. The moment the kingdom has a tariff, it has stopped being the kingdom.

What it does not mean. Not that those who preach the gospel may not be supported by others. Jesus immediately says the worker deserves his food (v. 10), and Paul defends the right of ministers to be paid (1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18). The point is that the gospel is never sold, and ministry is not done for money. Nor does the command to heal and raise the dead mean that every Christian today has these powers. These were special signs given to the apostles to confirm the message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4).

Where Christians differ: is this commission to heal and raise the dead for the church today? Continuationist Christians believe it is, at least in part, and point to Mark 16:17–18 and James 5:14–15, and to the absence of any text saying such gifts would end. Cessationist Christians hold that these powers were signs given to the Twelve, and to those closely linked with them, to confirm their message at the founding of the church. Verdict: the cessationist reading is the more likely. The signs are called the signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12), and Hebrews speaks of God bearing witness to the message by signs and wonders through those who first heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3–4). The church still prays for the sick, and God still heals in answer; but no one today holds the apostles’ authority to raise the dead or cleanse lepers at a word. This is a difference among godly Christians, to be held charitably.

So may churches charge for anything? They may cover costs honestly: a book costs money to print and a conference hall costs money to hire, and the worker deserves his wages. But some things must never carry a price: the preaching of the gospel, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, prayer, pastoral care, a welcome to the poor. Beware anyone who links God’s blessing to your giving, who promises healing or prosperity in return for a gift, or who treats the needy as less welcome than the wealthy. And in your own service, ask whether you would still do it if nobody paid you or thanked you. That is what freely given means.

In a sentence. The apostles were to announce the kingdom and show its power in works of healing, freely giving what they had freely received.

On a Tuesday. What have you freely received from God: forgiveness, grace, gifts, time? Give freely to others today, without expecting anything back. Choose one act of service this week for which you will get no credit and no return: help someone who cannot repay you, give time to someone who cannot advance you, forgive someone who has not earned it. That is the economy of the kingdom.

For worship. Everything we have from God came to us free, and none of it was cheap. The forgiveness we did not pay for, he paid for with his blood; the Spirit we did not buy, he poured out as a gift; the kingdom we could never earn, he gives to beggars. The King of glory runs a kingdom with no tariff and no admission charge, because he himself paid the whole price. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift (2 Corinthians 9:15).

parallels.desc: what I have I give you

verseByVerse.quote: Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts, no bag for your journey, or two tunics or sandals or a staff, for the laborer deserves his food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not take money, a travel bag, spare clothing, sandals or a staff. Travel light, and depend on God to provide through the people you serve: a worker deserves his food.

Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts. Coins were often carried in the folds of a cloth belt. Gold, silver and copper: no money at all.

No bag for your journey. A traveller’s bag for food and supplies, or possibly a beggar’s bag for collecting gifts. They were not to beg.

Or two tunics or sandals or a staff. No spare clothes, no extra sandals, no walking stick. (Mark says they could take a staff and sandals, Mark 6:8–9. The difference may be that Matthew means do not acquire additional ones, and Mark means take the ones you have.)

Matthew and Mark together. This is one of the most frequently cited contradictions in the Gospels, and it dissolves when the verbs are compared. Matthew’s word is not take but acquire: do not procure, do not get hold of. Mark’s is take: do not carry anything extra. Put them together and the sense is plain and consistent: do not go out and equip yourselves for this journey. Do not buy a staff for the road or a second pair of sandals for the wear; go as you stand, with the stick already in your hand and the sandals already on your feet. Every traveller in that country owned a staff and wore sandals; neither writer is discussing whether a man may walk shod. Both forbid the same thing, which is provisioning. Between them they describe one scene: twelve men leaving town with nothing in their hands but what they already had, and no visible means of getting home.

For the laborer deserves his food. Those who receive the gospel should support those who bring it. The disciples were to trust God to provide through hospitality. Paul quotes the same principle (1 Timothy 5:18). The support of gospel workers is not charity; it is what is owed.

The point. The mission was urgent, and the disciples needed to learn to depend on God. Travelling light also distinguished them from the travelling teachers who made money from their audiences. The worker who arrives with nothing shows that the kingdom has sent him; his survival is his master’s responsibility.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries. At the Last Supper, Jesus told the disciples that from then on they should take a moneybag and a knapsack (Luke 22:35–36). Conditions changed. But the principles remain: simplicity, urgency, dependence on God, and the duty of God’s people to support those who serve them with the gospel.

Should missionaries today raise support or earn their own living? Either can be right. Paul defended the right of gospel workers to be supported (1 Corinthians 9:14), and gladly received gifts from the Philippians (Philippians 4:15–18); yet he often worked with his hands as a tentmaker so as to be no burden and to set an example (Acts 18:3; 2 Thessalonians 3:8–9). What matters is that the worker depends on God whichever way the bread arrives, that the gospel is never sold, and that churches take seriously their duty to provide for those they send. If you support a missionary, you are not doing him a favour. You are a partner in his work.

In a sentence. The apostles were to travel light and depend on God’s provision through those who received them, since a worker deserves his food.

On a Tuesday. Do you support those who teach you God’s word (Galatians 6:6)? And what could you let go of to travel lighter in following Christ? Look at what you are carrying: possessions, commitments, worries about provision. Which of them would you be unable to put down if he asked? Then give, regularly and generously, to the people who bring you the word and to those your church has sent.

For worship. The Lord who sent his apostles with empty hands fed every one of them. When he asked them later whether they had lacked anything, they said, nothing (Luke 22:35). He owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10), and he has never sent a servant out and failed to provide for him. He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, will he not also with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32)?
verseByVerse.note: Coins were carried in the belt. The “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies.

parallels.desc: those who proclaim the gospel get their living by it

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it and stay there until you depart. As you enter the house, greet it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In each town, find someone worthy and stay with them until you leave. When you enter a house, greet it.

Find out who is worthy in it. “Worthy” here means a person open to the message, ready to welcome God’s messengers: someone like the “son of peace” in Luke 10:6. Not morally perfect, but receptive. The word (axios) runs through this paragraph four times: the labourer is worthy of his food; find who is worthy; if the house is worthy; if it is not worthy. And the definition is entirely practical. A worthy house is one that opens its door. There is no moral audit, no enquiry into the family’s reputation. Which is a mercy, since the alternative would have required twelve men with no local knowledge to assess the character of strangers in towns they had never entered.

And stay there until you depart. Do not move from house to house looking for better hospitality. Be content and avoid giving offence. The instruction is more pointed than it looks. The ancient world was full of travelling teachers, and they had a reputation: begin with whoever offers, and if a wealthier patron appears with a better table, move up. A Christian handbook from the following century, the Didache, warns that a travelling prophet who stays three days, or who asks for money, is a false prophet. Jesus forecloses the whole business in one clause. The first door that opens is the one you use.

As you enter the house, greet it. The normal greeting was Shalom, “peace” (Luke 10:5). From Jesus’ messengers, it was more than a polite word: it was a blessing, offering the peace of the kingdom. In that culture a greeting was understood to convey something, not merely to wish it.

What it does not mean. Not that only respectable or good people are “worthy” of the gospel. Jesus ate with sinners (9:10). Worthiness here is openness, not merit.

How can I show hospitality if my home is small or I live alone? Hospitality is not about the size of the house or the quality of the food. It is about an open door and an open heart. A bowl of soup at a kitchen table, a spare sofa for a visiting student, a cup of tea with a new family after church: these are hospitality in the New Testament sense (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9). If your home really cannot be opened, open your time instead: take someone out for coffee, give a lift, invite yourself to help in someone else’s home. The point is to receive Christ’s people as you would receive him.

In a sentence. The apostles were to stay with those who welcomed them and bring the blessing of peace to each household.

On a Tuesday. Hospitality to Christian workers is a ministry. Could you open your home to a missionary, a visiting preacher or a new believer? And when you are the guest, learn from these instructions: be content with what you are given, do not shop around for better treatment, and bring a blessing into the house rather than only taking one out.

For worship. The Prince of Peace sends his peace into ordinary houses, carried by men with dusty feet. He was himself a guest in many homes, and he has made his people a household where the door is open to the stranger. And one day he will receive us into his Father’s house, where he has prepared a place, and we will never again need to ask whether we are welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it, but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a house welcomes you, let your peace rest on it; if not, let your peace return to you. If a town or house rejects you and your message, shake its dust off your feet as you leave.

If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it. The blessing of peace comes on those who receive it. Peace here is the shalom of the kingdom: God’s blessing and salvation, the wholeness that comes with the arrival of God’s rule.

But if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. If they reject it, the blessing does not take effect on them. It is not wasted, but it is withdrawn. Jesus speaks of peace almost as a substance: it can come to rest on a house, or come back, undamaged, into the messenger’s hands, to be given somewhere else. That is worth having for anyone who has spoken about Christ to somebody who did not want it. Nothing was wasted and nothing was lost. It came back.

And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words. Rejection of the messengers and of their message. The condition is stated precisely: refusal to hear, not slowness to agree.

Shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town. Strict Jews returning from Gentile lands would shake off the dust from their feet, so as not to bring unclean soil into the holy land. For the disciples to do this to a Jewish town was a startling symbolic act: it declared that the town, by rejecting the Messiah, had made itself like a pagan land, and that the messengers were no longer responsible for it. Paul and Barnabas did exactly this at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51). It was a verdict delivered in mime: this place has put itself outside. And everybody who saw it would have understood it at once.

What it does not mean. Not an act of personal anger or contempt. It was a solemn warning, done with sorrow, leaving the town to God. Nor does it mean that Christians should give up quickly on people. The disciples’ mission was urgent and their time short; in ordinary life, Christians often keep loving and praying for those who reject the gospel for many years.

The freedom in it. The gesture is also a release. The messenger is not responsible for the result. He carries a message and offers a peace; if the door shuts, he shakes his feet at the gate and walks to the next town without dragging the failure along the road behind him. There is a great deal of freedom in that for anyone who has lain awake over somebody who would not listen. The loss, the gesture says, is entirely on the other side of the door.

When should I stop sharing the gospel with someone? Rarely, and never stop loving or praying. The apostles were on a short, urgent tour, and Jesus told them not to linger where the door was shut. In ordinary life, most of us live alongside the same people for years, and many come to faith slowly. But there is wisdom in knowing when to stop pressing. If someone has heard the gospel clearly and asks you not to raise it again, respect that, keep living it in front of them, keep praying, and be ready when they ask (1 Peter 3:15). Do not throw what is holy before those who only mock it (7:6). And remember that God can open a door you have no strength left to knock on.

In a sentence. Those who receive the messengers receive peace; those who reject them are solemnly left to God.

On a Tuesday. When someone rejects the gospel, you are not responsible for their response, only for your faithfulness. Leave the results to God. If there is someone whose rejection you have been carrying as your own failure, hand it back to God in prayer today, and ask him for the next person who might listen.

For worship. The Lord’s peace is never wasted. It rests where it is welcomed and returns to the hand that offered it, and it can never be used up. He offered himself to his own, and his own did not receive him, and he was not diminished by their refusal. To all who did receive him, he gave the right to become children of God (John 1:12). His is the peace that the world cannot give and cannot take away.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: Paul and Barnabas shake off the dust

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warned that on the day of judgment it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah than for a town that rejects his messengers.

Truly, I say to you. A solemn statement of Jesus’ authority (see 5:18).

It will be more bearable on the day of judgment. There are degrees of judgment. All who reject God face judgment, but not all equally (11:22–24; Luke 12:47–48). Scripture nowhere teaches that the lost are all in the same condition. There are degrees, and they follow the light each person received. Whatever else the judgement will be, it will be meticulous. God does not sweep humanity into two undifferentiated heaps; every case is weighed on exactly what that person had.

For the land of Sodom and Gomorrah. Cities destroyed by fire from heaven for their great wickedness, including violence, pride, sexual immorality and neglect of the poor (Genesis 18–19; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Jude 7). They became a byword for God’s judgment. Ezekiel’s summary is often a surprise: Sodom had pride, excess of food and prosperous ease, and did not help the poor and needy (Ezekiel 16:49). Genesis records the assault on the visitors, and it was real and wicked; but Ezekiel puts the arrogant, well-fed indifference first. The byword for judgement turns out to describe something rather close to a prosperous modern town, which is worth knowing before the name is used as a weapon against others.

Than for that town. A shocking comparison for Jewish hearers. Sodom was the worst example of a wicked city. Yet a town in Israel that rejects the Messiah’s messengers will face worse judgment. Why? Because greater light brings greater responsibility. Sodom never heard the gospel or saw the Messiah’s works. To reject him with full knowledge is a greater sin.

What it does not mean. Not that Sodom will escape judgment. Nor that sexual sin does not matter. The point is that rejecting Christ, with knowledge, is the most serious sin of all (John 3:18–19; Hebrews 10:26–29).

Who is most in danger from this verse? Not the people who never heard. The ones who have heard often, and well, and can predict the sermon, and have arranged their lives so that nothing in it ever has to be acted on. The principle cuts towards the religious reader, not away from him.

What about those who never heard the gospel? They are judged by the light they had, not by light they never received, and the judgement will be perfectly fair. But Scripture is clear that all have sinned against the light of creation and conscience and are without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:12–15), and that salvation is found only through faith in Christ (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). That is why Paul asks how they can believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14), and why the church sends missionaries. The right response to the question is not speculation but prayer, giving and going.
