(Infants who die in infancy, who cannot hear or understand, are in a different case: the elect among them are saved by Christ through the Spirit, Westminster 10.3.)

In a sentence. Those who reject Christ’s messengers, having heard the gospel, will face a heavier judgment than even Sodom.

On a Tuesday. You have heard the gospel more clearly than most people in history. Greater privilege brings greater responsibility. Do not treat it lightly. Think of the sermons you have heard and the Bibles you own. Is there one thing God has made plain to you that you have been arranging your life to avoid? Act on it this week, while it is still called today.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25). He weighs every soul with perfect justice, and no one will be punished for more than he knew or less than he deserved. And this same Judge sent his messengers to warn the towns before the day came, and then went himself to bear the judgement of all who would believe. Fire fell on Sodom; on Calvary the fire of God’s wrath fell on his Son, so that those who flee to him will never feel it. Justice and mercy have met in him.

parallels.desc: the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–42 — Persecution, Confession, and the Cross: The Cost of the Mission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of the mission discourse turns from method to cost. Jesus warns the disciples of coming persecution — before synagogues, governors, and kings — and promises the Spirit's help in that moment. He sets family divisions as the expected consequence of his mission and demands that disciples value him above father, mother, son, and daughter. The section culminates in the cross-bearing saying and the principle that whoever loses their life for Jesus will find it. Four things more. The backbone of vv. 26-31 is three "do not fear" commands, each with a different ground: because everything hidden will come out (v. 26), because there is a worse thing than dying (v. 28), because you are valued (v. 31) — the fear of being misrepresented, of being killed, and of being insignificant, each answered with a fact rather than an exhortation. On v. 28, the one to be feared is God, not Satan (who has no such authority, and cf. Lk. 12:5) — and the strangeness of hearing that beside "your Father" attends to sparrows is the point, not a problem. gehenna is a place name: the Valley of Hinnom, where children were burned to Molech until Josiah defiled the site (2 Kgs. 23:10; Jer. 7:31). The sparrow arithmetic is exact — two for a penny here, but five for two pennies in Luke 12:6, so the fifth was the makeweight thrown in free; and Luke's promise is that not one of them is forgotten. And vv. 29-31 need a guard, because they read like a promise of safety and cannot be: the sparrow falls, and by early tradition many of the men hearing this died violent deaths. The promise is not that the worst will not happen but that it will not happen unnoticed. Note too that v. 38 is the first mention of a cross in Matthew — and it comes six chapters before Jesus says anything about his own death (16:21), so the twelve heard it with no idea their master would die on one. Varus had crucified two thousand Jews within living memory; the image is the walk, carrying the beam past everyone you know. And "not peace but a sword" is glossed by Luke as division (Lk. 12:51) — while the Micah 7:6 Jesus quotes was a standard description of the birth-pangs of the messianic age, and its very next verse is "but as for me, I will look to the LORD".
verseByVerse.theology: The persecution discourse is not pessimism but realism: "a disciple is not above his teacher." Jesus himself will be persecuted; his followers will share his fate. The Spirit's provision in persecution is specific — not general spiritual support but particular words at the moment of trial. This is the promise that has sustained Christian martyrs across every century: the one who sends into danger is the one who speaks in danger. The fearlessness Jesus commands is grounded not in courage but in theology: God knows, God values, God reigns.
verseByVerse.examples: The cross-bearing saying (v. 38) appears here before the crucifixion — Jesus uses the cross as a metaphor before it is a fact. Every disciple must take up their own cross, not his. This is the death of the self-directed life: a public alignment with a man under sentence, at the cost of respectability and safety alike. The paradox of verses 39 is the deepest saying in the chapter: the one who clutches their life loses it; the one who surrenders it for Jesus finds it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. So be shrewd as snakes and innocent as doves. Be on your guard: people will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues.

The wider horizon. From verse 16 onward, Jesus looks beyond the first short mission to the whole future mission of the church: governors, kings, Gentiles, and persecution until he returns (vv. 18, 22–23). Much of this did not happen on the first mission, but it happened in Acts and has happened ever since.

Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves. Sheep are defenceless; wolves are predators. The disciples will be vulnerable in a hostile world. But note: “I am sending you”. Jesus knows exactly where he is sending them, and he is the Shepherd (9:36). The image is not of eventual triumph but of immediate vulnerability. He does not promise that his messengers will be safe. He promises that they are sent, and that the one who sends them is the Shepherd of the sheep.

So be wise as serpents. Snakes were proverbially shrewd and cautious (Genesis 3:1). Disciples must be wise, prudent and alert: not naive, not taking unnecessary risks, not provoking needless trouble.

And innocent as doves. “Innocent” (akeraioi) means pure, unmixed, without guile. Doves were proverbially gentle and harmless. Wisdom without innocence becomes cunning; innocence without wisdom becomes foolishness. Disciples need both.

What the wisdom looks like. Christians are sometimes taught to be suspicious of shrewdness, as though it were a failure of faith. It is not. Jesus declined to answer Herod at all (Luke 23:9), slipped away from crowds intending to seize him, and told these very men to flee from one town to the next under persecution (v. 23). Paul let himself be lowered over a wall in a basket (Acts 9:25) and used his Roman citizenship as a legal shield more than once (Acts 22:25; 25:11). So wisdom looks like this: do not be provocative about things that do not matter; do not hand opponents ammunition they have not earned; know when to speak and when to be silent; be careful what you put in writing; answer the question actually asked; and where the law protects you, use it without embarrassment.

What the innocence guards. The danger of shrewdness is that it curdles into cunning: the half-truth, the quiet manipulation, the small deceit that seems justified because the other side is fighting dirty. The dove forbids it absolutely. You may be as careful as you like about how you speak; you may not lie, spin, flatter or scheme. Wisdom chooses the moment; innocence keeps the hands clean while doing it. Held apart, each fails. Doves without serpents get needlessly destroyed and call it faithfulness: the Christian who picks avoidable fights and mistakes the damage for a cross. Serpents without doves survive every encounter, win most arguments, and lose the thing they were sent to carry. Jesus asks for both at once, in the same person, on the same afternoon.

Beware of men. Do not trust people naively. Opposition will come from people, including religious people. Jesus knew what was in man (John 2:25), and he tells his friends the truth before he sends them.

For they will deliver you over to courts. “Courts” is synedria, local Jewish councils (the word is related to Sanhedrin).

And flog you in their synagogues. Synagogues had authority to discipline Jews by flogging. The law allowed forty lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3), and the practice was thirty-nine, to avoid exceeding the limit. Paul received this five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should be suspicious of everyone, or that all opposition is persecution for righteousness. “Wise as serpents” includes not bringing trouble on ourselves by foolishness or rudeness. Nor does it permit deceit: the dove’s innocence rules out lies and trickery.

In a sentence. Jesus sends his disciples like defenceless sheep among wolves, so they must be wise and pure, and ready for opposition even from religious authorities.

On a Tuesday. Where do you need more wisdom in your witness, and where do you need more innocence? Ask God for both. Most of us lean one way by temperament. If you are naturally blunt, ask before your next difficult conversation whether this is the moment and the manner. If you are naturally careful, ask whether your caution has slid into evasion or flattery. Then pray James 1:5 and expect an answer.

For worship. The Good Shepherd sends his sheep among wolves, and never once forgets where he has sent them. He was himself the Lamb led to the slaughter, wise enough that his enemies could not trap him in his words, and so innocent that the judge who condemned him could find no fault in him. He was harmless, undefiled, separated from sinners (Hebrews 7:26). What he asks of us he first was for us, and the wolves who surrounded him could not prevent his rising.
verseByVerse.note: Synagogues had the authority to flog; the law allowed up to forty lashes, kept to thirty-nine in practice.

parallels.desc: five times the forty lashes less one

verseByVerse.quote: and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be dragged before governors and kings because of me, to bear witness to them and to the nations. When you are arrested, do not worry about what to say, because you will be given the words at that moment.

And you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake. Governors were Roman officials, like Pilate, Felix and Festus; kings were client rulers, like Herod Agrippa. Paul stood before all of these (Acts 23–26). Peter and John stood before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4–5). James was executed by Herod (Acts 12:2). Every category in this sentence was filled within thirty years, by the Twelve and by Paul, and finally Paul appealed to Caesar himself.

To bear witness before them and the Gentiles. Persecution becomes an opportunity for witness. The trial room becomes a pulpit. Paul preached to governors and kings because he was arrested (Acts 26:1–29). Here the Gentiles are mentioned: the mission will reach beyond Israel. They are forbidden to go to the Gentiles in verse 5 and told in verse 18 that they will be dragged to them. That is how it actually worked. The gospel did not reach the empire because a committee planned it. It reached the empire because Christians were arrested. Paul wrote several of his letters from custody, and the man who wanted to go to Spain arrived in Rome in chains at the government’s expense.

When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say. “Anxious” is the same word as in 6:25–34. Jesus forbids worry about a trial, as he forbade worry about food. Do not be anxious about your life, about tomorrow, and now about your defence.

For what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. God will provide the words when they are needed, as he provided for Moses (Exodus 4:12). Stephen spoke with such wisdom that his opponents could not resist it (Acts 6:10). Notice the shape of the promise. He does not promise they will be spared the trial, or acquitted. He promises that when the moment comes there will be something to say, which is precisely the fear, since what frightens most people about that scene is not the sentence but standing there with nothing in their mouth.

What it does not mean. Not that preachers do not need to prepare sermons. This is a promise for those suddenly put on trial for their faith, not an excuse for laziness in teaching. Paul urged Timothy to study and work hard at teaching (2 Timothy 2:15). Nor is it a promise of acquittal: Stephen spoke well and was killed (Acts 7). It is a promise for the dock, not the pulpit: it says nothing to a preacher who did not prepare, and everything to a Christian summoned without warning to answer for his faith.

What if I go blank when someone challenges my faith? It happens to most of us, and it is not a sign that God has left you. The promise here is first for the hour of real persecution, but the Father who gives words in a courtroom does not forget his children in a staffroom. Do what you can beforehand: know your Bible, be able to say simply what Christ has done for you, and think through the questions you are most often asked (1 Peter 3:15). Then in the moment pray silently, say what you know, and do not be afraid to say, I don’t know, but I will find out. Faithfulness is not eloquence.

In a sentence. Persecution will bring disciples before rulers as witnesses, and they need not worry about what to say, because God will give them the words.

On a Tuesday. If you are anxious about speaking of Christ in a hostile situation, pray, and trust him to help you in that moment. Think of the conversation you dread most, at work, in your family, online. Commit it to God today, and ask him to turn it into an opportunity to bear witness, as he turned Paul’s chains into a pulpit.

For worship. Our Lord stood before a governor and a king and made the good confession (1 Timothy 6:13). He was condemned so that his people, standing in the same kind of dock, might never stand alone. The God who makes the mouth gives the words (Exodus 4:11–12), and the plots of rulers against his Anointed end only in spreading his name to the ends of the earth. He sits in the heavens and laughs at their schemes (Psalm 2:4), and turns every prison into a pulpit.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death,
verseByVerse.commentary:
It will not be you speaking but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. Persecution will divide families: brother will betray brother to death, a father his child, and children their parents.

For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. The Holy Spirit will speak through them. This is the first mention of the Spirit in Matthew since 4:1. “The Spirit of your Father”: the same Father who cares for sparrows (v. 29) gives his Spirit to his persecuted children. The exact phrase occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and the wording is doing pastoral work. Jesus does not simply say the Spirit will speak, which would be true and cold. He says the Spirit of your Father. The one who supplies the words in the courtroom is named by his relation to them, and the relation is family. A man on trial for his life is being told that his Father will do the talking.

Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child. The gospel will divide families. In the early church, converts from Judaism or paganism were sometimes disowned, reported to authorities, or killed by their own families. This still happens today in many parts of the world. Micah 7:6 had described a time of such social breakdown (quoted in vv. 35–36).

And it happened. Not as a figure of speech. Roman justice ran on informers: accusation was a private matter, and there were rewards for it. The earliest surviving outside account of Christian persecution, the letter of Pliny to the emperor Trajan about AD 112, describes a stream of anonymous accusations naming Christians in his province. Somebody was writing those lists, and in a household the people who knew were relatives. The order of the discourse matters. Jesus warns of councils and floggings first, then governors and kings: public, formal, at the hands of strangers. And then, at the end of the escalation, he names the thing that is worse.

And children will rise against parents and have them put to death. The deepest bonds of human life will be broken by hatred of Christ. He does not soften it, and he does not promise it will not happen. He says it in advance, to men who had families, so that when it came they would know he had seen it coming and had not thought it too high a price.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should expect or provoke family division. The gospel brings peace to many families. But when family members reject Christ, loyalty to him may bring painful division.

How should I pray for persecuted Christians? Specifically and regularly, as for members of your own body, because they are (Hebrews 13:3). Pray that they will stand firm and not deny Christ; that the Spirit will give them words when they are questioned; that their families will be won rather than lost; that their persecutors will be converted, as Saul was; and that governments will allow them to live peaceful and quiet lives (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Find out about one country where Christians suffer and learn the names of a few believers there. Give to help them if you can. And let their courage shame our comfortable silence.

In a sentence. The Spirit will speak through persecuted disciples, even when their own families turn against them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for believers today who have been rejected or endangered by their families because of Christ, especially converts from other religions. And if your own family is merely cool towards your faith, thank God for the freedom you have, and use it.

For worship. The Father does not abandon his children in the dock. His Spirit speaks in them and for them, and when their earthly fathers turn against them, their Father in heaven claims them as his own. The Son was betrayed by one of his own household, and sold for silver, and he did not curse the betrayer. And when father and mother forsake me, the LORD will take me in (Psalm 27:10). That is a promise kept ten thousand times in the history of the church.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: and you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be hated by everyone because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. When you are persecuted in one town, flee to the next. You will not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.

And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. “All” means people of every kind, not literally every individual. “For my name’s sake”: because you belong to Jesus. The world hated him first (John 15:18–20). The scope is wide and the cause is specific: it is the name of Jesus that provokes the hatred, not the disciples’ personalities or methods.

But the one who endures to the end will be saved. “Endure” means to remain, to persevere, to hold on under pressure. “To the end” may mean to the end of one’s life, or to the end of the age. True faith perseveres. Those who fall away under persecution show that their faith was not genuine (13:20–21; 1 John 2:19).

When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. Fleeing persecution is not cowardice. The disciples are not to seek martyrdom, but to keep spreading the message. Persecution in Jerusalem scattered the church and spread the gospel (Acts 8:1–4). Martyrdom is not to be sought, and the next town still needs the gospel.

For truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. A difficult verse, and it must be faced honestly, because sceptics have made much of it. Albert Schweitzer built a whole portrait of Jesus on it: here, he claimed, Jesus predicted the end of the world within his disciples’ lifetime and was simply wrong. If that were the meaning, it would be a failed prophecy. But the key is the phrase the Son of Man comes. It is drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where the Son of Man comes not down to earth but up to the Ancient of Days, to be enthroned and given a kingdom. It speaks of his vindication and reign, and need not mean his final return at all.

Where Christians differ: which coming of the Son of Man is meant? There are three main views. 1. The resurrection and ascension. The Son of Man “comes” in vindication when he is raised and receives all authority (28:18; Daniel 7:13–14). 2. The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. A coming in judgment on the nation that rejected him (24:30, 34). 3. The second coming. The mission to Israel will continue until Christ returns at the end of the age; it will never be finished. Verdict: most likely the coming in judgment in AD 70 (view 2), within the generation of the disciples, as Jesus says in 16:28 and 24:34, though this event itself foreshadows the final coming. On any view, the point is: the mission to Israel is urgent, and it will not be complete before the Son of Man acts.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by endurance. Endurance is the evidence and fruit of true faith, and God himself gives it. Those whom God has saved, he will keep to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). This is the doctrine called the perseverance of the saints (Westminster 17). The warning and the promise belong together: God keeps his people precisely by moving them to persevere. Nor does Jesus’ word mean that he was mistaken about the timing of his return. It refers to a coming in his own generation.

If I must endure to the end, can I lose my salvation? No one whom God has truly saved will finally be lost. Jesus says of his sheep that no one will snatch them out of his hand or his Father’s (John 10:28–29), and Paul is sure that he who began a good work will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). But the way God keeps us is not by letting us coast; it is by working in us to keep believing, keep repenting and keep following. So the warning is real, and it is one of the means by which he keeps us. A believer may fall badly and for a time, as Peter did, but he will be brought back. If you are afraid of falling away, run to Christ with that fear. The fear itself is not the mark of the lost, who are untroubled; it is the Spirit stirring you to hold on.

In a sentence. Disciples will be hated for Christ’s name, but those who persevere to the end will be saved; they should flee persecution and keep spreading the message.

On a Tuesday. Endurance is built day by day. What is one small act of faithfulness you can do today to keep going? Read a chapter of Scripture when you do not feel like it; go to church when you are tired; confess the same sin again rather than hiding it; keep the promise you made. Perseverance is mostly made of ordinary days kept faithfully.

For worship. The Shepherd who sends his sheep among wolves also guarantees that he will bring them home. Not one whom the Father has given him will be lost (John 6:39). He endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and he who endured to the end for us is the one who keeps us to the end. Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before his glory with great joy, be glory and majesty, dominion and authority, for ever (Jude 24–25).

parallels.desc: the one who endures to the end

verseByVerse.quote: A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for a disciple to be treated like his teacher. If they called the head of the house Beelzebul, they will say even worse about the members of his household.

A disciple is not above his teacher. A proverb. Students do not expect better treatment than their teacher.

It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher. If Jesus was rejected and persecuted, his disciples should expect the same. Being like him is honour enough (John 15:20). It is a sufficient destiny, even a dignified one, to share the reception of one’s Lord.

If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul. The Pharisees had accused Jesus of casting out demons by the prince of demons (9:34; 12:24). “Beelzebul” was a name for Satan, perhaps meaning “lord of the dwelling” (which fits “master of the house”), or a form of Baal-zebub, meaning lord of the flies, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2). They called Jesus the devil.

A grim pun. The element zebul means an exalted dwelling, a lofty house, so Baal-zebul is something like lord of the house; Israelite writers seem to have enjoyed twisting it into Baal-zebub, lord of the flies, as an insult to a neighbouring god. Now read the verse with that in hand. The word for master of the house is oikodespotēs; the word for his household is oikiakoi. And the name they threw at him already meant, in its own language, house-lord. So the sentence runs: if they have called the head of the house the devil’s lord of the house, what will they call the servants? It is a grim joke, made by a man explaining to his friends that the worst thing anyone has said about him is going to be said about them.

How much more will they malign those of his household. If they insulted the head of the house, they will insult his family.

A ceiling and a floor. The proverb is usually quoted as a warning against arrogance, and it does that job. Here it is doing another. The natural reading of being slandered for one’s faith is that something has gone wrong, that a better Christian would have been better received. This verse removes that. The measure of a good disciple is not a better reception than the master got; it is the same reception. That sets a ceiling on the ambition and a floor under the discouragement. Nobody should expect the world to think better of him than it thought of Christ. And nobody who is thought badly of for Christ’s sake should conclude that he has failed.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should expect only rejection. Some will receive them (vv. 11, 40–42). But they must not be surprised when they are treated as their Lord was (1 Peter 4:12–14).

In a sentence. If the world called Jesus the devil, his disciples must expect similar treatment, and count it an honour to share his lot.

On a Tuesday. When you are misrepresented for your faith, remember what they said about your Master. You are in good company. Before you take it to heart, ask honestly whether it is for Christ or for your own folly (1 Peter 4:15). If it is for Christ, do not retaliate and do not despair. Rejoice, as the apostles did, that you were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

For worship. The Master of the house was called the prince of demons by the men he came to save, and he bore it in silence. He who is the radiance of the Father’s glory was named after the lord of the flies. He did not count it beneath him to be insulted for us, and he counts it an honour to share his name with those who are insulted for him. Blessed are you when others revile you on my account, for your reward is great in heaven (5:11–12).
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

parallels.desc: a servant is not greater than his master

verseByVerse.quote: So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. What I tell you in the dark, say in the light, and what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do not be afraid of them. Everything hidden will be revealed. What I tell you privately, speak in the light; what you hear whispered, proclaim from the rooftops.

So have no fear of them. The first of three “do not fear” commands (vv. 26, 28, 31). Fear of people is the great enemy of witness (Proverbs 29:25).

Three fears, three answers. Count them, because they are the backbone of the next six verses. Have no fear of them (v. 26), because everything hidden will come out. Do not fear those who kill the body (v. 28), because there is a worse thing than dying, and only one person controls it. Fear not, therefore (v. 31), because you are valued. Three fears: being misrepresented, being killed, being insignificant. He does not treat any of them as unreasonable, and he does not tell anyone to stop feeling them by an act of will. He answers each with a fact.

For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. The truth will come out. God will vindicate his people and expose their persecutors at the judgment. And the gospel, which now seems hidden and small, will be known by all. The verdict that matters is not the verdict of the council or the court but the verdict of the one who sees everything. The faithfulness of disciples, hidden in obscurity, and the wickedness of persecutors, disguised as respectability, will both be brought into the light.

What I tell you in the dark, say in the light. Jesus taught his disciples privately, often explaining things he did not explain to the crowds (13:10–11). After his resurrection, they must proclaim it all openly. What I tell you in the dark is not conspiracy; it is how a rabbi taught, a small circle, indoors, quietly, at the end of a day.

And what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops. Houses had flat roofs, used as public spaces. Announcements were made from rooftops, where they could be heard across the village. The gospel is not secret wisdom for a few, but public news for all. The instruction is about scale, not secrecy. The private tuition is the raw material of a public announcement, and nothing he said to them in a room was meant to stay there.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must be loud or aggressive. But they must not be silent from fear.

I am shy, and I find it very hard to speak about my faith. What should I do? Start where you are, not where the bold are. The housetop is wherever you can be heard: your kitchen table, a message to a friend, a quiet word at work. Shy believers are often the best listeners, and listening earns the right to speak. Pray for one opportunity a week, and when it comes, say one true sentence about Christ: that you go to church, that you pray, what he means to you. Ask a bolder friend to help you, and invite people to hear someone else preach. God does not need you to become someone else; he needs you not to be silent from fear. And he loves to use the weak (2 Corinthians 12:9).

In a sentence. Do not fear opponents, because the truth will be revealed; proclaim openly what Jesus taught privately.

On a Tuesday. What has Christ taught you in private, in your Bible reading and prayer, that you need to share with someone today? And notice whether your faith has become a purely private matter, deeply held and carefully never mentioned. That is the one form of Christian privacy this verse does not permit.

For worship. The day is coming when every secret will be told, and the hidden faithfulness of the least of Christ’s people will be announced before the whole creation. The Lord who taught a few fishermen in a quiet room has had his words shouted from the housetops of every nation for two thousand years. Nothing he says is lost, and nothing his people suffer for him is forgotten. He will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness, and then each one will receive his commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:5).
verseByVerse.note: Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Fear God, who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Yet that same God cares for sparrows, the cheapest of birds: not one falls to the ground apart from your Father.

And do not fear those who kill the body. The worst persecutors can do is kill the body. Jesus does not make light of it; being killed is a real and terrible thing. But it is less than what God can do.

But cannot kill the soul. The soul, the inner self, survives the death of the body. Persecutors cannot touch the believer’s relationship with God or eternal life. Here the Bible distinguishes body and soul, and teaches that the soul continues after death (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23).

Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. God. “Hell” is Gehenna (see 5:22). Fear of God is not cringing terror, but reverent awe of the one who holds final judgment. Fear of God drives out fear of people. Those who fear God fear nothing else (Isaiah 8:12–13).

Who is the one to be feared? Most readers assume God, and a minority through the centuries have argued for Satan, because it seems strange to be told to fear the Father in one breath and to trust him about sparrows in the next. The answer is God, and the reasons are decisive. The devil has no authority to destroy soul and body in hell; he is a creature under judgement himself, and nowhere in Scripture does he send anybody there. The whole passage contrasts two fears, of which the lesser is fear of men, and a warning to fear the devil would break the argument. And Jesus says it elsewhere in the plainest terms: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell; yes, I tell you, fear him (Luke 12:5). But the strangeness is real, and it is the point. The same God is named as the one to be feared above all and, in the next verse, as your Father who attends to the death of a bird. A God who were only terrible could not be loved, and a God who were only kind could not be trusted with anything that matters.

Gehenna. It is not a general word for the afterlife but a place name. The Valley of Hinnom ran along the southwest of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under Ahaz and Manasseh, until Josiah defiled the site so it could never be used for that again (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Jeremiah calls it the Valley of Slaughter. So the word carries a real ravine with a real history, the one piece of ground in Israel most associated with the destruction of the innocent, and Jesus uses it for the thing truly worth being afraid of.

Where Christians differ: does destroy mean that the lost cease to exist? Some (annihilationists, or conditionalists) take “destroy” to mean that the wicked cease to exist. But the same word is used of the lost sheep (v. 6), who are not annihilated but ruined, and Matthew uses it of wineskins that burst (9:17). Elsewhere Jesus speaks of eternal punishment (25:46), eternal fire (25:41) and unquenchable fire (3:12). Verdict: “destroy” means ruin, the loss of all that makes life life, not cessation of existence. The traditional view of hell as conscious, eternal punishment is the biblical one, which is why God is to be feared above those who can only kill the body.

Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food. A “penny” (assarion) was a small copper coin, about a sixteenth of a day’s wage. Luke says five sparrows for two pennies (Luke 12:6): buy four, and one was thrown in free. The fifth bird was the makeweight, worth nothing, not even counted in the price. And Luke’s form of the promise is that not one of them is forgotten before God. Not the four that were paid for. Not one, including the one nobody charged for.

And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. God is in control of the smallest events: the death of a sparrow. “Apart from your Father” means without his knowledge and will. This is the doctrine of providence: God governs all things, great and small (Westminster 5.1). If he governs the death of a sparrow, he governs the death of his children.

The balance. Fear God as the Judge; trust God as your Father. The same God who can destroy soul and body in hell is the Father who watches every sparrow. For those who belong to him, the fear of God becomes the foundation of confidence.

What it does not mean. Not that sparrows, or believers, never fall. They do. But they never fall outside the Father’s will. Persecution and death come, but not by accident.

If God governs everything, is he the cause of evil? No. Scripture holds two truths together. God governs all things, so that not a sparrow falls without him; and God is perfectly holy, never the author of sin, and never forces anyone to do evil (James 1:13). Those who persecute Christians are fully responsible for what they do. Yet God rules over their wickedness and turns it to his purposes, as Joseph said to his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The supreme example is the cross, where wicked men did what God’s hand had planned (Acts 4:27–28). The Westminster Confession puts it carefully: God orders all things, yet the sinfulness proceeds only from the creature (Westminster 5.4). That is why a believer can suffer injustice and still say, my times are in your hand (Psalm 31:15).

In a sentence. Fear God, not people, and trust him as your Father, who governs even the death of a sparrow.

On a Tuesday. Whose opinion do you fear most? Bring that fear to God, and let fear of him, and trust in his care, replace it. Write the name down if it helps: a boss, a parent, a group of friends, the online crowd. Then set beside it what this passage says: they can at worst kill the body, and the one who holds your soul is your Father. The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life (Proverbs 14:27).

For worship. The God who holds body and soul in his hand is the God who watches the cheapest bird in the market fall. He is so great that hell is in his power, and so tender that a sparrow does not drop to the ground without him. We fear him, and because we fear him we fear nothing else. And the Son who taught this went to Gehenna’s edge for us, bearing in body and soul the wrath we deserved, so that those who fear God might never be destroyed, and might call the Judge of all the earth their Father.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna. Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food; the “penny” was a small copper coin.

verseByVerse.quote: But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God knows even the number of hairs on your head. So do not be afraid: you are worth more than many sparrows.

But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Most people have over 100,000 hairs. God knows exactly how many. Nothing about you is too small for his attention. This is personal, detailed care. The number changes every day, nobody knows it about himself, and it seems far too trivial for heaven. Yet the Father has counted. And the tense is a perfect passive: they have been numbered and stand numbered. Not a running tally kept out of curiosity, but a completed reckoning.

Fear not, therefore. The third “do not fear” (vv. 26, 28, 31).

You are of more value than many sparrows. A gentle, almost humorous comparison: if God cares for sparrows, how much more for you, his children, made in his image and redeemed by his Son. Not merely more than two sparrows, but many. The argument moves from the known, that God cares for sparrows, to the certain: how much more for you.

The sparrow falls. Read straight, verses 29 to 31 sound like a promise of protection, and a good deal of shallow comfort has been built on them: God watches the sparrows, so nothing bad will happen to you. That is not what it says, and the context makes it impossible. The sentence before says, do not fear those who kill the body; the sentences after speak of losing your life for his sake. By early tradition many of the men being addressed died violent deaths, and James was beheaded little more than a decade later. And the sparrow saying itself says the bird falls. The promise is not that it is caught before it hits the ground; it is that it does not fall outside the Father’s knowledge and government. So the comfort on offer is not that the worst will not happen. It is that if it does, it will not have happened unnoticed, or outside his hand, or to someone he had lost track of. That is a smaller promise than the one people want, and a much stronger one than the one they usually get. A guarantee of safety would be worthless within a lifetime, since everybody dies. This one holds at the graveside.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s care guarantees freedom from suffering or death. The context is persecution, even martyrdom. But it guarantees that nothing happens by chance, and that God’s children are precious to him through all of it. Paul says nothing can separate us from God’s love, not even death (Romans 8:35–39).

The fear underneath. The logic, then, is not: you are safe, therefore fear not. It is: you are known and you are valued, therefore fear not. The fear being answered is not chiefly the fear of dying. It is the fear of dying for nothing, unremarked, with nobody keeping count. Somebody is keeping count, down to the hairs.

Then why did God let this happen to me? When suffering comes, this passage does not give us the reason, but it closes off the worst answers. It was not an accident; he was not looking the other way; you did not slip through his fingers; you are not worth less to him than you thought. Often we will not know why in this life, as Job never learned why. But we can know who: the Father who numbers your hairs, who did not spare his own Son, and who works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Bring the question to him honestly, as the psalmists did. He can bear your why, and he will hold you while you wait for the answer.

In a sentence. God knows you in every detail and values you greatly, so you need not fear.

On a Tuesday. Thank God that he knows you completely, down to the hairs of your head, and values you. When you next feel insignificant, overlooked at work, forgotten by friends, invisible in a crowd, say to yourself: my Father has counted my hairs. And when you are afraid of what might happen, remember that nothing can happen to you that he does not see and govern.

For worship. The God who names the stars and calls them all by name (Psalm 147:4) has counted the hairs on your head. He is never too great to notice us and never too busy to care. We are worth more than many sparrows, and we know exactly how much we are worth to him, because he paid for us with the blood of his Son. Our lives are hidden with Christ in God, and not one of us falls outside his hand.

parallels.desc: not one hair of his head shall fall

verseByVerse.quote: So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who openly acknowledges Jesus before people, he will acknowledge before his Father in heaven. But whoever denies him before people, he will deny before his Father.

So everyone who acknowledges me before men. “Acknowledge” (homologeō) means to confess, to declare publicly, to say the same thing. To acknowledge Jesus is to say openly that you belong to him and that he is Lord (Romans 10:9–10). Under persecution, this could cost one’s life. It is the ordinary word for a public legal declaration, and the whole discourse is set in a courtroom. The Greek construction is unusual, too, something like confess in me, as if the confession were made not only about him but from within him.

I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. At the final judgment, Jesus will say: this one is mine. Jesus presents himself as the one whose word decides our eternal destiny before God.

But whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. To deny Jesus is to disown him, to say “I do not know him”. Jesus will say the same of them: I never knew you (7:23).

Two courtrooms. The two halves of the sentence are built identically. The same verb, the same setting, the same authority. What is said in a village square in Galilee is reproduced, exactly, in the presence of God, and Jesus casts himself as the witness in both courts. That is the answer to the fear the passage has been addressing. These men were about to stand before people who could end them and be asked whether they were with him. He tells them what the scene looks like from the other side: whatever is said down here is being said up there, by him, about them.

Peter’s denial. Peter denied Jesus three times (26:69–75). Was he lost? No. He wept bitterly and was restored (John 21:15–19). The warning is about a settled, final rejection of Christ, not a moment of weakness followed by repentance. Peter’s denial and restoration show that Jesus is gracious to those who fall and return.

What the church learned. The church has had to face this question in earnest. In the persecutions under the emperors Decius and Diocletian, large numbers of Christians did deny Christ, some under torture, some by quietly buying a certificate saying they had sacrificed to the gods. When the persecutions ended, many wanted to come back, and the church had to decide whether this verse shut the door. There were rigorists who said it did, and the church did not follow them. The reason was in the New Testament itself: the man who denied Christ three times, with oaths, to a servant girl, was restored by name and given the flock to feed. Whatever verse 33 means, it cannot mean less mercy than Jesus showed to Peter.

What it does not mean. Not that every moment of cowardice or silence damns a person. All believers fail. But a life that refuses to acknowledge Christ when it counts shows that he is not truly treasured. Nor does acknowledging Jesus mean only words: our lives also confess or deny him (Titus 1:16).

I have kept quiet about my faith out of fear. Have I denied Christ? You have failed him, and that is worth grieving over, but you have not done what this verse warns against if you are grieved. Peter’s failure was worse than yours, and Jesus came looking for him. Confess it to God, plainly and without excuses, and receive his forgiveness (1 John 1:9). Then ask him for courage, and take the next opportunity, however small, to say that you belong to him. The difference between Peter and Judas was not the size of their failure but what they did next. Peter went back to Jesus.

In a sentence. Those who openly confess Christ will be confessed by him before the Father; those who finally disown him will be disowned.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to hide that you are a Christian: at work, among friends, online? Acknowledge him today, gently and clearly. It might be as simple as saying you were at church on Sunday, praying before a meal in public, or declining something and saying why. And if you have never confessed him publicly in baptism and church membership, ask whether it is time.

For worship. Imagine it: the Son of God standing before his Father and the holy angels, naming you as his. That is what he promises to everyone who is not ashamed of him. He was not ashamed of us when we were his enemies; he confessed the truth before Pilate and was crucified for it, and he is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11). And when we fail him, as Peter did, he comes to the shore and lights a fire and asks, do you love me? Blessed be the faithful witness, who never denies his own.

parallels.desc: if we deny him, he also will deny us

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not think that Jesus came to bring a peace that leaves everything undisturbed. He came to bring a sword: his call divides even families, setting a son against his father, a daughter against her mother.

Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. Surprising words from the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). Jesus does bring peace: peace with God (Romans 5:1), and peace among those reconciled to God (Ephesians 2:14). But the immediate effect of his coming is division, because people respond to him in opposite ways.

I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. The sword is a picture of division, not of violence by his followers. Jesus rebuked Peter for using a real sword (26:52). The sword cuts between those who follow him and those who reject him (Luke 12:51 says “division”). Hebrews 4:12 says that the word of God is sharper than any two-edged sword. Simeon said that Jesus was set for the fall and rising of many and as a sign that is opposed (Luke 2:34–35).

Two misuses. This verse is pulled in two opposite directions, and both are abuses. Critics quote it to show that Jesus was not the peaceable figure Christians claim. And a certain kind of believer quotes it as permission for a combative Christianity that treats conflict as proof of faithfulness. Both misread it. The sentence is about the effect of his coming, and Luke’s version supplies the interpretation with a different word: not peace, but rather division (Luke 12:51), diamerismos, a splitting into parts. The sword is not a weapon in anybody’s hand; it is what a blade does to a thing laid across it. And the man who said it told Peter to put his sword away, and healed the man Peter had struck (Luke 22:51). In the whole New Testament there is not one instruction to a Christian to use force for the faith.

For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Jesus quotes Micah 7:6, which describes a time of social and family breakdown in Israel’s sinfulness. Jesus uses it to describe the effect of his coming. When one member of a family follows Christ and others do not, their deepest loyalties now differ.

The birth pains of the Messiah. By Jesus’ day Micah 7:6 had become one of the standard descriptions of what would happen just before the Messiah came. The rabbis collected such signs, and a list preserved in the Mishnah runs through the disorders of the last days and ends with exactly these words of Micah. So when Jesus quotes it and says, I have come to set a man against his father, he is not only predicting trouble. He is taking a text everyone used for the birth pains of the messianic age and saying: this is now, and I am the reason.

Micah’s next verse. The passage he quotes does not end in the ruins. Micah’s next sentence is the turn: as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me (Micah 7:7). The chapter that describes a family in pieces goes on to become one of the great statements of confidence in the Old Testament, and ends with God delighting in steadfast love and casting all our sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:18–19).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should cause division in their families or treat unbelieving relatives with hostility. Peter tells believing wives to win unbelieving husbands by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2). The division comes from the different responses to Christ, not from Christian aggression. Nor does it mean that Jesus wants families to break up. He wants them all to follow him.

In a sentence. Jesus’ call divides people, even families, because some follow him and others do not.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has created tension in your family, keep loving and praying for them, and do not give up your loyalty to him. Pray Micah 7:7 as your own prayer, and wait for the God of your salvation. And if there is no tension, ask whether that is because your family loves Christ too, or because you have never let them see how much he means to you.

For worship. The Prince of Peace came with a sword, and the sword passed first through his own mother’s soul (Luke 2:35) and through his own body on the cross. The division he brings is the separating of light from darkness, so that at last there may be a peace that nothing can divide. He has made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and one day every family that is his will be gathered in, from every family of the earth, with no one at enmity ever again.

parallels.desc: son against father, daughter against mother

verseByVerse.quote: and a person's enemies will be those of his own household. Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A person’s enemies may be members of his own household. Whoever loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than Jesus is not worthy of him.

And a person’s enemies will be those of his own household. The end of the quotation from Micah 7:6. The worst opposition sometimes comes from those closest to us. The people most likely to oppose a new disciple are often not strangers but relatives whose own commitments feel threatened by his conversion.

Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. An astonishing claim. In Jewish law, honouring father and mother was one of the highest duties (Exodus 20:12). Jesus claims a loyalty above even that. Only God could claim such loyalty: the first commandment says, you shall have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3). Jesus is implicitly claiming to be God. Luke’s version uses stronger language: if anyone does not “hate” his father and mother he cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:26), a Hebrew idiom meaning “love less” (see 6:24).

And whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. Even our love for our children must come second to Christ.

Not worthy of me. Not fit to be his disciple. Not that anyone earns worthiness, but that a person who puts anything above Christ has not truly received him as Lord.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should love their families less, or neglect them. Christ commands love and care for family (15:4–6; 1 Timothy 5:8; Ephesians 5:25; 6:4). Loving Christ first actually makes us love our families better, with a love that is unselfish and rightly ordered. The point is priority: when loyalty to family and loyalty to Christ conflict, Christ must win. And this is not only for martyrs: it applies in decisions about career, marriage, where to live, and how to raise children.

Am I wrong to love my family so much? No. The verse does not set your love for them against your love for God, as though the affection itself were the problem. God commanded you to honour your parents, and he does not withdraw the command here. This is not a measurement of how warmly you may feel about people. It is about who wins when the two pull in opposite directions: when keeping your place in the family would require you to disobey Christ. Most days there is no conflict at all, and on those days loving your family with everything you have is obeying him.

Am I sure the division is over Jesus? This is the guard the passage most needs, because the sword he speaks of is one he brings; it is not one we are licensed to swing. Much family friction that gets filed under persecution is nothing of the kind. It is the Christian who has become insufferable: who corrects at the dinner table, cannot let a remark pass, and wears his disapproval where everyone can see it. Peter draws the line plainly: let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler (1 Peter 4:15). So run the test honestly. Are they rejecting Christ, or rejecting you, your tone, your superiority, your need to win? If it is the second, that is not a cross. It is something to repent of.

So what do I actually do? Keep honouring them, which costs more than arguing with them and persuades far more. Honour a mocking parent with courtesy, presence, practical help, and a refusal to retaliate. You may not obey anyone into sin, but you are nowhere permitted to be rude. Do not make your love conditional on their agreement, or you will prove their suspicion that faith has made you colder. Answer questions when they are asked, and resist preaching when they are not. And play a long game: how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband (1 Corinthians 7:16)? Households have been won slowly, by years of ordinary faithfulness, far more often than by argument.

And if the division never closes? Some do not, this side of eternity. Jesus does not promise reconciliation in this life. He promises that no one who has left house or family for his sake will fail to receive a hundredfold, and eternal life (19:29), and he says the loss is real enough to be worth mentioning. If you carry that grief, notice who is speaking to you. His own family once came to seize him because they thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), and his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). One of those brothers later opened a letter by calling himself a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1). He is not asking you to bear anything he declined to bear himself, and he has been known to finish these stories long after everyone else had given up on them.

In a sentence. Jesus must be loved more than our dearest family members, and whoever puts family above him is not fit to be his disciple.

On a Tuesday. Is there a family expectation or love that is competing with your obedience to Christ? Love your family by loving Christ first. Think of one decision in front of you, about where to live, how to spend Sunday, what to tell your children, where family pressure and Christ’s word pull apart. Decide it by asking what Christ wants, and then carry it out with as much kindness to your family as you can.

For worship. Who but God could ask to be loved above father and mother, son and daughter? Jesus asks it without apology, because he is the one from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named (Ephesians 3:15). And no father, mother, son or daughter ever loved us as he has: he left his Father’s side and gave himself for us. To love him first is not to lose our families but to receive them back from his hand, loved better than before. Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Psalm 73:25).

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does not take up his cross and follow Jesus is not worthy of him. Whoever holds on to his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for Jesus’ sake will find it.

And whoever does not take his cross and follow me. The first mention of the cross in Matthew. In the Roman world, crucifixion was the cruellest and most shameful form of execution, used for slaves, rebels and criminals. A condemned man carried his own crossbeam through the streets to the place of execution, in front of jeering crowds (27:32; John 19:17). The Romans had crucified thousands of Jews in Galilee after revolts. Everyone listening knew exactly what carrying a cross meant: a man walking to his death, publicly shamed, with no way back.

Before he had spoken of his own. Notice the order. Jesus first plainly predicts his death at 16:21, six chapters later, and Matthew says that from that time he began to show them, and Peter’s horrified reaction shows it was news. So when the Twelve heard whoever does not take his cross, they had no idea that their Master would die on one. The image was not yet about him. It landed on them as pure horror, with none of the softening that two thousand years of jewellery have supplied. They had probably seen it. After the revolt that followed Herod’s death, the Roman governor Varus is said to have crucified two thousand Jews at once, and there had been a rising led by Judas the Galilean within the memory of the older men present. Crosses beside roads were part of the furniture of an occupied country.

The walk, not only the death. The picture is the walk. A condemned man carried the crossbeam himself, through the streets, to the place: publicly, in front of his neighbours, already convicted, with no possibility of appeal. That is the image: not bear your troubles patiently, which is what the phrase has been reduced to, but walk out of your front door carrying the thing you are going to be killed on, past everyone you know. And notice, his cross: each man’s own. Christ’s cross was not shareable; he bore it alone, for us.

What taking up the cross means. Not putting up with ordinary hardships (“my bad back is my cross to bear”). It means dying to self: renouncing the right to run your own life, accepting rejection and shame for Christ, and being willing to die if necessary. It is a decisive, total surrender. Jesus will repeat it after he first predicts his own death (16:24), and Luke adds “daily” (Luke 9:23).

Is not worthy of me. See verse 37.

Whoever finds his life will lose it. “Life” (psychē) means the self, the soul, one’s whole life. Whoever tries to save their life by avoiding the cost of following Christ, protecting their comfort, reputation and safety, will in the end lose everything, including their soul (16:26). It is not the word for mere biological life, but for the whole of what a person is. Whoever succeeds in the project of securing himself, arranging his life round his own preservation and advantage, will find at the end that the thing he was protecting has evaporated.

And whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Whoever gives up their life for Christ, in martyrdom or in daily self-giving, will find true life: life with God now and for ever. The paradox of the gospel: the way to life is through death. Jesus himself walked it first (John 12:24–25). And the claim can be tested against ordinary experience long before death. People organised entirely around themselves are not, as a rule, the ones who seem most alive.

For my sake. Not any self-sacrifice, but sacrifice for Christ. Losing your life for a cause, a career or an ideology is not the same.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by suffering. Christ carried his cross to save us; we carry ours because we have been saved and now follow him. Nor does it mean that Christians should seek suffering for its own sake, or despise ordinary joys. The cross is the willingness to give up anything for Christ, not the rejection of God’s good gifts (1 Timothy 4:4).

What does carrying my cross look like on an ordinary day? Mostly it looks small and unseen. It is saying no to yourself so that you can say yes to Christ: telling the truth when a lie would be easier; giving up the evening you planned to help someone in need; refusing to join the gossip and accepting that you will be thought odd; obeying his word about money, sex or forgiveness when it costs you. It is accepting being misunderstood for him without retaliating. For some believers, it will one day mean prison or death. For most, it means a thousand daily deaths to self, each of them a step behind Jesus. And each one, he promises, is a finding and not a losing.

In a sentence. Following Jesus means dying to self like a condemned man carrying his cross, and those who lose their lives for him find true life.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to die to today, a right, a reputation, a comfort, in order to follow Jesus? Name one, and lay it down before him in prayer this morning. Then notice by evening whether you feel less alive for it, or more.

For worship. He told his disciples to take up a cross before they knew he would take up his. And then he did: he went out carrying his own cross to the place called the Skull (John 19:17), and there he lost his life so that we might find ours. Because he died, we die with him; because he rose, we find our life hidden with him in God. The way of the cross is the way he walked first, and it ends where his ended, in resurrection and glory. Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Galatians 6:14).
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet's reward, and the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person's reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever welcomes Jesus’ messengers welcomes Jesus, and whoever welcomes Jesus welcomes the Father who sent him. Whoever welcomes a prophet or a righteous person because of who they are will share their reward.

Whoever receives you receives me. The apostles are Jesus’ representatives (see v. 2). In Jewish thought, a man’s agent was as the man himself. To welcome them is to welcome Jesus. To reject them is to reject him (Luke 10:16).

The law of agency. The principle had a name in Jewish law, and knowing it makes the sentence precise rather than merely warm. A man’s agent is as the man himself. A legally appointed representative, a shaliach, carried the full standing of the one who sent him: to receive him was to receive the sender, to insult him was to insult the sender, and his acts within his commission bound the man who sent him. It governed betrothals, purchases and legal declarations. Everybody knew it. And the Greek word apostle is simply the Greek for this same office.

And whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Jesus is the Father’s agent. To welcome him is to welcome God (John 13:20). A chain of three: the apostle stands for Christ, and Christ stands for the Father.

Two ways it cuts. For anyone in Christian service, both are needed. The authority is real, and it is not his: a messenger is owed the reception due to his master, and nothing at all is owed to his personality. And the responsibility is real too, since an agent who goes beyond his commission binds nobody.

The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. “Because he is a prophet” means for the sake of his message, recognising him as God’s messenger. Someone who supports God’s messenger shares in the messenger’s work and reward. The widow of Zarephath, who fed Elijah, shared in God’s provision (1 Kings 17:8–16); the Shunammite woman who welcomed Elisha received a son (2 Kings 4:8–17).

And the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. “Righteous person” probably means an ordinary faithful disciple. Those who support and welcome believers because they belong to Christ share in their reward.

The motive is weighed. The phrase is repeated: because he is a prophet, because he is a righteous person, and in verse 42, because he is a disciple. Hospitality offered because the guest is impressive, or useful, or well connected, is an ordinary transaction and gets an ordinary return. Hospitality offered because of what the man carries, when there is nothing to be got out of him and some risk in being seen with him, is counted as a share in his work. And the reward is not a lesser payment for a supporting role. It is the same wage. In the kingdom’s accounting the man who preached and the woman who fed him are on the same line.

What it does not mean. Not that welcoming Christian workers earns salvation. The reward is God’s gracious recognition of faith shown in action. Nor does it mean that every person claiming to be a prophet should be welcomed (7:15). The welcome is for true messengers of Christ.

Do pastors today carry this authority? In part, and with a limit. A faithful minister of the gospel is Christ’s messenger, and when he speaks what Scripture says, he is to be received as one sent by Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20; 1 Thessalonians 2:13; Hebrews 13:17). But he is not an apostle, and his authority extends only as far as his message agrees with the word of God. An agent who exceeds his commission binds nobody. So receive faithful preaching as the voice of your Lord, support and honour those who bring it, and test everything by Scripture (Acts 17:11). No preacher’s personality, title or popularity adds anything to that authority, and none can replace it.

In a sentence. Welcoming Christ’s messengers is welcoming Christ and the Father, and those who support them share in their reward.

On a Tuesday. You may not be a missionary or preacher, but you can share their reward by welcoming, supporting and praying for them. Whom could you support this month? Write to a missionary your church supports and ask how to pray. Invite a visiting preacher for a meal. Give to a gospel worker who cannot repay you. In God’s accounting it is shared work, and a shared reward.

For worship. When we receive his servants, we receive Christ; when we receive Christ, we receive the Father. The Father sent the Son, and the Son sends his people, and in that chain of sending the God of heaven comes to the doors of ordinary homes. He does not forget the widow who shared her last bread or the woman who built a room for a prophet. He is the God who notices, who remembers, and who rewards beyond all we gave.

parallels.desc: the widow of Zarephath receives Elijah

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple, truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the smallest act of kindness, a cup of cold water given to one of Jesus’ humble followers because he is a disciple, will never go unrewarded.

And whoever gives one of these little ones. “Little ones” means humble, ordinary disciples, those who seem least important (18:6, 10, 14). The apostles were “little ones” too: unimpressive fishermen. And in this chapter the little ones are the Twelve at the very moment they are described: sent out with no money, no bag, no spare clothes, dependent on strangers for supper. That is what a little one is here: not a child, but an apostle, reduced by his instructions to someone who needs a drink of water and cannot pay for it.

Even a cup of cold water. The simplest, cheapest act of kindness. In a hot climate, cold water from a deep well was a real refreshment, but it cost almost nothing. Cold water, not simply water: it cost someone a little trouble to fetch. That is the size of the act being promised a reward. Not a house, not a large gift, not a year of service. Somebody walked to the well.

Because he is a disciple. Literally “in the name of a disciple”: because the person belongs to Jesus. The motive matters: kindness to a believer for Christ’s sake.

Truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward. God notices the smallest act of kindness done for his people. Nothing is wasted (25:40; Hebrews 6:10). The double negative in Greek (ou mē) is the strongest form of denial the language has: there is no possibility whatever that it will be lost.

The end of the chapter. The mission discourse began with authority to cast out demons and raise the dead (v. 8), and ends with a cup of cold water. Both matter to Jesus. Not everyone is called to great public ministry, but everyone can give a cup of water. Between those two ends the chapter has passed through floggings, courtrooms, family betrayal, hatred by all, and a cross. And the last word is not about heroism. It is about a person in a doorway who did one small kind thing for somebody with nothing, because of whom that somebody belonged to, and a guarantee, in the strongest form the Greek can manage, that it will not be lost.

What it does not mean. Not that kindness to non-Christians does not matter. Jesus commands love to all, even enemies (5:44). Here he speaks specifically of supporting his messengers. Nor does reward mean that we earn heaven; it is grace recognising the fruit of faith (see 6:1).

Will some Christians have greater rewards in heaven than others? Scripture speaks of rewards that differ (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Luke 19:16–19), and this verse is one of the promises. But they are rewards of grace, not wages earned. Every believer is accepted wholly because of Christ, and the works rewarded are works God himself prepared and enabled (Ephesians 2:10). Augustine said that when God crowns our merits he crowns his own gifts. And there will be no envy in heaven: every cup will be full, and every one of us will gladly cast our crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). The point of the promise is not to make us calculate, but to assure us that nothing done for Christ, however small, is wasted.

In a sentence. Even the smallest kindness to one of Christ’s humblest followers, done for his sake, will be rewarded by God.

On a Tuesday. What is a “cup of cold water” you could give to a fellow believer today: a meal, a text, a lift, a word of encouragement? Think of the least noticed person in your church, the one who never leads anything and whom nobody thanks. Do one small kind thing for them this week, because they belong to Christ. He will see it, and he will not forget.

For worship. Thank God that he notices every small act of love done for his people. The Lord of glory, who sent his apostles out with authority to raise the dead, ends his charge by promising a reward for a cup of water. Nothing is too small for his notice, because his people are not small to him. He who once sat thirsty by a well and asked a woman for a drink (John 4:7) will say on the last day, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (25:40). And he himself is the spring of living water, given freely to all who thirst.

parallels.desc: as you did it to one of the least of these

10.theology: Providence and mission. Matthew 10 grounds the missionary enterprise in the doctrine of divine providence. The disciples go out into hostility, vulnerability, and probable suffering — not because God has abandoned them but because God governs every detail of their mission. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that providence is not merely the general oversight of large events but the meticulous governance of all things, including the suffering of God’s people. This is not fatalism — it does not make the missionary passive — but it is the foundation of missionary courage. The one who governs the sparrow governs the jail cell, the court, and the execution ground.
10.examples:
Then: The Twelve went out with no bag, no extra tunic, no staff, wholly dependent on the hospitality of those who received the gospel. Their very poverty was a sign: the kingdom of heaven advances not by human resources but by divine power through human weakness.

Now: The church in every generation is sent as sheep among wolves. In contexts of comfort and freedom, the temptation is to reverse the commission: to make the church a refuge from the world rather than a mission into it. In contexts of persecution — which most of the global church knows — Matthew 10 is a survival manual. Fear not the one who can kill the body; fear the One who holds the soul.

11.title: Are You the One Who Is to Come?
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. <sup>2</sup>Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples <sup>3</sup>and said to him, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>4</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: <sup>5</sup>the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>6</sup>And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>7</sup>As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>8</sup>What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. <sup>9</sup>What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>10</sup>This is he of whom it is written, “‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>11</sup>Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. <sup>12</sup>From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. <sup>13</sup>For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, <sup>14</sup>and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. <sup>15</sup>He who has ears to hear, let him hear. <sup>16</sup>“But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates, <sup>17</sup>“‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’ <sup>18</sup>For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>19</sup>The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.” <sup>20</sup>Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. <sup>21</sup>“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>22</sup>But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>23</sup>And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades.
