For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. <sup>24</sup>But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.” <sup>25</sup>At that time Jesus declared, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; <sup>26</sup>yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>27</sup>All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. <sup>28</sup>Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. <sup>29</sup>Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. <sup>30</sup>For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is built around a single question: “Are you the one who is to come?” John the Baptist, the greatest of the prophets, sits in Herod’s prison and sends his disciples to ask Jesus the question. Doubt is not always the opposite of faith; sometimes it is faith in extremity, crying out for reassurance. Jesus answers with Isaiah’s sign: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news (Isa 35:5–6; 61:1). The messianic age has arrived. John is the last and greatest of the prophets, the Elijah who prepared the way, standing at the threshold of the new era.

The chapter turns on the city of unbelief. Chorazin, Bethsaida, Capernaum — cities that witnessed the greatest miracles in history — did not repent. They will face a worse judgment than Sodom. Privilege entails responsibility; greater revelation means greater accountability. The chapter closes with the most tender invitation in the Gospels: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” The King who demands a cross is also the Lord who bears the burden of all who come to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — John's Question, Jesus's Invitation: The Kingdom in Paradox
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist, imprisoned, sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who is to come. Jesus answers by pointing to his deeds and pronounces John the greatest of all born of women — yet the least in the kingdom is greater. He condemns the generation that rejected both John and himself, pronounces woes on unrepentant cities, and closes with the great invitation: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden." The chapter moves from doubt to judgment to grace. The most important thing in the chapter is something Jesus leaves out. His reply to John is stitched from Isaiah 35:5-6, 26:19 and 61:1 — and Isaiah 61:1 continues "to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound". That is the one clause in the whole quarry that speaks to a man in a cell, and it is the one clause omitted. He takes the poor and drops the prisoners, in a message sent to a prisoner who had asked. Which is why the last line is what it is: "blessed is the one who is not offended by me" — the kingdom has come, I am the one, and I am not getting you out. The reed (v. 7) was Herod Antipas's emblem, stamped on the coins of his new capital at Tiberias — and Herod is the man holding John; while "soft clothing in kings' houses" points at a palace with a prophet in camel hair underneath it. The Malachi quotation (v. 10) is altered in one pronoun: Malachi 3:1 has God say the messenger prepares the way "before me", and Jesus quotes it as "before your face... prepare your way". The way prepared for the coming of God is the way prepared for him, and the claim is made by changing a pronoun and saying nothing. "the least is greater" is not moral but chronological: John died before the crucifixion and never heard that the tomb was empty. Verse 12 is genuinely disputed — biazetai can be middle or passive, giving either "the kingdom suffers violence and violent men plunder it" (which fits a prophet in a dungeon) or "the kingdom is forcefully advancing and forceful men lay hold of it" (which fits Luke 16:16); both are held by serious men, and Luke's parallel tips the balance toward the second. On Elijah, John's flat "I am not" (Jn. 1:21) denies the popular expectation of the historical Elijah returning; Jesus affirms the office, as Gabriel had before John was born (Lk. 1:17). "a glutton and a drunkard" (v. 19) is a legal formula — the exact charge in the rebellious-son law of Deuteronomy 21:20, for which the penalty is stoning. Capernaum's doom (v. 23) quotes the taunt against the king of Babylon (Isa. 14:13-15), applied to a fishing village of fifteen hundred people — and all three towns named are now ruins, with Bethsaida's site still disputed. "the wise and understanding" (v. 25) is lifted from Isaiah 29:14, a judgement oracle against the religious establishment, and "little children" is nepioi, infants. And verse 27 is the "Johannine thunderbolt" — a sentence that reads like the fourth Gospel, found in Matthew and Luke and not in John, which disposes of the claim that a high Christology is late.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter's center is the paradox of the kingdom: John is the greatest prophet and yet less than the least kingdom citizen, because the kingdom has arrived in a greater reality than any prophet foresaw. The "violent" who take the kingdom by force are not the arrogant but the eager — those who press urgently into what God has opened. The cities of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum had seen the greatest miracles in history and remained unmoved; their judgment will exceed Sodom's because their privilege exceeded Sodom's.
verseByVerse.examples: The great invitation of verses 28-30 is the gospel in miniature. "All who labor and are heavy laden" — the exhausted self-righteous crushed by law-keeping, the sinners crushed by guilt, the anxious crushed by the weight of life. "Come to me" — not to a program, a religion, or a therapy, but to a person. The yoke of Jesus is easy not because it demands less but because it is borne with him, by one who is gentle and lowly in heart. Learning from him is not hard labor but rest — the deep rest of a soul that has found what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus had finished instructing the Twelve, he went on teaching and preaching in the towns of Galilee.

Meaning first. Matthew 11 is the chapter in which the kingdom meets every kind of response. John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask whether Jesus really is the one; Jesus answers from Isaiah and then praises John to the crowds. He compares his generation to sulky children who will play no game, pronounces woe on the towns that saw his mightiest works and did not repent, thanks his Father for hiding these things from the proud and revealing them to infants, and then, from the height of his unique knowledge of the Father, turns and calls every weary person to come to him for rest. The chapter that is full of rejection ends with the gentlest invitation in the Bible, spoken by the only man who ever described his own heart.

When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples. This is the second of five times Matthew rounds off a block of teaching with the same sentence, and the formula is worth seeing whole, because it is the skeleton Matthew hung his Gospel on and it is invisible until the five are laid side by side. When Jesus finished these sayings (7:28), after the Sermon on the Mount. When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples (11:1), after the mission charge. When Jesus had finished these parables (13:53). When Jesus had finished these sayings (19:1), after the teaching on life in the church. And when Jesus had finished all these sayings (26:1), after the teaching on the end, and then the passion begins. Five blocks of teaching, each sealed with the same words, in a Gospel written for Jewish readers. The Law came in five books; here is the word of the Lord in five discourses, delivered by a greater Moses who went up a mountain to give the first of them.

He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. Notice what the verse actually reports him doing. Having sent twelve men out to preach in the towns, he goes off to teach and preach in the towns himself. He does not delegate and withdraw, and he does not linger to be admired for the speech he has just given. The commissioning of others did not reduce his own work by a single village. And there is a quiet dignity in the phrase their cities: the towns of Galilee where these people lived. He works the same ground the Twelve are working, at the same time, and he does not send them anywhere he is unwilling to go himself. He sends his servants out, and then he goes out after them.

The new section. Chapters 11 and 12 set out the growing responses to Jesus, and they darken as they go: honest doubt (John’s question, 11:2–6), indifference (this generation, 11:16–19), unrepentance (the cities, 11:20–24) and open hostility (the Pharisees, chapter 12). In the middle of it all, like a spring in a desert, stands his invitation to the weary (11:28–30). Matthew wants us to feel that the Lord’s gentleness is not the gentleness of a man who has never been opposed. He offers rest in the very chapter in which he is being rejected.

Does this mean that those who serve Christ should never stop working? No. The point is that Jesus never asks of his servants what he will not do himself, not that rest is unspiritual. The same Lord took his disciples away to a desolate place to rest a while (Mark 6:31), slept in a boat in a storm, and withdrew to pray. What the verse rules out is the leader who hands every task to others and keeps the platform for himself. Those who lead in a church, a home or a ministry should still be found doing the ordinary work they ask others to do, and they should also keep the rest their Master kept.

In a sentence. After sending out the Twelve, Jesus went on teaching and preaching in the towns of Galilee himself.

On a Tuesday. If you lead anything, a family, a Bible study, a team, ask whether you still do the kind of work you ask of others. Jesus did not delegate everything; he kept working, in the same villages. And if you are one of the sent, take heart from the order of the verse: he sends you out, and then he comes after you. You never arrive anywhere he has not already chosen to go.

For worship. Here is a Lord who does not stand at a distance and direct the battle from a hill. He sends his servants into the towns and then walks into the same towns himself, teaching and preaching, until he walks at last into Jerusalem and the work no servant could do. Blessed be the Shepherd who goes ahead of his sheep and behind them, who never asks his people to bear what he has not first carried, and who is still going out after every messenger he sends.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples and said to him, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" And Jesus answered them, "Go and tell John what you hear and see:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist, in prison, heard about what Jesus was doing and sent his disciples to ask: are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?

Now when John heard in prison. Herod Antipas had imprisoned John for telling him that he could not have his brother’s wife, Herodias (14:3–4). The historian Josephus says John was held at Machaerus, a fortress-palace in the hills east of the Dead Sea. He had been there for months, perhaps a year, and he would not come out alive. This is not the John of the Jordan, calling crowds to repentance with burning certainty. This is a man in darkness, whose certainty is being tested by circumstances that do not fit what he expected. Prison does not destroy faith, but it strips it of comfort and forces it down to its foundations.

About the deeds of the Christ. The works of chapters 8 and 9: the healings, the exorcisms, the girl raised from the dead. Matthew calls them the deeds of the Christ on purpose: the reader is to know that these are the Messiah’s works, even while John is unsure. John still had disciples who visited him, and they brought him the reports.

Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? The one who is to come was a title for the Messiah (3:11; Psalm 118:26; Malachi 3:1). Why would John, who had baptised Jesus and seen the Spirit descend and heard the Father’s voice (3:13–17), ask this? Most likely because Jesus was not doing what John had expected. John had announced a Messiah with a winnowing fork and unquenchable fire, who would cut down every fruitless tree (3:10–12). Instead Jesus was healing, eating with sinners and showing mercy, while John sat in a dungeon and Herod went unpunished. Where was the fire? Where was the liberty to the captives that Isaiah had promised (Isaiah 61:1)? It is the most honest question in the Gospels. John is not pretending; he is genuinely uncertain.

Who is doing the doubting. Stay with this, because it is the passage for anyone whose faith has gone quiet, and there are far more such people in any congregation than ever say so. This is not a half-hearted man at the edge of the crowd. It is the prophet who saw the heavens opened, the man Jesus is about to call the greatest born of women (v. 11). If John can arrive here, then doubt is not proof that your faith was never real. Some of the darkest questions in the world are asked by people who are very far in, and they are usually asked from a prison of one kind or another: illness, grief, a marriage that failed, a prayer unanswered for years, where the God you trusted does not seem to be acting as you expected.

What John did with it. This is the whole difference between doubt that matures a person and doubt that dismantles him. John did not bury the question, and he did not walk away with it. He sent it to Jesus. Doubt carried toward Christ becomes faith with its foundations exposed; doubt carried away from him hardens into something else. So do what John did: say it out loud, to God, and to someone who will not panic when they hear it. A church where nobody may admit a hard question is a church that will lose the people who have one.

What Jesus does not do. He does not rebuke John or shame him, and he does not ask where his faith has gone. He does not treat the question as an insult. He sends back evidence, go and tell him what you hear and see, and treats an honest doubt as worth answering carefully. He is not fragile, and neither is the truth. You may bring him the question you are most afraid of.

What Jesus does not send back. This is the hardest part. He does not explain why John is in prison. He does not promise release. He does not say the sentence John most wanted to hear. John was beheaded there, still inside, without seeing the kingdom he had announced come in the way he had pictured. What Jesus sent was not an explanation of why this was happening, but a declaration of who he is. Very often that is the only answer given, and it turns out to be the one that holds when the other would not have.

Then read on. The best thing in this passage is easy to miss. The moment John’s messengers turn for the door, Jesus begins to speak to the crowd about him, and he praises him without reserve: no one greater has arisen. He does not say that John was great before he wavered. He does not mention the wavering at all. He defends the doubter in public, at the very hour of his doubting, and so far as we know John never heard a word of it. That is what your Lord says about you on the worst day of your faith, whether or not it ever reaches you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean John had lost his faith. He sent his question to Jesus himself, which is what faith does with doubt. Honest questions brought to Christ are not unbelief; the psalmists did the same (Psalm 13; 22). Nor does it mean John was wrong about the judgment. He was right that the Messiah would judge. What he did not yet see was that the judgment would come later, at Christ’s return, and that first the Messiah would come in mercy, and bear the fire himself at the cross.

Is it a sin to doubt? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. Unbelief refuses God’s word and turns away; doubt is faith struggling to hold on while something does not make sense. John doubted and Jesus called him great. Thomas doubted and Jesus showed him his hands. Scripture even says to have mercy on those who doubt (Jude 22). What matters is direction. Doubt nursed in private, used as a reason to stop praying or to stay away from God’s people, can harden. Doubt brought to Christ, in prayer, in the Scriptures and in honest conversation with a mature believer, is often how he deepens a faith that was resting on feelings rather than on him.

What if I bring my doubts to Jesus and nothing seems to change? Then you are where John was, and you are in good company. Jesus did not change John’s circumstances; he gave John himself to look at, and the Scriptures to hold. Keep doing the ordinary things: read the Gospels, where the deeds of the Christ are recorded; keep gathering with the church; keep praying, even if the prayer is only the question. Faith is not a feeling you must manufacture but a person you keep turning toward. Feelings of assurance often return slowly, and sometimes only later can you see that he was holding you all along.

In a sentence. John, in prison and puzzled that Jesus was not bringing judgment, brought his doubt to Jesus himself, and Jesus answered him with evidence and praised him in public.

On a Tuesday. When God does not act as you expected, and you are confused, take the question to Jesus as John did. Say it plainly in prayer. Then tell one trusted believer what you are struggling with, rather than carrying it alone. And if someone brings a doubt to you, answer as Jesus did: without shock, without shame, by pointing them to who he is.

For worship. Glory to the Christ who is not threatened by our questions. He received the doubt of the greatest of the prophets without a word of reproach, answered it from the Scriptures, and then stood before a crowd and honoured the man who had asked it. He did not open John’s prison, but he went into a darker prison for John, and for us, and came out of it on the third day. The fire John was waiting for fell, in the end, on the Lamb John had pointed to, so that doubters like John, and like us, would be gathered as wheat into the barn.
verseByVerse.note: John was imprisoned by Herod Antipas, according to Josephus in the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered by pointing to what was happening: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news. These are the signs Isaiah promised. Blessed is anyone who does not stumble over me.

Go and tell John what you hear and see. Jesus does not answer yes directly. He points to the evidence and lets John draw the conclusion from the Scriptures John knew. The deeds themselves are the answer, because they are the deeds Isaiah had said would mark the coming of God to save.

The blind receive their sight and the lame walk. Isaiah 35:5–6: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped, and the lame man shall leap like a deer. Isaiah 35 is a picture of God himself coming to save his people, and of the desert blossoming as he comes. The signs Jesus lists are the signs of the new creation, the reversal of every curse. John had read Isaiah. He would recognise the passage at once.

Lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up. Isaiah 26:19 promises that the dead shall live. Cleansing lepers is not in Isaiah’s lists, but Elisha did it (2 Kings 5), and Jesus has done it (8:2–3), touching the man nobody touched.

And the poor have good news preached to them. Isaiah 61:1: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. It is the passage Jesus read aloud in the synagogue at Nazareth and declared fulfilled (Luke 4:18–21). And the climax of the list is not a miracle at all. It is preaching: the gospel to the poor. The greatest of the signs is that the poor are told the good news.

The clause that is missing. Now read Isaiah 61:1 in full, and watch what happens. The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound. The one clause in the whole passage that speaks directly to a man in a cell, and Jesus leaves it out. He includes the poor and passes over the prisoners. To John. In prison. Who had sent to ask. In a man who has assembled a quotation from several passages with such care, that is very likely deliberate, and it means the answer is honest to the point of severity. The signs are real, the age has begun, the evidence is sufficient, and the prison door is not going to open. The day of vengeance in the next verse of Isaiah is not mentioned either. Jesus is gently telling John: I am fulfilling the promises, but in God’s order, mercy now and judgment later.

And blessed is the one who is not offended by me. “Offended” translates skandalisthē, from the word for the trigger of a trap, the stick that springs under a foot. It is not the language of intellectual objection but of a man walking along and being brought down suddenly by something he did not see. Blessed are those who do not reject Jesus because he does not fit their expectations. Many stumbled over a humble, merciful, suffering Messiah (1 Corinthians 1:23); many still do. Read as a general saying it is mild. Read as the ending of this particular message it is almost unbearable, and exactly right: the kingdom has come, I am the one, and I am not getting you out, and blessed is the man who can hold those three together without stumbling.

Who the beatitude was first spoken to. Not to sceptics, and not to enemies. To the greatest man born of women, at his lowest hour, through messengers, as the only comfort available. The comfort was not deliverance but a blessing on the man who can go on trusting without it. And it is a kindness, not a threat. Jesus is not scolding John for asking. He is naming, tenderly, the one real danger, that the Christ who is not doing what you expected might become the reason you turn from him, and he names it so that it will not happen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that miracles alone prove Jesus is the Messiah. False messiahs could appear to do signs (24:24). It is the combination of the works with Scripture’s promises, and above all the preaching of good news to the poor, that identifies him. Nor does the omission of judgment mean that Jesus will never judge. He will (25:31–46). The day of vengeance has been postponed, not cancelled, and the delay is itself mercy.

Why does Jesus not do miracles like these everywhere today? He still heals, and Christians are right to pray for the sick and to give thanks when he answers (James 5:14–16). But the signs in this list had a particular purpose: they were the credentials of the Messiah, the evidence Isaiah said would mark his coming, and they were continued through the apostles to confirm their message (Hebrews 2:3–4). This commentary holds, charitably towards brothers who differ, that those sign-gifts ceased with the apostolic age. The sign that has not ceased is the last one in the list: the poor still have good news preached to them. Every faithful sermon to needy people is the same work of the Messiah going on.

What if God does not rescue me from my prison? Then this verse was written for you. John was not rescued, and Jesus called him blessed if he did not stumble. God does sometimes open prison doors (Acts 12), and you may ask him to. But his love is not measured by whether he changes your circumstances. It is measured at the cross. A Christian can be in hospital, in debt, in grief, or in an actual cell, and still be in the kingdom and loved without limit. The question is not whether he will do what you want, but whether you will trust him if he does not.

In a sentence. Jesus pointed John to his works as the fulfilment of Isaiah’s promises, left out the release of prisoners, and blessed those who do not stumble over the way he fulfils them.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing about Jesus or his ways that troubles you most: the prayer he has not answered, the trouble he has not removed. Then look at what he has done, in the Gospels and at the cross, and set that beside it. Do not let the thing you do not understand trip you over the things you do. Trust his order: mercy now, and every wrong put right later.

For worship. Look at the signs: the blind see, the lame leap, the lepers are clean, the dead rise, and the poor hear good news. This is God himself come to save, exactly as Isaiah said. And look at the Saviour who sends them, who would not flatter even the greatest prophet with a promise he did not mean to keep, yet who walked into the deepest prison of all, death itself, and broke it open from the inside. The liberty for the captives that John did not receive in Machaerus he received at last in glory, and every one of Christ’s prisoners will receive it on the day the doors of every grave are opened.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers with the language of Isaiah’s promises.

parallels.desc: the blind see, the lame leap

verseByVerse.quote: As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings' houses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As John’s disciples left, Jesus spoke to the crowds about John. What did you go out to the desert to see? A reed blown about by the wind? A man dressed in soft, fine clothes? No: those are found in kings’ palaces.

As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John. Jesus turns from answering John to defending him, and he does it at once, so that no one in the crowd would think less of John because of his question. The timing is the tenderness. He waits until John’s disciples are leaving, so the praise is not flattery to be carried back, and then speaks it where everyone can hear.

What did you go out into the wilderness to see? Crowds had gone out in great numbers to hear John (3:5), walking for days into the desert. Jesus asks what they were looking for, and the question reaches the reader too. What do you go to church to find: comfort, or truth? A performer, or a word from God?

A reed shaken by the wind? Reeds grew thickly in the marshes along the Jordan and at the north end of the lake, bending with every breeze. So a shaken reed is first a picture of the ordinary: nobody walks into a desert to look at grass. And it is a picture of a weak man who bends with public opinion. John was not that. He stood firm against a king. But there may be a sharper edge. Herod Antipas founded a new capital on the lake shore, Tiberias, and the early coins he struck there seem to have carried a reed. If so, the question carries a second meaning: you did not walk into the wilderness to look at the man on the coinage. You went to see someone who was his opposite.

A man dressed in soft clothing? Fine, luxurious clothes, the dress of the wealthy and the courtier. John wore camel hair and a leather belt and ate locusts (3:4).

Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. That is not a general remark about luxury. There is a king’s house in this story, and a man in soft clothing in it, and another man underneath it in the dark wearing camel hair. John was in a king’s house too, in the dungeon and not the court. The crowd had gone out to the desert precisely because John was not like Herod’s courtiers, and Jesus is reminding them of what they knew and had perhaps begun to forget, now that the prophet was inconveniently in prison and asking awkward questions. His imprisonment is the mark of his faithfulness, not his failure. A prophet who ends in prison for speaking the truth has not mismanaged his calling; he has fulfilled it.

The temptation to become a reed. A shaken reed is the man who bends with whatever is blowing, and the temptation to become one is not usually felt as cowardice. It is felt as reasonableness, as not wanting to make a scene, as keeping the peace. John was in prison because he had told a king that he could not have his brother’s wife. By any sensible measure, that was an unnecessary thing to say. He said it, it cost him his head, and Jesus is about to call him the greatest man ever born.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that fine clothing or wealth is sinful in itself. Joseph of Arimathea was rich, and so was Lydia. The point is the contrast between John’s fearless integrity and the comfortable compromise of those who serve the powerful. Nor does it mean that a Christian should be harsh or look for confrontation. John spoke because the truth required it, not because he enjoyed a fight.

How do I know whether I am standing firm or simply being stubborn? Ask three questions. First, is the thing I am holding to clearly taught in Scripture, or is it my preference? John stood on God’s law about marriage, not on a personal opinion. Second, what does standing cost me, and what does bending gain me? If bending would bring comfort, approval or advantage, be suspicious of your reasons for bending. Third, am I saying it with love and for the other person’s good? John’s words to Herod were a call to repentance, not a performance. Firmness on what God has said, with gentleness in how it is said, is the mark of a prophet. Firmness on everything, with harshness, is just pride.

In a sentence. Jesus reminded the crowds that John was no weak reed bending with the wind or pampered courtier, but a man of unbending conviction who had gone to prison for the truth.

On a Tuesday. Think of the place this week where you are most tempted to bend: the conversation at work where everyone mocks the faith, the family gathering where a sin is celebrated, the friend whose choice you are expected to applaud. You do not need to make a speech. But you must not pretend. Decide now what you will not say, and what you will gently say if asked.

For worship. Christ is the Lord who honours faithfulness the world calls foolish. Kings’ houses were full of soft clothing, and he passed them by; he chose instead a man in camel hair in a dungeon, and called him great. He himself would stand before Herod and say nothing, and before Pilate and say the truth, and he would be clothed in a mock robe of purple and then stripped of it. The reed would be put into his own hand as a sceptre in scorn (27:29), and with that weakness he would conquer. Blessed is the King who was never shaken by any wind.

verseByVerse.quote: What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is he of whom it is written, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did you go out to see a prophet? Yes, and more than a prophet. John is the messenger of whom Malachi wrote: God’s messenger sent ahead to prepare the way.

A prophet? The people regarded John as a prophet (21:26), the first in Israel for about four hundred years. After the long silence since Malachi, a voice had come out of the wilderness again.

Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. Every other prophet spoke about a day he would not see. Moses died looking at the land from a mountain. Isaiah wrote seven centuries early. Daniel was told to seal up the words until the time of the end. John is the only one who could point with his finger and say: that man there. He was not only a prophet; he was himself the subject of prophecy, the last of the line and the only one who was not, in the end, still waiting. Which is what makes his question from prison so moving. The one prophet who saw the thing he had prophesied was, near the end of his life, no longer sure he had seen it.

This is he of whom it is written. Malachi 3:1, combined with words from Exodus 23:20, where God sends his angel before Israel through the wilderness.

Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. Here the boldest claim in the chapter is hidden in a pronoun. In Malachi, God is speaking: I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me, and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. The messenger goes ahead of God, to prepare for God’s own coming. Every Jew who knew the passage knew that. Now read it as Jesus gives it: before your face, your way. The first person has become the second. The Father is now addressing the Son, and the way that Malachi said was prepared for the arrival of God is the way prepared for Jesus. Nothing is argued and no claim is stated. A pronoun is changed, and a sentence about God coming to his temple becomes a sentence about the man standing in front of them. Once again Jesus is identified with the LORD himself (see 3:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that John was greater than Jesus. John’s greatness is borrowed: he was great because of whom he announced. He was the forerunner; Jesus is the Lord whose way he prepared, and John himself said that he must increase and I must decrease (John 3:30).

If Jesus is the LORD, is he the same person as the Father? No. Notice that in this very verse the Father speaks to the Son: I send my messenger before your face. There are two persons in the sentence, the one who sends and the one before whom the messenger goes. Yet the words of Malachi that belonged to the coming of God now belong to Jesus. That is the doctrine of the Trinity in seed form: one God, existing as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, distinct persons sharing one divine nature. Jesus is not a second god, nor merely the Father wearing a different mask. He is God the Son, come to his own temple.

In a sentence. John was more than a prophet: he was the messenger Malachi foretold, preparing the way for the Lord himself, who is Jesus.

On a Tuesday. You cannot be John, but you share his calling: to point away from yourself to Christ. Think of one person you will see this week and ask how you might prepare the way for him in their life, a kindness that makes them ask why, a word about what Christ has done for you, an invitation to hear the gospel. A forerunner is satisfied when people walk past him to the one he announced.

For worship. The God of Malachi said he would come to his temple, and he came. He came not with an army but as a carpenter from Nazareth, preceded by a man in camel hair, and the temple he came to was rebuilt in three days in his own body. All the prophets saw him from a distance and greeted him from afar; John saw him face to face and pointed. Now the One whose way was prepared prepares a way for us, through the curtain, into the presence of the Father, and he is himself the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one born of a woman is greater than John. Yet the least person in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. From the time of John until now, the kingdom has been advancing forcefully, and forceful people have been attacking it.

Among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Born of women means human beings. Of all the great people of the old covenant, Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Isaiah, none was greater than John. Why? Because of his unique place: he stood at the hinge of history and pointed directly to the Messiah. And remember when Jesus says it: on the day John sent to ask whether he was the one.

Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. The comparison needs to be made precise, because as it stands it can sound like an insult to John, and it is not one. The greatness in view is not moral or personal. Jesus is not saying that the least Christian is holier than John, which would contradict the first half of his own sentence. It is a matter of where a man stands in the story. John died before the cross. He never heard that the Lamb of God he had pointed to was killed at Passover, and he never heard that the tomb was empty. He worked entirely on the near side of the event, announcing a kingdom whose central act he did not live to see. Believers after the cross and resurrection see it fulfilled, receive the Spirit poured out at Pentecost, and know the whole gospel. Prophets and kings longed to see what they see (13:16–17; 1 Peter 1:10–12). Greatness here is privilege of position, not personal merit. The least believer knows what John did not, not because he is better but because he is later. He saw the dawn from a distance; the disciples live in the sunrise.

From the days of John the Baptist until now. From the start of John’s preaching to the present: a short span of time, but the turning point of history. Something changed when John began to preach. The waiting stopped.

The kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. One of the hardest sayings in the Gospels, and the honest thing is to show the problem. The Greek verb biazetai can be passive, suffers violence, or middle, forcefully advances, and the two produce different meanings. On the first reading, the kingdom has been attacked by violent men who try to seize or destroy it. John is in prison; Jesus will be killed; the disciples will be persecuted (10:16–25). On this view the violent are the Herods and the authorities, and the verse is a lament. The ESV text follows this reading. On the second reading, the kingdom has been forcefully advancing (the ESV footnote), and forceful people, those who press in with urgency, are laying hold of it: the tax collectors and sinners shouldering their way into a kingdom the respectable thought was theirs. Luke has a similar saying: everyone forces his way into it (Luke 16:16).

Where Christians differ over the violence. Both readings are held by careful scholars, and neither can be settled from the grammar alone. Verdict: the first fits best in Matthew’s context, between John’s imprisonment and the mounting opposition of chapters 11 and 12. Since John came, the kingdom has broken in with power, and it has met violent opposition. Both truths are taught in the Gospels, and the same period saw the kingdom advancing hardest and its herald in chains.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we must seize the kingdom by violence or human force. The kingdom is God’s gift to the poor in spirit (5:3). Nor does least in the kingdom mean that John is outside it. He will sit at the feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (8:11). He belongs to the age of promise, standing at its very end, and he is saved by the same Lamb he announced.

But I feel very ordinary. How can I be greater than John? Because the measure is not you but what you have been shown. The most privileged man of the old order would have given everything for what an ordinary Christian takes for granted on a wet Tuesday: that it is finished, that the grave is open, that God is not angry with those who are in Christ. You may never preach to crowds or stand before kings. But you know the name of the Saviour, the meaning of his death and the fact of his resurrection, and the Spirit lives in you. That is not a compliment to your character. It is a measure of the gift.

In a sentence. John was the greatest of the old era, yet the least in the kingdom has a greater privilege, and the kingdom, breaking in since John, has met violent opposition.

On a Tuesday. Before the day is out, say to God in your own words three things John never heard: that Christ died for sinners, that he rose, and that he has poured out his Spirit. Then let the privilege shape one thing you do. You know more than the greatest prophet. Live like someone who has seen the sunrise.

For worship. How great must the kingdom be, if its least citizen stands higher in privilege than the greatest man ever born of a woman? It is great because its King is great. Violent men laid hands on his herald and then on him, and thought they had stopped the kingdom by a cross. But the violence of the world was the very means by which the kingdom came, as the King bore the violence that our sins deserved. Now the gates stand open, and the least of his people walks in the full light of what the prophets only longed to see.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 12 is a notoriously difficult saying; it may describe the kingdom’s forceful advance or the violent opposition to it.

verseByVerse.quote: For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to accept it, John is the Elijah who was to come.

For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. The Law and the Prophets means the whole Old Testament, and the whole of it looked forward. It pointed to the coming of the Messiah and his kingdom, and John was the last voice of that age of anticipation. Unusually, Jesus says that the Law prophesied too. The law did not only command; it pointed ahead, in its sacrifices, its priesthood, its festivals and its very demands, to the One who would fulfil it (5:17).

And if you are willing to accept it. That is not how prophecy fulfilment is usually announced. There is a condition in the sentence, and it does not attach to the fact, John is what he is either way, but to the hearer’s willingness. Accepting John as the promised Elijah commits a person to something much larger. Elijah comes immediately before the day of the LORD. If the messenger has arrived, the one he announced is standing in front of you. Nobody can take the first half and leave the second. To receive John is to receive Jesus; to reject one is to reject both.

He is Elijah who is to come. Malachi 4:5–6, the last words of the Old Testament in our order, promised that God would send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD, to turn the hearts of fathers to their children. Many Jews expected Elijah himself to return, since he had not died (2 Kings 2:11). Jesus says John fulfilled the promise. John came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), dressed like him (3:4; 2 Kings 1:8), lived in the wilderness as he did, and preached repentance as he did. He even confronted a wicked king and his wife, so that Ahab and Jezebel are repeated in Herod and Herodias almost detail for detail.

But John denied being Elijah. The apparent contradiction deserves to be set out plainly. Here Jesus says of John that he is Elijah. In John’s Gospel the priests ask John directly whether he is Elijah, and he answers: I am not (John 1:21). The resolution turns on what the questioners meant. Popular expectation held that the historical Elijah, the man who had gone up in a whirlwind, would physically come back. That is what the priests were asking, and John’s answer was correct: he was not that man. He was Zechariah’s son, born in the hill country of Judea, and he knew it. What Jesus affirms is the other thing, which the angel had said before John was born: he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. Not the person, but the office. John denied being Elijah come back; Jesus affirmed that he was Elijah come again, in the only sense Malachi ever meant.

What it does not mean. It is not reincarnation, as some have claimed. Scripture nowhere teaches it, and John was a new person, born to Zechariah and Elizabeth, who fulfilled Elijah’s prophetic role. Nor do we wait for another Elijah before Christ returns. Jesus says the promise has been fulfilled (17:10–13).

How do I read the Old Testament as pointing to Christ without forcing it? Follow the lines the New Testament draws. Start with what a passage meant to its first readers, then ask how it fits the whole story that ends in Christ: a promise he keeps (Genesis 3:15), a pattern he fills (the Passover lamb, the priest, the king), a need he meets (the law’s demand that no one could keep), or a longing he answers (the psalmist’s cry). Jesus said all the Scriptures speak of him (Luke 24:27), but that does not mean every detail is a hidden code. Not every tent peg is the cross. Read whole passages, let the apostles guide you, and Christ will come into view naturally.

In a sentence. John ended the age of prophecy and fulfilled Malachi’s promise of the coming Elijah, so that to accept him is to accept the Lord he announced.

On a Tuesday. Next time you read the Old Testament, before you close it, ask one question: where is this pointing? Write down one way the passage prepares for Christ. Over a year you will find that the whole Bible has become one story, and that every road in it leads to the same person.

For worship. For a thousand years the Law and the Prophets spoke, and every sacrifice, every promise and every prophet was a finger pointing forward. Then the last of them came out of the desert, dressed like Elijah, and pointed with his own hand at a man in the queue for baptism. All of it was about him. The God who wrote the last line of the Old Testament kept his word to the letter, sent his Elijah, and then came himself, the great and awesome day of the LORD clothed in human flesh, to turn the hearts of rebels back to their Father.

parallels.desc: I will send you Elijah the prophet
in the spirit and power of Elijah

verseByVerse.quote: He who has ears to hear, let him hear. But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has ears, let them hear. Then Jesus asked what this generation was like: like children sitting in the market square, calling to their playmates.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. A phrase Jesus uses after important or puzzling teaching (13:9, 43), and it is doing more work than it looks. It is an odd thing to say: everybody in the crowd had ears. The point is that hearing in the sense that matters is not automatic. The sound arrives at every ear present and lands in some and not others. Which is precisely what he will say in the parable of the sower, and precisely what he thanks the Father for at the end of this chapter, that these things are hidden from the wise and revealed to infants. The call to hear and the teaching that hearing is given are not in competition. They stand ten verses apart in the same speech. It is a call to pay close attention, to understand and to respond.

But to what shall I compare this generation? This generation means the people of Jesus’ time, especially those who rejected both John and Jesus. In Matthew it is often a dark phrase: an evil and adulterous generation (12:39, 45; 16:4; 23:36).

It is like children sitting in the marketplaces. The marketplace (agora) was the town square, where children played while adults did their business. The picture is drawn from something Jesus had evidently watched, and it repays being seen properly. Children in a village square, playing at being grown-ups.

And calling to their playmates. The two great public events in the life of a Galilean village were weddings and funerals, and both were noisy. At a wedding there were pipes and dancing; at a funeral there were hired mourners, wailing and beating the breast. Children imitated both, as children everywhere imitate whatever the adults do most loudly. The game itself is explained in the next verse.

Does this generation include me? Jesus meant first the people who saw and heard him and rejected him. But the phrase describes a kind of heart as well as a period of time, and every generation has it: people who have heard God’s message and keep finding reasons not to respond. You are not part of this generation in Jesus’ sense if you have come to him in repentance and faith. But the warning is for everyone who still has ears and is still deciding what to do with what they have heard.

In a sentence. Jesus calls for careful listening and compares his generation to children in the market square who will join in no game.

On a Tuesday. Before you next hear a sermon or read the Bible, pray a one-line prayer: Lord, give me ears to hear. Then, afterwards, ask one question: what did God say, and what will I do? Hearing that does not go on to doing is only noise.

For worship. The Lord who made the ear (Psalm 94:9) stands in the marketplace and calls. He could have spoken only to angels; he chose to speak to farmers, fishermen and children in a square. And when ears are deaf he does not simply leave them so. He opens them, as he opened the ears of the deaf in Galilee, by the same word that once said, let there be light. Every person who has ever truly heard him has heard because he first spoke into their silence.

verseByVerse.quote: "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn." For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, "He has a demon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The children complain: we played wedding music, and you would not dance; we played funeral songs, and you would not mourn. So it was with John, who fasted and lived austerely, and people said he had a demon.

We played the flute for you, and you did not dance. Children played at weddings, with pipes and dancing. One group strikes up the wedding tune, and nobody dances.

We sang a dirge, and you did not mourn. So they switch to funerals, with wailing and beating the chest, and nobody mourns. Whatever is offered, the others sit there. Notice that the complaint is not that the second group played badly. It is that they would not play at all: not that they preferred a different game, but that no game was acceptable. The picture is of sulky, childish people who cannot be pleased. No key fits this lock.

The symmetry. Matthew has built it on purpose, and it is the whole force of the picture. The dirge that got no mourning corresponds to John, all fasting and warning and judgment. The pipe that got no dancing corresponds to Jesus, at Levi’s table and at the wedding at Cana and in the houses of sinners. Two men, opposite in every visible respect, and one generation with an answer ready for each. This generation is not weighing John against Jesus and preferring one. It is refusing both, and the refusals contradict each other.

For John came neither eating nor drinking. John lived an austere life: fasting, eating locusts and wild honey, drinking no wine (3:4; Luke 1:15). His message was the funeral song: mourn for your sins, for the axe is at the root.

And they say, He has a demon. His strictness was dismissed as madness or possession. It is the strongest thing that could be said, and it is the same accusation they made against Jesus (9:34) and will make again (12:24). It is the standard explanation for a man whose authority is undeniable and whose message is unacceptable: something is clearly at work in him, so it must not be God. And notice who said it. The people who called John demonised had not gone out to the wilderness to hear him. They had stayed at home and formed a view.

A diagnostic worth keeping. When the same person objects to strictness as fanaticism and to warmth as laxity, the objection is not really about either, and no change of manner will meet it, because the thing being resisted is not the manner. Unbelief is endlessly resourceful in finding objections. The problem was not the messengers’ style but the hearers’ hearts.

How do I tell a fair criticism of a preacher from this kind of excuse? Fair criticism asks whether what was said is true to Scripture, and it is willing to be answered. The excuse in these verses changes its complaint whenever the messenger changes, and is never satisfied. Ask yourself honestly: if this preacher did exactly what I say I want, would I then obey what he says from the Bible? If the honest answer is no, the problem is not the preacher. Christians may and should test teaching (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1). But testing is aimed at the message, and it ends in obedience when the message proves true.

In a sentence. Like sulky children who refuse every game, the people rejected John’s call to mourn, and dismissed him as demon-possessed.

On a Tuesday. List the reasons you have given, perhaps only to yourself, for not acting on something God has said through a preacher, a friend or the Bible. Too strict, too relaxed, too serious, too cheerful, too long. Then ask whether those reasons would survive if the messenger changed. If you would find another reason, the problem may be in you, and the remedy is repentance, not a better preacher.

For worship. God is patient with his people beyond all our deserving. He did not send one kind of messenger and give up. He sent the stern prophet in the desert, and then he sent his own Son to the dinner tables, and to both of them his generation said no. Still he did not withdraw the invitation. He played the funeral song so that sinners might mourn, and the wedding song so that they might rejoice, and in the end his Son both mourned at a tomb and promised a marriage supper. There is no tune God has not played to call us home.
verseByVerse.note: Children played at weddings and funerals; some refused whichever game was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, "Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds. Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus came, eating and drinking, and people said he was a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Yet wisdom is proved right by what it does. Then Jesus began to rebuke the towns where most of his miracles had been done, because they had not repented.

The Son of Man came eating and drinking. Jesus’ ministry was the wedding song: joy, feasting, the bridegroom present (9:15). He ate with all kinds of people, at Levi’s table and with Pharisees and with crowds on a hillside (9:10).

Look at him, a glutton and a drunkard. The insult is not casual abuse. It is a legal formula, and everybody hearing it knew it. Deuteronomy sets out what parents are to do with a son who will not be governed. They are to bring him to the elders at the gate and say that he is stubborn and rebellious, will not obey their voice, and is a glutton and a drunkard; and the men of the city are to stone him (Deuteronomy 21:20–21). So the crowd is not merely calling Jesus greedy. They are laying against him the formal charge for a son who has broken with his father’s authority, and the penalty attached to it is death. Said of this man, who always did what pleased his Father, it is a more terrible charge than any of them understood, and it ended, in a sense, as the law said it should: outside the city, condemned.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners! Meant with equal contempt, and gloriously true (9:10–13). It was intended as evidence for the prosecution. It has turned out to be the best short description of him anyone produced during his lifetime, and it was produced by his enemies. The church has treasured it ever since. Jesus is the friend of sinners.

The point. John fasted, and they rejected him; Jesus feasted, and they rejected him. The problem was not the messengers’ style but the people’s hearts. They did not want God’s message in any form it came.

Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds. Wisdom here is God’s wisdom, at work in both John and Jesus. In Proverbs 8 wisdom is personified, present with God at creation. Justified is a courtroom word: declared to be in the right, vindicated. The generation has delivered its verdict on John and on Jesus, and that verdict will itself be overturned, not by argument but by results: the changed lives of sinners who repented, and the works of the Christ (v. 2, where Matthew used the same word, deeds). Some see Jesus here as Wisdom itself in person, as Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). A small textual note: some manuscripts read by her children, as in Luke 7:35. Nothing turns on it. Either the deeds vindicate wisdom, or the people she produces do.

A comfort for the misunderstood. The vindication of wisdom is not usually an explanation. It is a harvest, arriving later, in front of people who were not there for the accusation. If you have obeyed God and been misread for it, you are standing where Jesus stood. You do not need to win every argument. Let the fruit speak, and let God choose the day.

Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. The tone changes sharply. Jesus has defended John; now he turns to judge. Mighty works (dynameis) are miracles, deeds of power. Their purpose was to lead people to repentance, and they had not. The towns that saw the most are the ones under the sharpest condemnation, because the greatest privilege carries the greatest responsibility. To see the greatest miracles in history and stay unchanged is not neutrality. It is the deepest rejection there is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Jesus approved of gluttony or drunkenness. He ate and drank in moderation and holiness; the accusation was slander. Nor does being a friend of sinners mean that he joined in their sins. He befriended them to call them to repentance (Luke 5:32), and they did not leave his table the same.

Did Jesus drink wine? Yes. He came eating and drinking, and the charge of drunkenness was slander. Scripture condemns drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), not the cup itself, and calls wine a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15). Christians are free to drink in moderation, and free not to, and the strong should take care not to wound a weaker brother’s conscience or tempt someone who struggles with alcohol (Romans 14:21). Anyone for whom drink has become a master should abstain completely; freedom in Christ is never freedom to be enslaved again.

What does it mean for me that Jesus is the friend of sinners? First, it means he is your friend, if you have come to him: not a reluctant master who tolerates you, but one who chose to eat with people like you. Second, it shapes how you treat those outside the church. Jesus went to their tables, listened to them and welcomed them, without approving their sin and without hiding his call to repent. That means real friendships with unbelieving neighbours and colleagues, meals and time, not only invitations to events. You will be misunderstood for it, as he was. Keep your own life clean while you keep your door open.

In a sentence. The people rejected Jesus’ joy as they had rejected John’s austerity, and even branded him a rebellious son, but God’s wisdom is proved right by its results.

On a Tuesday. Think of one person others avoid: the awkward colleague, the neighbour with a reputation, the young man nobody at church talks to. Make one move towards them this week, a coffee, a meal, a real conversation. Do it for the sake of the friend of sinners, who did the same for you.

For worship. They called him a glutton and a drunkard, and a friend of tax collectors and sinners, and they meant it as an indictment. We say it back to him as praise. He came eating and drinking because he is the Bridegroom, and he sat at the tables of the unclean because he had come to make them clean. The rebellious son of Deuteronomy was to be taken outside the city and put to death; the obedient Son was taken outside the city and put to death in the place of the rebels. Now he is preparing a table, and the guests will be the very people his enemies said he should not have eaten with.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, Chorazin and Bethsaida! If the miracles done in you had been done in the pagan cities of Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. On judgment day, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for you.

Woe to you. Woe is a cry of grief and warning, the opposite of blessed (5:3–12). It announces coming disaster, but with sorrow, not glee. The prophets used it (Isaiah 5:8–23). Jesus does not pronounce it as a man glad to be proved right. He pronounces it as one who will weep over Jerusalem (23:37).

Chorazin. A town about two miles (three kilometres) north of Capernaum, in the hills. Chorazin is not mentioned anywhere else in the Gospels except Luke’s parallel. The Gospels record no miracle there, yet Jesus says many were done, which shows that the Gospels record only a fraction of what he did (John 21:25). Today Chorazin is a field of black basalt ruins, including a later synagogue.

Bethsaida. A fishing village on the northern shore of the lake, the hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Jesus fed the five thousand nearby (Luke 9:10) and healed a blind man there (Mark 8:22–26).

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon. Tyre and Sidon were wealthy Gentile ports on the Mediterranean coast, north of Galilee, condemned by the prophets for their pride, wealth and wickedness (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28). To Jews they were symbols of pagan arrogance. The comparison is devastating: the pagan cities will fare better on judgment day than the privileged Jewish towns.

They would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Sackcloth was rough cloth of goat’s hair, worn in mourning. Ashes were sprinkled on the head or sat in. Both were signs of deep grief and repentance (Jonah 3:5–8; Daniel 9:3). Pagan Nineveh did it at one sermon from a reluctant prophet. The Jewish towns that saw the Son of God did not.

But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. Greater privilege brings greater responsibility (see 10:15). Greater light means greater accountability, and greater judgment if it is refused. The miracles of Jesus were not entertainment. They were the final call to repentance.

A question about knowledge. Notice that Jesus does not say that Tyre and Sidon might have repented. He says they would have. God knows not only what happens but what would have happened in other circumstances. He knows the road not taken as exactly as the road taken. That is a staggering claim about the mind of God, and it should not be hurried past. Some theologians call this middle knowledge, and use it to explain election: God chooses those he foresees would believe in the circumstances he places them in. The Reformed tradition affirms that God knows all possibilities, but holds that his decree, not his foreknowledge of what people would do, is the basis of election (Ephesians 1:4–5; Westminster 3.2).

Then why did God not send the miracles to Tyre? Thoughtful readers stop dead here. If he knew they would have turned, why were the works done in towns that would not? Be honest about what we are not told. Scripture nowhere explains why the light falls where it falls. It says that God determines the times and places in which people live (Acts 17:26), and it draws a line we are not invited to cross: the secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children (Deuteronomy 29:29). When Paul reached this wall he did not climb it; he asked instead who we are to answer back to God (Romans 9:20). And notice where Jesus aims the sentence. He is not lecturing on the distribution of grace across the nations. He is indicting two towns that saw everything and did nothing. The comparison measures their guilt, not Tyre’s. So the verse is a mirror, not a riddle. The question it presses is not why others were given less light, but what you have done with the light you were given, and the man asking the first question is very often avoiding the second.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God was unfair to Tyre and Sidon. They were judged for their own sins, according to the light they had (Romans 1:18–21; 2:12). But those who had greater light, and rejected it, are more guilty. Nor does it mean that miracles inevitably produce repentance. Chorazin saw them and did not repent. Repentance is the work of God in the heart.

Will some people be punished more than others in hell? Yes. Jesus says it will be more bearable for some than for others on the day of judgment (see also Luke 12:47–48). Hell is real, conscious and eternal, and no one there is innocent; but God is perfectly just, and the judgment of each person is measured by what they did with what they knew. The sobering application is not for the pagan who never heard but for the person who has heard the most. Every sermon, every Bible on the shelf, every praying parent adds to the light, and therefore to the accountability, of someone who will not come.

What about people who have never heard of Jesus? They will be judged for their own sins against the light they had, in creation and conscience, not for rejecting a gospel they never heard (Romans 1:20; 2:12–16). But no one is saved by that light. Salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–15). That is exactly why the church sends missionaries, and why the right response to this question is not speculation but prayer, giving and going.

In a sentence. The towns that saw Jesus’ miracles and refused to repent will face a heavier judgment than pagan cities that never saw them.

On a Tuesday. Write down the light you have received: a Christian upbringing, a Bible, faithful preaching, believing friends. Then ask what it has produced in you. Privilege that is ignored becomes judgment; privilege that is received becomes thanksgiving. Pray today for one unreached people group, who have far less light than you.

For worship. The God who knows every road not taken is the God who chose to send his Son down this one, to the hills of Galilee and to towns that would not listen. His judgment is exact, and his knowledge is perfect, and no one will be wronged on that day. And the same Jesus who pronounced the woes took the woe himself. He wept over the cities that would not come, and then he bore the wrath of God for all who would. Mercy has never been wasted by God, only refused by us.
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities. Sackcloth was coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Capernaum, Jesus’ own base, which thought itself raised high: it will be brought down to Hades. If Sodom had seen such miracles, it would still be standing. On judgment day it will be more bearable for Sodom than for Capernaum.

And you, Capernaum. Jesus’ own town (4:13; 9:1), the base of his ministry, the city most saturated with his presence and his works: the centurion’s servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, the paralysed man let down through the roof, Jairus’ daughter, and many more.

Will you be exalted to heaven? The words are a quotation, and the original is the most famous taunt in the Old Testament. Isaiah 14 addresses the king of Babylon, who said in his heart that he would ascend to heaven and set his throne above the stars of God, and was brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit (Isaiah 14:13–15). That is addressed to the proudest power on earth at the height of its arrogance. Jesus takes it and applies it to a fishing town on the north shore of a lake: perhaps a thousand or so people, a customs post, a synagogue and a beach. The disproportion is the point. Capernaum had no imperial ambitions. What it had was the Son of God living in it, and it received him as a local celebrity and went on with the fishing. And the sentence written for Babylon fits it exactly, because the pride that does not need God is the same in a palace and a fishing village.

You will be brought down to Hades. Hades is the Greek name for the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol), the lowest place. Here it means deep humiliation and judgment. And the ground itself has kept the record. All three towns named in these verses are gone. Chorazin is a field of ruins. Capernaum is an archaeological site with a fence and no inhabitants. The site of Bethsaida is still argued over, which is to say that the town Jesus named cannot now be found with certainty. They were not destroyed in any dramatic way that anyone recorded. They simply declined and emptied, and the lake went on without them.

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. Sodom, the most notorious city of judgment in the Bible (Genesis 19; 10:15), would have repented if it had seen what Capernaum saw. Sodom is gone, and so, now, is Capernaum.

But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you. Even Sodom’s judgment will be lighter than Capernaum’s. The irony is bitter: the town that hosted the Son of God will be brought lower than the town that became the byword for depravity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that everyone in Capernaum rejected Jesus. Peter, Andrew, Matthew and others came to faith there. The town as a whole did not repent. Nor does it mean that physical nearness to Jesus saves. Capernaum had Jesus living in it, and still did not repent.

A guard for the tender conscience. This passage frightens the wrong people. The condemnation falls on towns that watched the works and were unmoved. It is not aimed at the person who has heard a great deal and worries that he has not responded well enough. That worry is itself a response, and Chorazin was not troubled by anything. If you are troubled, go to Christ with it; the trouble is a sign that he is still speaking to you.

I grew up in church and know it all. Am I Capernaum? Only if you have heard it all and never actually turned to Christ. Capernaum’s sin was not that it saw much but that it did not repent. Familiarity is the danger: the gospel can become so ordinary that it no longer surprises you, and what no longer surprises you no longer moves you. The way out is simple and humbling. Stop treating your knowledge as if it were faith. Come to Jesus today as a sinner who needs him, as if you were hearing for the first time, and ask him to make the old words new.

In a sentence. Capernaum, which saw more of Jesus than any other town and still did not repent, will be judged more severely than Sodom.

On a Tuesday. Being near Jesus, at church, in a Christian family, among believers, is not the same as turning to him. Take ten minutes today to tell him plainly that you are a sinner, that you trust him and not your background, and that you want to follow him. If you have done that before, do it again; repentance is not a door you go through once but a road you keep walking.

For worship. The Lord of glory made his home in an ordinary town and walked its streets for months, healing its sick and eating at its tables. Such is the humility of the Son of God, that he would live among people who would ignore him. And such is his holiness, that he will not pretend their indifference did not matter. Proud Babylon fell, and proud Capernaum fell, but the King who lived in Capernaum was himself brought down to the grave, and raised from it, so that everyone who humbles himself might be lifted up with him and never be brought down again.
verseByVerse.note: Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus declared, "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very time, Jesus prayed: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and learned and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was your gracious will.

At that time Jesus declared. The word (apokritheis) literally means answered. Jesus responds to the unbelief of the cities by turning to his Father in prayer. That is the most striking thing about the passage. Rejection does not shake him; he rests in the Father’s plan.

I thank you, Father. Jesus calls God Father with the intimacy of the only Son. He gives thanks even in the face of rejection, at the turning point of the chapter.

Lord of heaven and earth. God is sovereign over all things. What he does, he has the right to do, and the Son delights in it.

That you have hidden these things. These things are the truths of the kingdom: who Jesus is, and what his works mean.

From the wise and understanding. The pairing is a set phrase from a judgment oracle. Isaiah puts it in God’s mouth against the religious establishment of his day: the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden (Isaiah 29:14). Paul quotes the same verse to explain why the cross looks foolish (1 Corinthians 1:19). So Jesus is not making a general remark about clever people. He is reaching for the specific text in which God says he will confound the professionally religious, and applying it to the men who have just decided that John had a demon and that he was a drunkard. They are not truly wise, but wise in their own eyes: the scribes, the Pharisees and the experts proud of their learning. God hides the truth from the proud, in judgment on their pride (1 Corinthians 1:18–29).

And revealed them to little children. The word is stronger than little children. Nēpioi means infants: those who cannot yet speak, entirely dependent, with no accomplishments and no capacity to acquire any. It is the disciples, fishermen, tax collectors and sinners. The contrast is not between the educated and the simple. It is between people who can do something and people who can do nothing at all. God reveals the truth to those who receive it as a child receives from a parent (18:3–4). Revelation is God’s gift: no one can work it out for himself (16:17).

Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. Literally, for thus it was good pleasure before you. The word (eudokia) is the same idea as Ephesians 1:5, 9: the Father’s sovereign good pleasure. Notice what the prayer does with the hiding. Jesus does not lament it or apologise for it. He thanks the Father for it. He does not merely accept this; he rejoices in it (Luke 10:21). That is the harder half, and it should not be softened. The concealment is God’s own act and his good pleasure, and the Son is glad about it. There is a mercy in it too, since a kingdom that could be reached by cleverness would be closed to almost everybody. But the passage does not offer that as an excuse. It offers thanks.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that education or intelligence are bad, or that God only saves the uneducated. The man praying this knew the Scriptures better than anyone alive and argued with the best-trained minds in the land, and beat them. He chose Paul, the most thoroughly educated man of his generation. The church has never been able to obey this Gospel without hard thinking, and it has suffered when it tried. What is condemned is not intelligence but self-sufficiency, and there is a form of it peculiar to the well-taught, which consists in having enough answers not to need anything. God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). Nor does God’s hiding make those who reject Christ innocent victims. They were responsible for refusing the light (vv. 20–24). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility stand side by side in this passage: the cities are condemned for not repenting (v. 20), and the Father hides and reveals according to his will (v. 25). And the very next verses invite everyone who is weary to come (v. 28). God’s sovereign choice does not limit the free offer of the gospel; it guarantees that some will come.

Where Christians differ over God’s choice. Arminians hold that God reveals the truth to those he foresees will be humble and believe, so that the little children are those who humble themselves and respond, and God reveals himself in answer to their openness. Reformed theology holds that God’s revealing is his sovereign, gracious choice, which creates the humility and faith (v. 27; Ephesians 1:4–5; 2:8). Verdict: God’s revealing is according to his good pleasure (v. 26), not caused by anything in us. The openness is itself God’s gift. That is why it is grace, and why there is no room for boasting. Yet Jesus sets this beside two other truths: the cities that did not repent are guilty, and the invitation that follows is to everyone who labours. God’s choosing never cancels human responsibility, and it never closes the door on anyone who comes.

Is it unfair of God to hide the truth from some? No. Those from whom it is hidden are not eager seekers turned away at the door. They are proud people who have already rejected the light they had, and God gives them over to what they chose (Romans 1:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:10–11). No one is owed revelation. That anyone sees is pure mercy. And no one who wants Christ is ever refused him; the wanting itself is the sign that the Father is revealing him.

How do I know whether I am one of the little children? Not by finding something impressive in yourself, but by the opposite. Do you know you cannot save yourself? Do you look to Christ and find him beautiful, and want him? Do the Scriptures speak to you, however imperfectly you understand them? Those are the marks of a heart to which the Father has revealed the Son. You did not produce them; they were given. And if you are unsure, do what the next verse says: come to him. No one who comes is turned away (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Jesus thanked the Father for hiding the truth from the proud and revealing it to the humble, according to his gracious will.

On a Tuesday. If you understand the gospel, it is because God revealed it to you, not because you were cleverer than your neighbour. Thank him for it by name today.
