Then come to his word this week as a child and not as a critic: open it asking to be taught, and obey what you understand before you argue about what you do not.

For worship. Here is the Son at prayer in the hour of his rejection, and his prayer is thanksgiving. He rejoices that the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, has chosen to pass by the proud and to bend down to infants. That is the gospel in a sentence: God does not wait for us to climb up to him, because we cannot; he stoops to those who can do nothing, and shows them his Son. Every believer is a witness that the Father’s good pleasure is kind, and the Son’s joy over it has not ended. He is glad about you.

parallels.desc: God chose what is foolish in the world

verseByVerse.quote: All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declares that the Father has handed over all things to him. Only the Father truly knows the Son, and only the Son truly knows the Father, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Then he invites everyone who is weary and burdened to come to him for rest.

All things have been handed over to me by my Father. All authority, all knowledge, all revelation. Before the resurrection Jesus already claims what he will declare after it: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (28:18). Handed over is the language of passing on an inheritance or a tradition. The Father has entrusted everything to the Son.

And no one knows the Son except the Father. The Son’s identity is a mystery known fully only to God. The crowds and the cities did not understand who Jesus was; only the Father knows him completely.

And no one knows the Father except the Son. An astonishing claim. That the Father knows the Son perfectly is not surprising; God knows everything. That the Son knows the Father with the same completeness, and that no one else does, places him on the far side of the line that divides creatures from God, because a creature does not comprehend his Maker. This is a claim to equality with God, as a son shares his father’s nature.

The thunderbolt. This verse has been nicknamed the Johannine thunderbolt: a sentence that reads exactly like the Gospel of John, dropped without warning into Matthew. The Father handing all things to the Son, the mutual knowing, the Son as the only one who can reveal the Father, the Son choosing to whom he does it: any of these would sit unremarked in John 5 or 10 (John 1:18; 10:15; 14:6–9). And it sits here, in Matthew, and again in Luke (Luke 10:22). That quietly disposes of an argument made for two centuries, that the high view of Christ is a late development found only in John while the earlier Gospels present a simpler figure. The same high view of Jesus is found in all the Gospels.

And anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Chooses (boulētai) means wills, decides. Knowledge of God comes only through Christ, as he chooses to reveal it. The Son does what the Father does: he reveals according to his will (vv. 25–26). And this last clause turns the whole thing outward: a door in a wall that was otherwise sheer.

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden. Then the most abrupt turn in the Gospel, and it should be felt. The sentence before is as high and remote as anything Jesus ever said: no one knows the Father, the knowledge is exclusive, it is given at the Son’s discretion. It is the language of a locked door. And the very next word is: come. No preparation, no conditions attached, no narrowing. Having just established that he alone holds the knowledge of God, he turns and calls anybody who is tired. The two halves belong together and neither works without the other. An invitation from someone with lesser credentials would not be worth accepting, and credentials without an invitation would leave everyone outside. The one who holds the only key opens the door himself and asks people in.

Who are the weary? Labour means to toil to the point of exhaustion. Heavy laden means carrying a heavy load, like a pack animal. Especially they are those burdened by the religious leaders’ demands: the scribes and Pharisees tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders (23:4). They are also everyone weary of sin and guilt, of trying to earn God’s favour, of anxiety and grief and the troubles of life: moral failure, religious performance, all of it. All are invited. All.

And I will give you rest. Not more rules, but rest. The word (anapausis) means refreshment, relief, ceasing from labour. Jesus offers what only God can give, rest for the soul (Jeremiah 6:16; Exodus 33:14, where the LORD promises his presence will go with Moses and give him rest). And he gives it himself, personally: I will give.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sovereign revealing contradicts the open invitation. Both are true together. The invitation goes to all; those who come are those to whom the Son reveals the Father. No one who comes will be turned away (John 6:37). Nor is the rest Jesus gives a life without effort or duty. It is rest from the burden of earning God’s favour and from the weight of sin, so that we can serve him freely (v. 29).

What does coming to Jesus actually look like? It is not a physical journey or a special ceremony. To come to him is to trust him: to stop relying on your own efforts to put yourself right with God, and to rely on him instead, on his death for sinners and his risen life. In practice it begins with prayer, in your own words: telling him that you are weary and guilty, that you believe he can give you rest, and that you give yourself to him. It continues every day, because Christians keep coming. Every time you are burdened, the invitation is still open.

I have come to Jesus, and I am still tired. What is wrong? Perhaps nothing. The rest he promises is first rest of soul: peace with God, freedom from condemnation, the end of trying to earn his love. It does not remove every burden of life at once, and it does not cure physical exhaustion; for that he also gave sleep and sabbath and the care of others. But ask honestly whether you have picked up again a yoke he lifted off: trying to prove yourself, carrying guilt he has forgiven, worrying over what you have handed to him. Bring that to him specifically. Coming is not once for all; it is the daily habit of laying things down.

In a sentence. Jesus, who alone knows the Father and has all authority, invites everyone who is exhausted and burdened to come to him for rest.

On a Tuesday. Name, to yourself, what is weighing you down today: guilt, anxiety, religious performance, a relationship, a decision. Then come to Jesus with it in prayer, now, in so many words. Do not wait to feel fit to come. The invitation is to the weary, not the rested.

For worship. Behold the Son, to whom all things have been handed over, who alone knows the Father as the Father knows him, who holds the only key to the knowledge of God. And behold what he does with it. He does not keep the door shut to protect his glory. He opens it, and calls the exhausted and the burdened, the failures and the frauds, by name, and says: come to me. All the authority of heaven bends down in one word of welcome, and the One who could command chooses to invite.

parallels.desc: the Father has given all things into his hand
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.quote: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take my yoke on you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. My yoke is easy and my burden is light.

Take my yoke upon you. A yoke was a wooden frame placed over the necks of two oxen so that they could pull a plough or a cart together. In Jewish teaching the yoke was a picture of submission: rabbis spoke of the yoke of the law and the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, meaning the acceptance of God’s rule and commandments, as interpreted by the teacher. The Pharisees’ yoke was heavy; their commands multiplied beyond bearing (23:4). Jesus invites people to take his yoke instead: to submit to him and become his disciples. Not the abolition of demand, but a different kind of demand, borne with him. Rest does not come by throwing off every yoke, but by taking the right one.

And learn from me. Become my disciples, my students. Learn his teaching, and learn him (Ephesians 4:20). The yoke is the classroom, and the teacher is pulling alongside.

For I am gentle and lowly in heart. Pause over these words, because the eye slides past them. In all four Gospels this is the only place where Jesus tells us what his own heart is like. He says many things about himself, the door, the vine, the bread, the light, but only here does he open the very centre of his being. And what is there? Not harsh and demanding. Not exacting and disappointed. Gentle and lowly. Gentle (praus) is the same word as meek in the beatitude (5:5). Lowly (tapeinos) means humble, unassuming, the very opposite of the proud religion that had been crushing these people. Unlike the harsh teachers who loaded burdens on others, Jesus is gentle with the weak and humble toward the lowly. He does not break a bruised reed (12:20). And this is the settled disposition of his heart, not a mood he is in on his better days. When you come to him weary, ashamed, having failed again, you are not coming to a reluctant judge who tolerates you. You are coming to the gentlest heart in the universe, who is more ready to receive you than you are to come. The Puritans loved to dwell here, and they were right to: this is the truest thing about Jesus, told to us in his own words, so that we would never be afraid to draw near.

And you will find rest for your souls. From Jeremiah 6:16, where God tells Israel to ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it, and find rest for their souls. But they refused to walk in it. Jesus offers the same rest, and he is himself the ancient path that Jeremiah’s generation would not take. The rest is not the rest of having nothing to do. It is the rest of Psalm 23, the rest of the sheep who has found the right shepherd.

For my yoke is easy. Easy (chrēstos) means kind, well-fitting, good. A carpenter like Jesus would have known how a yoke was shaped to fit the ox’s neck so that it did not chafe. His yoke fits. It is easy not because it asks little but because he bears it with us, and because it is the yoke of love and not of law-keeping to earn acceptance.

And my burden is light. Not that following Jesus involves no demands (16:24), but that his commands are not burdensome (1 John 5:3), because he gives the strength to keep them and carries the weight with us. The burden of earning salvation is replaced by the light burden of serving a gracious Master who has already saved us. Augustine said that the burden of Christ is like wings to a bird: they seem to add weight, but they lift it up.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the Christian life is effortless or free of suffering. Jesus has just spoken of persecution and the cross (10:16–39). The yoke is easy in comparison with the crushing burden of sin and works-religion, and because we bear it with him. Nor does rest mean laziness. Oxen in a yoke work, but they work beside a strong partner.

What is Christ’s yoke, concretely? It is his rule over your life, received as his disciple: his teaching to believe and his commands to obey, learned in his company. Concretely that means listening to his word, praying, belonging to his church, being baptised as he commanded, forgiving as you have been forgiven, and loving God and neighbour. It is not a new list of rules to earn his favour. It is the shape of life lived next to him, by people he has already accepted. The difference is not in how many commands there are but in who you are pulling with, and why.

If his burden is light, why does the Christian life feel so hard? Because it is hard, and Jesus never said otherwise: there is a cross in it, and a fight with sin, and suffering. But the hardness is the strain of growth and battle, not the crushing weight of having to save yourself. Often the heaviness we feel is not his yoke at all, but a yoke we made: perfectionism, people-pleasing, the need to be admired, worry about what we cannot control. Those chafe because they were never made for us. His yoke rubs only where our pride resists it, and the closer we walk with him, the lighter it becomes.

In a sentence. Submit to Jesus and learn from him, because he is gentle and lowly in heart, and his yoke is well-fitting and his burden light, giving rest to the soul.

On a Tuesday. Identify a yoke of your own making that you are carrying: perfectionism, people-pleasing, trying to earn God’s love by your performance, fear of what others think. Name it to Jesus, and ask him to take it. Then take one concrete step under his yoke instead: one command of his you will obey today, gladly, because you are already loved.

For worship. Blessed be the Lord who told us what his heart is like. He might have said that he is holy, and he is; that he is mighty, and he is; that he is just, and he is. But when he opened his heart to the weary, he said that it was gentle and lowly. The Lord of heaven and earth puts his neck into the yoke beside ours and takes the weight. He who had all things handed over to him took on himself the heaviest burden of all, the sin of his people, and carried it to the cross, so that nothing would be left for us but a yoke that fits and a burden that lifts like wings. There is rest for our souls, because there is such a heart in him.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals to pull together; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

parallels.desc: you will find rest for your souls
a yoke our fathers could not bear

11.theology: The gentleness of Christ. “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (v. 29) is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus describes his own inner character. The word “gentle” (praus) is the same word used of Moses in Numbers 12:3 and of the meek in the Beatitudes. Christ’s gentleness is not weakness but strength under restraint: the one who has all authority in heaven and earth bends to receive the weary. Thomas Goodwin wrote that Christ’s heart is more moved by our miseries than by all his own glory. The invitation “Come to me” is the theological centre of grace: not “make yourself worthy,” not “prepare yourself,” not “clean yourself up first,” but “come.”
11.examples:
Then: John the Baptist in prison represents every believer whose faith has been tested by circumstances that did not match expectation. The answer Jesus gives is always the same: look at what the Scriptures say I would do, and look at what I am doing. Faith is anchored in the word.

Now: The invitation of 11:28–30 is the greatest recruitment speech in history. Every generation of tired, guilt-laden, performance-exhausted people is addressed. The church that does not centre its preaching on this invitation has lost the gospel. The yoke of Christ is easy not because it makes no demands but because the one who makes the demands has already borne their weight.

12.title: Lord of the Sabbath
12.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. <sup>2</sup>But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” <sup>3</sup>He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup>how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? <sup>5</sup>Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? <sup>6</sup>I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. <sup>7</sup>And if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless. <sup>8</sup>For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>9</sup>He went on from there and entered their synagogue. <sup>10</sup>And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”— so that they might accuse him. <sup>11</sup>He said to them, “Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? <sup>12</sup>Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” <sup>13</sup>Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. <sup>14</sup>But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him. <sup>15</sup>Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all <sup>16</sup>and ordered them not to make him known. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: <sup>18</sup>“Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. <sup>19</sup>He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; <sup>20</sup>a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory; <sup>21</sup>and in his name the Gentiles will hope.” <sup>22</sup>Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. <sup>23</sup>And all the people were amazed, and said, “Can this be the Son of David?” <sup>24</sup>But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons.” <sup>25</sup>Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? <sup>27</sup>And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>28</sup>But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>29</sup>Or how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>30</sup>Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>31</sup>Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>32</sup>And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. <sup>33</sup>“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit. <sup>34</sup>You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. <sup>35</sup>The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. <sup>36</sup>I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, <sup>37</sup>for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” <sup>38</sup>Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” <sup>39</sup>But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. <sup>40</sup>For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. <sup>41</sup>The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>42</sup>The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>43</sup>“When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none. <sup>44</sup>Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. <sup>45</sup>Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.” <sup>46</sup>While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. <sup>48</sup>But he replied to the man who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” <sup>49</sup>And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>50</sup>For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”
12.overview:
Chapter 12 marks a decisive turning point in Matthew. The Pharisees, having sought ways to trap Jesus, now plot his destruction (v. 14). The conflict comes to a head over the Sabbath, the temple, and the identity of Jesus. Jesus makes two enormous claims: “something greater than the temple is here” (v. 6) and “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” (v. 8). The temple was the dwelling place of God; the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant. To claim authority over both is to claim divine identity.

The chapter also introduces the sin against the Holy Spirit — attributing the works of the Spirit to Beelzebul. This is not a sudden slip but the settled, hardened rejection of the evidence of God’s kingdom. The Pharisees have seen the blind healed, the deaf hearing, the demon-possessed set free; they call it the work of Satan. This deliberate, informed, hardened reversal of moral and spiritual categories is the sin that cannot be forgiven — not because the blood of Christ is insufficient but because the one who commits it has placed himself permanently beyond repentance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Lord of the Sabbath and Servant of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 12 opens the extended conflict section of Matthew. The Pharisees attack Jesus twice on Sabbath observance: first for his disciples plucking grain, then for healing a man with a withered hand. Jesus defends both from Scripture and declares himself Lord of the Sabbath. The Pharisees then plot his destruction, and Matthew quotes Isaiah's first Servant Song at length, identifying Jesus as the gentle, bruised-reed-not-breaking Servant of the LORD. Note the link across the chapter break: "at that time" follows immediately on the offer of rest (11:28-29), so the man who has just promised rest is challenged about the day of rest. And Matthew alone adds that the disciples were hungry, because that is the hinge of the argument — David was hungry too. The charge was not theft (Deut. 23:25 permits plucking by hand) but Sabbath-breaking: rabbinic tradition listed thirty-nine forbidden classes of work, and reaping, threshing and winnowing are among them. The David precedent is stranger than it looks — David lied to Ahimelech, and the episode ends with Doeg reporting it and Saul slaughtering eighty-five priests (1 Sam. 22:18-19). Jesus reaches for an incident with a body count, and the parallel is exact: the anointed king not yet in his kingdom, hungry, with his men, pursued. The priestly argument: the Sabbath doubled the temple workload (two extra lambs, Num. 28:9-10), so the Sabbath has always yielded to something. And "something greater than the temple" is neuter — as are "greater than Jonah" (v. 41) and "greater than Solomon" (v. 42). Three times in one chapter, and the three are the pillars of Israel's life: the temple where God met his people, the prophet through whom he spoke, the king through whom he ruled. The trap at v. 10 is precise: rabbinic law allowed Sabbath healing only where life was in danger, and a withered hand is not — so the honest answer on their terms was "wait until sundown", and Jesus heals anyway. Note which day the murder plot is formed on: restoring a hand is a Sabbath violation; convening to arrange a killing is not. Mark records the only named anger of Jesus in the Gospels at exactly this point (Mk. 3:5). And the Servant Song is the longest OT quotation in Matthew — used, remarkably, to explain not a miracle but the absence of spectacle.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath controversies reveal the Pharisees' fundamental error: they have turned a gift (the Sabbath rest) into a burden, and a sign (rest pointing to God's shalom) into a system of control. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he fulfills it. He is the one in whom the true Sabbath rest is found (11:29) — the rest that the weekly day always pointed toward. The Servant Song quotation (Isa. 42:1-4) interprets his retreat from conflict not as weakness but as fulfillment: the Servant does not "quarrel or cry aloud" but pursues justice to victory through gentleness.
verseByVerse.examples: The healing of the withered hand poses the sharpest question of the controversy: "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" Jesus answers with an argument from worth: if you would rescue a sheep that fell in a pit on the Sabbath, how much more a person? The comparative worth of persons over animals is the premise; the compassionate action follows from it. Every Sabbath restriction that would prevent healing a human being has missed the Sabbath's point — the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, "Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One Sabbath, Jesus’ hungry disciples picked heads of grain as they walked through a field and ate them. The Pharisees protested that they were breaking the Sabbath.

Meaning first. Matthew 12 is the chapter in which opposition to Jesus hardens into a plot to kill him. It opens with two Sabbath disputes, in a grainfield and in a synagogue, where Jesus claims to be greater than the temple and Lord of the Sabbath, and heals a man’s withered hand. The Pharisees begin to plan his death, and Matthew answers with the longest Old Testament quotation in his Gospel: Isaiah’s portrait of the gentle Servant who will not break a bruised reed. Then the Pharisees say that Jesus casts out demons by Satan. Jesus shows the charge is absurd, announces that the kingdom of God has come, warns of the blasphemy against the Spirit, refuses any sign but the sign of Jonah, and ends by pointing to his disciples: here is my family. Through it all one claim rises: something greater than the temple, greater than Jonah, greater than Solomon is here.

At that time. The phrase links this straight back across the chapter break. Matthew has just recorded the invitation: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; you will find rest for your souls (11:28–29). And the very next thing that happens is a fight about the day of rest. The man who has offered rest to the exhausted is immediately challenged by men who had made the day of rest into work. Matthew has not arranged that by accident. The whole Sabbath controversy is to be read in the light of the offer made three verses earlier. Who gives true rest: the Pharisees’ rules, or Jesus?

The Sabbath. The seventh day, Saturday, from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday. God commanded Israel to rest from work on it, remembering both his own rest after creation (Exodus 20:8–11) and his rescue of Israel from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:12–15). It was a sign of the covenant between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13–17), a weekly gift of freedom for people who had once been slaves without a day off. By Jesus’ time Jewish teachers had built a detailed system of rules about what counted as work. The Mishnah, a later collection of rabbinic teaching, lists thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, among them reaping, threshing, winnowing and preparing food.

His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. Matthew adds a detail that Mark and Luke do not: they were hungry. He puts it in because it is the hinge of the argument he is about to record. David was hungry too, and that is the whole reason the precedent applies. They were not making a point about Sabbath law. They were walking through a field and had not eaten. The law allowed travellers to pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field, though not to put a sickle to it (Deuteronomy 23:25). So nobody is accusing them of theft. The issue was the day.

Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath. The charge is precise. A man walking through a field, pulling heads of grain, rubbing them between his palms to loosen the husk (Luke 6:1), and blowing the chaff away has, on a sufficiently determined reading, performed three of the thirty-nine forbidden works before breakfast: reaping, threshing and winnowing. That is the accusation. Not greed, not trespass. Harvesting, on a technicality, in a quantity that would fit in two hands. And they hold Jesus responsible, as a teacher was for his students. Notice too how closely they were watching. They are not concerned with the disciples’ hunger; they are concerned with the breach of their interpretation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the Sabbath command itself was bad or unimportant. It was God’s gift. The problem was the Pharisees’ traditions, which had turned the day of rest into a burden, and their harsh spirit, which cared more for the rule than for the hungry men in front of them. Jesus will answer them from the written Scriptures themselves, David, the priests and the prophets, against the tradition that had hardened around them.

Is it wrong for my family to have its own rules for Sunday? No. A family may wisely decide how it will keep the Lord’s Day: no homework, no shopping, a shared meal, a walk, time with church friends. Such arrangements can be a great blessing. The Pharisees’ fault was not having practices but treating their own additions as God’s law and condemning others by them. So keep your household customs, and explain them to your children as gifts, not as the measure of holiness. And never judge another Christian family because they draw the lines in a different place.

In a sentence. The Pharisees accused Jesus’ hungry disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking grain, according to their own rules.

On a Tuesday. Make a short list of the rules you live by that are not actually in the Bible: about clothes, music, schooling, drink, how others should spend Sunday. They may be wise. But ask whether you have begun to judge others by them. When you notice yourself watching someone else’s field to see what they are picking, stop, and ask instead whether they are hungry.

For worship. How kind is the God who gave his people a day of rest, and how kind is the Son who would not let it become a burden. The Pharisees watched the disciples’ hands; Jesus saw their hunger. The Lord who gave manna in the wilderness and a double portion before the Sabbath is the Lord who stood in this field, and he is still more concerned that his people are fed than that his critics are satisfied. He came to give rest, and he will not let anyone turn his gift into a yoke.
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered from Scripture: have you not read what David did when he and his men were hungry? He went into the house of God and ate the holy bread that only priests were allowed to eat.

Have you not read. Jesus says it six times in Matthew, always to the professionally religious: here, again two verses later, on divorce (19:4), on the children’s praise (21:16), on the rejected stone (21:42) and on the resurrection (22:31). He never asks a crowd that. He asks it of the men who had committed the text to memory, and the question is not whether they know the words but whether they have understood what they were reading. Of course they had read it. They had not understood it. It is the most withering thing a teacher can say to a scholar, and it is his standard opening.

What David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him. 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David was fleeing from King Saul. He came to the tabernacle at Nob and asked the priest Ahimelech for food, and there was none except the holy bread. And look at the state David was in. He was on the run from a king who wanted him dead. He told Ahimelech he was on the king’s business, which was not true. And the day ended in one of the worst atrocities in the Old Testament: Doeg the Edomite, who was standing there, reported it, and Saul had eighty-five priests of Nob put to the sword with their families (1 Samuel 22:18–19). Jesus reaches for an incident with a body count. Not a tidy precedent, but a desperate, compromised, disastrous day in the life of the anointed king who had not yet come into his kingdom.

How he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, were set on a golden table in the holy place each Sabbath, before the LORD (Leviticus 24:5–9). When they were replaced, the old loaves were eaten by the priests only, in a holy place.

Which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests. David broke a ceremonial law and was not condemned. The priest gave him the bread, and Scripture does not criticise it.

The argument. Two points. First, human need, hunger, can take priority over ceremonial rules. God’s ceremonial laws were never meant to keep people starving. Second, David was God’s anointed king, and he and his men were allowed this exception. And the parallel is exact. Here is the anointed King who has not yet come into his kingdom, hungry, with his men, pursued by the authorities. If the son of Jesse could eat the holy bread on such a day, the Son of David and his men may take a handful of grain.

A note for a reader with a harmony. Mark’s account names Abiathar as high priest at the time (Mark 2:26), while 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech, his father. It is a genuine difficulty, and several answers have been proposed, including that Mark’s phrase means in the passage about Abiathar, who is the dominant figure of that section. Matthew names nobody, so nothing here turns on it; it is noted only so that it is not a surprise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God’s laws can be ignored whenever it is convenient. Jesus is distinguishing God’s moral law from ceremonial regulations, and showing that the ceremonial laws were meant to serve people, not to harm them. Nor does it mean that the end justifies any means. David’s lie to Ahimelech is not approved; the bread is.

How do I tell God’s moral law from the ceremonial law? The ceremonial law covered the sacrifices, priesthood, festivals, food laws and rules of ritual purity. It was given to Israel as a picture of Christ and his cleansing, and it is fulfilled in him, so Christians no longer keep it (Hebrews 9–10; Mark 7:19; Colossians 2:16–17). The moral law expresses God’s unchanging character. It is summed up in the Ten Commandments and in loving God and neighbour, and the New Testament repeats it: do not murder, steal, lie or commit adultery, honour your parents, worship God alone. A useful test is whether the New Testament renews a command or says it is fulfilled. The one commandment Christians debate is the fourth, discussed at vv. 7–8.

In a sentence. Jesus pointed to David eating the holy bread to show that ceremonial rules give way to human need, especially for God’s anointed King and his men.

On a Tuesday. God’s laws are for our good. When a religious rule in your church or your own life hurts someone in real need, ask whether it has been misunderstood. Then look for one practical way this week to put someone’s need ahead of your convenience or your custom.

For worship. Behold the true Son of David, hungry in a cornfield with his men, rejected by the authorities, not yet on his throne. David received the holy bread from a priest; Jesus is himself the bread of life, and he gives himself to his hungry followers. The priests of Nob died because David came to them. The great High Priest would die so that hungry sinners could come to him, and eat, and live.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gave a second argument: the priests in the temple work on the Sabbath, offering sacrifices, and are not guilty. And something greater than the temple is here.

Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? The priestly argument is stronger than it looks. The Sabbath did not reduce the temple’s workload; it doubled it. The daily offering was one lamb morning and evening, and on the Sabbath two more lambs were added (Numbers 28:9–10). The bread of the Presence was changed on the Sabbath (Leviticus 24:8). And a boy born on a Sabbath was circumcised on the following Sabbath, because the eighth day is the eighth day (John 7:22–23). So on the one day in seven when all Israel rested, the priests worked harder than usual, inside the sanctuary, by God’s command, and no one had ever suggested they were sinning. That establishes the principle Jesus needs: the Sabbath yields to something, and it always has. The question was never whether there are higher obligations, but what they are. Temple service took priority over Sabbath rest.

I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. An astonishing claim. The temple was the most sacred place on earth, where God dwelt among his people and toward which the whole nation faced to pray. Jesus says something greater is here: himself. If temple service could override the Sabbath, how much more the service of the one greater than the temple. Jesus is God present among his people (1:23; John 2:19–21).

Three times greater. The Greek is neuter: not someone greater, but something. A reader might take that as modesty until he notices that Jesus does it twice more in this chapter: something greater than Jonah (v. 41), something greater than Solomon (v. 42). Three times, all neuter, all in one chapter. And the three things named are the three pillars of Israel’s life: the temple, the prophet and the king. The place where God met his people, the voice that called them back, the throne that ruled them. He does not merely say he is a better temple, a better prophet and a better king, which would already be blasphemy if it were not true. He says that something greater than all three is here, standing in a cornfield in the middle of an argument about breakfast. All three were God’s arrangements, and the arrangements are being quietly fulfilled in the presence of the One they were arranged for. The neuter may point to Jesus himself or to the kingdom he brings, but the point is the same.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Jesus despised the temple. He called it his Father’s house (21:13). But he is its fulfilment. The temple pointed to God dwelling with his people; in Jesus, God is with us in person.

What does this mean for where I worship? It means no building is a temple now. A church building is a useful room, not a holy house where God lives more than elsewhere. The temple of God today is Christ himself, and in him his people: you, together, are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit dwells in you (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22). So you meet God not by going to a sacred place but by coming to Christ, wherever you are. And you are part of a holy temple whenever the church gathers, which is a reason to gather gladly and not to treat it as optional.

In a sentence. If priests may work on the Sabbath for the temple, how much more may Jesus’ disciples serve him, since he is greater than the temple.

On a Tuesday. Pray today in an ordinary place, at the sink, on the bus, at your desk, and remember as you do that you need no temple to meet God, because the One greater than the temple has opened the way. Then plan to be with his gathered people on the Lord’s Day, the living temple where he has promised to be.

For worship. For a thousand years Israel faced the temple, and the smoke of sacrifice rose day and night, and the priests served without rest even on the day of rest. Then the Lord of the temple came, and stood in a field, and said quietly that something greater was here. He is the place where God and man meet. His body was destroyed and raised in three days, and in him we are brought near. Worship him, greater than the temple: God with us, in person.
verseByVerse.note: The priests worked hardest on the Sabbath, offering extra sacrifices.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you had known what this means, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice," you would not have condemned the guiltless. For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you had understood what God meant by “I desire mercy, not sacrifice”, you would not have condemned the innocent. For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. Hosea 6:6. Matthew is the only Gospel writer who quotes it, and he quotes it twice: once at Levi’s table, when the Pharisees objected to the company Jesus kept (9:13), and once here, when they object to his disciples eating. Both times the subject is food, and both times the objectors are Pharisees. At 9:13 Jesus told them to go and learn what the verse means; here he says that if they had known what it means, they would not have condemned the guiltless. God values compassion above ritual. Hosea was writing to a nation whose religious machinery was in excellent order and whose life was rotten: plenty of sacrifice, no faithfulness. God’s complaint was not that they had stopped worshipping but that the worship had become a substitute for what it was meant to produce. That is exactly the charge here, and it should make a careful reader uncomfortable. The men in this story were not lax. They were the most rigorous, disciplined, scripturally literate people in the land, and their failure came at the point of their strength.

You would not have condemned the guiltless. The disciples were innocent. They had broken the Pharisees’ traditions, not God’s law.

For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. The climax. The Sabbath was God’s day, the Sabbath to the LORD your God (Exodus 20:10). Jesus claims authority over it: he has the right to say what the Sabbath means and how it should be kept. Only God could make this claim. As the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3), the author of the law is also its most authoritative reader. Mark adds that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

The Sabbath and Christ. But there is more in the title than authority. Read straight on from the invitation a few sentences earlier: I will give you rest (11:28). Then: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. Matthew has set those side by side deliberately. The Sabbath was never merely a day off; from the beginning it was a signpost. God rested on the seventh day of creation, and Israel kept the day as a weekly rehearsal of a rest still ahead, a rest Joshua did not finally give them (Hebrews 4:8–9). Every Sabbath Israel ever kept was a finger pointing down the centuries at something it could not itself supply. Hebrews says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, entered by faith in Christ (Hebrews 4:1–11). So when Jesus calls himself lord of the Sabbath, he is not only claiming the right to interpret the day. He is claiming to be what the day was about. The rest the seventh day promised is finally not a date on the calendar but a Person, and he is standing in a cornfield being told off for letting hungry men eat. The Pharisees were guarding the signpost so fiercely that they could not see they were arguing with the destination. After his resurrection on the first day of the week, Christians gathered on that day, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Jesus abolished the principle of rest and worship. He kept the Sabbath himself, worshipping in the synagogue (Luke 4:16). But as Lord of the Sabbath, he fulfils it.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Some (Seventh-day Adventists, Seventh Day Baptists) hold that Christians must keep Saturday as the Sabbath. Many Reformed and Presbyterian Christians (following Westminster 21.7–8) hold that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy with rest from ordinary work and devotion to worship. Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day is binding as the Sabbath (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5), while Sunday is the Lord’s Day for the church’s gathering. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest. The Lord’s Day is not a burden of rules but a privilege: a gift for gathering with God’s people for worship and for rest. Christians who keep a stricter Sabbath should be respected, and none should be judged by others in this (Colossians 2:16).

Is it wrong to work on a Sunday? Some work must be done on any day: nurses, doctors, police, carers, farmers with animals. Jesus defended works of necessity and mercy, and no Christian in such a job should feel second-class. But where you have a choice, guard the gathering of the church; it is commanded whatever view of the day you hold (Hebrews 10:25). Do not let Sunday become simply another day for catching up on work or shopping by default. And if your employer requires Sunday work regularly, look for ways still to worship with God’s people, perhaps at another service, and keep some real rest elsewhere in your week.

In a sentence. Jesus, the Lord of the Sabbath, shows that God values mercy above ritual and that he himself is the true rest the Sabbath pointed to.

On a Tuesday. Look at your diary for next Sunday. Is there room for unhurried worship, real rest and some deed of mercy, or is it a day like any other? Plan it as a gift. And this week, ask whether any of your religious habits have become a substitute for mercy: the prayer that is said while the needy neighbour is ignored, the attendance that never reaches out.

For worship. The Lord of the Sabbath is the Lord of creation, who rested on the seventh day not because he was tired but because his work was very good. And he is the Lord of the new creation, who cried on the cross, it is finished, and rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose on the first day of the week. In him the long signpost has reached its destination. He desires mercy, and he has shown it, and he gives his weary people a rest that no law could give and no accuser can take away.

parallels.desc: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: He went on from there and entered their synagogue. And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" — so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue that Sabbath was a man with a withered hand. The Pharisees asked Jesus whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, looking for a reason to accuse him.

He went on from there and entered their synagogue. Their synagogue: the Pharisees’. Matthew uses the possessive repeatedly (4:23; 9:35; 10:17; 13:54), and it is the language of a man describing an institution that has begun to close against Jesus. It was his synagogue too, in every sense that mattered. By the time Matthew wrote, it was theirs. The tension is rising.

And a man was there with a withered hand. A hand shrunken or paralysed; the word suggests it had dried up. Luke says it was his right hand (Luke 6:6), which meant he probably could not work. In that economy a one-handed man did not earn a living. But his condition was not life-threatening.

Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? The trap is more precisely made than it appears, because the rabbinic position on this exact question was settled and everybody in the synagogue knew it. The rule was that danger to life overrides the Sabbath. If a man’s life is at risk, you act: you dig him out of rubble, you treat the wound, and the Sabbath waits. That principle is generous and right. But the corollary was equally firm: where there is no danger to life, it waits. A chronic condition had been there for years and would still be there tomorrow. Now look at the man. A withered hand: useless, the ruin of his living, but not dangerous. So by the standard of the day the answer was obvious. Wait until sundown, heal him then, and nobody objects. That is exactly what makes it a trap. They are not asking whether healing is good. They are asking whether it is urgent, and the honest answer, on their terms, is no.

So that they might accuse him. Their question was a trap, not an honest inquiry. They wanted to bring a charge against him. They used a suffering man as bait. The man’s need is incidental to their agenda; he is a prop in their argument. When a suffering human being becomes a means to score points, something has gone deeply wrong with the religion.

Why did Jesus not simply wait until the evening? Because the man’s hand was not the only thing being decided. Jesus heals him anyway, in the synagogue, in front of them, on that day, when a delay of a few hours would have cost nothing and avoided everything. What was on trial was whether the day God gave for rest and restoration could be used to restore somebody, and answering that on Monday would have answered nothing. Jesus was not being provocative for its own sake. He was refusing to let a man’s suffering be postponed to keep a man-made rule intact.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that asking questions about God’s law is wrong. Good questions are how we learn. The problem was their motive.

In a sentence. The Pharisees used a disabled man as bait, asking whether healing on the Sabbath was lawful in order to accuse Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Notice the next time you are in a religious discussion whether you are seeking the truth or trying to win. And notice the people in the conversation: is anyone being treated as an example, a case or an issue, rather than as a person? Put the person first.

For worship. Into a synagogue full of watching eyes walks the Lord who sees what they cannot. They saw a test case; he saw a man. They saw an opportunity to accuse; he saw a hand to restore. The God who formed Adam’s hands from the dust has not forgotten one of the hands he made, and he would rather walk into a trap than leave it withered.
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. In the rabbis’ rulings, healing a condition that was not life-threatening had to wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: if one of your sheep falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will you not pull it out? A person is worth far more than a sheep. So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.

Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? Most rabbis permitted rescuing an animal on the Sabbath, or at least feeding it until the next day. (The community of the Dead Sea Scrolls was stricter and forbade it.) Jesus appeals to their own practice. The precedent they already accept commits them to the conclusion they want to deny.

Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! An argument from lesser to greater. If you would help an animal, how much more a human being, made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27; 9:6; see 10:31). The worth of a person made in the image of God is the anchor of the whole argument. The Sabbath was given to honour human dignity by giving rest; healing a person on it honours its purpose far better than leaving him to suffer.

So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. The Sabbath was made for doing good, not for preventing it. Mark adds Jesus’ question: is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? (Mark 3:4). And the irony is plain: Jesus was doing good on the Sabbath, while the Pharisees were about to plot his death (v. 14). It is not merely permitted to do good on the day of rest. It is fitting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the Lord’s Day is like any other day, to be spent on ordinary work. It means that works of mercy and necessity are fitting on the day of rest. Westminster speaks of the day spent in public and private worship, and in the duties of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.8).

Does this mean animals do not matter? No. A righteous man cares for the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10), and the Father feeds the birds and notices every sparrow (6:26; 10:29). Jesus assumes that rescuing the sheep is right. His point is not that animals are worthless but that people are worth far more, because they alone bear God’s image. A culture that will spend lavishly on pets and little on the poor, or that protects animals while despising unborn or disabled human beings, has reversed the order Jesus taught.

Does any of this bind me? Two Sabbath controversies in fourteen verses leave a reader with an obvious and practical question. Should Christians keep a Sabbath, and is Sunday it? Believers who love the Scriptures land in two places here. Some hold that the fourth commandment stands with the other nine as part of the moral law, and that the day has moved to the first of the week in honour of the resurrection, so the Lord’s Day is to be set apart from ordinary work for worship and rest. That is the historic Reformed and Puritan position, and it has produced some of the most joyful, well-ordered lives the church has seen. Others hold that the Sabbath belonged to the shadows that have found their substance in Christ, and that no particular day now binds the conscience, pointing to Paul, who writes that one person esteems one day as better than another while another esteems all days alike, and tells them both to stop judging each other (Romans 14:5–6). The second fits the New Testament better and is the view taken here (see vv. 7–8): Paul calls the Sabbath a shadow whose substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), the apostles laid no Sabbath on the Gentile churches (Acts 15:28–29), and the church gathered on the first day without calling it a Sabbath (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2). Even so, Paul’s chief concern is to forbid the quarrel, and that should shape how firmly any of us holds an opinion here.

Where both sides agree. Notice how much is shared, because that is where the practical wisdom lies. The pattern of rest is older than Israel and older than Sinai: God rested on the seventh day of creation and blessed it (Genesis 2:2–3), long before there was a commandment about it. It was given as a gift and not a burden: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). Gathering with God’s people is commanded whatever your view of the day (Hebrews 10:25). And we are creatures with limits, made to stop, which no theological position changes.

Where the danger lies for us. The Pharisees’ error was too much Sabbath, fenced with rules; ours is almost never that. It is a life with no boundary in it anywhere: work bleeding into every evening, a phone that never stops, Sunday spent catching up. Almost nobody in our culture needs protecting from excessive rest. So whatever your conviction about the day, put a real boundary somewhere in your week and defend it: work put down, worship unhurried, time with people who are not a task. Do it not to earn anything, but because you are a creature and not a machine, and because the day was always a signpost to the Person who is your rest (11:28). And one guard, from the men in this story. The moment your practice becomes a stick to measure other people with, you have reproduced their mistake exactly, whichever side of the question you are on. They were so busy guarding the day that they resented a hungry man eating and a crippled man being healed on it. If your Sabbath makes you censorious, it has stopped being rest.

In a sentence. If people rescue sheep on the Sabbath, how much more may Jesus heal a person, for it is right to do good on the Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Plan one deed of mercy for next Lord’s Day: visiting someone lonely, inviting a newcomer for a meal, phoning someone housebound, helping a neighbour. Let the day of rest become a day of doing good, and notice how much more like a gift it feels.

For worship. We are worth more than sheep to him. That is the astonishing logic of this verse, and the cross carries it further than the Pharisees could imagine. The Good Shepherd did not only lift his sheep out of the pit; he went down into it himself and laid down his life for them. Of how much more value is a man than a sheep? The answer is written in the blood of the Lamb of God, who counted his people worth his own life.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told the man to stretch out his hand. He did, and it was restored, as healthy as the other. But the Pharisees went out and began plotting how to destroy Jesus.

Stretch out your hand. A command he could not obey in his own strength, and Jesus’ command carried the power to obey it. That is always the pattern of the gospel: he commands what we cannot do, and in the trusting act of obedience the power comes. And notice what he asks. A withered hand is a thing you keep in your sleeve. The man had had years of practice keeping it out of sight, and he is told to hold it out in the middle of a synagogue with every eye in the building on him. The healing did not come first. He had to extend the ruined thing before there was anything to see.

And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. Jesus did no work in the Pharisees’ sense: he did not touch the man or use any treatment. He spoke, and the man stretched out his hand. There was nothing to charge him with except the healing itself. The verb for restored (apokathistēmi) means put back to its former condition. It is the word the disciples use when they ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6), and the related noun is the one Peter uses for the time of restoring all things (Acts 3:21). So a small, unmistakable sample of the last day happened in a synagogue on a Sabbath morning, in one man’s hand.

But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him. The first mention in Matthew of a plot to kill Jesus. Notice which day the conspiracy is formed on. The complaint was that healing a man on the Sabbath was work. The response is to go out and hold a meeting about how to kill him. Matthew does not comment. He puts the two clauses in one sentence and lets the reader do the arithmetic: restoring a hand is a Sabbath violation; planning a murder is not. Mark adds that they plotted with the Herodians, supporters of Herod (Mark 3:6), unlikely allies against Jesus. And Mark tells us what Jesus felt in the synagogue: he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). It is the only place where the Gospels use the word anger of Jesus, and this is what provoked it. Not the plot against his life, which he bore calmly for three years, but the willingness to watch a crippled man stay crippled rather than lose an argument.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that all Pharisees were murderous. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea came to faith, and Paul was a Pharisee. But this group’s religious zeal had become hatred of the very God they claimed to serve.

What is my withered hand? It may be a sin you have hidden for years, a shame you never speak of, a wound you protect, a weakness you are embarrassed by. Jesus does not usually heal what we refuse to bring out. Stretching it out means telling him the truth about it in prayer, and often telling a trusted brother or sister as well (James 5:16). It feels like exposure. It is the moment healing begins, because you are holding out to him the very thing you could not fix.

In a sentence. Jesus healed the man’s hand with a word, and the Pharisees, enraged, began plotting to kill him.

On a Tuesday. Religious zeal without love can become cruel. Ask God to show you where your devotion to being right has made you hard toward someone. And bring to him today, specifically, the withered thing you have been keeping in your sleeve.

For worship. Here is the Lord who restores. With a word he put back a hand that had withered, and gave a glimpse of the day when he will restore all things. And the men who watched went out to kill him. He knew it, and he healed anyway. The hand that was restored that morning would be among the hands stretched out to receive him as risen Lord; the hands that conspired would one day help nail his to a cross. And by those pierced hands he restores everything that sin has withered.

parallels.desc: seeking to kill him over the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all and ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing about the plot, Jesus withdrew. Large crowds followed him, and he healed them all, but ordered them not to make him known.

Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. Not out of fear, but because his time had not yet come (26:18). He would not provoke a premature confrontation; the cross would come on the Father’s timetable, not the Pharisees’. The verb (anachōreō) is one Matthew uses again and again. Joseph withdrew to Egypt with the child, and then to Galilee (2:14, 22). Jesus withdrew when John was arrested (4:12). He withdraws here, and will again when he hears John has been beheaded (14:13), and once more to the region of Tyre and Sidon (15:21). Always away from danger, never presented as cowardice: a man keeping to a timetable his enemies are not setting. And every time, Matthew notes that the withdrawal is followed by more ministry, not less.

And many followed him, and he healed them all. Stop on that sentence. He has just been condemned, in effect, for healing on a Sabbath. A plot is under way to kill him. And he leaves the district and goes on healing everybody who comes, which is a sufficient answer to the suggestion that he withdrew out of fear. Opposition did not stop his compassion.

And ordered them not to make him known. What he stops is not the work but the publicity. Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a miracle-worker, or to stir up political hopes of a warrior Messiah (see 8:4). And the reason Matthew gives is striking. A hunted man has an obvious reason to keep quiet, and Matthew declines that explanation. He does not say Jesus kept it quiet so that his enemies would not find him. He says it happened to fulfil what was spoken by Isaiah, and then quotes four verses about a Servant who does not shout in the street. The Messiah is a quiet, gentle Servant, not a loud self-promoter.

Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because before the cross, the news that a miracle-working Messiah had come would have been heard as a call to arms against Rome, and would have drawn crowds who wanted bread and victory but not a crucified Saviour. Jesus would not be made king on those terms (John 6:15). After his death and resurrection, when the meaning of his messiahship was clear, the command changed: go and make disciples of all nations (28:19). So the silence was for a season. Our calling now is to speak, and to speak above all of the cross, which is what the silence was protecting.

In a sentence. Jesus withdrew from his enemies but kept healing the crowds, without seeking publicity.

On a Tuesday. Do one good thing today that no one will ever know you did. Notice the small tug to mention it to someone. Jesus did good without seeking attention, and the Father who sees in secret is enough of an audience (6:4).

For worship. Admire this Saviour. Hunted, he heals. Plotted against, he keeps on giving. Condemned for mercy, he goes somewhere else to be merciful to everyone who comes. He does not need the crowd’s applause and he does not fear the council’s threats, because he is doing his Father’s will on his Father’s timetable. And still today he heals them all who come, every sinner who comes to him for cleansing, without exception.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy of the Servant: God’s chosen and beloved one, in whom he delights. God puts his Spirit on him, and he will announce justice to the nations.

This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah 42:1–4, the longest Old Testament quotation in Matthew. Matthew quotes Scripture constantly, usually a line or two. This is the one place he stops the story and lets a prophet speak at length, and he does it to explain not a miracle or a claim but a man’s decision to avoid a confrontation and ask people to keep quiet. The thing being explained is not spectacular. It is the absence of spectacle. The passage is the first of four Servant Songs in Isaiah (42:1–9; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12), which describe the Servant of the LORD, who brings justice and salvation and suffers for the sins of the people.

Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. The Father’s voice at Jesus’ baptism said almost exactly this (3:17), and Matthew has waited nine chapters to show the reader which text it came from. So the Father’s declaration over his Son at the beginning of his ministry echoed the first Servant Song, together with Psalm 2:7. From the outset the identity being announced was not simply the Messiah but the Servant, and every Jew who followed the reference would have known that the songs run on to Isaiah 53, to a man despised and rejected, wounded for transgressions not his own. Jesus is the Servant. His greatness is the greatness of a servant (20:28).

I will put my Spirit upon him. Fulfilled when the Spirit came upon Jesus at his baptism (3:16). And Jesus casts out demons by this Spirit (v. 28), which is why the charge that he works by Beelzebul, a few verses later, is so terrible.

And he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. Justice (krisis) means God’s right order, his righteous rule and judgment, set right in the world. The Servant brings it not only to Israel but to the nations. Matthew stresses this: the Messiah is for the Gentiles too (v. 21; 28:19). The one the Pharisees plot to destroy is the one the Father has appointed to reach every nation.

An honest note on the text. Matthew’s Greek here matches neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament exactly, and seems to be his own rendering: closer to the Hebrew in places, closer to the Greek in others, independent in a few. That is not a defect. He is a Jewish writer reading a Hebrew Bible for readers who use Greek, and he translates as he goes. What he does not do is bend the sense. The Servant of Isaiah 42 is chosen, Spirit-anointed, quiet, gentle with the damaged and destined for the nations, and that is precisely the man Matthew has been describing for eleven chapters, most recently walking away from an argument he could have won.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that justice is only political or social. It includes God’s whole saving order: forgiveness, righteousness, and the setting right of every wrong. Nor does the Servant’s quietness mean he is weak; the same song says he will not grow faint until he has established justice in the earth (Isaiah 42:4).

If Jesus is God, how can he be God’s servant? In becoming man, the eternal Son took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). He did not stop being equal with the Father; he added a human nature and, as man and as our Mediator, he obeyed the Father perfectly, even to death on a cross. So the Father can call him my servant and my beloved in the same breath. The Servant is not a lesser being; he is the Son stooping to do the work of a servant for us.

In a sentence. Jesus is Isaiah’s chosen and beloved Servant, filled with God’s Spirit, bringing God’s justice to the nations.

On a Tuesday. The Lord of glory chose the shape of a servant. Find one place today to serve without title or credit, perhaps in your home, at work or in church, and do it as one who follows the Servant.

For worship. Hear the Father speak of his Son: my servant, my chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul delights. The delight of God rests on Jesus, and on everyone who is in him. The Spirit rests on him without measure. And the justice he brings is not only for Israel but for the coastlands, the far nations, people like us. The Servant who was despised by the experts in a Galilean synagogue is the one in whom the soul of God is well pleased forever.

parallels.desc: my chosen servant, with my Spirit upon him
the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Servant will not quarrel or shout or make a noise in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smouldering wick, until he brings justice to victory.

He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. The Servant is not a noisy self-promoter, a political agitator or a street-corner demagogue. He does not force his way. That explains why Jesus withdrew and told people not to publicise him (vv. 15–16). The Pharisees quarrel, plot and cry aloud with accusations; the Servant does not.

A bruised reed he will not break. Picture the two things Isaiah chose. A reed is a hollow stalk from the riverbank, used for a pen or a simple pipe. Once it is cracked and bent, it will not write and it will not play, and the ordinary thing to do with it is snap it and throw it away. The Servant does not.

And a smoldering wick he will not quench. A lamp-wick with no flame left is a thread of smoke and a smell in the room, and you pinch it out and replace it. The Servant shields it instead and gently fans it back to flame. Both images are of things a reasonable person discards, because they have stopped being useful and are now merely untidy. That is the picture. And the promise is that he will not do it.

Who are they? The weak, the failing, the crushed, those with almost no faith left, those whom others have given up on: the sick he healed, the sinners he ate with, the weary he called (11:28). The Puritan Richard Sibbes wrote a famous book on this verse, The Bruised Reed (1630), to comfort struggling Christians: Christ is gentle with weak faith. And this was written about somebody, and it should be said to somebody. If your faith is down to a flicker; if your praying has shrunk to a sentence or two, and not good ones; if you turn up to church out of habit rather than hunger and feel a fraud for being there; if you have failed at the same thing so many times that you have stopped making promises about it, this verse has your name on it. He is not standing over you with his fingers ready to pinch. And notice where Matthew has placed this quotation: immediately after the Pharisees walk out to plan a murder (v. 14). The world around him was as hard as it gets, and this is the sentence Matthew reaches for to describe how he treats the weak in the middle of it.

Until he brings justice to victory. His gentleness is not weakness. He will persevere until justice triumphs completely. The gentle Servant is also the conquering King. And this is the guard that keeps the comfort from going soft. He will not break the reed, but the sentence goes on to victory: the tending has a destination. He is not indifferent to your ruin; he is patient with it, and he intends to finish the repair. Gentleness here is not the absence of purpose but the manner of it.

The reed in his hand. There is one more thing, which Matthew will show you if you read to the end of his book. When the soldiers dressed Jesus as a mock king, they put a reed in his right hand for a sceptre, and then took the reed and struck him on the head with it (27:29–30). The bruised reed was handled the way bruised reeds are always handled: snapped, mocked and used to hit somebody. He went through that so that he would never have to do it to you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ is soft on sin or never confronts evil. He rebuked the Pharisees fiercely (chapter 23). His gentleness is for the broken and the repentant; his severity is for the proud and hard-hearted.

Does his gentleness mean he never disciplines me? No. The Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and sometimes that discipline is painful: a sin exposed, a plan frustrated, a hard season. But his discipline is never meant to break you. It is the pressure of a hand straightening a bent reed, not snapping it; the breath that fans a wick, not the fingers that pinch it. If you are under his correction, it is because he has not given up on you. The gentlest heart in the universe is also the most determined to make you whole.

In a sentence. The Servant is gentle with the weak and failing, never crushing them, and he will persevere until justice triumphs.

On a Tuesday. If your faith feels like a smouldering wick, bring it to Christ as it is; he will not snuff it out. Then think of one bruised reed around you, a struggling believer, a discouraged friend, a person who has failed publicly, and be gentle with them this week. A word, a note, a meal. Treat them as he treats you.

For worship. Blessed be the Servant who does not break bruised reeds. He could have crushed his enemies with a word, and he spoke words of healing instead. He could have discarded the weak, and he gathered them. He let himself be bruised and mocked with a reed in his hand, so that no reed in his keeping would ever be thrown away. And he will not stop until justice is victorious, until every flicker of faith he has guarded becomes a flame in the light of his glory.
verseByVerse.note: A bruised reed and a smouldering lamp-wick are pictures of the weak and failing, easily finished off.

parallels.desc: he will not cry aloud, nor break a bruised reed

verseByVerse.quote: and in his name the Gentiles will hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in his name the nations will put their hope.

And in his name the Gentiles will hope. The end of the quotation from Isaiah 42:4. His name means his person, character and authority. The nations, who were without hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12), will find hope in the Servant. Not in the Pharisees’ religion, not in Rome’s armies, not in Israel’s privilege, but in his name. The Pharisees rejected him; the nations will trust him.

An honest textual note. The last line differs from the Hebrew. Isaiah 42:4 in the Hebrew reads that the coastlands wait for his law; Matthew has in his name the Gentiles will hope, following the Greek tradition. The two are not far apart: the coastlands are the Gentile lands, and waiting for his instruction is close kin to hoping in his name. But the difference is real, and a reader comparing the passages should know it is there rather than wonder.

Two reeds. Matthew has put two reeds a chapter apart. In chapter 11 Jesus asked the crowd whether they had gone out to see a reed shaken by the wind (11:7), the emblem of the man who bends whichever way the weather goes. Here the Servant will not break a bruised reed (v. 20). The same plant, and two entirely different things done with it. There is the reed a man can become, blown about and worth nothing. And there is the reed a person can be reduced to, already crushed, no use to anybody. Jesus has no patience with the first and will not lay a finger on the second.

The direction. What is not in doubt is the direction of the song. It ends by reaching past Israel to everybody else, and Matthew puts that sentence at the exact point where Israel’s leaders have begun plotting to kill him. The nations get their hope in the same paragraph in which his own people decide he must die. And the cross they plan will not end his name; it will make it the name above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). Their murder becomes his throne.

What does it mean to hope in his name? Hope in the Bible is not wishful thinking but confident expectation resting on a promise. To hope in Jesus’ name is to rest your future, your forgiveness, your eternity and your daily needs on who he is and what he has promised, rather than on your own record, your health, your money or your country. It shows itself in prayer offered in his name, in steadiness when things fall apart, and in patience as you wait for his return.

In a sentence. The nations will put their hope in the Servant, Jesus, whom his own people rejected.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for one nation, by name, where few know Christ, that people there will find their hope in him. And if you are a Gentile believer, thank God that you are one of the coastlands this song was waiting for.

For worship. We were the far nations, without hope and without God in the world. And the Servant’s song reached across the sea to us. The name the rulers of Israel tried to blot out is now spoken in every language under heaven, and the nations have found in it what no empire, philosophy or religion could give.
