Glory to Jesus, the hope of the Gentiles, whose name is above every name, at which every knee shall bow.

parallels.desc: the coastlands wait for his law
in him will the Gentiles hope

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–50 — The Unforgivable Sin, the Sign of Jonah, and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter's second half escalates the conflict. Jesus heals a blind and mute demoniac; the Pharisees attribute it to Beelzebul. Jesus dismantles the accusation with three arguments, then pronounces the solemn warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The scribes and Pharisees demand a sign; Jesus offers only the sign of Jonah. The chapter ends with a redefinition of family: those who do the will of the Father are Jesus's true mother and brothers. Four things more. The crowd's question in v. 23 expects the answer no — closer to "this can't be the Son of David, can it?" They are edging toward a confession and flinching. And the title fits this miracle exactly: Solomon, David's son, had a reputation as master of spirits, and Josephus describes a Jewish exorcist working "according to the methods of Solomon" — with a ring and a root. Jesus says "go". Luke records v. 28 with one word different — "by the finger of God" (Lk. 11:20), which is a quotation: it is what Pharaoh's magicians said when they could no longer reproduce the plagues (Exod. 8:19). The exorcisms are a new exodus, and the Pharisees are standing where the magicians stood. "come upon you" is ephthasen — arrived, overtaken; not an offer drawing near but a thing that has landed. "every careless word" is argos, literally not-working: the unemployed remark that achieved nothing and was forgotten within the hour — and the guard that "by your words you will be justified" is forensic, evidence rather than payment. Both witnesses at the judgement are Gentiles: Nineveh, capital of the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, which had one reluctant preacher; and the queen of Sheba, who had a rumour and a long journey. Neither had Scripture, temple, covenant or promise. The returning Spirit finds the house "empty, swept, and put in order" — three approving words, and the first is fatal. It is not a passage about losing salvation; there is no indwelling in the story, which is the whole problem. And v. 50 names brother, sister and mother — but not father, because the Father is already in the sentence (cf. 23:9). Mark tells us why the family came: they thought he was out of his mind (Mk. 3:21); John notes his brothers did not believe (Jn. 7:5); and Mary is in the upper room in Acts 1:14. She did not stay outside.
verseByVerse.theology: The blasphemy against the Holy Spirit — attributing the Spirit's work to Satan — is the one sin Jesus calls unforgivable. It is not unforgivable because it exceeds God's mercy but because it closes the door through which mercy enters: it calls the Spirit of conviction a demon, and the person who has hardened to that degree has no remaining capacity to receive the grace they are calling evil. The Pharisees are approaching this condition, if they have not already reached it. The warning is pastoral, not vindictive: it is the warning of a doctor who sees a patient choosing death.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign of Jonah — three days and three nights in the earth — is the only sign Jesus offers to an evil and adulterous generation. The resurrection is the final and definitive sign, the one that vindicates all his claims. No amount of healing, no accumulation of miracles, will convince those whose hearts are already set against him; only the empty tomb is sufficient — and even that will not convince those determined not to believe (28:13-15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. And all the people were amazed, and said, "Can this be the Son of David?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to Jesus, and he healed him, so that he could speak and see. The crowds were amazed and asked: could this be the Son of David?

A demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute. A threefold ruin: possessed, blind and mute. He could not see who had come to him, could not ask for anything, and had no power to resist what was in him. There is no record of his faith, because there could not be: a blind mute cannot approach and cannot request. Matthew says only that he was brought. Somebody else carried the whole transaction, which is worth knowing for anyone praying for a person who is past asking for themselves.

And he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. Complete healing, and freedom from the demon, all at once. The man who had been shut in on every side now sees the face of the one who freed him and speaks his first words in his presence.

Can this be the Son of David? The crowd were amazed, and the question is more hesitant in Greek than in English, and the hesitation is the point. Matthew uses a construction that expects the answer no. It is closer to: this cannot be the Son of David, can it? The crowd is not making a confession; it is edging toward one and flinching. They have seen enough to raise the question and not enough to want to own it. That is very often how faith begins, and it is worth saying so, because the sentence is usually read as enthusiasm, and it is the sound of people saying something they are not ready to have overheard. They are close to faith (see 1:1; 9:27).

Why Son of David. The title is exactly right for this miracle, for a reason easy to miss. Son of David means the Messiah. But in Jewish tradition it also recalled Solomon, David’s son, who had acquired a reputation as a master of spirits. Josephus records the tradition and describes a Jewish exorcist named Eleazar drawing a demon out of a man in front of the emperor Vespasian, using a ring and a root, by the methods said to come from Solomon. So a man who casts out demons with a word is not merely doing something impressive. He is doing what the son of David was famous for, without the ring, the root or the incantation. The crowd puts those together and reaches, tentatively, for the title. And the Pharisees, hearing the crowd say it, produce their explanation within a verse.

Is demon possession real today, and what should I think about it? Scripture treats demonic oppression as real, and missionaries in many lands have met it. But two guards are needed. First, many conditions that look strange are medical or psychological, and they should be treated with medical care, prayer and patience, not labelled demonic. Second, there is no need for rituals or special techniques. Jesus cast out demons by a word, and Christians resist the devil by faith in Christ, prayer, the word of God and the fellowship of the church (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). A believer, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, cannot be possessed by a demon (see on vv. 44–45).

In a sentence. Jesus freed and healed a blind, mute, demon-possessed man, and the crowds began, hesitantly, to wonder if he was the Messiah.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone in your life who is past asking for help, too far from God, too bound, too blind? Bring them to Jesus in prayer today, by name, as someone carried this man. And if you are like the crowd, wondering but not yet confessing, do not stop at the question. Wonder must become faith.

For worship. This is the Son of David, greater than Solomon, who needs no ring and no root and no spell, because the spirits obey his voice. He opened the eyes of a man who could not look for him and the mouth of a man who could not call for him. So he does still. Every one of us was brought to him blind and mute in our sins, unable to see him or to ask; and he spoke, and we saw, and we spoke his praise.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, "It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons." Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, "Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees answered that Jesus cast out demons only by the power of Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Jesus, knowing their thoughts, replied: every kingdom divided against itself is ruined, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand.

But when the Pharisees heard it. They saw the crowds moving toward faith and acted to stop it.

It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons. The most important thing in this verse is what the Pharisees do not say. They do not say it did not happen. A blind, mute, possessed man is standing there seeing and talking, and the official response is not that the crowd is mistaken or the man was faking. It is an explanation of the mechanism. That pattern holds throughout the Gospels, and it is a considerable piece of evidence. His enemies had every motive to deny the works, and they never do. The council later says this man performs many signs and treats it as the problem (John 11:47). The charge at his trial is blasphemy, not fraud. Even the story spread after the resurrection concedes the empty tomb and disputes only how it got that way (28:13). The argument in the first century was never about whether he did these things, but about whose power he did them by. Beelzebul was a name for Satan (see 9:34; 10:25, where the note explains the name as something like lord of the house). This is the most serious accusation they could make: Jesus is in league with the devil.

Knowing their thoughts. As in 9:4. They had spoken, and the verse says so; but he answers what lay underneath the sentence rather than the sentence itself. Matthew does not pause over it. Jesus knows the heart, as only God does (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10).

Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste. Civil war destroys nations, and history, including Israel’s own, was full of examples. And notice the logic descends in three steps: kingdom, city, house. That is not decoration. He starts at the largest scale and narrows, and the last word is the one he needs, because in four verses he will describe Satan as a strong man whose house is being robbed (v. 29).

And no city or house divided against itself will stand. Division destroys families and communities. The reasoning is simple enough for a child to follow, and that is deliberate. If the accusation were true, the devil is dismantling his own operation, one prisoner at a time, in public, on request. No power in history has ever run that way.

Why did they not simply deny the miracle? Because they could not. Too many people had seen the man before and after. That is why the Gospels’ accounts of Jesus’ works are so hard to dismiss: the people who most wanted them to be false admitted they had happened. Faced with undeniable evidence they would not accept, they chose a theory that let them keep their hatred. It is a warning for every age. The problem with unbelief is rarely a lack of evidence; it is what the heart will do with the evidence.

In a sentence. The Pharisees could not deny the miracle and so claimed Jesus worked by Satan’s power, and Jesus began to show the absurdity of the charge: a divided kingdom cannot stand.

On a Tuesday. Division destroys. Is there a quarrel in your family or church that you have been feeding rather than healing? Take one step toward peace this week (Ephesians 4:3). And when you meet evidence of God’s work that you would rather not accept, in Scripture or in someone’s changed life, ask whether your heart is looking for a way around it.

For worship. Here is the Lord who reads the heart. Nothing hidden in us is hidden from him: not the thought behind the word, not the motive behind the question. And still, knowing all, he answers patiently and reasons with his enemies. His kingdom is not divided. Father, Son and Spirit are perfectly one in the work of salvation, and that undivided kingdom will stand forever, when every rival realm has fallen.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan, probably related to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.

verseByVerse.quote: And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Satan drives out Satan, he is fighting himself; how could his kingdom stand? And if Jesus drives out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do the Pharisees’ own followers drive them out? They will judge you.

And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. The first argument: the charge is absurd. Satan would be destroying his own work. Why would he free the people he had enslaved?

How then will his kingdom stand? Satan has a kingdom, an organised realm of evil (Colossians 1:13; Ephesians 2:2; 6:12). He is wicked, but he is not foolish enough to destroy it from within.

And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? The second argument: inconsistency. And it needs one fact to land properly: Jewish exorcism was a real and respected practice. Josephus describes it and treats it as an ancient national skill. The book of Acts records seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva going about Ephesus attempting it, badly in that instance (Acts 19:13–16). Your sons means the Pharisees’ followers or other Jewish exorcists of the time. So Jesus is not scoring a point off a hypothetical. He is pointing at practitioners the Pharisees knew and approved, possibly men in their own circle.

Therefore they will be your judges. The trap closes neatly. If exorcism as such is satanic, their own people stand condemned. If it is not, then their explanation of his exorcisms was invented for the occasion. Their own followers expose their inconsistency.

The difference they could not explain. Every exorcist of the period worked with apparatus: names, rings, roots, formulas, the invocation of a higher authority. The whole art consisted in knowing what to say and what to hold. Jesus says go, and it is over. That is the thing the Pharisees cannot fit anywhere. A man working with borrowed authority has to name his source. A man who never names one is either a fraud, in which case the demons would not leave, or he is not borrowing. They have grasped that he is not borrowing. Their only remaining move is to name the wrong owner.

What it does not mean. Jesus is not here approving every exorcist or saying how they succeeded. He is using the Pharisees’ own approval of them to expose their double standard. The point is not what the sons did, but how the Pharisees judged.

In a sentence. The Pharisees’ charge was absurd, since Satan would not fight himself, and inconsistent, since they approved of their own exorcists.

On a Tuesday. Watch for double standards in how you judge others, especially people you dislike. Is there someone whose good deeds you explain away while praising the same deeds in your friends? Name that to God, and ask him for fair judgment and a generous heart.

For worship. Every other power in the world borrows its authority; the Son of God has it in himself. No ring, no formula, no higher name invoked, because there is no higher name. He speaks and the darkness leaves. And this Lord, who needs no help to defeat the devil, has chosen to share his victory with weak people like us, so that the name we pray in is his.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” probably means Jewish exorcists of their own circle.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Or how can someone enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if Jesus drives out demons by the Spirit of God, then God’s kingdom has arrived. No one can enter a strong man’s house and steal his goods without first tying him up. Jesus has bound the strong man, Satan, and is plundering his house.

But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons. The third and decisive argument: the true explanation is God’s Spirit, who came upon Jesus at his baptism (3:16; 12:18). Luke records the same sentence with one word different: by the finger of God (Luke 11:20). And the finger of God is a quotation. It occurs at one memorable moment in Israel’s story: Egypt, the third plague, when Pharaoh’s magicians, who had matched Moses until then, could not produce the gnats and said to their king, this is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19). That is the sentence in which the professional opposition concedes. So the exorcisms are being cast as a new exodus: a stronger power arriving in enemy territory, prisoners being taken out of a house that had held them, and the resident experts unable to reproduce it. Which puts the Pharisees exactly where Pharaoh’s magicians stood, watching something they cannot do and cannot explain, and choosing the other answer.

Then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Here Matthew uses kingdom of God, not his usual kingdom of heaven. The verb (ephthasen) is stronger than has come. It means to arrive, to reach, to overtake: to get somewhere before you expected. The kingdom has not merely drawn near; it has landed on them. The exorcisms are proof that God’s reign has broken into the world in Jesus, here and now. This is the already of the kingdom. And it is the sting in the sentence. He does not say the kingdom has come to you, as an offer. He says it has come upon you, and the men it has overtaken are the ones explaining it away.

Or how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? A parable, and the picture is a burglary. The strong man is Satan. His house is the world, or the people he holds captive; his goods are the people he enslaves. Nobody walks into an occupied house and starts carrying out the furniture while the owner is standing there. The goods come out only after the owner is on the floor. So every demon that leaves is not a negotiation; it is evidence that somebody has already been dealt with in the next room. The image is Isaiah’s before it is his. Can the prey be taken from the mighty? the prophet asks, and answers that even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, for the LORD will do it (Isaiah 49:24–25). He raises it as an impossibility and then says God will do it anyway.

Then indeed he may plunder his house. Jesus is the stronger one (3:11; Luke 11:22). He has bound Satan, beginning with his victory in the wilderness (4:1–11), and completing it at the cross (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15; John 12:31). Every exorcism, and every person set free from sin, is Jesus plundering Satan’s house.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Satan is now powerless or inactive. He still prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). But he is bound in the sense that he cannot stop the advance of the gospel or hold on to those whom Christ frees.

Where Christians differ over the binding of Satan. Revelation 20:1–3 pictures Satan bound so that he can no longer deceive the nations. Reformed amillennialists see this binding as beginning with Christ’s first coming, which is the present gospel age, not a future millennium; premillennial readers take that passage as a future binding during a thousand-year reign after Christ returns. Verdict: Satan is bound now, in the sense this verse describes (Luke 10:18; Colossians 2:15), and the gospel is plundering his house among the nations. He is still active and dangerous, but restrained, and that fits what Jesus says here.

If Satan is bound, why is there still so much evil? Because bound does not mean idle. A dog on a chain can still bark and bite anyone who wanders within reach. Satan still tempts, accuses, deceives individuals and stirs up persecution. What he cannot do is stop the gospel from going to the nations, prevent the elect from being gathered, or keep any person Christ sets free. The binding is about the advance of the kingdom, not the end of all evil. That end comes at Christ’s return, when the devil will be thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10).

In a sentence. Jesus drives out demons by God’s Spirit, proving that God’s kingdom has come and that he has bound Satan and is setting his captives free.

On a Tuesday. Whatever has held you captive, a habit, a fear, a lie you have believed about yourself, Christ is stronger. Name it to him today and ask him to set you free, and tell a mature Christian, so that you are not fighting alone. And when you share the gospel, remember that you are not trying to win an argument with a strong man. The strong man is already bound.

For worship. Praise Christ, the stronger one. He walked into the house of the strong man, the world under the power of darkness, and bound him. In the wilderness he refused him; at the cross he disarmed him; at the empty tomb he left him with nothing. And now, all through this age, he carries the prisoners out one by one, each of us once Satan’s goods, now Christ’s treasure. The finger of God that wrote the law on stone has written freedom on our hearts.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty
he disarmed the rulers and authorities

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no neutral ground: whoever is not with Jesus is against him, and whoever does not gather with him scatters. Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not.

Whoever is not with me is against me. In the war between Jesus and Satan, there is no neutrality. Not to side with Jesus is to side with his enemy. Neutrality toward Jesus is not neutrality; it is opposition in practice. The Pharisees thought they were serving God; by opposing Jesus, they were serving Satan.

And whoever does not gather with me scatters. A picture from shepherding, or from harvest. Jesus is gathering his flock or harvest (9:36–38); those who do not help him gather are scattering it.

Two sayings that seem to clash. A reader who knows the other Gospels may pause here, because Jesus appears to say the opposite elsewhere: the one who is not against us is for us (Mark 9:40; Luke 9:50). Both are his words, and both are true, because they answer different questions. Here he is speaking of a man’s own standing before Christ, and on that there is no neutral ground: you are either gathering with him or scattering, and indifference is a verdict. There he was speaking about someone else, an outsider casting out demons in his name whom the disciples wanted to stop because he was not of their company, and the rule for judging other people’s work is the opposite of the rule for judging yourself. Be strict with your own allegiance and generous about somebody else’s. Most of our trouble comes from getting those two the wrong way round.

Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people. Do not let the warning at the end of this verse swallow the promise at the beginning of it. The sentence contains the widest offer in the Gospel and the single exception to it, in that order, and most readers only ever hear the second half. Weigh the word every, and weigh the company Jesus kept. This is the Gospel in which a tax collector gets up from his booth and is made an apostle; and the same Lord defends a woman with a reputation in a Pharisee’s house and promises a thief on a cross paradise that afternoon (Luke 7:36–50; 23:43). And blasphemy is the strongest word available: not weakness or failure but speech against God himself. The man who wrote these words down had collaborated with an occupying power against his own people. The man who would carry the gospel across the empire had held the coats at a stoning, and later described himself as formerly a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent who received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13). No sin is too great to be forgiven, if it is repented of.

But the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. The one exception, which verse 32 explains. Whatever a reader is carrying, the thing never said aloud to anyone, the thing said about God in a hospital corridor at the worst hour of a life, the years spent arguing against him, this verse was drafted wide enough on purpose. There is exactly one sin named here as beyond forgiveness, and the next entry sets out why the person who fears he has committed it is, by that very fear, showing that he has not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a person can be neutral about Jesus and safe. Nor does it mean that we should be suspicious of every Christian outside our own circle. About Jesus himself there is no neutrality; about those doing good in his name we should not be suspicious.

What if someone I love seems neutral, neither for nor against? Jesus’ words mean they are not safe while they stay there, however kind or respectful they are. That should move you to pray for them and to speak to them, gently and honestly, not to write them off. Neutrality is often a holding position, and people move from it. Many who once shrugged at Christ have come to love him. Keep loving them, keep praying, and look for natural ways to tell them why Jesus matters to you.

In a sentence. No one can be neutral about Jesus, and while every sin and blasphemy can be forgiven, blasphemy against the Spirit cannot.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly: am I with Jesus, gathering with him, or only watching from the side? There is no safe middle. Then think of one way you could help him gather this week: an invitation, a conversation, a prayer for a named friend.

For worship. Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven. Hear the breadth of it. The mercy of God is wide enough for tax collectors and prostitutes, for persecutors and thieves, for blasphemers like Saul of Tarsus and deniers like Peter. It is wide enough for you. Only one door is shut, and it is shut from the inside, by those who will not come. Glory to the Saviour whose blood cleanses from every sin, and whose arms are open to the worst.

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who speaks against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but anyone who speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or the age to come. A tree is known by its fruit: make the tree good, and the fruit will be good.

Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. People who misunderstood Jesus, or spoke against him in ignorance, could be forgiven. His identity was partly veiled during his earthly life. Peter denied him and was forgiven; Paul persecuted him and was forgiven.

But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. What is this unforgivable sin? In context, the Pharisees had seen the Spirit’s work clearly, the casting out of demons, and deliberately called it the work of Satan (vv. 24, 28). They were not ignorant; they were calling light darkness and good evil, against the evidence, because they hated Jesus. Mark adds the explanation: because they were saying, he has an unclean spirit (Mark 3:30). It is a settled, defiant, clear-eyed hatred of the light: the heart so hardened that it looks straight at the work of God and calls it the work of the devil, and feels no grief at doing so.

Why is it unforgivable? Not because God’s grace is too small, but because this sin rejects the only source of forgiveness. The Holy Spirit is the one who convicts people of sin and draws them to Christ (John 16:8–11). To reject his testimony deliberately and finally, calling it satanic, is to shut the only door to forgiveness. Such a person does not want forgiveness and will not repent. It is a settled, wilful hardening of the heart against God’s clear revelation of Christ. The sin forecloses forgiveness not by a limit on God’s mercy but by a person’s self-exclusion from it.

If you are afraid you have committed it. No verse in Scripture has frightened tender souls more than this one, so the pastoral word must be said plainly. If you are afraid you have committed the unforgivable sin, that very fear is the surest proof you have not. The person who commits it has no desire for Christ and no fear of having offended him. But a trembling conscience, a longing to be right with God, a dread of having sinned against him: these are the Spirit’s own work in a soul, and the Spirit does not grieve over a heart he has abandoned. As the old pastors said, the tears you weep over this question are tears the unpardonable sin never sheds. Come to Christ; he has never yet cast out one who came (John 6:37).

Either the tree is good and its fruit good, or the tree is bad and its fruit bad. A tree is known by its fruit (7:16–20). The fruit of Jesus’ ministry, people freed, healed and restored, is good; so the tree, Jesus, is good, not satanic. And the Pharisees’ fruit, slander and plotting murder, reveals what they are. Good fruit does not come from a bad tree.

What it does not mean. It is not a single careless word, a doubt, a blasphemous thought that flashes through the mind unwanted, or a sin committed in weakness, even a serious one. It is a settled, deliberate rejection of Christ in the face of the Spirit’s clear witness. And either in this age or in the age to come does not imply that other sins may be forgiven after death, as in the later doctrine of purgatory. It is a Jewish way of saying never, as we might say not now, not ever. The whole Bible knows only one place of forgiveness, and it is here, in this life, at the foot of the cross (Hebrews 9:27).

Can this sin still be committed today? Some think it was possible only for those who saw Christ’s own miracles and called them Satan’s. Others think it recurs wherever someone knowingly and finally rejects the Spirit’s witness to Christ (see Hebrews 10:26–29). The second is the more likely. Either way, the person who fears he has committed it shows by that fear that he has not; the hardened heart does not grieve.

What about horrible thoughts about God that come into my mind against my will? These torment many sincere believers, especially in times of anxiety or depression. A thought you hate, resist and are distressed by is not blasphemy against the Spirit; it is a burden you are carrying, and often an attack of the enemy or a symptom of an anxious mind. Do not argue with it endlessly or keep checking whether you meant it. Tell God that you reject it and love him, turn your mind to a promise of Scripture, and if it persists, speak to a pastor and, if needed, a doctor. Christ is not angry with you for being tormented.

In a sentence. Those who deliberately call the Spirit’s clear work in Christ the work of Satan reject the only source of forgiveness, and so cannot be forgiven.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you have committed this sin, read John 6:37 aloud today and come to Christ: he will not turn you away. If you do not fear it, take the warning seriously in another way: do not grow used to resisting what you know God is saying to you. Hardness begins with small refusals.

For worship. How tender is the Spirit, who convicts us of sin and draws us to Christ, and whose very conviction is the proof that we are not abandoned. How patient is the Son, who forgave those who spoke against him in ignorance, and prayed for those who nailed him to the cross. And how great is the mercy of the Father, who shuts the door only on those who will not have it opened. Every trembling sinner who comes is welcome, and none has ever been cast out.

verseByVerse.quote: You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called the Pharisees a brood of snakes: how can evil people say good things? What fills the heart comes out of the mouth. A good person brings good things out of the good stored in them; an evil person brings evil out of the evil stored in them.

You brood of vipers! The phrase occurs three times in Matthew. John the Baptist said it first, at the Jordan, to Pharisees and Sadducees coming for baptism (3:7). Jesus says it here, and once more in the last week, in the temple, at the climax of the woes (23:33). Three times, all aimed at the same people. And the first man to say it was beheaded, and the second was crucified. The picture is of a nest of small poisonous snakes: not a single obvious danger but a mass of them, hard to see, lethal by accident as much as by intent. And in a chapter about what comes out of a mouth, the choice of animal is exact: the viper’s danger is all in its mouth. Their poisonous slander showed their nature.

How can you speak good, when you are evil? Words reveal character.

For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The word (perisseuma) means overflow, surplus, what spills when a container is full. So speech is not primarily a decision. It is a leak. What comes out under pressure is not what a person has chosen to say but what there was too much of to keep in. That is why the test is so reliable and so unwelcome. A man can control his words while he is thinking about them; nobody controls what he says when he is startled, or tired, or contradicted in front of others. That is when the level shows. The Pharisees’ slander against Jesus was not a slip; it revealed hatred in their hearts. It was their own self-portrait.

The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good. Treasure here means a storehouse. What we store in our hearts, our thoughts, loves and beliefs, eventually comes out in our words (6:21).

And the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. Evil stored in the heart produces evil words.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every harsh word reveals a wholly evil heart. Christians still sin with their tongues (James 3:2). But our words are a window into our hearts. And the passage does not say the storehouse cannot be changed; the whole New Testament is about hearts being given new contents. It says the mouth reports the current stock honestly. So the solution is not just to control our speech, but to have our hearts changed, which only God can do.

May I call people a brood of vipers? No. Jesus forbade calling a brother a fool (5:22). Here he speaks as prophet and judge to hardened teachers who had just blasphemed the Spirit. His disciples are not licensed to copy the words as personal abuse (James 3:9–10; Titus 3:2), though there are times when false teaching must be named sharply (Galatians 1:9; Titus 1:13). The tone of a Christian online or in argument should be marked by gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), even when the content is firm.

How do I change what is in my heart? Not by willpower alone, but by what you let fill it. God changes the heart by his Spirit, and he does it through means: his word read, heard and memorised (Colossians 3:16), prayer, worship with his people, and repentance whenever you hear something ugly come out of yourself. Notice what you feed on: what you watch, read and listen to most. The right response to hearing something ugly come out of your mouth is therefore not merely to resolve to say less. It is to ask what has been going in, and to bring that to God.

In a sentence. Our words overflow from what fills our hearts, revealing whether they are good or evil.

On a Tuesday. Listen to your own words today, especially when you are tired, interrupted or contradicted. Write down one thing you said that surprised you. Then ask what in your heart it came from, confess it to God, and ask him to fill that place with something better.

For worship. There was once a heart so full of good treasure that every word that overflowed from it was grace and truth. Never once did a careless word come from the mouth of Jesus. Even on the cross, under the greatest pressure ever borne, what spilled out was forgiveness for his enemies and comfort for a thief. Out of the abundance of his heart he spoke, and it was love. And he gives that heart’s Spirit to us, so that one day our mouths too will speak only praise.

parallels.desc: what comes out of the mouth

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On judgment day, people will give an account for every careless word they have spoken. By your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned.

I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak. The adjective is precise and unusual. Argos is a compound of a- and ergon: literally not-working, unemployed, idle. It is the word used of the labourers standing in the marketplace with nothing to do (20:3, 6), and of those who learn to be idlers, going about from house to house (1 Timothy 5:13). So the words in view are not primarily the wicked ones. They are the idle ones: the remarks that were doing no job at all. Not the calculated lie or the deliberate cruelty, which any conscience flags, but the throwaway: the comment that cost nothing, meant nothing, achieved nothing, and was forgotten within the hour by everybody except the person it was about. The joke at someone’s expense, the gossip, the casual remark. That is what will be given account for. And if even careless words matter to God, how much more deliberate ones like the Pharisees’ slander.

The setting. That sounds intolerable until the setting is remembered. It is said in the middle of an argument in which men have just called the Holy Spirit a demon. It is not a general anxiety about small talk. It is the conclusion of a paragraph about a mouth revealing a heart, and the point is that nothing is exempt from the disclosure, not even the material we discount ourselves.

For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned. Justified here means declared righteous at the final judgment. And the language is a courtroom’s. In a court, evidence does not create a fact; it establishes one. The words are exhibits, not payment. What they demonstrate is what was in the storehouse, and the storehouse is what grace changes and nothing else does. At the judgment our words will show whether our hearts belonged to God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we are saved by our words, as if careful speech earns heaven. The man who said it would shortly die to secure acquittal on entirely different grounds, and Paul spends most of Romans establishing the point: we are justified by faith in Christ (Romans 3:28). But words, like works, are evidence of genuine faith or its absence (James 2:18; 3:2–12). A person whose heart has been changed will have changed speech. Nor does it mean every careless word will condemn a believer. Christ’s blood cleanses them from all sin, including sins of the tongue (1 John 1:7). So the verse is terrifying to a man who thinks his words are trivial, and it is not terrifying to a man whose heart has new contents and whose tongue keeps embarrassing him. Those are two different situations, and this sentence distinguishes them. But no one should treat words lightly.

What do I do about words I said that I cannot take back? Confess them to God specifically, and believe that in Christ they are forgiven; you will not be condemned for them on the last day. Then, where you can, go to the person you hurt and apologise plainly, without excuses. Where a word has spread, gossip for instance, correct it with the people who heard it. Some damage takes time to heal, and you may need to show changed speech over months. But do not live under a cloud. The same Lord who weighs every word has spoken a better word over you: no condemnation (Romans 8:1).

In a sentence. God will judge every careless word, because our words reveal our hearts, though believers are justified by faith and their words are evidence, not payment.

On a Tuesday. If you had to give an account for every word you said yesterday, what would it reveal? Ask God to forgive your careless words, and pray Psalm 141:3 before your first conversation today: set a guard over my mouth. Then say one word today that does a job: an encouragement, a thank you, a truth spoken in love.

For worship. Every word will be weighed, and only one man’s words were ever found entirely without fault. He is the Word made flesh, and every word that came from his mouth was true and good and timely. And this same Word speaks for us now at the Father’s right hand, an advocate whose plea is his own blood. Our careless words are many; his word of pardon is greater. Praise the Judge who will hear every word, and the Saviour who has already answered for ours.

parallels.desc: death and life are in the power of the tongue

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, "Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you." But he answered them, "An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some scribes and Pharisees asked Jesus for a sign. He replied that an evil and adulterous generation demands a sign, but no sign will be given except the sign of the prophet Jonah.

Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you. Note how they address him, because Matthew has been keeping score. In this Gospel, disciples say Lord and outsiders say Teacher. The scribe who volunteered to follow said Teacher (8:19). The rich young man said Teacher (19:16). The Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Herodians say Teacher (22:16, 24, 36). And Judas, alone among the Twelve at the Last Supper, says Rabbi while the rest say Lord (26:22, 25). The address is the assessment. These men have come to test a religious lecturer, and their opening word says so before the request does. A sign means a miraculous proof of his authority, something spectacular, on their terms.

The sign that had just happened. The request is astonishing in its position. They have just watched a man who was blind, mute and possessed walk away seeing, speaking and free (v. 22). That was the sign. It had happened in front of them, and it was the reason for the whole argument that followed, and they called it Satan’s work. So what they mean by a sign is something other than evidence. They want a demonstration on demand, of their choosing, on their terms: the very thing the devil had proposed in the wilderness, when he invited Jesus to throw himself from the temple, and Jesus refused there too (4:5–7). Their request was not honest seeking but unbelief demanding more.

An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign. Adulterous is not casual abuse. It is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God. Israel’s covenant with God is described throughout the prophets as a marriage, which is why unfaithfulness is adultery; Hosea was told to marry an unfaithful woman so that the nation could see itself (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3). To call a generation adulterous is to say that it is not a stranger to God but a wife who has gone elsewhere. That is why the demand for a sign is so galling. A wife does not require her husband to prove his identity.

But no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. Jesus will not perform on demand. The refusal is not a withholding of evidence from honest seekers; it is a refusal to play the game of the hardened heart, which will always require more evidence as a reason for never believing. The only sign they will get is the sign of Jonah, which he explains next.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that asking God for help or reassurance is always wrong. Gideon asked for a sign, and God graciously gave it (Judges 6:36–40). The problem is demanding proof from a heart that has already decided not to believe.

Is it wrong to ask God for a sign when I have a decision to make? It is not wrong to ask God for wisdom, and he promises to give it (James 1:5). But the normal way God guides his people now is through his word, which is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17), through prayer, through wise counsel from mature Christians, and through the ordinary circumstances he arranges. Setting tests for God, if the phone rings in the next five minutes I will take the job, is risky: it treats chance events as messages and can bypass the wisdom he has already given. Pray, search the Scriptures, seek counsel, then decide, trusting that he directs the steps of those who seek him (Proverbs 3:5–6).

In a sentence. Jesus refused to perform signs on demand for an unfaithful generation that had just rejected the sign in front of them, except for the sign of Jonah.

On a Tuesday. Are you asking God to prove himself on your terms while ignoring the evidence he has already given: the Scriptures, the cross, the empty tomb, his faithfulness in your life? Write down three things he has already shown you. Then trust him with the thing you are asking about.

For worship. How patient is the Bridegroom with his faithless bride. They demanded proof of him while he was healing their sick in front of them. And he did not abandon them to their demand. He promised them one sign, the greatest of all, and then he went and gave it: his own death and resurrection. God has never needed to prove himself to us. That he does, at the cost of his own Son, is pure grace.
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jonah was three days and nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and nights in the heart of the earth. The people of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn this generation, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and something greater than Jonah is here.

For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish. Jonah 1:17. Jonah was swallowed by a great fish and then came out alive. It was like a death and resurrection, and Jonah himself describes it that way. Inside the fish he prays a psalm: out of the belly of Sheol he cried, and God heard his voice; the deep surrounded him; he went down to the land whose bars closed upon him for ever; and God brought up his life from the pit (Jonah 2:2–6). That is not the language of a man in an awkward situation. It is the language of a man describing his own death, from underneath.

So will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Jesus predicts his death, burial and resurrection. The sign of Jonah is the resurrection: the greatest sign of all, and the one that makes all other signs unnecessary. And notice the phrase he chooses for the tomb. Not in the grave, but in the heart of the earth, answering Jonah’s heart of the seas (Jonah 2:3). So the sign is not merely a three-day interval. It is the whole of what Jonah’s prayer describes: going down into the place from which nobody negotiates a return, and being brought up out of it, and brought up specifically so that Gentiles could be preached to.

How is Friday to Sunday three days and three nights? Jesus was buried on Friday afternoon and rose on Sunday morning, which looks like only two nights. The answer is the Jewish way of counting time: any part of a day was reckoned as a whole day and night. So Friday, Saturday and Sunday were counted as three days and three nights, even though only part of Friday and part of Sunday were involved. Scripture counts this way elsewhere. Esther calls a fast for three days, night or day, and then goes to the king on the third day (Esther 4:16; 5:1); the same idiom appears in 1 Samuel 30:12–13 and 2 Chronicles 10:5, 12. A few have proposed a Wednesday crucifixion to fit a literal seventy-two hours, but the Gospels’ own timing, that Jesus rose on the third day and not the fourth (16:21; 27:63–64), fits the ordinary Jewish reckoning best.

The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, Israel’s most brutal enemy, a pagan city of great wickedness. When Jonah preached, the whole city repented, from the king down (Jonah 3:5–10). At the final judgment their example will condemn this generation, which did not repent.

For they repented at the preaching of Jonah. Jonah was a reluctant, angry prophet who performed no miracles and preached a short message of judgment. Yet Nineveh repented.

And behold, something greater than Jonah is here. Jesus is greater than Jonah: a willing Saviour, not a reluctant prophet; the Son of God, not a mere messenger; working miracles, not only preaching. Jonah was swallowed unwillingly; Jesus lays down his life of his own accord. And there is a last irony in the comparison. Jonah went into the deep because he was running from the commission to preach to pagans. Jesus goes into the earth in order to fulfil it. If Nineveh repented at Jonah, how much more should Israel repent at Jesus.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the story of Jonah is merely a myth. Jesus treats Jonah and the repentance of Nineveh as real history, alongside his own resurrection. Nor does three days and three nights require exactly seventy-two hours.

Was Jonah a real person? Many critics treat the book as a parable. But Jesus sets Jonah beside his own death and resurrection and says the men of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment (see also Luke 11:30). That makes best sense if the events happened, and the more likely reading is that Jesus believed they did. Jonah is also named as a historical prophet in 2 Kings 14:25. If the Lord of the Scriptures treated the account as history, his people may do the same without embarrassment.

In a sentence. Jesus’ death and resurrection will be the sign of Jonah, and repentant Nineveh will condemn a generation that would not repent at one greater than Jonah.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection is the sign God has given. If you have doubts, do not ask for a new sign; study the one already given. Read one Gospel’s account of the resurrection this week slowly. And ask: have I repented at the preaching of one greater than Jonah, or only listened?

For worship. Jonah went down into the deep running from God, and was brought up by mercy. The Son of God went down into the heart of the earth running toward the will of God, carrying our sin, and on the third day the earth could not hold him. Here is the sign no one could forge: a tomb empty, and death swallowed up in victory. Nineveh repented at one sentence from a sulking prophet; how shall we not fall down and worship the risen Lord?
verseByVerse.note: “Three days and three nights” was a way of counting any part of a day as a day. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

parallels.desc: three days and three nights in the fish

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of the South will also rise at the judgment and condemn this generation, because she travelled from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and something greater than Solomon is here.

The queen of the South. The queen of Sheba, from south-west Arabia (modern Yemen), about 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometres) from Jerusalem. She came to test Solomon with hard questions, was overwhelmed by his wisdom, and praised his God (1 Kings 10:1–13). She was a Gentile.

Will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it. She made a long, costly journey to hear wisdom; this generation would not walk a few steps to listen to Jesus. And notice who the two witnesses for the prosecution are: the men of Nineveh (v. 41) and the queen of the South (v. 42). Both are Gentiles. Nineveh was the capital of the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom and carried ten tribes away for ever, the cruellest power in Israel’s memory, whose kings boasted in inscriptions of the cruelties they inflicted. And the queen came from the far southern end of the known world, a pagan monarch on a trade mission. Neither had the Scriptures, the temple, the covenant, the prophets or the promises. Nineveh had one reluctant preacher and a single sentence of warning; Sheba had a rumour about a clever king and a long journey. Both responded. And they will be on their feet at the last day against people who had everything, watched Jesus heal a blind mute, and called it Beelzebul. It would have been unbearable to hear.

For she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. Solomon was the wisest king in Israel’s history, the son of David, and his wisdom drew the nations.

And behold, something greater than Solomon is here. Jesus is greater than Solomon: the true Son of David, Wisdom itself (11:19; 1 Corinthians 1:24, 30; Colossians 2:3). And look at how the comparisons are built. Jonah was a prophet, and a poor one: he ran away, sulked and wanted the city destroyed. Solomon was a king, and ended badly. They are not Israel’s finest; they are simply the two who reached the Gentiles. Set against them: something greater than Jonah, something greater than Solomon, both neuter, both the same construction as verse 6. In this chapter Jesus has claimed to be greater than the temple (v. 6), than Jonah the prophet (v. 41) and than Solomon the king (v. 42): greater than priest, prophet and king. The temple was the place, the prophet was the voice, the king was the throne. All three are named in one chapter, and the same word is used of what has arrived to fulfil them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Gentiles are saved by seeking wisdom or by their sincerity. The queen praised Israel’s God; Nineveh turned to him at his word. Their example condemns those who had more light and refused it. Salvation still comes only through the One greater than Solomon.

In a sentence. A Gentile queen who travelled far for Solomon’s wisdom will condemn those who ignored one far greater than Solomon.

On a Tuesday. What effort do you make to hear the wisdom of Christ? The queen travelled 1,200 miles for a lesser king. Is there a Bible study, a sermon, a book of Scripture you have been meaning to get to? Make the journey this week: set aside the time, and go.

For worship. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. The queen of Sheba saw Solomon’s court and there was no more breath in her. What will it be to see the King greater than Solomon in his glory, the one who is the wisdom of God and who became for us righteousness, holiness and redemption? Kings will bring their glory to him, and the nations will come from the ends of the earth, and we who were far off will stand among them, breathless with praise.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, in south-west Arabia.

parallels.desc: the queen of Sheba visits Solomon

verseByVerse.quote: Then it says, "I will return to my house from which I came." And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When an unclean spirit leaves a person, it wanders looking for rest and finds none. Then it says: I will go back to my house. It finds the house empty, swept and tidy, and brings back seven other spirits worse than itself. The person ends up worse than before. So it will be with this evil generation.

When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest. Deserts were thought of as the haunt of demons (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). The spirit is restless without a person to inhabit.

I will return to my house from which I came. The person is still its house, because no one else has moved in.

And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. The three descriptions are the whole parable, and they are all approving words. Nothing is dirty. Somebody has been at work: the place has been cleared out, the floor has been swept, the furniture arranged. On any inspection it would pass. And the first of the three is the fatal one: empty. The house is not reoccupied. It is in excellent condition and there is nobody in it, which is exactly the state a life is left in by a reformation that goes no further than removal. The habit was given up, the company was dropped, the language cleaned. Nothing has moved in.

Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself. Seven: a complete number. A full occupation.

And the last state of that person is worse than the first. Reformation without regeneration leaves a person more vulnerable than before. It produces a clean space and no defender.

So also will it be with this evil generation. The application is stated outright, which is unusual for a parable. He means the generation in front of him. They had had a genuine national awakening: enormous crowds going out to the Jordan, confessing sins, being baptised by John, and the healings and exorcisms of Jesus. The house had been swept. And then the one who was to fill it arrived, and they said he had a demon. Within forty years the temple was rubble, in the disaster of AD 70, and the last state was worse than the first.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a true believer, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, can be repossessed by demons or lose his salvation. There is no indwelling in the story; that is the entire problem. A house with an occupant is not vacant, and the New Testament’s word for a believer is precisely that God has taken up residence: he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). The warning is about moral reform without new birth: cleaning up one’s life without receiving Christ. Getting rid of bad habits is not enough; the heart must be filled with Christ.

I have given up some bad habits. How do I make sure the house is not empty? Ask first whether Christ himself lives there: have you trusted him, not just tidied up for him? Then fill the space deliberately. When you stop one thing, put something better in its place: time with God’s word where the screen used to be, friendship in the church where the old company used to be, serving others where the old habit used to sit. Paul’s pattern is always put off and put on (Ephesians 4:22–32). An emptied life is not a safe life; it is a vacant one, and the previous tenant knows the address.

In a sentence. Moral cleaning without being filled by God leaves a person, or a nation, worse off than before.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith only a tidying-up of your life, or have you received Christ himself to fill it? If you have recently given something up, decide today what you will put in its place, and tell a Christian friend so they can help you keep at it.

For worship. We could sweep our own houses, but we could never fill them. Only God can live in a human heart, and he has chosen to. The Father and the Son make their home with those who love Christ (John 14:23), and the Holy Spirit takes up residence as in a temple. No empty house for his people, but a dwelling filled with God. And the One who fills it is stronger than every spirit that would return, so the house he has entered he will never leave.

parallels.desc: the last state worse than the first

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. Someone told him, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was still speaking, his mother and brothers stood outside, wanting to speak to him. Someone told him they were waiting.

His mother and his brothers. Mary and Jesus’ brothers, James, Joseph, Simon and Judas, with sisters also mentioned (13:55–56). Mark tells us plainly why they came: his family went out to seize him, for people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21, 31). They were not paying a visit. They had come to take him home, and the reason given was that he had lost his reason. His brothers did not believe in him at this time (John 7:5). After the resurrection they became believers. James became a leader of the Jerusalem church and wrote the letter of James, which he opens by calling himself a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ; and Judas, Jude, wrote the letter of Jude (Acts 1:14; 15:13; Galatians 1:19). It took a resurrection.

Stood outside, asking to speak to him. Outside the house or the crowd. Physically, and perhaps spiritually, they were outside. The interruption is public, in the middle of his teaching, and it is the occasion for one of his most searching sayings.

Textual note. Some important early manuscripts omit verse 47, the report that his mother and brothers were standing outside asking to speak to him. It may have been accidentally skipped because verses 46 and 47 end with almost the same words, and a copyist’s eye could jump from one to the other. Verdict: probably original; it is needed for verse 48 to make sense. Nothing turns on it either way.

On the brothers. Christians have read this in three ways, and it is worth knowing them without heat. The oldest Eastern view takes them as Joseph’s children by a previous marriage, and so stepbrothers. The Western Catholic view, from Jerome onward, takes them as cousins, since the word for brother can stretch that far in Semitic usage. The Protestant view takes them at face value as later children of Joseph and Mary, pointing to Matthew’s wording that Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (1:25), and to Luke calling Jesus her firstborn (Luke 2:7). The plain reading favours the third, and it is followed here. But the virgin birth, which is what actually matters and which all three views affirm, is untouched by the question, and it would be a poor use of a passage about family to be uncharitable about a point on which sincere Christians differ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Jesus’ brothers must be cousins or Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. The natural reading is that they were Mary’s later children (see 1:25).

My family thinks my faith has made me strange. What should I do? You are in good company: Jesus’ own family thought he had lost his mind. Stay patient and loving. Keep honouring your parents and serving your family in practical ways, so that the change in you is seen in kindness, not only in words (1 Peter 3:1–2). Do not give up following Christ to keep the peace, but do not be harsh or superior either. And keep praying. His brothers came to believe; the family that stood outside ended up in the upper room.

In a sentence. Jesus’ mother and brothers, who did not yet understand him, came wanting to speak to him and take him home.

On a Tuesday. Pray by name today for any member of your family who does not yet believe. And do one practical kindness for them this week, without preaching, as the love of Christ made visible.

For worship. The Son of God was misunderstood by his own household. He grew up with brothers who did not believe him and who came to take him home as a madman. He bore that too, for us. And look at what grace did with that family: the brother who thought him mad became the servant who called him Lord, and the mother who stood outside was found praying among his disciples. No one is too close to him to need his grace, and no one is too far from him to receive it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 47: “Someone told him, ‘Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, asking to speak to you.’”

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to the man who told him, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked: who is my mother, and who are my brothers? Pointing to his disciples, he said: here are my mother and my brothers.

Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? A shocking question in a culture where family was everything. Jesus is not rejecting his family, but redefining what family means in God’s kingdom. And it is worth being honest about how hard the saying is. His mother is outside. She had carried him, had been told by an angel who he was, had watched shepherds arrive and kept all these things in her heart. She is standing in the street unable to get in, and he does not go out. The Gospel does not soften that, and neither should a commentary.

And stretching out his hand toward his disciples. A gesture of welcome and claim, and Matthew uses the identical verb (ekteinas) as in verse 13. It is what he told the man with the withered hand to do, and what that man did before anything was healed. So the chapter has two outstretched hands in it. A ruined one, held out on command in front of a hostile congregation, and restored. And this one, held out over a circle of ordinary men to say: here is my family.

Here are my mother and my brothers! His disciples are his true family. The bond of faith is deeper than the bond of blood. The church is not a voluntary association or a religious club; it is a family, brothers and sisters with God as Father (23:8–9), with all the obligations, closeness and mutual care that family implies.

Where Mary ended up. Mary is in the upper room after the ascension, named among those devoting themselves to prayer with the apostles (Acts 1:14). She did not stay outside. The circle he pointed at that day was the one she joined. She got in, not as his mother, which had never been in doubt, but by the door he was describing, which was open to her on the same terms as everybody else. That is the answer to the discomfort of the scene. He is not disowning her. He is telling her, in the hearing of the whole room, that the relationship she is about to need is not the one she already had.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Jesus despised his mother. On the cross he provided for her care (John 19:26–27). Nor does it mean that natural family does not matter (15:4–6). But family loyalty is not the highest loyalty (10:37). And this passage gives no support for devotion to Mary as a mediator. Jesus pointed away from his family to his disciples, and Mary herself was saved by faith in her Son like everyone else (Luke 1:47).

If the church is my family, what do I still owe my natural family? A great deal. Scripture commands children to honour their parents (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:2), husbands and wives to love and be faithful to each other, parents to raise their children in the Lord, and anyone who does not provide for his relatives to be counted worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). Jesus himself cared for his mother from the cross. The church does not replace those duties; it sets them in order. Christ comes first, so that when family demands conflict with obeying him, you follow him. But in ordinary life, following him means loving your family better, not less.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that his disciples are his true family, a bond deeper than blood.

On a Tuesday. Your church is your family. Who in it needs a brother, sister, mother or father this week: a widow, a student far from home, a single parent, a new believer whose own family has turned away? Invite one of them for a meal.

For worship. With the same gesture that healed a withered hand he gathered a family. He looked at fishermen and tax collectors and called them his brothers. He is not ashamed of them, and he is not ashamed of us (Hebrews 2:11). The eternal Son, who had the Father’s love from before the world began, stretched out his hand over ordinary sinners and said, these are mine. And in the end his own mother came in by the same door, and found that her Son was her Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.

For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven. Membership in Jesus’ family is not by birth but by doing God’s will: repenting, believing in Jesus and obeying him (7:21; John 6:29). It is the same standard given for entering the kingdom. Anyone may join.

Is my brother and sister and mother. Count the relations he names, and then count the one he does not. Brother, sister, mother: three. He does not say father. The omission cannot be accidental, because the missing word is standing in the sentence already: the will of my Father in heaven. There is a father in the verse, and the place is taken. He will say it outright in the last week: call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven (23:9). In a household there is one father, and the family being described has one, and he is not in the room. And notice sister. Jesus includes women explicitly, in a culture that routinely kept them at the edge of religious life. In the church there are spiritual mothers, sisters and brothers. Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

What this family is. That quietly settles what this new family is. It is not an association of like-minded people, and it is not a replacement for the household. It is a household, with siblings and a mother’s place in it, and one Father, and everybody else at the same level under him. That is why the obligations are what they are. Christians are not asked to be fond of each other, which is beyond arranging. They are told what they are: people with the same Father, which is a fact about the arrangement rather than a description of the feeling. He was standing in a house, with his own mother outside and his brothers convinced he was out of his mind, when he said it. It cost him something to define the family that way, and it is the definition under which the church has lived ever since: held together not by temperament, nation or blood, but by one Father in heaven and a will that everybody in the room was learning to do badly. The men he stretched his hand over would all abandon him within a year, and not one of them was struck off the list.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we earn a place in Jesus’ family by our works. Doing the Father’s will begins with believing in the Son he sent (John 6:29). Those adopted into God’s family by grace (Ephesians 1:5) show it by doing his will.

I am single, or my family has rejected me. Does this promise mean anything for me? It means everything. Jesus promised that no one who has left home or family for his sake will fail to receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life (Mark 10:29–30). The church is meant to be that hundredfold. If you feel alone, tell your pastor or a mature believer; you are not imposing. And if you belong to a church, make it your business that no single person, widow or rejected believer in it lacks a family table to sit at.

In a sentence. Everyone who does the Father’s will belongs to Jesus’ family, with one Father in heaven.

On a Tuesday. If you trust and obey Christ, he calls you his brother or sister. Live today as a member of his family: pray for one brother or sister by name, and think of someone in your church you have never really spoken to, and change that this Sunday.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he is not ashamed to call you his brother or sister. The Son by nature made us sons and daughters by grace, and shares with us his own Father. We were outsiders, standing in the street; he stretched out his hand and drew us in. He did not strike off the disciples who fled, and he will not strike off us. One Father in heaven, one elder Brother who died for his family, and a household gathered from every nation, learning together to do the will of God, and kept by his love for ever.

parallels.desc: you are my friends if you do what I command

12.theology: Christ as the fulfilment of the Sabbath. The Sabbath controversy of chapter 12 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the antitype of every Old Testament type. The Sabbath rest of creation (Gen 2) and covenant (Exod 20) pointed forward to the final rest that God’s people would enjoy in the new creation. Hebrews 4 draws this line explicitly: the rest that Joshua could not give, the rest that the weekly Sabbath symbolised, is found in Christ. When Jesus says “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath,” he is claiming to be both the giver and the substance of that rest. The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is a weekly proclamation that the rest has arrived in Christ and will be consummated at his return.
12.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ religion had become a burden rather than a delight. Rules multiplied around the Sabbath until the day of rest was a day of anxiety. Jesus exposed the inversion: when religious observance crushes the people it was meant to bless, something has gone terribly wrong.

Now: The temptation of every religious tradition is to mistake the form for the substance, the sign for the thing signified. The Sabbath becomes a test case: are we worshipping the living God who gives rest, or performing compliance with a schedule? The Lord’s Day is meant to be a foretaste of heaven, a weekly resurrection celebration, not a legal obligation. Christ is Lord of it — and he gives it as a gift.

13.title: The Kingdom in Parables
13.text: <sup>1</sup>That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. <sup>2</sup>And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach. <sup>3</sup>And he told them many things in parables, saying: “A sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them. <sup>5</sup>Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, <sup>6</sup>but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. <sup>8</sup>Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. <sup>9</sup>He who has ears, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” <sup>11</sup>And he answered them, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. <sup>12</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>13</sup>This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. <sup>14</sup>Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: ”’“You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.” <sup>15</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>16</sup>But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. <sup>17</sup>For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. <sup>18</sup>“Hear then the parable of the sower: <sup>19</sup>When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. <sup>20</sup>As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, <sup>21</sup>yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. <sup>22</sup>As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>23</sup>As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” <sup>24</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, <sup>25</sup>but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. <sup>26</sup>So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. <sup>27</sup>And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?’ <sup>28</sup>He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ So the servants said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and gather them?’ <sup>29</sup>But he said, ‘No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. <sup>30</sup>Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, “Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’” <sup>31</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. <sup>32</sup>It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.” <sup>33</sup>He told them another parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened.” <sup>34</sup>All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. <sup>35</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.” <sup>36</sup>Then he left the crowds and went into the house.
