And his disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” <sup>37</sup>He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. <sup>38</sup>The field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, <sup>39</sup>and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. <sup>40</sup>Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. <sup>41</sup>The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers, <sup>42</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>43</sup>Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear. <sup>44</sup>“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. <sup>45</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls, <sup>46</sup>who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. <sup>47</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind. <sup>48</sup>When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. <sup>49</sup>So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous <sup>50</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>51</sup>“Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.” <sup>52</sup>And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.” <sup>53</sup>And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there, <sup>54</sup>and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? <sup>55</sup>Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? <sup>56</sup>And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?” <sup>57</sup>And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.” <sup>58</sup>And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the third great discourse of Matthew — a collection of seven parables about the kingdom of heaven. Jesus shifts to parables at a moment of escalating opposition (chapters 11–12), and explains to his disciples that parables reveal to the insiders and conceal from the hardened outsiders. This is not capricious; it is the judicial hardening of those who have repeatedly refused the light (v. 15, quoting Isa 6:9–10).

The parables themselves paint a picture of a kingdom that is present but not yet consummate, growing but not yet glorious, mixed but not yet purified. The mustard seed and leaven speak of unexpected, hidden growth from small beginnings. The wheat and tares speak of a kingdom growing alongside counterfeit until the final harvest. The treasure and pearl speak of the surpassing value of the kingdom that makes all sacrifice worthwhile. Together they answer the perennial question: why is the kingdom not more obvious? Because this is the age of seed-sowing, not harvest. The harvest is coming.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — The Parable of the Sower and the Mystery of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes to the seashore and teaches in parables for the first time in Matthew. The parable of the sower describes four kinds of reception of the kingdom's word — the path, the rocky ground, the thorns, and the good soil. When the disciples ask why he teaches in parables, Jesus answers that parables reveal the kingdom to those with ears to hear and conceal it from those whose hearts are hardened. He then interprets the parable of the sower in detail. What the summary cannot hold. First-century sowing came before ploughing, not after: a man broadcast seed across the whole field as it stood and then turned the soil to cover it. So the sower is not careless — the path, the rock shelf and the thorn roots are all ground he is about to plough, and the parable is about ground rather than about a fool with a bag. "rocky ground" is not soil with stones in it but a shelf of limestone a few inches down, extremely common in Galilee — and thin soil over rock warms faster, which is exactly why that seed comes up first. The fastest green in the field is growing over the shallowest ground. The yields are the point and are usually skimmed: a normal harvest returned seven to tenfold, so thirty is triple a good year and a hundredfold is what Genesis records of Isaac as a Mark of extraordinary blessing (Gen. 26:12). One patch of good ground repays the whole sowing many times over — the parable is not pessimistic arithmetic. On the hardening, Matthew and Mark genuinely differ: Matthew has "because (hoti) seeing they do not see"; Mark has "so that (hina)... lest they should turn and be forgiven" (Mk. 4:12). Consequence and purpose. Both are in the Isaiah passage both writers quote — "their eyes they have closed" is active and theirs, and "lest they should turn, and I would heal them" is purpose and God's. Anybody who resolves that has dropped one half. Isaiah 6:9-10 is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts; it is the settled apostolic explanation for Israel's unbelief. And "grown dull" is epachynthe, thickened — the language of a callus, which is formed by repetition rather than by one injury.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable of the sower is really a parable of soils — the sower and the seed are constant; the variable is the heart that receives the word. The four soils are not four types of people as if fixed in their category, but four ways the same heart can receive or resist the word. The parable is both diagnostic (what kind of soil am I?) and eschatological (the harvest will reveal what was real). The interpretation makes explicit that the word of the kingdom is the seed and the devil, persecution, worldly care, and the deceitfulness of riches are the enemies of fruitfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: The mystery of the kingdom — given to the disciples, hidden from others — is not arbitrary divine caprice but the consistent pattern of revelation-and-response: those who have ears to hear receive more; those who have closed their ears lose even what they have. The disciple's responsibility is to cultivate the good soil of an open, honest, persevering heart — "hear the word and understand it" (v. 23) — so that the seed which is sown can bear its appointed fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same day, Jesus sat by the Sea of Galilee. So many people gathered that he got into a boat and taught from it, while the crowd stood on the shore.

Meaning first. Matthew 13 is the third of Jesus’ five great teaching sections: the parables of the kingdom. It follows directly from the growing rejection of chapters 11 and 12, and it answers the question that rejection raises. If the kingdom has really come in Jesus, why do some receive him and others refuse him, and why is evil still everywhere? The parables answer: the kingdom comes quietly, like seed; it meets different kinds of soil; it grows hidden, from tiny beginnings, until it fills the world; it is worth more than everything a man owns; and good and evil will grow side by side until the harvest, when the Son of Man will sort them for ever. The chapter ends in Nazareth, where the people who knew Jesus best stumble over him, a living picture of the hard ground.

The connection. Why do some receive Jesus and others reject him, if the kingdom has really come? The parables answer it from the farm, the kitchen, the market and the lake: the kingdom comes quietly, like seed; it meets different kinds of soil; it grows hidden; and good and evil will exist side by side until the final harvest.

That same day. The day of the Beelzebul controversy and the sign of Jonah (chapter 12), and Matthew has built a link across the chapter break.

Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. Which house? The one he was in at the end of chapter 12, when his mother and brothers were standing outside unable to reach him, and he stretched out his hand over his disciples and said, here are my mother and my brothers (12:46–50). He leaves that house and goes and sits by the sea. Matthew has put a scene about who truly belongs to him immediately before a teaching about who truly receives his word, and the join is the same day. And he sat. Teachers sat to teach (5:1). A rabbi stood to read the Scripture and sat down to expound it, as Jesus did in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:20). Nothing about this is casual. The crowd stands; the teacher sits.

So that he got into a boat and sat down. The boat, pushed a little out from the shore, became a pulpit, and the water carried his voice to the crowd. The north-west shore of the lake near Capernaum has a small natural bay, and its shape has long been noticed: the ground rises from the water in a curve, and a voice from a boat a few yards out carries remarkably well up the slope. Visitors have tested it and been surprised. Whether or not this is the exact spot, the arrangement is sound. A man standing on a beach is heard by the first few rows. A man sitting in a boat pushed out a little, with water in front of him and a natural amphitheatre behind, can be heard by thousands. He did not have a building, so he used the shape of the ground.

And the whole crowd stood on the beach. Crowds in large numbers, as throughout Galilee. And within that crowd were all four soils of the parable he was about to tell. The same word would be sown on all of them; what happened next would depend not on the word but on the hearts that received it.

Why does Jesus teach in stories at all? Because stories reach people who would not sit through a lecture, stay in the memory long after an argument is forgotten, and require the hearer to think. A parable also leaves a person free to walk away with only a story, or to ask what it means and receive more. Jesus will explain this himself in verses 10–17. For now, notice that the Lord of glory sat in a fishing boat and talked about seed and soil, weeds and yeast, nets and pearls. He made the deepest truths of God out of ordinary things, so that ordinary people would meet them every day.

In a sentence. Jesus left the house and taught the great crowds from a boat beside the lake.

On a Tuesday. Jesus used whatever was at hand, a boat and the shape of a shore, to teach. Look for an ordinary opportunity this week to share God’s word: a meal table, a car journey, a walk with a friend. You do not need a building or a platform to speak of Christ.

For worship. The Word through whom the sea was made sat in a boat upon it, and spoke. He who could have thundered from Sinai chose to speak from a fishing boat to farmers and fishermen, in words they could carry home. Blessed be the Teacher who comes down to where we are, sits among us, and turns the things we handle every day into windows on the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach; the boat let the crowd on the shore hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them many things in parables, saying: "A sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus taught in parables. The first: a farmer went out to sow seed. As he scattered it, some fell on the path, and birds came and ate it.

Parables. A parable (parabolē, something thrown alongside) is a story or picture from everyday life placed alongside a spiritual truth to illustrate it. The Hebrew equivalent (mashal) includes proverbs, riddles and illustrations. Jesus’ parables use farming, fishing, cooking, buying and selling. They usually make one main point, sometimes a few; they are not detailed allegories where every detail has a hidden meaning, though Jesus does interpret some details (vv. 18–23, 36–43).

A sower went out to sow. In Galilee seed was usually sown by hand, scattered broadly from a bag. And one fact about first-century farming removes a misreading that has troubled many readers. The usual complaint is that the sower seems incompetent: much of his seed lands where no farmer would put it. Why scatter good grain on a footpath, a rock shelf and a thorn patch? The answer is that in that land the ploughing often came after the sowing, not before. A man broadcast the seed across the whole field as it stood, stubble, path and all, and then turned the soil over to cover it. So what looks like carelessness is standard practice: he is sowing the ground he is about to plough. The path is a right of way the villagers had beaten across the field. The thorns have been cut back, and their roots are still there. He is not wasteful; he is sowing a field, and a field in that country has all of this in it. The parable is not a story about a fool with a bag of seed. It is a story about ground. And it is a picture of the gospel: sown generously, without visible selection, on every kind of heart.

And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path. The path was the hard-trodden footpath through the field. The soil was packed hard by feet, and the seed could not sink in. On every other soil the seed at least goes in. Here it does not: it lies on top, in plain sight.

And the birds came and devoured them. Seed lying on the surface was eaten at once. The birds do not have to dig. The interpretation names them: the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown (v. 19). And notice how little time there is in that picture. No struggle, no gradual erosion, no argument. The word arrives, does not go in, and is gone before the man has walked home.

The four soils. The parable is often called the parable of the sower, but its focus is on the four kinds of soil: the path, the rocky ground, the thorns and the good soil. The seed is the same; the soils differ. Jesus explains it in verses 18–23.

Is the problem ever the seed? Never. The word of God is the same wherever it falls, and it is always good. When people do not respond to faithful preaching, the fault is not in the gospel, and the remedy is not to change the message into something more acceptable. The sower in the parable is not told to sow different seed on the path. He keeps sowing the same seed everywhere, and the harvest comes from the good soil.

In a sentence. In the first parable a farmer scatters seed across his field, and some falls on the hard path, where birds eat it at once.

On a Tuesday. The parable will ask you what kind of soil your heart is. Begin today by noticing how you receive God’s word: does it go in, or does it lie on the surface until something carries it off? Before you read or hear the Bible next, ask God to make your heart soft enough to take it in.

For worship. How generous is the Sower. He does not measure out the seed only for the ground that looks promising. He flings it across the whole field, path and rock and thorn alike, because his word is abundant and his mercy is wide. Every one of us who now bears fruit was once hard ground, and he sowed on us anyway. Glory to the Lord of the harvest, who scatters the good seed of his word with an open hand.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell on rocky ground, with little soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow, but when the sun rose it was scorched and withered, because it had no root.

Other seeds fell on rocky ground. Not soil full of stones, but a thin layer of soil over a shelf of limestone bedrock lying a few inches below the surface, which is extremely common in Galilee. A farmer walking his land knows where the shelves run, because the plough tells him.

Where they did not have much soil. Shallow.

And immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil. The agriculture is exact, and it explains why the shallow seed comes up faster. Thin soil over rock warms up quicker than deep soil: the stone holds the heat of the sun and gives it back, so the seed sprouts ahead of everything else in the field. That is why Matthew writes immediately. The fastest green in the field is growing over the shallowest ground, and it is coming up early because there is rock underneath. It looked promising. It looked better than its neighbours for two or three weeks.

But when the sun rose they were scorched. Then the roots go down and hit the shelf. They cannot go through it, so they turn and run sideways in the few inches available, and the plant is left holding a large amount of leaf on almost no anchorage and almost no water. And then the heat comes. In that country it can be the hot east wind off the desert, which arrives in a day and draws the moisture out of everything standing. The deep-rooted plants reach down and survive it. The shallow ones cannot. The same sun that made them sprout quickly also killed them.

And since they had no root, they withered away. No root, no endurance. And the picture should not be softened. The parable does not describe a man who was never affected. It describes the most impressive-looking plant in the field. Whatever this hearer had, it was visible, and it was ahead of everybody else’s, and the thing that made it grow so fast was the same thing that killed it.

How can I tell whether my own faith has roots? Roots are invisible, so you cannot tell by how you feel on a good Sunday. You tell by what holds when the heat comes. Has your faith survived a disappointment, an unanswered prayer, mockery, a loss, a season with no feelings at all? Do you keep coming to God when it brings you nothing you can see? Roots grow down in the dark: through steady reading of Scripture, honest prayer, belonging to a church where you are known, and obedience when it costs. If you are not sure, do not panic. Ask God to deepen you, and start putting down roots today.

In a sentence. Seed on shallow, rocky ground sprouted quickly but withered in the heat, because it had no root.

On a Tuesday. Quick enthusiasm is not the same as deep roots. Choose one root-growing habit and begin it this week: a fixed time for reading a Gospel, a weekly conversation with a mature Christian, or a passage of Scripture learned by heart. Roots are grown before the heat, not during it.

For worship. There is One whose roots went down through every rock of suffering and found the water of his Father’s will. He was a root out of dry ground (Isaiah 53:2), and the scorching sun of God’s wrath beat on him at the cross, and he did not wither. Because he endured, those who are rooted in him will endure. Praise the Lord who plants his people like trees by streams of water, whose leaf does not wither (Psalm 1:3).
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked it. But other seed fell on good soil and produced a crop: a hundred, sixty or thirty times what was sown. Whoever has ears, let them hear.

Other seeds fell among thorns. Ground where thorn roots remained. The thorns had been cut back and had not yet appeared when the seed was sown.

And the thorns grew up and choked them. The thorns grew faster and stronger, taking the light, water and nourishment. The plants survived, but produced nothing.

Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain. Deep, soft, clean soil.

Some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. The numbers are the part everybody skims, and they are the whole point of the parable. A normal harvest in that country returned perhaps seven to ten times what was sown. A tenfold yield was a good year: enough to feed the household, keep next year’s seed and pay what was owed. So take the figures again with that in hand. Thirtyfold is three times a good year. Sixtyfold is six times. A hundredfold is a harvest nobody in the audience had ever seen. Genesis records exactly one: Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold, and the LORD blessed him (Genesis 26:12). It is offered there as a mark of extraordinary divine favour.

The arithmetic turned upside down. Read quickly, it is a discouraging story: three failures and one success, a hard word about how few last. Read with the yields in place, it is nothing of the kind. One patch of good ground at a hundredfold repays the entire sowing many times over, the losses on the path, the rock and the thorns included. The sower does not come home at a loss. He comes home with more than he can carry. God’s kingdom will succeed abundantly. And notice that the good soil is not uniform. Even among those who truly receive the word, the return varies, and no explanation is offered for the difference. Not every believer bears the same quantity of fruit, but every true believer bears fruit. What is not offered is any category of good soil that produces nothing.

He who has ears, let him hear. A call to listen carefully and respond (see 11:15). The parable has just described four ways of hearing, and it ends by telling the crowd to do the fourth, which is a strange instruction if hearing were simply a matter of sound arriving. The words are now in every ear present, and what happens next is not a matter of volume. The parable is itself a test of the hearer.

Should I compare my fruit with other Christians’? No. The parable expressly allows for thirty, sixty and a hundredfold, and gives no ranking among them. Some believers have great gifts, long lives and wide influence; others are faithful in a small corner for many years, or are ill, or young in the faith. The question is not whether you produce as much as someone else but whether the word is bearing real fruit in you: more love for God and people, more holiness, more trust. Comparison breeds either pride or despair, and the Lord of the harvest is the only one who measures the yield.

In a sentence. Seed among thorns was choked, but seed in good soil produced an extraordinary harvest that more than repaid all the losses.

On a Tuesday. Are there thorns growing alongside God’s word in your heart, quietly crowding it out? Name one. And if you sow the word, in a class, a family, a friendship, take heart from the numbers: do not measure your work by the path and the rock. The good soil will repay it all.

For worship. The harvest of God is not meagre. From a handful of fishermen in Galilee he has raised a multitude no one can number, from every nation, tribe, people and language. The seed that fell into the ground and died, the Son of God himself, has borne much fruit (John 12:24). Thirty, sixty, a hundredfold: the Lord of the harvest is lavish beyond all our counting, and every grain in his barn will be to the praise of his glorious grace.
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the disciples came and said to him, "Why do you speak to them in parables?" And he answered them, "To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples asked why Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables. He answered: the secrets of the kingdom have been given to you to understand, but not to them. Whoever has will be given more; whoever does not have will lose even what he has.

Why do you speak to them in parables? Jesus had taught plainly before (chapters 5–7). Now he uses parables to the crowds. Why? And the disciples’ question is itself a mark of good soil: they come to Jesus for explanation rather than assuming they understood or giving up. They are distinguished from the crowd not by superior intelligence but by their posture: they come with their questions, and they are with him when the crowd has gone home.

To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven. The word is mystēria, mysteries, and the English is misleading. In ordinary Greek religion a mystery was something permanently withheld from outsiders, disclosed only to initiates. That is not what the word means here. Its background is Daniel, where the same term describes the king’s dream: a thing genuinely hidden, which no wise man in Babylon could reach by cleverness, and which God then revealed (Daniel 2:28–30). A biblical mystery is not a puzzle to be solved but a secret that has been told (see Ephesians 3:3). So the disciples have not been let into a club. They have been let in on something, and the difference matters, because a mystery religion keeps its content in, and this one is about to be proclaimed from the housetops (10:27). The mystery here is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, but not in the way people expected: not with crushing force, but like seed, hidden and growing, received by some and rejected by others, until the harvest.

It has been given. The passive points to God as the giver. Not achieved, not deduced, not earned by closer attention. The disciples were, on the evidence of this very chapter, no quicker than anybody else; they had to ask for the explanations. What separated them from the crowd was not capacity but a gift, and the sentence says so about both halves. Understanding the kingdom is a gift (11:25–27; 16:17).

But to them it has not been given. To the unbelieving crowds and leaders, who have rejected Jesus (chapters 11–12).

For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance. A principle of spiritual life. Those who receive and respond to the truth receive more understanding. Faith grows by use.

But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Stated flatly it sounds like a rule for concentrating wealth. What it actually describes is how attention to God works, and anybody who has learned anything will recognise it. A man who uses what he understands finds it opening out; a man who does not use it finds it closing. Nothing was confiscated. It went unused, and it went. Truth ignored is lost. There is no stable middle: the soul either grows in the light or loses its capacity to receive it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God is unfair, hiding the truth from people who wanted it. Those who did not receive it had already hardened their hearts (v. 15; 12:24). Nor does it mean that the disciples were cleverer. Their understanding was a gift.

If understanding is a gift, what can I do about it? Ask for it, and use what you have. Those two go together throughout Scripture: God gives wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), and to the one who has, more will be given. So pray before you read the Bible, read it regularly, ask questions of those who know it well, and above all obey what you already understand. Many people want more light while ignoring the light they have. The disciples did not understand everything; they simply kept coming to Jesus and asking.

In a sentence. Jesus gives understanding of the kingdom’s secrets to his disciples as a gift, while those who reject the light lose even what they had.

On a Tuesday. Think of one thing in Scripture you clearly understand and have not yet acted on: a person to forgive, a habit to drop, a kindness to do. Do it this week. Then ask God for more light, and expect him to give it.

For worship. The secret hidden from the wise of Babylon, hidden from the ages and generations, has been told to fishermen. God has opened his counsel to the humble and let them in on the purpose he formed before the world began: that his kingdom would come in his Son. It has been given. Every grain of understanding we have of Christ is a gift from the Father’s hand, and every gift of light is a promise of more.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: to everyone who has will more be given

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: "You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks in parables because, though people see, they do not truly see; though they hear, they do not truly hear or understand. This fulfils Isaiah’s prophecy.

This is why I speak to them in parables. Parables both reveal and conceal. To those open to the truth they illuminate; to those who have hardened their hearts they remain riddles, and that is itself a judgment. Those who want to understand will ask, as the disciples do; those who do not want to will receive a story they can enjoy without being confronted.

Because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. They saw the miracles and heard the teaching, but did not grasp what they meant: physical sight without spiritual sight. The word for understand (syniēmi) runs through this whole chapter, six times in all (vv. 13, 14, 15, 19, 23, 51). Its root sense is putting things together. It is not a word about intelligence but about the word being joined to a life.

Matthew and Mark. A reader with Mark open will find a real difference here, and it should be met head on. Matthew writes that Jesus speaks in parables because seeing they do not see: the parables respond to a condition that already exists. Mark records the same conversation with the words so that they may indeed see but not perceive, lest they should turn and be forgiven (Mark 4:12): the parables are given with a purpose. One reads as consequence, the other as intention. The difference is not a copying error, because both writers then quote the same passage of Isaiah, which contains both ideas. These are two true angles on one thing, and Scripture declines to collapse them. Matthew has the human side: they had already stopped their ears, and the parables meet them where they had put themselves. Mark has the divine side: God is not a bystander to that process, and a judicial hardening is truly his act. Anybody who resolves that tension has done so by dropping one half, and the New Testament never does.

Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled. Isaiah 6:9–10, from Isaiah’s call. God sent Isaiah to preach to a people who would not listen, and told him in advance that his preaching would harden them further. This passage is among the most quoted in the New Testament. It appears here, in Mark and Luke, in John (12:39–41) and in Acts (28:25–28), and Paul takes up the same theme (Romans 11:8). It is the settled apostolic explanation for why the message about Israel’s Messiah was so widely refused by Israel. And the explanation they reached for was not an accident of history or a failure of communication, but a text from the day a prophet was commissioned.

You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. The emphatic Hebrew form, hearing you will hear: plenty of hearing, but no understanding.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Jesus was trying to prevent people from being saved who wanted to be. The hardening is a judgment on those who have already rejected the truth. God gives them over to what they have chosen (Romans 1:24). Nor does it mean that parables are meant only to confuse. They also teach; the disciples received the explanations, and many who heard the parables later understood.

Could I be hardened without knowing it? It is possible to grow dull slowly, and that is why the warning is given. But the sign of the hardening in this passage is a settled refusal of Christ, a heart that no longer wants him. If you are troubled by this question, read the Gospels with a desire to know Jesus, and find that you want him, that desire is the opposite of hardness. The remedy for creeping dullness is not fear but turning: come back to him, ask him to soften your heart, and he will (Ezekiel 36:26).

In a sentence. Parables conceal truth from those who have hardened their hearts, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy that they would hear but not understand.

On a Tuesday. You can sit through sermons for years and not truly hear. Before Sunday, pray specifically: Lord, give me ears that hear and a heart that understands. After the sermon, write down one sentence about what God said and what you will do. That is how the word is joined to a life.

For worship. The God who sent Isaiah to a deaf people is the God who sent his own Son to a blind generation. He is just when he gives the proud over to the darkness they chose. And he is merciful beyond measure when he opens blind eyes that never asked to see. Every believer stands where the crowd stood, and should have stayed deaf; it is his grace alone that has made us hear.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them." But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah’s prophecy continues: the people’s heart has grown dull, their ears hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, so that they will not turn and be healed. But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.

For this people’s heart has grown dull. The verb (epachynthē) comes from the word for thick or fat. The heart has thickened. It is the language of tissue coarsening, of a surface becoming callused: something once sensitive has been overlaid until it no longer registers what touches it. And a callus is not formed by a single injury. It is formed by repetition, the same friction in the same place over a long time, until the body protects itself by growing a layer that cannot feel. That is exactly the condition described. Nobody in this crowd decided one morning to stop understanding. They had heard and set it aside, and heard again and set it aside, and the setting aside had become a habit.

And with their ears they can barely hear. Hard of hearing.

And their eyes they have closed. Notice: they closed their own eyes. The verb is active and theirs. The blindness is their own choice, and God’s judgment confirms it.

Lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them. This clause has troubled every serious reader, because it sounds as though God withholds sight in case somebody is healed, and the words must not be softened. Two things hold it in place. The first is the order in the sentence. Before the lest comes their eyes they have closed. The judicial hardening is not the first move; it is God’s ratification of a shutting that was already done. The second is what Scripture does with the theme elsewhere. Paul writes of Israel’s hardening and then asks whether they stumbled in order to fall, and answers with the strongest negative Greek possesses: by no means (Romans 11:11). The hardening is real, judicial, and not final. Turn is repentance. And the tragedy is in the last words: if they turned, God would heal them. He is willing to heal; they are not willing to turn.

But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. The turn is abrupt. After all of that, the disciples are told they are the happy ones, not because they are better, but because God has opened their eyes and ears. The same beatitude form as 5:3–12, and it echoes the blessing on the pure in heart, who shall see God (5:8). It is a beatitude on an organ, not on an achievement.

The balance. The hardening is both God’s judgment and the people’s own choice. They closed their eyes; God confirmed it. Pharaoh hardened his heart, and God hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exodus 8:15; 9:12). The disciples see because God gave them sight. In both cases God is sovereign, and people are responsible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God refuses those who come to him. Whoever comes will be received (John 6:37). The hardening falls on those who have refused to come.

How do I keep my heart from growing dull? A callus grows where the same friction is repeated and ignored, so the guard is to stop ignoring it. When God’s word touches a sore place, respond at once: confess, obey, or at least pray about it honestly, rather than filing it away. Keep company with believers who will speak plainly to you (Hebrews 3:13 says to exhort one another daily, so that none is hardened by sin’s deceit). And keep coming to Christ himself, not only to religious routine. A heart that is regularly brought to him stays soft.

In a sentence. The people closed their own eyes and hardened their hearts so they would not turn and be healed, but the disciples are blessed because God has opened their eyes.

On a Tuesday. Think of something God has been saying to you for a long time that you keep setting aside. That is where a callus grows. Respond to it today, in one concrete act, before the friction becomes a habit.

For worship. Blessed are our eyes, if they see Christ. We did not open them. Our eyes were closed like everyone else’s, and our hearts were thick. But the God who said let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). He who wills to heal has turned us, and healed us. Glory to the Father who opens blind eyes, and to the Son who is the light they see.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. Hear then the parable of the sower:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many prophets and righteous people longed to see what the disciples see, and to hear what they hear, but did not. Jesus then explains the parable of the sower.

For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it. Abraham, Moses, David, Isaiah and the faithful of Israel looked forward to the Messiah, but died without seeing him (Hebrews 11:13, 39–40). Peter, who was standing there, spent years thinking about this sentence and eventually wrote down what it meant to him: the prophets who prophesied of the grace that was to be ours searched and inquired carefully what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted Christ’s sufferings and the glories after them; it was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but us, in things into which angels long to look (1 Peter 1:10–12). That says three extraordinary things. The prophets did not fully understand their own writings; they searched into what they had written. They were told they would not live to see it. And the angels are still leaning over the edge of it: the word Peter uses is the one for stooping to peer into something, the same verb John uses of the disciple bending to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5).

And to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. The teaching of the Messiah himself. Consider what was happening on that beach. Isaiah wrote about a child born and a government on his shoulder, and died. Micah named the village and never saw it. David wrote a psalm about pierced hands a thousand years before anybody in Israel had seen a crucifixion (Psalm 22:16). Every one of them worked in the dark, on material they could not fully read, for an audience not yet born. And a group of fishermen and a tax collector are sitting in the shade listening to the Messiah himself explain a story about seed, casually, in the ordinary daylight of an ordinary day, with the possibility of asking him a further question. Prophets longed for it. Angels bend down to look at it. The Twelve had it as their normal working conditions.

Hear then the parable of the sower. Jesus explains it to those who have been given understanding. He does not say here who the sower is; the point is the soils. But in the next parable he says that the one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man (v. 37), so the sower is first Jesus himself, and then those who preach his word after him.

With all this in view. The greatest privilege of hearing calls for the deepest response of hearing. That is why the then matters: with all of this in view, the prophets longing, the angels looking, the Messiah present, now listen carefully. The appropriate response to such privilege is not complacency but urgent, attentive hearing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the Old Testament saints were lost or had no real faith. Abraham rejoiced to see Christ’s day (John 8:56); they were saved by trusting the promise of the same Saviour. The difference is not between saved and unsaved but between promise and fulfilment, shadow and substance.

Do I really have more than the prophets? In privilege of knowledge, yes. You know the name of the Messiah, the meaning of his death, the fact of his resurrection, and you have the Spirit poured out and the whole Bible in your hands. Isaiah would have given anything for one afternoon with a Gospel. That does not make you holier than Isaiah, but it does make you more accountable, and it should make you far more thankful.

In a sentence. The disciples see and hear what the prophets longed for, and Jesus explains the parable to them.

On a Tuesday. You know more of Christ than Abraham, Moses and Isaiah did. Read one of Isaiah’s prophecies of Christ today, Isaiah 53 perhaps, and then thank God that you know whom it was about.

For worship. For centuries the prophets wrote by candlelight about a dawn they would never see. The angels have bent down ever since to look into it. And it has come: the Christ of the prophets has spoken, suffered, risen and reigns, and the gospel the angels marvel at has been told to us. Blessed are the eyes that see what we see. Glory to God, who saved the best wine for last and poured it out for his people in the fullness of time.

verseByVerse.quote: When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seed on the path is the person who hears the message of the kingdom and does not understand it: the evil one comes and snatches it away. The seed on rocky ground is the person who hears the word and receives it at once with joy.

When anyone hears the word of the kingdom. The seed is the word: the message of the kingdom, the gospel (Luke 8:11 calls it the word of God).

And does not understand it. Not merely intellectual failure, but refusal to take it in. Here is the chapter’s key word again, syniēmi, putting things together. The path-hearer’s problem is not that the word was too difficult. It is that nothing was joined to anything: the seed sat on top of a life it never connected with. The heart is hard, like a trodden path, and the word lies on the surface. Many hear sermons this way: the words enter the ears but never reach the heart.

The evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. The birds are Satan. The verb (harpazō) is the violent one: to seize, the word used of a wolf snatching the sheep (John 10:12) and of the crowd trying to take Jesus by force (John 6:15). He takes the word before it can take root, through distraction, doubt, mockery or forgetfulness. Paul says the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4).

This is what was sown along the path. The first soil: hard, unresponsive.

As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy. The second soil, and the detail that ought to unsettle a certain kind of Christian gathering. Joy. Not grudging assent or mere agreement, but the visible, immediate, delighted response that everybody in Christian work is glad to see and inclined to count. Quick, joyful, impressive. It looks like conversion. And it is the mark of the soil that fails.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that joy in receiving the gospel is suspicious. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit, and good soil also receives the word with joy (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The problem with the rocky soil is not joy but lack of root (v. 21). What the passage does is remove joy from the list of reliable signs, because the one soil explicitly credited with immediate joy is the one that will not be there in a year. That is a hard word for any ministry that measures by response. The path shows nothing and the rocky ground shows everything, and the only soil that can be identified with certainty is the one still standing at harvest.

Were the rocky and thorny hearers ever truly saved? Some Christians read them as real believers who later fall away. The more likely reading is that they show a profession that was never new birth: no root, no fruit, and they did not last (1 John 2:19; John 8:31). The response was real as far as it went, but it was not the work of the Spirit that endures. That is why the parable is a warning and not a threat to those who have truly come to Christ: the mark of the good soil is fruit and endurance, and those whom God has truly given new birth he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6).

How do I stop the birds taking the word? By giving the word somewhere to go before anything can carry it off. After a sermon or a time in Scripture, do not rush straight into conversation about something else. Pause, pray over what you heard, write down one sentence, talk about it with someone on the way home, act on it that day. The birds feed on seed that lies on the surface. The more quickly the word is turned into prayer and obedience, the less there is lying about to be taken.

In a sentence. Some hearers do not take the word in, and Satan snatches it away; others receive it quickly and joyfully, but without depth.

On a Tuesday. After you hear a sermon this Sunday, take five minutes before you speak to anyone else to reflect and pray over it, so that the birds do not take it away. And if you work with new believers, rejoice in their joy, but care for their roots: teach them, visit them, walk with them through the first heat.

For worship. The enemy snatches; the Saviour sows again. Satan’s birds have carried off seed from every one of us, and still the Lord of the harvest has not given up on his field. He keeps sending his word, Sunday after Sunday, year after year, and where it finally sinks in, he guards it, so that no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand. Praise the faithful Sower, whose patience is longer than our hardness.

verseByVerse.quote: yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rocky-ground hearer has no root and lasts only a while. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away. The thorny ground is the one who hears the word, but the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke it, and it produces nothing.

Yet he has no root in himself. The response is shallow. It has not gone down into the heart and will. And notice: in himself. The shallowness is an inner condition. The persecution does not cause it; it reveals what was already lacking. Root depth is not visible on the surface; it is revealed by the weather.

But endures for a while. For a time, it looks real.

And when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word. The scorching sun (v. 6). Trouble comes because of the word: opposition, mockery, loss. Christianity costs something.

Immediately he falls away. Falls away (skandalizetai) is the trap word, from the name for the stick that springs a snare. It is the same verb Jesus used in his message to John in prison: blessed is the one who is not offended by me (11:6). So the rocky-ground hearer does not resign. He is tripped. The picture is not of a man weighing the evidence and withdrawing, but of somebody walking along and going down suddenly over something he did not see coming, which is what persecution feels like to a person who did not expect the Christian life to cost anything. As quickly as he came, he goes. The faith that sprang up overnight withers overnight.

As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word. The third soil. This person goes further. The word takes root and grows. Nothing in this soil is dramatic: no snatching, no scorching, no falling away in a crisis.

But the cares of the world. Cares is the same word as the anxiety of 6:25–34. Worries about life: money, health, family, work, the future. Not open sin, but ordinary preoccupations that crowd out God.

And the deceitfulness of riches. The word (apatē) means a deliberate deception, a con. Money is described here not merely as dangerous but as a liar, something that makes a promise and does not keep it. What does it promise? Security, mostly: that when there is enough, the anxiety will stop. It promises satisfaction and happiness and does not deliver (6:19–24; 1 Timothy 6:9–10), and it makes people feel they do not need God. Mark adds the desires for other things (Mark 4:19). And notice that the same soil contains opposites: the worry of not having enough and the illusion of having it. Those look like different problems, and the parable files them together, because they choke the same plant and are the same preoccupation seen from either end.

Choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. The plant survives, but bears no fruit. It simply produces nothing over a long period while remaining green, and the verse is careful to say what is missing rather than what went wrong. This person may stay in church for years, but their life shows no real fruit, because worry and wealth have crowded out the word. Here is the test, and it is quieter than the others. Not have you fallen away, which a person would notice, but: what is there to show? Take the last five years. Something should have come off this plant by now.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that true believers can lose their salvation. The rocky and thorny soils describe people who appeared to receive the word but never truly did. Their faith was never rooted (1 John 2:19). Jesus’ point is that a real response is shown by perseverance and fruit. Nor does it mean that every Christian who worries or has money is thorny ground. The danger is when these things choke the word, so that it bears no fruit.

I am a Christian and I worry a great deal. Am I thorny ground? Not necessarily. Many true believers struggle with anxiety, and Jesus’ answer in chapter 6 is not condemnation but an invitation to trust the Father who feeds the birds. The thorny ground is the heart where worry and wealth have taken over, so that the word is crowded out and nothing grows. If your worries drive you to pray, to Scripture and to Christ, the word is not being choked; it is being tested. Bring your cares to him by name (1 Peter 5:7), and where anxiety is severe, seek help from your pastor and, if needed, your doctor.

In a sentence. Shallow hearers fall away when trouble comes, and preoccupied hearers let worry and wealth choke the word until it bears no fruit.

On a Tuesday. Look at two honest witnesses to what crowds your heart: where your mind goes when it is unoccupied, and your calendar and bank statement. Name one thorn you find there and cut it back this week: one subscription, one late-night habit, one anxious rehearsal you will turn into prayer instead.

For worship. Christ wore the thorns. The curse that made the ground bring forth thorns and thistles (Genesis 3:18) was pressed into a crown and pushed onto his head. He bore the curse of our choked and fruitless lives, so that the word might grow free in us. And he is the treasure that exposes the lie of riches: in him are riches that do not deceive, the unsearchable riches of Christ, and a peace that worry cannot steal.

verseByVerse.quote: As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it. That person bears fruit: a hundred, sixty or thirty times what was sown.

As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. Understanding here means grasping the word with the heart, receiving it deeply, joining it to life. Luke says: holding it fast in an honest and good heart, and bearing fruit with patience (Luke 8:15). The good soil hears, understands, holds fast and endures. Understanding in Matthew is not mere comprehension; it is the comprehension that changes the one who comprehends.

He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty. Fruit is the mark of the good soil: a changed life, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), good works (Ephesians 2:10), and other people brought to Christ. The amounts differ, but all good soil bears fruit. God is not demanding equal output; he is producing real fruit from truly changed hearts.

Where does good soil come from? Not from our own efforts. Every heart by nature is hard like the path (Ephesians 2:1–3). God must make the soil good: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), opens hearts to listen (Acts 16:14), and gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). But we are called to receive the word humbly (James 1:21) and to guard our hearts.

Which soil am I? Now use the parable for the purpose it was given, because it is not a scheme for classifying other people. Jesus told it to a mixed crowd and ended it with he who has ears, let him hear. The only honest question is which soil I am, and it is worth asking with specific tests rather than in a vague fog. The path: is there any real hearing at all, or does it slide off the surface? A usable test is not how much you know but when Scripture last changed a decision you had already made. The rocky ground: is the faith attached mainly to feeling, and does it fold when following costs something? Test it against the last time obedience was truly expensive. What happened? And the thorny ground, which is the one most readers of a commentary should worry about, because it is not rejection but crowding. Nothing is refused; the word is simply squeezed into a smaller and smaller corner by things that are not even sinful. Test it by looking at where your mind goes when it is unoccupied, and at your calendar and your bank statement, which between them are a fairly ruthless account of what you actually care about.

Is the soil fixed? This is the question that decides whether the parable crushes you or helps you, because if it is fixed, the honest reader who finds himself among the thorns has just been handed a life sentence. It is not fixed, and the Bible is emphatic about it. Real soil cannot change itself; people are not real soil. Hosea says to a hard-hearted nation, break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD (Hosea 10:12), and Jeremiah says, break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns (Jeremiah 4:3), which is God commanding the very change the metaphor might seem to rule out. And underneath the command is the promise that makes it possible: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). That is the one thing no field can do for itself, and it is precisely what he undertakes to do.

The remedy for each soil. If you have recognised yourself somewhere in the first three, that recognition is not a verdict; it is the beginning of the remedy, and it is more than the crowd on the beach ever got. If the ground is hard, ask him to break it, and put yourself where the word is faithfully preached until it does. If the trouble is shallowness, the answer is roots, and roots grow in the dark: from knowing the Scriptures well enough to stand when the feelings have gone, and from being known by people who will not let you drift. If it is thorns, they have to be named and cut one at a time, because nobody has ever drifted out of thorns; the choking is what happens when nothing is done.

The lessons of the parable. For hearers: test what kind of soil you are, and pray for a receptive heart. For preachers and witnesses: do not be discouraged when many do not respond. And notice what the parable does not say, which is a comfort to anyone who sows and sees little. Three soils out of four came to nothing, and the harvest was still thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. The sower is not told to stop scattering, or to sow more carefully, or to blame himself for the path and the rocks. He is told what the ground does. Keep sowing. The problem is never the seed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the parable divides people into four fixed types for ever. By God’s grace, hard ground can be broken, and rocky soil can be deepened. Nor does it mean that fruitful Christians are better than others. All fruit is God’s work (John 15:5).

In a sentence. The good soil hears and understands the word, holds it fast, and bears an abundant harvest of fruit.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, in so many words: Lord, make my heart good soil for your word. Then take one of the tests above and answer it honestly in writing. And keep sowing the word, in your home, your work, your friendships, whatever response you see.

For worship. Every good heart in the world was once a path, a rock or a thorn patch, and God made it good. He broke up fallow ground that would never have broken itself; he took out hearts of stone and gave hearts of flesh; he sent his Son as the seed that fell into the earth and died, and from that one grain has come a harvest of thirty, sixty and a hundredfold that will fill his barns for ever. The fruit is his, the soil is his, the seed is his, and so is all the glory.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–58 — Six More Parables: The Kingdom's Hidden Growth and Coming Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six parables follow the sower: the wheat and weeds (growing together until harvest), the mustard seed (tiny beginning, great growth), the leaven (invisible transformation of the whole), the hidden treasure and pearl of great price (discovering and selling everything for the kingdom), and the dragnet (mixed catch sorted at the end). Jesus then returns to Nazareth, where his neighbors take offense at him. More to notice. The weed has a name: zizania is bearded darnel, and three facts make the parable bite. It is indistinguishable from wheat until the ear forms — Jewish tradition treated it as degenerate wheat. It is poisonous, regularly fungus-infected, and the Latin temulentum means drunken because that is how a person looks who has eaten the bread. And sowing it in an enemy's field was a crime under Roman law, which means it happened often enough to legislate for. The master's refusal to weed is agriculturally exact — darnel roots interlace with wheat roots. This was the text at the centre of the donatist controversy, and Augustine answered the rigorists from it; but note the guard runs both ways, since "let both grow together" is not a ban on church discipline (18:15-17). Discipline addresses conduct and is reversible; what is forbidden is sorting by identity, which requires seeing the ear before it has formed. On the mustard seed objection — orchid seed is smaller — three answers: it was a proverb for the very small, the comparison is among seeds a farmer actually sowed ("in his field"), and this is ordinary descriptive speech, as when we say the sun rises. And the image of a great tree with birds nesting is imperial — Nebuchadnezzar's dream tree (Dan. 4:12), Ezekiel's Assyria and his cedar (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6). Jesus attaches empire-language to a garden herb. The chapter is bracketed by a door: he goes out of the house to the crowds (v. 1) and back into the house for the explanations (v. 36). "the field is the world" — not the church, and Jesus defines it explicitly. The two kinds are described by parentage, not performance, which is why sorting by inspection cannot work. The reapers are angels, and the harvest is the end of the age — the sorting is removed from human hands and from the growing season in one sentence. Note also that the weeds are gathered out of his kingdom (v. 41), so the kingdom in its present form contains what will have to be removed; and "causes of sin" is skandala, the trap-word running through 11:6, 13:21 and 13:57. The dragnet is a sagene, not a cast-net — it sweeps everything, and Levitical law (Lev. 11:9-12) meant a Jewish crew sorted catch into permitted and forbidden every working day. And v. 52's scribe trained for the kingdom is very probably Matthew's self-portrait: the evangelist who quotes the Old Testament some sixty times, structures his book in five discourses, and alone records this saying.
verseByVerse.theology: The parables of growth — mustard seed and leaven — correct the disciples' expectation that the kingdom would arrive with obvious power and immediate separation of righteous from wicked. The kingdom begins invisibly, grows slowly, works from within, and will only be sorted at the harvest. The "already-not-yet" structure of the kingdom is the key: it is genuinely present now (the treasure is in the field; the leaven is in the dough) but not yet fully revealed (the harvest is coming). Patience and trust in the hidden growth are the kingdom virtues these parables require.
verseByVerse.examples: The two treasure parables (hidden treasure, pearl) express the supreme value of the kingdom: it is worth selling everything to obtain. The joy of the man who finds the treasure is the joy of someone who has found what makes every other thing trivially small by comparison. This is the experience of genuine conversion — not reluctant sacrifice but joyful exchange, because the thing found is worth infinitely more than everything surrendered. The kingdom is not burdensome; it is the treasure that makes all other burdens light.

verseByVerse.quote: He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told another parable. The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and went away.

He put another parable before them. The second of seven parables in this chapter. It addresses the question every serious believer asks: if the kingdom has come, why is there still so much evil in the world, and why are there false believers among the true? Why does God not sort them at once?

The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field. May be compared means: this is what the kingdom is like, in this respect. The man is the Son of Man (v. 37). The good seed is his; the field is his.

But while his men were sleeping. That is not an accusation. It is simply night, and men sleep at night. The parable does not fault the household for failing to mount a watch over a field, and no reading should make it a lesson about vigilance. What the phrase does is locate the sabotage where sabotage always happens: unobserved, at a time when nobody could reasonably have been looking, in a way that left no trace until months later.

His enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. The weeds are almost certainly darnel (zizania), bearded darnel, a ryegrass that looks almost identical to wheat in its early stages. Only when the heads form can they be told apart. And notice where the enemy sows: among the wheat, through the middle of it, not round the edges or in a corner that could be written off, so that the two crops would come up interleaved and no line could ever be drawn between them. The enemy did not merely add something bad to the field. He arranged it so that removing the bad would cost the good. Sowing darnel in someone else’s field as an act of revenge was a known crime; Roman law had provisions against it. Everybody listening would have known of such a case.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God is careless or that evil happened without his permission. The sleeping servants simply mean it happened secretly. Jesus explains the meaning in verses 36–43.

Where did evil come from, if God made everything good? The parable gives the answer Scripture gives everywhere: an enemy has done this (v. 28). God is not the author of sin. He made the world very good (Genesis 1:31), and evil entered through the rebellion of the devil and of humanity (Genesis 3; John 8:44). Yet nothing happens outside God’s rule: the enemy works in God’s field, under God’s permission, until God’s harvest. Scripture does not explain fully why God allowed evil, but it shows us where it is going: to the fire, while God brings good out of what the enemy meant for harm (Genesis 50:20; Romans 8:28).

In a sentence. In a second parable, an enemy secretly sowed poisonous weeds among a man’s good wheat.

On a Tuesday. Evil is real, and it often works secretly. Do not be naive about it in the world or in the church. But do not be anxious either: the field belongs to the Son of Man, and the enemy works only until the harvest.

For worship. The field is the Lord’s, and the good seed is the Lord’s. No enemy, however cunning, can take the field from its owner. The devil sows by night and slips away; the Son of Man sows in the daylight and stays, and he will be there at the harvest. Praise the Lord of the field, whose good purpose no sabotage can overthrow.
verseByVerse.note: The weeds are probably darnel, a poisonous grass that looks like wheat until the heads form.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, "Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the wheat grew and formed heads, the weeds appeared too. The servants asked their master: didn’t you sow good seed? Where did the weeds come from?

So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. The weed has a name, and once it is known the parable sharpens. Darnel is indistinguishable from wheat. Not similar: indistinguishable by eye, until the heads form. The blade, the height, the colour and the habit are the same. Jewish tradition even regarded it as a degenerate form of wheat rather than a separate plant, which shows how close the resemblance is. Only when the ear comes does the difference appear: wheat bears heavy golden grain and bows over; darnel bears small dark seed and stands up straight. And it is harmful. The seed is commonly infected with a fungus, and eating it produces dizziness, nausea and vomiting. Its Latin name, temulentum, means drunken, because that is how a person looks who has eaten bread made from contaminated flour. In quantity it can kill. So the parable trades on both properties at once: false disciples cannot be told from the true in the early stages, and they are not neutral presences but harmful ones.

Sir, did you not sow good seed in your field? The servants know their master sowed only good seed.

How then does it have weeds? The ancient question: if God is good and his work is good, where does evil come from? And with the darnel known, the question is not puzzlement but alarm. The servants have discovered that a field they believed was clean is full of something that looks like food and is not, in quantities they cannot estimate, and it is too late to do anything about it before harvest. It is the perennial question of the troubled pastor and the puzzled believer.

The church’s experience. This is the pastoral reality the parable describes, first in the world and, in its own way, in the visible church. False profession can look exactly like real faith in its early stages. The difference appears only as growth and fruit become visible over time. That is why it is foolish to declare too quickly that someone is or is not a true Christian, and why the fruit of a life over years matters far more than the impression of a season.

How should I react when someone I trusted in church turns out to be false? With grief, but not with despair or cynicism. Jesus warned us that it would happen: there would be weeds among the wheat until the end. A leader’s fall or a friend’s betrayal does not prove that the gospel is false; it proves that the enemy is active. Where wrongdoing must be dealt with, it should be dealt with properly, and any abuse reported to the proper authorities. Then keep your eyes on Christ, who is never false, and remember that the field is still his.

In a sentence. As the crop matured, the weeds became visible, and the servants asked in alarm where they had come from.

On a Tuesday. When you see evil in the world, or even in the church, you are not the first to ask where it came from. Bring the question to the Master, as the servants did, rather than nursing it in bitterness.

For worship. There is one field-owner who is never deceived by appearances. He knows the wheat from the darnel when every eye in the field is fooled, because he knows the seed he sowed. The Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19). We may be confused; he never is. Glory to the Son of Man, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and who will bring every hidden thing to light.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "An enemy has done this." So the servants said to him, "Then do you want us to go and gather them?" But he said, "No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master said: an enemy has done this. The servants asked whether they should go and pull up the weeds. He said no: in pulling up the weeds you might uproot the wheat with them.

An enemy has done this. Evil is not God’s work. It is the work of an enemy, the devil (v. 39). The master’s answer is a diagnosis rather than an explanation. It says who, and it does not say why, and the parable never comes back to that.

Then do you want us to go and gather them? The servants want to remove the weeds immediately.

No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. The master’s reasoning is agriculturally exact, which is worth saying because it is often treated as a piece of theological convenience. Darnel roots do not grow beside wheat roots; they interlace with them. In a field where the two have come up together and stood for weeks, pulling one out lifts the other. Any farmer in the audience knew it, which is why the servants do not argue. And at that stage they might mistake wheat for weeds. So the refusal is not sentimentality about the weeds. It is a judgment about what would be destroyed in removing them.

A long history. This parable was at the centre of the Donatist controversy in North Africa in the fourth and fifth centuries. After the persecutions, a rigorist party held that the church must be visibly pure, that clergy who had lapsed under pressure were no longer clergy, and that a mixed church was no church at all. Augustine answered them from this passage: the field contains both, the servants are not the reapers, and the demand for a perfectly pure church before the harvest is a demand God has refused. That argument has had to be made again and again, because the instinct is always sincere. It arises from a genuine love of holiness, and it tends to produce the same result: the sharper the sieve, the more wheat goes out with the darnel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the church should never exercise discipline over its members. Jesus himself commands church discipline (18:15–20), and Paul tells the Corinthians to remove a man living in open sin (1 Corinthians 5). In Jesus’ explanation, the field is the world (v. 38), not the church. The point is that God’s people must not try to remove all evil from the world by force before the judgment. That task belongs to God at the end. The distinction is between two different works. Discipline addresses conduct; it is corrective, aimed at restoration, and can be reversed. What the master forbids is an attempt to sort people by their final identity, to decide who is finally wheat and who is finally weed, and that is forbidden because it requires seeing the ear before the ear has formed.

Does this mean the church should tolerate sin or abuse? No. The parable is about the world and the final judgment, not about ignoring wrongdoing in the church. Sin among members must be addressed lovingly and firmly (18:15–17; Galatians 6:1). Abuse must never be tolerated or covered up; it must be stopped, the vulnerable protected, and crimes reported to the civil authorities, whom God has appointed to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). What the parable forbids is something else: Christians trying to purge the world of unbelievers by force, or pretending that they can see into hearts as only God can.

In a sentence. The master forbids pulling up the weeds now, because the wheat would be damaged with them.

On a Tuesday. Be patient with a world where good and evil grow together. Do not try to take God’s place as the final judge of who is in and who is out. But do the work that is yours: correct gently, protect the weak, and pray for those who look like weeds today. God will sort it out in his time, without any mistakes.

For worship. How careful is the Lord with his wheat. He would rather let the weeds stand a season than lose a single stalk of his grain. Not one of his people will be uprooted by mistake, because the harvest is in his hands and not ours. The same patience that leaves the weeds standing is the patience that kept us standing, when we too were indistinguishable from the darnel. Praise the Master whose care for his own is exact.

parallels.desc: do not pronounce judgment before the time

verseByVerse.quote: Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, "Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn." He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let both grow together until the harvest. Then I will tell the reapers to gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, and gather the wheat into my barn. Then Jesus told another parable: the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed planted in a field.

Let both grow together until the harvest. Good and evil will exist side by side in the world until the end of the age (v. 39). The patience of the growing season is not laxity toward evil but wisdom about timing. The judgment is not avoided; it is only delayed.

And at harvest time I will tell the reapers. The reapers are the angels (v. 39).

Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned. Dried darnel was used as fuel. The weeds’ end is fire: judgment.

But gather the wheat into my barn. The wheat, God’s people, are gathered safely into his kingdom (3:12). The harvest verdict is certain and final.

He put another parable before them. The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. The third parable begins, and it follows without pause. The mustard seed is explained in the next entry. The contrast between beginning and end is the point: the kingdom’s origin is astonishingly small, a band of Galilean disciples around a travelling teacher, and its destiny is vast.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the wicked and the righteous are indistinguishable for ever, or that God is indifferent to evil. The delay is mercy, giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and it ends in a sure judgment.

Why does God wait so long? Because he is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). Every year of delay is another year in which the gospel goes out and people who were living like weeds are brought to new birth. You may be one of them; most Christians can name a time when, if the harvest had come, they would not have been ready. The waiting is hard for those who suffer from evil, and Scripture lets them cry how long? (Revelation 6:10). But the delay is not forgetfulness. The date is fixed, and on that day every wrong will be put right.

In a sentence. Good and evil will grow together until the harvest, when the weeds will be burned and the wheat gathered into God’s barn.

On a Tuesday. The delay of judgment is a time of mercy. Use it. Pray this week by name for someone who does not yet know Christ, and look for a chance to speak to them of him while the field is still growing.

For worship. The harvest is coming, and the barn is ready. Every grain of the Lord’s wheat will be gathered in: not one blown away, not one left in the field, not one burned with the weeds. He who began the sowing will finish the harvest. Until then he waits, with a patience that has saved multitudes, and when he comes he will gather his people home with joy.

parallels.desc: the wheat gathered, the chaff burned

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches." He told them another parable. "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mustard seed is the smallest of seeds, but it grows into the largest of garden plants, a tree in which birds come and nest. The kingdom is also like yeast that a woman mixed into a large amount of flour until all of it was leavened.
