It is the smallest of all seeds. The black mustard seed was proverbially tiny, about a millimetre across. Jews spoke of something as small as a mustard seed (17:20), and the rabbis used it as their standard measure of the very small. An objection is often raised: the mustard seed is not the smallest seed in the world; orchid seed, for example, is finer. Three things settle it. First, smallest of all seeds was a proverb, as English speaks of a grain of sand without conducting a survey. Second, the comparison is inside a category the sentence supplies: a man took and sowed in his field. Among the seeds a Galilean farmer actually handled, mustard was the smallest, and orchids were not among them. Third, this is ordinary speech, which Scripture uses constantly. We say the sun rises without asserting that it goes round the earth. Jesus speaks as people spoke.

But when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree. The mustard plant grew in one season to two or three metres (eight to ten feet), large enough to look like a tree and for birds to perch in. It is not a tree, strictly; it becomes one in the loose sense. And there is something close to a joke in it.

So that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches. A great tree with birds in its branches is not a neutral image. It is imperial. Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a tree at the centre of the earth, immense, with the birds of the heavens living in its branches (Daniel 4:10–12, 20–22). Ezekiel uses the same picture for Assyria, and for the cedar God himself will plant on the mountain of Israel, under which birds of every sort will nest (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6). That is the language of empires that shelter the nations. And Jesus attaches it to a garden herb. It is exactly the correction his hearers needed. They were expecting the cedar, the kingdom arriving with obvious magnificence. He gives them mustard: something small enough to be overlooked, fast enough to be underestimated, growing in a vegetable patch, and ending up with the nations sheltering in it.

Are the birds a bad sign? Some note that birds stand for the evil one earlier in the chapter (vv. 4, 19), and read these birds as a corrupted church. But the image here comes from Ezekiel and Daniel, where birds nesting in a great tree picture nations sheltering in a kingdom. The same image can mean different things in two different parables, and the good sense is the more likely here.

The meaning. The kingdom began in an obscure way: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve ordinary disciples, rejected by the leaders. It looked insignificant. Yet it would grow into a worldwide kingdom. Today the church is found in nearly every nation.

He told them another parable. The kingdom of heaven is like leaven. Leaven was a lump of old, fermented dough kept from the previous batch and mixed into new flour to make it rise, like yeast.

That a woman took and hid in three measures of flour. Three measures (sata) was a very large amount of flour, perhaps forty litres, enough to make bread for a hundred people or more. Sarah used the same amount when baking for the Lord’s visit (Genesis 18:6). Hid is the word used: the leaven disappears into the dough.

Till it was all leavened. The leaven works quietly, invisibly, from within, until it has permeated everything. The kingdom does not change the world chiefly by outward force, the constant temptation of political religion, but by the hidden work of the Spirit in human hearts, spreading through the whole.

The two parables together. The mustard seed shows the kingdom’s outward growth: from small beginnings to great size. The leaven shows its inward growth: quiet, hidden, pervasive transformation from within.

But leaven usually means evil. A reader who knows his Bible may balk here, and the objection is a good one. Elsewhere leaven often stands for corruption. Israel swept it out of the house before Passover (Exodus 12:15); Paul says a little leaven leavens the whole lump, speaking of tolerated sin (1 Corinthians 5:6–8); and Jesus will warn of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, meaning their teaching (16:6). So some have read this parable as evil corrupting the church. It is an honest reading, but it does not sit well with the sentence itself. Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like leaven, exactly as he has just said it is like a mustard seed, and in both he describes growth from something small to something total. A warning would be a strange thing to introduce with those words and then leave unexplained. The better answer is that leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading. A small hidden agent works quietly through a large mass until nothing is unaffected. Sin does that, which is why Paul and Jesus both use the picture of sin. The kingdom does that too. Here the point is its spreading power, not its moral quality.

What it does not mean. The parable does not promise that the whole world will become Christian before Christ returns.

Where Christians differ over the leaven and the end of the age. Postmillennialists read these parables as promising that the gospel will gradually Christianise the world, leading to a golden age before Christ’s return. Amillennialists see the parables as describing the kingdom’s sure growth through the whole gospel age, alongside continuing evil (the weeds), until the harvest at Christ’s return. Verdict: amillennial. The kingdom will grow powerfully among all nations, but good and evil grow together until the end.

Our church is small and seems to be making no difference. Does this parable apply to us? Yes, it was told for exactly that situation. The kingdom always looks small at the start and hidden in the middle. You cannot see leaven working, and nobody admires a mustard seed. God’s measure is faithfulness, not size: a small church that preaches Christ, prays, loves its members and serves its neighbours is the leaven in the dough of its town. Do not despise the day of small things (Zechariah 4:10). Keep sowing, keep praying, and leave the growth to God.

In a sentence. The kingdom starts small but grows into a great tree that shelters the nations, and works quietly from within like yeast until it permeates everything.

On a Tuesday. Do not despise small beginnings: a small Bible study, a single conversation, a little act of faithfulness, one child taught to pray. God’s kingdom grows from mustard seeds. Do one small, hidden thing for Christ today and trust him with what it becomes.

For worship. Look at what God has done with a mustard seed. A baby in a manger, a carpenter in Nazareth, twelve frightened men, a body in a borrowed tomb, and from that the church of every nation, a tree in whose branches the peoples of the earth have found shelter. And look at the leaven: hidden in human hearts, it has changed families, cities and centuries, and it is not finished. The kingdom of our God is growing still, and one day it will fill the earth.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man. Three measures of flour is a very large batch — about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

parallels.desc: birds nest in the cedar’s branches

verseByVerse.quote: All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: "I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus taught the crowds in parables, and said nothing to them without a parable. This fulfilled the words of the psalm: I will open my mouth in parables; I will declare what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.

All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. Nothing. That is a sweeping statement about the public teaching at this stage, and Mark says the same while adding the other half: privately to his own disciples he explained everything (Mark 4:33–34).

This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet. Psalm 78:2. The psalm was written by Asaph, who is called a seer (2 Chronicles 29:30), which is why Matthew calls him a prophet. Psalm 78 is one of the longest psalms in the Bible, seventy-two verses in which Asaph retells Israel’s history from the exodus to David, with the failures left in. And its stated purpose is that the next generation might know these things and set their hope in God, and not forget his works (Psalm 78:6–7). So the text Matthew reaches for to explain teaching in parables is itself a piece of parable-teaching: a long story told to children so that they would not repeat what their fathers had done. The method is older than the Gospel, and it was always aimed at the next generation rather than the current experts.

I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world. In Psalm 78, Asaph retells Israel’s history as a lesson, revealing its meaning: God’s faithfulness and Israel’s unfaithfulness. Jesus is the greater teacher who reveals God’s purposes, hidden from the beginning and now made known in the kingdom. And hidden since the foundation of the world is the phrase to hold. What is being disclosed on that beach is not new information about God’s plans. It is old, older than Israel, older than Abraham, in place before there was anything to plan for, and it had been kept.

A chapter bracketed by a door. Matthew has drawn the structure like a diagram. At verse 1 Jesus goes out of the house to the crowd; at verse 36 he leaves the crowds and goes into the house with the disciples for the explanation. Out of the house to the parables, back into the house for the meaning.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the psalm was a direct prediction about Jesus. Matthew sees a pattern: as Asaph used parables to reveal hidden truth, so Jesus fulfils and surpasses him.

What does fulfil mean when Matthew uses it like this? Matthew uses fulfil in more than one way. Sometimes a prophet directly predicted an event, such as the birthplace in Bethlehem (2:5–6). Sometimes, as here, an Old Testament person or pattern is filled out and completed in Christ: Asaph taught Israel’s history in parables, and Jesus, the greater teacher, reveals God’s hidden purposes in parables. Both are real fulfilment, because the whole Old Testament is moving toward Christ. When you meet the word, ask whether it is a prediction kept or a pattern completed.

In a sentence. Jesus taught the crowds in parables, fulfilling the psalm’s picture of one who reveals what has been hidden from the beginning.

On a Tuesday. God’s purposes are not random. What has been hidden from the foundation of the world is now revealed in Christ. Take the psalm’s purpose as your own this week: tell a child, or a younger Christian, one story of what God has done, so that they may set their hope in him.

For worship. Before the mountains were brought forth, God had a purpose of grace, and he kept it hidden through the long ages, until the fullness of time. Then his Son opened his mouth in a fishing boat and uttered it. The counsel of eternity spoken in the language of farmers. Glory to the God whose plan is older than the world and whose Son is its living word.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm’s author, Asaph, is called a seer in Chronicles; Matthew calls him “the prophet.”

parallels.desc: I will open my mouth in a parable

verseByVerse.quote: Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, "Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field." He answered, "The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left the crowds and went into the house. His disciples asked him to explain the parable of the weeds. He said: the one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.

Then he left the crowds and went into the house. Away from the crowds, to teach his disciples privately. This movement is the hinge of the chapter. Verse 1: he went out of the house and sat beside the sea, and the crowds gathered. Verse 36: he left the crowds and went into the house, and the disciples came. Everything the crowd hears is a story; everything the disciples receive is the meaning, and the door between them is the same door, opened twice in thirty-five verses. It is what he told them at verse 11: to you it has been given. Matthew has built the chapter to show it.

Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field. The disciples asked, and Jesus answered. Those who seek understanding receive it (v. 12). And notice: they did not understand it either. It is easy to imagine the Twelve as insiders who followed everything, and the plain evidence of this chapter is that they were as lost as anyone and simply asked. The difference between the fourth soil and the others is not comprehension. It is what a man does when he has not understood.

The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. Jesus himself (see 8:20). He is the sower of the kingdom. And the title is the largest claim in the parable. It comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man is brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion and a kingdom that shall not pass away. It is the title Jesus uses of himself more than any other, and here it belongs to the sower. So the man scattering seed, the ordinary figure walking a Galilean field, turns out to be the figure of Daniel’s vision. And he will appear again at verse 41, sending the angels to reap. The same person plants and harvests. Nothing in the field belongs to anybody else.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that only Jesus may sow. Those who preach his word after him are sowing his seed in his field (see on v. 18). But they sow as his servants, and the field and the harvest remain his.

What should I do when I do not understand a passage of Scripture? Do what the disciples did: ask. Ask the Lord in prayer, because understanding is his gift. Ask other Christians, your pastor, a good study Bible or commentary. Read the passage again in its context, and compare it with clearer passages on the same subject. Do not pretend you understand when you do not, and do not give up and conclude the Bible is impossible. Some things become clear only over years. Meanwhile, live by what is plain, which is most of it.

In a sentence. The disciples asked Jesus to explain the parable of the weeds, and he began by identifying the sower as himself, the Son of Man.

On a Tuesday. When you do not understand something in Scripture, ask the Lord, and keep seeking. Write down one question about the Bible you have been carrying and take it this week to someone who can help.

For worship. The Son of Man of Daniel’s vision, to whom the Ancient of Days gave an everlasting kingdom, walked into a house in Galilee and explained a story to fishermen who had not understood it. The Judge of all the earth is also the patient Teacher of slow disciples. He sows, he explains, he waits, and he will reap. From first seed to final harvest, the kingdom is his.

verseByVerse.quote: the field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The field is the world. The good seed is the people of the kingdom. The weeds are the people of the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.

The field is the world. Not the church, but the whole world. Five words in this verse have done more work in church history than almost any phrase in the parables, and they are exact. It is the one element of the parable Jesus defines most explicitly. Read as a picture of the church, the parable becomes an argument for tolerating anything inside the congregation, which is what it has often been made to say, and which collides head on with chapter 18 and with Paul, who tells a church to remove a man. Read as Jesus defines it, the picture is of the whole human community, with two kinds of people growing side by side in it, indistinguishable to the eye, until the end of the age (see v. 29).

And the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. True believers, God’s people. In 8:12, sons of the kingdom referred to those who seemed to be heirs but were excluded; here it refers to the true heirs.

The weeds are the sons of the evil one. Those who belong to Satan, sharing his character (John 8:44; 1 John 3:10). And the two kinds are described by parentage, not by performance. That is Semitic idiom: a son of something belongs to it, bears its character, comes from it. The distinction is not simply that one group behaves well and the other badly; it is that they have different origins. That explains why the sorting cannot be done by inspection: parentage is invisible, and the wheat and the darnel look alike precisely because appearance is not what is being sorted.

And the enemy who sowed them is the devil. Satan works in the world to oppose God’s kingdom, planting his own people among God’s.

The harvest is the end of the age. The end of the present world, at Christ’s return (24:3; 28:20). So not now, not in any reformation or purge or council, and no amount of zeal can bring the date forward.

And the reapers are angels. Angels will gather people for judgment (24:31; 25:31). So not us. Not the servants who volunteered in verse 28, and not their successors. The parable takes the sorting out of the growing season and out of human hands in one sentence, and it leaves the church with a quite different job in the meantime: to sow, to pray, to bear fruit and to wait.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that people are born as wheat or weeds and cannot change. Paul was a persecutor and became an apostle. The parable describes the state of the world at the harvest, not a fixed destiny regardless of response. Nor does it teach that the devil creates people. He sows them in the sense of influencing them and placing them to oppose God’s work.

Can the weeds ever become wheat? The parable describes how things stand at the harvest, not a fixed caste in the growing season. Sons of the evil one are brought out of that condition by new birth, transferred from the domain of darkness to the kingdom of God’s beloved Son (Colossians 1:13; John 1:12–13), and that is why the gospel is preached to all. Some object that the image makes conversion impossible, but the parable is about the end of the age, not the beginning of a life. Every Christian was once a child of wrath like the rest of mankind (Ephesians 2:3).

In a sentence. In the world, the Son of Man’s people and the devil’s people grow together until the angels gather them at the end of the age.

On a Tuesday. The world is a mixed field. Do not be surprised by evil around you, and do not lose heart: the harvest is coming. Meanwhile, do the servant’s work, not the reaper’s. Pray for the neighbour who seems furthest from God; he may yet be wheat.

For worship. The field is the world, and the whole world is his. The Son of Man has planted his people in every nation, among every kind of opposition, and not one of them will be lost among the weeds. And by a wonder no farmer has ever seen, his word turns darnel into wheat, makes sons of the evil one into sons of the kingdom, and gives them a new Father. Blessed be the Lord of the harvest, who changes the very nature of the seed.

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe

verseByVerse.quote: Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the weeds are gathered and burned, so it will be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom everything that causes sin and all who do evil.

Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The certainty of judgment. The kingdom in its present form is mixed; it will not always be.

The Son of Man will send his angels. Jesus is the Judge, and the angels are his (16:27; 24:31). He who now sows will then reap. And notice the possessive. Angels belong to God throughout the Old Testament: they are his host, his messengers. Here they are the Son of Man’s, sent at his order, carrying out his judgment in his kingdom. The possessive is not decorative, and no first-century Jew would have missed it.

And they will gather out of his kingdom. One phrase that should stop a reader: out of his kingdom, not out of the world. Christ’s kingdom now extends over the whole world (28:18), though not all acknowledge it. So in its present form the kingdom’s territory contains things that will have to be removed. The harvest is described as a clearing operation within the King’s own realm rather than a conquest of someone else’s. At the end, everything that opposes him will be removed.

All causes of sin. Literally all stumbling blocks (skandala): everything that leads people into sin. It is the trap word again, used in the message to John in prison (11:6) and of the rocky-ground hearer who falls away (13:21). So what is gathered out at the end is, in the first instance, whatever in the field brought others down. That makes the judgment less abstract: someone will be there partly because of what he did to somebody else’s faith.

And all law-breakers. Those who live in lawlessness (see 7:23), apart from God’s will.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the judgment is impersonal or careless. The Son of Man himself sends the angels, and he knows every one in the field.

Will I be judged for causing others to stumble? Jesus takes it very seriously (18:6–7). If you have led others into sin, by example, teaching, pressure or abuse, the first thing to do is repent before God and, where possible, put it right with those you harmed. Christ’s blood covers that sin too, for all who come to him (1 John 1:7). Then guard your life now: think about what your example teaches others, especially the young and weak in faith (Romans 14:13).

In a sentence. At the end of the age, Christ’s angels will remove from his kingdom everything that causes sin and everyone who does evil.

On a Tuesday. One day every cause of sin will be removed. Long for that day, and begin now to remove the stumbling blocks in your own life. Ask whether anything you do, say, post or allow is tripping up someone weaker. Change it this week.

For worship. The day is coming when nothing in all the kingdom of Christ will cause anyone to stumble. No temptation, no deceiver, no snare, no sin. The Son of Man will clear his realm of every trap, and his people will walk through it without fear of falling. Praise the King whose kingdom will be pure, whose judgment will be perfect, and whose mercy has already gathered us out of the darkness that would have been our end.

parallels.desc: I will sweep away the stumbling blocks
he will send out his angels

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evildoers will be thrown into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom. Whoever has ears, let them hear.

And throw them into the fiery furnace. A picture of hell (Daniel 3:6; Revelation 20:15). Fire is a picture of God’s holy judgment. Jesus does not soften the end.

In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Grief and anguish (see 8:12).

Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. A quotation from Daniel. At the very end of his book, Daniel is told that those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above, and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars for ever and ever (Daniel 12:3). That sentence comes immediately after the clearest statement of resurrection in the Old Testament: many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt (Daniel 12:2). So Jesus is not reaching for a poetic flourish. He is quoting the passage that stands closest to what he is describing, in the book from which he takes his favourite title for himself. And he sharpens it. Daniel says the wise will shine like the sky and like the stars. Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun. Stars are many and distant and easily lost in a city. The sun is the thing you cannot look at directly. It is the same picture used of his own face on the mountain of transfiguration, where his face shone like the sun (17:2). Whatever happened to him there is what is being promised to them here. The righteous, freed from all sin, will be glorified, reflecting God’s glory (Philippians 3:21; 1 John 3:2).

In the kingdom of their Father. The possessive again, and this time it is theirs. The kingdom has been the Son of Man’s throughout the explanation; in the last clause it becomes the Father’s, and the ones shining in it are his children.

He who has ears, let him hear. A call to take this seriously (see v. 9). The same formula closes the explanation as closed the parable: once for the crowd on the beach, and once for the Twelve in the house. It is a quiet way of saying that being on the inside of the door does not exempt anybody from the call to hear.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the righteous are those who earned righteousness by their works. They are those made righteous by God’s grace in Christ (5:6; Romans 3:22–24). Nor is hell a mere metaphor without reality. The pictures (fire, darkness, weeping) describe a real, terrible and conscious condition of separation from God’s favour, under his just judgment, and it is eternal (see 3:12; 25:46).

How can a loving God send people to hell? Because he is also holy and just, and sin is not a small thing to him. Hell is not God losing his temper; it is God giving rebels the just reward of their rebellion, and the weeds of this parable are those who have refused him to the end. The question is not finally whether God is loving enough, but how he can be just and still forgive anyone. The answer is the cross, where the fire of judgment fell on Christ in the place of all who trust him (Romans 3:26). No one goes to hell who wanted Christ. Anyone may still come to him today.

In a sentence. The wicked will be thrown into the fire of judgment, and the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Let both ends of this verse shape your week. Pray for someone who is heading for the furnace without Christ, and speak to them if you can. And when you are discouraged by your own dimness, remember what is promised: you will shine like the sun.

For worship. The furnace is real, and the light is real. The Son of Man who will send his angels went himself into the fire of God’s judgment at the cross, so that all who belong to him would never feel it. And the glory that blazed from his face on the mountain he will share with his people, who will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. We who were darnel will stand as wheat in the light of God, and our faces will shine with the glory of the One who loved us.

parallels.desc: the wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky

verseByVerse.quote: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. A man found it, hid it again, and in his joy sold everything he had and bought that field. It is also like a merchant searching for fine pearls.

The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. In a world without banks, people often buried valuables in the ground for safekeeping, especially in times of war, and invasion was frequent. Sometimes the owner died, and the treasure was forgotten.

Which a man found and covered up. Perhaps a labourer ploughing someone else’s field stumbled on it by accident. Nothing in the story suggests he had any interest in treasure that morning. He put a spade into something and stopped.

Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. The key word is joy. He does not sell everything grudgingly, as a painful sacrifice, but gladly, because the treasure is worth far more than everything he owns. Everything in the sentence turns on four words, in his joy he goes, and the selling of everything is what joy looks like when it has found something worth more than everything. Selling it all feels like nothing compared to what he gains. This is conversion at its truest: not the grim duty of giving up good things for God, but the delighted exchange of lesser goods for the supreme good. The kingdom found makes everything else look small by comparison: not worthless, but small.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls. Pearls were among the most valuable things in the ancient world, more valuable than gold. A merchant dealing in pearls would search far and wide for the best ones, and he had spent years training his eye for exactly this.

The two parables. They are a matched pair with one deliberate difference, and the difference is the point. The treasure is found by accident; the pearl is found after searching. So the pair covers the two ways people arrive. Some are ambushed: they were not seeking anything, and the kingdom turned up in the middle of an ordinary working day. Some search for years, know roughly what they are after, and find it at last. The parables refuse to make either route the only one. Either way, when they find it, they give up everything for it with joy.

Is Jesus approving of sharp practice? People stumble over the man’s conduct, and it is worth answering. He finds treasure in a field that is not his, covers it again, says nothing to the owner, and buys the field. Two things. First, a parable makes one point, and its details are scenery rather than moral instruction. Jesus tells stories about a dishonest manager, an unjust judge and a thief in the night, and commends none of them; he takes one feature of each and uses it. Here the feature is joy. Second, the man’s conduct was probably less questionable than it sounds to us. The law of the time seems generally to have attached what was buried in a field to the field itself, so the honest route to the treasure ran through buying the field. He could have pocketed it and walked away; instead he paid for the ground it lay in. Either way, it is not what the story is about.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we can buy the kingdom by giving up our possessions. The kingdom is God’s gift (5:3). The parables show the worth of the kingdom and the response it calls for: giving up everything to have it. Nor is Jesus commenting on property law; the parable is about the value of the kingdom.

Who is the man who sells everything? Most read him as the believer, who gives up all for the kingdom because he has seen its worth. Others read him as Christ, who gave all to buy his people (Ephesians 5:25). The first is the more likely, since the next parable makes the same point about a merchant. But the believer buys nothing that earns grace; the invitation is to come and buy without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1). The price is the glad surrender of everything else to Christ. That surrender is real, though it does not always mean literally selling everything (19:21).

So what do I actually have to give up? Everything, in the sense that nothing may be held back from Christ’s ownership: your money, time, ambitions, relationships, reputation and future all become his. In practice that does not usually mean selling your house. It means holding everything with an open hand, giving generously, dropping whatever he forbids, and being willing to lose anything he asks for. The test is the one in the parable: when you think about what following Christ costs you, does it feel like a loss, or like a bargain? The man in the field was not brave. He was glad.

In a sentence. The kingdom is worth more than everything we have, and those who find it, by accident or after long searching, give up everything for it with joy.

On a Tuesday. Does following Christ feel like a sacrifice, or like a treasure? Write down three things you have in Christ that money cannot buy. Then ask God to show you one thing you are still holding back, and open your hand.

For worship. There is a treasure in the field of this world worth more than all the gold of the nations, and it is Christ. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in him is forgiveness, life and the friendship of God. And the wonder is that the Father led us to it. Some of us stumbled on it unlooking; some of us searched for years. All of us, having found it, find that we have lost nothing and gained everything. Blessed be the God whose kingdom is our joy.
verseByVerse.note: With no banks, people commonly buried valuables in the ground. Pearls were among the most prized luxuries of the ancient world.

parallels.desc: counting everything as loss for Christ

verseByVerse.quote: who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the merchant found one pearl of great value, he went and sold everything he had and bought it. The kingdom is also like a net thrown into the sea, which caught fish of every kind.

Who, on finding one pearl of great value. One pearl, worth more than all his others. The merchant who has handled fine pearls all his life recognises it at once; his expertise serves the discovery. He does not need to be told what it is worth.

Went and sold all that he had and bought it. As with the treasure. The kingdom is worth everything. And the joy is not in the sacrifice. A man who exchanges everything he owns for something worth vastly more has not sacrificed; he has traded up, and he knows it, and he is delighted. That is a useful test of how a person actually regards Christ. Whether following him feels like a cost being paid or a bargain being struck says more about the valuation than any statement of belief.

Christ the pearl. Many have seen Christ himself as the pearl of great value, worth giving up all for (Philippians 3:7–8). Paul counted everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord. To have the kingdom is to have the King.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea. A dragnet (sagēnē): a long net with floats on top and weights at the bottom, drawn between two boats or pulled to shore from the beach, sweeping everything in its path. Not the cast-net a man throws from the shore, which is aimed. A dragnet is not aimed; it takes what is in the water, and the sorting is a separate operation done later on the sand.

And gathered fish of every kind. Good and bad, clean and unclean. The parable shifts from the individual finding the kingdom to the gathered community: the preaching of the kingdom gathers broadly, and the church should not be surprised that it contains both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the church should be careless about the gospel it preaches in order to gather more. The net is the gospel of the kingdom, and it gathers widely because it is offered to all, not because it is watered down.

How can I value Christ more? Not by trying to work up feelings, but by looking at him. The merchant valued the pearl because he looked at it with a trained eye. Train yours: read the Gospels slowly, notice what Christ is like and what he has done, meditate on the cross, sing about him, spend time with Christians who love him. Ask God to show you his worth (Ephesians 1:17–18). As you see more of him, other things will look smaller, not because they are worthless, but because he is greater.

In a sentence. The merchant gave up everything for one priceless pearl, and the kingdom is also like a net that gathers every kind of fish.

On a Tuesday. Is Christ your pearl of great value? Name one thing you would be unwilling to give up for him, and bring it to him honestly in prayer today. And cast the net: invite someone this week to hear the gospel, whatever kind of fish they seem to be.

For worship. Christ is the pearl beyond price, and he is also the merchant who gave everything. He left the riches of heaven and became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). We are not worth a pearl; he made us his treasured possession. Glory to the Lord whose worth is greater than all the world, and who counted us worth his life.
verseByVerse.note: A dragnet was drawn between boats or to shore, catching everything in its path.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the net was full, the fishermen pulled it ashore, sat down, and sorted the good fish into baskets and threw away the bad. So it will be at the end of the age: the angels will come and separate the evil from the righteous.

When it was full, men drew it ashore. The net gathers until it is full. The Sea of Galilee makes this parable exact.

And sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. The lake holds many species, and the law made an unavoidable distinction among them: only fish with fins and scales could be eaten (Leviticus 11:9–12). Everything else, catfish among them, was unclean. So a Jewish fisherman hauling a dragnet up that beach was sorting his catch not merely into saleable and unsaleable but into permitted and forbidden. The scene Jesus describes was the ordinary end of every working day for men in his audience: the net up on the sand, the crew sitting down beside it, and the long business of going through the pile by hand. And the two adjectives are worth having. The good fish are kala, fine, sound. The bad are sapra, which is not small or inferior but rotten: the word used of the bad tree that cannot bear good fruit (7:17–18). The category is not disappointing fish. It is fish that have gone off. Sorting was a careful, final process.

So it will be at the end of the age. The same lesson as the weeds: the final separation (vv. 40–43). And the repetition is deliberate. The wheat and the weeds ended with the reapers separating and burning. The dragnet ends with the angels separating and burning. Two different pictures, a field and a lake, farming and fishing, arrive at the same conclusion in the same chapter. Matthew is not padding. He has given the warning twice, in the two industries his first readers worked in, so that nobody could file it as farming imagery and move on.

The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous. The angels, not human beings, will do the sorting. Only God can judge the heart perfectly. The fishermen who drew the net are not the ones who do the final sorting; they bring in the catch.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we should be careless about who is in the church. But the net gathers all kinds through the preaching of the gospel; final separation belongs to God.

How can I be sure I will be among the good on that day? Not by your own goodness, which is never enough, but by belonging to Christ. The righteous in this parable are those made righteous by faith in him (Romans 5:1). The marks that you belong to him are that you trust him, love him, and are being changed by him, however imperfectly; and his promise is that whoever believes in him has eternal life and will not come into judgment (John 5:24). Look to Christ, not into the net. Assurance grows as you look at him and see his work in you.

In a sentence. Like fishermen sorting their catch, the angels will separate the evil from the righteous at the end of the age.

On a Tuesday. The gospel net catches all kinds of people. Cast it widely: be friendly to the person at church who seems unpromising, and do not decide in advance who will or will not be saved. Leave the final sorting to God, and give yourself to the fishing.

For worship. Jesus called fishermen and made them fishers of men, and the net of the gospel has been sweeping the sea of the nations ever since. It will be drawn ashore when it is full. Not one fish will be lost that belongs to him, and not one will be wrongly sorted. Praise the Lord who gathers, who judges with perfect knowledge, and who has made us clean through his blood.
verseByVerse.note: Fish without fins and scales were unclean under the law and could not be sold as food.

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Have you understood all these things?" They said to him, "Yes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evil will be thrown into the fiery furnace, with weeping and gnashing of teeth. Jesus asked his disciples: have you understood all these things? They said yes.

And throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The same words as verse 42. Jesus repeats the warning: the judgment is real and terrible.

Have you understood all these things? Understanding is the mark of good soil (v. 23). The verb is syniēmi again, the word that has run through the whole chapter, and this is its sixth and last appearance. It is put to them now as a direct question. The chapter has been about the difference between hearing and understanding, and it ends by asking the Twelve which side of that line they are on. He asks not to quiz them but to call them to account for their hearing.

They said to him, Yes. One word in Greek, nai. And it is worth being honest about what it was worth. Within a few chapters Peter will be told get behind me, Satan, for objecting to the cross. They will argue about which of them is greatest. They will fail to cast out a demon because of their little faith. At the supper they will still be asking where he is going, and by the end of that night every one of them will be somewhere else. So their yes was not false, and it was not adequate either. Their understanding was real, though limited (16:9–11). They had grasped the outline of what he said and almost nothing of what it would cost.

The mercy in his response. That is a mercy for anybody who has ever said yes to God and discovered later how little he knew he was agreeing to. Jesus does not correct them. He accepts the answer, and then adds one more parable, about a householder bringing out treasure both old and new, as though to say: good, and there is a great deal more in the store.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the disciples now understood everything, or that understanding is complete in this life. Understanding grows as we keep company with Christ.

I said yes to Christ but understood so little. Was my faith real? Almost certainly, if you meant it and have kept coming to him. No one understands the gospel fully when they first believe; the disciples did not. Faith is trusting Christ with what you know of him, and the knowing grows. What matters is not how much you understood at the start but that you are still with him and still learning. Jesus accepted the disciples’ small yes and went on teaching them. He does the same with you.

In a sentence. After repeating the warning of judgment, Jesus asked whether the disciples had understood, and they said yes, a real but small yes that he received and built on.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus asked you whether you have understood his teaching, what would you say? Pick one parable from this chapter and explain it to someone else this week. You will find out how much you understand, and you will understand it better.

For worship. How patient is the Teacher of slow disciples. He knew how little their yes contained, and he received it, and he did not let them go. He would take the same men through his death and resurrection and the gift of his Spirit until they understood enough to turn the world upside down. He has received our small yes too, and he will finish what he began.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old." And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every teacher of the law who has become a disciple of the kingdom of heaven is like the owner of a house who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old. When Jesus had finished these parables, he moved on.

Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven. A scribe was a teacher of the law (see 2:4). A scribe trained for the kingdom (literally discipled) is one who has become Jesus’ disciple. And this is very probably Matthew’s own self-portrait, one of the most attractive readings in the Gospel. Consider who is writing this book: a man who quotes the Old Testament more than any other evangelist, who arranges his Gospel in five discourses echoing the five books of Moses, who stops his story again and again to say this was to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet, who alone records this saying, and whose name appears in his own list of apostles with a description no other Gospel adds: Matthew the tax collector (10:3). A man who kept records for a living and knew the Scriptures well enough to weave them into every chapter. If anybody in the New Testament is a scribe trained for the kingdom, bringing out things old and new, it is the author of this sentence.

Is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old. Treasure here means the storeroom, the place where treasure is kept: the householder goes to the store and fetches things out. The old treasures are the Old Testament: the law, the prophets and the promises. The new treasures are the teaching of Jesus and the gospel of the kingdom. A good teacher uses both, showing how the new fulfils the old (5:17). And the order matters: new first. A scribe of the old school brought out the old; this one has something recent to put beside it, and he leads with it. But he does not discard the old, and that is the whole force of the sentence. He has not replaced his library. He has had something added to it that makes the rest legible. Augustine summed it up: the New Testament is concealed in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New.

And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there. The formula ending the third great discourse (see 7:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the new replaces the old entirely, nor that the old is enough without the new. Both are needed, understood together. The Old Testament is not a preface that can be skipped now that the New has come, and the New is not intelligible without it. Darnel and dragnets and mustard seed mean what they mean because Daniel and Ezekiel and the psalms of Asaph stand behind them.

Is this only for preachers? No. Every Christian is to let the word of Christ dwell in him richly, teaching and admonishing one another (Colossians 3:16), and parents teach their children daily. Your storeroom is filled by reading both Testaments over years, and you bring out of it whenever you encourage a friend, answer a child’s question or comfort someone with a promise. You do not need to be learned; you need to be a disciple who keeps adding to the store.

In a sentence. A disciple trained in the kingdom brings out both the old treasures of the Old Testament and the new treasures of Jesus’ teaching, showing how the new fulfils the old.

On a Tuesday. Read both Testaments. If you have only read the New, begin a plan this week that includes the Old. When you read the Old, look for Christ; when you read the New, look for the Old Testament roots. Bring out both.

For worship. God wrote one book in two Testaments, and both are about his Son. The law, the prophets and the psalms were the old treasure, kept for centuries in Israel’s storeroom; Christ came and brought them out and showed what they had always meant. Now the whole house is full, and every disciple may go to it and bring out riches. Blessed be the Lord who has given us the Scriptures, old and new, and in them himself.

parallels.desc: not to abolish but to fulfil

verseByVerse.quote: and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, "Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came to his hometown, Nazareth, and taught in their synagogue. The people were astonished: where did this man get this wisdom and these miracles? Isn’t he the carpenter’s son? Isn’t his mother Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon and Judas?

And coming to his hometown. Nazareth, where he grew up (2:23).

He taught them in their synagogue. On the Sabbath. Luke records a similar visit, perhaps the same one (Luke 4:16–30).

So that they were astonished. At his wisdom and power. Their astonishment is genuine. They are not stupid, and at the start they are not hostile.

Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? A fair question, with an answer they would not accept: from God. That is the right question.

Is not this the carpenter’s son? Carpenter (tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Mark calls Jesus himself the carpenter (Mark 6:3). They knew him as a manual worker, who had built their houses and mended their ploughs. How could an ordinary tradesman have such wisdom? They had no category for the incarnation: God in an ordinary man.

Is not his mother called Mary? They knew his family well. Every one of these questions is accurate. They have the family right, the trade right, the names right. Nobody in Nazareth is mistaken about a single fact.

And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? Jesus’ brothers, most naturally Mary’s later children (see 1:25). The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life, have taken them to be either cousins (so Jerome) or children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (so the Orthodox). The words themselves most naturally mean what they say: these are the later sons and daughters of Joseph and Mary, the younger half-brothers and half-sisters of Jesus, born, unlike him, in the ordinary way. Matthew has already hinted as much, saying Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (1:25), and Luke calls Jesus her firstborn (Luke 2:7). There is no need to protect Mary’s honour by keeping her a perpetual virgin; her honour is that she bore and raised the Son of God, and then was a mother to his brothers.

The brothers who came to believe. There is gospel gold here. These brothers did not believe in him during his ministry (John 7:5), yet after the resurrection we find them in the upper room praying (Acts 1:14). James later led the Jerusalem church and wrote the letter of James; Judas, Jude, wrote the letter of Jude. What turns a sceptical younger brother into a man who calls his own brother the Lord? Only an empty tomb. The conversion of the brothers of Jesus is one of the quiet, powerful evidences that he rose.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that there was anything shameful about Jesus’ ordinary background. The Son of God worked with his hands for years, dignifying all honest labour. The problem was that familiarity bred contempt. They reduced him to what they already knew instead of letting what they saw revise what they knew.

Does my ordinary work matter to God? Yes. The Lord of glory spent most of his earthly life as a craftsman in a small town, and the Father was well pleased with him before he had preached a sermon (3:17). Work done honestly and for God’s glory is never wasted, whether it is building, cleaning, teaching, caring or keeping accounts (Colossians 3:23–24). You do not need a religious job to serve Christ. Do your ordinary work well, as for him.

In a sentence. The people of Nazareth were astonished at Jesus’ wisdom and miracles, but could not accept that the carpenter they knew could be more than he seemed.

On a Tuesday. Familiarity can blind us to Jesus. Have you grown so used to the stories that they no longer astonish you? Read one familiar Gospel story today as if for the first time, and ask: who is this man?

For worship. The hands that formed the stars planed wood in Nazareth. The Word through whom all things were made lived thirty years as a village carpenter, so ordinary that his neighbours could not see past it. Such is the humility of God. And such is his power, that the brothers who grew up with him and doubted him came at last to worship him as Lord. Glory to the Son who became so lowly that he could be overlooked, and who is so glorious that he will be worshipped for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?" And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aren’t all his sisters here with us? Where did he get all this? They took offence at him. Jesus said: a prophet is not without honour except in his hometown and in his own household.

And are not all his sisters with us? Jesus had sisters too, unnamed. All suggests at least two, perhaps more. Jesus grew up in a large family. And notice the present tense: his sisters are with us, still living in the village, presumably married locally. Their neighbours could point to their houses. Nothing about this family was mysterious, and that was the difficulty.

Where then did this man get all these things? The same question they opened with, asked the second time as an objection rather than an enquiry. That is the whole tragedy of the passage. They began by asking where it came from, assembled a complete and correct account of everything they knew about him, found that it did not explain what they were looking at, and concluded that the problem was with him. The evidence had raised a question their information could not answer. The right response was to widen the information. They narrowed the evidence instead.

And they took offense at him. Took offence (eskandalizonto) means stumbled over him, the chapter’s trap word (see 11:6). It has run all through this material: the message to John (11:6), the rocky-ground hearer who falls away (13:21), the causes of sin gathered out at the harvest (13:41), and now his own village. They did not argue him down. They tripped over him, over the very thing that should have made him easiest to believe, which was that they had known him all his life. He did not fit their expectations. They knew his family, his job and his ordinary life; they could not believe he was the Messiah.

A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household. A proverb. People find it hardest to accept greatness in someone they grew up with. Even Jesus’ own brothers did not yet believe (John 7:5). God’s messengers are often received everywhere except at home. He was rejected not by strangers but by neighbours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a believer must expect never to be heard at home, or should stop speaking to family. The proverb describes a common pattern, not an iron law; Jesus’ own family came to faith.

How do I live as a Christian among people who knew me before? Expect it to be hard, as it was for Jesus, and do not be bitter about it. Those who remember your past may doubt your change, and some may resent it. Let your life do much of the speaking: patience, honesty, kindness, steadiness over years (1 Peter 2:12). Speak of Christ when there is opportunity, simply and without preaching at people. And remember that many who first took offence later believed. The proof that Jesus was who he said was not argued into Nazareth; it walked out of a tomb.

In a sentence. His hometown took offence at Jesus because they knew him and his family too well to believe.

On a Tuesday. If your family or old friends find it hard to take your faith seriously, Jesus understands. Keep living faithfully among them, and pray for one of them by name each day this week.

For worship. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). Even the town where he learned to walk would not have him. He bore that dishonour in his own household, among his own neighbours, and went on loving them. And to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God. Glory to the despised prophet of Nazareth, who is the King of kings.

parallels.desc: his own people did not receive him

verseByVerse.quote: And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief.

And he did not do many mighty works there. Mark says he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them (Mark 6:5).

Because of their unbelief. Not because Jesus’ power was limited by their unbelief, as if he were helpless. Rather, miracles were signs meant to call people to faith; where people refused to believe, signs had no purpose. Jesus would not perform for sceptics (12:39). And unbelief closes the door to what God offers. Mark adds that Jesus marvelled at their unbelief (Mark 6:6).

Handle it carefully. That sentence must be handled carefully, though, because it is one verse away from a cruelty that has done a great deal of damage. Read carelessly it says: miracles run on faith, so if God has not acted in your situation, the fault is the thinness of your believing. Some have been told exactly that over a hospital bed. It is not what the verse means. Look at what it actually reports. He did not do many mighty works there, and Mark, telling the same visit, says he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Even in that atmosphere, some were healed. So this is plainly not a mechanism in which a quantity of faith buys a quantity of power. And set it beside the rest of the Gospel: he heals a paralysed man on the strength of his friends’ faith and not his own (9:2), he raises the dead, who by definition contribute nothing, and he restores people who do not yet know who he is. Faith is the open hand, never the currency.

What unbelief prevented. What Nazareth’s unbelief actually prevented was simpler and sadder. They did not bring their sick to him, because they had already settled who he was: the carpenter’s boy, whose family lived down the road. You cannot receive what you have decided not to come for. The verse describes a town that had made up its mind, not a formula governing answered prayer. If you have prayed and not received, this passage is not an accusation against you; the note at 8:16–17 sets out what may and may not be expected, and Paul, whose faith was equal to anything, asked three times and kept his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

The warning that is here. But do take the warning that is truly here, because it is aimed at exactly the sort of person who reads commentaries. The people who got least from Jesus in his whole ministry were the ones who had been nearest to him longest. They were not hostile; they were familiar. They had him filed. A lifetime of church can do the same thing to a soul: the sermons heard before, the passage you already know, the quiet assumption that there is nothing here you have not met. Nazareth is what happens when knowing about him has replaced knowing him, and this chapter has already told you what that ground is called.

The end of the chapter. The chapter of parables ends with a living example of the hard soil: the people who knew Jesus best did not receive him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that faith is a power that makes God act, or that a lack of miracles always shows a lack of faith. God is sovereign in what he does (Romans 9:15–18). But faith receives what God gives, and unbelief refuses it.

So should I pray for healing at all? Yes. Jesus welcomed the sick, and Scripture tells us to pray for them and ask the elders to pray (James 5:14–15). Pray with honest trust, asking boldly and leaving the answer to his wisdom: your will be done. Sometimes he heals; sometimes he gives grace to bear what remains, as with Paul; always he will heal completely at the resurrection. Use doctors and medicine as gifts of his providence. And never tell a suffering believer that their illness continues because they lack faith.

In a sentence. Because of their unbelief, Jesus did few miracles in his hometown, not because his power failed but because they would not come to him.

On a Tuesday. Unbelief shuts out blessing, and familiarity breeds it. Ask God to replace your doubts with trust, and to make you hungry again for a Christ you may have filed away. Then bring him one real need today, as Nazareth would not.

For worship. The Lord of all power stood in Nazareth with healing in his hands, and they would not come. He marvelled at their unbelief, and still he laid his hands on the few who did. Such is his patience, and such is his kindness. And for us, who have heard so much and so long, he is still the same: mighty to save, ready to heal, astonishing to all who will look at him again. Praise the Christ whom familiarity cannot diminish, whose mercies are new every morning.

13.theology: The hiddenness and growth of the kingdom. The parables of Matthew 13 develop a theology of the kingdom that runs against both triumphalism and despair. Against triumphalism: the kingdom grows secretly, like leaven, not by worldly power or coercion. Against despair: the smallest seed becomes the largest tree; the handful of leavened dough leavens the whole batch. The kingdom’s smallness is not its failure but its method. Reformed theology has always insisted that the church advances through the ordinary means of grace — word, sacrament, prayer — not through political power or cultural dominance. The harvest will be glorious; the sowing is patient.
13.examples:
Then: The disciples were living through the mustard-seed phase of the kingdom. From their vantage point, a small band of Galileans following a rabbi who was being plotted against by the religious establishment, the kingdom’s glory was not obvious. Jesus tells them: do not judge the end by the beginning.

Now: Every era of church history has felt like the mustard-seed phase. Persecution, secularisation, nominalism — all seem to contradict the kingdom’s advance. The parables of Matthew 13 are the antidote to both despair and triumphalism. The Sower keeps sowing. The leaven keeps working. The net keeps gathering. The harvest belongs to the Lord.

14.title: Bread in the Wilderness
14.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, <sup>2</sup>and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>3</sup>For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, <sup>4</sup>because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” <sup>5</sup>And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. <sup>6</sup>But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod, <sup>7</sup>so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. <sup>8</sup>Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.” <sup>9</sup>And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. <sup>10</sup>He sent and had John beheaded in the prison, <sup>11</sup>and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. <sup>12</sup>And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. <sup>14</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick. <sup>15</sup>Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves.” <sup>16</sup>But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat.” <sup>17</sup>They said to him, “We have only five loaves here and two fish.” <sup>18</sup>And he said, “Bring them here to me.” <sup>19</sup>Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>20</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>21</sup>And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>22</sup>Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. <sup>23</sup>And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone, <sup>24</sup>but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. <sup>25</sup>And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. <sup>26</sup>But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, “It is a ghost!” and they cried out in fear. <sup>27</sup>But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>28</sup>And Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” <sup>29</sup>He said, “Come.” So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. <sup>30</sup>But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me.” <sup>31</sup>Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” <sup>32</sup>And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. <sup>33</sup>And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.” <sup>34</sup>And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. <sup>35</sup>And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick <sup>36</sup>and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 moves from Herod’s banquet of death (John’s head on a platter) to Jesus’ banquet of life (five thousand fed in the wilderness). The contrast is deliberate. Herod’s table is supplied by cruelty, vanity, and the murder of a prophet. Jesus’ table is supplied by compassion, prayer, and the creative power of the Creator multiplying what is surrendered to him. John’s death is the herald’s fate; Jesus will face his own; but the meals he gives point beyond death to the resurrection feast.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (besides the resurrection). Matthew frames it with Exodus typology: a desolate place (wilderness), manna-like provision, the Shepherd feeding his people. Jesus looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives — the same fourfold action he will perform at the Last Supper. Every Lord’s Supper echoes this meal. The chapter closes with Peter walking on water — and sinking. The disciples worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Death of John and the Feeding of the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus and fears John has risen from the dead. Matthew then narrates the death of John the Baptist — arrested for condemning Herod's marriage to his brother's wife, beheaded to fulfill a rash oath at a banquet. Jesus withdraws on hearing the news, but the crowds follow him. He heals them and then feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish. The feeding is the great Eucharistic sign, anticipating the Last Supper and the heavenly banquet. What the summary cannot hold. Herod is a tetrarch, not a king — Herod the Great's realm was quartered at his death and this son got Galilee and Perea. He wanted the higher title, went to Rome to ask for it, and was exiled for his trouble. He came to power soon after the nativity and was still in power at the crucifixion, and Luke has Pilate send Jesus to him during the trial (Lk. 23:12). His explanation is theologically bizarre: nobody in Judaism expected an individual to be raised in the middle of history, so "this is John, he has been raised" is not a belief he is reaching for — he has invented it on the spot, and said it to his servants, the people who had watched the platter come in. On the geography, Josephus names the prison: Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea with luxurious apartments above and cells below — so the banquet and the dungeon were in the same building. He also names the girl: Salome. And Matthew calls her a korasion, the diminutive, the same word used of Jairus's twelve-year-old (9:24-25) — a child, put up to it, who goes out to ask her mother what to say. The oath is a quotation: Mark gives it in full, "up to half my kingdom" (6:23), which is what Ahasuerus says to Esther three times, at her banquets (Est. 5:3, 6; 7:2). A drunken king, a rash promise, a woman with a prepared request, a man's life in the balance — and every element inverts. Esther's request saved a people from a murderer; this one murders a prophet. Note too that Herod and the chief priests are restrained by the same calculation, in almost identical words: both fear the crowd "because they held him to be a prophet" (14:5; 21:46). And verse 12 is the quietest sentence in the chapter — John's disciples walked into a royal fortress to ask for the body, buried what there was, and then went to the one man who had told them who John was. Matthew records no reply. The next thing Jesus does is withdraw; the next thing after that is to feed five thousand men, besides women and children. On the day he heard.
verseByVerse.theology: John's death is the dark center of the chapter: the fate of the forerunner anticipates the fate of the one he announced. Herod's fear that Jesus is John raised from the dead is simultaneously wrong (Jesus is not John) and prophetically ironic (the resurrection John could not achieve, Jesus will). The feeding of the five thousand is the messianic act par excellence: the shepherd-king who provides bread for his people in the wilderness, echoing the manna of the Exodus. Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives — the fourfold action of the Last Supper.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' protest — "we have only five loaves here and two fish" — is the protest of faith that has not yet learned what it is living with. They are calculating from what they have; Jesus acts from who he is. "Bring them here to me" is the word for every situation where human resources fall desperately short of human need. The miracle occurs not in the disciples' hands but in his: he takes, blesses, breaks, gives — and twelve baskets remain. Twelve: one for each tribe of Israel, one for each disciple. The abundance of the kingdom always exceeds the need.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, and he said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod the ruler of Galilee heard about Jesus and said to his servants: this is John the Baptist, raised from the dead. That is why these powers are at work in him.

Meaning first. Matthew 14 sets two banquets side by side. The first is Herod’s birthday feast in a fortress palace, supplied by vanity, lust and fear, and its last course is the head of a prophet on a serving dish. The second is a meal on the grass in a desolate place, supplied by compassion and prayer, where a grieving Jesus feeds a city from a boy’s lunch. Then, in the dark, he comes to his struggling disciples walking on the sea, says the words God spoke from the burning bush, catches a sinking Peter by the hand, and receives the first confession of this Gospel: truly you are the Son of God. The chapter shows what the kingdoms of this world serve at their tables, and what the King of heaven serves at his, and who it is that walks on the waters that frighten us.

At that time Herod the tetrarch. This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great (2:1). When his father died in 4 BC, Rome carved the kingdom into pieces, and this son received a quarter of it, Galilee and Perea (east of the Jordan), with the rank of tetrarch rather than king. The title originally meant ruler of a fourth part and came to mean a minor ruler, below a king. It is worth knowing how much this man overlaps with the life of Jesus. He came to power soon after the nativity and was still in power at the crucifixion, ruling the district where Jesus grew up for almost the whole of his earthly life. Luke records Pilate sending Jesus to him during the trial, and the two rulers becoming friends that day (Luke 23:12). Jesus once called him that fox (Luke 13:32). He wanted the higher title badly, and in the end it ruined him (see on vv. 9–10).

Heard about the fame of Jesus. News of the miracles, and perhaps of the Twelve going out through the villages (10:1–8), had reached the palace. The kingdom of heaven was being proclaimed in Herod’s own territory, and the first thing it did in his heart was not to call him but to haunt him.

This is John the Baptist. Herod said it to his servants, and that detail is worth weighing. These were the people who had been in the palace on the night of the banquet, who had seen the platter carried in, and who now had to stand there while their master worked out loud through what he had done. His explanation is theologically bizarre. Nobody in Judaism expected a single individual to be raised in the middle of history; resurrection was a doctrine about the last day and the whole people. So he has not reached for an available belief. He has invented one on the spot. That is what a guilty conscience does. It is not reasoning from the evidence; it is being visited. The man who silenced the prophet cannot silence the memory of the prophet’s voice.

He has been raised from the dead. Some people thought Jesus was Elijah or one of the prophets (16:14); Herod thought he was John. And there is a dark irony in it. His superstitious terror came close to a truth he never grasped. One greater than John had indeed come, and he would rise from the dead, not as a ghost to frighten a murderer but as the firstfruits of a new creation.

That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him. John did no miracles in his lifetime (John 10:41). Herod imagined that a John back from the grave would have new powers. Guilt is a busy theologian. It confirms that John was innocent and that the deed was murder, and it supplies explanations faster than reason can check them.

What it does not mean. Not that Herod believed in Jesus. His fear was superstition and guilt, not faith. Luke adds the sequel: Herod sought to see him (Luke 9:9). He got his wish at the very end, and when he finally had Jesus in front of him he asked for a conjuring trick, received silence, and treated him with contempt (Luke 23:8–11). Fear of God is the beginning of wisdom only when it brings a man to repentance. Herod’s remained dread.

Is a troubled conscience a good thing or a bad thing? It depends entirely on where it sends you. A conscience that accuses you is God’s mercy, a warning light on the dashboard. Herod’s did its work faithfully: it would not let him forget. The tragedy is that he treated the light as the problem and never went to the one person who could deal with what it was reporting. Two men in the Gospels were tormented by what they had done to an innocent man. Judas carried it alone and was destroyed by it; Peter carried it to Jesus and was restored. If something you did years ago still visits you, the remedy is not distraction or self-punishment but confession to God, and where possible putting it right, and then believing that the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).

In a sentence. Haunted by guilt, Herod thought Jesus was John the Baptist, whom he had executed, raised from the dead.

On a Tuesday. A guilty conscience cannot be silenced by killing the messenger, or by moving house, or by staying busy. Notice the explanations you reach for when something unsettles you, and ask whether they are reasoning or self-defence. If your conscience is troubled, take it to Christ today, by name and in detail. He forgives what you cannot forget.

For worship. The Lord whom Herod feared is the Lord who forgives. The same Jesus whose rising Herod dreaded rose in fact, and he rose for the guilty, so that men who have done terrible things to the innocent might hear their consciences answered instead of only silenced. There is no voice from the past that his blood cannot speak louder than. It speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24), and a better word than the blood of John.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea. A tetrarch was a ruler of part of a divided kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because John had been saying to him, "It is not lawful for you to have her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod had arrested John, put him in chains and imprisoned him because of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife. John had told him: it is not lawful for you to have her.

For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison. Matthew now goes back to explain how John died. John had been in prison since 4:12. Josephus tells us where: Machaerus, a fortress palace Herod the Great had built on a ridge east of the Dead Sea, in the bleakest country in the region. It was a stronghold with luxurious apartments above and cells below, a place where a ruler could entertain guests and hold prisoners at the same time. Josephus adds that Herod also feared John’s influence over the people.
