For the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife. Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great, and so the niece of both her husbands. She had been married to Antipas’s half-brother. On a visit to Rome, Antipas fell for her; both divorced their spouses and married each other. Antipas’s first wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, fled to her father, who later went to war with Antipas and defeated him. Josephus saw that defeat as God’s judgment on Herod for killing John.

Philip or Herod? The name in this verse has drawn fire, and a reader who has met the objection deserves the answer. Josephus names Herodias’s first husband as Herod, another son of Herod the Great, and says that Philip the tetrarch married Salome, Herodias’s daughter. Critics have concluded that the Gospels muddled the family. They have not, and the tangle is of Herod’s own making. Herod the Great had at least ten wives and a swarm of sons, and he named a remarkable number of them after himself; there are several men called Herod in this family and more than one called Philip, and Josephus himself gives some of them two names. A son known formally as Herod and familiarly as Philip is entirely possible, and Matthew’s readers, close enough to know the family gossip, would have needed the second name precisely to tell one brother from another. We meet the same convention with the man who wrote this Gospel, called Matthew here (9:9) and Levi in Mark 2:14. It does not touch the point of the passage: whichever brother she left, the marriage was unlawful and John said so. But it is worth knowing that where the Gospels can be checked against an independent historian they hold up under checking, and that an apparent collision, patiently examined, usually turns out to be a detail we were missing rather than an error the writer made.

Because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her”. “Had been saying”: repeatedly, not once in a heated moment. The law forbade a man to take his brother’s wife while the brother was alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). And the marriage was built on two divorces that had no ground God recognises; neither spouse had been unfaithful or had deserted (see 5:32; 19:9; Westminster 24.5–6). John did not qualify his condemnation for the sake of safety or soften it for political convenience. He said to the ruler’s face what was true. Like Elijah confronting Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21), the man who came in the spirit of Elijah (11:14) stood up to a king and his queen, and like Elijah he found that the queen was the more dangerous of the two.

What it does not mean. Not that preachers should comment on every personal sin of every politician, or that the pulpit is a place for campaigns. But John shows that God’s law applies to rulers as much as to anyone; that there is no class of person above the seventh commandment; and that faithful servants of God must sometimes speak hard truths to power, at personal cost.

Why did John make a private marriage a public issue? Because it was not private. Herod was the ruler of God’s people in Galilee, and his marriage was a public act that told a whole province that the law of God could be set aside by anyone with enough power. John was a prophet, and a prophet’s office is to say what God says about what is done in the open. He was not gossiping or settling a score; he was calling a man to repentance, and Mark tells us Herod kept going back to listen (Mark 6:20). The aim of rebuke is always the sinner’s rescue. Most of us will never address a ruler, but we will face moments when a friend, a relative or a colleague does something openly wrong, and silence would be the comfortable cowardice. Speak, privately where you can, humbly always, and for his good.

In a sentence. John was imprisoned for telling Herod, again and again, that his marriage to his brother’s wife broke God’s law.

On a Tuesday. Are you willing to say a true thing that may cost you, when love for God and for the person in front of you requires it? And when someone says a true and costly thing to you, will you be Herod, who listened and resented, or will you thank them?

For worship. Behind John’s courage stands a greater faithfulness. Christ also stood before rulers, before the high priest, before Pilate, before this same Herod, and witnessed the good confession (1 Timothy 6:13). He did not soften the truth to save himself, and he did not keep silent to save himself either; he kept silent to save us. The Lord who gave John a tongue that would not bend is the Lord whose own word never once bent, and whose truth is the only ground any of us has to stand on.
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

parallels.desc: the nakedness of your brother’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. But when Herod's birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod wanted to kill John, but he feared the people, who regarded John as a prophet. But on Herod’s birthday, Herodias’ daughter danced before the guests and pleased Herod.

And though he wanted to put him to death. Mark tells us the other side: Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted him dead, while Herod feared John, knowing he was a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe; he was greatly perplexed by him, and yet heard him gladly (Mark 6:19–20). Herod’s heart was divided. He was drawn to John’s message and he resented it. He wanted the prophet silenced and could not stop going to listen to him. It is one of the most recognisable portraits in Scripture: a man who enjoys sermons and will not obey them.

He feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. Fear of public opinion restrained him, not conscience. And set the two rulers side by side, because Matthew does. In seven chapters the chief priests will want Jesus dead and hesitate for exactly the same reason: they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet (21:46). Almost identical words. The tyrant and the temple establishment are governed by the same calculation, and neither is restrained by conscience for a moment. What restrains them is a headcount, and in both cases it only postpones matters.

But when Herod’s birthday came. A lavish banquet for his nobles, military commanders and the leading men of Galilee (Mark 6:21). And remember where it was. If Josephus is right about Machaerus, the birthday feast and the cell were in the same building. The music was audible from the dungeon.

The daughter of Herodias danced before the company. Josephus names her Salome, Herodias’s daughter by her first marriage; she later married her great-uncle Philip the tetrarch. The scene is often painted as seduction by a grown woman, and the text does not say that. Mark and Matthew call her a korasion, the diminutive, a little girl, the same word used of Jairus’s twelve-year-old daughter (9:24–25). She was probably in her early teens. For a princess to dance before a hall of drinking men was shameful in itself, and the sequel shows what kind of dance it was. She is a child, put up to it by her mother and used by the adults in the room.

And pleased Herod. He was delighted, very likely drunk, and inflamed. The powerful man who yielded to popular fear now yields to appetite: two forms of weakness, and between them they will seal John’s fate.

What it does not mean. Not that the girl was innocent of what she did next, for she asked for it herself. But the passage puts the heavier weight on the adults: the mother who used her child as an instrument, and the stepfather who took pleasure in what he should have stopped. Those who lead the young into sin carry a terrible responsibility (18:6).

Can a person enjoy good preaching and still be lost? Yes, and Herod is the proof. He sent for John, listened to him gladly, was troubled by him, and protected him, and none of it was repentance. Enjoying truth is not the same as submitting to it; being moved is not the same as being changed. The test is not whether you like the sermon but whether you obey the word, especially the part that touches the one thing you are determined to keep. Herod’s one thing was Herodias. If there is one area of your life where you have quietly decided God’s word will not be allowed to reach, that is where Herod’s danger lives. The remedy is to name it to God today and ask him for the grace to let it go.

In a sentence. Herod wanted John dead but feared the people, until his stepdaughter’s dance at his birthday banquet pleased him.

On a Tuesday. Herod liked to hear John but would not obey him. Listening to God’s word without obeying it leaves the heart open to disaster, because the day always comes when the unconfronted sin meets an opportunity. Ask yourself which comes first in you when the word of God and the opinion of the people around you pull in different directions.

For worship. How different is the King we serve. Herod’s birthday was celebrated with a dance and a death. The birth of Christ was celebrated by angels singing glory to God and peace among men. Herod’s table fed the appetite of a few powerful men; Christ’s table, a few verses later, feeds the hungry poor. Herod could not rule his own desires; Christ was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and he rules his kingdom with a righteousness that never once gave way to the crowd.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

verseByVerse.quote: so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. Prompted by her mother, she said, "Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Herod swore an oath to give her whatever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she said: give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.

So that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. A rash, extravagant oath, made in drunken excitement before guests. Mark gives the full wording: whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom (Mark 6:23). And that is a quotation. King Ahasuerus says it to Esther, at her banquets (Esther 5:3, 6; 7:2). The elements line up exactly: a king at a feast, an enormous promise, a woman with a prepared request, and a man’s life hanging on what she asks for. Then everything inverts. Esther used her request to save a people from a murderer; this one is used to murder a prophet. Esther risked her life going in unbidden; this girl is sent in. In Esther the villain ends on his own gallows; here the villain gets what she wants and walks away. The Persian court behaved better than the Jewish one. And Herod had no kingdom to give in any case, only what Rome allowed him. Jesus had warned against careless oaths (5:33–37); here is the kind of mouth he meant.

Prompted by her mother. Matthew’s word suggests she was pushed forward, instructed. Mark fills in the gap: the girl went out and asked her mother what she should ask for, and came back in haste with the answer and one addition of her own, at once (Mark 6:24–25). Herodias had wanted this for months and had been blocked. She does not appear at the feast, does not make the request, and never speaks in the scene. She arranged the conditions, waited, and used her daughter as the instrument. Hatred is patient in its own way.

She said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter”. A horrifying request, spoken at a feast. A platter was a serving dish: John’s head would be brought in like a course. And one word in it is pure cruelty: here. Not have him executed, but here, on a dish, now, while the guests are still at the table. It is designed to make retreat impossible and to turn a murder into the evening’s entertainment. The one who preached repentance is murdered by the very sins he named.

Should I keep a promise I now regret? Usually, yes. Scripture honours the man who swears to his own hurt and does not change (Psalm 15:4), and a Christian’s word should be reliable even when keeping it is costly or inconvenient. But there is one clear exception, and Herod stands in it: no promise can bind you to sin. An oath to do evil is void from the moment it is spoken, and keeping it doubles the sin rather than redeeming it. If you have promised something wrong, the right course is to confess the rash promise, refuse to fulfil it, and accept whatever embarrassment follows. And if you are not sure whether a promise falls into that category, take counsel from a mature believer before acting.

In a sentence. Herod rashly swore to give the girl anything, and at her mother’s prompting she asked for John’s head on a platter.

On a Tuesday. Rash promises made in the heat of the moment can trap us: the yes said to impress, the commitment made because the room was watching. Be slow to promise and quick to keep, and never let a promise bind you to sin. Let your yes be yes and your no be no (5:37).

For worship. There is a King who also made a promise at a table, and it was not rash. On the night he was betrayed he took the cup and promised his blood for the forgiveness of sins (26:28), and he kept it the next day, at the cost of his life, not to save his face but to save ours. Every promise of God finds its Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). Herod swore and kept his word to destroy a righteous man. Christ swore and kept his word to rescue the unrighteous.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. He sent and had John beheaded in the prison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king was distressed, but because of his oaths and his dinner guests, he ordered it to be done. He sent and had John beheaded in prison.

And the king was sorry. Matthew records the sorrow, and it makes the surrender worse. Herod knew it was wrong. He was sorry. And he did it anyway. This is sin at its most nakedly human: not ignorance, not compulsion, but the choice of pride over what is right. And notice the word king. In verse 1 Matthew called him the tetrarch, the accurate title. Here he is the king, the courtesy his court and his vanity gave him, and the word carries a bitter providence. The title Antipas did not have, he ached to have, and it was Herodias who drove that ambition. A few years later she pressed him to sail to Rome and ask the emperor for the royal title; instead he was accused, stripped even of his tetrarchy, and exiled to Gaul in AD 39 (so Josephus). The woman for whom he broke God’s law and shed a prophet’s blood steered him to his ruin. Sin keeps its promises exactly backwards. He grasped at a crown and lost the little he had. Whoever loves his life loses it (John 12:25) is written across his whole story.

But because of his oaths and his guests. This phrase is the exact anatomy of how a decent impulse gets overruled. His oaths: a rash promise to a dancing girl, which no court on earth would have held him to and which any decent man breaks. Herod treated it as binding because breaking it would have cost him something. And his guests: that is the real one. The room was full of the people whose opinion of him made up his standing. So a man who privately admired John, and had gone to some trouble to keep him alive, had him beheaded before the evening was over, because of what a roomful of officials would think if he did not. He valued his reputation above an innocent man’s life. Nothing in this story requires Herod to have wanted it, and that is what makes it so recognisable. He did not lose an argument with his conscience; he simply valued the opinion of the people in the room above the life of a man in the cellar, and the whole thing took about a minute. An oath to do evil should be broken, not kept: an oath cannot bind anyone to sin (Westminster 22.4), and no one may vow to do anything God’s word forbids (Westminster 22.7).

He commanded it to be given. The king who could not command himself commands a death.

He sent and had John beheaded in the prison. John, the greatest of those born of women (11:11), the forerunner of the Messiah, was killed at a drunken party to satisfy a vengeful woman and a weak man’s pride. He died alone in a dungeon, without a trial, without a farewell. And his death is a foreshadowing. Another innocent man will be killed by a ruler who knows he is innocent, wants to release him, and gives way to the crowd (27:24). The forerunner went before his Lord in his preaching, and he went before him in his death.

What it does not mean. Not that God had abandoned John. John had finished the work God gave him: to prepare the way of the Lord (3:3). From the world’s point of view his death was a squalid tragedy; from God’s, it was the end of a faithful race. Jesus had already honoured him as the greatest of the old order (11:11), and he is now with the Lord whose way he prepared.

Why did God let John die like that? This is the question every believer asks when the faithful suffer and the wicked feast. Scripture does not pretend it is easy. But it gives us three things to hold. First, God was not absent; John’s life was not taken from God’s hands but placed in them, and precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15). Second, John’s death was not wasted; it is part of the pattern by which the kingdom advances, through the suffering of its servants and supremely through the suffering of its King. Third, the story is not finished. Herod’s banquet was not the last word on John; the resurrection will be. The one who was silenced in a dungeon will stand in glory, and Herod will stand before the Judge. When you see the righteous suffer, do not conclude that God has lost control. Look at the cross, where the worst injustice in history was the very means of our salvation.

In a sentence. To save face, Herod had John beheaded, though he knew it was wrong.

On a Tuesday. Fear of losing face leads people to terrible choices, and most of them are small and quick. Where are your guests? Whose opinion is in the room when you decide? Be willing to admit a wrong promise or decision publicly rather than compound it, and decide now, before the moment comes, that the opinion of God outweighs the opinion of the table.

For worship. Herod was sorry and did it anyway; Christ was sorrowful even to death and did the Father’s will anyway, and his obedience saved us while Herod’s cowardice destroyed a prophet. The Lord who let his forerunner be silenced in a dungeon did not leave him there. He went down into death himself, and broke it open from the inside, and the head that rested on Herod’s platter will one day be lifted up in glory by the King whose way it prepared.
verseByVerse.note: Antipas was only a tetrarch, but was popularly called king.

verseByVerse.quote: and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, who brought it to her mother. John’s disciples came, took his body and buried it. Then they went and told Jesus.

And his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. Matthew narrates it without comment, because no comment is adequate. The horror is told plainly. Evil in power can be grotesque, and Scripture does not look away from it.

And his disciples came and took the body and buried it. Verse 12 is one of the quietest sentences in the Gospel, and it deserves to be read slowly. They came, and that took courage. These are the followers of a man executed for criticising the ruler, walking into a royal fortress to ask for the corpse, which is precisely what Joseph of Arimathea will do at another execution, and Mark says he took courage to do it (Mark 15:43). They took the body; the head had gone to Herodias. They buried what there was. Proper burial mattered deeply in Jewish life, and this was the last act of love available to them.

And they went and told Jesus. Having done the last thing that could be done for their master, they walked to the one man in the country who had told them who John was. They had been rivals, in a sense. These are the disciples who came to complain that Jesus’ followers did not fast (9:14), and who carried John’s anxious question from prison (11:2–3). There had been a certain awkwardness between the two groups all along, and John himself had settled it: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30). When their teacher was dead, they knew where to go. Some of John’s disciples had already followed Jesus (John 1:35–37); now the rest came to him.

Matthew records no reply. The next verse is: now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew. He said nothing that anybody wrote down. He went away to be alone, which, for the man who had called John the greatest born of women, who was his kinsman, and who had stood in the Jordan and been baptised by him, is a more eloquent record than any sentence. And then the crowds followed him round the lake, and he came ashore and had compassion on them and healed their sick, and then fed all of them. On the day he heard.

What it does not mean. Not that God was absent, or that evil had won. His purposes went on. The worst the world could do did not stop the kingdom; it drove John’s friends to Jesus.

What do I do with grief that has no explanation? Do what John’s disciples did. They did not first work out why God had allowed it, and they did not pretend it was not terrible. They did the practical things love required, and then they went and told Jesus. Prayer in grief does not need to be tidy. It can be nothing more than telling him what happened. And notice that the one they told was himself grieving. You do not bring your sorrow to a Saviour who is above it, but to one who was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3), and who knows what it is to lose a friend to cruelty.

In a sentence. John’s disciples buried his body and brought the news to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When you are grieving or shocked by evil, do what John’s disciples did: do the next loving thing, then tell Jesus. And when someone else is grieving, be one of the people who come and carry the body: turn up, help with the practical things, and say little.

For worship. The forerunner’s disciples came to the Lamb their master had pointed to (John 1:29), and they did not come in vain. He did not send them away with an explanation; he received them in his own grief. Blessed be the Saviour who is the place where every broken loyalty and every unexplained loss can finally be brought, and who will one day wipe away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard the news, he withdrew by boat to a remote place to be alone. But the crowds heard and followed him on foot from the towns. When Jesus landed and saw the great crowd, he had compassion on them and healed their sick.

Now when Jesus heard this. The death of John: his relative, his forerunner, the man who baptised him, the greatest born of women.

He withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. To grieve, to pray, and perhaps to step out of Herod’s reach for a while. Mark adds that the Twelve had just come back from their mission and needed rest (Mark 6:30–31). Luke places the scene near Bethsaida (Luke 9:10), on the north-east shore of the lake. Jesus was truly human. He needed solitude, and he grieved.

But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. They walked round the shore and arrived before him (Mark 6:33). They needed him too much to honour his solitude.

When he went ashore he saw a great crowd. His time alone was gone before it began. He came to be alone, and found thousands.

And he had compassion on them. Deep, gut-level compassion, the word splanchnizomai, the churning of the inward parts, the same word as 9:36. In his own grief, Jesus did not turn the crowds away in irritation. He saw their need, and his heart went out to them. The healer who was grieving still healed. His mercy is not contingent on his personal comfort.

And healed their sick. Compassion in action. He did not only feel for them; he did something.

Three things for the tired and grieving. Slow down over these two verses, because three things sit in them that a tired or grieving reader needs, and one guard that keeps them from being turned into a whip. The first: he grieved. Told that his cousin had been beheaded to amuse a dinner party, the Son of God went away by himself. That ought to settle a question that torments sincere Christians, whether sorrow is a failure of faith. It is not. It is what love does when it loses something, and here it is done by the only person who never sinned. If you have been made to feel that your grief is unspiritual, or that you should have got over it by now, this verse is your answer. The second: he withdrew deliberately, and more than once in this chapter. Solitude was not an indulgence he permitted himself when nothing else was pressing; it was a necessity he arranged. You are not more robust than he was. The third, and the hard one: he did not get it. Instead of the solitude he had gone looking for, he found several thousand people wanting things from him. And he did not send them away.

What it does not mean. This is exactly where the passage gets misused into a theology of burnout, as though the Christian ideal were a person who never rests and always serves. Read the whole chapter. He withdraws here; and after the feeding he makes the disciples get into the boat, dismisses the crowds himself, and goes up the mountain alone to pray (v. 23). He got his solitude. It came later that night, but it came, and he took it. The pattern is not the abolition of rest but its postponement, once, under a particular pressure, followed by actually taking it. Jesus often withdrew to pray (Mark 1:35; Luke 5:16). Rest is necessary. But when real need interrupted him, he responded with compassion, not resentment.

What does this mean for me when the demands never stop? For the parent of small children, the one nursing a dying relative, the pastor, the carer who cannot see the end of it, take all four things together. Grief needs room and is allowed. Withdrawal has to be planned, because it will never happen by accident. Interruptions will come, and compassion rather than resentment is only possible for someone who is not treating exhaustion as a permanent policy. And what is taken from you now must be taken back later, as he took it. Notice where the day’s resources came from: he fed a city from a boy’s lunch, and the one place he went for supply was up a mountain by himself with his Father. That is still where it comes from. Ask for help from your church too; the body of Christ exists so that no one carries everything alone (Galatians 6:2).

In a sentence. Grieving John’s death, Jesus sought solitude, but when the crowds found him, he had compassion and healed them.

On a Tuesday. How do you respond to interruptions, especially when you are tired or sad? Notice the moment today when someone needs you at the worst time, and ask God in that moment for Jesus’ compassion. Then look at your diary and make sure there is a mountain somewhere in the week.

For worship. Here is the heart of our Lord: grieving, interrupted, worn out, and moved with compassion. He did not love the crowd because it was convenient or grateful or deserving; he loved it because that is what he is. And he is the same today. The Lord who would not send away the crowd on the worst day of his life will not send you away on the worst day of yours. We have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and whose compassion has never once run dry.
verseByVerse.note: Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida, at the north end of the lake.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves." But Jesus said, "They need not go away; you give them something to eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the evening, the disciples came to Jesus: this is a remote place, and it is getting late. Send the crowds away so they can go to the villages and buy food. Jesus answered: they do not need to go away. You give them something to eat.

Now when it was evening. Late afternoon, as the light was fading, on the same day John’s disciples brought the news.

This is a desolate place. “Desolate” (erēmos) means wilderness, the same word used of the wilderness where John preached (3:1) and where Jesus was tempted (4:1), and in the Greek Old Testament of the wilderness where Israel wandered. The setting is chosen for us: Israel in the desert, hungry, and God feeding them with bread from heaven (Exodus 16). A reader steeped in the Old Testament knows what kind of story is about to happen.

And the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves. It deserves saying that this was a sensible plan, because the disciples are usually treated as faithless here. It is late, there is nothing here, send them off in time to reach the villages before dark. Nobody would be harmed by it. It is the responsible, administratively sound answer, and it has exactly one defect: it gets the crowd off their hands. The disciples saw the problem but not the solution, and they assumed the crowd was not their responsibility.

But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat”. The pronoun is emphatic: you yourselves, give them to eat. He is not making a suggestion; he is putting the crowd’s dinner on their account. That is a startling thing to do to twelve men whose entire supply is a boy’s lunch, and John tells us why he did it: he said this to test Philip, for he himself knew what he would do (John 6:5–6). The impossibility was deliberate. He asked them for something he knew they could not produce, to find out what they would say. And hold the first clause: they need not go away. The disciples’ solution was dispersal; his was provision. The difference between those two instincts has divided Christian ministry ever since, because sending people somewhere else to be dealt with is always available and always looks like good sense.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus expected them to solve the problem by their own resources. He wanted them to see their inadequacy and his sufficiency, and to learn that the place where human resources end is not the place where his work ends.

Does this mean the church must meet every need it sees? No church can do everything, and Jesus himself did not heal every sick person in Israel. But this verse forbids one particular reflex: treating needy people as someone else’s problem by default. Before you say send them away, ask what Jesus has already put in your hands, and whether he might be testing you with this need as he tested Philip. Sometimes the right answer really is to refer someone elsewhere. But it should be the answer of prayer and love, not of convenience. The church’s first instinct toward the hungry, the lonely and the lost should be to bring them closer to Jesus, not to move them along.

In a sentence. When the disciples wanted to send the hungry crowd away, Jesus told them to feed it themselves.

On a Tuesday. When you see an overwhelming need, at the school gate, in the family, at church, do you say send them away, or do you ask Jesus what he would have you bring? Name one need you have been quietly hoping someone else will deal with, and ask him today what your part is.

For worship. They need not go away: that is the voice of the Shepherd. The world says go and buy for yourselves. He says come, everyone who thirsts; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat (Isaiah 55:1). The Lord who would not dismiss a hungry crowd in a desolate place is the Lord who does not dismiss sinners at the end of their resources. No one who comes to him is told to go elsewhere for bread.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "We have only five loaves here and two fish." And he said, "Bring them here to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples said: we have only five loaves and two fish. Jesus said: bring them here to me.

We have only five loaves here and two fish. John’s account adds the detail that changes the arithmetic from small to almost comical. The loaves and fish were not the disciples’ rations. Andrew found them: there is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:9). Barley was the cheap grain, the poor man’s bread. And the word for the fish is a diminutive: little fish, the dried or salted sort eaten as a relish with bread rather than as a meal. So what is brought to Jesus is a child’s packed lunch, five small barley rolls and a couple of dried fish, against a crowd of perhaps fifteen thousand. Andrew’s own comment on it is the honest one: but what are they for so many?

And he said, “Bring them here to me”. Four words in the Greek, and they do not ask for more. He does not say find more, or see what else you can raise, or we shall have to take a collection. He asks for the ridiculous thing they have already assessed and dismissed. The miracle does not happen in the disciples’ hands; it happens in his. But their obedience in bringing what seems useless is the first step. Human insufficiency, surrendered to divine sufficiency, is the way the kingdom’s abundance comes.

The arithmetic. Most of us do the disciples’ sums instinctively: measure the need, measure the resource, conclude that the gap is unbridgeable, and start looking for a way to reduce the need. That calculation is almost always correct, and it is the reason a great deal never gets attempted. What the passage adds is one term the arithmetic leaves out. The five loaves were genuinely inadequate. They were also genuinely all that was required, because the multiplying did not happen in the boy’s basket or in Andrew’s hands. The instruction is not to pretend the loaves are enough. It is to hand them over anyway.

What it does not mean. Not that if we give God something he is obliged to multiply it into whatever result we want, or that giving is a technique for getting. The boy did not give his lunch as an investment. And not that small things matter less to God than large ones. He chose to work through the smallest gift available, and he still does.

But what can my little actually do? Probably much less than you would like, if you mean what it can do by itself. That is the point. The question Jesus asks is not how much you have but whether you will put it in his hands. A widow’s two small coins, a cup of cold water, an hour of listening, a short prayer, a Sunday school class of four children: Scripture is full of tiny things that God made great. You will often never see the multiplication; the boy only saw it because he was there. Give what you have, faithfully and without measuring, and leave the arithmetic to the Lord who owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10).

In a sentence. The disciples had almost nothing, and Jesus told them to bring it to him.

On a Tuesday. What small thing do you have, a skill, some time, a little money, a spare room, a phone call you could make, that you have dismissed as too small to matter? Bring it to Jesus today, in prayer, and then give it.

For worship. Bring them here to me: it is the word of the Creator, who once made everything out of nothing and is not troubled by little. He does not need our loaves, and he delights to use them. Blessed be the Lord who takes what is laughably inadequate, a boy’s lunch, a fisherman’s faith, a sinner’s broken heart, and makes it enough, because in his hands nothing given is ever wasted.
verseByVerse.note: John adds that the loaves were barley loaves, the bread of the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told the crowds to sit on the grass. He took the five loaves and two fish, looked up to heaven, gave thanks, broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, who gave them to the crowds. Everyone ate and was satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve baskets full of leftover pieces.

Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass. Mark adds that it was green grass, and that they sat in groups by hundreds and by fifties (Mark 6:39–40). Spring, near Passover (John 6:4). And the scene would have reminded any Israelite of a psalm: he makes me lie down in green pastures (Psalm 23:2). The Good Shepherd, who had seen them as sheep without a shepherd (9:36), is making his flock lie down and feeding them. The orderly companies even recall Israel encamped in the wilderness under Moses.

And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. As the head of a Jewish household did at every meal, Jesus thanked God for the food. The Jewish blessing over bread ran: blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. Prayer is the setting of the miracle. The Son of God looks up to his Father before he does what only God can do.

Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples. Count the verbs, because Matthew’s readers would have recognised them at once. He took, blessed, broke and gave. That is the sequence Matthew records again, in the same order and almost the same words, in an upper room on the last night: Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples (26:26). And Luke records them a third time, at a table in Emmaus, where two men who had walked seven miles with a stranger recognised him at the moment he did this, and their eyes were opened (Luke 24:30–31). Three meals: a hillside, an upper room, an inn. The same four movements each time, and on the third occasion they were enough to identify him without a word. The feeding looks forward to the Lord’s Supper and beyond it to the great banquet of the kingdom (8:11).

And the disciples gave them to the crowds. He could have distributed it himself. What actually happened is that twelve men who had just said the thing was impossible spent the next hour walking up and down a hillside handing out food that would not stop coming out of their own hands. Whatever they understood about him before that evening, they had a new fact by the end of it: the supply ran through them and did not come from them. That is the shape of all ministry since. Christ provides; his servants carry.

And they all ate and were satisfied. Not a taste, but a full meal. The verb (chortazō) is used of animals being fed to the full, eaten to the point of stopping. It is the word of the Beatitude: those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be satisfied (5:6).

And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Twelve baskets: perhaps one for each of the disciples who had doubted, or a sign of provision for the twelve tribes of Israel. The baskets (kophinoi) were the wicker baskets Jews carried for food on a journey. And the surplus at the end was far larger than the supply at the beginning. He did not merely stretch five loaves; he produced a meal for a city and had more left than he started with. God’s provision is not barely enough. It overflows.

The background. God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16). Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, and there was some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus feeds thousands with five. Moses prayed for bread; Jesus gives it himself. He is the greater Moses and the greater Elisha. And John, recording the same day, tells us what Jesus said the next morning: I am the bread of life (John 6:35). The manna kept a nation alive for forty years and then it stopped, and everyone who ate it died anyway (John 6:49). This bread does not run out, and neither do those who feed on it. What the crowd received in their hands that evening was a picture of what they were being offered in him.

What it does not mean. Not that the people simply shared lunches they had hidden, as some interpreters have suggested. They were in a desolate place, the disciples had only five loaves and two fish, twelve baskets were left over, and the crowd wanted to make Jesus king because of what they had seen (John 6:14–15). That is a response to a sign, not to a picnic. The Gospel writers describe a miracle of creation. All four Gospels record it, the only miracle besides the resurrection that all four tell.

Does this mean God will always give me what I need materially? God has promised to care for his children, and Jesus tells us not to be anxious about food and clothing, because our Father knows we need them (6:25–33). He does provide, usually through ordinary means: work, family, the generosity of the church. But this miracle is not a guarantee that believers will never go hungry; Paul knew hunger and plenty (Philippians 4:12), and Christians in famine and persecution have died poor. What it guarantees is something larger: that the Lord who feeds is present with his people, that he is never short of resources, and that he will give us everything we truly need, above all himself, the bread that lasts to eternal life (John 6:27). Pray for daily bread, work for it, share it, and trust him with the rest.

How does this meal relate to the Lord’s Supper? The feeding is not the Supper, but it points to it. At the Lord’s Table the same Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives, and believers receive him, not in the bread as though it were changed, but truly and spiritually by faith, feeding on his body broken and his blood shed for us (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23–26). The hillside teaches us how to come to the Table: hungry, empty-handed, sitting down where we are told, and receiving from his hands. And it teaches us what the Table promises: a day when the whole people of God will sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom (8:11), all fed, all satisfied, with baskets to spare.

In a sentence. Jesus, the Shepherd of Psalm 23 and greater than Moses, fed the crowd abundantly from five loaves and two fish, through his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your food today, as Jesus did, and mean it. Remember that he provides through ordinary people, including you; ask whose hands you could put bread into this week. And when you next come to the Lord’s Table, come as that crowd sat on the grass: needy, expectant, and ready to be satisfied.

For worship. Here is the Lord of Psalm 23, spreading a table in the wilderness. Here is the bread of heaven, broken so that the hungry may live. The same hands that took and blessed and broke the loaves on the hillside would be taken and broken on the cross, and from them flows a supply that a world of sinners has never exhausted. They all ate and were satisfied. One day every child of God will say the same, at the marriage supper of the Lamb, and there will be twelve baskets left over.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with some left over
he took bread, blessed and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About five thousand men ate, not counting women and children.

And those who ate were about five thousand men. “Men” (andres) means adult males. Mark, Luke and John all give five thousand men. Men were the unit normally counted for an assembly in that culture.

Besides women and children. Matthew alone adds these four words, and they can be misread. Read carelessly, it sounds dismissive, as though the women and children did not count. It is the opposite. The other three leave a reader with the impression that five thousand people were fed. Matthew is the one who tells us the real number was considerably higher, and that the reported figure had left people out. He is correcting an undercount, not making one. The women and children ate too, and the Lord who fed them wanted it recorded.

The scale. The total may have been fifteen or twenty thousand people. A crowd like that in first-century Galilee is not a large meeting; it is a city. Capernaum may have held around fifteen hundred people. Tiberias, Herod’s new capital, perhaps eight or ten thousand. So the number of people sitting on that hillside was greater than the population of any town on the lake, gathered with no notice, on foot, in a place with no food, because they had heard where he had gone. And every one of them ate. The precise count is Matthew’s way of insisting on the factual reality of the miracle: this happened, to this many people, and the evidence was counted.

In a sentence. Five thousand men, and many more women and children, were fed.

On a Tuesday. God’s provision is never small, and no one in the crowd is too insignificant to be counted by him. Trust him with the needs that seem too big. And if you feel overlooked in your church or your family, remember that Matthew made sure the uncounted were written into the story.

For worship. The Lord who fed a city in the wilderness counts the ones others leave out. He knows the number of the stars and calls them all by name (Psalm 147:4), and he knows the women and children on the grass. Not one of his flock is a statistic to him, and not one will be missing when the great multitude that no one can number stands before the throne (Revelation 7:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — Walking on Water and Healings at Gennesaret
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up the mountain alone to pray. In the early morning hours the disciples are struggling against the wind; Jesus walks to them on the sea. Peter walks on the water toward Jesus, sinks when he doubts, is rescued, and worship breaks out in the boat. They land at Gennesaret, and Jesus heals all who touch the fringe of his garment. Four things more. "he made the disciples get into the boat" is anankazo, to compel — the word for forcing someone to do what they do not want. They did not want to go, and John supplies the reason: the crowd was about to seize him and make him king (Jn. 6:15). Thousands of people on a Galilean hillside who have just watched dinner appear out of nothing is a political event, and the country had seen risings before. He got the twelve off the beach before it could form. The boat is "beaten" by the waves — basanizomenon, a word for torture, used of the demons begging not to be tormented (8:29). And "the fourth watch" is Roman reckoning, three to six in the morning: they had been rowing since evening, roughly nine hours, and had covered three or four miles of a lake they could normally cross in two (Jn. 6:19). Note that they were exactly where he had sent them — this was not a wrong turning, and Mark says he saw them from the mountain (6:48). Mark preserves one clause Matthew omits and it is the strangest in the account: "he meant to pass by them" (6:48). Read flatly that is baffling; but passing by is technical Old Testament language for a theophany — what God does for Moses in the cleft of the rock (Exod. 33:19-22) and for Elijah at Horeb (1 Kgs. 19:11). The intention was to be seen. He does not ask for ability; he asks to be commanded, having just watched a word do this to five loaves. The record stands that one man got out of a boat in a gale in the dark and walked on a lake, and Matthew reports it in a single sentence. Finally, "the fringe of his garment" is the kraspedon, the tzitzit commanded in Numbers 15:38-39 — and the Hebrew for the corner of a garment, kanaph, also means wing. Malachi's last page promises that "the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings" (Mal. 4:2). They were reaching for the corners of the robe of the one Malachi described, and finding that it was there.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus walking on the water is another creation-sovereignty miracle: the same one who stilled the storm (8:26) now walks on it. In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8; Ps. 77:19). Jesus is doing what God does. Peter's walking on the water is the only time anyone but his Master is recorded doing this, and it happens not by Peter's power but by Jesus's command: "Come." The sinking and rescue express the pattern of every disciple's faith: bold initial response, fear when looking at the circumstances, cry for help, rescue by the one who is always within reach.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' worship in the boat — "Truly you are the Son of God" — is the first time in Matthew that the disciples make this full confession. The storm-stilling produced "What sort of man is this?" (8:27); the water-walking produces "Truly you are the Son of God." The miracles are cumulative revelation. Each display of his authority over creation moves the disciples closer to the full confession that Peter will make at Caesarea Philippi (16:16). Faith grows through the accumulation of evidence seen with open eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately Jesus made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. Then he went up the mountain alone to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.

Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat. The verb is not merely strong; it is the word for force. “Made” (ēnankasen, from anankazō) means compelled, constrained. It is the word Paul uses of trying to force people to blaspheme (Acts 26:11) and of Peter compelling Gentiles to live like Jews (Galatians 2:14). So the disciples did not want to go, and he overrode them. John supplies the reason: perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself (John 6:15). A crowd of fifteen thousand on a Galilean hillside, having just watched a man produce dinner out of nothing, is a political event. That is the raw material of a rising, and the country had seen several. What was being averted was not embarrassment but a messianic revolt with Jesus at its head and twelve very willing lieutenants. He got the disciples off the beach before the crowd could reach them.

While he dismissed the crowds. He refused the crown they offered. Satan had offered him all the kingdoms of the world without a cross (4:8–10); now the crowd offers him Galilee without one. His kingdom would come by way of the cross, not by an uprising, and the crown he would wear in Jerusalem was made of thorns.

He went up on the mountain by himself to pray. Consider what that day had held. It opened with the news that John had been beheaded. He tried to get away by boat and was followed round the lake by thousands. He healed their sick. He fed all of them. He broke up a movement that wanted to crown him. He sent his friends away over the water. And then, at last, he got what he had set out for that morning, and used it to pray. Jesus prayed at moments of crisis and decision (26:36–46; Luke 6:12). The feeding of a city did not replace his need for communion with his Father; it increased it.

When evening came, he was there alone. Solitude with God. The Gospels record him going off alone to pray only a handful of times, and this is one of them: after the largest public success of his ministry, on the day he heard his kinsman had been murdered.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus did not care about the crowds. He had fed and healed them. But he would not let them define his mission. Compassion gave them bread; wisdom refused them the thing they wanted most, because it was not the thing they needed.

Why would Jesus refuse to be made king? Was he not the King? He was, and is. But the crowd wanted a king on their terms: one who would fill their stomachs and drive out the Romans, a Messiah without a cross and a kingdom without repentance. To accept their crown would have been to become a different kind of Messiah from the one the Father sent, and to leave their real enemy, sin and death, untouched. He would be enthroned, but through suffering, and his throne would be at the right hand of God (26:64). The same temptation comes to us whenever we want Jesus for what he can give us in this life rather than for who he is. He will not be that kind of king, because he loves us too much to be so small.

In a sentence. Jesus sent his disciples away, refused the crowd’s political hopes, and went up the mountain alone to pray.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus needed to be alone with the Father after the busiest and best day of his ministry, so do you, especially after success, when the temptation is to ride the moment. Find time today, even a few minutes, alone with God. And notice which crowns you are being offered that would take you away from the path he has given you.

For worship. The King of kings would not be crowned by a hungry crowd, because he had come to be crowned with thorns for them. He would not seize a throne; he would lay down his life and take it up again. And while his friends were struggling on the sea below, he was on the mountain praying, as he still is: he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). Our safety in the night does not rest on our rowing but on his prayers.
verseByVerse.note: John says the crowd wanted to make him king by force.

verseByVerse.quote: but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By then the boat was far from land, battered by the waves, because the wind was against them. In the early hours of the morning, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea.

But the boat by this time was a long way from the land. John says they had rowed three or four miles (John 6:19), about halfway across the lake.

Beaten by the waves. “Beaten” (basanizomenon) is a word for torture. It is used of the demons pleading not to be tormented (8:29), of the paralysed servant suffering terribly (8:6), and of torment in judgment. Matthew has taken a word for what is done to a person under interrogation and applied it to a boat.

For the wind was against them. They were struggling against a strong headwind for hours. Unlike the storm in 8:24, Jesus is not in the boat. And here is the detail that will not be improved on: they were where he had sent them. This is not a storm they sailed into by poor judgment. He put them in that boat, over their objection, and pointed them at the far shore. The wind was against them in the middle of an errand they had been compelled to undertake.

And in the fourth watch of the night. Jews divided the night into three watches, Romans into four. Matthew uses the Roman reckoning, so this is between three and six in the morning, the darkest hours, the hours of deepest sleep and lowest human resilience. They had got into the boat at evening. That is somewhere around nine hours of rowing into a headwind, in the dark, on a lake they knew, going nowhere. Mark says they were making headway painfully (Mark 6:48).

He came to them, walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea. He alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea (Job 9:8); his way was through the sea, his path through the great waters, yet his footprints were unseen (Psalm 77:19). In Scripture the sea pictures chaos and danger, the deep that only God can master. Jesus walks on the waves as their Lord, doing what Job said only God does.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was unaware of their struggle during those hours. Mark says he saw them straining at the oars (Mark 6:48), which in the dark, from a mountain, three or four miles offshore, is its own kind of statement. His timing was deliberate. Nor does it mean he walked along the shore or on a sandbar, as some have suggested. The boat was a long way from the land, Peter also walked and sank, and the disciples worshipped. Nothing in the account can be explained away.

If I am struggling, does that mean I have taken a wrong turn? Not necessarily, and this passage is the proof. It is a common and comfortable idea that difficulty means you are out of God’s will. On this occasion the headwind was blowing against men who were exactly where they had been told to be, and it blew for nine hours, and the one who sent them was on a hill watching. Hardship can be a sign that you need to repent of something, and it is right to ask. But it can equally be the ordinary weather of obedience. Keep rowing in the direction he gave you, keep praying, and do not read his apparent absence as his indifference. He sees you at the oars.

Why does Jesus so often seem to come so late? The fourth watch tells us he waited until they were at the end of their strength. He was not cruel and he was not careless. He was teaching them what they could not learn on a calm night: that their safety rested on him and not on their rowing. He came when coming would show them who he was. Most believers can look back on a long night when help came at the last possible moment, and see afterwards that it was the right moment. His delays are never desertions, and he is never late by his own clock.

In a sentence. After the disciples had struggled all night against the wind, Jesus came to them walking on the sea, as only God can.

On a Tuesday. If you have been straining at the oars for a long time, in a marriage, a job, an illness, a ministry that seems to go nowhere, Jesus sees you. Keep at the task he gave you. He will come at the right time, and he may come walking on the very thing that is beating you.

For worship. The waves that tortured the boat were a floor under his feet. The God who trampled the sea at creation, who made a path through the Red Sea for his people, came to his friends across the water in the dark. Nothing that frightens us is beyond his reach or above his feet. He watched them from the mountain, he came to them in the fourth watch, and he is still the Lord over every deep in which his people labour.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch of the night ran from about 3 to 6 a.m.

parallels.desc: who alone trampled the waves of the sea
your way was through the sea

verseByVerse.quote: But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, "It is a ghost!" and they cried out in fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified and cried out in fear: it is a ghost! But Jesus spoke to them at once: take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.

They were terrified, and said, It is a ghost! Mark records one clause here that Matthew leaves out, and it is among the strangest sentences in the Gospels: he meant to pass by them (Mark 6:48). Read as ordinary narrative that is baffling, a man walking past a boat in distress. But passing by is technical language in the Old Testament, and it belongs to one kind of scene. Moses asks to see God’s glory and is told that God will make all his goodness pass before him, and put him in a cleft of the rock while his glory passes by (Exodus 33:19–22). Elijah at Horeb is told to stand on the mountain, and the LORD passed by (1 Kings 19:11). It is not indifference; it is the vocabulary of a theophany, God making himself visible by going past. So the intention was to be seen. He came out on the water so that they would look up and see who was walking on it. Which they did, and concluded it was a ghost.

And they cried out in fear. The word is phantasma, and their reaction is not scepticism but terror. Sailors feared spirits of the sea, and in the dark before dawn they saw a figure walking on the water. Experienced fishermen screamed. And it is worth noticing that men who had spent the night fighting a hopeless sea were more frightened by the sight of him than by the wind. The supernatural was correctly perceived and wrongly named.

But immediately Jesus spoke to them. He did not leave them in their fear for a moment. He does not begin by stopping the wind; the wind blows for the whole of the next four verses. What arrives first is a voice across black water saying who it is.

Take heart. Be of good courage, the same word he spoke to the paralysed man and to the woman who touched his garment (9:2, 22).

It is I. In Greek, egō eimi, literally I am. It can simply mean it’s me, and it does. But it is also the name of God revealed to Moses at the burning bush: I AM WHO I AM (Exodus 3:14). And it is God’s own word in Isaiah: I am he; I, I am he who comforts you (Isaiah 43:10–13, 25; 51:12). In John’s Gospel the same two words will get him nearly stoned (John 8:58–59) and will throw an arresting party to the ground (John 18:5–6). In English it reads as an identification. In Greek it is that, and it is also the Name. Walking on the sea and saying I am, Jesus reveals himself as the LORD.

Do not be afraid. The word God so often speaks when he reveals himself to someone undone by the encounter: to Abraham (Genesis 15:1), to Joshua (Joshua 1:9), to Israel (Isaiah 41:10). First the voice, then the hand. Take heart, it is I, do not be afraid: three short sentences, and the middle one holds the other two up.

Was Jesus really claiming to be God? Taken alone, it is I could be an ordinary greeting. But nothing here is alone. He is doing what the Old Testament says only God does, walking on the sea; he is passing by, the language of God’s self-revelation to Moses and Elijah; he speaks the words of the divine name; and the scene ends with the disciples worshipping him, which he accepts, though every faithful Jew knew that worship belongs to God alone (4:10). Matthew is not leaving us to guess. The man in the boat with them is the LORD who made the sea.

In a sentence. When the disciples thought Jesus was a ghost, he comforted them with words that reveal who he is: take heart; I am; do not be afraid.

On a Tuesday. In your darkest fear, listen for Jesus’ voice in his word: take heart; it is I; do not be afraid. Notice too how often the thing that frightens us most is Jesus himself coming to us in a form we did not expect, in a loss, a delay, a disruption. Ask whether what you are afraid of might be the way he is coming.

For worship. I AM walked on the sea that night, and the name that blazed in the bush spoke gently to twelve frightened men. The holy God who told Moses no one could see his face and live came near enough to be seen in the dark, and the first thing he said was take heart. That is the glory of our Lord: infinite majesty, coming toward us across the waves with comfort in his mouth.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

parallels.desc: when you pass through the waters

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter answered him, "Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water." He said, "Come." So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter answered: Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water. Jesus said, come. So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water toward Jesus.

And Peter answered him. Only Matthew tells this part of the story. Peter, impulsive and bold, as always.

Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water. The condition is not a doubt, and the Greek settles it. The construction is the one that assumes the thing is true: closer to since it is you, or if it is you, as it is. He is not testing whether the figure is a ghost; he has heard the voice and believed it. And what he asks for is a command. That is the theologically careful part of an otherwise reckless request. He does not ask for the ability, or announce that he will try. He asks Jesus to order him, because he has grasped that a word from this man is what makes a thing possible, which is exactly what he has just watched happen to five loaves. He wants to be where Jesus is, doing what Jesus does.

He said, “Come”. One word, with all authority. The command created the ability to obey it, as Christ’s commands always do.

So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. This sentence ought to stop every reader. He walked on water. Not far, and not for long, and it ends badly enough that the failure is what everybody remembers. But the record stands: one man in the history of the world got out of a boat in a gale in the dark and walked on a lake, and Matthew reports it in a single sentence without commentary. Peter is usually treated as the cautionary tale of this passage. It is worth noticing that the other eleven are still in the boat, and that nothing whatever is said about them.

Came to Jesus. The direction matters. He does not walk about on the water, or walk to the shore, or demonstrate anything. He goes toward the person who called him, which is the only thing the water was ever going to be crossed for. For a brief moment Peter is doing what Jesus does, where Jesus does it, by Jesus’ word alone. That is the shape of all discipleship.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should demand miracles or take reckless risks to prove their faith. Peter acted on Jesus’ explicit command. Faith obeys Christ’s word; it does not invent its own tests (4:5–7). Wanting an adventure is not the same thing as being sent, and the desire to do something dramatic for God is not itself a call.

How do I know whether Christ is calling me to step out? Today Christ’s commands come to us in Scripture, not in voices across the water, and the canon is closed. So begin there: is the step clearly required or clearly permitted by his word? Much of the time the boat we need to leave is not mysterious at all: the apology we have not made, the witness we have not given, the generosity we keep postponing. Those need no special guidance; he has already said Come. For larger choices that Scripture does not settle, such as a move, a job or a ministry, pray, weigh your gifts and circumstances honestly, seek the counsel of mature believers and your church, and then act in faith. You will not be given a voice, but you will not be left without wisdom (James 1:5).

In a sentence. At Jesus’ command, Peter stepped out of the boat and walked on the water toward him.

On a Tuesday. Is there a step of obedience that Christ has clearly called you to in his word, and you have stayed in the boat? Name it, and take it today. The water will only hold you while you are walking toward him.

For worship. Come: one word from the Lord of the sea, and the sea became a road. He still speaks that word, to the weary, to sinners, to the frightened: come to me (11:28). The one who called Peter across the waves is the one who calls us across everything that stands between us and him, and his call carries its own power to obey it. Blessed be the Lord whose commands are enablings, and whose invitation is the ground under our feet.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records Peter walking on the water.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, "Lord, save me." Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Peter saw the wind, he was afraid. He began to sink and cried out: Lord, save me! Jesus immediately reached out his hand, caught him, and said: you of little faith, why did you doubt?

But when he saw the wind, he was afraid. Notice what actually went wrong, because it was not the getting out. Jesus had said Come. And it was not the wind either: the wind was already blowing when he climbed over the side, and nothing changed in the weather. What changed was where he was looking. He sank at the moment the storm became more real to him than the word that had sent him into it. Faith looks at Christ; fear looks at circumstances.

And beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me”. The shortest prayer in the Bible, and one of the best. Three words in English, from a man with his mouth full of water and no time to make it respectable. No eloquence, no formula, just desperate trust. Peter knew where to turn even as he sank. It was enough. Do not wait until you can compose something better; you will drown politely. Cry out now, in the shape the panic actually takes.

Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him. Immediately: no delay, no lecture first. The rescue comes before the rebuke. The Psalms had sung of this hand: he sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters (Psalm 18:16; 144:7). The hand of God in the psalm is the hand of Jesus on the lake.

O you of little faith, why did you doubt? “Little faith” (see 6:30; 8:26). “Doubt” (distazō) means to waver, to be in two minds, pulled two ways. Peter had real faith, enough to step out of the boat, but it wavered. The order matters. Only after his grip was on him, above the water, with the sinking over, did Jesus say this. The rebuke is real, but that is the tone to hear it in. It is not contempt from the shore; it is the question of a man holding you up. And it is a real question: why? There was no reason to doubt. Nothing had changed except where Peter was looking.

Who sinks. Notice that Peter is the only man other than his Master ever to have walked on water, and he is the only man in that boat who failed at it. The other eleven had a dry night and no story. This particular humiliation is only available to people who attempted something, and there is a kind of safety that is really just refusal.

What it does not mean. Not that Peter’s faith was worthless. He walked on water, which no one else did. But it was mixed with doubt. Nor does sinking mean that Jesus abandoned him. Even when our faith fails, Christ holds us: if we are faithless, he remains faithful (2 Timothy 2:13). Our safety rests on his grip, not ours.

Was it presumption if I stepped out in obedience and it went wrong? Perhaps, but do not assume it. This is the passage for anyone who stepped out at Christ’s word and went under: the ministry that did not flourish, the costly obedience that has so far produced nothing but water round the ankles. Sinking is not evidence that the step was wrong. Before you conclude that, check where your eyes have been. Peter’s step was right; his gaze drifted. The remedy was not to climb back into the boat in shame but to cry to Jesus, and to be held. If you are sinking now, the prayer is the same and the hand is the same.

Does little faith mean I am not saved? No. Jesus calls Peter a man of little faith, not a man of no faith, and he catches him. Saving faith is not measured by its strength but by its object. A weak hand that grips a strong Saviour is safe, because the Saviour grips back. Many true believers waver, and Scripture is full of them; the man who cried I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24) was heard. Bring your little faith to him and ask him to increase it. He does not break a bruised reed (12:20).

In a sentence. When Peter looked at the wind instead of Jesus, he began to sink, cried for help, and Jesus caught him at once.

On a Tuesday. What wind are you staring at today: the bank balance, the diagnosis, the hostile colleague, the news? It may be real, but it is not new, and it is not the most real thing in the picture. Turn your eyes back to Jesus, by opening his word and believing what he says there. And if you are sinking, pray Peter’s prayer: Lord, save me.

For worship. Lord, save me, and immediately the hand. Every one of us is saved by that same hand, reaching down into waters we could never climb out of, and it is a hand that would soon be pierced. He did not wait for Peter to deserve rescue or to pray properly; he caught him while he was going under. So he caught us, while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8). And no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28): the grip that held Peter above the lake holds every one of his own for ever.

parallels.desc: save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck
he drew me out of many waters

verseByVerse.quote: And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, "Truly, you are the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they climbed into the boat, the wind stopped. The disciples in the boat worshipped Jesus, saying: truly you are the Son of God.

And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. Note what stops the wind. In chapter 8, on this same lake, he was woken in a swamped boat and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm (8:26). He spoke to it. Here he says nothing. When they got into the boat, the wind ceased. No command is recorded. He steps over the side and it stops. Nine hours of headwind end without a word being spoken to it. His presence is enough. John adds that immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going (John 6:21).

And those in the boat worshiped him. “Worshipped” (prosekynēsan) means bowed down before him, the word for prostration, the worship the magi gave him (2:11) and the worship Jesus told Satan belongs to God alone (4:10). He does not refuse it.

Saying, “Truly you are the Son of God”. Compare what the same men said after the earlier storm: what sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him? (8:27). A question. Now: truly you are the Son of God. A statement, with truly in front of it, offered as worship. Two storms, two responses, and between them the disciples have moved from asking what sort of being he is to telling him what he is, on their faces, in a wet boat, at dawn. They have seen him feed thousands, walk on water, say I am, catch Peter, and still the wind. This confession anticipates Peter’s at Caesarea Philippi (16:16) and the centurion’s at the cross (27:54).

The first to say it. Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi is usually called the turning point, and rightly, in the sense that Jesus receives it there formally and builds on it. But it is not the first time the words are said. They are said here, two chapters earlier, by the whole crew, and the ground of them is not an insight into his identity but a night of being terrified and then rescued. The theology at Caesarea Philippi came out of a conversation. This came out of the water. Twelve men who had spent the night convinced they were going to drown, and who had watched one of their number sink and be caught, were the first in this Gospel to get the sentence right.

What it does not mean. Not that their understanding was complete. They still did not understand that the Son of God must suffer (16:21–23), and Mark says their hearts were still hardened about the loaves (Mark 6:52). But they had seen enough to worship, and worship is where understanding grows.

What does Son of God mean here? In the Old Testament, Israel and its kings could be called God’s son, meaning chosen and beloved. But the disciples are not using it loosely. They say it while bowing down to a man who walks on the sea and speaks the divine name. Matthew means far more: Jesus is the eternal Son, sharing the nature of the Father, the one the Father himself called my beloved Son at his baptism (3:17). Only the Son knows the Father, and only he can reveal him (11:27). To call Jesus the Son of God is to confess that when you look at him, you are looking at God come to us.

In a sentence. When Jesus stilled the wind by his presence, the disciples worshipped him and confessed him as the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. Your storms are where your confession of Christ is meant to grow. Look back at the last hard season you came through and ask what you learned about who he is. Then say it to him, in your own words, as worship.

For worship. Truly you are the Son of God. The wind stops when he steps into the boat, and the worship begins. He is the eternal Son who made the sea, and the Son who came into our boat, took our flesh, and went down into the deepest waters of all on the cross, so that the storm of God’s wrath might cease for us. One day his whole church will be brought safe to the land where they were going, and the confession first made in a wet boat at dawn will be sung for ever: worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:12).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret. The people recognised Jesus and sent word throughout the region, and brought all their sick to him.

They came to land at Gennesaret. The plain of Gennesaret is a crescent of land on the north-west shore of the lake, about three miles long and a mile deep, between Capernaum and Magdala. It was famous. Josephus describes it at length and calls its fertility extraordinary: walnuts, palms, figs and olives growing side by side, which normally need different climates, and grapes and figs available for ten months of the year. The lake itself was sometimes called the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1). So this is not open country. It is the most productive and most densely settled ground on the lake, and the boat has come ashore in the middle of it.

And when the men of that place recognized him. The verb suggests identification, working out who this is. His fame had gone before him.

They sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick. Messengers went out. Whole villages were told. And what came back was all who were sick, carried on mats along the paths of a fertile plain, from every direction, to a beach. They did not keep him to themselves. And the contrast is worth sharpening with a name. Nazareth asked where then did this man get all these things, and took offence, and Matthew’s verdict was that he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief (13:57–58). Gennesaret asked nothing. It sent runners. The difference between the two places is not information; Nazareth had more of it, thirty years of it. The difference is what each did in the first hour after finding out he was there.

In a sentence. At Gennesaret, people recognised Jesus and sent through all the region to bring their sick to him.
