On a Tuesday. When you know where Jesus can be found, tell others and bring them to him. Who in your street, your office or your family is sick in body or soul and has never been brought? You cannot heal them, but you can pray for them by name, and you can invite them to hear him.

For worship. The same Jesus, two receptions: Nazareth offended, Gennesaret running. And he is the same Lord in both, full of power and willing to heal. Blessed be the Saviour whose fame is good news, who did not grow tired of the sick being carried to him from every direction, and who still receives all who are brought.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They begged him to let the sick just touch the fringe of his cloak, and all who touched it were healed.

And implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. The woman with the bleeding had done exactly this (9:20–22), and news of her healing had evidently spread. Now whole crowds reach for what she reached for. And the word for what they reach for opens something remarkable. Kraspedon is the tassel, the fringe God commanded every Israelite to wear on the four corners of his outer garment, with a blue cord in it, a tassel to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD (Numbers 15:38–40; Deuteronomy 22:12). So Jesus wore them. He kept that law like any faithful Jew. The sick of Gennesaret were reaching for a tassel on the corner of his cloak.

Healing in its wings. The Hebrew word for the corner of a garment is kanaph, and kanaph also means wing. It is the ordinary word for a bird’s wing, and it is used of the corners of a robe throughout the Old Testament. Ruth asks Boaz to spread his wings, his garment’s corner, over her (Ruth 3:9); God says he spread his over Israel (Ezekiel 16:8). And the last page of the Old Testament contains this promise: for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:2). Healing in his kanaph: in his wings, or in the corners of his garment. Whether or not the crowds at Gennesaret had worked that out, that is what they were doing: reaching for the corners of the robe of the one Malachi said would rise with healing in them, and finding that it was there.

And as many as touched it were made well. “Made well” (diesōthēsan) means brought safely through, thoroughly healed; it is built on the word for being saved. Not one was turned away. Not most; not those who touched it in the right frame of mind, or who had understood the prophecy, or who could say afterwards exactly what they had believed. As many as touched it: every single one, including whoever was last in the queue and whoever got there by being carried. The faith that reaches for the edge of his garment is faith in its least impressive form, not a full confession, just an outstretched hand. And the kingdom’s mercy is not fussy about its channel.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ clothes had magical power, or that relics or objects carry healing power. The power was Jesus’ own, received through faith (9:22). The tassel was only the place where the hand met him.

Should I expect healings like these today? God still heals, and we should pray for the sick with real expectation, as James tells us to (James 5:14–15); many believers have seen remarkable recoveries in answer to prayer. But these mass healings belonged to the arrival of the King. Jesus’ miracles, and the signs given through the apostles, marked out the Messiah and confirmed the new revelation (Hebrews 2:3–4). We believe, as many Reformed Christians do, that the gift of working miracles at will passed with the apostles, and we hold that view charitably towards brothers and sisters who see it differently. So pray for healing, boldly. Use doctors gratefully; they too are God’s gift. And when healing does not come, remember that every believer will be made completely well at the resurrection, when every touch of Gennesaret becomes permanent.

In a sentence. Everyone who touched even the fringe of Jesus’ garment in faith was completely healed.

On a Tuesday. You cannot touch Jesus’ cloak, but you can come to him in faith through prayer, and your faith does not need to be eloquent to reach him. Bring the sick you love to him by name today. No one who comes to him is turned away.

For worship. The Sun of righteousness had risen, and there was healing in his wings. As many as touched him were made whole. That is the gospel in one line: not most, not the worthy, not the theologically precise, but as many as come. The hem that the sick of Gennesaret reached for belonged to the one whose garments would be divided by soldiers at the cross, where he bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, and by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:4–5).
verseByVerse.note: The fringe was the tassel the law required on the corners of a garment.

parallels.desc: the woman who touched the fringe

14.theology: Christ as the true bread from heaven. John 6 makes explicit what Matthew implies: the feeding of the five thousand points to Christ as the bread of life. He is the antitype of the manna — not merely a physical provision for the body but the living bread who gives eternal life to all who feed on him by faith. The Lord’s Supper is the sacramental extension of this meal: in it, we receive not merely bread and wine but Christ himself, the bread of heaven, by faith. The wilderness feeding thus stands at the intersection of Exodus typology, Eucharistic anticipation, and kingdom eschatology: we are fed by Christ in the wilderness of this age until the great feast of the new creation.
14.examples:
Then: Five loaves and two fish were laughably inadequate for five thousand people. The disciples knew it. Jesus knew it. He asked for them anyway. What he asks for is never the measure of what he can do with it.

Now: Every pastor, teacher, parent, and missionary knows the feeling of inadequate resources — not enough time, energy, money, or skill. Matthew 14 is not a promise that resources will always multiply visibly, but it is a call to bring what we have to Jesus and trust him with the rest. The twelve baskets of leftovers are the testimony: what is given to Christ is never wasted, and rarely runs out.

15.title: What Defiles a Person
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, <sup>2</sup>“Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat.” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? <sup>4</sup>For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>5</sup>But you say, ‘If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God,” <sup>6</sup>he need not honor his father.’ So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. <sup>7</sup>You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: <sup>8</sup>“‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>9</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’” <sup>10</sup>And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand: <sup>11</sup>it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person.” <sup>12</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” <sup>13</sup>He answered, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. <sup>14</sup>Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” <sup>15</sup>But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us.” <sup>16</sup>And he said, “Are you also still without understanding? <sup>17</sup>Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? <sup>18</sup>But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person. <sup>19</sup>For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. <sup>20</sup>These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. <sup>22</sup>And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon.” <sup>23</sup>But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us.” <sup>24</sup>He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” <sup>25</sup>But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.” <sup>26</sup>And he answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>27</sup>She said, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” <sup>28</sup>Then Jesus answered her, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed instantly. <sup>29</sup>Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. <sup>30</sup>And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them, <sup>31</sup>so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. <sup>32</sup>Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.” <sup>33</sup>And the disciples said to him, “Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.” <sup>35</sup>And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, <sup>36</sup>he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>37</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>38</sup>Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>39</sup>And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 confronts the deepest corruption in religion: the substitution of human tradition for the word of God. The Pharisees have constructed an elaborate system of ritual purity — washings, dietary rules, oral traditions — that they treat as divinely binding. Jesus cuts through it all with a single theological move: defilement is not external but internal. The heart is the problem. No ceremony can cleanse it; only the blood of the covenant can reach it.

Then, in a jarring turn, Jesus goes to Gentile territory and encounters a Canaanite woman whose persistence in faith stands in shaming contrast to the Pharisees' hypocrisy. She is the wrong ethnicity, the wrong gender, the wrong religion — and Jesus commends her as having “great faith.” She is the second Gentile in Matthew to receive this commendation (after the centurion in chapter 8). The kingdom breaks every ethnic and ritual boundary. The chapter closes with a second feeding miracle — four thousand this time, in Gentile territory — extending the bread of the messianic banquet to the nations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — What Defiles a Person: Tradition and the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharisees from Jerusalem confront Jesus about his disciples eating without washing hands. Jesus counters by exposing how their tradition nullifies the command to honor parents, then teaches the crowd that defilement comes from within, not without. He explains privately to the disciples: it is what comes out of the heart that defiles a person — evil thoughts, murder, adultery, all the rest. What the summary cannot hold. The handwashing was not about dirt. It is netilat yadayim, a ritual pouring in prescribed quantity and order to remove ceremonial uncleanness — a man with filthy hands who performed it was clean, and a man who had scrubbed and not performed it was not. And the Torah requires it of priests, before the altar, on pain of death (Exod. 30:19-21); the tradition had extended priestly purity to everybody at every meal. The impulse is not contemptible — if Israel is a kingdom of priests, why not treat the table like the altar? — but it had become the thing a delegation walked ninety miles from Jerusalem to complain about. Watch the structure of the reply: they ask why his disciples break the tradition; he asks why they break the commandment for the sake of their tradition. Same verb, nouns exchanged, and it puts them on trial in one sentence. Note also that he says "your tradition" twice, where they had said "the tradition of the elders" — a phrase that gives it distance and belongs to nobody. And the two texts he cites are the fifth commandment and its capital sanction (Exod. 21:17), so nobody can claim a small matter is being inflated. "hypocrite" is the Greek theatre word for the masked actor — and the mask was not a disguise but a device for projecting a character to people too far off to see a face. Matthew uses it thirteen times, more than the rest of the New Testament together. On the quotation, Matthew follows the Greek of Isaiah 29:13, which sharpens the Hebrew rather than altering it. "in vain" is maten — not wrongly, not insincerely: useless, which is a colder verdict than hypocrisy about men who fasted twice a week and tithed their herb garden. And note what he does at v. 10: he stops answering the delegation, calls the crowd, and gives the answer to them directly.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy exposes the Pharisees' deepest error: they have allowed their oral tradition to override the written word of God. The corban rule (declaring assets dedicated to God, thereby relieving oneself of the duty to support parents) is the example Jesus uses — a legal fiction that honored the letter of piety while violating the command to honor father and mother. Isaiah's word stands: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." External religion without heart-transformation is hypocrisy by definition.
verseByVerse.examples: The list of defiling things in verses 19-20 is a heart-audit: from the inside come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are not random vices; they map onto the second table of the Decalogue. Jesus is saying: the law you claim to keep is being broken from the inside out. Clean hands matter less than clean hearts — and clean hearts are precisely what the Pharisees have not addressed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, "Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and scribes came from Jerusalem and asked Jesus why his disciples broke the tradition of the elders: they did not wash their hands before eating.

Meaning first. Matthew 15 asks where uncleanness really lives and who may come to God’s table. A delegation from Jerusalem complains that Jesus’ disciples eat without the ritual washing of hands. Jesus answers that their tradition has cancelled the commandment of God, that worship from the lips without the heart is useless, and that what defiles a person is not food going in but sin coming out of the heart. Then he walks out of Israel altogether, and a Canaanite woman, from the most alien people a Jew could name, kneels before him and asks for nothing but crumbs, and is praised for great faith. The chapter ends on the Gentile side of the lake with the lame walking, the mute speaking, a crowd glorifying the God of Israel, and four thousand men fed in the wilderness. The religious experts who had everything went home offended; the outsiders who had nothing went home fed. What God wants is not clean hands but a new heart, and the only one who can give it is the Lord who welcomes outsiders to his table.

Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem. This is a delegation. Matthew says they came from Jerusalem, ninety miles on foot, four or five days’ walk, to a lakeside district in Galilee. Nobody makes that journey to raise a question about hand hygiene. The religious capital has sent a deputation north, perhaps to investigate him, and the opposition that began in 12:14 is now organised. And the opening charge is that his men eat wrong.

Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? The tradition of the elders was the large body of oral rules that earlier teachers had built around the law of Moses, to apply it to every situation of life and to put a fence around it, so that no one would break it even by accident. The Pharisees believed this oral law had been given to Moses at Sinai alongside the written law and handed down by word of mouth. It was later written down in the Mishnah, about AD 200. To break it was, in their framework, about the gravest charge there was.

For they do not wash their hands when they eat. It was not about hygiene, and it was not about dirt. The washing in question was a ritual pouring of water over the hands, in a prescribed quantity and order, to remove ceremonial uncleanness picked up from the marketplace, from Gentiles, from unclean objects (Mark 7:3–4). A man with visibly filthy hands who had performed it was clean; a man who had scrubbed them and not performed it was not. So nobody is accusing the disciples of eating with dirty hands. They are accusing them of eating without a rite. And the rite was for priests. The law commands the washing of hands and feet for Aaron and his sons before they approach the altar, on pain of death (Exodus 30:17–21). That is the whole of the biblical requirement, and it applies to men on duty in the sanctuary. What the tradition had done was extend priestly purity to everybody, at every meal, for ever.

A serious idea. The impulse behind it is not contemptible, and it should be said. If Israel was a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6), why should every table not be treated like the altar? It was a serious idea, seriously held, by devout men. And it had become the thing they walked ninety miles to complain about. That is how human religion usually goes wrong: not by beginning in wickedness but by beginning in zeal and ending by putting its own careful additions in the place of God.

What it does not mean. Not that tradition is always bad. The church has good traditions: creeds, confessions, forms of worship, patterns of Christian life, which faithfully express Scripture, and Paul tells believers to hold to the traditions he taught them (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The problem comes when human tradition is put on the same level as God’s word, or above it (v. 3), and when people are judged by it as though God had commanded it.

How do I tell a good tradition from a bad one? Ask three questions. Does it come from Scripture, or only from us? Does it serve what God commands, or does it crowd it out? And are we binding it on other people’s consciences, so that someone who does not keep it is treated as less faithful? A church may sing certain hymns, meet at certain times, and follow certain orders of service, and these can be wise and helpful. But the moment they are treated as marks of true godliness, or used to look down on believers who do things differently, they have become the tradition of the elders. Hold your customs with an open hand and God’s commands with a closed one.

In a sentence. Religious leaders from Jerusalem challenged Jesus because his disciples did not keep the elders’ rule of ritual handwashing.

On a Tuesday. Are there religious habits you treat as if they were God’s commands, and judge others for not keeping: a style of dress, a translation, a way of keeping Sunday, a form of schooling, a list of things a real Christian would never do? Name one, and ask honestly whether God said it or you did.

For worship. The God whose holiness the Pharisees tried to fence with water is holier than all their washings could reach, and more merciful than all their fences allowed. He sent his Son not to add rules to our hands but to make clean our hearts by his own blood. How kind is the Lord who, when we try to manage holiness ourselves, comes to us himself, and offers us not a better rite but a new heart.
verseByVerse.note: The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law. The washing was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God commanded, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered with a question: why do you break God’s commandment for the sake of your tradition? God commanded: honour your father and mother, and whoever curses father or mother must be put to death.

And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? Watch the exchange as a piece of argument, because the structure is exact and it is devastating. They ask: why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? He answers: and why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? The same verb, break, thrown straight back, with the two nouns exchanged. They accused the disciples of breaking the tradition; he accuses them of breaking the commandment, by means of the tradition. It is not a change of subject and it is not evasion. It is the same charge at a higher level, and it puts them on trial in one sentence. Notice also the possessive, which he uses three times in this passage: your tradition. They had called it the tradition of the elders, a phrase that gives it weight and distance, as though it descended from Moses and belonged to nobody in particular. He calls it theirs. Whatever its pedigree, the men in front of him are the ones enforcing it, and they will answer for it. Human, not divine.

For God commanded. Jesus treats the words of Moses as God’s own command (compare Mark 7:10, where he says Moses said). What Scripture says, God says. There is no gap between the written word and the voice of God, and that is the whole ground on which Jesus judges their tradition.

Honor your father and your mother. The fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12), which Paul calls the first commandment with a promise (Ephesians 6:2), and the first of those that govern how we treat one another. Honour includes respect, obedience when young, and practical care in old age, including financial support.

Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die. Exodus 21:17. “Revile” means to curse, to speak evil of, to treat with contempt. God took this so seriously that it was a capital crime in Israel. And the two texts are chosen with care. He does not pick a peripheral regulation to make his point. He goes to the Ten Commandments, and then to the death penalty behind it, so that when he shows in the next two verses what their rule does to it, nobody can suggest a small matter is being inflated.

Does that death penalty still apply? No. Jesus cites it to show how seriously God takes the fifth commandment, and how guilty the Pharisees were in evading it. The civil penalty belonged to Israel’s law as a nation under God, and it expired with that nation’s civil order (Westminster 19.4). The moral duty to honour parents still stands for Christians (Ephesians 6:1–3), and its seriousness has not changed. What has changed is that the sanction for breaking it now falls not on the offender at the hands of the state but was borne for every repentant child of God by Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus accused the Pharisees of breaking God’s commandment to honour parents for the sake of their own tradition.

On a Tuesday. How are you honouring your parents? If they are old, their care is a command of God, not an optional kindness. If they are difficult, honour still means respect in speech, patience, and practical help. If they are gone, honour their memory and thank God for what he gave you through them. And if your parents wronged you, honouring them never means pretending abuse was not abuse or putting yourself back in danger; it means refusing contempt and doing them what good you safely can.

For worship. There was one Son who honoured his Father perfectly, in every word and work, and who from the cross still honoured his earthly mother, giving her into the care of the beloved disciple (John 19:26–27). Christ kept the fifth commandment for us, and bore the curse of every child who has dishonoured father or mother, so that we might be adopted into a family where we cry, Abba, Father (Romans 8:15).

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, "If anyone tells his father or his mother, 'What you would have gained from me is given to God,' he need not honor his father." So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you teach that if someone tells his parents, “What you would have received from me is given to God”, he no longer needs to honour his father. So for the sake of your tradition you have made God’s word void.

But you say. In contrast to what God said (v. 4). The two sentences stand side by side: God commanded; but you say. That is the whole controversy in five words.

If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God”. Mark gives the Aramaic word: Corban, meaning an offering dedicated to God (Mark 7:11). A son could declare his property Corban, dedicated to the temple. Once declared, it could not be used to support his parents, though he could often keep using it himself during his lifetime. It became a legal loophole: a way to escape the duty of caring for ageing parents while appearing pious.

He need not honor his father. By their tradition, such a vow had to be kept, even if it meant breaking the fifth commandment. The rule meant to honour God’s holiness had been used to dishonour God’s command.

So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. “Made void” means cancelled, nullified, made of no effect. Their human rule had overruled God’s clear command. Mark adds: and many such things you do (Mark 7:13). Jesus does not call this a lapse or an imbalance. He calls it making void the word of God, which is about as strong as language gets, and he says it to the most devout men of their generation, who would have been genuinely shocked to hear it.

The manoeuvre. Name the move itself, because its shape long outlived the practice. A man owed his parents support. He could not simply refuse; that would be plainly wrong, and everyone would say so. So he found a religious way of being unavailable: the money was dedicated, his hands were tied by piety, and the duty was not neglected but outranked. Nobody has ever needed to be taught that move. It survives wherever a religious activity is used to excuse a moral one. I am too committed at church to visit my mother. I give generously, so my brother’s situation is someone else’s problem. I am busy with the Lord’s work, which is why my children see so little of me. Each sentence is true on its face, and each is Corban. The tell never changes: the thing being done for God happens to be precisely the thing that lets you off something costly, unglamorous and explicitly commanded.

The principle. Whenever human tradition contradicts Scripture, Scripture must win. This is the Reformation principle of sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority over the church’s traditions, and nothing is to be added to it, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or by the traditions of men (Westminster 1.6, 1.10). The Reformers used this passage against medieval traditions that they believed had overruled the word of God: the sale of indulgences, purgatory, the withholding of the cup, and rules that bound consciences where God had left them free.

What it does not mean. Not that giving to God is wrong, or that we should not give generously to the church. Dedicating property to God was honourable. But no religious giving can replace the God-given duty to care for one’s family, and anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). So the test is not whether the religious activity is good. It is what it is being used to avoid.

What if caring for my parents conflicts with serving God? Usually it does not, because caring for them is serving God. Scripture never sets the two against each other. There may be real decisions to make, about money, time, where to live, whether a parent should move in or receive professional care, and faithful Christians will reach different answers. But the question is never whether to honour them; it is how. Talk to them, to your siblings and to your church. Share the load where you can. And if a parent opposes your faith or your obedience to Christ, you must obey God rather than man (10:37; Acts 5:29), while still showing them every honour and kindness you can.

In a sentence. The Pharisees used a religious vow to escape caring for their parents, cancelling God’s word by their tradition.

On a Tuesday. Put it to your own week: is there a duty I am dodging, and is my reason for dodging it a spiritual one? A religious-sounding excuse for avoiding a clear duty, at home, at work or in your family, is Corban. Name it, and do the duty.

For worship. How faithful is the Lord, who never once used his heavenly business as a reason to neglect us. The Son of God, about his Father’s great work of redemption, still stopped for a blind beggar, still touched a leper, still fed a hungry crowd, and still provided for his mother as he died. His word cannot be made void; heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not pass away (24:35).
verseByVerse.note: Mark gives the formula its Aramaic name, Corban — “given to God.” Property declared dedicated could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied rightly about you: this people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.

You hypocrites! The word is worth having exactly, because English has borrowed it and worn it down. Hypokritēs was a technical term of the Greek theatre: the actor, the man who speaks from behind a mask. It carried no moral charge; it was simply a job. What gives it its edge in the Gospels is what the mask was for. In a Greek theatre the mask was not a disguise; it was how a character was presented, at scale, to a crowd who could not see a face at that distance. The mask projected. So the accusation is not primarily that they are lying about themselves, though they are. It is that what an audience sees is a constructed exterior designed to be read from a long way off, and behind it there is a man whose own face is doing something else. Matthew uses the word thirteen times, more than the rest of the New Testament together, and almost always of these men (see 6:2).

Well did Isaiah prophesy of you. Isaiah 29:13. Isaiah spoke to his own generation, but his words describe every generation with the same disease. And Isaiah’s setting is not what one would expect. Isaiah 29 is addressed to Jerusalem, to Ariel, the city where David encamped, in a chapter about a people who cannot read a sealed book. The complaint is not that they had abandoned religion. It is that they were performing it accurately and had gone somewhere else while doing so. Seven hundred years later, a deputation from that same city walks ninety miles to complain about handwashing, and has its own mail read to it.

This people honors me with their lips. They said the right words: prayers, praise, religious language, scrupulous and correct.

But their heart is far from me. Their inner life was not given to God. They went through the motions without love. This is the heart of the matter. Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). God has never wanted lips without a heart. He has always wanted the heart, and lips that speak from it.

Does this condemn all church tradition? No. Creeds, confessions and orders of worship can serve the church well, and there is great wisdom in the prayers and hymns of past generations. Traditions become wrong when they are bound on the conscience as if they were God’s commands, or when they override what God has plainly commanded. The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches give tradition authority alongside Scripture; Reformed churches hold that Scripture alone is the final rule, and that every tradition must answer to it. That is the stance of this commentary: we receive the wisdom of the church gratefully, and test all of it by the Bible.

How do I know if my worship is only lip-service? Everyone who sings in church has caught his mind wandering, and that alone does not make you a hypocrite. The danger Isaiah describes is settled, not momentary: religion that has become a performance, kept up for others, with no desire for God behind it. Some signs: you are more concerned with how worship looks than with whom it is for; you feel nothing about God from Sunday to Sunday; and the words you sing never touch what you do. If that frightens you, the remedy is not to stop worshipping but to ask God for a new heart (Psalm 51:10), and then to come honestly, telling him exactly where your heart is.

In a sentence. Jesus called the Pharisees hypocrites, fulfilling Isaiah’s description of people who honour God with their lips while their hearts are far from him.

On a Tuesday. When you sing or pray on Sunday, is your heart near to God, or only your lips? Pick one line of a hymn you will sing this week, and mean it all week.

For worship. There was one man whose lips and heart were never apart. Every word Christ spoke to his Father came from a heart wholly given to him, and he could say, I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). He is the true worshipper the Father seeks (John 4:23), and he offered himself without mask and without reserve on the cross, so that people like us, with divided hearts, might be brought near and given hearts that love God.

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men." And he called the people to him and said to them, "Hear and understand:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their worship is empty, because they teach human rules as if they were God’s commands. Then Jesus called the crowd and said: listen and understand.

In vain do they worship me. “In vain” is matēn, meaning to no purpose, without effect, uselessly. Not wrongly, and not insincerely. Useless. That is a colder verdict than hypocrisy, and it should be felt as one. These men prayed at fixed hours, fasted twice a week, tithed their herb garden, and kept a purity code more demanding than the law required. And the assessment is not that it was inadequate but that it accomplished nothing whatever. Worship offered without the heart, according to human rules, achieves nothing before God.

Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. Notice the mechanism, because it is not what people usually imagine happening. Nobody in this story has thrown Scripture out. The Pharisees revered it, memorised it, and would have died for it. What went wrong is that human material had been promoted into the same category. Once a tradition is taught as doctrine, it acquires the authority of the thing it was built to protect, and from that moment it can overrule it, which is precisely what verses 5 and 6 describe happening to the fifth commandment. The danger is not irreverence. It is reverence attached to the wrong object, by people who can no longer tell which of their convictions came from God. Paul warns against the same thing: rules of do not handle, do not taste, do not touch, which have an appearance of wisdom and no value against the flesh (Colossians 2:20–23).

A note on the quotation. Matthew follows the Greek version of Isaiah 29:13, which reads in vain do they worship me. The Hebrew runs slightly differently: their fear of me is a commandment taught by men. The Greek sharpens what the Hebrew implies. Isaiah’s complaint is that reverence for God had become a matter of learned human procedure, and the Greek states outright what that makes of the worship. Nothing is invented; the emphasis moves.

The regulative principle. The Reformed tradition draws from verses like this that God is to be worshipped only in the ways he has appointed in Scripture, and not according to human imaginations and inventions (Westminster 21.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession says the same at 22.1). Others hold that whatever Scripture does not forbid is permitted in worship. Both agree that no human rule may be imposed on the conscience as if it were God’s command, and that worship must be shaped by God’s word rather than by our preferences.

And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand”. The turn in verse 10 is a deliberate public act. He has been answering a delegation from Jerusalem; he stops, summons the crowd, and says the next thing to them. The ordinary people standing about, who had been told all their lives that these were the men who understood, are made witnesses to the argument, and are then given the answer directly rather than through the usual channel. The issue matters for everyone. And the second verb, understand, is the one that has been running since chapter 13 (13:13–15, 51), now asked of the crowd rather than the experts.

What does it mean that worship can be in vain? It means God does not accept worship simply because it is offered, or because it is sincere, or because it is elaborate. He accepts worship that comes through Christ, from a heart that trusts him, in the way he has appointed. That should humble us and free us. It humbles us because we cannot impress God by effort, beauty or tradition. It frees us because the simplest prayer of a believing child, the plainest service of a small church reading Scripture, singing and praying in the name of Jesus, is not in vain. God is not looking for performance. He is looking for faith.

In a sentence. Worship according to human rules taught as divine commands is useless before God, so Jesus called the crowd to listen and understand.

On a Tuesday. Test what you believe and practise by Scripture: is this God’s command, or a human tradition? Take one conviction you hold strongly about how Christians should live or worship, and find where the Bible teaches it. If you cannot, hold it more lightly, and never bind it on anyone else.

For worship. The Lord who rejects empty worship is the same Lord who makes worship full. Through Christ, our great high priest, our poor prayers and praises are made acceptable to God, perfumed with his intercession (Revelation 8:3–4). We do not come with clean hands of our own making; we come in the name of the one who washed us, and in him we worship not in vain but in spirit and truth.

verseByVerse.quote: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person." Then the disciples came and said to him, "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of it. Then the disciples told Jesus that the Pharisees were offended by what he said.

It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person. “Defiles” (koinoi) means makes common, unclean, unfit for God’s presence. The Pharisees taught that eating with unwashed hands, or eating unclean food, made a person unclean before God. Jesus says food cannot make a person morally unclean. To ears trained to think of defilement as chiefly ritual and dietary, it would have sounded revolutionary.

But what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person. Words, and the heart from which they come (vv. 18–19; 12:34). Real uncleanness is moral and spiritual, not ritual. The Pharisees’ whole system of defilement faced outward, and the problem was inward.

Then the disciples came and said to him, Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying? “Offended” (eskandalisthēsan) means scandalised, made to stumble. Jesus had swept away a central part of their purity system in one sentence. The disciples seem anxious; it is never comfortable to watch your teacher offend the most respected men in the nation. Jesus’ response is not an apology but a deepening (vv. 13–14).

What about the food laws? The claim that Jesus is speaking only about handwashing needs qualifying, because Mark, telling the same scene, adds a sentence Matthew does not: thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). A reader with both Gospels open may feel the two pulling in different directions. They are not. What Jesus says here is the principle; Mark supplies the conclusion the principle was always going to force. And the conclusion was not obvious even to the men in the room. If Peter had understood that afternoon that all foods were clean, he would not have needed a sheet let down from heaven three times, years later, before he would eat with a Gentile, and he still argued with the voice that told him to (Acts 10:9–16). The church would take years, a vision, a council and a good deal of correspondence to work it through. So both writers are right, and the difference between them is the difference between a seed and its fruit. Matthew, writing for Jewish readers, records what Jesus said. Mark, writing for Gentiles among whom the question had become urgent, tells his readers where it led.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament food laws were wrong. They were God’s commands for Israel, teaching the difference between clean and unclean and setting Israel apart from the nations (Leviticus 11:44–47). But they were symbols pointing to inner purity, and they are fulfilled in Christ. The ceremonial laws were never abolished by being broken; they were fulfilled by the arrival of what they pointed to, and this sentence in a Galilean courtyard is the moment the shadow began to give way. Christians are free to eat any food with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5), while taking care not to make a weaker believer stumble (Romans 14).

Should I worry about offending religious people? Not when the offence comes from the truth. The disciples were troubled that the Pharisees were offended, and Jesus did not retract a word. We should never offend needlessly, by rudeness, pride or careless speech, and Paul tells us to give no offence to Jews or Greeks or to the church of God in matters of freedom (1 Corinthians 10:32). But the gospel itself offends people who are trusting in their own goodness, and no amount of tact will make it otherwise. The question to ask is not whether someone was offended, but whether what offended them was Christ’s word or our manner.

In a sentence. Food cannot make a person unclean before God; what comes out of the heart through the mouth does.

On a Tuesday. What comes out of your mouth reveals your heart. Think back over this week: the sharp reply, the gossip, the boast, the complaint, the kind word, the prayer. What have your words revealed?

For worship. The Lord who declared all foods clean is the Lord who declares sinners clean. He did not sweep away the shadows to leave us with nothing; he swept them away because he himself is the substance. In him, the Jew and the Gentile who were kept apart by the food laws now sit at one table, and the heart that no washing could touch is made clean by his blood. What God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:15).

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them alone: they are blind guides. And if a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.

Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Israel was pictured as God’s planting, the branch of his planting, the planting of the LORD that he might be glorified (Isaiah 60:21; 61:3). The Pharisees and their teaching were not planted by God, however ancient and elaborate, and they will be removed in judgment. Compare the weeds among the wheat (13:24–30). What God did not plant cannot last; what he plants cannot be uprooted.

Let them alone. The sentence that ought to stop a reader. It is startling in the mouth of Jesus. He has just been told that the Pharisees were offended by what he said, and this is his response: not an explanation, not another attempt, not go and put it right with them. Leave them. Let them go. That has to be held with care, because it is not a general licence to give up on people. The man saying it wept over Jerusalem, went on preaching to these same men until the last week of his life, and prayed for the people driving nails into him. But it is in the text, and it means something. There is a point at which further argument is not owed, where a man has seen enough, decided, and hardened, and the loving thing is not to keep supplying material. Paul reaches the same conclusion: after warning a divisive person once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him (Titus 3:10). It is a permission, not an instruction, and it is given about religious leaders rather than about the lost. For the disciples it means: do not worry about offending them, do not follow them, do not try to win their approval.

They are blind guides. The two words do not go together. A guide is a man hired precisely because he can see the road, and this one cannot, and has not mentioned it, and is being paid for it. The Pharisees saw themselves as a guide to the blind (Romans 2:19). Jesus says they are blind themselves. They cannot see the truth about God, so they cannot lead others to it. Matthew will use the phrase again in chapter 23, where it becomes a refrain (23:16, 24).

And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit. A proverb, and the consequence is put with no cruelty at all. Pits were common hazards: cisterns, wells, ditches. Not the guide only. The tragedy of bad teaching is that the teacher is rarely the only casualty, and in this picture he is not even the one who most deserves to be in the hole.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should ignore false teachers. Elsewhere we are told to beware of them (7:15) and elders are told to rebuke them (Titus 1:9–11). But we must not seek their approval, or follow them.

How do I know if my teacher is a blind guide? Test what he says by Scripture, as the Bereans tested even Paul (Acts 17:11). A faithful teacher points you to Christ and his finished work, not to himself or to a system of extra rules. He submits his own words to the Bible, explains it rather than adding to it, and lives in a way that matches what he teaches. Watch for warning signs: a teacher who is always adding requirements God did not give, who cannot bear to be questioned, who treats Scripture as a springboard for his own ideas, or who makes the gospel about something other than sin, grace and Christ. Read your Bible for yourself, belong to a church that is accountable, and do not follow anyone you could not follow with your Bible open.

In a sentence. Teachers whom God has not planted will be removed; they are blind guides, and those who follow them will fall with them.

On a Tuesday. Whom are you following spiritually: which preachers, writers, podcasts, voices online? Make sure they can see, by testing them against Scripture. And if you teach anyone, a class, your children, a friend, ask whether you are pointing them to the word or to yourself.

For worship. Blessed be the Father who plants, and whose planting cannot be uprooted. Every soul he has planted in Christ will stand when the whole field of human religion is cleared. And blessed be the true Guide, the light of the world, of whom it is promised that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "Explain the parable to us." And he said, "Are you also still without understanding?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter asked Jesus to explain the saying. Jesus said: are you still without understanding?

But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us”. Notice what Peter calls it. It was not a parable. Verse 11 is a plain statement, with no story, no image, and nothing hidden. Peter files it as a riddle because it cannot mean what it appears to mean. He has been raised on food laws that God himself gave, and the sentence he has just heard sounds as if it dismantles them, so he assumes there must be a second level. He is wrong about the form and right about the size of it. Peter, as spokesman, asks for the meaning, and asking is good (13:36).

And he said, Are you also still without understanding? A gentle rebuke, and the word in it is the chapter 13 word. “Without understanding” (asynetoi) is the negative of the verb that ran through the parables: they do not understand; the one who hears the word and understands it; and at the end, have you understood all these things? To which the disciples had answered yes (13:51). That was two chapters ago. Here the same men are told they are still without understanding, and the adverb does the work. Their yes had been honest, and it had been thin. And the little word also puts them, for a moment, in the same column as the crowd and the Pharisees. After all his teaching, the disciples were still thinking about purity in the Pharisees’ way. Old habits of thought die hard. But Jesus explains, patiently.

Slow learners. It is a mercy that Matthew records this, and he records it repeatedly. These men are not presented as spiritual naturals who grasped things the rest of us would not. They were slow, they asked for basic things to be explained twice, and one of the two whose names we know best is the one asking here. Matthew was one of them, and he puts his own slowness in the book.

Is it wrong to need things explained again? No. Jesus’ rebuke is real, because the disciples had been given so much, but he does not refuse to explain. He goes straight on to teach them. Some believers feel ashamed that they still do not understand parts of the faith they have heard for years, or are afraid to ask in Bible study in case they look foolish. Ask anyway. Ask your pastor, ask a mature friend, ask God as you read. The only thing worse than being slow to understand is pretending you understand when you do not.

In a sentence. Peter asked for an explanation, and Jesus gently rebuked the disciples for still not understanding, and then explained.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is patient with slow learners. Keep asking him to help you understand. Take one thing in the Bible you have never really grasped, and ask someone about it this week.

For worship. How patient is our Teacher. He bore with men who said yes and did not understand, who heard and forgot, who asked the same questions twice, and he never gave up on them. He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures in the end (Luke 24:45), and he sent the Spirit of truth to guide them into all the truth. He is as patient with us, and as determined.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and out of the body? But what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and this defiles a person.

Whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled. The physiology is deliberately plain, and the Greek is blunter than most translations. He is not being coarse for effect. The argument requires the route to be traced: in at the mouth, through the gut, out of the body. At no point does it pass through the heart. Whatever a food is, it never touches the part of a person where defilement happens. It cannot affect a person’s standing with God.

Matthew’s silence. Mark records the same saying and then adds, in his own voice, thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). Matthew records the argument and leaves out the conclusion. That is unlikely to be an accident, and the likeliest explanation tells us something about who each man was writing for. Mark writes for Gentiles, for whom the question was settled and the implication welcome. Matthew writes for Jewish Christians, for whom the food laws were their grandmothers’ whole practice, and for whom this was the most painful issue in the early church, the one that split Peter and Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14) and required a council in Jerusalem (Acts 15). He gives them the words of Jesus and lets them draw it out.

But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart. In Scripture the heart is not the seat of the emotions as against the head. It is the whole interior control room: thinking, willing, deciding, loving, remembering. Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life (Proverbs 4:23). So out of the heart does not mean out of the feelings. It means out of the place where a person is actually operating from, and the mouth, on this account, is simply the outlet where that becomes audible (12:34).

And this defiles a person. The source of real uncleanness is inside us, not outside us.

The significance. This was revolutionary. The Pharisees’ whole system located defilement outside the person: in food, in objects, in contact with unclean people. They tried to stay pure by avoiding contact with the unclean. Jesus says the problem is within. You cannot stay pure by avoiding the world, because you carry the source of impurity in your own heart. Only a new heart can make a person clean (Ezekiel 36:25–26; Psalm 51:10).

So should Christians not bother avoiding bad influences? We should, but for the right reason. Scripture tells us to flee youthful passions (2 Timothy 2:22) and warns that bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33). Avoiding temptation is wise, because temptation feeds what is already in the heart. But it is not what makes us clean. The person who has cut out every bad film and every worldly friend can still be proud, bitter and unloving, because the root was never outside. So guard your eyes and your company, yes, and do not mistake that for holiness. Holiness begins with a heart made new by the Spirit and kept close to Christ.

In a sentence. Food passes through the body and cannot defile; what defiles comes from the heart.

On a Tuesday. You cannot keep yourself clean simply by avoiding bad places and people. The danger is within. When you sin this week, resist the instinct to blame what was around you, the traffic, the tired children, the colleague, and ask instead what it showed you about your heart. Then ask God for a clean one.

For worship. The Lord who knows what comes out of the heart knows what is in it, and he is not repelled. He came for precisely those whose hearts were the problem. Create in me a clean heart, O God (Psalm 51:10) is a prayer he delights to answer, and he answers it not with advice but with his Spirit, writing his law on the hearts that once broke it.
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean.”

parallels.desc: out of the abundance of the heart

verseByVerse.quote: For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness and slander. These are what defile a person. Eating with unwashed hands does not.

For out of the heart come evil thoughts. First, and the source of all the rest: evil thoughts, the inner reasonings, plans and intentions of the heart. Sin begins in the mind before it becomes action, desire conceiving and giving birth to sin (James 1:14–15). The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? (Jeremiah 17:9).

Murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. The list follows the order of the second table of the Ten Commandments: the sixth (murder), the seventh (adultery and sexual immorality), the eighth (theft) and the ninth (false witness and slander). These are what make a person unclean before God. The Pharisees had policed the outside while the inside went unexamined, and the law they claimed to keep was being broken from the inside out.

Sexual immorality. Porneia: every kind of sexual sin outside the marriage of one man and one woman (see 5:32).

Slander. Blasphēmiai: speech that damages others, or insults God. The tongue that never touched an unwashed loaf can be defiled by a single sentence.

These are what defile a person. Not food, but sin. Clean hands and a dirty heart: defiled. Unwashed hands and a heart made new: not defiled.

But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone. Jesus returns to the original question (v. 2) and dismisses it. The whole elaborate handwashing tradition could not address the real problem of human defilement, because it addressed the wrong organ.

What it does not mean. Not that every person commits every one of these sins in action. But the seeds of all of them are in every human heart, and only God’s grace keeps them from growing (5:21–28). Nor does it mean that outward actions do not matter. They matter because they reveal and express the heart.

If the trouble is my heart, how can it ever be changed? This is the hardest question in the chapter, and it must not be left hanging. If the heart is the very thing doing the wanting, I cannot repair it with itself. This is what the older theologians meant by total depravity, and the term is often misheard. It does not mean every person is as wicked as he could possibly be; it means there is no part of us, mind, will or affections, that the corruption has not reached, so there is no clean corner left to start the repairs from. So the cure cannot be a better tradition, a stricter rule or a firmer resolution. It has to be a replacement. And God promised exactly that, centuries before this argument: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezekiel 36:26). That is not reform; it is transplant. It is the Spirit’s work, purchased at the cross toward which this whole Gospel is walking. Jesus is not telling you to try harder at the impossible. He is telling you where the disease is, so that you will stop treating your hands and bring him your heart.

Am I really changed if I still find these things in my heart? Yes, if you hate them and fight them. A new heart is not yet a perfect heart. The old sinful nature remains in believers until death, and the Christian life is a lifelong war between the flesh and the Spirit (Galatians 5:17; Westminster 13.2). What changes at new birth is that sin no longer reigns: you now grieve over what once pleased you, confess what you once excused, and want God more than you want the sin. Finding evil thoughts in yourself does not prove you are unconverted. Being untroubled by them would be far more worrying. Keep confessing, keep fighting, and keep looking to Christ, whose righteousness, not your progress, is your standing before God.

In a sentence. Evil thoughts and the sins they produce come from the heart and defile a person, not unwashed hands.

On a Tuesday. Which of these sins finds a home in your heart, even if it never becomes action: the murderous resentment, the lustful imagining, the envy that would take what is another’s, the lie you rehearse, the slander you enjoy hearing? Confess it to God by name, and ask him to cleanse you. Then do one thing that starves it.

For worship. Here is the diagnosis no one else would make, and here is the physician who made it. The Lord who sees every evil thought in us did not stand at a distance with a list. He took that list upon himself. He who knew no sin was made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21), so that hearts which produced murder, adultery, theft and slander might be washed, sanctified and justified in his name (1 Corinthians 6:11). He did not come to wash our hands. He came to give us new hearts, and he paid for them with his own.

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–39 — The Canaanite Woman and the Feeding of the Four Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman cries out for her demon-oppressed daughter. After testing her faith through apparent reluctance, he heals the daughter and commends her great faith. Jesus then returns to Galilee, heals many on a mountain, and feeds four thousand people from seven loaves and a few fish. More to notice. This is the one time in his ministry that Jesus goes into Phoenicia — he had already crossed to the Gentile east bank at 8:28 and will go north to pagan Caesarea Philippi at 16:13, but Tyre and Sidon are foreign soil. Tyre and Sidon are Phoenician cities outside Israel, outside Herod's jurisdiction — and in the Old Testament they are bywords, with Ezekiel devoting three chapters to Tyre's fall and Jezebel a Sidonian princess. That is the address he withdraws to after Jerusalem sends a deputation about hand washing. And Matthew's word for her is deliberately archaic: Mark calls her a Syrophoenician, the ordinary current term; Matthew calls her a Canaanite — the Old Testament name for the nations Israel was to drive out, rarely heard in his day. He has reached back for maximum freight, and then has her say "Son of David". On the dogs, Greek has two words: kyon is the street scavenger and the word used when "dogs" is an insult (7:6; Phil. 3:2), and Jesus does not use it. He uses kynarion, the diminutive — the animal that lives in the house, belongs there, and is fed there. The saying is about order, not worth. But the shock should not be dissolved: he ignored her, the disciples asked him to send her away, and he answered her kneeling with a proverb about dogs. What resolves it is the outcome rather than the vocabulary. Her reply begins "yes, LORD" — she agrees, disputes nothing, and adds only "for even", staying inside his picture and finding that it contains her. And Jesus commends faith of this order in only two people: this woman (great is your faith) and the centurion (with no one in Israel have I found such faith, 8:10) — both Gentiles, both asking for somebody else, and neither present when the healing happens. The crowd at vv. 29-31 is Gentile, and Matthew signals it by how they worship: they glorified "the God of Israel", which is what an outsider says. Which explains the second feeding — and the two are not one story twice. The basket words differ consistently: kophinos at the five thousand (a small stiff wicker basket a Jew carried his own food in) and spyris at the four thousand (a hamper big enough to hold a man — the one Paul was lowered down the Damascus wall in, Acts 9:25). Jesus himself distinguishes the two events at 16:9-10.
verseByVerse.theology: The Canaanite woman episode is one of the most theologically dense in Matthew. Jesus's apparent reluctance — "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" and the difficult "dogs" saying — is best understood as testing her faith rather than expressing genuine exclusion. Her response — "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table" — is the model of faith that does not demand, does not argue, does not claim rights, but presses through apparent rejection on the strength of the Savior's character. Jesus pronounces her faith "great" — the only time this word is used of any individual's faith in the Synoptics.
verseByVerse.examples: The second feeding (four thousand) parallels the first (five thousand) but occurs in Gentile territory — the region of the Decapolis. Where the first feeding fed a Jewish crowd (twelve baskets, echoing the twelve tribes), the second feeds a largely Gentile crowd (seven baskets, echoing the seven Gentile nations of Canaan). The Messiah who first came to the lost sheep of Israel is already extending his table to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, "Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman from that area came out crying: have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely oppressed by a demon.

And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. Gentile territory on the Mediterranean coast, north of Galilee, in modern Lebanon (see 11:21). Two things about this scene are more remarkable than they appear, and the first is simply where it takes place. This is the only occasion in the Gospels on which Jesus goes outside the borders of Israel altogether. He had crossed to the Gentile east bank before, among the Gadarenes and their pigs (8:28), and he will go north to pagan Caesarea Philippi (16:13); but Tyre and Sidon are Phoenicia, foreign soil, outside Herod’s jurisdiction, outside anything that could be called the land of promise. And in the Old Testament these two cities are bywords. Ezekiel devotes three chapters to the fall of Tyre; Isaiah, Joel and Amos pronounce against them. Jezebel was a Sidonian princess, and her marriage brought Baal into Israel. That is where he withdraws to, perhaps for rest and to escape the hostility of the Pharisees, straight after a delegation from Jerusalem has come north to complain about handwashing. Having just declared that food does not make people unclean, he goes among the people Israel considered unclean.

And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out. The second remarkable thing is the word Matthew chooses for her, and it is deliberately archaic. Mark calls her a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth (Mark 7:26), the ordinary geographical description a first-century writer would use. Matthew calls her a Canaanite. It is the Old Testament word, the name of the nations Israel was commanded to drive out of the land, the people of Jericho and Ai, the ones whose religion the whole law was designed to fence against. It is rather as if a modern writer described someone as a Philistine. Matthew has reached back over a thousand years for a term with maximum freight, and it can only be on purpose: he wants the reader to feel the full distance between this woman and the covenant before she opens her mouth. And yet Rahab, another Canaanite woman, is already in Jesus’ family tree (1:5).

And was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David”. Then she opens her mouth and says: Son of David. A Canaanite, using Israel’s messianic title, correctly, in Gentile country, while back in Galilee the scribes who owned that title were arguing about whether his men had washed properly. She recognises who Jesus is, as the blind men did (9:27). And have mercy: she knows she has no claim on him. Her faith begins with who he is, not with any merit of her own.

My daughter is severely oppressed by a demon. She pleads for her daughter, not for herself. A mother’s desperate love, and a need she cannot meet. She does not argue about whether she deserves help; she simply names him and names the need. That is always the starting point of prayer.

What does severely oppressed by a demon mean? The Gospels describe people under the cruel control of evil spirits, often with physical or mental suffering as a result, and Jesus always treated this as real and always had authority over it (4:24; 8:28–34). It is not simply an old word for illness, for the Gospels distinguish the two (4:24). Nor should we think every trouble today is demonic. The New Testament warns us that we wrestle against spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12), but it gives believers armour, not anxiety: the truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, the word and prayer. A Christian indwelt by the Holy Spirit cannot be owned by a demon, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

In a sentence. In Gentile territory, a Canaanite woman cried to Jesus as the Son of David, begging mercy for her demon-oppressed daughter.

On a Tuesday. Whom do you plead for before Jesus: a child, a friend, someone in deep trouble you cannot reach? Bring them to him as this mother did, by name, asking for mercy. And notice where the most surprising faith in this chapter comes from. Do not write off anyone as too far from God to cry to him.

For worship. The Son of David had come to the borders of Canaan, and the oldest enemy of Israel cried out to Israel’s King for mercy. That is what his kingdom is like. The Lord who once commanded Israel to drive the Canaanites out came himself to draw a Canaanite in, and he has been gathering strangers into his family ever since, from every nation that once was far off (Ephesians 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast north of Galilee. Mark calls her a Syrophoenician; Matthew uses the old name Canaanite, Israel’s ancient enemies.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, "Send her away, for she is crying out after us." He answered, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus did not answer her a word. His disciples urged him to send her away, because she kept crying after them. He answered: I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

But he did not answer her a word. A startling silence. Jesus, who always had compassion, said nothing. It is the hardest moment in the episode. Her position is harder than the storm at 8:24 or the delay on the road to Jairus’s house (9:18–26). This is not sleep and it is not lateness. She asks and receives nothing at all; then she asks again and gets what sounds like a closed door. His silence was not a refusal. It was a test of her faith, which would make it shine all the brighter, and the outcome proves it. Sometimes God is silent before he answers.

And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us”. They found her annoying and embarrassing. Send her away may mean give her what she wants and be rid of her, or simply be rid of her. Either way they had no compassion for her. And it is the same instinct as the evening of the five thousand: send them away (14:15). Persistent need that complicates the journey is always tempting to dismiss.

He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”. The same principle as 10:6. Jesus’ mission during his earthly ministry was first to Israel, the people of the covenant. This was God’s order: to the Jew first, and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16). Christ became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy (Romans 15:8–9). The woman was outside that mission. And yet the statement of the mission is a context, not a ceiling. She will press past both the silence and the mission statement.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was prejudiced against Gentiles, or that he did not care about her. He had already healed a Gentile’s servant (8:5–13). He was stating God’s plan for his earthly ministry, and testing her, as the outcome shows.

Did Jesus come only for the Jews? His earthly ministry was directed to Israel, as he told the Twelve (10:5–6), because God’s promises came first to them. The mission to all nations came after the resurrection, when he sent his disciples to make disciples of all nations (28:19). Yet even here he blesses a Gentile woman, a foretaste of the other sheep he must also bring, so that there will be one flock, one shepherd (John 10:16). From the very beginning God promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Israel first was always the road to the world, never a wall against it.

How do I keep praying when God is silent? Watch what she does, because it is the most instructive thing in the chapter. She does not withdraw offended, which most of us would call self-respect. She does not argue that the arrangement is unfair. She keeps coming, and she never once rests her case on herself. There is no protest that she deserves better, no account of how long she has waited. Her whole argument is about what he is like. If you are praying into silence, that is the shape to copy: not louder, and not a better case for your own deserving, but persistence, with the plea fastened to his character rather than your merit. Jesus told a parable precisely so that we would always pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Silence is not his last word.

In a sentence. Jesus at first was silent, and then explained that his mission was to Israel, while the disciples wanted her sent away.

On a Tuesday. If God seems silent to your prayers, keep praying. Write down what you are asking and why you believe he is able and kind. And when someone’s need is inconvenient to you, notice whether you are saying, with the disciples, send her away.

For worship. The silence of Christ was never cold. It was the last thing standing between her and a sentence she would otherwise never have heard, and a daughter healed that hour. He was not withholding from her; he was drawing out of her something she did not know was there. So it is with all his delays toward his people. The Shepherd of Israel had his eye on a Canaanite all along, and he is drawing his other sheep from every land, until the flock is complete.

parallels.desc: the lost sheep of the house of Israel
a servant to the circumcised, that the Gentiles might glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: But she came and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, help me." And he answered, "It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But she came, knelt before him, and said: Lord, help me. He answered: it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.

But she came and knelt before him. She would not be put off. She came closer, past the silence and past the disciples, and bowed down before him. The verb is the worship word, prosekynei. A Canaanite woman on her knees in Phoenicia, doing what the Pharisees of Jerusalem had never done.

Saying, “Lord, help me”. The simplest prayer, stripped of all argument and claim. She drops the title Son of David, which belonged to Israel and had not moved him, and appeals simply to him as Lord. She does not dispute his mission; she simply keeps her need in front of him.

And he answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs”. A hard saying. The children are Israel; the bread is the blessing of the Messiah’s ministry; the dogs are Gentiles. Jews often called Gentiles dogs as an insult. But the diminutive has to be pressed, because it is the difference between a slur and a household. Greek has two words. Kyōn is the dog of the streets and the rubbish heaps, a scavenger, unclean and dangerous, and that is the word used when dog is an insult: do not give what is holy to the dogs (7:6); look out for the dogs (Philippians 3:2). Jesus does not use it. He uses kynarion, the little dog, the one that lives in the house. And the picture changes entirely. This is not a pack outside the gate; it is a family at a meal with a pet under the table. The dog belongs there. It is fed there. What is being said is not you are vermin but the children eat first, which is a statement about order, not about worth. Mark adds the word first: let the children be fed first (Mark 7:27), implying that the Gentiles’ turn would come. The woman hears that instantly, which is why her reply works.

The difficulty, honestly. The difficulty should not be dissolved entirely. He ignored her. The disciples asked him to send her away. He told her his commission did not extend to her. And then, when she knelt and said Lord, help me, he answered with a proverb about dogs. No amount of word study makes that gentle, and readers who feel the shock of it are reading correctly. What resolves it is not the vocabulary but the outcome: within two verses he calls her faith great, grants her request without qualification, and heals the girl at a distance that same hour. Whatever he was doing, it was not refusing her. He was drawing something out of her, and what came out is the finest reply anybody gives him in the Gospel.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was cruel or contemptuous. His words were a test, drawing out her faith, and they used a picture that left room for her answer. Nor does it mean that Gentiles are inferior. The priority of Israel was a matter of God’s order in history, not of human worth. Within months, the gospel would go to all nations (28:19).

Why would Jesus test someone who was already desperate? Because the test was for her good and for ours. Gold is tested by fire not to destroy it but to show it is gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). Her faith was already there, given by God; the test brought it into the open, strengthened it, and made her an example to every generation of the church. And the test was never as hard as it sounded, because the one testing her already intended to give her everything. When God allows hard things in the lives of his people, he is not looking for an excuse to say no. He is preparing a greater yes. We do not always see the purpose at the time, but we can trust the heart of the one who sets the test.

In a sentence. She knelt and pleaded, and Jesus tested her with a picture of the children’s bread not being given to the household dogs.

On a Tuesday. When God’s answer seems hard, keep coming. Persistent, humble prayer is never rejected by him. Kneel, if it helps you, and say the simplest prayer there is: Lord, help me.

For worship. Lord, help me: and the Lord who heard it is the same Lord who hears it now, from every Canaanite heart that has nothing else to say. He is the true Bread, given not only for Israel but for the life of the world (John 6:51). The children’s bread was broken on the cross, and there was more than enough for the children, and the crumbs fed the nations.
