verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table.

verseByVerse.quote: She said, "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table." Then Jesus answered her, "O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire." And her daughter was healed instantly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She said: yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. Jesus answered: woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire. And her daughter was healed at that moment.

Yes, Lord. Her reply is a single small word longer in Greek than the English suggests, and everything turns on it. Nai, kyrie: yes, Lord. She agrees. That is the whole foundation of her argument. She does not dispute the order he has described, does not claim it is unfair, does not point out that her daughter is suffering, does not appeal to her own decency. She accepts his words and takes the place he has given her.

Yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. She has taken the picture he offered and stayed inside it, and found that the picture itself contains her. If the household is as he says, then there is a floor under the table, and things fall onto it, and the little dog that lives there eats them. Nothing has to be taken from the children. Nothing has to be rearranged. She is asking for what drops. It is a brilliant and humble answer. She does not ask for the children’s place, only for a crumb, and she understands that Jesus’ power is so great that even a crumb of it is enough to heal her daughter. The children can keep their bread; there is more than enough for her too.

Twice in this Gospel. Twice somebody argues with Jesus and wins, and both times it is a Gentile. Neither wins by disputing him. The centurion accepts that he is unworthy to have Jesus under his roof (8:8), and this woman accepts that she is not a child of the house, and both press through on the strength of what they have grasped about him rather than about themselves.

Then Jesus answered her, O woman, great is your faith! In the Gospels Jesus speaks of great faith in exactly two people: this woman, and the centurion, of whom he said that not even in Israel had he found such faith (8:10). Two commendations of great faith in the whole record, and both are Gentiles, and both are pleading for somebody else, a daughter or a servant, and neither ever sees Jesus perform the healing. The disciples were often called men of little faith (8:26; 14:31; 16:8). This woman’s faith was great because it was humble (she claimed nothing), persistent (she would not give up), and confident in Jesus’ power and mercy (she was sure that a crumb would do). He went north to Phoenicia to find her.

Be it done for you as you desire. Jesus gives her exactly what she asked, without qualification.

And her daughter was healed instantly. At a distance, like the centurion’s servant, from that hour.

The lesson. The Pharisees had all the privileges of the children and rejected the bread; a Canaanite woman had no privileges and received it by faith. It is a picture of the gospel going to the nations, and of the faith God honours: humble, persistent, and trusting entirely in his grace.

Does great faith mean I will always get what I ask? No. Her faith was great not because it forced Jesus’ hand but because it trusted his heart. Faith is not a technique for obtaining outcomes; it is reliance on Christ. She asked for something that was in line with his compassion and his power, and he granted it. Sometimes believers with great faith pray for healing and do not receive it in this life, as Paul did not have his thorn removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). That is not proof of weak faith. Great faith asks boldly, humbly and persistently, and then trusts the Lord with his answer, knowing that whatever he gives will be good.

Is it wrong to argue with God in prayer? It depends on how. Scripture is full of believers who plead with God: Abraham for Sodom, Moses for Israel, the psalmists asking how long. What God rejects is arguing from our own deserving, or disputing his word. This woman shows the right way. She agreed with everything Jesus said and pleaded on the basis of his own words and character. That is how to wrestle in prayer: take hold of his promises and his nature, and say, Lord, you are like this, so please do this.

In a sentence. The woman humbly asked only for a crumb of Jesus’ mercy, and he praised her great faith and healed her daughter.

On a Tuesday. Great faith is humble faith. Come to God claiming nothing, but trusting everything to his mercy. Take one promise of his word this week and plead it back to him, saying yes, Lord, and then asking.

For worship. Yes, Lord, and the crumbs fell. Blessed be the Lord whose table is so rich that its crumbs heal, whose mercy is so wide that there is more than enough for outsiders like us, and who delights to praise the faith he himself has given. We who were once far off, without hope and without God in the world, have been seated not under the table but at it, as children, by the grace of the Son of David.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went on along the Sea of Galilee, went up on a mountain and sat down. Great crowds came to him, bringing the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute and many others, and laid them at his feet, and he healed them.

Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. Mark places this in the Decapolis, the mainly Gentile region east of the lake (Mark 7:31). He had left Jewish territory at verse 21 and has not come back. The crowd that follows was probably largely Gentile.

And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. Matthew has used that pairing once before, at the opening of the Sermon on the Mount (5:1): the same two verbs, the same posture of authoritative teaching. On that mountain he taught. On this one he heals, and Matthew records no word at all.

And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others. The list is a quotation in substance. Isaiah had written: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isaiah 35:5–6). That is the passage Jesus sent back to John in prison as evidence that the promised age had begun (11:5). Here Matthew simply reports it happening, in bulk, on a hillside. And the location is the thing to notice, because Isaiah 35 is about the desert blossoming and a highway called the Way of Holiness on which the redeemed come home to Zion. It is happening on the wrong side of the lake, among the nations.

And they put them at his feet, and he healed them. Not brought them to him, which is what Matthew usually writes. They were put down, which tells you these were people who could not stand, carried some distance by others, and laid on the ground in front of a seated man. It is a picture of complete dependence. And the word for what happened to them is one clause: he healed them. No preaching is recorded, no dialogue, no faith examined, and nobody is asked anything. They were put down at his feet, and picked up again whole.

Why did Jesus heal so many, when he does not heal everyone today? These healings were signs that the King had come and the new creation had begun, exactly as Isaiah promised. They were previews of the resurrection, when there will be no lame, blind or mute at all. God still heals in answer to prayer, but he has not promised to heal every illness now, and believers still suffer and die. We do not believe the gift of miraculous healing at will continues in the church as it was given to Christ and the apostles, though we hold that view charitably towards brothers who differ. What does continue is what these healings pointed to: the King who has authority over every disease, and the promise that every one of his people will be raised whole.

In a sentence. Great crowds, probably largely Gentile, brought their sick to Jesus on a mountain and laid them at his feet, and he healed them.

On a Tuesday. Lay your needs at Jesus’ feet today in prayer, and the needs of those who cannot bring themselves. Some people will only come to him if they are carried. Whom could you carry?

For worship. Isaiah’s desert blossomed on a Gentile hillside, and the tongue of the mute sang for joy. The Lord who healed them all without a word is the Lord who will one day make all things new, when the redeemed come home to Zion with singing and everlasting joy upon their heads, and sorrow and sighing flee away (Isaiah 35:10).
verseByVerse.note: Mark places this in the Decapolis, the Gentile region east of the lake.

parallels.desc: the lame leap and the mute sing

verseByVerse.quote: so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, "I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled made well, the lame walking and the blind seeing, and they glorified the God of Israel. Then Jesus called his disciples and said: I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me three days and have nothing to eat.

So that the crowd wondered. Amazement at God’s power: the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, the blind seeing (the full list is in the verse).

And they glorified the God of Israel. Four words that suggest who this crowd was, easy to read past. The qualifier of Israel is what an outsider adds, distinguishing this God from the gods he grew up with. So the people on that mountain were Gentiles, and Matthew signals it by the way they worship rather than by stating it. It is the moment the prophets foresaw: many peoples saying, come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob (Isaiah 2:2–3).

Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd”. The word is physical. Splanchnizomai comes from the noun for the inward organs. It is not pity considered at a distance; it describes something that happens in the body. The Gospels use it almost only of Jesus. Matthew has it of the shepherdless crowds (9:36), of the sick at the first feeding (14:14), of two blind men on a road (20:34), and here, of a Gentile crowd.

Because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. Three days. That is not an afternoon’s crowd. These people had camped on a hillside in Gentile country for three days, and whatever food they brought ran out. Some had come a long way (Mark 8:3). Their hunger for him had outlasted their bread.

And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way. The concern is not spiritual and he does not dress it up as such. He is thinking about people collapsing on the walk home. And notice the order of his priorities. He has spent three days healing them. The healing is over, the teaching is done, and the last thing on his mind before they disperse is whether they will get home without falling over. Jesus cares about bodies.

Does Jesus care about my ordinary practical needs? Yes. This verse is one of the plainest proofs. The Son of God, who had just healed every kind of disease, was concerned about whether people had enough to eat for a walk. Our Father knows what we need before we ask him (6:8), and we are told to cast all our anxieties on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). Nothing in your life is too small or too ordinary to bring to him: the bills, the car, the meals, the long walk home. That does not mean he will always provide in the way we expect. It does mean he is never indifferent.

In a sentence. The largely Gentile crowd glorified Israel’s God for the healings, and Jesus had compassion on them after three days without food.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cares about practical needs as well as spiritual ones. Notice the hungry around you, literally: the neighbour who is struggling, the family at church under pressure, the person at the food bank. Meet one practical need this week in his name.

For worship. The Gentiles glorified the God of Israel, and the God of Israel had compassion on the Gentiles. The Lord whose heart was moved for a hungry crowd is the Lord whose heart has always been toward the nations. He who opened his hand to satisfy the desire of every living thing (Psalm 145:16) stood on a mountain in the Decapolis, and would not send them away hungry.
verseByVerse.note: “The God of Israel” may suggest a largely Gentile crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples said to him, "Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?" And Jesus said to them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven, and a few small fish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples said: where can we get enough bread in this remote place to feed such a crowd? Jesus asked how many loaves they had. They said: seven, and a few small fish.

Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd? The most astonishing sentence in the chapter, and it should not be smoothed over. These are the same men, the same twelve who, not long before, had each carried a basket of leftovers away from a hillside where five loaves had fed a crowd of much the same size. And they ask the question as though it had never happened.

Two feedings, not one. Some have found this so implausible that they have argued the two feedings must be one story told twice. Jesus himself settles it. A chapter later he asks them whether they remember the five loaves for the five thousand and how many baskets they gathered, and the seven loaves for the four thousand and how many baskets they gathered (16:9–10). He treats them as two events and rebukes the disciples for failing to learn from either. So the implausibility is real, and it is in the men rather than in the record. And that is one of the quiet arguments for the Gospels’ honesty. A writer inventing a movement’s founding generation does not make them look like this. Matthew was one of the Twelve; he is describing his own lapse of memory and putting his name on the book.

How many loaves do you have? As before, Jesus starts with what they have, not with what they lack. No rebuke is recorded here; that will come later, at 16:8–11, and it is sharp. In the moment he simply asks what is in the bag.

They said, “Seven, and a few small fish”. More than last time, and a smaller crowd, and still nothing like enough. They had improved slightly on the arithmetic and not at all on the conclusion.

Why do I forget God’s past help so quickly? Because we are like these disciples. We believe after the miracle and doubt before the next one; each new need feels as if there had never been any previous provision. The remedy Scripture gives is deliberate remembering. Israel was commanded to remember the way the LORD had led them (Deuteronomy 8:2), to set up stones as memorials, to teach their children. The Lord’s Supper is itself a commanded act of remembrance. Keep a record of answered prayers and past mercies, tell them to others, and when a new crisis comes, read them back to yourself before you start to calculate. Faith remembers what grace has done; unbelief only counts what is in the bag.

In a sentence. The disciples, forgetting the earlier miracle, asked where bread could be found, and had only seven loaves and a few fish.

On a Tuesday. Remember God’s past provision when you face new needs. Write down three times he has helped you before, and read them over when you are tempted to panic.

For worship. How patient is the Lord with forgetful people. He did not cancel the second feeding because the disciples had forgotten the first. He asked them gently what they had, and fed the crowd anyway. His mercies are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23), not because our memories are good but because his faithfulness is great.

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told the crowd to sit on the ground. He took the seven loaves and the fish, gave thanks, broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground. As before (14:19). There is no mention of green grass this time; perhaps it was later in the year. The same Shepherd seats his flock.

He took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples. Then the sequence, the same as before and the same as it will be at the Last Supper: took, gave thanks, broke, gave (14:19; 26:26). The second verb here is eucharisteō, giving thanks, rather than the blessing of chapter 14. The two are interchangeable in this pattern, and both appear in the accounts of the Last Supper. It is the word from which the church later took the name Eucharist for the Lord’s Supper. Before he does what only God can do, the Son thanks his Father.

And the disciples gave them to the crowds. Again Jesus works through his disciples. The men who had just asked where bread could possibly come from spent the next hour handing it out. They distribute what they cannot produce. That is the shape of all ministry: the minister is not the source but the channel, and the source is always the one who took, gave thanks, broke and gave.

What it does not mean. Not that this meal was itself the Lord’s Supper, or that the bread became something other than bread. The pattern points forward to the Table, where believers receive Christ spiritually by faith, and backward to the manna in the wilderness. Every meal Jesus gives is a sign of the greater gift of himself.

In a sentence. Jesus gave thanks, broke the loaves, and gave them through his disciples to the crowd.

On a Tuesday. You are one of the disciples who distribute what Christ provides: his word, his comfort, his practical help. You will never be the source; you do not need to be. Whom could you serve today with what he has given you?

For worship. Before the bread was broken, thanks was given, and the Son of God taught Gentiles on a hillside what it is to receive everything from the Father’s hand. One night soon he would give thanks again, over bread that meant his own body, and then go out to be broken. Every crumb that has fed the church since came from that thanksgiving and that breaking.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples gathered seven baskets full of leftover pieces. Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.

And they all ate and were satisfied. Full provision, as before. Everyone ate to the point of stopping.

And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. The two feedings differ in a way that is invisible in English and decisive in Greek, and it answers anyone who says this is the same story twice. At the five thousand, twelve baskets were taken up, and the word is kophinos, a small stiff wicker basket, the sort a Jew carried his own food in when travelling, so as not to depend on Gentile provisions; Roman satirists mocked Jews for going about with one. Here, seven baskets are filled, and the word is spyris, a large hamper, big enough to hold a man. It is the basket Paul was let down the wall of Damascus in (Acts 9:25). Two different objects, consistently used: kophinos every time the five thousand is mentioned, spyris every time the four thousand is, in Matthew and in Mark, and in Jesus’ own recollection at 16:9–10. That is not how a duplicated story behaves. And the numbers may be saying something too. Twelve may recall Israel’s tribes. Seven may suggest completeness, and some have seen in it the seven nations of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:1). Twelve baskets on the Jewish shore; seven on the Gentile one.

Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. Matthew adds the same four words he added at the first feeding (14:21), and both times he is spelling out what the round number leaves out. The actual crowd was very likely eight or ten thousand people, which means the two feedings were closer in size than the round numbers suggest, and the Gentile one was still larger than any town on the eastern shore.

A different event. This is a different event from the feeding of the five thousand, and the details differ throughout: five thousand on the Jewish side and four thousand in the Gentile Decapolis; five loaves and seven; twelve small baskets and seven large hampers; a crowd there for an afternoon and one that had been with him three days. Jesus himself names both separately (16:9–10). Even the disciples’ baffling forgetfulness is not the seam of a clumsy editor but the very thing the text is exposing: the slowness of the human heart to carry yesterday’s grace into today’s need. Two feedings, two peoples, one Lord who is bread enough for Jew and Gentile alike.

The leftovers. Seven hampers of surplus, gathered after everybody had eaten their fill, from seven loaves, in a desolate place, among foreigners. Nothing is said about what happened to them. Somebody, presumably, ate them on the road home, and in a story about a man who did not want people fainting on the way, that may well be the point of gathering them.

What it does not mean. Not that this is a duplicate account of the same miracle. The numbers, place, baskets and audience differ, and Jesus distinguishes them.

Why does it matter that there were two feedings? Because it shows the heart of Jesus is the same for Gentiles as for Jews. The first feeding fed Israel in the wilderness, as the manna had; the second fed the nations, on the far shore, after a Canaanite woman had asked for crumbs and been given far more. Together they say that Christ is the bread of life for the whole world, and that the table of the kingdom has room for every people. If you are not Jewish, this is your feeding. You were the crowd on the far side of the lake, and he would not send you away hungry.

In a sentence. Four thousand men, besides women and children, ate and were satisfied, and seven large baskets were left over.

On a Tuesday. God’s provision overflows. If he has given you more than you need this week, ask who the leftovers are for. And thank him that his table has room for you.

For worship. They all ate and were satisfied, Jew on one shore and Gentile on the other, and there were baskets to spare on both. This is the Lord of the whole earth, the bread of life broken for the world. From every tribe and language and people and nation he is gathering a people to sit down at his table, and there will be enough, and more than enough, for every one.
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets is different from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand, and could mean a large hamper.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After sending the crowds away, Jesus got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.

And after sending away the crowds. This time he dismissed them with their needs met: healed, taught and fed. He sent them away only when they were ready to go.

He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan. An honest note on the place name, since a reader with two Bibles open will find two different words. Matthew has Magadan; Mark has Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10); and some manuscripts of Matthew read Magdala. None can be identified with certainty. The likeliest account is the ordinary one: a stretch of shoreline with more than one landmark on it, named differently by different people, as a traveller today might say he landed at Dover or in Kent. Magdala, the home town of Mary Magdalene, sat on the western shore, and a small harbour there has been excavated. Nothing hangs on it, and Matthew’s geography is not usually vague; this is one obscure landing place on a lake.

The end of an arc. What the verse does mark is the end of a long journey. He left Jewish territory at verse 21 and has not been back since. In between: a Canaanite woman commended for great faith, a mountain of Gentile sick healed without a word, a crowd glorifying the God of Israel, and four thousand men fed with seven hampers to spare. Now he crosses back, and the very first thing that happens on the other side is that the Pharisees and Sadducees come and ask him for a sign (16:1). Matthew sets the two scenes side by side without comment. Gentiles who had nothing glorified the God of Israel on a hillside; the men who had everything met the boat and asked for evidence. The great commission of chapter 28 is not a new idea. It is the conclusion of what these chapters have been showing all along.

In a sentence. Jesus dismissed the crowds and crossed to the region of Magadan.

On a Tuesday. Jesus moved from place to place, meeting needs wherever he went, on both sides of every border. Where might he be sending you this week, and who on the other side of some line you have drawn might be waiting for what you have been given?

For worship. The Lord crossed the lake and crossed the boundaries, and his compassion had no ethnic limit. The boundary between Jew and Gentile that the Pharisees guarded so carefully was already giving way under the feet of the Messiah, who would soon tear it down in his flesh and make the two one new people (Ephesians 2:14–16). Blessed be the Shepherd who has other sheep, and who will not rest until every one of them is home.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Magadan is uncertain; Mark names it Dalmanutha.

15.theology: Total depravity and the need for regeneration. Matthew 15:18–19 is one of the clearest statements of the doctrine of the heart’s corruption in the Gospels. The evil that defiles comes not from outside but from within — from the heart that Jeremiah described as “deceitful above all things” (Jer 17:9). Reformed theology insists that this corruption is total in extent (reaching every faculty) though not infinite in degree (common grace restrains it). The implication is that the solution must be equally radical: not education, not ceremony, not moral effort, but the new heart promised in Ezekiel 36:26 — “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” That is the work of regeneration by the Spirit, purchased by the cross of Christ.
15.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ tradition had become a way of performing piety while avoiding its cost. The Corban ruling let a man appear devout while dishonoring his parents. Religion had become a loophole system. Jesus shut it down.

Now: Every generation finds ways to honour God with the lips while protecting the heart from real submission. Theological correctness without personal holiness, church attendance without costly love, tithing without generosity of spirit — all are versions of the Pharisaic trap. The Canaanite woman is the antidote: no credentials, no performance, just desperate faith in the mercy of Christ. That is always enough.

16.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. <sup>2</sup>He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’ <sup>3</sup>And in the morning, ‘It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. <sup>4</sup>An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” So he left them and departed. <sup>5</sup>When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. <sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>7</sup>And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.” <sup>8</sup>But Jesus, aware of this, said, “O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread? <sup>9</sup>Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>10</sup>Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>11</sup>How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>12</sup>Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” <sup>14</sup>And they said, “Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” <sup>15</sup>He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” <sup>16</sup>Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. <sup>18</sup>And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. <sup>19</sup>I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” <sup>20</sup>Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. <sup>21</sup>From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. <sup>22</sup>And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” <sup>23</sup>But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>24</sup>Then Jesus told his disciples, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>25</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. <sup>26</sup>For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul? <sup>27</sup>For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. <sup>28</sup>Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the turning point of Matthew’s Gospel. Peter’s confession — “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” — is the summit of the disciples’ journey of recognition. Jesus affirms it as divinely revealed, not humanly deduced, and builds the future of his church on this confession. But he immediately turns to the cross: the Christ, the Son of the living God, must go to Jerusalem and die. Peter, who has just made the highest confession of faith in the Gospel, immediately becomes “Satan” — a stumbling block — by refusing the necessity of the cross.

The pairing is deliberate and profound. You cannot confess Jesus as Christ without receiving the cross. Caesarea Philippi was a pagan city at the foot of Mount Hermon, a centre of Roman imperial cult and pagan worship. Here, at the edge of empire and paganism, Jesus declares that he will build his church — and the gates of hell will not prevail. The church is built on the confession, and on Peter only as the first man to make it; and it advances not by cultural power but by the cruciform mission of a cruciform King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Sign of Jonah, Peter's Confession, and the Keys of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven. Jesus refuses, offering only the sign of Jonah, and warns the disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. At Caesarea Philippi he asks the disciples who they say he is, and Peter confesses: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus pronounces a blessing on Peter, declares he will build his church on this rock, and gives him the keys of the kingdom. Then, having accepted the confession, he forbids them to repeat it (v. 20): the title is true, but it is sealed until the cross can say what kind of Christ he is.
verseByVerse.theology: Peter's confession is the christological climax of the first half of Matthew's Gospel. The question Jesus asks — "But who do you say that I am?" — is addressed to the disciples after they have lived with him through chapters 4-15. Peter's answer is the only possible answer for those who have truly seen: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus responds with the foundational promise of the church's existence: "I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." The church does not build itself; it is built by Christ on the confession of who he is. The first half of the section is a study in reading. Men who can forecast weather cannot read the moment they are standing in (vv. 1-4), and the only sign they will get is a grave and an empty tomb. The leaven warning that follows (vv. 5-12) names the two ways a faith is brought under human management: the Pharisees added to God's word until their tradition outranked it, the Sadducees subtracted from it until nothing supernatural was left, and verse 12 calls the two of them one teaching. And the section closes on a deliberate silence (v. 20). The confession is true and the definition in the hearers' heads is false, so the title goes under guard until Jerusalem explains it — and the ban is lifted only when the risen Christ commands the nations to be told (28:19).
verseByVerse.examples: "Who do you say that I am?" is the question every person must answer. The crowds reach for the biggest names they have — John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah — and every one of them belongs to the past and is a forerunner, a signpost rather than a destination. Peter offers the only category that fits the evidence: Messiah, Son of the living God. The confession is the door through which everything else follows — the keys of the kingdom, the binding and loosing, the promise that the church will stand against the gates of hell. The church is not a human institution that may or may not endure; it is Christ's building, constructed on the indestructible foundation of the confession that he is Lord. Two practical edges run through the same section. The leaven warning is spoken to the Twelve about themselves, with no opponent present — it is not a licence to hunt heresy in other people but a question about which way your own faith drifts when nobody is checking: toward a list of things you are careful about, or toward a quiet removal of everything in the Bible that would be awkward to say out loud at work. And the silence of verse 20 is a warning to anyone impatient for results: it is entirely possible to get a man to say the right sentence about Jesus by leaving out what it costs. Our Lord had that option, with a crowd ready to take it, and chose silence instead.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. He answered them, "When it is evening, you say, 'It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees and Sadducees came to test Jesus, demanding a sign from heaven. He answered: in the evening you say, it will be fair weather, for the sky is red.

Meaning first. Matthew 16 is the hinge of the Gospel. It opens with men who can read the sky but not the Son of God standing in front of them, demanding a sign from heaven and being promised only the sign of Jonah: a grave and an empty tomb. It moves to a boat where the disciples, worried about bread, are warned about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, the two ways a faith is brought under human management. Then, at Caesarea Philippi, among pagan shrines and a great rock face, Jesus asks the question on which everything turns, and Peter answers it: you are the Christ, the Son of the living God. On that confession, and on the confessing apostle, Christ promises to build his church, and death itself will not prevail against it. And from that moment he begins to tell them plainly that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and be raised. The man who has just been called blessed tries to stop him and is called Satan, and every disciple is called to deny himself, take up his cross and follow. The chapter shows us who Jesus is, what he came to do, and what it means to belong to him: a crucified King, a church that cannot die, and a life that is found only by being given away for his sake.

And the Pharisees and Sadducees came. Normally rivals (see 3:7), they now join forces against Jesus. The Pharisees were strict about the law and its traditions; the Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who held only the five books of Moses and denied the resurrection. They agreed on almost nothing, and would not normally have been in the same room. Shared opposition to Jesus united them.

And to test him. “Test” (peirazontes) is the word used of the devil tempting Jesus in the wilderness (4:1, 3). Their request was not honest seeking but a trap, and it was the devil’s own kind of request: prove yourself on our terms.

They asked him to show them a sign from heaven. Not another healing, which they had already explained away as the work of Satan (12:24), but a spectacular sign in the sky, something above the argument, too large to be disputed: Elijah calling down fire (1 Kings 18:38), or manna falling again. They had already asked for a sign and been refused (12:38–39). The signs Jesus had given were being dismissed; what they wanted was one that would compel belief without requiring trust.

He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’”. A red sky in the evening meant good weather the next day. Farmers and fishermen read the sky expertly. Jesus begins with something they are good at. The capacity to read signs is not missing in these men; what is missing is the willingness to read the one in front of them.

Textual note. Verses 2b–3 (“When it is evening … the signs of the times”) are missing in some important early manuscripts. A reader with an open Bible will notice the brackets and footnote before he notices anything else, and nobody has told him what to make of it. The facts are these. Two of the oldest and best copies of Matthew, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, do not have these words, nor do several early translations, and Jerome in the fourth century remarked that most of the copies in front of him lacked them. Many later manuscripts do have them. One likely explanation is that a copyist who knew the similar saying in Luke (Luke 12:54–56) filled in what looked to him like a gap in Matthew, the same movement of a scribe’s hand that we meet at Matthew 17:21 and 18:11. Others argue the other way: that copyists in Egypt, where a red morning sky does not forecast a storm as it does in Palestine, dropped a line of weather lore that made no sense where they lived. Verdict: the evidence is divided; the saying is certainly authentic as Jesus’ teaching (Luke has a parallel), whether or not Matthew wrote it here. The ESV includes it.

How much is at stake? Very little, which is the usual outcome of these questions and is worth feeling. Every word of the exchange that carries the weight stands in undisputed text: they came to test him, they demanded a sign from heaven, and he answered that an evil and adulterous generation would be given none but the sign of Jonah. Matthew has already given us the same refusal in full (12:38–39), and the rebuke about reading the sky is beyond dispute in Luke. Not one thing taught in this chapter depends on the answer. The bracket marks a question about a copyist. It does not mark a doubt about the Lord’s words. And it is a mark of the care with which God has preserved his word that we can see the evidence so plainly and lose nothing by it.

In a sentence. Jesus’ united opponents demanded a sign from heaven to test him, and he began by pointing out how well they read the weather.

On a Tuesday. Demanding proof on our terms is not seeking God. If you find yourself saying I would believe if only, ask whether you are gathering evidence or setting conditions. Look at the evidence he has already given: his word, his works, his cross and his empty tomb.

For worship. The Lord who was tested by the devil and by the religious leaders never once performed to order, and never once failed to give what was truly needed. He did not owe his enemies a sign, and yet he gave the greatest sign of all, rising from the dead for the very generation that demanded proof. How patient is the God whose evidence is everywhere, written in the sky they read so well, and written supremely in the Son they would not see.

parallels.desc: reading the sky but not the times

verseByVerse.quote: "And in the morning, 'It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.' You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah." So he left them and departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the morning you say, it will be stormy today, because the sky is red and threatening. You know how to read the sky, but you cannot read the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but none will be given except the sign of Jonah. And he left them.

And in the morning, “It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening”. A red sky in the morning warned of storms. The English proverb says the same: red sky at night, shepherd’s delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd’s warning.

You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. They could read the weather, but not God’s work in history. The signs of the times were all around them: the healings, the feedings, the teaching with authority, the fulfilment of prophecy, the ministry of John. The kingdom had arrived, and they could not see it, because they did not want to (13:13–15). Men who could forecast tomorrow’s weather could not read the moment they were standing in.

An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign. The same words as 12:39. Adultery is an odd charge to bring against men who have asked for evidence. But it is not a charge about their morals; it is a charge about their marriage. Through the prophets God had described his covenant with Israel as a wedding, and every turning to another god as a wife’s unfaithfulness (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3). So the word means that they were bound to God in covenant and were standing in front of his Son asking him to prove himself, the way a wife asks for one more piece of evidence from a husband she has already decided to leave. The request sounds neutral. It is being made from inside a marriage that has already gone cold.

But no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. Matthew has already told us what it is: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (12:40). His death and resurrection. And notice what kind of sign that is. They asked for a sign from heaven, something in the sky, beyond dispute. What they are promised is a sign from underneath: a grave. God answers the demand for overwhelming proof with a corpse and an empty tomb, which is to say he answers it in the one way that cannot be watched from a safe distance. There is a second edge to Jonah too. Nineveh repented at a preacher who gave them no sign whatever, and the men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment beside men who were given every sign and wanted one more (12:41). The greatest sign was coming, and even then the leaders would not believe; they paid the guards to say the body had been stolen (28:11–15).

So he left them and departed. The last six words. He does not argue. He does not perform. He walks away from men who are still standing there waiting to be impressed, and Matthew reports it as flatly as a man closing a door. It is a solemn moment, and it is worth sitting with how quiet a judgment can be. To be contradicted by Christ is a mercy; Peter is about to receive one of the hardest contradictions in the Gospels and be kept. To be left by him is something else entirely. These men got exactly what they had asked for, an end to the conversation, and the getting of it was the punishment. There is a point when God leaves people to their unbelief.

Is it wrong to ask God for a sign? Most believers have at some point said, in a hospital corridor or at two in the morning, Lord, if this is really you, show me something. Is that person under this rebuke? Almost certainly not, and it matters that he knows it. Scripture is not against asking. Gideon asked twice, with a fleece, and was answered twice without reproach (Judges 6:36–40). Ahaz was told to ask for a sign, refused out of false piety, and was given the greatest sign in the Old Testament anyway (Isaiah 7:10–14). In this very Gospel, John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, and received no rebuke, only the evidence and then a public commendation (11:2–11). The difference is never the asking. It is what the asking is for. These men had watched the healings and filed them under demonic power; they were not gathering evidence but auditioning a candidate they had resolved to reject. The frightened believer who asks for help is doing the opposite: he wants the evidence to work. Even so, the normal way God guides and assures us now is through his written word, applied by his Spirit, not through signs. Ask for help, and then open your Bible.

In a sentence. The religious leaders could read the weather but not the signs of God’s kingdom, and Jesus refused them any sign but his resurrection, and left them.

On a Tuesday. Are you skilled at reading the markets, the news, the culture or the politics, and blind to what God is doing? Pray for eyes to see. And if you have been keeping Christ at arm’s length until he proves himself further, consider that the sign you have been given is an empty tomb, and that it asks to be trusted, not merely examined.

For worship. The sign of Jonah is the gospel itself: the Son of Man swallowed by death and given back on the third day. God gave a wicked generation the very sign that would save the world, and he gives it still. Jonah went down into the deep and came up to preach to Nineveh; Christ went down into death and rose to send his preachers to every nation. Blessed be the Lord whose answer to our demand for proof was not a fire from the sky but his own Son, laid in a grave and raised in glory.

verseByVerse.quote: When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. Jesus said to them, "Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples crossed the lake, they had forgotten to bring bread. Jesus said to them: watch out, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. Mark says they had only one loaf with them in the boat (Mark 8:14). After two feedings with baskets to spare, they were down to one loaf, and worried.

Jesus said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees”. Take the picture seriously before taking the point. Leaven in that world was not a sachet bought at a shop; it was a lump of last week’s dough, gone sour, kept back and worked into the new batch. A woman needed only a small piece for a whole baking. Nothing about the process is visible and nothing about it is fast. The dough does not decide to change. It is changed, quietly, from the inside, by something already folded into it before anyone was watching, and by the time the difference can be tasted there is no separating it out again (see 13:33). In Scripture leaven often pictures a corrupting influence that spreads quietly: a little leaven leavens the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Galatians 5:9). At Passover Israel had to remove every trace of leaven from their homes (Exodus 12:15). And the verb is watch: keep watching, a standing habit, not a single inspection. Jesus warns his disciples that the teaching and attitudes of the religious leaders could spread into their own hearts without their noticing.

The guard. This verse is a favourite of the wrong sort of Christian, so one guard. It is not a commission to go looking for heresy in other people. Look at who is being addressed: he says it to the Twelve, about themselves, when there is not a Pharisee in sight. Leaven is not what you detect in someone else’s loaf; it is what is already working in yours. False teaching must be named and resisted in the church, and elsewhere Scripture tells us how. But this warning begins at home.

In a sentence. Jesus warned his disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

On a Tuesday. Wrong ideas spread quietly. What influences are working their way into your thinking without your noticing: the assumptions of your workplace, the tone of what you watch, the voices you scroll past every evening? Name one, and hold it up to Scripture this week.

For worship. The Lord who warns us is the Lord who keeps us. He knows the hidden leaven in our hearts better than we do, and he does not leave us to discover it too late. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), so that the old leaven might be cleaned out and we might keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; it often pictures a corrupting influence.

parallels.desc: a little leaven leavens the whole lump

verseByVerse.quote: And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, "We brought no bread." But Jesus, aware of this, said, "O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples discussed it among themselves: it is because we brought no bread. Jesus, knowing this, said: you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves that you have no bread?

And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread”. Look at what actually happened in that exchange, because it is funnier and sadder than a failure of doctrine. He said one word, leaven, and what they heard was bread. They thought he was rebuking them for forgetting it, or warning them not to buy bread from Pharisees. They were not disputing with him or even disagreeing. They simply were not listening, because their heads were full of an empty bag, and a man with an empty bag hears every subject as a comment on his bag. Whatever he had said that morning was going to come out sounding like lunch. They were thinking on the level of food while he was speaking of the spirit.

The preoccupied mind. That is a test worth running on yourself, and it is uncomfortably easy to run. Think of the last sermon you heard, or the last chapter you read, and ask what it had turned into by the time you reached the car. A man worried about money will hear a sermon on the sovereignty of God and come out thinking about his mortgage. A lonely woman will hear a sermon on the church and come out counting who did not speak to her. This is not wickedness. It is what a preoccupied mind does with everything it is handed, and it is why the Twelve could be given a warning about false teaching and come away discussing catering.

But Jesus, aware of this. Again he knows their thoughts (9:4; 12:25). Nothing said in the boat is hidden from him.

O you of little faith. One word in Greek, oligopistoi, and it is very nearly Matthew’s own word. He uses it of the man anxious about clothing (6:30), of the Twelve in the storm (8:26), of Peter on the water (14:31), here in the boat, and once more at the foot of the mountain (17:20). Notice who receives it every time. It is always disciples. He never once calls a Pharisee a man of little faith. It is a family word, spoken only to people who are already inside. Their worry about bread showed they had not trusted him.

Why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread? After two miraculous feedings, why worry about bread? The Lord of the harvest does not run out.

Does little faith mean I am not really a Christian? No, and this is where the mercy hides. He does not say you of no faith, or you unbelievers, though he has that vocabulary and uses it of other men. He weighed what they had, found it small, said so, and then kept them in the boat, took them north to Caesarea Philippi, and within days called one of them blessed and took three of them up a mountain. Little faith is not a verdict of exclusion. It is a diagnosis delivered by a physician who has no intention of discharging the patient. And notice what the cure turns out to be. He does not tell them to try harder, or to generate more confidence, or to stop feeling anxious. He asks them a question about the past. The opposite of little faith, in this scene, is memory.

In a sentence. The disciples misunderstood Jesus and worried about forgetting bread, and he rebuked their little faith.

On a Tuesday. What practical worry are you discussing endlessly, with your spouse, with yourself at three in the morning, when you could simply bring it to Jesus and trust him with it? Name the bag you are carrying, and give it to him.

For worship. How gentle is the Lord with his little-faith people. He knows our thoughts, he sees our empty bags, he hears us mutter about bread while he speaks of eternal things, and he does not throw us out of the boat. He corrects us, and keeps us, and leads us on. The bruised reed he will not break (12:20), and the smallest faith that clings to him is held by a hand that never lets go.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you still not understand? Don’t you remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?

Do you not yet perceive? The yet implies a growth he expected and had not seen. After all they had seen, they still did not understand.

Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Twelve baskets (14:20). Watch how precisely he makes them do it, because he is not asking for a general feeling of gratitude. He asks two questions with the numbers left in: five loaves, five thousand, how many baskets; seven loaves, four thousand, how many baskets. Those men had carried the baskets. The arithmetic had gone through their own arms. He is not saying remember that I am generous. He is saying count.

Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Seven baskets (15:37). Jesus reminds them of both feedings separately, and Matthew has kept even the detail that the two sets of baskets were different: twelve small hand baskets at the first, seven large hampers at the second, a different word each time. Their memory of God’s past provision should have removed their anxiety. Forgetting what God has done lies at the root of much unbelief: Israel forgot his works and the wonders he had shown them (Psalm 78:11, 42). Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits (Psalm 103:2).

Try the equivalent. Without inventing anything, name three specific things you were genuinely afraid of five years ago, the ones that woke you at night, and say what became of each. Most Christians cannot do it. Not because God did nothing, but because we carry the fears forward and leave the answers behind us on the road. The bag we keep is the one with tomorrow’s worry in it; last year’s rescue is set down somewhere and not picked up again. That is exactly the condition of the men in this boat, and it is why a written page at the back of a Bible, dated and specific, what was asked and what happened, is worth more to a frightened man at three in the morning than a shelf of resolutions.

What if I remember and I am still afraid? Then hold this honestly, or remembering becomes another burden. Remembering is not a technique that makes anxiety disappear; it did not work that way for the Twelve. They will fail again at the foot of the next mountain, and in the end every one of them will run. So a person who does his remembering faithfully and is still afraid has not fallen out of the story; he is standing exactly where the apostles stood. Keep remembering anyway, and pray your fear to God rather than about him (Philippians 4:6–7). And see what their Lord does with a memory as poor as theirs. He puts the question to them, gets no good answer, and then walks them north and asks them who he is, and when one of them gets it right he calls him blessed. He rebuked their memory. He did not revise his plans for them.

In a sentence. Jesus reminded the disciples of both miraculous feedings, to show that they had no reason to worry about bread.

On a Tuesday. Remember how God has provided for you in the past. Recall a specific time today, with the details left in, and write it down. Let it strengthen your trust for the thing you are facing now.

For worship. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Romans 8:32). That is the great memory to which every smaller memory points. The twelve baskets and the seven hampers were only previews of the cross, where God gave the greatest gift of all to people who would forget him by morning. And he remembers us still, every one, by name.

verseByVerse.quote: How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can you fail to understand that I was not talking about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Then they understood that he meant their teaching, not the yeast in bread.

How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Jesus speaks in pictures, and they must learn to think spiritually. And count how often he has to say it. He gives the warning in verse 6. They mishear it. He asks them a string of questions. Then he gives the same warning again in almost the same words, and only after that does Matthew write, then they understood. He repeated himself. He was not too grand to repeat himself, and there is not a syllable in the text suggesting he found it beneath him.

Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He repeats the warning.

Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Their teaching, and it is worth naming what these two teachings actually were, since the men are usually left as vague villains. The Pharisees added. They built a fence of tradition around the law to keep people from breaking it, and the fence ended up outranking the law it was built to protect. Matthew has just shown it working, one chapter back, where a man could dedicate his money to the temple and leave his parents unsupported (15:6). Luke calls their leaven hypocrisy (Luke 12:1), and with it came the demand for signs while rejecting the evidence. The Sadducees subtracted. They held only the five books of Moses, denied the resurrection, denied angels and spirits (Acts 23:8; see them arguing it at 22:23), ran the temple, and had made their working peace with Rome. What is left after that subtraction is a religion with nothing supernatural in it at all, competently administered and politically safe. Mark adds the leaven of Herod (Mark 8:15): political worldliness.

One teaching. Notice the grammar of verse 12, because it carries more than it looks. It does not say the teachings of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees. It says the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees: one warning covering two parties who agreed on almost nothing. That is the diagnosis, and it is sharper than either party alone. Adding to God’s word and subtracting from it arrive at the same place: a faith that has been brought under human management. One puts man’s word alongside God’s; the other takes God’s word out of God’s hands. Either way you end up with a religion no larger than the men running it, which is exactly the size of religion that can demand a sign from heaven and then refuse the one it is given.

Which way do I drift? Both leavens are still in production, and each has a congregation that finds it comfortable. So put the question to yourself rather than to the church down the road. Which way does your own faith drift when nobody is checking? Toward a list of things you are careful about, which you could keep whether or not God were alive? Or toward a quiet, respectable removal of everything in the Bible that would be embarrassing to say out loud at work: miracles, judgment, the exclusive claims of Christ, the parts of his ethics your friends find old-fashioned? Answer honestly. Nobody drifts toward both at once, and almost nobody drifts toward neither. The cure for both is the same: let Scripture be the whole word of God, no more and no less, and let it judge you.

The difference between them. Set the disciples beside the men he had left standing on the shore, because the contrast is the point of the whole passage, and it is not what we would expect. The difference between the Pharisees and the Twelve here is not intelligence, and it is not performance. Both groups failed to read what was in front of them. The Pharisees demanded evidence with the evidence already in their hands; the disciples had watched two crowds fed and were still counting loaves. Measured by results, the score is level. The difference is one thing only: one group could still be told. That is why verse 4 ends with him departing and verse 12 ends with them understanding. He walked away from the closed mind. He stayed in the boat with the slow one.

What it does not mean. Not that every Pharisee or Sadducee taught nothing true. Jesus says elsewhere to do what the scribes teach from Moses, but not what they do (23:2–3). The danger was their characteristic errors, which could spread unnoticed.

How teachable am I? The question to bring away from this is not whether you understand your Bible well. It is what happened the last time somebody showed you that you had a passage wrong: a preacher, a book, a friend who loved you enough to risk it. Not whether you turned out to be right, but whether you could be told. A Christian who is often wrong and always teachable is in the boat. A Christian who is usually right and cannot be corrected is standing on the shore.

In a sentence. The disciples finally understood that Jesus was warning them against the corrupting teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

On a Tuesday. The two main dangers are still with us: legalism, which adds rules and breeds pride, and scepticism, which doubts the supernatural and makes peace with the world. Which one are you more tempted by? Ask someone who knows you well, and listen to the answer.

For worship. Then they understood: three words that cost him a whole conversation, a string of questions and a repetition, and he paid for them without complaint. It is the same patience that will keep this same set of men through a denial, a scattering and a locked room, and that keeps every one of his people still. It ought to make a slow learner love him rather than despair of himself. He does not walk away from those who can still be told; he stays in the boat and teaches them until they see.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that the Son of Man is?" And they said, "Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples: who do people say the Son of Man is? They answered: some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.

Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi. A Gentile city about twenty-five miles (forty kilometres) north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, at one of the sources of the Jordan, about as far from Jerusalem as Jesus ever took his disciples. It had long been a centre for the worship of the Greek god Pan: there was a great cave and spring at the foot of a cliff, with shrines carved into the rock face. Herod the Great built a white marble temple there to Caesar Augustus. His son Philip rebuilt the town and named it Caesarea in honour of Caesar, adding Philippi after himself to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast. So against a backdrop of pagan gods, emperor worship and a great rock, Jesus asks who he is.

Who do people say that the Son of Man is? The turning point of Matthew’s Gospel. Jesus has taught and worked for months. Now he asks what people have concluded. And he uses his own favourite title for himself, Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7 who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom (see 8:20).

Some say John the Baptist. Like Herod (14:2).

Others say Elijah. The prophet whose coming was promised before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5).

And others Jeremiah. Only Matthew mentions Jeremiah; Mark and Luke say only one of the prophets. Of all the names available, why that one? Jeremiah was the prophet who stood in the temple courtyard and told the worshippers that the house they trusted in would be pulled down; who was called a traitor for it and dropped into a cistern; who wept over a city that would not hear him; and who, in the middle of the wreckage, announced a new covenant written on hearts instead of stone (Jeremiah 7; 31:31–34; 38:6). Some Jewish traditions also expected Jeremiah to return before the Messiah. Someone in the crowd had watched Jesus, looked for a category, and reached for the rejected prophet of a doomed temple and a coming covenant. It is the shrewdest guess of the three, and it is nearer the mark than the man who made it can have known, for every part of that description is about to happen.

Or one of the prophets. All were complimentary opinions. People held Jesus in high regard as a great prophet. But none was high enough.

What the answers share. Every one of them belongs to the past. John had been beheaded two chapters ago (14:10); Elijah was taken up centuries before; Jeremiah had been in his grave six hundred years. To account for a living man standing in front of them, the crowd had to go to the graveyard. Nobody alive would do, and no ordinary category was large enough; the best the public could manage was to say that one of the giants must have come back. And they share something sharper still. John was the forerunner. Elijah was the herald. Jeremiah and the prophets pointed forward. Every popular answer makes Jesus the signpost and not the destination, a very great man on the road to someone greater.

What it does not mean. Not that these opinions were wicked. They were honourable, but inadequate. Many today hold similar views: Jesus was a great teacher, a prophet, a good man, a moral genius born ahead of his time, one of the great spiritual figures of history. Look at the shape of them. Every one is warm, every one is respectful, and every one leaves the man who says it with nothing whatever to do on Monday. A signpost asks nothing of you. You admire it and drive on. That is why it will not do to sneer at the crowd. Their answers were reverent, sincere and generous; they were paying him the highest compliment their vocabulary allowed. It is entirely possible to hold Christ in the very highest regard your categories permit, to speak of him with real warmth, and to have missed him altogether, and to be perfectly polite the whole time.

Why is a great teacher not enough? Because Jesus did not leave that option open. A mere teacher does not forgive sins against God (9:2–6), accept worship (14:33), claim to be the only one who knows the Father (11:27), or say he will judge the world (16:27). If those claims are false, he is not a great teacher but a deceived or deceiving one. If they are true, he is far more than a teacher. The one answer that does not fit the evidence is the polite one. When a friend says Jesus was a good man, you can agree warmly, and then ask what they make of the things he said about himself.

In a sentence. At Caesarea Philippi, among pagan shrines, Jesus asked who people thought he was, and the answers, though honourable, all fell short.

On a Tuesday. What do people around you say about Jesus: at work, in your family, online? Listen carefully, without scorn, and notice how often the answers are kind and too small. Be ready, gently, to say who he truly is.

For worship. The crowd went to the graveyard for names to describe him, and none was big enough, because he is not one of the dead come back. He is the living one, who was dead and is alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18). John pointed to him, Elijah heralded him, Jeremiah foretold his new covenant, and all the prophets bore witness to him (Acts 10:43). He is not the signpost. He is where every signpost was pointing.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Sea of Galilee, with a shrine to the god Pan.

parallels.desc: Herod thinks he is John raised

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "But who do you say that I am?" Simon Peter replied, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus asked: but who do you say that I am? Simon Peter answered: you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

But who do you say that I am? Feel the force of the question before the answer. In Greek the pronoun is plural, emphatic and put at the front: you, as against all of them, who do you say that I am? He has let them repeat the opinion of the villages, listened to it, and then swept it off the table. Reported answers will not do. He is asking what these men, who have eaten with him and watched him and been rebuked by him, will now say for themselves. It is not enough to know what others think. Everyone must answer this question personally, and it is the most important question anyone will ever answer.

The question behind every pew. It deserves to be turned round on the reader, because it is the one question in the Bible that a whole lifetime of church attendance can be conducted without ever answering. A man may attend for forty years, recite a creed, sing every hymn, hold every correct sentence about Christ, and hold all of it as information received rather than as something he has ever once said. So run the test, and run it honestly. If the question were put to you with nothing to recite, no creed, no hymn, nobody else’s phrasing to borrow, what would you say? Not what is true. What you would say. And a guard, because that test can be misheard as a demand for eloquence or for feeling. It is neither. Peter’s answer is one short sentence. Nor is it a demand that your life has already caught up with it: this same man is about to be called Satan before the conversation ends, and within a year he will swear in a courtyard that he never knew him. The question is not whether you can say it beautifully. It is only whether it is yours.

Simon Peter replied. As spokesman for the Twelve, as so often.

You are the Christ. The Messiah, the Anointed One, the promised King of David’s line (see 1:1). Not merely a prophet who points to the Messiah, but the Messiah himself, the one all the prophets were pointing to.

The Son of the living God. Not only a title of the Davidic king (Psalm 2:7), but more. The disciples had already confessed him as the Son of God after he walked on the water (14:33); now Peter says it with the full weight of all they have seen. Not a son of God in the general sense in which Israel was called God’s son, but the Son, in a relationship with the Father that belongs to him alone (11:27). And the living God is not a decorative phrase. It is the Old Testament title that sets the true God against dead idols (Joshua 3:10; Psalm 42:2; Jeremiah 10:10), the phrase the shepherd boy threw at a giant when he asked who this man was to defy the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:26). It was especially fitting here, surrounded by the shrines of Pan and the temple of Caesar. Peter confesses that Jesus belongs to the one true, living God as his unique Son.

The same words at the trial. The phrase has one more appearance in this Gospel that should make a reader sit still. At the trial the high priest stands up and says: I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God (26:63). The question is almost word for word what Peter says here. Peter says it and is called blessed; Jesus agrees to it and is condemned to die for it. The very sentence that opens heaven to a fisherman is the sentence that sends the Son of God to a cross. He knew that when he asked the question.

Had Peter not already said something like this? Andrew had told him, we have found the Messiah (John 1:41), and Peter later confessed Jesus as the Holy One of God (John 6:69). Those confessions were real but partial; the disciples’ idea of the Messiah was still shaped by hopes of a political deliverer, as Peter’s rebuke in verse 22 shows. What is new here is the full content, the Son of the living God, given by the Father after all they had seen, and received by Jesus as the foundation of his church.

What it does not mean. Not that Peter fully understood what he said. He immediately showed that he did not understand that the Messiah must suffer (v. 22). But his confession was true, and it was revealed by God.

In a sentence. Peter confessed that Jesus is the Messiah and the Son of the living God.

On a Tuesday. Who do you say Jesus is? Not who your parents, your church or your culture say, but you. Say it to him today, in your own words, in prayer. And if you cannot yet say it, ask him to show you, as the Father showed Peter.

For worship. You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. This is the confession of the whole church in every age, the song of martyrs and children, of apostles and of the thief on the cross. He is the Anointed King whom the prophets longed to see, the eternal Son who shares the Father’s life, the living God come among dead idols and dying men. And he asked the question knowing that the answer would cost him his life. Every time we confess him, we are confessing the one who was condemned for these very words, so that we might be blessed for saying them.

parallels.desc: “you are the Holy One of God”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because no human being revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! “Bar-Jonah” is Aramaic for son of Jonah (John calls his father John, John 1:42; 21:15, perhaps a variant of the same name). Jesus calls him blessed: favoured by God, the word of the Beatitudes (see 5:3). It is the only time in this Gospel that Jesus pronounces a beatitude on a named individual.

For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you. “Flesh and blood” means human beings, human reasoning. Peter did not reach this conclusion by his own cleverness, or because others told him, or by adding up the evidence more carefully than the crowd. The crowd had the same evidence and reached for the graveyard.

But my Father who is in heaven. God revealed it to him. Saving knowledge of Christ is always a gift of God’s grace. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (11:25–27); no one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). True knowledge of Jesus is always given, never achieved.

If faith is a gift, can I take any credit for believing? None at all, and that is the joy of it. If your faith were your own achievement, it would be as fragile as you are, and you could boast of it. Because it was revealed to you by the Father, it rests on his purpose, not your cleverness (Ephesians 2:8–9). That does not make your believing unreal; Peter really spoke, and you really trust. It means that when you confess Christ you are not displaying your insight but receiving his grace. And it is a reason to pray for those who do not yet see: the same Father who opened Peter’s eyes can open theirs.

And I tell you, you are Peter. “Peter” (Petros) means rock or stone. Jesus had given Simon this name when they first met (John 1:42); now he explains it. Peter has said who Jesus is; now Jesus says who Peter is.

And on this rock I will build my church. A wordplay: Petros (Peter) and petra (rock). In Aramaic, which Jesus probably spoke, both would be Kepha (Cephas). What is this rock? The main views:

1. Peter himself. Peter, as the first to confess Christ and the leader of the apostles, is the foundation stone on which Christ builds his church. This fits the wordplay best. It does not exclude the other apostles: the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20; Revelation 21:14), with Peter first among them. Peter did lead the early church: he preached at Pentecost (Acts 2) and opened the door to the Gentiles (Acts 10).
