2. Peter’s confession. The truth Peter confessed, that Jesus is the Christ, is the rock. Many Reformers held this.

3. Christ himself. Christ is the rock and the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8).

The argument from the Greek. Older Protestants often pressed the Greek: you are Petros, a stone, and on this petra, bedrock, I will build, as though Jesus deliberately distinguished the man from the confession. That argument is weaker than it looks, for in Aramaic both words are the one word Kepha, and Petros is masculine only because it has become a man’s name. Honesty admits that Peter himself is most likely the rock. The real answer to Rome is not to deny that, but to see how Peter is the rock. Verdict: the most natural reading is Peter himself, as the confessing apostle, the first stone of the foundation. But this gives no support to the papacy. Nothing in the text speaks of successors, of Rome, or of a supreme authority over the other apostles. Peter’s foundational role, like that of all the apostles, was unique and unrepeatable: a foundation is laid only once. The rock is Peter as the confessor of Christ: Peter and his confession cannot be separated.

The place. Caesarea Philippi gives the words a setting that is hard to forget. Carved into the cliff face at the heart of the city was the cave sanctuary of Pan; a spring surged from within the cave and seemed to disappear into the depths, and some ancient writers spoke of the opening as a way down to the underworld. It is in front of a great rock, crowded with the shrines of dead gods and the temple of a man who was worshipped as a god, that Jesus announces the building of his church on a living confession and declares that the gates of death will not prevail against it. Matthew does not draw out the setting, and we should not lean on it too heavily. But it is hard to stand there without hearing it.

I will build my church. “Church” (ekklēsia) means assembly, the gathered people of God. This is the first time the word appears in the New Testament, and it is on his own lips; it occurs only here and at 18:17 in all four Gospels. The Greek Old Testament used it for the assembly of Israel gathered before God at the mountain (Deuteronomy 4:10). He is not founding a society. He is claiming a very old one and building it on himself. “My” church: it belongs to Christ. “I will build”: Christ himself builds it. The church is his work, not ours. The church does not build itself; it is built by Christ on the confession of who he is.

And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. “Hell” here is Hades, the realm of the dead (ESV footnote), not Gehenna, the place of judgment, which Matthew uses freely elsewhere (5:22; 10:28; 23:33). “Gates” stand for the power of a city, and the gates of Hades is an ordinary Hebrew way of speaking of the power of death itself (Job 38:17; Isaiah 38:10). So the promise is more exact than the slogan, and far better. Death will not overcome Christ’s church. And consider who is saying it: a man who a few verses later tells these same friends that he is going to Jerusalem to be killed, and that on the third day he will be raised. The gates of death will not prevail against his church because they will not prevail against him. Christ, who will rise from the dead, holds the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). His people will be raised; the church cannot be destroyed. It is not a garrison pinned behind its walls; it is the people of the risen Christ, and the gates of death will open before them on the last day.

Where Christians differ: Peter and the papacy. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter the head of the whole church, that Peter was the first bishop of Rome, and that his authority passes to each pope as his successor. Orthodox and Protestant churches reject this. Peter was a leader among the apostles, but Paul rebuked him publicly (Galatians 2:11–14); James led the council at Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21); and Peter called himself a fellow elder (1 Peter 5:1). The New Testament says nothing about successors to Peter’s role or about Rome. Verdict: Peter had a unique foundational role, which no successor inherits. The church’s authority now rests on the apostolic teaching preserved in Scripture.

The Roman case at full strength. Fairness requires the Roman case to be heard properly, because stated in a line it sounds like mere assertion, and it is a great deal better than that. Peter is not prominent by accident of temperament. Matthew numbers him and nobody else: first, Simon, who is called Peter (10:2). He is named more often than all the others together. And three times, in three different Gospels, our Lord speaks to him alone in terms he uses of no one else: here he is given a new name and the keys; in the upper room he is told that Jesus has prayed for him in particular, and that when he has turned again he is to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:31–32); and by the lakeside after the resurrection he alone is charged three times to feed the sheep (John 21:15–17). Rock, keys, shepherd. Then comes the strongest piece: a foundation is not an event but a permanent fact. If Christ founded a visible church on a man, and that church is to stand until he returns, then surely the office outlives the man who first held it, as offices do in Scripture, from Moses to Joshua, from Aaron to his sons, and from Judas to Matthias, chosen so that another might take his office (Acts 1:20).

The answer. That is a serious argument and it deserves better than a slogan. Three things answer it. First, the one apostolic vacancy the New Testament actually fills is filled on a condition that closes the category. The replacement had to be a man who had been with them from John’s baptism to the ascension, and a witness of the resurrection (Acts 1:21–22). Only one generation could ever meet that. And when James the brother of John is put to the sword a few chapters later, nobody replaces him at all (Acts 12:2). The New Testament’s own precedent for apostolic succession is a door that shuts by design. Second, the foundation argument proves less than it needs to. Grant that a foundation is permanent; that is the Protestant point. But Paul says the household is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). If a permanent foundation required a living succession of foundation stones, we should need successors to the prophets too, and nobody argues that. A foundation is permanent by staying laid, not by being laid again every generation. The apostles hold the church up still, and we meet them where they are: in what they wrote. Third, everything the New Testament singles Peter out for is a first, not a permanence: first to confess, first to preach when the Spirit fell, first through the door into Samaria and into a Gentile house. A man who opens a door has done something that by its nature cannot be done twice, and there is no office in being the man who went first. And most telling of all, five verses on, this same rock is called Satan. The honour is real, and it is grace; but it is the honour of a forgiven confessor, not the founding of a throne.

If the church cannot be defeated, why do churches close? This has to be said carefully, because a confident sentence here sits one step from a cruelty. This is a promise about the church, and it is not a promise that your congregation or your denomination will survive. Congregations close. Denominations grow proud and cold and are buried. Seven churches in Asia received letters from the risen Christ himself, and not one of them exists today; Ephesus had Paul for three years and John in his old age, and its lampstand was removed as it had been warned (Revelation 2:5). So if you have watched your own fellowship shrink to nine people and then to none, and quietly wondered whether this verse failed, be told plainly that it did not, and that nothing here is aimed at you. What is guaranteed is that Christ will never be without a church, that he is the one building it, and that death will never get the doors shut. Two thousand years on, having outlived every empire that set out to finish it, the promise has held in precisely the terms it was made.

In a sentence. Jesus blessed Peter for a confession revealed by the Father, and promised to build his church on Peter, the confessing apostle, a church that death itself cannot overcome.

On a Tuesday. Christ is building his church, and nothing can destroy it. When you are discouraged about the church, its failures, its smallness, its quarrels, remember whose church it is and who is building it. Then take your place in it: a living stone in a real congregation, not a spectator of the building site.

For worship. I will build my church: the Lord of glory has staked his own name on a people. He is the cornerstone, chosen and precious; he laid the foundation in the apostles and their confession; he is laying living stones on it still, from every nation; and he went down through the gates of death and came out again, so that those gates can never hold his people. Every empire that ever threatened his church is a ruin now. His church is still singing, and on the last day it will be presented to him in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27).
verseByVerse.note: Bar-Jonah means “son of Jonah.” Peter means “rock.” The ESV notes that “hell” here renders Hades, the realm of the dead; its gates stand for the power of death. A play on words: “Peter” (Petros) and “rock” (petra) are closely related Greek words.

parallels.desc: built on the foundation of the apostles

verseByVerse.quote: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will have been loosed in heaven. Then he strictly told the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.

I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Keys represent authority: to open and shut, to admit and exclude. Every phrase here has a history behind it, and without the history the keys are only a metaphor. Isaiah 22 is the passage in view, and it is a small domestic drama. Shebna is steward over King Hezekiah’s household, a self-important official caught cutting himself a splendid tomb in the rock, and God announces that he will be removed and another man, Eliakim, installed. The words of installation are these: I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open (Isaiah 22:22). The key was a large thing carried on the shoulder, worn where everyone could see it, the badge of the office. And note what the office is. The steward is not the king. He is the man who runs the king’s house and decides who is brought into the king’s presence. And the risen Christ takes that very sentence for himself: the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut (Revelation 3:7). The key is his. He hands a servant the use of it. He does not hand over the house.

Peter using the keys. Jesus gives Peter authority to open the kingdom to people, and Luke shows him using it. A key opens a door, and Peter opens three. At Pentecost he preaches and three thousand Jews enter (Acts 2:14–41). In Samaria the half-caste neighbours whom no respectable Jew would eat with are let in (Acts 8:14–17). On a rooftop in Joppa he is argued out of a lifetime’s revulsion, walks into a Gentile house, and the door to the nations stands open from that day to this (Acts 10). Three doors, each opened once and never needing to be opened again. By the council of Acts 15 it is James who sums up and gives the ruling, and after that chapter Peter disappears from Luke’s account. That is not the career of a man administering a permanent office. It is the career of a doorkeeper who has finished with the doors. The keys are the preaching of the gospel, which opens the kingdom to those who believe and shuts it to those who refuse. The scribes, by contrast, shut the kingdom in people’s faces (23:13).

The Isaiah argument. This is where the Roman argument is at its most impressive. Isaiah 22 is about a post, not a man: Shebna is removed and Eliakim installed, and the stewardship continues while the king’s house continues. So, the argument runs, if Jesus reached for this text, he instituted a stewardship that is filled again when its holder dies. But the oracle does not end where the argument stops quoting it. Three verses later the picture is reversed: the peg fastened in a secure place will give way, and be cut down and fall, and the load on it will be cut off (Isaiah 22:25). On the usual reading, Eliakim himself comes down and takes the household with him. That is a strange charter for an office that cannot fail. Isaiah gives a stewardship with the steward’s collapse written into the same paragraph, which is exactly what happens here, four verses later, when the man holding the keys is called Satan.

And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven. “Bind” and “loose” were rabbinic terms meaning to forbid and permit, and also to condemn and acquit. The Greek tense is a future perfect: “shall have been bound in heaven”. The apostles do not decide things that heaven then must follow; they declare on earth what God has already decided in heaven. Their authority is to declare God’s will, not to create it. Some reply that the construction is an idiom and will not bear so much weight, and the grammar alone may not settle it. But the rest of the New Testament settles the direction, because the apostles never once invent terms of admission. Peter at Pentecost does not decide who may be saved; he tells a crowd what God has done and what they must do about it. The key does not make the door. It opens the one the King built.

And whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. To declare what is permitted, and to pronounce forgiveness to those who repent (John 20:23).

The same authority given to all. In 18:18, Jesus gives the same authority to bind and loose to all the disciples, and to the church in its discipline. After the resurrection the authority to forgive and to retain is breathed on the gathered disciples together (John 20:23). Whatever the keys are, Jesus distributes them almost at once. The keys belong to the church as a whole, exercised through the preaching of the gospel and the discipline of the church (Westminster 30.2). Churches order this differently: some through elders, some through the gathered congregation with its elders, and the confessions differ on the details. All agree that the keys work only through the word.

What this means on an ordinary Sunday. It sounds remote until you see where it lands. When a church hears someone confess Christ, baptises him and receives him to the Lord’s Table, it is not offering an opinion about his prospects; it is doing on earth a thing Christ authorised, and heaven is not indifferent to it. When a church, after long patience, must finally tell an unrepentant member that his life and his profession no longer agree (18:15–17), that is not a committee being unkind; it is the same key turned the other way, in the hope of his return. This is why belonging to a real congregation is not an optional extra for people who happen to like institutions: the keys were given to a church, not to individuals with Bibles and strong opinions. And it is why the keys are terrible in the wrong hands, which is the substance of what the Reformers said when forgiveness was being sold at a church door. The abuse of the keys does not abolish them. It makes their right use urgent.

Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. This looks like an anticlimax and is nothing of the kind. He has just called Peter blessed for saying it, and now forbids them to say it to anybody. Why put a true confession under guard? Because the word was true and the definition in the hearers’ heads was false. Christ, in Galilean mouths, meant a son of David with an army who would clear the Romans out of the country (see 8:4; 14:22). Say that word in a village and you do not gather disciples; you start a rising. The disciples themselves did not yet understand that the Messiah must suffer and die (v. 21). A man misunderstood in silence can still be explained later; a man acclaimed on the wrong terms cannot, because every cheer makes the correction more expensive. Only after the cross and resurrection could the title be proclaimed without misunderstanding.

The seal lifted. Look at the very next verse, where the seal and the explanation arrive together: silence imposed in verse 20, and in verse 21 he begins for the first time to tell them plainly that he must go to Jerusalem and be killed. Nor does the seal stay on. At the trial, put on oath and asked whether he is the Christ, the Son of God, he answers openly (26:63–64), because by then the cross is close enough that the word cannot be misheard. And after the resurrection the charge is reversed: go and make disciples of all nations (28:19). What was forbidden in a Galilean village is commanded to the ends of the earth. There is a warning in that sequence for anyone impatient for results. It is perfectly possible to get someone to say the right sentence about Jesus by leaving out what it costs, and to count the sentence as a conversion. Our Lord had that option, with a crowd ready to take it, and chose silence instead.

What it does not mean. Not that a church or minister can forgive or condemn arbitrarily. The keys work only in line with God’s word. Nor does it support the Roman Catholic doctrine of papal authority or priestly absolution as an independent power.

Can my pastor forgive my sins? Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7), and he does so through Christ, when we repent and believe. What a minister can do, and must do, is declare that forgiveness with authority: tell a repentant sinner, on the basis of God’s word, that his sins are forgiven in Christ. That declaration is not a power of its own; it is the gospel spoken to you personally, and it is meant to be believed. You do not need a priest to confess to before God will hear you; you may go straight to him through Jesus (1 John 1:9; Hebrews 4:16). But there is real help in confessing to a trusted fellow believer and hearing God’s promise spoken aloud (James 5:16).

In a sentence. Jesus gave Peter the keys of the kingdom: authority to open it by the gospel and to declare on earth what God has decided in heaven.

On a Tuesday. Every time you share the gospel, you are using the keys: opening the kingdom to those who will believe. Whom could you tell this week what God has done in Christ? And if you have drifted from a local church, ask whether you have left the place where Christ put the keys.

For worship. The key of David is in the hand of Jesus, and what he opens no one can shut. He opened the kingdom of heaven to all believers by his death, and he opens it still, through the plain preaching of his gospel, to Jews and Samaritans and Gentiles, to people like us. No council can shut out one whom he has let in, and no power on earth or under it can unlock a door he has closed. He is the King of the house and its door (John 10:9), and he keeps it open for every sinner who comes.
verseByVerse.note: Keys give authority to open and shut. “Bind” and “loose” were used of forbidding and permitting.

parallels.desc: the key of the house of David
the same authority given to all the disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — The First Passion Prediction and the Call to Cross-Bearing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the moment of Peter's confession, Jesus begins to teach that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day. Peter rebukes him; Jesus rebukes Peter with the sharpest words in the Gospel: "Get behind me, Satan!" He then calls the crowd and disciples to cross-bearing: whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. The section ends with a warning about the coming of the Son of Man in his Father's glory. Between the two he asks what a man could possibly hand over in exchange for his soul (v. 26), and he closes by promising that some standing there will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (v. 28) — a promise kept six days later on the mountain, as one of the men who heard it says himself (2 Pet 1:16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The first passion prediction marks the watershed of Matthew's Gospel: the confession at Caesarea Philippi is the turning point from which Jesus now sets his face toward Jerusalem. The cross is not an unexpected tragedy but the appointed path. Peter's rebuttal — "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you" — is the most natural human response and the most spiritually dangerous: it substitutes human preferences for divine purpose. "You are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men" is the diagnosis of every theology that wants a cross-free Christianity. The section then puts a price on the choice. Verse 26 is a market question — what sum would buy back a soul? — and it is left unanswered until 20:28, where the Son of Man gives his own life as the ransom no man could pay. Verse 27 supplies the frame: he will repay each person according to what he has done. That is not a scoreboard, for Matthew twice rules one out — the impressive workers of 7:21-23 are turned away because they were never known, and the sheep of 25:31-46 cannot remember their own good deeds. Works are the evidence of a righteousness received, never the ground of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The cross-bearing saying moves from Jesus's cross to the disciple's: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me." The disciple's cross is not their personal hardships and inconveniences; it is the public cost of standing with a man under sentence, and the losing of a life organised around self-interest in order to find one organised around Christ. The paradox of verse 25 — finding life through losing it — is the gospel in miniature: the life surrendered to Jesus is the life truly found. Verse 26 makes the same point as a transaction. Ask a man what he would take for his car and he names a figure; ask what he would take for his son and he refuses the category outright. There is one thing in his possession that no market will quote, and it is himself. And verse 28 shows how this Master treats frightened followers: the cross-bearing call is issued on a Monday, so to speak, and by the following week three of them have been taken up a mountain and shown what the road ends in. The order of those two events is the mercy in them, and it is set out at vv. 23-24.

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From then on, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised. Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him: far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.

From that time Jesus began. The second great turning point in Matthew. The same phrase opened his public ministry: from that time Jesus began to preach, repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand (4:17). Now it opens his teaching about the cross. From here on, Jesus’ face is set toward Jerusalem.

To show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem. “Must” (dei): it is necessary, by God’s plan. Not an accident or a tragedy, but the purpose for which he came: to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). The Scriptures required it (26:54; Luke 24:26). He was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

And suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes. The three groups who made up the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council. The leaders of God’s people would reject God’s Messiah. The builders would reject the stone (21:42).

And be killed. A shocking statement. The Messiah was expected to conquer, not to die.

And on the third day be raised. The resurrection is part of the plan from the start, not an afterthought. Suffer, be killed, be raised: the three stages are specific, and the third is in the first announcement. Jesus predicted his death and resurrection three times (16:21; 17:22–23; 20:18–19). The disciples heard the death, but apparently not the resurrection.

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. Peter, who had just confessed Jesus as the Christ, now presumes to correct him. He took hold of him and drew him aside. “Rebuke” is a strong word, the word Jesus uses against demons and the wind (8:26; 17:18): he scolded him. The man who confessed the Son of the living God is now trying to redirect the living God from his stated purpose.

Far be it from you, Lord! Literally mercy to you, meaning God forbid!

This shall never happen to you. Peter loved Jesus and could not bear the thought of his death. And his idea of the Messiah had no room for suffering. A Messiah who dies is a defeated Messiah.

Ninety seconds. Hold the two halves of this conversation together, because the distance between them is very short. In verse 16 Peter says the most exalted sentence any human being has said so far in this Gospel, and Jesus tells him no man taught it to him; the Father did. In verse 23 the same man, in the same conversation, is called Satan. Same afternoon, same mouth, and no interval in which he might have gradually declined. That ought to reorganise how a Christian reads his own life. Revelation received does not immunise you against the next hour. The highest moment and the worst are not separated by decades in most people; they turn up in the same week, and sometimes in the same conversation. If your walk with God consists of genuine heights followed by collapses that embarrass you, you have not discovered that you are a special case. You have discovered that you are Peter, and Peter is the normal one.

Love that tempts. Look at where the collapse came from, because it is not where we expect. Peter is not being wicked here. He is being protective. Far be it from you, Lord is affection talking; it is what you say to someone you love who has just told you he is going to die. That is precisely what makes it dangerous. The worst advice most of us ever receive comes from people who love us and cannot bear to see us suffer, and the worst advice we give ourselves is nearly always dressed as care. Satan did not need to find an enemy for this errand. A devoted friend did it for him, sincerely, out of love, within a minute of a God-given confession.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was a victim of circumstances. He went to the cross willingly, by the Father’s plan. No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:17–18; Acts 2:23).

Why did Jesus have to die? Could God not simply forgive? God is merciful, and he is also just. He cannot pretend sin does not matter, any more than a good judge can wave away a crime. The Old Testament sacrifices taught Israel that sin brings death and that forgiveness comes through a substitute’s blood (Leviticus 17:11). Jesus is the true substitute. He bore the penalty our sins deserved, the curse of God’s law, in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24), so that God might be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). That is why he must go to Jerusalem. The must is not a cruel necessity laid on him from outside; it is the necessity of love determined to save sinners without denying justice.

In a sentence. Jesus began to teach that he must suffer, die and rise, and Peter, who could not accept it, rebuked him.

On a Tuesday. Do you want a Christ without a cross, a Christianity without suffering? Peter did. Accept God’s way, even when it is not yours. And when someone who loves you urges you away from a costly obedience, listen kindly, and then ask whether their advice is setting its mind on the things of God or of man.

For worship. He must go, and he went. The Son of God set his face toward Jerusalem knowing every step of what waited there: the elders, the scourge, the nails, the grave. No friend’s pleading turned him aside, because he loved his friends too much to spare himself. And the third day was in the plan from the first word. Blessed be the Lord whose must was our salvation, and whose road to the cross ran on, past it, to the empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: But he turned and said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man." Then Jesus told his disciples, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turned and said to Peter: get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, because you are thinking not as God thinks, but as people think. Then he told his disciples: anyone who wants to follow me must deny himself, take up his cross and follow me.

But he turned and said to Peter, Get behind me, Satan! Astonishing words, minutes after Jesus called Peter blessed. The sharpest rebuke in the Gospel, directed at the man just named the rock. Peter was speaking Satan’s words: the same temptation Satan offered in the wilderness, the crown without the cross (4:8–10). Jesus used almost the same words then: Be gone, Satan! Satan can use even a loving friend to tempt us. “Get behind me” may also mean: get back in your place as a follower, behind me, not in front, not steering.

You are a hindrance to me. “Hindrance” is skandalon, a stumbling block, a trap. A wordplay: Peter, the rock on which the church would be built, has become a stone to trip over. The same stone can be a foundation or an obstacle, depending on whether it stays where Christ has put it.

For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man. Peter was thinking by human standards: success, safety, power, a Messiah who wins without bleeding. God’s way was the way of the cross.

Severity and commitment together. Watch what Jesus does with him, because this is the part that carries a reader through the rest of his life. He rebukes Peter about as hard as anyone is rebuked in the Gospels, and he does not dismiss him. Six days later Peter is one of the three taken up the mountain (17:1). He will go on to deny his Lord outright, with oaths, in a courtyard, and will be restored and commissioned by a charcoal fire (John 21:15–19). Full severity and unbroken commitment, held together at the same moment. We find that combination almost impossible to imagine, which is why we keep expecting our failures to end the relationship. They did not end his. Do not read your worst moment as your verdict.

Then Jesus told his disciples, “If anyone would come after me”. Not only for the Twelve, but for anyone. Discipleship is defined. And note the order of the three commands, and who gives them: deny, take up, follow, and the following is behind him, on a road he walks first. He is not asking for anything he declined to do himself.

Let him deny himself. Not deny himself things (like chocolate in Lent), but deny his self: say no to self as the master of his life. Matthew tells you exactly what the word means, because he uses it again in this Gospel for the most famous denial in history. It is the word for what Peter does in the courtyard when he says I do not know the man (26:70–74). To deny is to disown, to refuse to be identified with, to decline to take someone’s side. So to deny yourself is to do to your own claims what Peter did to Jesus: to hear the demand of your own comfort, your own reputation, your own being in the right, and answer, I do not know him. Not to despise yourself. To stop automatically taking your own side. Peter would later deny Jesus; disciples must deny themselves instead. For what this does and does not mean in daily life, see the note on dying to self at Philippians 3:10.

And take up his cross. Like a condemned man carrying his crossbeam to execution (see 10:38). The phrase has been flattened until it means a chronic complaint, a difficult relative, a job you dislike, anything one has to put up with. Hear it as the men on that road heard it. A man carrying a crossbeam through a town was not carrying a burden; he was walking to his own execution, in public, and everyone who saw him knew he was not coming back. A cross is not a weight you carry. It is a death you have agreed to: a willingness to die, to self and if necessary physically, for Jesus.

Is my illness my cross? Not in the sense Jesus means, and the distinction is worth keeping. Your illness, your difficult marriage, your bad back, your awkward colleague, your ageing parents: these are afflictions, and Scripture has a great deal to say about them, and God is deeply present in them. But your cross is the specific cost of following Jesus, the thing you would not be bearing if you were not his. The promotion refused because the figures would have to be wrong. The relationship ended because it could not continue in obedience. The truth told when silence would have been cheaper. The money given that you had other plans for. The reputation you have quietly lost among people whose good opinion you wanted. The reason for insisting on this is not pedantry. Calling an ordinary hardship a cross is a way of feeling that discipleship is costing us something when it may be costing us nothing at all. Luke adds one word that settles the shape of it: daily (Luke 9:23). It is not one dramatic renunciation, remembered for years. It is a small repeated decision, most of which nobody sees.

And follow me. Walk behind him, on the road he walks, which leads to the cross and through it to resurrection. And see the mercy of the arrangement in this very chapter: he says all this, and six days later he takes three of them up a mountain and lets them see the far side of it. He does not ask anyone to carry a cross on bare instruction. He shows them the glory first.

What it does not mean. Not that self-denial earns salvation, or that Christians should hate themselves. Self-denial is the response of those who have been loved and saved. Nor does it mean that Peter was demon-possessed or not a true disciple. He was a true disciple who, in that moment, spoke Satan’s thoughts.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked Peter for speaking Satan’s temptation to avoid the cross, and called every disciple to deny himself, take up his cross and follow.

On a Tuesday. Where do you need to say no to yourself today in order to follow Jesus? Look for the moment when your comfort, your reputation or your need to be right demands a hearing, and answer it as Peter answered the servant girl: I do not know him. Then follow, one step behind your Lord.

For worship. He never asks us to go where he has not gone first. The Lord who called us to deny ourselves denied himself all the way to the cross; he did not please himself (Romans 15:3). The one who told us to take up a cross carried his own, out of the city, to the place of the skull, and died on it for the very disciples who could not bear the thought. And the road behind him does not end at the cross. It ends where his ends: in resurrection and glory, at the Father’s right hand.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever wants to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for Jesus’ sake will find it. What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses his soul? What can he give in exchange for his soul?

For whoever would save his life will lose it. “Life” (psychē) means the self, the soul, life itself. Those who try to protect their life, comfort and success by avoiding the cross will lose what matters most (see 10:39). Self-preservation destroys.

But whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Those who give up their lives for Christ will find true and eternal life. Self-surrender, for him, saves.

One word, four times. Read it in Greek and the two verses close up into a single argument. Life in verse 25 and soul in verse 26 are the same word, psychē, and it occurs four times in three sentences. Our English versions change the word halfway through, and the change hides the logic. He is not moving from a point about earthly life to a separate point about eternal souls. He is running one word through one argument: the self you clutch, you lose; the self you hand over, you get back; the self cannot be bought at any price; and there is not a second one available for another attempt. You have one self, and every day you are spending it on something.

For my sake. Before that is applied, one guard, because the sentence is regularly used to bully decent people. Nothing here forbids ambition. A person is not more spiritual for wanting less; Scripture tells him to work well, provide for his household and be good at what he does. And note the three words that keep this from being a general commendation of sacrifice: for my sake. Jesus does not praise losing your life as such. People lose their lives for a country, a company, a cause, a reputation, and lose them altogether. The clause that turns a loss into a finding is not the size of the sacrifice but the name of the person it is made for. Self-denial is not the point of Christianity. He is.

For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? A business question: what is the profit? Imagine gaining everything the world offers: wealth, power, fame, pleasure. If you lose your soul, you have made the worst trade in history. The devil offered Jesus the whole world (4:8–9); Jesus refused.

Or what shall a man give in return for his soul? The word behind in return is antallagma, the sum handed over in an exchange, the price. So he is inviting a bid: name the figure. And the terrible thing about the question is not that the price is high; it is that there is no price at all. Everything else a man owns converts into something else. A house converts into money, money into time, time into comfort. There is exactly one item in his possession that no market will quote, and it is himself. Nothing can buy back a lost soul. Psalm 49:7–9 says that no one can ransom another, for the ransom of their life is costly. Only Christ can pay that price (20:28).

The four-second test. Ask a man what he would take for his car, and he names a figure. His house, and he names a figure, perhaps after a pause. Ask him what he would take for his son, and the question stops being a question: he does not calculate slowly and arrive at a large number; he refuses the whole category, and is offended that it was raised. Jesus is saying that this is what a soul is, and that most people who would be outraged by the second question have been quietly answering the first one about themselves for years, at rates they would be ashamed to write down.

The answer to the question. Left there, it is a lecture on prudence. Matthew does not leave it there. The question of verse 26 is asked and not answered, and four chapters later the same Gospel supplies the only answer ever given: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). The word for the life he gives is psychē, the same word as here, and the ransom is the price paid to buy a person out. So the question stands unanswered for four chapters and then the questioner answers it himself, and not with a sum. He knew the arithmetic when he asked. He knew that no one in that circle, and no one since, had anything in his hands worth a single soul, and that every one of them had already sold his own cheaply and could not buy it back. And knowing it, he walked from this conversation to Jerusalem, carried the price to the counter himself, and paid it in the only currency the exchange would accept, which was his own life.

How do I know if I am trading my soul? Not usually by one dramatic bargain, but by a hundred small ones. Ask what you will not give up for Christ; that is where your price is set. Ask what you think about when your mind is free, what you would be most devastated to lose, what you sacrifice your time with God and your family for. If the answer is a career, an image, a relationship, a comfort, take it to Christ honestly. The remedy is not to despise those good things but to hold them under him, and to receive them back from his hand. And if you see that you have been selling yourself cheaply for years, the good news is in verse 26’s answer: Christ came to buy back exactly such people.

In a sentence. Those who cling to their lives lose them, and those who give them up for Christ find them, because nothing in the world is worth one’s soul, and only Christ could pay its ransom.

On a Tuesday. What are you trading your soul for: a career, a relationship, comfort, the approval of people who will not remember you in fifty years? Count the cost honestly, on paper if it helps. Then spend one hour this week on something only Christ will ever repay.

For worship. The One who warned men not to sell themselves for the world is the One who bought them when they already had. He gave his own soul as the price for ours, and the Father accepted the payment, and raised him from the dead to prove it. There is no other transaction like it in the universe, and the church has never got over it. You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20): not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19).

parallels.desc: the ransom of a life is costly

verseByVerse.quote: For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of Man is going to come with his angels in his Father’s glory, and he will repay each person according to what he has done. Truly, some standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.

For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father. The one who must suffer (v. 21) will come in glory. The suffering Servant is also the glorious Judge of Daniel 7:13–14 (see 8:20). The cross and the glory are not alternatives; the glory comes through and because of the cross. And this is the frame for the call to carry a cross: nothing spent on him will be lost.

And then he will repay each person according to what he has done. From Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12: God judges each person according to their works. At the final judgment, Christ will judge (25:31–46). Our works will show whether we truly followed him (7:21–23).

Judgment by works? An honest Protestant reader stops dead at this clause. Judgment by works, on the lips of Jesus, in the same paragraph as the cross. Say the awkward thing first: the New Testament teaches this everywhere and never apologises for it, and Matthew insists on it most of all: the men turned away in 7:21–23, the account rendered for every careless word in 12:36–37, the sheep and the goats separated by what was and was not done in 25:31–46. The resolution is not a softening of the words but a question about what a court is for. Two different questions are asked at any trial: on what ground is this person received, and what was this person actually like? Righteousness is received and never earned; that is settled at the cross. But a righteousness that has been received always shows, and faith in itself is invisible. God does not hold an invisible judgment. The deeds are the visible form of the thing, produced in evidence, the way a man’s handwriting is produced to show whose hand it was.

Not an audit. Matthew rules out a scoreboard twice over, in two scenes that should be read together. In 7:21–23 the people rejected are not rejected for a low total; their works are impressive, prophecies and exorcisms and mighty deeds, and the verdict against them is not that they did too little but that they were never known: I never knew you. Works could not supply the relationship. In 25:31–46 the sheep are astonished by their own record and cannot remember any of it: when did we see you hungry? On a scoreboard, nobody is surprised by his own score. Together those scenes tell you what kind of judgment this is. It is not an audit. It is a recognition.

Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. A puzzling verse, and one of those most often produced as proof that Jesus was mistaken. Read flatly, it sounds like a dated prediction that failed: he promised to return before his hearers died, and they died, and he did not come. “Taste death” means die. What coming did Jesus mean? Several views:

1. The transfiguration. Six days later, three of the disciples saw Jesus in his glory (17:1–8). All three Synoptic Gospels place this saying immediately before the transfiguration, suggesting a link. Peter later described the transfiguration as seeing the power and coming of the Lord Jesus Christ (2 Peter 1:16–18).

2. The resurrection and ascension. Jesus received all authority and came into his kingly reign (28:18).

3. Pentecost and the spread of the church. The kingdom came with power (Mark 9:1).

4. The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. A coming in judgment within that generation (24:34).

Coronation, not arrival. The phrase itself matters. The Son of Man coming in his kingdom is throne-room language borrowed from Daniel, where the figure moves toward the Ancient of Days to be crowned, rather than toward earth to be seen (Daniel 7:13–14). So the sentence need not be about the last day at all. Matthew puts the same question before us twice more, at 10:23 and at 24:34, and answers it in both. And the objection usually pressed against the transfiguration reading deserves an answer: if Jesus meant an event six days away, why speak so solemnly of some not tasting death, as though the interval were long? First, the emphasis falls on some: he has just spoken of the last day in verse 27, and now he distinguishes; that day is not what you are about to see, but a few of you are about to see something of it. Second, all three Gospels place the saying right before the transfiguration and then date the transfiguration to the following week, which is as loud a piece of arrangement as the Evangelists ever make. Third, and best, one of the men standing there tells us what he thought he had seen. Writing near the end of his life, Peter defends the promise of Christ’s coming by appealing to that mountain: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, for we were with him on the holy mountain (2 Peter 1:16–18). The man who heard the promise cites its fulfilment. Verdict: the transfiguration is the first fulfilment: a preview of his glory seen by some of those standing there. His resurrection and enthronement are the full reality the transfiguration previewed. On any view, Jesus was not mistaken about his return: he was speaking of events within his disciples’ lifetimes.

The timing of the promise. See what kind of word this is, coming where it comes. These men have just been told that their Master is going to Jerusalem to be killed and that they must take up a cross behind him. It is the bleakest hour of their training. Into it he drops a promise: before you die, some of you are going to see who I really am. He gives three of them a look at the far side of the cross first.

What it does not mean. Not that we are saved by our works. Christ will judge according to works, as the evidence of faith or unbelief (see 7:21). Those who are in Christ are judged as forgiven, and their works, imperfect as they are, will be graciously rewarded.

Should the judgment frighten me? Look at whom he is saying it to. These are men who could not follow a warning about bread that morning, one of whom has just been called Satan and will in due course deny him with oaths. He tells them about the judgment not to terrify them but to steady them, as the reason they can afford to lose their lives: the Son of Man is coming in his Father’s glory, and nothing spent on him will be mislaid. A believer who examines his own deeds and finds them thin has not thereby discovered that he is lost. There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The question at that day is not how much was done. It is whose you were, and the deeds are only how that shows. If you belong to him, the Judge is your Saviour, and his coming is your hope. If you do not, the right response to this verse is not despair but to come to him today, while the door is open.

In a sentence. The suffering Son of Man will come in glory to judge everyone, and some of the disciples would see a preview of his kingly glory before they died.

On a Tuesday. Live today as one who will stand before Christ the Judge, and as one who belongs to him. Do one thing this week that only makes sense if he is really coming back: a gift no one will repay, a kindness no one will see, a truth spoken that costs you.

For worship. The Son of Man who went to the cross is coming in the glory of his Father with all his angels, and every eye will see him. The one who was judged in our place will sit as Judge, and those who are his will find that the Judge is the Lamb who was slain for them. Six days after this promise three men saw his face shine like the sun. One day his whole church will see it, and be like him, for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

16.theology: The church and the confession. Matthew is the only Gospel that records Jesus using the word “church” (ekklesia — the called-out assembly), and it appears on his lips in only two passages: here, and again in the discipline of 18:17. His promise is breathtaking in its confidence: he will build it, not we; and it will endure against all opposition. The church’s indestructibility rests not on its institutional strength or cultural influence but on the identity of its Lord and the truth of its confession. When the church loses the confession — that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God — it loses the rock on which it stands. The Reformation was at its heart a recovery of this confession: Christ alone, known through Scripture alone, received through faith alone, to the glory of God alone.
16.examples:
Then: Caesarea Philippi was the last place you would expect the church to be founded — a pagan city, politically dangerous territory, far from Jerusalem’s religious centre. Jesus chose it deliberately. The church is born at the margins, in hostile territory, by a divine confession that overturns every human calculation.

Now: The question “Who do you say that I am?” is not a theological quiz but an existential confrontation. Every person who hears the gospel must answer it. Correct doctrine about Jesus (acknowledging him as a great teacher, a moral exemplar, a historical figure) falls short of Peter’s confession. Jesus demands a verdict — not about what others say, but about what you say. The church is built on those who answer as Peter answered, by the same Spirit who revealed it to him.

17.title: The Transfiguration
17.text: <sup>1</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. <sup>2</sup>And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light. <sup>3</sup>And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. <sup>4</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>5</sup>He was still speaking when, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” <sup>6</sup>When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified. <sup>7</sup>But Jesus came and touched them, saying, “Rise, and have no fear.” <sup>8</sup>And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Tell no one the vision, until the Son of Man is raised from the dead.” <sup>10</sup>And the disciples asked him, “Then why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?” <sup>11</sup>He answered, “Elijah does come, and he will restore all things. <sup>12</sup>But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man will certainly suffer at their hands.” <sup>13</sup>Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them of John the Baptist. <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the crowd, a man came up to him and, kneeling before him, <sup>15</sup>said, “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and he suffers terribly. For often he falls into the fire, and often into the water. <sup>16</sup>And I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him here to me.” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed instantly. <sup>19</sup>Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said, “Why could we not cast it out?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “Because of your little faith. For truly, I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.” <sup>22</sup>As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men, <sup>23</sup>and they will kill him, and he will be raised on the third day.” And they were greatly distressed. <sup>24</sup>When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax went up to Peter and said, “Does your teacher not pay the tax?” <sup>25</sup>He said, “Yes.” And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do kings of the earth take toll or tax? From their sons or from others?” <sup>26</sup>And when he said, “From others,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are free. <sup>27</sup>However, not to give offense to them, go to the sea and cast a hook and take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a shekel. Take that and give it to them for me and for yourself.”
17.overview:
The Transfiguration is a window into eternity opened for three disciples on a mountain. For a moment the veil of Jesus’ humanity is drawn back and the uncreated glory of the Son shines through: his face blazes like the sun, his garments become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear — the Law and the Prophets — converging on the one they pointed to, discussing the “exodus” he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The Father speaks from the cloud — the shekinah glory — as he did at the baptism: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.”

The Transfiguration is the answer to Peter’s confusion in chapter 16. Peter could not accept a suffering Messiah. The mountain shows him why the cross is not a defeat: the one who will be crucified is the radiant Son of God, whose glory is momentarily unveiled. The cross does not contradict his glory; it is the appointed path through which his glory reaches the world. The disciples descend the mountain and immediately confront a demon-possessed boy they could not heal — from glory to weakness, from the height to the valley of need, which is always where the church must work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days after Peter's confession, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured before them — his face shining like the sun, his clothes white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him. A cloud overshadows them and the Father's voice speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him." The disciples fall on their faces; Jesus touches them and they see no one but Jesus alone. Coming down, he forbids them to speak of the vision until he is raised from the dead, and answers their question about Elijah: Elijah has already come, in John the Baptist, and was not recognised but treated however his enemies pleased — and so also, he says, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.
verseByVerse.theology: The Transfiguration is the mountain-top confirmation of Peter's confession: the Son of God whose glory was hidden in flesh is momentarily unveiled. Moses (the law) and Elijah (the prophets) appear alongside Jesus — the whole of the Old Testament represented — and then disappear. Jesus alone remains. The command "listen to him" supersedes Sinai and Carmel: not the law through Moses, not the prophetic word through Elijah, but the Son himself who is their fulfillment. The disciples' prostration and their rising at Jesus's touch enact the pattern of every encounter with the holy: undone by the presence, restored by the touch of grace. There is a quiet fitness in which two men were chosen to stand there. Moses and Elijah are the two men in the Old Testament who met God on Horeb, and each was given something less than an unveiled sight of his glory: Moses was hidden in a cleft of the rock and shown only the back of the glory as it passed (Exod 33:18-23), and Elijah wrapped his face in his cloak at the mouth of the cave and would not look (1 Kings 19:9-13). Now the two of them stand on a mountain with the glory in front of them, unveiled and in the open, holding a conversation with it. What neither prophet was permitted to see, both of them at last see in the face of a Galilean carpenter. And the descent (vv. 9-13) attaches the vision to the cross: the silence is to hold until the resurrection, and the Elijah question is answered by pointing at a man already dead. John came in Elijah's spirit and power and was killed on a whim; the pattern of the forerunner is the pattern of the King.
verseByVerse.examples: The descent from the mountain with the charge to silence (until the resurrection) and the discussion about Elijah frames the Transfiguration within the larger passion narrative. The glory on the mountain will be followed immediately by the failure to heal the epileptic boy in the valley — the constant movement between mountain-top and valley-floor, between the unveiled glory and the demanding need. The disciples are not left on the mountain; they descend with Jesus to where the need is. Two practical edges run through the descent itself. The first is the order to say nothing (v. 9): three men walk down to nine colleagues who were not invited and are about to have the worst day of their ministry, and they are to keep the greatest experience of their lives to themselves. Not everything God gives is given for circulation; some of it is given to be carried. The second is the plain warning of vv. 12-13. God's own forerunner, the greatest man born of women, was beheaded because a king did not want to look foolish in front of his dinner guests, and God did not prevent it. Faithfulness does not purchase a comfortable outcome. What it secures is a place in a pattern that runs through the Son himself and out the far side on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days later, Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain by themselves. There he was transfigured before them: his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became as white as light.

Meaning first. Six days after Jesus told his disciples that he must suffer and die, and that they must take up their crosses behind him, he took three of them up a high mountain and let them see who he is. His face shone like the sun, Moses and Elijah spoke with him about the death he would accomplish in Jerusalem, and the Father’s voice from the cloud said: this is my beloved Son; listen to him. Then they came down into a valley of failure and torment, where Jesus healed a boy his disciples could not help, spoke again of his betrayal and resurrection, and paid a temple tax he did not owe. The whole chapter says one thing: the way of the cross is the way of the Lord of glory, and the glory is real before the cross, through it, and on the far side of it.

The connection. Six days earlier, Jesus had told his disciples that he must suffer and die, and that they must take up their crosses (16:21–28). He had promised that some would see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom before they died (16:28). Now three of them see his glory, and the promise is kept with the ink barely dry. These are men who have just been told to carry a cross behind a Master going to Jerusalem to be killed. He takes them up a hill and shows them who it is they are following. He does not explain the glory to them. He lets them look at it. The transfiguration assures them that the way of the cross leads to glory.

And after six days. An unusually precise time marker, and it may echo Moses on Mount Sinai: the cloud covered the mountain six days, and on the seventh day God called to Moses out of the cloud (Exodus 24:16). A reader with a parallel Bible will notice that Luke says about eight days (Luke 9:28). Luke has written about, and the ordinary Jewish way of counting includes the day you start from and the day you finish on, which turns the same interval into eight. It is one span counted in the two normal ways.

Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother. The inner circle (see 4:21; 26:37), the three who will also be taken further into the garden of Gethsemane. Moses also took a smaller group up the mountain (Exodus 24:1, 9). Jesus himself chooses who comes and when; nobody climbs this mountain on his own initiative.

And led them up a high mountain by themselves. Which mountain? Matthew says only a high mountain, and the honest answer is that we do not know. Ancient tradition settled on Tabor in Galilee, and there are churches on it; but Tabor is under two thousand feet and had a fortified settlement on its summit in that century. Six days earlier this party was at Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Hermon, which climbs to about 9,200 feet (2,800 metres) and carries snow most of the year. Hermon is the likelier candidate. Matthew did not think the location worth recording, which is itself a hint about where he wants the eye to go. Mountains in Scripture are places where God reveals himself: Sinai, Carmel, Zion.

And he was transfigured before them. “Transfigured” (metemorphōthē, from which “metamorphosis” comes) means changed in form. The verb is passive, but what changed was not his nature, and this is the hinge of the whole scene. Nothing was added to Jesus on that mountain. Something stopped being hidden. The glory that was always his as the Son of God, veiled by his ordinary human appearance, shone through. It was not a light shining on him from outside, but the glory within him shining out. John says, we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father (John 1:14). Paul uses the same word for believers being transformed into his image (2 Corinthians 3:18; Romans 12:2).

And his face shone like the sun. Set him beside the man who will shortly be standing next to him and the difference is exact. When Moses came down from Sinai his face shone so that Israel was afraid to come near him, because he had been speaking with God (Exodus 34:29–35). That light was borrowed, reflected off a glory that was not his, and it faded, and he put a veil over it so that they would not watch it die away (2 Corinthians 3:13). Here nothing is reflected and nothing is veiled. Moses’ face reflected God’s glory; Jesus’ face shines with his own. In Revelation, John sees the risen Christ with a face like the sun shining in full strength (Revelation 1:16).

The promise out of sequence. Matthew chose his comparison with care, because he has used it once before. Four chapters back, explaining the weeds and the harvest, Jesus said that at the end the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (13:43). Now Matthew writes that his face shone like the sun. The same phrase, the same Gospel, the same speaker. What he had promised was waiting at the end of the world is standing in front of them on a hillside in the middle of it, out of sequence, so that three frightened men would have something to remember.

And his clothes became white as light. In Daniel 7:9 the Ancient of Days had clothing white as snow. Jesus appears clothed in divine glory, the glory of the God whom no one can approach (1 Timothy 6:16).

The thirty years. Sit for a moment with what the veil implies, because it is harder to take in than the blaze. If this was in him all along, then it was in him at Nazareth. For something like thirty years that face had been an ordinary face in an ordinary village. The neighbours watched him grow up. His mother washed his clothes. Men came to the workshop about a yoke or a door frame and haggled over the price, and went away with no idea at all; later they would say, dismissively, is not this the carpenter’s son? (13:55). All that time, this was what was under the surface, held back, day after day, by a decision he kept making (Philippians 2:6–8). The wonder of the transfiguration is not that he shone for an hour. It is the thirty years he did not.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus became divine at this moment, or that his glory was borrowed. The transfiguration revealed what he always was. Nor was it a dream or a hallucination. Peter later wrote: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty (2 Peter 1:16–18).

Did Jesus stop being human while he shone? No. The transfiguration did not turn his humanity into something else, nor did it mix his two natures together. The same man who had walked up the hill, with real lungs out of breath from the climb, stood there in light, and he walked down again. What the three saw was the one person, truly God and truly man, with the divine glory no longer hidden by the humble form he had taken. This also shows what our future is: our bodies too will be changed to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21), still human, but human as God always meant it to be.

Why only three disciples? Not because the other nine were less loved. God gives particular sights to particular servants for the sake of all the rest. Peter, James and John were to be pillars of the church (Galatians 2:9), and their testimony was meant for everyone, including us, which is why Peter wrote it down (2 Peter 1:16–18). If you have never seen anything like this, you have not been passed over. You have been given it the way the church has always been given it: by trustworthy eyewitnesses, in Scripture.

In a sentence. On a high mountain, three disciples saw Jesus’ hidden divine glory shine out, a preview of his glory after the cross.

On a Tuesday. The Jesus you follow on the road of the cross is the Lord of glory. When the road is hard and he looks small in your life, as he looked small in Nazareth, remember that the smallness is the veil and not the face. Whatever you are carrying today, you are carrying it behind someone whose face is like the sun.

For worship. Here is the Lord of glory, who hid that glory in a carpenter’s shop for thirty years and in a body that would be nailed to a cross, and who let it shine for one hour on a mountain so that his friends would not lose heart. The light did not fall on him; it came out of him. He is the radiance of the glory of God (Hebrews 1:3), and he chose to be looked at without being recognised so that he could be pierced for us. The face that shone like the sun was spat upon, and the same face will be the light of the city of God, which has no need of sun or moon (Revelation 21:23).
verseByVerse.note: The mountain is unnamed; tradition says Tabor, but Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, is also suggested.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. And Peter said to Jesus, "Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Elijah appeared, talking with Jesus. Peter said: Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah.

And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. Moses, through whom God gave the law, and Elijah, the great prophet, together represent the Law and the Prophets: the whole Old Testament. Both had met God on a mountain (Moses on Sinai, Exodus 24; Elijah on Horeb, the same mountain, 1 Kings 19). Both had mysterious departures: God buried Moses (Deuteronomy 34:5–6), and Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). And both were expected before the end: a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15) and Elijah before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). Moses had once begged, please show me your glory, and was hidden in a rock while it passed (Exodus 33:18–23). Now, fourteen centuries after he was refused entry to the land of promise, he stands on a mountain with the Lord of glory and sees it face to face.

What they talked about. Luke tells us: his departure (literally his exodus), which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The man who led the first exodus is talking with the man who will lead the last one, out of a slavery deeper than Egypt. The glory was not an alternative to the cross; it was a conversation about the cross. The Law and the Prophets point to it, and the whole Old Testament here gathers round the Son to discuss the one event it was written to announce.

And Peter said to Jesus, Lord, it is good that we are here. Peter was right: it was good. But as usual he spoke too quickly. Mark adds, kindly, that he did not know what to say, for they were terrified (Mark 9:6). It is the speech of a man overwhelmed.

If you wish, I will make three tents here. “Tents” (skēnas) are booths or shelters. At the Feast of Tabernacles (Booths), Jews lived in temporary shelters to remember the wilderness journey (Leviticus 23:42–43). Peter may have wanted to prolong the moment, to stay on the mountain in glory rather than go down to the cross. Or he may have thought the kingdom had now come. His if you wish at least puts his Master’s will above his own preference.

Worship reaching for permanence. Peter’s instinct is one every Christian will recognise, and it deserves more than a smile at his expense. Something overwhelming has happened, and his immediate reaction is to make it permanent: build something, stay here, do not let this end. That is not a foolish impulse. It is worship reaching for permanence. It is wrong all the same, and the passage shows why twice over. A shelter built to keep them all up there would have been a shelter built against the very thing Moses and Elijah were talking about. And when Peter has finished speaking, God answers the offer of a tent by sending his own: the cloud overshadows them, and it is not made of anything Peter could have assembled. You cannot house this glory. It houses you.

One for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah. Peter’s deeper mistake was to put Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah, three great men, three equal tents. The Father’s voice immediately corrects him (v. 5).

How did the disciples know who they were? The text does not say; the recognition was part of what God showed them. There were no portraits of Moses or Elijah, and they needed none. When God reveals something, he gives the understanding with it.

What it does not mean. Not that the dead can be contacted, or that Christians should seek visions of the saints. This was a unique event of revelation, initiated by God. Scripture forbids seeking contact with the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and it gives no warrant for praying to departed saints. Nor does it mean that Moses and Elijah were equal to Jesus. They came to speak with him about his work. What the scene does show is that the faithful dead are alive with God: Moses had died fourteen centuries earlier, and here he is, himself, talking. God is not the God of the dead but of the living (22:32).

When the closeness of God fades. There are seasons when God feels near: a conference, a retreat, a Sunday when the singing landed somewhere it usually does not, a stretch of months when prayer came easily. Almost everyone is given some. Nobody keeps them. And when the sense of it goes, people conclude either that they have sinned it away or that it was never real. Look at what happened to these three. Within a day they came down into a shouting argument, a desperate father, a boy convulsing in the fire, and nine colleagues who had just failed in public. The glory did not follow them down in any visible form. What they brought down was a memory and a sentence: this is my beloved Son; listen to him. That was the point of the mountain: not the feeling, but a clearer sight of who he is, to be carried into a valley where nothing would look glorious at all.

Where the glory is kept now. Peter tells us himself, decades later, what he did with it. He appeals to that day as proof that the church’s hope is no cleverly devised myth, and then, having played his eyewitness card, says something surprising: we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place (2 Peter 1:16–19). The man who saw the face shine like the sun points his readers not to another mountain but to their Bibles. That is where the glory is kept for the rest of us. So do not try to rebuild the tent. Take what you were given, and go down.

Is it wrong to long for those moments again? No. To long for God’s nearness is the cry of the psalms (Psalm 42:1–2; 63:1). What goes wrong is making the feeling the measure of your faith, or chasing it as the goal. Ask God for it, thank him when he gives it, and do not doubt him when he withholds it. His presence is promised (28:20); the sensation of it is a gift he gives as he wills. A believer who walks for months in the dark and keeps trusting is not less spiritual than one on the mountain. Often he is further on (Isaiah 50:10).

In a sentence. Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets, appeared and spoke with Jesus about his coming death, and Peter wanted to build shelters to stay.

On a Tuesday. Like Peter, we sometimes want to stay on the mountain of spiritual experience rather than go down into ordinary obedience. Christ calls us down with him. If last Sunday or last year was a high point and today feels flat, do not try to rebuild it. Take the sentence you were given, open your Bible, and do the next thing he has told you to do.

For worship. The whole Old Testament came to this hillside to speak with him. Moses, who saw only God’s back, saw his face at last; Elijah, who once sat under a broom tree wishing to die, stood in glory beside the one who would die for him. The law and the prophets had been talking about this one man for fifteen centuries, and when they finally met him they talked about his cross. Blessed be the Son who is the subject of all Scripture, and who would not stay on the mountain because his people were in the valley.
verseByVerse.note: Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets. The tents may recall the Feast of Booths.

verseByVerse.quote: He was still speaking when, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him." When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said: this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him. The disciples fell on their faces, terrified.

He was still speaking when, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. God interrupts Peter. The cloud is the cloud of God’s presence, the Shekinah glory: the cloud that led Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), covered Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:15–18), filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35) and the temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). Bright, because God’s glory filled it. On the one occasion in the Gospels when the Father issues an order, he interrupts a man in the middle of a sentence to say: stop talking and listen to my Son. It is not a cruelty; Peter was frightened and meant well. But the impulse to organise the moment is very nearly always louder than the impulse to hear.

And a voice from the cloud said. God the Father speaks, as at Jesus’ baptism (3:17). Weigh how rare this is. God the Father speaks audibly three times in the four Gospels: at the baptism, here, and once more in Jerusalem in the last week (John 12:28). Twice he identifies his Son. Once, and only once, he commands anything at all.

This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. The same words as at the baptism, and they are not one statement but Old Testament strings sounded together, which a Jew on that mountain would have heard. This is my beloved Son is the enthronement psalm, where God says to his king, you are my Son; today I have begotten you (Psalm 2:7). With whom I am well pleased opens the first of the Servant songs: behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights (Isaiah 42:1), the Servant who will not break a bruised reed. Jesus is not one among three, but the unique Son.

Listen to him. The new words, from Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him: it is to him you shall listen. King, Servant and Prophet, in a single breath, from the throne. And notice whose words the third is. Deuteronomy 18 is Moses speaking, and Moses is standing right there. The Father, with Moses at his Son’s shoulder, quotes Moses’ own promise and points it at Jesus. That is not a slight on Moses; it is Moses getting what he was promised. The next verse of Deuteronomy tells you what kind of sentence this is: whoever will not listen to the prophet’s words, God himself will require it of him (Deuteronomy 18:19). Listen to him is not a recommendation. Moses and Elijah were God’s servants who spoke for him; Jesus is God’s Son, and his word is final (Hebrews 1:1–2).
