Twenty-odd verses earlier the man speaking here said it would be better for someone who damages one of these little ones to be drowned with a millstone round his neck (v. 6). The Jesus who tells you to stop counting is the Jesus who said that. Both sentences are his, and neither cancels the other: he takes what was done to you more seriously than you do, and he still will not let it own you. Forgiving does not mean that the wrong goes unreported or unpunished; God has appointed the authorities to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and he himself will judge (Romans 12:19).

The prison he builds himself. That is the reason the command is mercy rather than cruelty. Look at the first servant’s afternoon. He has just been released from a debt no lifetime could clear, and he spends it with his hands round somebody’s throat over a sum he could have written off without noticing. He walks out of the throne room a free man and immediately builds himself a prison. That is what unforgiveness does: it keeps the offender living rent-free in a life he has otherwise left, and hands him a second victory he did not earn. Christ is not asking you to say the wrong was nothing. He is asking you to stop carrying the man who did it. (What forgiving does and does not require, and what to do when you cannot get there yet, is set out at 6:14–15.)

In a sentence. Hearing the same plea he had made, the forgiven servant refused mercy and threw his fellow servant into prison.

On a Tuesday. When someone asks you for patience or forgiveness, remember the words you have used with God.

For worship. The King heard our plea and did far more than we asked; he did not lock us up until we paid. He takes the wrongs done to his people more seriously than they do, and he will right every one of them. And he offers the wounded something the world cannot: a way to put down the weight of the offender without pretending the offence was small, by laying it in the hands of the God who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: When his fellow servants saw what had taken place, they were greatly distressed, and they went and reported to their master all that had taken place. Then his master summoned him and said to him, "You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the other servants saw what had happened, they were deeply distressed, and went and told their master everything. Then the master summoned him: you wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.

When his fellow servants saw what had taken place, they were greatly distressed. The injustice grieved them. Matthew uses a phrase he has used once before, in the previous chapter: greatly distressed (elypēthēsan sphodra), the identical words used of the disciples when told their Lord would be killed (17:23). What broke the disciples open at the news of the cross is what breaks these men open at the sight of cruelty between two of the forgiven. It is meant to be the same grief.

The bystanders. These servants are the only bystanders in the parable, and they are almost certainly the reader’s part in it. We come expecting to be the man forgiven a fortune, or on a bad day the man being throttled. But most Christians, most of the time, are the third group: the ones who saw it happen and had to decide what to do about something that was not their business.

And they went and reported to their master all that had taken place. They did not take revenge themselves; they brought it to the king. Look at what they did not do. They did not discuss it among themselves and leave it there. They did not form a party. They did not go and confront the man, which was not theirs to do; nothing had been done to them. They went to the one person with the standing and authority to act, and told him all of it. That is the road for a Christian who has watched another treated cruelly in a matter not his own. Verse 15 still stands: if he has sinned against you, go to him first, alone. But when the wrong was done to somebody else and the pattern is plain, the route is upward, not sideways, and the difference between reporting and gossiping is exactly the difference between the one you take it to and the people you tell it to.

Is reporting someone a betrayal of Christian love? No. These servants are the heroes of the scene. Bringing a wrong to those with the authority to deal with it, church leaders for sin in the church, the police for a crime, is not gossip, slander or disloyalty; it is love for the victim and obedience to God, who has appointed both (Hebrews 13:17; Romans 13:4). What is wrong is telling everyone except the people who can act. And where the wrong is abuse, especially of a child, reporting to the authorities is not optional and must never be delayed for a private conversation first.

Then his master summoned him and said to him, You wicked servant! “Wicked” is a strong word. His failure to forgive was not a small weakness but a great evil. And it is the only name the king ever gives him. He does not say, you are still in debt. He does not reopen the ledger. The charge is not arrears; it is character.

I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me. The master reminds him of the grace he received. All of it. Simply because he asked. Not because the man deserved it, not because he promised, not because the schedule looked workable. He asked. That is the entire reason on the record, and it was enough.

In a sentence. The other servants reported the cruelty, and the king called the unforgiving servant wicked, reminding him of the vast debt he had been forgiven.

On a Tuesday. Remember the grace you received when you asked God for mercy. It changes how you treat others. And if you have seen cruelty in your church that is not yours to confront, take it to those who can act, and to no one else.

For worship. The whole reason on the record for our forgiveness is that we asked. Not our merit, not our promises, not our improvement: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). And the God who forgives so freely also sees every cruelty done among his people and grieves over it. He is the King to whom every wrong may be brought, and he never fails to act.

verseByVerse.quote: "And should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" And in anger his master delivered him to the jailers, until he should pay all his debt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Should you not have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you? In anger his master handed him over to the jailers until he paid back everything he owed.

And should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you? The heart of the parable, the question that answers itself. Mercy received obliges mercy given. “As I had mercy on you”: the measure and motive of our forgiveness is God’s forgiveness of us (Ephesians 4:32; Colossians 3:13). Not as a burden laid on the forgiven, but as the natural overflow of what grace produces in them.

And in anger his master delivered him to the jailers. “Jailers” (basanistais) literally means torturers. Prisoners were sometimes tortured to make their families pay. The king’s feelings are named twice in this story and only twice: he is moved with pity at a man who cannot pay, and he is angry at a man who will not forgive. The thing that finally provokes him is not the sixty million. It is the hundred.

Until he should pay all his debt. Which he never could. The forgiveness is withdrawn. The original debt returns.

Does until mean the punishment will end? This phrase, with 5:26, has been cited in support of purgatory, a punishment after death that ends when the debt is discharged (see on 5:25–26). But this verse adds an argument the other cannot. The debt is ten thousand talents, and the parable has spent its whole length making sure you understand it could never be paid by the man who owed it. So the until is not a sentence with a term attached; it is a door that does not open. Scripture knows no purgatory: Christ’s sacrifice cleanses his people fully (Hebrews 10:14), and those outside him bear a punishment that is eternal (25:46).

What it does not mean. Not that God forgives and then takes back his forgiveness from true believers. Parables make a main point and should not be pressed on every detail. The point is that a person who refuses to forgive shows they have never truly received God’s forgiveness into their heart. The unforgiving servant did not understand grace; he was still thinking of debts and payments. Those whom God has truly forgiven are changed by it (Luke 7:47).

Can forgiveness be taken back? Three things, in order. First, a parable makes a point and is not a system. This Gospel likens the Lord’s return to a burglar at night (24:43), and uses leaven for the corruption of the Pharisees in one chapter (16:6) and for the kingdom of heaven itself in another (13:33). The pictures are chosen for one point of contact and do not carry their luggage with them. Second, the whole New Testament falls the other way: an unforgiving heart is evidence, not cause. And the parable has already told us what happened: the man never understood he had been released. He walked out believing he had been granted an extension (see on vv. 25–26). You cannot lose what you never actually took. Third, do not defuse the verse. Jesus told this story to frighten people, and the next sentence says so: so also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you. Assurance and complacency are not the same thing, and it is complacency this is aimed at.

If I cannot forgive yet, is this verse my sentence? Look hard at the man in the story before accepting that. He is not lying awake wrestling with a wound. He is not trying and failing. He is a man who, within the hour of being released from a debt no lifetime could clear, has his hands round a colleague’s throat over three months’ wages, and then puts a man who begged him into prison. This parable is about contempt, not difficulty. A reader who wants to forgive and cannot yet get there is not in this parable at all. He is back at verse 22, where the number is seventy-seven, which is not only a demand but a promise that there is room to keep coming back to it. The question is not whether you have arrived. It is which way you are facing.

In a sentence. The king asked why the servant had not shown the mercy he received, and handed him over to pay the whole debt.

On a Tuesday. Is there anyone you have thrown into prison in your heart, refusing to release them? Let them go, as God has let you go.

For worship. The God whose anger is kindled by contempt for mercy is the God whose own mercy has no bottom. He was moved with pity over a debt we could not pay, and the only thing that angers him in this story is mercy refused to others. Every believer stands in that throne room forgiven, not by a king who tore up paper, but by a Father who gave his Son. And those he has truly released, he never hands over to the jailers, for there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

parallels.desc: as God in Christ forgave you
as the Lord has forgiven you

verseByVerse.quote: So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart.

So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you. A solemn warning. God will deal with the unforgiving as the king dealt with the wicked servant (see 6:14–15).

If you do not forgive your brother from your heart. Not just with words, or outwardly, while holding a grudge inside. Real forgiveness comes from the heart: releasing the debt inwardly, refusing to nurse resentment, and wishing the other person good. This is impossible for us by nature; it is possible only for those who have been forgiven, by the Spirit’s work.

What from the heart rules out. Take it concretely, because in the abstract everyone agrees. It rules out the forgiveness that is announced and then produces a relationship which is polite, correct, and thirty degrees colder than before. It rules out the forgiveness that keeps the file open in case it is needed later: the grievance not pressed but carefully preserved, in good condition, where it can be reached. And it puts a question against the sentence people say most often, I have forgiven him but I will never forget it, which is sometimes an honest description of how memory works and sometimes a way of keeping the debt on the books.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving others. God’s forgiveness comes first (vv. 27, 32). But those who refuse to forgive show that they have not received it. Nor does forgiving “from the heart” mean that we must feel warm feelings toward the person immediately. Forgiveness is first a decision to release the debt, which feelings may follow slowly. Struggling to forgive a deep wound is not the same as refusing to forgive.

What it does not require. Say plainly what it does not require, because this verse frightens the wrong people. It does not require a feeling; the servant’s failure was not a shortage of warmth. It does not require amnesia; nobody is obliged to develop a bad memory. It does not require that trust be restored or that anyone place himself back within reach of harm (see on vv. 21–22), nor that a crime go unreported. And it does not require that the whole thing be finished today. Forgiveness from the heart is a decision about what you will do with a debt, taken once and then renewed every time the memory comes back with the bill in its hand, which is exactly why the number he gave Peter was seventy-seven and not one.

How do I actually forgive someone from the heart? Begin before God, not before the person. Tell God honestly what was done and how much it hurt; the psalms give you words for that. Then, deliberately, hand the debt to him: I release this person from what he owes me, and I leave justice to you (Romans 12:19). Pray for the person, even if all you can manage is, Lord, deal with him in mercy. When the memory returns, and it will, do the same again, without despair. Refuse to rehearse the grievance to others. And keep looking at the cross, because the power to forgive comes from seeing how much you have been forgiven.

The frame of the chapter. Stand back and look at the two sentences that bracket this discourse. It opens with a question: who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? It ends with this warning about forgiving a brother from the heart. Between them stand a child set in the middle, a millstone, a severed hand, a shepherd out after one sheep, three patient stages of correction, two or three witnesses in a front room, and a king with two debtors. Jesus never comes back to the word greatest. He does not need to. The answer to the disciples’ question turns out to be the man who forgives, because he is the man who has grasped what he was forgiven. They asked for a league table and were handed a mirror.

In a sentence. God will deal with those who do not forgive from the heart as the king dealt with the unforgiving servant.

On a Tuesday. Name, before God, the person you find hardest to forgive. Ask him for grace to forgive them from the heart, remembering your own great debt.

For worship. Thank God for forgiving you a debt you could never pay. And see what the parable could not show. The king in the story cancelled ten thousand talents at no cost to himself; he tore up a paper and was poorer only on an accounting sheet. God’s forgiveness of the same debt was not arranged that way. The one telling this parable was soon to set out for Jerusalem, and what it cost to have the record destroyed was not ink. That is why the man who has understood it cannot go out and throttle anybody. He knows what the paper was written on: the blood of the Son of God, poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28).

parallels.desc: if you do not forgive others

18.theology: Forgiveness and the gospel. Matthew 18:21–35 is among the most searching passages in the Gospels on the nature of Christian forgiveness. The parable does not ground forgiveness in the worthiness of the offender or the severity of the offence but in the prior, overwhelming forgiveness of God. This is the gospel logic of ethics: we forgive because we have been forgiven a debt we could never pay. The Reformers called this the indicative grounding the imperative — what God has done for us in Christ is the foundation and motive for what we are to do for one another. Forgiveness is not optional for the Christian; it is the evidence that the gospel has actually taken root in the heart.
18.examples:
Then: The disciples’ argument about greatness was entirely natural — they had left everything and wanted to know what the return on their investment would be. Jesus placed a child in their midst and dismantled their entire framework. The kingdom does not run on the world’s economy of status and reward.

Now: Church conflict is the great test of whether the gospel has penetrated the heart. It is easy to believe in forgiveness in the abstract; it is hard to forgive the specific person who sinned against you specifically. The unforgiving servant stands as a warning: the one who has truly received grace cannot hoard it. The debt we have been forgiven is always larger than the debt we are asked to forgive.

19.title: Marriage, Children, and the Rich Young Man
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus had finished these sayings, he went away from Galilee and entered the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. <sup>2</sup>And large crowds followed him, and he healed them there. <sup>3</sup>And Pharisees came up to him and tested him by asking, “Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause?” <sup>4</sup>He answered, “Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female, <sup>5</sup>and said, ‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? <sup>6</sup>So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>7</sup>They said to him, “Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?” <sup>8</sup>He said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. <sup>9</sup>And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery.” <sup>10</sup>The disciples said to him, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.” <sup>11</sup>But he said to them, “Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. <sup>12</sup>For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this receive it.” <sup>13</sup>Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people, <sup>14</sup>but Jesus said, “Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven.” <sup>15</sup>And he laid his hands on them and went away. <sup>16</sup>And behold, a man came up to him, saying, “Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?” <sup>17</sup>And he said to him, “Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments.” <sup>18</sup>He said to him, “Which ones?” And Jesus said, “You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, <sup>19</sup>Honor your father and mother, and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>20</sup>The young man said to him, “All these I have kept. What do I still lack?” <sup>21</sup>Jesus said to him, “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus said to his disciples, “Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven. <sup>24</sup>Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>25</sup>When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?” <sup>26</sup>But Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” <sup>27</sup>Then Peter said in reply, “See, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?” <sup>28</sup>Jesus said to them, “Truly, I say to you, in the new world, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. <sup>29</sup>And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life. <sup>30</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.
19.overview:
Chapter 19 moves through three encounters that together form a sustained meditation on what it means to enter the kingdom. Marriage (vv. 1–12) is grounded in creation: the one-flesh union is God’s design, not a human arrangement, and cannot be dissolved at will. Children (vv. 13–15) are welcomed against the disciples’ protests: the kingdom belongs to those who come with empty hands. The rich young man (vv. 16–30) turns away sorrowful: he has great possessions, and they have him.

The three encounters build to the chapter’s most important theological statement: “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” Salvation is not a human achievement; it is a divine act. The disciples’ astonished question — “Who then can be saved?” — is the right question, and Jesus’ answer is the heart of the gospel: not the most religiously qualified, not the wealthiest, not even the morally most impressive, but those in whom God himself works the miracle of new birth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea, healing crowds. The Pharisees test him with the divorce question: is it lawful to divorce for any cause? Jesus answers by returning to creation — one man, one woman, one flesh — and distinguishes Moses' concession from God's original design. The disciples are troubled; Jesus adds teaching on celibacy. Children are brought to Jesus; the disciples rebuke those who bring them; Jesus rebukes the disciples and pronounces the kingdom belongs to such as these. At the centre of the exchange stands the one exception he names — sexual immorality (v. 9) — and the section closes with him laying his hands on the children and going away (v. 15), the last thing he does in that place.
verseByVerse.theology: The divorce question was a live controversy in first-century Judaism between the school of Shammai (divorce only for sexual immorality) and the school of Hillel (divorce for any cause, including burning the food). Jesus does not take sides in the rabbinic debate; he goes behind Moses to creation. The "hardness of heart" that occasioned the Mosaic permission (Deut. 24:1) was always a concession to human sin, not God's design. Jesus restores the original standard: what God has joined, let not man separate. Verse 9 adds the one exception Jesus names, and it is not the whole of Scripture's teaching: Paul supplies a second ground, when an unbelieving spouse deserts (1 Cor 7:15), and the Reformed churches have long held these two and no others. But the exception is a fence, not a loophole — its purpose is to guard the one-flesh covenant against the hardness of heart that treats it lightly. That must be said in both directions. Nothing here requires anyone to remain in a house where they are being harmed: separation for safety is nowhere forbidden (1 Cor 7:11), a spouse who makes a home unsurvivable has deserted it in substance whoever physically leaves, and the previous chapter has already said what Christ thinks of the man who damages one of these little ones (18:6). See the verse-by-verse on vv. 9-10.
verseByVerse.examples: The episode with the children immediately follows the marriage and divorce discussion — the connection is not incidental. The children whom the disciples dismiss as unimportant are the very ones who most perfectly embody the kingdom: they have no legal standing, no social status, no achievement to present. "Of such is the kingdom of heaven" — the kingdom belongs to those who receive it as a child receives a gift, with open hands and no pretense of deserving. Verse 15 is easily read past and should not be. Straight after the disciples had turned these families away, the last recorded act of Jesus in that district is that he laid hands on their children while the parents who had been told off stood watching. The people who received the blessing are the ones who declined to be embarrassed out of the queue. But the verse is not a guarantee that every child of a believing home will come to faith, and a parent grieving over a grown son who wants none of it must not read it as a verdict on their parenting.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus had finished these sayings, he went away from Galilee and entered the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. And large crowds followed him, and he healed them there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus finished these teachings, he left Galilee and went into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.

Meaning first. Jesus leaves Galilee for the last time and sets out on the road to Jerusalem and the cross, and on the way he is asked two questions about what a man may keep. Pharisees ask how easily a man may divorce his wife, and he takes them back to creation: God made them male and female and joins husband and wife into one flesh, so that divorce is permitted only where the covenant has been broken by sexual unfaithfulness, and never as a convenient exit. Then a rich young man asks what good deed will win eternal life, and Jesus shows him that his wealth is his god, and that salvation is impossible with man but possible with God. Between the two scenes he takes little children in his arms and blesses them, because the kingdom belongs to those who come with nothing. The chapter ends with a promise of thrones and a hundredfold, and a warning: many who are first will be last. All of it is spoken by the one who was on his way to give up everything for us.

Now when Jesus had finished these sayings. The formula ending the fourth great discourse (see 7:28). Matthew uses it exactly five times (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; here; 26:1), closing the five great blocks of teaching around which he has built his Gospel. Readers have long heard an echo of the five books of Moses: a new lawgiver on a mountain, with five books of his own. Whether or not Matthew intended it, the effect is plain: the long teaching in Galilee is finished, and from this verse on the road leads to Jerusalem.

He went away from Galilee. A turning point. Jesus leaves Galilee for the last time before his death. From here he travels toward Jerusalem and the cross (16:21; 20:17–19).

And entered the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Probably Perea, the region east of the Jordan, ruled by Herod Antipas, the same ruler who had executed John the Baptist for speaking against his marriage (14:3–4). The question about divorce that follows was politically dangerous here. It was in Perea, at the fortress of Machaerus, that Antipas had imprisoned and beheaded John, and Matthew has told us what John said to earn it: it is not lawful for you to have her (14:4), a public verdict on the tetrarch’s marriage. Herodias was still alive. So when Jesus crosses into that territory and the first thing that happens is that Pharisees ask him whether it is lawful to divorce a wife, the question is an invitation to repeat, in Herod’s own district, the offence for which the last preacher lost his head. The test had a body attached to it.

No lowering of the voice. Notice what he does with the danger, which is nothing at all. He does not lower his voice or leave the district or give an answer with room to move in. The chapter that follows is the strongest thing said about marriage anywhere in the Gospels, and it is said within reach of the man who killed the last person to raise the subject.

And large crowds followed him, and he healed them there. His compassion continues on the road to the cross. That is nine words in English, and behind it stand hundreds of individual people whose lives were permanently altered on an ordinary afternoon, every one of them a story somebody told for the rest of his life, and not one of them written down. Most of what Jesus did is not in the book (John 21:25), and what is in the book is enough.

In a sentence. Jesus left Galilee for the last time and travelled south toward Jerusalem, healing the crowds on the way.

On a Tuesday. Jesus kept serving others as he walked toward his own suffering. Can you serve others even in your own hard season? And when you must speak the truth in a place where it is unwelcome, remember that he did not lower his voice.

For worship. He set his face toward Jerusalem knowing exactly what waited there, and still he stopped for every sick person in the crowd. His compassion did not shrink as the cross came nearer; it was the same compassion that took him to the cross. And he walked unafraid into the territory of the king who had killed his forerunner, because no Herod could take his life from him; he would lay it down of his own accord (John 10:18).
verseByVerse.note: “Judea beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pharisees came up to him and tested him by asking, "Is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?" He answered, "Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some Pharisees came to test Jesus: is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason at all? He answered: have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female?

And Pharisees came up to him and tested him. A trap. Whatever he said would offend someone: one of the rabbinic schools, or Herod, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias.

Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause? The debate between the two great rabbinic schools of the day (see 5:31–32). The school of Shammai held that Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed divorce only for serious sexual sin. The school of Hillel held that a man could divorce his wife for “any cause”: if she burned his food, or if he found someone prettier. Hillel’s view was the popular one. The Pharisees wanted Jesus to take sides.

For any cause. The phrase is not loose wording but a technical term, and everyone in the crowd knew it. Deuteronomy 24:1 allowed a man to divorce his wife if he found in her some indecency, in Hebrew literally the nakedness of a matter. Shammai’s school read the two words as one thing and limited divorce to sexual indecency. Hillel’s school split them and made the second a separate ground: some indecency, or a matter, any matter. The Mishnah preserves how far it ran: a man might divorce his wife if she spoiled a dish, and Rabbi Akiba added, if he found another woman more attractive. So the Pharisees are asking Jesus to endorse the position that had already won, and which most men in the crowd were living by. To answer as he is about to answer was to tell a large number of ordinary, respectable men that what they had done was adultery. He does it anyway, in Herod’s Perea, on the day he arrived.

He answered, Have you not read. Instead of entering the rabbinic debate, Jesus goes back to Scripture, and to the beginning (see 12:3). It is a deliberately barbed question. These were professional readers of Scripture. Matthew has Jesus put it to them several times (12:3, 5; here; 21:16, 42; 22:31), and it never means, are you unfamiliar with the text. It means: you know this passage perfectly, you can recite it, and you have arranged your life so that it does not govern you. That is worth taking personally. A man may know his Bible thoroughly and use his knowledge chiefly to locate the room he is allowed to move in.

That he who created them from the beginning made them male and female. Genesis 1:27. God created humanity in two sexes, male and female, both in his image. Marriage is grounded in creation, not in culture. Jesus moves the question from what is permitted to what God intended. They asked about the exit; he answered about the entrance. They wanted the conditions under which a marriage may be dissolved; he told them what a marriage is. Every argument about how far a thing may be pushed is settled, if it is settled at all, by going back to what the thing was for, and it cannot be settled while both parties are standing at the exit measuring the door.

One man and one woman. Jesus grounds marriage in creation, not in culture: one man and one woman, joined as one flesh. That excludes same-sex marriage, and it excludes polygamy, which the Old Testament records but never commends.

The question that gives itself away. There is a test buried in the shape of their question that anybody can run. When you find yourself asking how far you may go, how much you may keep, how long you may stay angry, what exactly counts as a lie, notice that the question itself has already told you something. Nobody asks where the boundary is unless he is standing near it and hoping it is further out than he fears. The Pharisees asked it about marriage; the disciples will ask their own version a few verses later; and both times the answer comes back not as a line but as a purpose.

Why does it matter that God made us male and female? Because our bodies and our sex are not accidents or mere raw material for us to redefine; they are God’s good gift, part of his design. Man and woman are equal in dignity, both bearing his image, and different in ways that complement each other, and marriage brings that difference together in one flesh. This is why the church cannot treat marriage as whatever a culture decides it is. It also means that everyone who struggles with these questions, including those who feel at odds with their own body, is to be met with truth and with great compassion, as a fellow image-bearer, not as a problem.

In a sentence. When the Pharisees tested him about grounds for divorce, Jesus went back to creation: God made them male and female.

On a Tuesday. When facing a hard ethical question, start where Jesus started: what was God’s original design? And if you notice yourself asking how far you may go, ask instead what the thing was made for.

For worship. He is the one who created them from the beginning, for all things were made through him (John 1:3). The Creator himself stood among the Pharisees and told them what he had meant when he made man and woman. He is not a lawyer arguing over clauses but the Author explaining his own work, and his design is good. Blessed be the Maker who did not leave us to define ourselves, but made us male and female in his image, for his glory.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce: some allowed it for almost any cause, others only for sexual immorality.

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: "and said, 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh'? So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. So they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no one separate.

And said, Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife. Genesis 2:24. Jesus says God said it: the words of Scripture are God’s words. In Genesis the sentence is the narrator’s comment; Jesus attributes it to the one who created them. Scripture speaks, God speaks.

Leave. Marriage creates a new household. The primary loyalty shifts from parents to spouse. Not abandoning parents, who must still be honoured (15:4), but forming a new family unit. And the order is not decorative. A great deal of trouble in the early years of a marriage is a leaving problem rather than a cleaving problem: a man who still runs decisions past his mother, a woman whose father remains the final court of appeal on her husband, a couple whose Christmases are still arranged by somebody else. You cannot glue something that is still attached to what it was fixed to before.

Hold fast. “Hold fast” (kollēthēsetai) means to be glued, joined, bound. It describes a permanent, faithful commitment.

And the two shall become one flesh. A union of the whole person: physical (sexual union), but also emotional, spiritual and social: sharing one life. Paul calls it a profound mystery that pictures Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Take one flesh literally enough to feel it, because the phrase has been worn smooth. It does not mean the couple are close or well suited. It means that something which was two has become one thing, and so they can no longer be separated, only torn. That is why the ending of a marriage does not feel like the ending of any other relationship. A partnership can be dissolved and both partners walk away whole. Cutting one flesh in two does not produce two people; it produces two halves, and they bleed for years. Anyone who has been through it already knows this, and has usually been told he should be over it by now.

So they are no longer two but one flesh. Jesus draws the conclusion: marriage makes a new unity.

What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. The key sentence. God himself joins a husband and wife. Marriage is not merely a human contract that can be dissolved whenever people choose; it is a covenant made before God, which he has sealed (Malachi 2:14–16). No human authority, neither husband nor court, has the right to undo what God has done. The verb is synezeuxen, yoked: not a knot but a harness, two animals under one beam, pulling the same load, unable to turn without the other turning. And the subject of the verb is God.

Is a marriage without God really a marriage? Yes. On the authority of this sentence, two unbelievers in a registry office with no prayer said over them and no thought of God in the room are joined by God. He does the yoking whether or not he was invited to the wedding. There is no such thing as a merely civil marriage in heaven’s records. So a believer who married before conversion is truly married, and a marriage that began badly is still a marriage to be honoured and kept (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).

Let not man. Notice who is forbidden to separate them. Let not man is not addressed only to the husband and wife. It reaches the judge who grants divorce lightly, the friend who has been advising for months that she deserves better, the parent who never accepted the marriage and has been waiting, the colleague who makes the affair easy. There are usually more hands on a broken marriage than the two belonging to the couple.

What it does not mean. Not that divorce is never permitted in any circumstances (v. 9; 1 Corinthians 7:15). But it means that divorce is always a tearing of what God has joined, a tragedy, never merely a lifestyle choice. And the passage shows God’s design for marriage as one man and one woman, for life. The historic Christian view of marriage and sexuality is grounded here, in Jesus’ own words about creation. It should be held with conviction and with compassion for those who struggle.

Does let not man separate mean a wife must stay with a husband who abuses her? No. Abuse is never to be tolerated, and nothing in this verse requires anyone to remain in danger. Separation for safety is not forbidden anywhere in Scripture (1 Corinthians 7:11), and violence should be reported to the police. The one who separates what God has joined, in such a case, is the abuser, by his cruelty, not the wife who escapes it. What Scripture says about the marriage bond itself is set out on verses 9–10.

In a sentence. In marriage God joins a man and a woman into one flesh, and no one has the right to separate what God has joined.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, your marriage is God’s joining. Treat it as sacred today: with a word of love, a kindness, or an apology. If you are newly married, ask honestly whether you have yet left, as well as cleaved. And never be one of the hands that helps pull someone else’s marriage apart.

For worship. Behind every marriage stands a greater one. The profound mystery of one flesh points to Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:32): the Son of God who left his Father’s side to hold fast to his bride, who became one with her, and who will never let her go. What God has joined, no man can separate, and what Christ has joined to himself, neither death nor life nor anything in all creation can tear away (Romans 8:38–39). Every faithful marriage is a small sermon on the faithfulness of the Bridegroom.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?" He said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees asked: then why did Moses command a man to give a certificate of divorce and send her away? Jesus said: because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.

Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away? They refer to Deuteronomy 24:1–4. They call it a command.

Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives. Jesus corrects them: Moses did not command divorce; he permitted it. Watch the verb change hands, because the whole exchange turns on it. They had taken a permission and promoted it to a duty, which is exactly what a hard heart does with a concession: what is tolerated becomes normal, what is normal becomes expected, and within a generation somebody is citing the concession as though it were the command. The law of Deuteronomy 24 regulated divorce, which was already happening, to protect women from even worse treatment: the certificate gave the woman legal proof that she was free to remarry. It was a concession to human sin, not God’s ideal. “Hardness of heart” means stubbornness, a heart closed to God and to love.

What Deuteronomy actually commands. Deuteronomy 24 will not carry what they wanted it to carry, as anyone can see by reading it slowly. The passage is one long sentence, and divorce appears only in the opening conditions: if a man divorces her, and if she marries another, and if the second husband also divorces her or dies. The actual command does not arrive until verse 4: her first husband may not take her back. Moses is not legislating divorce at all. He is regulating a remarriage, and mentioning divorce only as the miserable background everybody knew about. The Pharisees had built a licence out of a subordinate clause.

Her shield, his sword. The certificate they cite as a man’s right was in fact a woman’s protection. A wife discarded without documents was in an impossible position: she could not prove she was free, no man would risk marrying her, and she was exposed to the charge of adultery if she tried. The written certificate stood between her and destitution. So the very provision quoted here as evidence that a man may send his wife away was designed to restrain the man and to shield her. They had turned her shield into his sword.

Your hardness of heart. Mark the pronoun. He does not say their hardness, of a generation dead a thousand years. He says your, to the men in front of him, who had come with a question designed to get somebody killed. Sklērokardia is a hard word: not weakness, not confusion, but a heart gone stiff, unable to bend where it should. The concession was not made because the situation was complicated. It was made because men were like that, and are.

But from the beginning it was not so. God’s original design, before sin, was lifelong marriage. Laws that regulate sin do not change God’s ideal.

Should a country have divorce laws at all, then? Yes, and notice that Jesus does not abolish the provision he has just put in its place. This is one of the most useful principles in Scripture for living in a world that is not going to be made Christian by legislation: God legislates for the world as it is without ever lowering what he made it for. A merciful provision for a broken situation is neither an endorsement of the breaking nor a recommendation to use it. That the law permits a thing settles nothing about whether you should do it, and it is possible to be entirely within your legal rights and standing exactly where Jesus says the hardness of heart is.

What it does not mean. Not that Moses’ law was wrong, or that God approved of easy divorce. The law reflected God’s mercy in a sinful world, limiting harm. Nor does “hardness of heart” mean that every divorced person is hard-hearted; often the hard heart is in the spouse who caused the breakdown.

In a sentence. Moses permitted divorce as a concession to human hardness of heart, but God’s design from the beginning was lifelong marriage.

On a Tuesday. Is there hardness in your heart toward your spouse, family member or friend? Ask God to soften it. And watch for the moment when something you once knew was merely tolerated begins to feel like your right.

For worship. God is so merciful that he restrains the damage even of our hardness, and so holy that he never lowers the standard to meet it. He wrote a law to shield discarded women in a world of hard men, and then he sent his Son to give us new hearts. I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). What Moses could only regulate, Christ came to heal.

verseByVerse.quote: And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery." The disciples said to him, "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another commits adultery. The disciples said: if that is how things are between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.

And I say to you. With his own authority (see 5:22). Not as the scribes, quoting the schools, but as the Lord of the law.

Whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery. Divorce for “any cause” does not dissolve the marriage in God’s eyes. A second marriage after such a divorce is adultery, because the first marriage still stands. The exception is “sexual immorality” (porneia), sexual unfaithfulness, which breaks the marriage covenant. In that case, the innocent party may divorce and remarry (see 5:32). Jesus is stricter than both rabbinic schools: stricter than Hillel, and closer to Shammai, but grounded in creation, not in debate about Deuteronomy.

The disciples said to him, If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry. The disciples are shocked. They had assumed the easy divorce of their culture. If marriage is for life, with no easy way out, is it wise to marry at all? Their reaction shows how radical Jesus’ teaching was. Their conclusion misses the point but captures the weight: marriage is not a social convenience; it is a covenant with something of the permanence of God’s own covenants. They sense it, even if their response is flight rather than faithfulness.

Where Christians differ: may the innocent party remarry? Those who hold that remarriage is never allowed while a former spouse lives have serious reasons: Mark and Luke record no exception (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18), Paul says a wife is bound while her husband lives (Romans 7:2–3), and many in the early church held this view. Others read the exception only of unfaithfulness during betrothal. The historic Reformed reading is the more likely, because Jesus’ exception is a real exception, and Paul shows that the bond can be released (1 Corinthians 7:15). Sexual immorality covers adultery and sexual sin of the same gravity. And the exception permits divorce; it does not command it. Where there is repentance, reconciliation is the better path. Verdict: divorce is permitted only for adultery (sexual immorality) or for desertion by an unbelieving spouse, and in those cases the innocent party is free to remarry (Westminster 24.5–6); on no other grounds may the bond be dissolved.

Two grounds and no others. Because this touches real and painful lives, two things should be said plainly. First, Matthew’s single exception is not the whole of Scripture’s teaching. Paul gives a second ground: when an unbelieving spouse deserts a believer, the brother or sister is not enslaved (1 Corinthians 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long held, with the Westminster Confession, that there are two grounds on which the marriage bond may be broken and the innocent party freed to remarry, adultery and desertion, and no others (Westminster 24.5–6). Those who took a stricter line (no remarriage ever) or a looser one (Hillel’s any cause) both miss the balance of the whole. Second, and more importantly: none of this is a loophole to be worked but a fence around something holy. Jesus’ aim is not to license divorce but to guard the one-flesh covenant against the hardness of heart that treats it lightly.

Why Mark and Luke have no exception. A reader with Mark or Luke open will notice that Matthew twice records an exception (5:32; 19:9) and they record none: whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery (Mark 10:11; Luke 16:18). Critics say Matthew softened his Lord. But this is how people have always spoken. A father who says, we do not lend the car out, is not lying when he lends it to his own son in an emergency; the rule is stated as a rule, and the known qualification is not repeated every time. Mark and Luke give the principle in its blunt form, which is where its force lies. Matthew, writing for Jewish readers to whom the Shammai and Hillel quarrel was a live argument, records the qualification Jesus actually made, because his readers were the very people who would ask. Neither says what the other denies.

What about a marriage that is destroying somebody? For some readers this is the only question in the chapter: the husband who is violent, the wife whose rage has made the house unsafe, the parent whose drinking has turned a home into somewhere the children brace themselves to enter. Matthew names one ground and Paul a second, and neither uses the word. Does Christ require a battered woman to stay? He does not, and it will not do to be vague about it, because vagueness here has cost real people a great deal. Three things are true, and the order matters.

Separation for safety. First, and before any question of divorce arises at all: separation for safety is nowhere forbidden in Scripture. Paul contemplates a wife who has separated and simply tells her to remain unmarried or be reconciled (1 Corinthians 7:11); he lays down no conditions for the separating and attaches no shame to it. Getting out of reach of a dangerous man is not a step toward divorce. It is a step toward not being killed, and nothing in this chapter stands in its way. It is also, very often, the only thing that has ever cost him anything, and therefore the only thing that has ever made repentance a live possibility. Violence and threats are crimes, and they should be reported to the police.

The children. Second, the children are not a secondary consideration. A parent who removes them from a violent house is obeying rather than disobeying, and the man who tells her otherwise should be asked to read the previous chapter aloud, where the Lord who forbids the easy divorce says that a man who causes one of these little ones to stumble would be better off in deep water with a millstone round his neck (18:6).

Desertion judged by its substance. Third, on the bond itself. The Reformed churches held that the marriage bond may be broken by adultery or by desertion, and the men who framed that were not innocent about cruelty. Desertion was never treated as a question of geography alone. A husband who makes a home unsurvivable has deserted the marriage as surely as one who packs a bag; he has simply arranged for his wife to do the walking. Judging desertion by its substance rather than by who physically left the house is not a modern loophole. It is what the older pastors meant, and it is why they said the innocent party is not to be held bound.

Not settled alone. Two things follow. This is a matter to be taken to a church rather than settled alone, which is precisely why the previous chapter placed such judgments in the hands of a congregation and its elders (18:15–20), and why a wounded person needs people around her who will look at the evidence. And any church that hears such a case and answers by sending a woman home to try harder, or by weighing a man’s standing in the congregation against what she has described, has not been careful with Matthew 19. It has been careless with a life, and it should be told so plainly. Abuse is never to be tolerated, and it is never to be handled privately: the authorities must be told.

What of someone who divorced without biblical grounds, or who divorced and remarried before becoming a Christian? The guilty party who repents is called to remain single or be reconciled (1 Corinthians 7:11), though Reformed churches differ on remarriage in that case. Those already remarried are not to break up the second marriage; it is a real marriage, and the call is to repent of how it began and to live faithfully in it. The phrase commits adultery describes how the second marriage began, not a sin repeated every day it continues.

What it does not mean. Not that divorced and remarried people can never be forgiven, or must divorce again. Divorce and remarriage outside these grounds is sin, but sin can be forgiven, and second marriages are real marriages to be honoured from then on. Nor does the exception mean that divorce is required after adultery: reconciliation is better where possible. The Westminster Confession adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15) as a second ground (24.6) (see 5:31–32).

A fence, not a cage. Look last at what our Lord is actually protecting in this passage. He is not defending an institution against the people inside it. Every stroke of it, the one flesh, the yoking, the refusal of the convenient exit, is meant to make a marriage the one place on earth where a human being is safe for life. A reading of it that shuts somebody inside cruelty has taken the fence he built around a person and used it as a cage.

If my own marriage has already broken, is there hope for me? Yes. To any reader whose marriage has already broken, through your sin, or another’s, or a tangle of both: there is no sin here that the blood of Christ does not cover, and no past so broken that grace cannot make something new of what remains. The gospel meets us not in the marriage we should have had but in the life we actually have. If you sinned, confess it plainly to God and, where it is wise, to those you wronged, and receive his forgiveness. If you were sinned against, bring your grief to the one who was himself betrayed. And find a church that will walk with you rather than define you by it.

In a sentence. Divorce and remarriage except for sexual unfaithfulness is adultery, a teaching so strict that the disciples thought it better not to marry.

On a Tuesday. Marriage is a serious commitment. If you are considering marriage, count the cost. If you are married, keep your vows. And if you know someone in a marriage that has become dangerous, help them to safety and to people who can act, rather than telling them to try harder.

For worship. Here is the Lord who speaks with his own authority over marriage, because he is the Bridegroom whose love for his bride never fails. Our unfaithfulness to God is the adultery the prophets mourned, and he did not divorce us; he came after us, paid for our sin, and made us his own (Hosea 3:1; Ephesians 5:25–27). He is stricter than any rabbi about the covenant, and kinder than any of them to the broken. He guards the weak, he forgives the guilty, and he makes all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, "Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this, receive it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: not everyone can accept this saying, but only those to whom it is given. Some are eunuchs from birth, some were made eunuchs by others, and some have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let anyone who can accept this accept it.

Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. “This saying” is probably the disciples’ remark that it is better not to marry (v. 10). Not everyone can live a single life. It is a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7). Jesus does not command celibacy but honours it as a gift given to some for the sake of the kingdom.

For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth. A eunuch was a man unable to marry or father children. Some were born unable, because of physical conditions.

And there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men. Men castrated as servants for royal courts, a common practice in the ancient world (Acts 8:27). Under the law of Moses, eunuchs were excluded from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1), but God promised them an everlasting name in his house (Isaiah 56:3–5). This middle category is nearly always skipped: people made this way by others, by circumstances entirely outside their control, and in the ancient world often by an act of cruelty.

And there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Not literal self-mutilation, but people who choose to remain unmarried and celibate in order to serve God’s kingdom more fully. Jesus himself was unmarried. Paul was single and commended singleness for those who have the gift, because it allows undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35). Jesus names all three kinds in one breath and honours the calling in all three; its dignity is not reserved for those who volunteered.

Let the one who is able to receive this receive it. It is a calling for some, not a command for all.

The third kind is figurative. The third kind of eunuch is figurative: those who give up marriage for the kingdom, not those who mutilate themselves. Nor does this require ministers to be unmarried; Peter had a wife (8:14; 1 Corinthians 9:5), and Paul expects overseers to be husbands (1 Timothy 3:2). The eunuchs from birth were those born unable to marry; the text is about that incapacity, not about sexual orientation.

What it does not mean. Not that marriage is less holy than singleness, or that single people are second-class Christians. Both are callings from God (1 Corinthians 7:7). The Reformers rejected the medieval idea that celibacy is a higher spiritual state, and that clergy must be celibate (1 Timothy 4:1–3). And it does not mean literal castration: the early church condemned Origen for doing that. Some today read “eunuchs from birth” as a reference to people with same-sex attraction, but that is not what the word means; it refers to physical inability to father children. What the verse does show is that Jesus honours those who are single, whatever the reason, and that a single life can be lived fully for God. Christians who remain single and celibate out of faithfulness to Christ, including those who experience same-sex attraction, are following a path Jesus honours here.

If I did not choose to be single, how can it be a gift? The objection is entirely fair. A gift is normally something you wanted and unwrapped. Many single Christians did not choose this and would exchange it tomorrow: the woman who hoped to marry and is now fifty, the widower, the person whose marriage ended and who will not remarry, the believer whose convictions about sexuality mean marriage is not open to him. Told that their situation is a gift, they may feel asked to be grateful for a loss. But in the New Testament a gift (charisma) is grace given for a purpose, not a pleasure guaranteed. Paul’s thorn was no delight either, and what he was promised in it was not enjoyment but sufficient grace (2 Corinthians 12:9). So what is promised is not that you will like it. It is that there is grace enough for it; that it is a genuine vocation rather than a waiting room for real life to begin; and that it is not a lesser existence. The most completely human being who ever lived was single, and so was the apostle who wrote most of the New Testament.

What the church owes. Jesus says it later in this same chapter: everyone who has left houses or family for his sake will receive a hundredfold (v. 29), which Mark spells out as brothers, sisters, mothers and children now in this time (Mark 10:30). That is not decoration. It is a debt. A congregation that preaches marriage constantly and has no place at its tables for the unmarried has left half its members outside the promise its Lord made. If you carry singleness as a grief, say so plainly to God and to somebody who will not rush you; Scripture has ample room for people who wanted a good thing and did not receive it, and it never once calls that unbelief.

In a sentence. Some people cannot marry, and some choose singleness to serve God’s kingdom; it is a gift given to some, not a command for all.

On a Tuesday. How does your church treat single people? Honour them as Jesus does, and include them as family. Invite someone single to your table this week, not as a guest to be entertained but as family.

For worship. The Lord of glory lived his whole earthly life unmarried, and no one was ever more fully human or more fruitful. He gave himself entirely to his Father’s business and to his bride, the church, and he has a place in his house for every single, widowed, childless and overlooked believer. To them he promises a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isaiah 56:5). In him no life given to God is a lesser life.
verseByVerse.note: A eunuch was a man unable to marry or father children. Some, like Paul, remained single to serve the kingdom.

parallels.desc: a name better than sons and daughters

verseByVerse.quote: Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people, but Jesus said, "Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then children were brought to Jesus so that he could lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people. But Jesus said: let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.

Then children were brought to him. Luke says they were infants (Luke 18:15). Parents brought them, probably mothers.

That he might lay his hands on them and pray. Jewish parents brought children to rabbis and elders to be blessed. Laying hands on someone was a sign of blessing (Genesis 48:14). It is the most natural thing a believing parent can do.

The disciples rebuked the people. They thought Jesus was too busy and important for children, and that they were protecting him. They had forgotten the lesson of 18:1–5, given only a chapter before, with a child standing in the middle of them.

But Jesus said, Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them. Mark says Jesus was indignant (Mark 10:14). Jesus welcomes children. No one is too small or unimportant for him. The word for hinder (kōlyō) is used elsewhere of barriers placed before those seeking to come to Christ (Acts 8:36; 10:47). The disciples are putting a fence where Jesus wants a door.

For to such belongs the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom belongs to those who are like children: humble, dependent, receiving it as a gift (18:3–4). Not such as these will eventually be admitted, but theirs is the kingdom. The children possess what the adult disciples are still learning to receive.

What it does not mean. Not that children are automatically saved by being children, or that they do not need Christ. They are sinners by nature too (Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3). But Jesus welcomes them and blesses them.

Where Christians differ: infant baptism. Paedobaptists often cite this passage in support of baptising infants: if the kingdom belongs to children, they should receive the sign of the covenant. They set it beside the covenant sign given to Abraham’s children (Genesis 17:7), Peter’s word that the promise is for you and for your children (Acts 2:39), and the whole households baptised in Acts. Credobaptists respond that this passage says nothing about baptism; Jesus blessed the children and prayed for them, he did not baptise them; and baptism signifies faith and union with Christ, which a person must profess. Every baptism the New Testament describes follows a profession of faith. Honesty requires admitting that this point lands: a case for infant baptism has to be built from the shape of the covenant across both Testaments rather than from these verses, and that wider case is less convincing than the plain New Testament pattern of baptism after faith (see on Acts 2:39). Verdict: credobaptist, held charitably. The passage teaches that children are welcome to Christ and should be brought to him in prayer and teaching, but it does not mandate infant baptism. Both sides agree that Christian parents must bring their children to Jesus.

What both sides can take home. What this text does settle is smaller and sharper. The only people rebuked in the story are the ones who thought children were a distraction from the real work. Whatever a church concludes about the water, a church that treats its little ones as an interruption to be managed until they are old enough to matter has been told plainly to stop it. He did not tolerate them; he called for them, and he laid his hands on every one.

Do children who die in infancy go to heaven? This verse does not say that children are innocent; Jesus has just warned that we must become like them, not that they are sinless (18:3). But it shows his welcome to them, and Scripture gives grieving parents real hope. David said of his dead infant, I shall go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and the historic Reformed confessions teach that elect infants who die in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (Westminster 10.3). Many Christians are confident that God, the Judge of all the earth, will do right by every child who dies before it can believe. We do not have a verse that says so in plain words, but we have the character of the God who said, let the little children come to me.

So should I wait for my children to choose for themselves? No. Credobaptists wait for a credible profession of faith before baptism, but no one should wait to bring children to Christ. Pray for them and with them from the day they are born; read them the Bible; bring them to worship; tell them the gospel plainly and often; and call them to trust Christ for themselves. Children can truly believe, and Jesus wants them near him. A child who asks to follow Jesus should be taken seriously and gently helped, and when his faith is credible, he may be baptised.

In a sentence. When the disciples tried to keep children away, Jesus welcomed them, for the kingdom belongs to such as these.

On a Tuesday. How can you bring children to Jesus: your own, or those in your church? Pray for them by name, and teach them about him. And when children are noisy in church, remember who was rebuked in this story, and it was not the children.

For worship. The King of heaven, on his way to Jerusalem, stops for babies. He is indignant when anyone keeps them from him, and he says the kingdom belongs to such as these. This is our Saviour: not too busy, not too important, not too holy to take a child in his arms. He gathers the lambs in his arms and carries them in his bosom (Isaiah 40:11), and grieving parents may lay their hope on the heart of the one who said, let them come.

verseByVerse.quote: And he laid his hands on them and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus laid his hands on them and went on his way.

And he laid his hands on them. He blessed them, as the parents had asked. Mark says he took them in his arms (Mark 10:16). Jesus had time for children, even on the road to the cross. Read it against what had just happened, because the sequence is the point. The apostles had just been turning these families away. Now Jesus puts his hands on their children, one by one, and hands laid on a group of children is not a gesture made in a moment. The parents who had been told off by the inner circle stood there and watched it happen.

Who brought them. Somebody thought it worth the walk, in the heat, with small children, on the chance of getting near. And when the men closest to Jesus told them they were wasting his time, an intimidating thing then and now, they did not take the children home. The people who received the blessing are the ones who declined to be embarrassed out of the queue.

Bring them. So the instruction to a parent or grandparent is not complicated, and it is not sentimental. Bring them. Put them where Christ is, week after week, when it is inconvenient and when they are difficult and when they are old enough to say they would rather not. Pray with your hand on them, out loud, using their name, which is as nearly as we can manage the thing happening in this verse. And do not be argued out of it by anyone who implies that the serious work of the church is going on elsewhere; that argument was made once already in this passage, by better men than will make it to you, and it was publicly overruled.

Does this promise that my children will become Christians? No, and the verse is quietly used to wound. Scripture is honest about godly parents whose children went their own way, and so is every congregation that has been going long enough. A mother or father grieving over a grown son who wants nothing to do with any of it must not read these verses as a verdict on their parenting or as a promise that failed. What is here is a picture of Christ’s disposition toward children, warm, unhurried and personally given, and an instruction about the church’s. That disposition has not altered for a man of forty who was once carried up to him. Keep praying; the arms that held these children are still open.

And went away. He continued his journey to Jerusalem. He blessed them, and left. Every one of those children grew up in a country that would crucify him within months, and Matthew does not tell us what became of a single one of them. The blessing was not a promise of a smooth life. It was a real thing, done by real hands, on an ordinary afternoon, by a man on his way to Jerusalem.

In a sentence. Jesus blessed the children with his hands and continued his journey.

On a Tuesday. Pray for a child by name today, and if it is your own, with your hand on his head. Do not let anyone embarrass you out of bringing your children near to Christ.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he welcomes the small and unimportant, including you. The hands that rested on those children would soon be nailed to a cross, and they carry the marks still. He blessed them on his way to die, and he died that the blessing might be real. The Lord who had time for children on the road to Calvary has time for every one of us now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — The Rich Young Man and the Great Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young man asks what good deed will earn eternal life. Jesus directs him to the commandments; he claims to have kept them all. Jesus says: sell your possessions, give to the poor, and follow me. The man goes away sorrowful, for he has great wealth. Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. The disciples are astonished. Jesus promises rewards for those who have left everything to follow him, and closes with the great reversal: the first shall be last and the last first. Two exchanges inside the section carry more weight than their length. Jesus meets the opening question with one of his own — why do you ask me about what is good, when there is only one who is good (v. 17)? And after the camel and the needle, Peter asks what the Twelve, who did leave everything, will have for it (v. 27); the promise of thrones and a hundredfold is his answer, and verse 30 is the warning attached to it.
verseByVerse.theology: The rich young man's failure reveals the nature of the commandment he thought he kept: "love your neighbor as yourself" (v. 19) was the final commandment in Jesus's list, and the sell-everything command is the test of whether it is actually operative. One cannot love one's neighbor as oneself while sitting on wealth that could address their need. The commandment was kept in its visible form (no theft, no fraud) but not in its spirit (genuine love that costs something). Jesus's diagnosis is precise: the man's wealth is not neutral; it is the specific obstacle between him and eternal life. Verse 17 is regularly produced as proof that Jesus denied being God — he pointed away from himself, so he cannot have thought himself divine. But he does not say I am not good. He asks a question, and the question is a door: you have called goodness a deed you can perform and me a teacher who knows the trick, and there is only One who is good, so think again about what you are asking and whom you are asking. The rest of the Gospel will not let the denial stand — this is the man who forgives sins as only God can (9:2-6), who says the Lord of the Sabbath is standing here (12:8), and who claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18).
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' astonishment at the camel-and-needle saying reflects their assumption that wealth is a sign of divine blessing — the standard view. Jesus upends the assumption: wealth is a spiritual obstacle, not an advantage. The camel through the needle's eye is not a metaphor for difficulty but for impossibility — making the way of salvation clear. "With God all things are possible" is the only resolution: the rich man cannot save himself; only God can accomplish the transformation that makes a rich man enter the kingdom. Guard that promise, since it has been lifted off the page and attached to whatever a reader happens to want. The word this has an antecedent, and the antecedent is the salvation of a rich man; it is not a general assurance that anything is obtainable with enough belief. And Matthew has left the proof at the far end of his book. When the crucifixion is over, a man comes to Pilate for the body — and Matthew alone tells us he was rich, plousios, the same word used here of the man who cannot get in (27:57). The needle did not widen and the camel did not shrink. God did the thing he said only God could do.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a man came up to him, saying, "Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?" And he said to him, "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man came to Jesus and asked: Teacher, what good thing must I do to have eternal life? Jesus said: why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.

And behold, a man came up to him. Matthew later calls him young (v. 20); Luke calls him a ruler (Luke 18:18), probably a leader in a synagogue. He was wealthy (v. 22). He had everything his culture valued: youth, wealth, position, morality and religious seriousness.

Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life? “Eternal life” means the life of the age to come, life in God’s kingdom (v. 23). His question assumes that eternal life is earned by doing something good: one more deed, one more achievement. It frames eternal life as a transaction: what can I perform to secure it?

Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. Mark and Luke record his question as “Good Teacher” and Jesus’ answer as “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:17–18). Jesus is not denying that he is good or that he is God. He is making the man think. Only God is truly good. If the man calls Jesus good, does he realise what he is saying? And goodness is not found in doing one good deed, but in God himself.

Did Jesus deny being God? No, though this verse is regularly produced as proof that he did. Read the sentence again and see what it does. Jesus does not say, I am not good. He asks a question, and the question is a door: you have called goodness a thing you can do and me a teacher who can tell you the trick; there is only One who is good, so think again about what you are asking, and whom you are asking. He is not refusing the title. He is telling a man who used it casually that he has no idea what he has just said. And the rest of the Gospel refuses to let the denial stand: this is the man who forgives sins as only God can (9:2–6), who says the Lord of the Sabbath is here (12:8), who receives worship without once waving it away (14:33), and who at the end claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). A man building a case against his own deity does not talk like that.

Matthew’s wording. Matthew has him ask about what is good rather than why do you call me good. It is often said that Matthew tidied the wording to protect his Christology. More likely he gives the exchange in compressed form, keeping its point, as he does elsewhere (compare 9:18 with Mark 5:23). The man came asking what good deed he must do; Matthew holds question and answer together, and the reply is the same in both: goodness is not a deed in your hand, it is a property of God, and you have come to the one place where the two meet without knowing it.

If you would enter life, keep the commandments. Jesus points him to God’s law. Not because the law can save, but because the law reveals God’s goodness and shows us our sin (Romans 3:20; 7:7). Jesus will show the man that he has not kept the law as he thinks.

Does this teach salvation by works? No. Perfect obedience would bring life, but no sinner can offer it (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10–12). Jesus uses the law here to expose the young man’s need, which is why he goes on to say that salvation is impossible with man but possible with God (v. 26).
