What it does not mean. Not that Jesus teaches salvation by keeping the law. He is using the law to expose the man’s heart. Nor does it mean that Jesus denied his own deity. The way he speaks of “one who is good” invites the man, and us, to recognise who Jesus is.

In a sentence. A man asked what good deed would earn eternal life, and Jesus pointed him to the one good God and his commandments.

On a Tuesday. Do you think of eternal life as something you earn by doing enough good? It is a gift from the only one who is good.

For worship. There is only one who is good, and he was standing in the road, talking to a young man who did not know whom he was addressing. All goodness flows from God, and in Jesus the goodness of God walked the roads of Judea. He alone kept the commandments perfectly, and he gives his righteousness to those who could never keep them. The good deed the man wanted to do was done by the Good One himself, at the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke record the question as “Good Teacher.” Luke calls him a ruler.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, "Which ones?" And Jesus said, "You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother, and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man asked: which commandments? Jesus said: you shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, honour your father and mother, and you shall love your neighbour as yourself.

He said to him, Which ones? Perhaps he wanted to know which ones mattered most, or to check that he had kept them. His question gives him away. A man who asks which commandments has already turned the law into a syllabus and is asking what is on the examination. He is not asking how to love God; he is asking which items he will be marked on, so that he can tick them off and know where he stands. It is the most common way there is of holding a religion, and it is comfortable precisely because a list can be finished.

You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother. The sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth and fifth commandments: the second half of the Ten Commandments, about how we treat others (Exodus 20:12–16).

And, You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18, which sums up the second half of the law (22:39; Romans 13:9). And the addition is as pointed as the omissions. Every other item on his list can be obeyed by sitting still; a man asleep is keeping five of them. This one cannot be kept by not doing something, and it has no upper limit, which is why it is the one item on the list the young man cannot tick.

What is missing. Jesus does not mention the tenth commandment: you shall not covet (Exodus 20:17). Nor the first: you shall have no other gods. These are the commandments the young man will be shown to have broken: his wealth was his god, and he coveted it. Jesus recites a list with the man’s own sin carefully removed, lets him answer all these I have kept, and then in the next breath asks him for the one thing the missing commandments were about. It is the method Nathan used on David, who angrily passed sentence on a man who stole a lamb (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

A conscience made of prohibitions. The young man’s instinct is everybody’s. Asked what you got wrong last week, you would almost certainly name things you did: a temper lost, a sharp reply, a lie about why you were late. Very few of us would name the person we did not visit, the money we did not give, the conversation we avoided because it would have cost an evening. A conscience built entirely out of prohibitions can be satisfied by half past ten in the morning, and that is exactly what recommends it.

Why does Jesus list the commandments if no one can keep them? Because the law is a mirror before it is a ladder. Its first work for a sinner is to show him what he is, so that he will look for a Saviour (Galatians 3:24). But the law is not thrown away after that. For the believer, the commandments remain God’s good guide to a life of love (Romans 13:8–10), kept now not to earn life but out of gratitude for life freely given. Read them both ways: as the verdict that sends you to Christ, and as the shape of the life Christ is producing in you.

In a sentence. Jesus listed the commandments about loving one’s neighbour, leaving out the ones about coveting and other gods.

On a Tuesday. Go through the Ten Commandments slowly today, especially the first and the tenth. Which ones expose your heart? And name one good thing you failed to do this week, not just a wrong thing you did.

For worship. The Lord who gave the law on Sinai stood on a road in Judea and used it as a surgeon uses a knife: precisely, gently, to reach the one place that needed healing. He knows exactly which commandment is our undoing, and he does not expose it to shame us but to save us. And he himself loved his neighbour as himself, and more: he loved his enemies to the death.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour and adds Leviticus 19:18.

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: The young man said to him, "All these I have kept. What do I still lack?" Jesus said to him, "If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young man said: I have kept all these. What do I still lack? Jesus said: if you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.

All these I have kept. He was sincere. Outwardly, he had kept these commands from his youth (Mark 10:20). He was not a hypocrite in the usual sense. But he had not understood the depth of the law (5:21–48): love for one’s neighbour includes the poor, and loving God means having no other god. By the standard he had been given, it may have been perfectly true, and that is the most frightening thing about him. He is a decent, careful, religious man who had done everything he understood himself to have been asked.

What do I still lack? He knew something was missing. Despite his morality, he had no assurance of eternal life. His honest question is the most hopeful thing about him. And nobody asks it unless something has been nagging at him. He did not need information; he needed to hear it said aloud by someone with the authority to say it.

If you would be perfect. “Perfect” (teleios) means complete, whole (see 5:48). What he lacked was wholehearted devotion to God.

Go, sell what you possess and give to the poor. Jesus puts his finger on the one thing that held his heart: his wealth. It was his god. To keep the first commandment, he must let it go. And to love his neighbour as himself, he must give to the poor. Jesus gives no rule about percentages and no general call to moderation. He names the specific object that had this specific man, and asks for exactly that. So the question to bring away is not how much is enough, but what is mine.

And you will have treasure in heaven. See 6:19–21. He would exchange earthly treasure for heavenly. Jesus is not confiscating. He is prising the man’s fingers off something small so that his hands are free for something enormous.

And come, follow me. The real issue. Not only giving away money, but following Jesus. Eternal life is found not in doing a good deed, but in following the one who is good. The removal exists for the sake of the last clause.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must sell everything they own. Jesus did not command this of everyone: Zacchaeus gave away half (Luke 19:8), and Joseph of Arimathea remained rich (27:57). He commanded it of this man, because wealth was his idol. The principle for all is that nothing may come before Christ, and everything we have belongs to him. Nor does it mean that giving away possessions earns eternal life. The man needed to give up his false god to follow the true one. Stewardship is not covetousness: Christians may own property and save wisely, but must hold it as God’s, use it generously, and be willing to give it up if Christ asks.

Where Christians differ: counsels of perfection. Medieval Catholic teaching distinguished between commands for all Christians and “counsels of perfection” (poverty, celibacy, obedience) for those seeking a higher spiritual state, especially monks and nuns. The Reformers rejected this two-level Christianity: every Christian is called to total devotion, in whatever calling God gives. Verdict: there is one standard of discipleship for all; Jesus addressed this man’s particular idol. Does if you would be perfect mean there is a higher class of Christian, as some teach of vows of poverty and celibacy? No. Jesus means complete, wholehearted devotion, the same word he used in 5:48, and he calls this man to it because wealth was his rival god. The call is to every disciple; what it costs varies from person to person.

How do I find my one thing? Sit still for a minute and most people can name the thing they would least like Christ to ask them for. It is not always money. It may be a relationship you know is pulling you away, a career you have quietly made the point of your life, your reputation, a plan for your children, an addiction you manage rather than end, a grudge you have decided to keep, or simply the fear of what people would say. The tell is the flinch. And the test is not whether you would be willing in principle, because principle costs nothing. It is what happens when the thing is actually named, out loud, and asked for.

What if I find my one thing and cannot let it go? Then you have not failed the test; you have arrived where the gospel starts. When the disciples ask who then can be saved, Jesus does not say, those with the strength to let go. He says that with man it is impossible, and with God all things are possible (v. 26). Bring the clenched hand to him, honestly, and ask him to open it. He does not wait for you to free yourself before he receives you. He frees those who come.

In a sentence. When the young man asked what he still lacked, Jesus told him to give up the wealth that ruled his heart and follow him.

On a Tuesday. What would Jesus put his finger on in your life, the one thing that holds your heart? Are you willing to let it go? Name it before God today, and ask him for the grace to open your hand.

For worship. Mark tells us that Jesus looked at him and loved him (Mark 10:21). His command was not harshness but love, the love of the one who was himself rich and for our sake became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He asked this man for everything because he was offering him everything: treasure in heaven, and himself. He never asks us to give up anything that he has not first given up for us, and he never takes anything from us without giving us more.

verseByVerse.quote: When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. And Jesus said to his disciples, "Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the young man heard this, he went away sorrowful, because he had great wealth. Jesus said to his disciples: truly, it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.

When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful. The only person in the Gospels who walked away from Jesus’ personal call sad. He wanted eternal life, but not at that price. He was sorrowful because he knew what he was choosing. Weigh what has happened, because it is unique in this Gospel. Jesus personally invites this man with the same words that emptied a fishing boat and a tax booth. Fishermen left nets. A tax collector left a table with money on it. This man went home. Matthew never tells us his name.

Grief is not repentance. He was not scornful. He went away sorrowful, which means he knew Jesus was right. That is the disturbing thing about him: he felt everything a man ought to feel, and did nothing. A person can be moved almost to tears by a sermon on Sunday, know while it is happening that it describes his own life, and have altered nothing by Wednesday, and then mistake being moved for being changed. The most dangerous condition in this passage is not the hard heart. It is the softened one that goes home anyway.

For he had great possessions. Or rather, his possessions had him. He thought he owned his wealth; it owned him. They were not his property but his prison, and he chose to stay in it.

Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven. Wealth makes it hard to enter the kingdom. Why? Because wealth gives a false sense of security and independence. It makes people feel they do not need God. It competes for the heart’s loyalty (6:24). It chokes the word (13:22). It is very hard for someone with much to come to God as a child with nothing (18:3; 5:3).

The danger named precisely. Vague warnings about materialism change nobody, so name the danger exactly. The trouble with money is not that it is evil; it is that it quietly removes the daily experience of dependence. A man who can solve most of his problems by paying for them will, across twenty years, gradually stop asking anyone for anything, and never notice it happening, because every decision along the way was sensible. He did not rebel against God. He simply stopped needing him for anything specific, and a faith with nothing specific left in it goes thin without ever being renounced.

What it does not mean. Not that rich people cannot be saved, or that poverty earns salvation. Abraham and Job were rich and righteous. Jesus will immediately say that with God all things are possible (v. 26). But wealth is a real spiritual danger. And by world standards, most people in Western countries are rich. Scripture is full of wealthy believers: Abraham with his herds, Job at both ends of his book, and the women who paid for this very ministry out of their means and stayed to the end when the men had gone (27:55–56; Luke 8:3). This is a warning about a specific danger and an honest statement of the odds. It is not a sentence.

A ten-second test. When did you last pray about something that money could not also have fixed? For most people in a comfortable country the honest answer is: about health, and about people I love. That is why illness and bereavement so often turn out to be where God is finally met. They are the two remaining rooms in a wealthy life where a cheque does nothing at all.

How much should I give? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage for Christians, though many find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point. It gives principles instead: give regularly and in proportion to what you have (1 Corinthians 16:2), give generously and cheerfully, not reluctantly (2 Corinthians 9:6–7), care for your own household (1 Timothy 5:8), support those who teach you the word (Galatians 6:6), and do not forget the poor (Galatians 2:10). A useful test is whether your giving costs you anything you notice. If it never does, it is probably not yet generous. Above all, give as one who belongs to Christ, because the giving is the opening of a hand, and the hand is the heart’s.

In a sentence. The young man went away sad because he would not give up his wealth, and Jesus warned that riches make it hard to enter the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. By global standards, you are probably rich. How does your wealth affect your trust in God and your generosity? Pray today about something money cannot fix, and give away something that costs you.

For worship. The one who watched that young man walk away is the one who owned the cattle on a thousand hills and had nowhere to lay his head. He never needed wealth to be secure, because his security was his Father. And he became poor so that the rich might be freed from their riches and the poor made rich in him. The treasure the young man refused is the treasure Christ himself is, and it never rusts.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God." When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, "Who then can be saved?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. When the disciples heard this, they were astonished: who then can be saved?

It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The camel was the largest animal in Palestine; the eye of a needle the smallest opening. A deliberately absurd, impossible picture, like the rabbinic saying about an elephant going through a needle’s eye. In Palestine the largest animal to hand was a camel; in Babylon it was an elephant. Everyone who first heard this knew it was a joke about impossibility, and nobody was laughing.

Softenings. Some have suggested a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle’s Eye, through which a camel could squeeze by kneeling, but there is no evidence such a gate existed, and it weakens Jesus’ point. Others suggest a misreading of kamēlos (camel) as kamilos (rope), but that too is unnecessary; a handful of late manuscripts read it, and it is a scribe’s improvement, not Matthew’s word. The giveaway is that both softenings pull in exactly the same direction: they are attempts to make the sentence survivable. Jesus means it is humanly impossible.

Than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. Matthew here uses “kingdom of God”, which he usually calls “kingdom of heaven” (v. 23). The two mean the same thing.

When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished. In their culture, wealth was often seen as a sign of God’s blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1–14). If the rich, whom God has blessed, cannot be saved, who can? A rich man was not merely a man with resources; he was a man whose life displayed that God was pleased with him. And this rich man was also young, morally serious, scrupulous about the commandments, and willing to walk up to a travelling rabbi in public and ask what he still lacked. He was the strongest candidate any of them had ever seen. They had just watched the front-runner walk away down the road.

Saying, Who then can be saved? Exactly the right question. If salvation depends on human ability, no one can be saved. Almost nobody asks it honestly, because almost everybody keeps a private category of people who obviously qualify: the missionary, the pastor’s wife, the old woman in the third row who has prayed for forty years and never said a sharp word. As long as that category exists, salvation remains comfortably plausible and somebody else’s problem. Jesus has just abolished the category. Not one name survives it.

The clearing of the ground. That is not cruelty; it is the necessary clearing of the ground. Nobody has ever heard the next verse, that with God all things are possible, until he has first stopped believing that with men some things are. The astonishment of verse 25 is not a failure of faith. It is the first correct reaction anybody in this chapter has had.

What it does not mean. Not that wealth is a sign of God’s favour, as the prosperity gospel teaches. Jesus overturns that idea. Wealth is not a proof of blessing, and it can be a great obstacle.

In a sentence. Jesus said it is harder for a rich person to enter the kingdom than for a camel to go through a needle’s eye, and the astonished disciples asked who then can be saved.

On a Tuesday. Never think of your wealth as proof that God approves of you. It is a responsibility, and a danger. And give up your private list of people who obviously qualify for heaven, including yourself.

For worship. The needle’s eye is closed to every one of us, rich and poor, good and bad. And that is where the glory of God begins to shine, because the door that no man can open has been opened by the one who said, I am the door (John 10:9). Salvation is not a narrow squeeze for the deserving. It is a miracle for the impossible, worked by a God who delights to do what we cannot.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus looked at them and said, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." Then Peter said in reply, "See, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked at them and said: with man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible. Peter said: we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?

But Jesus looked at them and said, With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible. The heart of the passage. Salvation is impossible by human effort, for rich and poor alike. No one can save himself. But God can do the impossible: he can save anyone, even the rich, by changing the heart (Genesis 18:14; Jeremiah 32:17). Salvation is God’s work from start to finish (Ephesians 2:8–9). Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector, was saved (Luke 19:1–10). Matthew keeps the detail that he looked at them (emblepsas), a straight, deliberate look, before he spoke. A dozen frightened men were held in his eye for a moment before they were told the thing that would settle them.

The staircase removed. This sentence turns the chapter over. Everything up to here has been about what a man must do: keep the commandments, which ones, sell what you have, come and follow. And now: with man this is impossible. The chapter has spent twenty-five verses building a staircase, and this sentence removes it. The young man arrived asking what good deed must I do to have eternal life, and the final answer is that there is no deed. He asked exactly the right person, and went home a few verses before the answer came.

What this promise covers. Guard the promise, because it has been lifted off this page and printed on more posters than almost any other sentence in Matthew, and attached to whatever the reader happens to be hoping for. The word this has an antecedent, and the antecedent is the salvation of a rich man. It is not a general assurance that anything you want is obtainable if you believe hard enough. It is the specific promise that the one thing which genuinely cannot be done, the unfastening of a heart welded to its possessions, is precisely the thing God does. And the phrase has an old home. When Sarah laughed at the promise of a son, the LORD asked, is anything too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). The impossibility there was a settled biological fact too, and the answer was a baby.

The rich man at the tomb. Matthew, who never wastes a word, has left the proof at the far end of his book. When the crucifixion is over and the disciples have scattered, a man comes to Pilate and asks for the body. Mark calls him a respected member of the council; Luke calls him good and righteous. Matthew alone tells us he was rich, plousios, the same word used of the man who cannot get in (27:57). The same writer, using the same word, shows us a rich man who is a disciple, spending his money, his position and his new tomb on a body nobody else would claim. The needle did not widen and the camel did not shrink; God did what he had said only God could do.

Then Peter said in reply, See, we have left everything and followed you. Peter compares the disciples with the rich young man. They did what he would not: they left their boats, nets and families (4:20, 22; 9:9).

What then will we have? An honest question, perhaps with a trace of self-interest. What is the reward for leaving everything? And the striking thing is that it is not rebuked. Jesus answers it, at length. Christianity is not indifferent to reward, and a piety that claims to want nothing at all is not more spiritual than Peter but less truthful; this Gospel has already told these men to lay up treasure in heaven (6:19–21), which is an instruction to want something. The trouble in Peter’s sentence is not the wanting. It is the small word we. He has just watched another man fail the test, and he has begun to compare.

If salvation is God’s work, does it matter what I do? Yes, though not in the way the young man thought. God saves by changing the heart, and a changed heart follows Christ, repents, gives and obeys (Philippians 2:12–13). Our actions do not earn salvation; they are what salvation looks like when God has done his work. And the impossibility of saving ourselves is exactly what frees us to come: you do not have to manage it, only to ask. Anyone, however far gone, may call on him today, and he who began the work will finish it (Philippians 1:6).

In a sentence. Jesus declared that salvation, impossible for humans, is possible with God, and Peter asked what reward the disciples would receive for leaving everything.

On a Tuesday. Who do you know who seems impossible to save? With God, all things are possible. Pray for them.

For worship. Thank God that he did for you what was impossible for you to do. He looked on helpless men and spoke the word that settles every heart: with God all things are possible. He gave a son to Sarah and Abraham when they were as good as dead, and he raised his own Son from the grave. The God who brings life from barren wombs and sealed tombs is the God who brings the rich and the poor, the moral and the ruined, through the eye of the needle into his kingdom. Salvation belongs to our God (Revelation 7:10).

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, in the new world, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: truly, in the new world, when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses, family or lands for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.

Truly, I say to you, in the new world. “The new world” (palingenesia, “regeneration”, “rebirth”) means the renewal of all things at Christ’s return: the new heavens and new earth (Acts 3:21; Romans 8:19–23; Revelation 21:1–5). Creation itself will be born again. Matthew uses of the creation the word the New Testament elsewhere uses of a person (Titus 3:5). Whatever happens to a Christian is going to happen to the world.

When the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne. From Daniel 7:9–14. The Son of Man will reign and judge (25:31).

You who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. The apostles will share Christ’s rule over the renewed people of God. “Judging” may mean ruling, as Israel’s judges ruled: they governed and rescued rather than merely passed sentence. The twelve tribes picture the whole people of God (see 10:1). Paul says all the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2).

Judas in the room. Read the promise with the room in mind, because Judas Iscariot is standing in it. You who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones is said, without a glance sideways, to twelve men one of whom will sell him for silver before the Passover. Jesus is neither mistaken nor being kind at the expense of the truth. He addresses the apostolic company as a body, and Acts shows the vacant seat being filled when the man who forfeited it had gone to his own place (Acts 1:20–26). But do not hurry past what it means that the sentence could be spoken at all. It is possible to stand inside the circle to whom the promise is made, to hear it addressed to you personally, and not to be in it.

Who are the twelve tribes of Israel, and when will this happen? Premillennial readers take it of ethnic Israel in a future earthly kingdom. The more likely reading is that it describes the renewal of all things at Christ’s return (the new world), and that the twelve tribes stand for the whole people of God, as the twelve gates and twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem suggest (Revelation 21:12–14). Christians who agree on this still differ on whether Scripture promises a future turning of the Jewish people as a whole to Christ (Romans 11:25–29); that question is not settled by this verse.

And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name’s sake. Not only the Twelve, but every disciple who gives up things for Jesus.

Will receive a hundredfold. In this life, in the family of God: brothers, sisters, mothers and homes in the church (Mark 10:30 adds “with persecutions”). Every believer who loses family for Christ gains a much larger family. Read what is on the list of things surrendered: houses, brothers, sisters, father, mother, children, lands. Then read what the hundredfold is made of: the same items. It is not a promise that a man who gives up one house receives a hundred houses. It is a promise that a man who loses a family receives a family a hundred times its size, which is a plain description of what the church is whenever it is working properly. Four relatives lost; four hundred gained.

Somebody is paying this cost today. The promise is theoretical to most readers in a comfortable country, who have left little for Christ and know it. But somebody is paying it now: the convert from Islam whose family holds a funeral for him while he is alive and never speaks his name again; the young woman in a Hindu village whose marriage, inheritance and place at the table all go on the day she is baptised; the believer who loses land because the village will not sell to a Christian. For them verse 29 is the promise they staked everything on. And Christ did not say they would feel a hundredfold; he said they would receive it, and the only place on earth where that can be handed over is a congregation. As with the unmarried (see on vv. 11–12), this is not a sentiment. It is a debt. So the honest question for the reader who has surrendered nothing is whether anybody, anywhere, is receiving their hundredfold through you.

And will inherit eternal life. The very thing the rich young man wanted (v. 16) and walked away from. It is given as an inheritance, a gift, not a wage.

Does this mean I may neglect my family for Christ? No. This does not license a believer to neglect his family; Jesus condemned that (15:3–6), and Paul says it denies the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). It describes the cost when loyalty to Christ and loyalty to family conflict.

What it does not mean. Not that we follow Jesus to get material rewards, as the prosperity gospel teaches. The hundredfold is chiefly the family of the church, and eternal life. Nor does it mean that the church replaces Israel in a way that excludes Jewish people. The twelve tribes picture the whole restored people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ.

In a sentence. In the renewed creation, the apostles will share Christ’s rule, and everyone who has given up anything for him will receive far more and inherit eternal life.

On a Tuesday. What have you given up for Christ? He has not forgotten it. Look around at your church family: they are part of the hundredfold. And look for someone who has lost family for Christ, and be family to him.

For worship. The Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, and the whole creation will be born again. Nothing given up for him is lost: not a house, not a brother, not a field. He is no man’s debtor. He repays a hundredfold now and gives eternal life to come, and the greatest gift in that inheritance is himself. The fishermen who left their nets will reign with him, and so will every forgotten believer who lost everything for his name. Blessed be the King who makes all things new.
verseByVerse.note: “The new world” is the renewal of all things at Christ’s return.

parallels.desc: I am making all things new

verseByVerse.quote: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But many who are first will be last, and the last first.

But many who are first will be last. The rich young man was first in the eyes of the world: rich, young, moral, important. He ended last, walking away from the kingdom. And notice the word many, which is doing careful work. He does not say all. A mechanical inversion, in which being at the front automatically damns and being at the back automatically saves, would only be the same league table turned upside down, and people enjoy that arrangement rather too much, as anyone knows who has met the Christian quietly proud of having nothing to be proud of. It is a warning, not a formula.

And the last first. The disciples, poor fishermen and a tax collector, were last in the world’s eyes. They will be first, sitting on thrones. The kingdom reverses the world’s rankings.

A warning too. “But” suggests a warning to Peter and the disciples, after his question about reward (v. 27). Do not assume you will be first. Those who think they deserve a reward may find themselves last. Jesus immediately tells a parable about this (20:1–16), which ends with the same words (20:16). See where it falls: not after the rich man’s departure, but after Peter’s what then will we have? and the enormous answer he was given. The men most in danger of finishing last are the men who have this moment been promised that they will be first. He hands them the throne and, without a pause, warns them what being handed a throne does to a man. The saying is a pair of brackets, and between them stands a story about men who worked all day in the heat and could not be glad about the wage given to men who worked an hour.

The long-serving. So it lands on the long-serving rather than the newcomer. The man who has given thirty years and cannot rejoice when the convert of six months is asked to do the thing he had always assumed would come to him. The unwritten order of seniority no church admits to having and every member could recite. The faithful couple who say nobody knows what this congregation has cost them, who are telling the truth, and are in more danger for it than the newcomer who has cost it nothing. Length of service is real and God does not forget it (v. 29 has just said so). It simply does not establish a position in the queue.

The comfort in it. It cuts the other way too. The reader who came late, who wasted the years everyone else was building on, who contributes little and is privately certain he belongs at the back, is the one this sentence was spoken to encourage. He is not told his lateness does not matter. He is told who decides the order.

What it does not mean. Not that every poor person will be first and every rich person last. The reversal is about God’s grace and human pride: those who rely on their own merit, status or sacrifice will be last; those who come with empty hands will be first.

Will there be ranks in heaven, then? Scripture speaks of rewards differing according to faithfulness (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Luke 19:17–19), so there is some sense in which God honours his servants differently. But no one in heaven will be there by merit, everyone will be there by grace, and no one will be resentful. The joy of each will be full, and every crown will be cast before the throne (Revelation 4:10). The point of this verse is not to help us calculate our place but to stop us calculating at all.

The shape of the chapter. Look at who has walked through it. Men arguing about the legal minimum a husband may keep. Children with nothing to contribute, nearly turned away at the door. A young man with everything, who went home. And twelve who had left everything, and were already, within the hour, counting what it was worth. The chapter opened with a question about how much a man is permitted to keep. It closes with a warning about how much a man can lose by being sure he is near the front.

In a sentence. God’s kingdom reverses the world’s rankings, and those who think themselves first may find themselves last.

On a Tuesday. Do you secretly think you deserve more from God than others because of what you have given up? Let grace keep you humble. And rejoice, out loud, the next time someone newer than you is honoured.

For worship. The first became last for us. The Son of God, who was first of all, took the last place: the servant’s towel, the criminal’s cross, the borrowed tomb. Therefore God has highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9), and in him the last are made first. We will not stand in his kingdom by seniority or sacrifice, but by the grace of the one who went to the back of the line for us. Blessed be the Lord who decides the order, and who has put the undeserving at his table.

parallels.desc: the same saying ends the next parable

19.theology: Monergism and the impossibility of self-salvation. Matthew 19:26 is the clearest statement in this Gospel of the Reformed doctrine of monergism: God alone works the miracle of salvation; unaided human will cannot accomplish it. The rich young man is not an extreme case; he represents every human being before the grace of God. His idolatry is more visible than most, but every person has a god that competes with Christ. The new birth — God’s sovereign act of grace that overcomes the resistance of the sinful will — is what makes it possible for anyone to sell all, follow Christ, and inherit eternal life. This is the good news hidden inside the severe word: with God, even this is possible.
19.examples:
Then: The rich young man came running (Mark 10:17) — he was eager, sincere, morally serious. He went away sorrowful. Sincerity and moral seriousness are not sufficient for salvation. Only the miracle of grace is sufficient.

Now: Every generation has its version of the young man’s idol — wealth, reputation, career, family, comfort, security. Jesus’ question to every person is the same: what is the one thing you are not willing to surrender? That is the idol that must go. The command is not an obstacle to grace; it is the exposure of where grace needs to go.

20.title: First and Last
20.text: <sup>1</sup>“For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. <sup>2</sup>After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, <sup>4</sup>and to them he said, ‘You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you.’ <sup>5</sup>So they went. Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. <sup>6</sup>And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, ‘Why do you stand here idle all day?’ <sup>7</sup>They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them, ‘You go into the vineyard too.’ <sup>8</sup>And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first.’ <sup>9</sup>And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. <sup>10</sup>Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more, but each of them also received a denarius. <sup>11</sup>And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, <sup>12</sup>saying, ‘These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’ <sup>13</sup>But he replied to one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? <sup>14</sup>Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. <sup>15</sup>Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?’ <sup>16</sup>So the last will be first, and the first last.” <sup>17</sup>And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, <sup>18</sup>“See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death <sup>19</sup>and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day.” <sup>20</sup>Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. <sup>21</sup>And he said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?” They said to him, “We are able.” <sup>23</sup>He said to them, “You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” <sup>24</sup>And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. <sup>25</sup>But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>26</sup>It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>27</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be your slave, <sup>28</sup>even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>29</sup>And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. <sup>30</sup>And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>31</sup>The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>32</sup>And stopping, Jesus called them and said, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>33</sup>They said to him, “Lord, let our eyes be opened.” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is structured around the inversion of worldly values. The parable of the workers in the vineyard opens with the same reversal that closed chapter 19: “the last will be first, and the first last.” Those hired at the eleventh hour receive the same wage as those who worked all day. The vineyard owner’s generosity is not unfair to the all-day workers (he pays exactly what was agreed) but it offends their sense of merit-based distribution. The parable is not about labour economics but about grace: God owes nothing to anyone; every denarius of salvation is sheer mercy.

The third passion prediction follows (vv. 17–19), and immediately James and John’s mother requests the seats of honour. Jesus responds with the kingdom’s law of greatness: the leader is the servant, the first is the slave. He grounds it in his own mission: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” This is the only place in Matthew where Jesus explicitly calls his death a ransom. The chapter closes with two blind men healed on the Jericho road — men who call him “Son of David” and, having received their sight, follow him on the road to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The parable of the workers hired at different hours — dawn, nine, noon, three, and five — all receiving the same denarius wage at day's end. Those hired first complain; the owner insists he has done them no wrong and is free to be generous with his own resources. "So the last will be first, and the first last." The parable illustrates the preceding reversal saying and the nature of God's grace: it is not a reward calculated by duration of service but a gift determined by sovereign generosity. Two mechanics inside the story carry it. Only the dawn workers negotiate a figure; everyone hired later goes into the vineyard on the owner's character alone, with no number (vv. 3-4, 7). And the owner instructs that the last be paid first (v. 8) — he could have paid in the obvious order and bought the dawn men's contentment for nothing, and instead he arranges for them to watch.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable's offense is intentional: the all-day workers' complaint is understandable by any standard of fairness. They worked more; they should receive more. The owner's response demolishes the complaint: he paid exactly what was agreed; his generosity to others does not diminish what they received. The problem is not injustice but envy — "is your eye evil because I am good?" The evil eye (stinginess, grudging spirit) cannot tolerate grace extended to others. The parable indicts the spirit of religious entitlement that calculates reward rather than receiving grace. Two further things the parable does deliberately. It sets the wage by need rather than by output: a denarius was a day's keep for a household, and an hour's honest pay would have sent the last man home with enough for nobody. There is only one wage in the story because there is only one thing God has to give, and eternal life does not come in grades. And the men who grumble are the only men on the estate with a figure in their heads — a man holding a contract can be disappointed, while a man trusting a person cannot, since the promise was kept. Note too that the eleventh-hour men are not blamed for their idleness: because no one has hired us (v. 7) stands without qualification.
verseByVerse.examples: The owner of the vineyard represents God, whose generosity is not constrained by human calculations of desert. Those hired last — with no track record, no extended service, no obvious claim — receive the same gift as those who bore the burden and heat of the day. This is the gospel: the deathbed convert and the lifelong believer receive the same eternal life, because eternal life is not a wage proportional to service but a gift given by the one who owns the vineyard. The men left standing have a name in every congregation: the long-term unemployed, the believer converted at sixty who does the arithmetic and concludes he has nothing to bring, the chronically ill Christian who cannot do the things his church visibly counts. And notice the direction of travel in every scene — not one labourer in the parable finds his own way to the vineyard. Each is there because the owner came down to the market and found him standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. He agreed to pay them a denarius for the day and sent them into his vineyard.

Meaning first. Matthew 20 is the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem, and it is held together by one question: what is God like when he gives? It opens with a parable told in answer to Peter, who has just asked what the disciples will get for leaving everything (19:27). A landowner hires labourers at dawn, and then keeps going back to the marketplace all day, until at five in the afternoon he is still finding men nobody wanted; and at evening every one of them receives a full day’s wage. Salvation is not pay earned by the hour but a gift handed out by a generous master, and the only man who goes home bitter is the one who was counting. Then Jesus tells the Twelve, for the third time and in the plainest words yet, that he is going up to be mocked, flogged, crucified and raised. James and John immediately ask for the two best seats in the kingdom, and he answers by defining greatness as service and naming his death as a ransom paid in the place of many. The chapter ends outside Jericho, where two blind beggars cry for mercy, are healed, and follow him up the road to the cross. From first to last it shows us a Lord who goes out to the people left standing.

The connection. “For” ties this parable to the saying just before it: many who are first will be last, and the last first (19:30). Peter had asked what reward there would be for those who had given up everything, and Jesus had promised thrones and a hundredfold (19:28–29). Then, so that the promise would not be turned into a ledger, he tells this story, and he ends it with the same saying turned round (v. 16). The whole parable sits inside those two brackets, and Matthew is telling us how to read it: as the worked example of what Jesus had just said to twelve men who had been promised thrones and had started counting.

Stand in the marketplace at first light. Before a word of the theology, see the scene. A day labourer in that country owned nothing but his hands. He had no contract, no notice period and no savings. He came down to the square before dawn and stood where he could be seen, and if a landowner picked him he ate that night and his children ate, and if nobody picked him they did not. The law itself assumed the knife edge he lived on: the hired worker was to be paid his wage on the same day, before the sun went down, for he is poor and counts on it (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). That is why everybody in this parable is paid at evening, and it is why standing unhired at five in the afternoon is not an inconvenience. It is a disaster with a family attached to it.

For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house. Fix one thing before the story runs. Jesus does not say the kingdom of heaven is like a wage system, or like a day’s labour, or like a vineyard. He says it is like a master of a house: a person. The landowner pictures God. Every question the parable raises about fairness is going to be answered not with a principle but with a man, and by the end the only question left on the table will be what sort of man he is.

Who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. Notice the detail the parable will repeat until it cannot be missed: he went out. This man has a foreman, as verse 8 tells us, and he does not send him. He walks down to the market himself at dawn, and again at nine, and at noon, and at three, and again at five when there is barely an hour of daylight left and no sane employer is still hiring. Five times in one day the owner of the vineyard comes out to the square where the unwanted men are standing. Whatever else this parable is about, it is not chiefly about the workers. Every scene in it turns on a man going out again. At harvest time, especially the grape harvest in September, extra hands were needed urgently before the autumn rains came, and so the labourers gathered in the marketplace at dawn, hoping to be hired.

His vineyard. Nor is the vineyard a neutral setting. Israel had been God’s vineyard since Isaiah sang over it and found wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7), and every hearer knew it. So the field in this story is the people of God, and the labour in it is the work God gives his own to do. That matters when the grumbling starts. The men who complain are not outsiders resenting the church from a distance. They are inside the vineyard, and they have been working in it since dawn.

After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day. A denarius was the standard day’s wage for a labourer, about enough to feed a family for a day. It is worth being clear that there is nothing generous about it yet. The master pays the market rate, agrees it openly, and sends them off. No one is being done a favour in verse 2. The story opens as an entirely ordinary piece of business, which is exactly why what happens at the end lands as hard as it does. He sent them into his vineyard, and the working day ran from sunrise to sunset, about twelve hours.

Is a deathbed conversion real? Yes. The thief on the cross received the whole of salvation in his last hours: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). And in this parable the men hired at the eleventh hour receive exactly the same wage as the men hired at dawn. A person who turns to Christ at eighty, or in a hospital bed, is not given a smaller salvation or a back seat. But nothing here licenses delay. The late workers were hired the moment they were called and went at once, and nobody in the parable chose to wait until five because he had heard the pay was the same. Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and the man who plans to come at the last hour has no promise that he will be offered one.

In a sentence. A landowner hired workers at dawn for an agreed fair wage of a denarius for the day.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly how you picture your life with God. As an arrangement: so much faithfulness on your side, so much blessing on his, with the books checked from time to time? Or as being hired by a person who came looking for you when you had nothing? Most Christians would deny the first and live it anyway. Notice the next time you say, or think, after all I have done. That phrase is the sound of a contract, and this parable is about to take it apart.

For worship. The God of this parable does not sit in his house waiting for applications. He goes out, himself, at first light, to the square where the men with nothing are standing, and he keeps going out all day long. That is what he did when he came looking for Adam in the garden, when he called Abram out of Ur, when he went down to Egypt to bring out a nation of slaves, and when his Son came into the world to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). Every one of us who is in the vineyard is there because the Master came down to the market and found us standing.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. The working day ran from sunrise to sunset.

parallels.desc: do not hold back a hired worker’s wages overnight

verseByVerse.quote: And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and to them he said, "You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you." So they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About nine in the morning he went out and saw others standing idle in the marketplace. He told them: you go into the vineyard too, and I will give you whatever is right. So they went.

And going out about the third hour. Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour was about nine in the morning. He saw others standing idle in the marketplace: unemployed workers, waiting to be hired. “Idle” does not mean lazy. It means without work, and the reason, as the last group will say, is that no one had hired them.

Whatever is right I will give you. Something changes at nine in the morning that the parable never draws attention to, and everything later depends on it. The dawn men had negotiated: a denarius, agreed, settled before a foot went into the vineyard. These men are offered no figure at all. Whatever is right, dikaion, whatever is just, I will give you, and that is the whole of it. They have a promise and a person, and no number.

So they went. That is a considerable thing for a man with nothing in the house to do on a stranger’s word, and the parable simply records it. Every group after the first goes into that vineyard on the character of the owner rather than on terms. Only one group in the story has a contract. And that turns out to be the difference between the men who end the day content and the men who end it bitter. A man holding a contract can be disappointed. A man trusting a person has nothing to measure the outcome against except the one who promised, and the promise was kept. The dawn workers were not cheated of a penny. They were simply the only men on the estate with a figure in their heads to compare things to, and by evening the figure had become a grievance.

The test. It goes deeper than it first appears. Most Christians could not say out loud that they deal with God on terms, and many do it anyway. The tell is not what you say when things go well; it is what rises in you when they go badly. A man on a contract feels cheated: after all these years, after all I have given up, after the way I have kept myself. A man who is trusting a person is bewildered and frightened and goes on trusting, because his confidence was never in the arithmetic. Ask which of those two was closer to your own heart the last time God did not do what you expected.

Is it wrong to make agreements, or to want to know where I stand? No. The parable is not against agreements. The dawn men did nothing wrong in accepting a denarius, and the master never suggests they did; he will treat the agreement as binding and honour it to the coin. Contracts are good and proper among men, and God himself binds himself by covenant promises you may hold him to. The trouble comes when a man carries a wage contract into a relationship that was never a wage arrangement, and then reads every kindness God shows to somebody else as a clause he has been denied. God’s promises are to be trusted, not invoiced.

In a sentence. At nine in the morning the landowner hired more workers, promising to pay whatever was right, and they went on his word.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time God did not do what you expected: the prayer that seemed unanswered, the door that closed. What was the first sentence that came into your head? If it was something like I deserved better than this, you were holding a contract. Take it to him and lay it down, and say instead the sentence the nine o’clock men lived by: whatever is right, you will give. Then go back to the work he has given you today without waiting to see the figure.

For worship. Every promise of God rests on what God is, and that is why it is safe to walk into his vineyard without a number. He cannot lie (Titus 1:2). He has never once given his people less than was right, and on the cross he gave them infinitely more. Abraham went out not knowing where he was going, because he knew who had called him (Hebrews 11:8). The Master’s whatever is right turned out, at evening, to be everything.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m.

verseByVerse.quote: Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, "Why do you stand here idle all day?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went out again at noon and at three in the afternoon and did the same. And about five in the afternoon he went out and found others standing there. He asked them: why have you been standing here idle all day?

Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. Noon, and then three, and the master is still coming out. He keeps going back to bring more people in.

And about the eleventh hour. About five in the afternoon, with the working day ending at six. These workers would hardly be worth hiring for one hour, and no ordinary employer would do it. He went out and found others standing: the last of the unemployed, perhaps the weakest, the oldest or the least wanted, whom no one had chosen.

Sit with what that standing had been like. They had been in that square since before dawn, in the same place, for eleven hours. Four separate times they had watched an employer walk in, look along the line, choose other men, and walk out again with them. Four times they had straightened up and been passed over. By the middle of the afternoon a man in that line has stopped arranging his face. He is not hoping any more; he is simply standing there because going home is worse, and because his wife will ask.

Why do you stand here idle all day? Read the master’s question in the tone the next verse requires, not the tone we expect. It sounds like an accusation and is nothing of the kind: their answer will satisfy him completely and he will hire them on the spot. It is the question of a man who has walked up to people nobody else has spoken to all day and asked them what happened.

These men have a name in every congregation. The one who has been out of work long enough that the sympathy has run out and people have started to theorise about him. The believer converted at sixty who does the arithmetic on the years and concludes he has nothing to bring. The disabled or chronically ill Christian who cannot do any of the things his church visibly counts, and sits through another meeting hearing about the workers who can. The person who has never in his life been picked first for anything, and has quietly built a whole theology out of it. If you have ever thought that the useful part of your life is behind you and you arrived too late to matter, this is the hour you were hired in.

The direction of travel. It is the same in every scene, and it is the opposite of what religion usually describes. Not one man in this parable finds his way to the vineyard. Nobody knocks at the estate, nobody applies, nobody hears there is work going and walks out to ask for it. Every labourer in the story is in that vineyard because the owner came down to the market and found him standing there. That is grace before a single coin changes hands: the call comes from his side.

What do I do with the years I wasted before I came to Christ? Grieve them honestly, because the years were real and some of what was lost cannot be recovered. But do not let the grief tell you a lie about the present. The eleventh-hour men did not spend their one hour lamenting the eleven; they worked, and at evening they were paid in full. God says he will restore the years the locust has eaten (Joel 2:25), and he does it not by giving the years back but by making what is left fruitful far beyond its length. Serve gladly in the hour you have, and leave the arithmetic to the Master.

In a sentence. The landowner kept hiring throughout the day, and at five o’clock, an hour before the end, he was still finding men no one had chosen.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your church who is most obviously standing in the square: overlooked, unchosen, slightly hard work. This week, go out to him the way the master did. Ask a real question and wait for the answer. And if you are the one standing there, hear the question as it was meant: not why are you useless, but come, there is work for you too.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest is not finished at noon. He was still going out at the eleventh hour, and he still is. He went out to Rahab in a doomed city, to Ruth from Moab, to a thief at the very end of his life on a cross. He is the God who comes for the ones nobody picked, and his Son was himself despised and rejected, the stone the builders passed over, so that the men left standing could be brought in.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m., the eleventh about 5 p.m. — an hour before the day ended.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Because no one has hired us." He said to them, "You go into the vineyard too." And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, "Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said: because no one has hired us. He told them: you go into the vineyard too. When evening came, the owner told his foreman: call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and ending with the first.

Because no one has hired us. That is the whole answer, and the parable lets it stand without a word of qualification. They were not lazy and they were not hiding. They had been available since dawn and the market had looked at them and chosen somebody else, over and over, until the day was nearly gone. The reason they had done no work was that no one had given them any. The parable is not sentimental about idleness, and it does not say that standing about is the same as working. What it does is refuse to blame these men for a condition that was done to them, and then put them in the vineyard for the last hour of the light.

You go into the vineyard too. No interview, no explanation of terms, not even the whatever is right the nine o’clock men were given. Just go. There is an hour left; go and have it. They are simply welcomed.

And when evening came. Sunset, the time the law set for paying wages (Deuteronomy 24:15). In the story it is simply the end of the working day; in the meaning, evening pictures the end of the age, when the Lord settles accounts with his servants. The owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, the manager who handled the payroll, to call the labourers and pay them.

Beginning with the last, up to the first. This is the most deliberate sentence in the parable. Think what it would have cost the master to do it the other way round. Pay the dawn men first, and they take their agreed denarius and walk home perfectly satisfied, and never learn what happened at the far end of the queue. Not one word of complaint is ever spoken. The master could have bought their contentment for nothing, simply by paying in the obvious order. He arranges for them to watch instead. He has the last men paid first, in full view, while the men who have been there since dawn stand in the line and do the arithmetic.

Diagnosis, not cruelty. That order is not carelessness, and it is not meant to wound. God does not conceal his kindness to other people in order to keep us comfortable, and this parable says so on purpose. He lets us see what he has given somebody else, because what rises in us when we see it is the truest thing anyone could tell us about ourselves, and until it rises it cannot be dealt with. So the next time you find out what somebody else was given, remember that the information did not reach you by accident, and it was not sent to make you miserable. It was sent the way a doctor sends a man for a scan.

Does every detail, like the foreman, stand for something? No. A parable is a story with one main point and a few telling details, not a code in which every item has a hidden meaning. The foreman is there because a real estate had one, and because the payroll had to be handled by someone. The master, the vineyard, the hiring and the pay plainly carry the meaning; the foreman, the hours and the marketplace furnish the scene. Reading too much into the furniture is how parables have been made to say almost anything, so hold on to what Jesus himself draws out in verse 16.

In a sentence. The landowner hired even the last, unwanted workers, and at evening ordered that the last be paid first while the first looked on.

On a Tuesday. In God’s kingdom the order of the world is reversed, and those who seem last may be first. This week, when you hear of someone else’s blessing, a promotion, a healing, a child’s conversion, a fruitful ministry, notice the first thing that moves in you. If it is gladness, thank God. If it is a small cold drop of something else, do not ignore it: that is the scan, and the Master is showing you what needs his care.

For worship. The day of evening is coming for every one of us, when the Lord of the vineyard calls his workers in. And the One who settles the accounts is not a stranger reading a ledger. He is the Master who hired us when no one else would, who knows exactly how little we brought, and who has already decided to be generous. Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes (Luke 12:37); and he himself, Jesus says, will dress himself for service and serve them.

parallels.desc: give him his wages on the same day

verseByVerse.quote: And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more. But each of them also received a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those hired at five o’clock came, and each received a full denarius. When those hired first came, they expected to receive more, but each of them also received a denarius.

And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. A full day’s wage for one hour’s work. They would be able to feed their families that night. Picture their faces as the coin was put into their hands: men who had expected a twelfth of a denarius, or nothing at all, holding the whole day’s keep.

What the master was doing with that coin. A denarius was not a lavish sum; it was a day’s keep: bread, oil, whatever a household needed to get to tomorrow. The eleventh-hour man had earned, strictly, about a twelfth of it. If he had been paid a twelfth he would have gone home with enough for nobody. So the master does not pay him what his hour was worth. He pays him what his household needs. The wage in this parable is not set by output at all; it is set by need and by the master’s goodness, and once you have seen that, the shape of the whole gospel is standing there in a coin.

Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more. Do the arithmetic the dawn men did, because their reasoning is not stupid; it is consistent. One hour has just been paid a denarius. Twelve hours at that rate comes to twelve denarii. Any accountant in the world would have signed off the expectation. But look at the verb Matthew chooses: enomisan, they supposed, they assumed. Nobody had told them anything of the kind. The master had made them one promise and kept it exactly. The extra eleven denarii existed nowhere but in their own heads, and they had spent the walk up the line building it.

But each of them also received a denarius. Exactly what they had agreed (v. 2). And here is why the dawn men cannot be given twelve. There is only one wage in this story, and it is the whole of what the master has to give. Eternal life does not come in grades. There is no larger portion of God available to a man who has been at it longer, because God is not a quantity you accumulate. The first workers were not given less than they deserved; they were given everything there is, which is precisely what the last men were given, and the reason it feels like an insult is that they had been thinking of it as pay.

Disappointment over things he never said. Here is a test most of us fail regularly and quietly. A great deal of the disappointment Christians carry with God is disappointment over things he never promised. He did not promise that the marriage would be easy because you waited. He did not promise that the child raised in the faith would keep it, or that the years of service would be recognised, or that the diagnosis would go the other way. Somewhere along the way an arrangement got built that he was never party to, and when it did not arrive it felt exactly like a broken promise. Go back through the grievance sometime and ask, item by item, which of these he actually said. The list is usually shorter than the grievance, and the difference between them is the size of the bitterness.

But does God not promise to bless obedience? He does, and those promises are real (Psalm 1; Galatians 6:9). But look at what he actually promises: his presence, his care, a harvest in due season, and a reward that is itself his gift. He does not promise a particular outcome on a particular timetable, measured against what other people receive. The sting in this verse is not that the dawn men were promised nothing. It is that they added to what they were promised, and then held the master to their additions.

In a sentence. The last workers received a full day’s wage, and the first workers, expecting more, received the same.

On a Tuesday. Would you be glad or resentful if someone who came to faith on his deathbed received the same eternal life as you? Try the question with a real name: the relative who mocked your faith for forty years, the man who did real harm and then repented in prison. If your honest answer is resentment, you have found the place where you still think of heaven as pay.

For worship. The coin in every hand at evening is the same coin because the gift is God himself, and there is no more of him to give than all of him. The apostle who laboured for decades and the thief who believed for an afternoon stand before the same Saviour, washed in the same blood, heirs of the same inheritance. Christ did not purchase a graded heaven. He purchased his people, entire, and gives each of them the whole of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, saying, "These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they received it, they grumbled against the landowner: these last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.

And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house. “Grumbled” is the word used of Israel murmuring in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8; 1 Corinthians 10:10): a people fed with bread from heaven every morning, complaining about the menu. It is the sound of people who have been given everything and are watching what somebody else got.

These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us. The complaint is articulate and, by human standards, fair. Twelve hours of summer work in a vineyard against one hour in the cool of the evening, and the same pay? Who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat: the sirocco, the hot east wind, made afternoon work exhausting. But notice what they actually say. Their complaint was not that they had been cheated, but that others had been treated as equals. You have made them equal to us. Their problem was comparison, and equality was what offended them.

Nothing had happened to them. Look closely, because the parable is doing something precise. Their wage had not been cut. Their hours had not been lengthened. The coin in their hand was the coin they had been content to work all day for. Every fact about their own situation was exactly as agreed and exactly as they had been satisfied with that morning. One thing changed: they saw somebody else’s pay. That is the whole mechanism of envy. Envy is the one sin that has never made anybody better off, including the person committing it. It cannot take anything from anyone. All it can do is alter how you feel about what you have, and it is extremely good at that. A man happy at dawn is bitter by dusk with the same denarius in his pocket.

Who are they? They are like the Pharisees, who grumbled that Jesus welcomed tax collectors and sinners and ate with them (9:11; Luke 15:2), and like the Pharisee at the meal who watched a sinful woman being forgiven (Luke 7:39–47). They are like the elder brother in the parable of the prodigal son, standing outside while the fatted calf was killed for the younger (Luke 15:28–30). In the setting of Matthew they also fit Israel’s leaders, who had borne the yoke of the law for centuries and resented the Gentiles and outcasts being brought in on equal terms. And they are like Peter, who had just asked what he would get for leaving everything (19:27). Anyone who serves God for a long time can fall into this attitude, which is why the parable is told to disciples.

How do I break envy when I find it in myself? The master’s cure is a question, and it can be borrowed: did you not agree with me for a denarius? Go back to what you were actually given, and say it out loud if it helps. Then do three things. Name it to God as sin rather than as a grievance, since it will always present itself as a grievance; that is its disguise, and the disguise is why it survives so long in respectable people. Thank him deliberately and specifically for your own denarius. And pray for the person by name, asking God to give him more of the very thing you envy. It is close to impossible at first, and it works.

In a sentence. The first workers grumbled that latecomers had been made equal to them, after they had worked all day in the heat.

On a Tuesday. The Christian version is easy to recognise once you know the shape. Someone comes to faith at fifty and appears to have skipped the decades you spent under obedience. Someone else’s ministry flourished while yours never did. Someone got the marriage, or the child, or the health, or simply the easier road, and you notice, in the place where gladness ought to be, a small persistent coldness. Do you resent grace shown to others? That resentment shows you think you have earned God’s favour. Find the coldness this week and bring it into the light.

For worship. Look how the master speaks to the man who complains: he calls him friend, and reasons with him at the gate. Luke’s elder brother is left in the same place at the end of his story, standing outside the party with his father still pleading with him. That is the patience of God with grumbling servants. He fed a murmuring nation for forty years in the wilderness, and he still comes out to the ones who stand outside arguing about fairness, with the door open behind his voice.

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to one of them, "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The landowner answered one of them: friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give this last man the same as I give you.

Friend. But he replied to one of them, Friend: the first word out of the master’s mouth is the one to stop on, and it is not the warm word we hear in English. Hetairos is a polite but cool address, used to someone who is in the wrong, and Matthew uses it exactly three times. Here, to the man grumbling at the pay table. At 22:12, to the guest found without a wedding garment, moments before he is thrown into the outer darkness. And at 26:50, in Gethsemane, from Jesus to Judas with the kiss still on his face: Friend, do what you came to do. Every one is addressed to a man in the wrong, and every one is courteous. It is not the word for a man you are close to. It is the word you use to a man you are still treating civilly when both of you know what he is doing.

I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? The argument is unanswerable. Every fact is on the master’s side. The wage was named before the work; the work was done; the wage was paid in full and on time. Justice was done, and the fair agreement was honoured. There is no case here at all. The grievance is not that the man received too little. It is that somebody else received the same.

Take what belongs to you and go. There is an edge under the courtesy that is easy to miss. He gets exactly what he bargained for, down to the coin, and then he is dismissed with it. There is nothing else coming, because he asked for terms and he has been given terms. A man who insists on strict justice from God will receive strict justice, and it is difficult to think of a more frightening thing to be granted. The eleventh-hour men went home with the same coin and something the grumbler never got near: they knew it was a gift.
