I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. The verb is thelō, I will, I want to. Not I am obliged, not the accounts require it. He wanted to. The generosity is the owner’s free decision, and he is sovereign over his gifts. That is the only reason given in the whole parable for the eleventh-hour denarius, and no other reason is ever offered anywhere in Scripture for why God saves anybody. He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, according to the purpose of his will (Ephesians 1:4–5), and not because of anything he saw in us.

Is God being cold to the grumbler? No, and the scene is worth reading again for how he handles him. He does not have him removed. He does not answer him through the foreman. He comes to him personally, calls him by a courteous name, sets out the reasoning step by step, and asks him two questions, which is more than the complaint deserved and more patience than most of us would show. The coolness of the word friend is a warning, not a rejection: it tells the man he is standing in a dangerous place. But the master is still standing there talking to him, and the conversation is an invitation to see the gift for what it is.

In a sentence. The landowner said he had been perfectly fair to the first workers, and was free to be generous to the last.

On a Tuesday. God never treats anyone unfairly. But he is free to give more than anyone deserves, and he does. Next time you hear yourself appealing to fairness in your prayers, stop and ask whether you really want what you are asking for. Then pray the other way: not give me what is fair, but have mercy on me, a sinner (Luke 18:13). That is the prayer of the eleventh-hour men, and it is always answered with the full wage.

For worship. I will, he says, and that is the deepest word in the parable. The salvation of every one of his people comes down to the good pleasure of God: not his obligation, not our claim, but his wanting to. He wanted the thief on the cross. He wanted the persecutor on the Damascus road. He wanted you. And because the reason lies in him and not in us, it cannot be undone by anything we discover about ourselves later. The Father who willed it gave his Son to accomplish it, and what he wills, he does.

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" So the last will be first, and the first last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or are you envious because I am generous? So the last will be first, and the first last.

Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Here is the sovereignty of God, and it needs its guard on both sides. This is not a God who does as he likes and calls it righteousness. The master has just shown, point by point, that he has wronged nobody, and he does not appeal to his rights until after he has cleared himself on justice. Sovereign generosity is not caprice. But nor is it negotiable. Salvation and its rewards are his to give as he wills: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (Romans 9:15–16). He owes no one more than justice, and he is free to give grace. What is his is his, and grace is not a substance that gets thinner when it is shared. Nobody in that line was given less because somebody else was given something.

Or do you begrudge my generosity? The English hides how sharp this is. Word for word it reads: is your eye evil because I am good? An evil eye was the Jewish idiom for envy and stinginess: a man with a good eye is open-handed, and a man with an evil eye is the grudging one who cannot bear to give or to see giving (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 23:6; 28:22). Matthew’s readers had met it already in the Sermon on the Mount: if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness (6:22–23), set in the middle of a passage about money and treasure. So the master’s question is a diagnosis of an organ. The problem is not the wage; it is the eye that looked down the line.

Because I am good. Notice which way the sentence runs, because it is not what we would write. He does not say, is your eye evil because they are undeserving. He says, because I am good. The goodness of God is what has provoked the reaction. That is a startling account of what is wrong with us, and far more searching than a charge of greed: there is something in a fallen man that can be made bitter by God being kind where he did not expect him to be. Jonah had it, sitting outside Nineveh, angry enough to die because God was gracious and merciful (Jonah 4:1–3).

So the last will be first, and the first last. The same saying as 19:30, turned round, closing the brackets around the parable. Those who came last, and received grace, are first. Those who think they deserve more, and grumble at grace, are last. Matthew wants it read not as a lesson in employment practice but as Jesus’ answer to twelve men who had been promised thrones and had begun to calculate.

The meaning. The parable is about grace. Eternal life is not a wage earned in proportion to work, but a gift given equally to all who are called into the kingdom, whether early or late. The thief on the cross, saved in his last hour, receives the same eternal life as the apostles (Luke 23:43). Grace is offensive to those who think in terms of merit. It is wonderful to those who know they have none.

What it does not mean. Not that there are no different rewards in God’s kingdom. Elsewhere Jesus teaches that faithfulness will be rewarded according to what each has done (16:27; 25:14–30; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). The parable’s point is that salvation itself, entry into the kingdom and eternal life, is all of grace, and no one can complain about God’s generosity to others. Nor does it encourage people to put off coming to God until the last moment. The latecomers came as soon as they were called. And it is not a parable about employment law, or a model for paying workers.

Does the one denarius mean there are no differences of reward in heaven? The wage everyone receives is eternal life, God himself, and that is the same for all. Other passages speak of different rewards and responsibilities (Luke 19:17–19; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but those rewards are themselves grace, God crowning his own gifts, and no one in heaven will envy another. A thimble and a bucket can both be full. The saint with the larger capacity will not look down on the other, and the other will not look up in resentment, because envy is one of the things that does not get through the gate.

Then why work hard for Christ, if the late convert gets the same? Because the work was never the price. The dawn men had the privilege of a whole day in the vineyard: the Master’s company, his purpose, the joy of fruit, and freedom from the misery of the square. Paul worked harder than all the apostles and called it the grace of God that was with him (1 Corinthians 15:10). Those who serve longest are not the most owed but the most blessed. If you resent the hours, you were treating them as payment; if you see them as a gift, you will wish the late arrivals had come sooner, not that they had been paid less.

The mercy in the arithmetic. There is a kindness here the grumbler never saw. If the kingdom really paid by the hour, the man who came in at the eleventh hour would have almost nothing, and the man who came in at dawn would spend eternity knowing exactly how much of it he had earned. Both would be intolerable. What the master does instead is hand every one of them the entire day’s keep and shut the ledger, and the only man who goes home unhappy is the one who kept it open.

In a sentence. God is free to be generous, and those who resent his grace to others show that they think they have earned it.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice when someone who seems undeserving comes to faith. You were undeserving too. Pick one person this week whose blessing you find hard to celebrate, and celebrate it anyway, in words, to his face or to God. Gladness at another’s grace is one of the surest signs that you have understood your own.

For worship. The Master’s eye is good. He looks down the line at men who have nothing and is glad to give them everything, and nothing done by the grudging can make him grudging. The full wage was paid at evening because the full price had been paid by another: the Son who worked the whole day in the heat without one hour lost, and then gave his life so that latecomers like us could be called friends without the coolness, and receive from him the very joy of his Father’s house.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “do you begrudge” is literally “is your eye bad” — an idiom for envy.

parallels.desc: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–34 — The Third Passion Prediction, the Mother's Request, and Two Blind Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus gives the fullest passion prediction yet: delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, crucified, raised. Immediately the mother of James and John asks for her sons to sit at Jesus's right and left in his kingdom. Jesus corrects the request: greatness is service, and the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. Two blind men at Jericho cry out "Son of David, have mercy on us" and receive their sight. Between the request and the healing the other ten turn on the two brothers (v. 24) — not from principle but because they wanted the same thing and were beaten to it — and Jesus answers all twelve rather than the two who asked.
verseByVerse.theology: The timing of the mother's request — immediately after the passion prediction — reveals the distance between the disciples' understanding and Jesus's reality. He has just announced crucifixion; she asks for thrones. The response of Jesus is not irritated dismissal but patient teaching: "You do not know what you are asking." The cup he must drink and the baptism he must undergo are not metaphors for achievement but for suffering. The right and left are not his to give; they are the Father's appointment. The contrast between the Gentile rulers who "lord it over" others and the Son of Man who gives his life is the most concentrated leadership theology in the Gospels. Two things guard it from becoming a slogan. Jesus does not abolish ambition: the sentence is whoever would be great among you, and only the object of the wanting is changed. And the standard is not an attitude but a cross — he does not say be like a servant, he says the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. The many of v. 28 is Isaiah's word for a multitude nobody could number (Isa 53:11-12), not a word that fences people out.
verseByVerse.examples: The two blind men at Jericho echo the two blind men of 9:27-31. The title "Son of David, have mercy on us" is the messianic title of chapter 9, and it elicits the same response: Jesus stops, asks, heals. Their sight is the last healing miracle before the triumphal entry — a fitting preparation for Jerusalem. Those who cry "Son of David" will soon hear the crowds cry "Hosanna to the Son of David." The blind who gain sight anticipate the seeing of what Jerusalem refuses to see. Matthew also asks the same question twice in this chapter, and the two answers are the spine of it: What do you want? to the mother of James and John (v. 21), and What do you want me to do for you? to the beggars (v. 32). One asks for the two best seats in the kingdom; the other asks for eyes. And in both Jericho scenes the obstacle between a needy person and Christ is the crowd already following him — as it was with the children in the previous chapter (19:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside privately and told them: we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death.

And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem. Going up is not a figure of speech. Jericho sits in the Jordan rift some 250 metres (800 feet) below sea level; Jerusalem stands about 750 metres (2,500 feet) above it, high in the Judean hills, and the road between them climbs the whole of that in some fifteen miles of bare rock and ravine. Every pilgrim used the phrase and meant it literally. They are climbing, in a crowd, at Passover, and the man at the front of the column knows precisely what is waiting at the top. Mark says he walked ahead of them, and they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid (Mark 10:32).

He took the twelve disciples aside. Picture it on a packed festival road. He pulls the Twelve out of the stream of singing pilgrims to tell them, quietly and on the move, that he is going up there to be killed. He did not want them to hear it later, and he did not want them to hear it from anyone else.

See, we are going up to Jerusalem. Jesus walks toward the cross deliberately. This is the third time he has told them, and each telling is more exact than the last. At 16:21 it was suffering at the hands of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and being killed. At 17:22–23 it was being delivered into the hands of men who would kill him. Now it is the chief priests and scribes condemning him, the Gentiles receiving him, mocking, flogging, and crucifixion, named for the first time. He has been walking toward this for months and telling them in instalments, and the detail he has kept until last is the manner of the death.

He looked straight at it. Hold that beside the way most of us handle what is coming. We manage dread by not looking directly at it: by keeping the appointment vague, by not asking the consultant the second question, by leaving the letter unopened on the side. Jesus did the opposite. He named it, in detail, out loud, three times, months in advance, to people who did not want to hear it, and then he set his face to the hill and kept climbing. Whatever strength he had for Jerusalem, he did not get it by refusing to look at Jerusalem.

And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. Read the verb in the middle of it (see 17:22). Delivered by whom? Judas will do it, and the Sanhedrin will do it, and Pilate will do it, and every one of them will be fully answerable for it. But the passive sits there unexplained, the way it does all through Isaiah 53, and Peter will say the quiet part out loud at Pentecost: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Both halves of that sentence are true at once. Nobody took him up that road against his will, and nobody who sent him to his death was excused because God had planned it.

And they will condemn him to death. The Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, would pass the sentence: he deserves death (26:66).

If God planned the cross, how could Judas and the leaders be guilty? Scripture holds both together without embarrassment, and so must we. God ordains all that comes to pass, yet he is not the author of sin, and the will of the creatures is not violated (Westminster 3.1). Judas acted freely, out of his own greed and unbelief, and was fully responsible; God, in the same events, was working out the salvation of the world. Joseph said it to his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). You cannot fully see how the two fit, but you can see why it matters: the worst thing human beings ever did was not outside God’s hand, and so nothing done to you is either.

In a sentence. On the way up to Jerusalem, Jesus told the Twelve privately that he would be handed over to the Jewish leaders and condemned to death.

On a Tuesday. Jesus walked toward suffering on purpose, for you. Is there something ahead of you that you have refused to look at: a conversation, a diagnosis, a duty? Name it to him today, plainly, as he named Jerusalem. Then take the next step up the road, knowing he has walked it before you and walks it with you.

For worship. The Son of God went up to Jerusalem the way a man walks into a fire to bring someone out. He knew every step of the climb, every face that would turn against him, and he went at the front of the column. No one forced him. The plan of the Father and the love of the Son were one and the same, and the road that led to his death was the road he had chosen from before the foundation of the world, for us.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day.

And deliver him over to the Gentiles. The Romans. Under Roman rule the Jewish council could not carry out the death penalty itself (John 18:31); only the governor could. And notice who does what. The chief priests and scribes condemn; the Gentiles mock, flog and crucify. Jew and Gentile, the covenant people and the nations, each contribute their own portion to the same crucifixion. Nobody in the story gets to stand outside it, which is precisely the point when the ransom is named in verse 28.

To be mocked and flogged and crucified. The third prediction of his death is the most detailed, and the first to name crucifixion. Take the verbs at their weight, since familiarity has worn them smooth. Mocked is not teasing. Matthew will show us what it means: a scarlet robe thrown over a torn back, a crown of thorns pressed down, a reed put in his hand for a sceptre, soldiers kneeling in front of him and hailing him King of the Jews before they spat on him (27:27–31). Flogged is the Roman scourge, a whip with pieces of bone and metal tied into its leather thongs, which often tore the skin to shreds; Roman citizens were legally exempt from it and slaves were not, and some victims died under it before the cross was reached (27:26). And crucified (27:35) was the most cruel and shameful death the Romans used. It was so far beneath a citizen’s dignity that Cicero said the very word should be kept away from Roman ears. It was the death kept for slaves and rebels, a detail worth carrying nine verses forward, where the same man tells his friends that whoever would be first among them must be a slave, and then says what he came to do. Everything happened exactly as he said.

And he will be raised on the third day. Then the fifth verb, which he has never once left out. Three predictions, and three times the resurrection is attached to the end of the sentence. Jesus knew the end of the story. And the disciples remember none of it. When the women come to the tomb, the angel does not break news to them; he reminds them: he is not here, for he has risen, as he said (28:6). It had been said plainly, three times, on an open road.

A strange comfort. The men closest to him, who heard all three predictions from his own mouth, retained nothing useful from them and fell apart entirely when it happened. Their failure to take it in did not derail a single detail of it. He was not depending on their understanding to get it done, and he is not depending on yours. Your salvation rests on what he did, not on how well you grasp it.

Why did the disciples not understand something said so plainly? Because it did not fit what they already believed. They expected a Messiah who would conquer, and a crucified Messiah was a contradiction in terms, a stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23). Luke says the saying was hidden from them (Luke 18:34). We do the same: we hear the parts of Scripture that fit our hopes and quietly file away the parts that do not. The remedy is to read what is actually there, and to ask the Spirit to open our eyes, as Jesus later opened theirs when he explained from all the Scriptures that the Christ must suffer and enter his glory (Luke 24:26–27, 45).

In a sentence. Jesus foretold that the Romans would mock, flog and crucify him, and that he would rise on the third day.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knew every detail of what he would suffer, and went anyway. That is the measure of his love. When you are tempted to think he does not understand what you are going through, remember the robe, the reed, the whip and the nails, and that he saw all of them coming. Then remember the third day, which is the last word on every one of them.

For worship. Mocked, flogged, crucified, raised: four verbs for what was done to him, and a fifth for what the Father did. The robe of mockery became the robe of righteousness he puts on his people; the reed of the soldiers was answered by the sceptre of all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18); the cross of the slave became the throne of the Lamb. He saw all of it coming, and he never once left the resurrection off the end of the sentence.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the first to name crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. And he said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the mother of James and John came to Jesus with her sons, knelt before him and asked for a favour. He asked what she wanted. She said: grant that my two sons may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.

Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons. Right after Jesus spoke of his death. She was probably Salome, who was present at the crucifixion (27:56; Mark 15:40), and possibly the sister of Jesus’ mother Mary (John 19:25), which would make James and John Jesus’ cousins. That may help explain the boldness of the request: family has claims.

And kneeling before him she asked him for something. Kneeling is the posture of petition and even worship (2:11; 8:2; 9:18): respectful, but with a selfish request. And the timing is the shock. Jesus has just announced, in the most specific terms yet, that he is going up to be crucified, and the family of Zebedee responds with a request for thrones.

Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom. The right and left of a king are the places of highest honour and power, the first and second ministers of state. They took Jesus’ promise of twelve thrones (19:28) and wanted the best two. They still imagined an earthly, political kingdom, coming soon.

Mother or sons? A reader with Mark open will stop here, because there the brothers make the request themselves (Mark 10:35). Which was it? It is often said that Matthew moved the words onto their mother to spare the two apostles. That explanation is worth resisting, for two reasons. First, Matthew is not a man who spares people: he records Peter called Satan (16:23), the disciples fleeing (26:56), and his own name in the list as Matthew the tax collector (10:3). Second, and decisively, look at the very next verse. Jesus does not answer the mother. He says, you do not know what you are asking, and in the Greek every you is plural, addressed to the sons; it is the sons who reply, we are able. Three verses later the ten are indignant, and not with her: they are indignant at the two brothers (v. 24). Matthew’s own account, read to the end, has James and John behind the request, exactly as Mark says. So both are true, and anyone who has watched a family do this will recognise it: the sons wanted the thrones and sent their mother to ask. Matthew tells you who spoke; Mark tells you whose ambition it was.

The irony. The ones who would be at Jesus’ right and left when he was enthroned as King of the Jews were two criminals crucified with him (27:38). James and John had asked for the two places nobody would have wanted if they had understood what was being requested.

Is it wrong to want to be great, or to pray for my children’s success? Not in itself. Jesus does not rebuke the wanting to be great; in verse 26 he redirects it. And a mother’s prayer for her sons is a beautiful thing. What was wrong here was the object and the motive: honour above others, sought by influence, in a kingdom misunderstood. Pray for your children to be near Christ, to be faithful and fruitful and to serve; pray that they will be great in the only way the kingdom counts greatness. Pray less for their position and more for their character, and leave their place to the Father.

In a sentence. Right after Jesus spoke of his death, James and John, through their mother, asked for the highest places in his kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Are you seeking position, recognition or status, even in Christian service? The test is simple: how do you feel when someone else is given the job, the platform or the thanks you hoped for? And notice whether you ever ask for things through others to avoid the embarrassment of asking yourself. Bring your ambitions to Jesus in your own voice; he will tell you the truth about them, kindly.

For worship. The King to whom this mother knelt did not throw her request back in her face. He would make her sons great, but not the way she imagined: by giving them his cup, his Spirit and his kingdom, and by going first to the cross where the places at his right and left were taken by thieves. The throne he was going to was a cross, and the glory he would share with his people was purchased there.
verseByVerse.note: In Mark the brothers ask for themselves. Comparing the women at the cross, their mother may be Salome.

parallels.desc: the mother of the sons of Zebedee at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?" They said to him, "We are able." He said to them, "You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: you do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink? They said: we can. He said: you will drink my cup, but to sit at my right and left is not mine to grant; it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.

You do not know what you are asking. The pronouns have already shifted. She asked; he answers you, plural, and it is the two sons who reply (see on vv. 20–21). They did not understand that the way to glory was through suffering.

Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink? The cup has to be understood, or the answer is unintelligible. In the prophets the cup is not an image of hardship in general; it is a very specific vessel. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Psalm 75:8). Isaiah calls it the cup of his wrath and pictures Jerusalem staggering after drinking it (Isaiah 51:17). Jeremiah is handed it and made to take it round the nations (Jeremiah 25:15–16). So when Jesus asks two ambitious young men whether they can drink the cup he is about to drink, he is not asking whether they can cope with a hard road. He is telling them what he is going up to Jerusalem to receive, and it is not chiefly nails. It is the wrath of God against sin, poured out and drained to the bottom by somebody who never earned a drop of it. Jesus would drink this cup at the cross, bearing God’s judgment on sin in his people’s place. In Gethsemane he prayed that it might pass from him, if possible (26:39), and then took it.

We are able. Brave, entirely sincere, confident and ignorant, spoken by men with no idea what they had just volunteered for. Within days they would be asleep in the garden and then running away in the dark.

You will drink my cup. He does not call them liars. They would share his sufferings, though not his atoning work, and they did, in two shapes so different that nobody would have guessed they were the same drink. James was the first of the apostles to be martyred, killed with the sword by Herod Agrippa about AD 44 (Acts 12:2). John outlived them all and suffered exile on the island of Patmos on account of the word of God (Revelation 1:9), watching his friends die one by one. A short violent cup and a long lonely one. The cup is not one flavour, and a Christian who has been given the slow version should not conclude he was given the easy one.

But to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant. Guard this carefully. It is not Jesus disclaiming authority: this is the man who ends the book saying all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (28:18). It is the Son declining to act outside the Father’s arrangement, which is the pattern of his whole earthly life. Within the Trinity the Son willingly does the Father’s will (John 5:19, 30).

But it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father. The Father has already decided. Rewards in the kingdom are God’s gift, prepared in advance, not won by ambition (25:34). And the practical edge is sharper than it looks: position in the kingdom is not open to lobbying. There is no queue to join and no case to put, and the sooner a Christian believes that, the sooner he is free of a great deal of exhausting comparison. It cuts the other way too, and that is the comfort in it. If your place cannot be secured by asking, it cannot be lost by somebody else asking either. Nobody can manoeuvre you out of what the Father has prepared, because it was never in the gift of anyone who could be manoeuvred.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciples’ sufferings atone for sin. Only Christ drank the cup of God’s wrath; his followers share in suffering for his sake (Colossians 1:24; 1 Peter 4:13). Nor does “not mine to grant” mean that Jesus is less than God. He speaks as the Son who willingly submits to the Father’s plan.

If Jesus drank the cup of wrath, why do Christians still suffer? Because there are two cups, and only one of them was his alone. The cup of wrath, God’s judgment on sin, he drained completely; not a drop of it is left for those who are in him (Romans 8:1). The cup his disciples share is the cup of suffering for his sake: opposition, loss, hardship, sometimes death, borne in fellowship with him. Your suffering is never God punishing you for sins Christ already paid for. It is the road the Master walked, now walked with him, and it ends where his ended, in glory (Romans 8:17).

In a sentence. Jesus told the brothers they did not understand the cup of suffering they were asking to share, and that places of honour are the Father’s to give.

On a Tuesday. Following Christ means sharing his cup of suffering. Are you prepared for that, or only for glory? If your cup at present is a long, quiet, unremarkable one, a caring role that never ends, an illness that never lifts, a faithfulness nobody sees, do not think it is a lesser discipleship than the martyr’s. It is the same cup, poured slower.

For worship. He drank it. The cup that would have been ours for ever, foaming with the wrath of a holy God, he took into his own hands in the garden and drained on the cross, until he could say, it is finished (John 19:30). And because he drank it to the dregs, the cup he hands his people is a different cup altogether: the cup of salvation (Psalm 116:13), the cup of the new covenant in his blood, and one day the new wine he will drink with us in his Father’s kingdom (26:29).
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is an Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. But Jesus called them to him and said, "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the other ten heard about it, they were angry with the two brothers. Jesus called them together and said: you know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great men exercise authority over them.

And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. Not moral superiority. They were angry because two of them had tried to get ahead, probably because they wanted the same places themselves. Their indignation shows the same ambition, and the rivalry inside the Twelve is laid bare.

But Jesus called them to him. Gently, all of them, to teach them. He does not address only the two who asked. The ten were indignant precisely because they wanted the same thing, and nobody in the room got to hear this as advice for somebody else.

You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them. Both verbs he uses carry the same prefix, kata, meaning down upon. Katakyrieuousin: they lord it down over them, dominate, rule harshly for their own benefit. And their great ones exercise authority over them, katexousiazousin: they bring their authority down on them. In the Roman world power meant domination. The emperor and his officials ruled by force and fear, and expected to be served; the disciples had seen it in the Herods and the Roman governors. Greatness in the world means having others under you. Jesus describes it without a flicker of admiration, and the kingdom inverts it entirely.

Where does this show up today? Not only in tyrants. It appears in the husband who uses his headship to get his own way, which is the very opposite of the self-giving love Scripture means by headship (Ephesians 5:25), and abuse is never to be tolerated under any name. It appears in the pastor who treats disagreement as rebellion, the manager who enjoys making people wait, the parent who rules by temper, the committee member who guards his territory. The question is never whether you have authority, but which way it presses: down on people, for your sake, or under them, for theirs.

In a sentence. When the ten were angry at the brothers’ ambition, Jesus reminded them how worldly rulers dominate those under them.

On a Tuesday. How do you use whatever authority you have: at work, at home, in church? To dominate, or to serve? Ask the people under you what it is like to be on the other end of your authority, and listen without defending yourself. Their answer will tell you more than your intentions do.

For worship. The One who had every right to lord it over us never once did. He had all authority, and he used it to call twelve quarrelling men to himself and teach them patiently. The Lord of glory stooped down, not to crush, but to lift: he holds the stars in his right hand and lays that same hand on the heads of his frightened servants (Revelation 1:16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: "It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be your slave," "even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It must not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be your slave, just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

It shall not be so among you. The church must be different from the world. Leadership in Christ’s community is not domination. This is not merely ethical advice but a redefinition of what greatness is: what the kingdom calls great is the opposite of what the world calls great. Since servant leadership has become a phrase on conference brochures, it is worth pinning down what Jesus actually says, because the words have content and the slogan often has none.

But whoever would be great among you must be your servant. Start with something he does not do: he does not abolish ambition. The sentence is whoever would be great among you; the wanting is allowed to stand, and only its object is changed. James and John are not rebuked for wishing to matter. They are told they have misunderstood what mattering is. A Christian is not required to want nothing; he is required to want the right thing, which turns out to be a towel rather than a throne. “Servant” (diakonos) is the word for someone who waits at table: practical, unglamorous work done for the comfort of other people. Greatness in the kingdom is measured by service.

And whoever would be first among you must be your slave. “Slave” (doulos) goes further still: someone with no rights, who belongs to another; not his time, not his preferences, not his reputation, not his plans for the afternoon. The first must be lowest of all. Jesus uses both words in ascending order, which is the opposite direction from the one careers normally travel.

How do I tell a servant from someone using the word? The tests are uncomfortable. A servant is available: he does not control his own diary the way a master does. A servant does work that nobody sees and nobody thanks him for, and keeps doing it when the thanks do not come. A servant can be interrupted. And the sharpest test of all: you can tell a servant by how he behaves when he is treated like one. Anyone can adopt the language while quietly requiring the deference; the moment of truth is when the deference is not given.

Even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. Jesus himself is the model, and he does not say be like a servant; he says this is what I came to do. The Son of Man of Daniel 7 is the one whom all peoples, nations and languages should serve (Daniel 7:14). He came to serve. The figure to whom the whole world owes service came to be the servant of the world. At the Last Supper he would take a towel and wash his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17).

And to give his life as a ransom for many. The heart of the gospel, in Jesus’ own words. A “ransom” (lytron) was the price paid to set a slave or prisoner free. The transaction was concrete and public: the sum was brought to the owner or the magistrate, it was paid, and the captive walked free. One person’s payment produced another person’s freedom. In the Old Testament the word was used for the price that redeemed a life that was forfeit (Exodus 21:30; 30:12). Jesus gives his life as the price to set his people free from sin, death and God’s judgment. “For” (anti) means in place of, instead of: a substitute. Not merely for the benefit of, but one thing given in the place of another. Jesus dies in the place of many. This echoes Isaiah 53:10–12, where the Servant makes his soul an offering for guilt and bears the sin of many. The Son of Man who commands servanthood in the verses before demonstrates it in its ultimate form: the cross is the supreme act of service, and the service that makes every other service possible.

For many. “Many” is a Hebrew way of speaking of a great number, as in Isaiah 53:11–12. It stresses the vast number saved by the one who dies. Reformed theology sees here the definite purpose of the atonement: Christ died for “his people” (1:21), “the many”, and actually secured their redemption. The gospel offer goes to all (28:19); the ransom actually frees those for whom it was paid.

Does many mean not all? Begin where the objection is weakest. In Hebrew and Aramaic “the many” is not a word that shuts people out; it means the multitude, the great mass. Isaiah uses it exactly so of the Servant who makes many to be accounted righteous and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:11–12), the passage Jesus is echoing, and Paul can move between “the many” and “all” without feeling he has changed the subject (Romans 5:15–19). So the word itself is not a fence; it is a word for a crowd nobody could count. Underneath, though, is a real question Christians have long divided over. Scripture also says Christ gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6; see 1 John 2:2). Reformed churches answer that the key is what a ransom does. A ransom is not an offer; it is a payment. Money laid on the table for a hundred prisoners does not make a hundred men releasable; it releases them. If Christ’s death merely made salvation possible for everyone and certain for no one, it would be the one ransom in history that might be paid and leave the captive in his cell. So the cross actually secured the freedom of those it was given for, which is why the New Testament speaks of it as purchasing a people and not merely an opportunity (Acts 20:28; Ephesians 5:25). The “all” texts are read as all kinds of people, Jew and Gentile, rulers and subjects. Other believers who love the same Lord read those texts more broadly, and they should be heard with respect and never caricatured.

Then how do I know I am one of the many? Not by working it out first. This doctrine has sometimes been used to frighten people it was meant to comfort, and no one in Scripture is ever sent to look for his name on a list before coming. The invitation is unrestricted: let the one who desires take the water of life without price (Revelation 22:17), and there is no small print under it. You find out you were among the many the way the eleventh-hour workers found out they were in the vineyard: by coming when called, and being handed the wage. Whoever comes to Christ will never be cast out (John 6:37). The doctrine is not a gate to be checked before you approach. It is the discovery, afterwards, that the price of your freedom was paid before you ever thought to ask.

What it does not mean. Not that the ransom was paid to Satan, as some early church writers suggested. Scripture does not say to whom the ransom was paid; it focuses on what it accomplished. But the broader teaching of Scripture shows that Christ satisfied God’s justice by bearing the penalty for sin (Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21). This is penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty our sin deserved, in our place. Nor does servant leadership mean that leaders have no authority. Jesus had all authority, and used it to serve. Elders are to lead, and to be followed (Hebrews 13:17), but as servants.

Two guards on servant leadership. One on each side. This is not the abolition of authority. Jesus gave commands, appointed leaders, rebuked error and made decisions; he did not run a committee, and a leader who will not lead is not being humble but leaving people unshepherded. Servant leadership is authority exercised for the good of those under it rather than for the comfort of the one holding it: a description of how power is used, not a reason to give it up. But the other guard matters more, because it is the commoner failure. A man who wears the phrase as a title while making every decision alone, resenting every challenge and requiring loyalty from everyone beneath him has kept the substance of what Jesus forbade and taken the vocabulary of what he commanded. That is worse than the Gentile rulers, who at least did not pretend. The elder is to shepherd not domineering over those in his charge, but being an example to the flock (1 Peter 5:3).

Where Christians differ: the atonement. Some see Christ’s death mainly as an example of self-giving love (the moral influence view), or as a victory over evil powers (Christus Victor). These contain truth: the cross does show love (1 John 4:10) and defeat Satan (Colossians 2:15). But Jesus’ word “ransom … in place of many” points to substitution at the centre. Verdict: penal substitution is the heart of the atonement, with example and victory flowing from it.

In a sentence. In Christ’s community, greatness is service, because the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom in the place of many.

On a Tuesday. How can you serve someone today in a way that costs you something: your time, your comfort, your preference? Look for the job in your home or church that nobody wants and nobody will notice, and do it without mentioning it. And when you are treated like a servant, overlooked, interrupted, taken for granted, take it as the test Jesus set, and pass it quietly, for him.

For worship. The Son of Man, before whom every nation will one day bow, came not to be served but to serve, and the deepest service he did was to die. He laid his own life on the table of divine justice as the price of our freedom, in our place, and the captives walked out. He did not offer a ransom that might work. He paid one that did, and the many he paid for will stand around his throne, a multitude no one can number, singing that he was slain and by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!" The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they left Jericho, a great crowd followed him. Two blind men sitting by the road heard that Jesus was passing and cried out: Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David! The crowd rebuked them and told them to be quiet, but they shouted all the more.

And as they went out of Jericho. Jericho lay about fifteen miles (twenty-four kilometres) northeast of Jerusalem, in the Jordan valley, about 250 metres (800 feet) below sea level. It was the last stop on the pilgrim road to Jerusalem. A great crowd followed him: pilgrims heading up for Passover.

Leaving or entering? Matthew and Mark place the healing as Jesus was leaving Jericho, but Luke sets it as he drew near (Luke 18:35). The likeliest answer is simple once you know the ground. There were two Jerichos about a mile apart: the old ruined mound of Joshua’s city, and the new Jericho that Herod had built beside it, with its palaces and gardens. Jesus could be leaving the one and approaching the other at the same moment, so both descriptions could be literally true of one scene seen from two sides. That is one likely explanation among several offered, and none requires a contradiction.

And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside. Mark names one: Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46). Matthew mentions two, as he often does (see 8:28). Mark and Luke fix on the one memorable, named man, while Matthew, careful of the whole, notes that there were two. One never denies a second.

When they heard that Jesus was passing by. This was their only chance. He would not come this way again; he was on his way to die. They seized the moment.

They cried out, Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David! They recognise him as the Messiah, the Son of David (see 9:27; 15:22), the very title the crowds will shout at the entry into Jerusalem days later (21:9). The blind see what many sighted people do not. Two men who could not see anything shouted the one title on that road that was actually true, while a crowd with perfect eyesight told them to stop making a scene.

The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent. Here is the detail that ought to make a churchgoing reader uncomfortable. It is not the town officials who tell these men to be quiet, and it is not the Romans. It is the crowd: the people who were at that moment following Jesus up the road. The people walking with him were the ones trying to silence the people calling out to him. Matthew showed us this once already, when the disciples turned away the families bringing children (19:13). Twice in two chapters the obstacle between a needy person and Christ is the group already committed to him. They thought the blind men a nuisance, unworthy of the teacher’s attention.

Who has learned to keep quiet in our church? Every congregation has ways of signalling that a particular sort of person is making things difficult: the man whose questions hold everything up, the woman whose crisis has gone on too long, the family whose children are loud, the person whose need is chronic and will not resolve into a tidy testimony. Nobody says be quiet. The crowd in this story probably thought it was being helpful, keeping the road clear for an important man on important business. Ask seriously who has learned to keep his voice down in your church, and who taught him; then make room for him to cry out.

But they cried out all the more. The opposition made them louder. They had nothing to lose that they had not already lost, they knew exactly how much they needed, and they were not going to be silenced by people whose eyes worked. Persistence (15:22–28): nothing would stop them.

Does persistent prayer twist God’s arm? No, and this passage is often turned into a technique. Their persistence is not what obtained the miracle, and shouting longer is not a lever that moves God. Jesus is not worn down here; he is not reluctant at any point, and there is no hint that a quieter pair would have been left blind. Persistence in prayer is not leverage. It is what real need looks like from the outside. They kept calling because they had no alternative, and they had worked out who was walking past. So keep praying, not to change his heart, which is already kind, but because he is the only one who can help.

In a sentence. Two blind men cried out to Jesus as the Son of David, and when the crowd tried to silence them, they shouted all the louder.

On a Tuesday. Do not let anyone silence your prayers to Jesus, including the voice in your own head that says you have asked too often. Cry out all the more. And watch that you are never the crowd: when someone in need interrupts the programme, be the one who brings him nearer, not the one who tells him to wait.

For worship. Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David: the oldest prayer of the church, first shouted by two blind beggars at the side of a road. He has never refused it. The King of David’s line, on his way to his throne by way of a cross, was within earshot of the least of his subjects, and their cry was the truest confession on the road that day. He is still within earshot, and the crowd has never yet been loud enough to drown out a sinner calling for mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Mark names one of the men, Bartimaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: And stopping, Jesus called them and said, "What do you want me to do for you?" They said to him, "Lord, let our eyes be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stopped, called them and asked: what do you want me to do for you? They said: Lord, let our eyes be opened.

And stopping, Jesus called them. Look at what he does before anything else. He is in a column of pilgrims going up to the Passover at which he will be executed; he has just told the Twelve in detail what is waiting at the top of the road; the crowd around him is large and moving and has already tried to shut these men up. And he stops it. The whole procession waits at the roadside while the Son of David deals with two men everybody else had classified as an interruption. If you want to know what he is like under the heaviest pressure a human being has ever carried, this is the answer: he stops. They mattered to him.

What do you want me to do for you? Matthew has put the same question twice in one chapter, and it is the spine of the whole thing. To the mother of James and John, in verse 21: what do you want? To two beggars on the Jericho road: what do you want me to do for you? Same questioner, same chapter, same courtesy, and two answers that could not be further apart. One asks for the two best seats in the kingdom. The other asks for eyes. The brothers asked for status; the blind men asked for mercy.

He asks anyway. He could see they were blind; the whole road could see it. He does not need the information. He asks because he will not treat a man as a case to be processed when he can treat him as a person to be spoken to, and because he wanted them to express their need and their faith. There is nothing efficient about that question, and he asked it with Jerusalem in front of him.

Lord, let our eyes be opened. A simple, specific request. Between them, the two petitions in this chapter teach a man how to pray. The mother asked for something that would put her sons above the other ten. The blind men asked for something they could not obtain anywhere else, could not manufacture and could not pretend to have. Nobody fakes sight. That is what made it a good request: not that it was modest, because it was not modest at all. Opening the eyes of the blind was a work the Old Testament reserves for God himself (Psalm 146:8; Isaiah 35:5). It was enormous. It was simply honest.

Should I ask God for specific things, or only pray “your will be done”? Both, and this scene shows how they fit. Jesus invites a specific answer, and the blind men give one. Vague prayers are often a way of protecting ourselves from disappointment, or of hiding what we really want. Tell him plainly what you want, as a child tells his father, and then entrust the answer to his wisdom, as Jesus himself did in Gethsemane: let this cup pass, yet not as I will (26:39). Specific asking and humble yielding belong together in the same prayer.

In a sentence. Jesus stopped for the blind men and asked what they wanted, and they asked for their sight.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus asked you today, what do you want me to do for you, what would you say? Run the question on yourself and do not tidy the answer. Most of us would hear ourselves asking for something nearer the thrones than the eyes: for the situation to resolve in our favour, for the person who was wrong about us to be shown wrong, for the position or the outcome. It is worth knowing that about yourself. It is not a reason to despair; it is a reason to ask him for better wants, which is itself a prayer of the second kind.

For worship. The Lord of glory, walking to the cross, stopped for two beggars. That is not an exception to his greatness; it is what his greatness is. The God who counts the stars and calls them all by name is the same God who heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds (Psalm 147:3–4), and in Jesus he stood still on a dusty road and asked two blind men what they wanted. He has never been too busy for a sinner who calls.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes. Immediately they received their sight and followed him.

And Jesus in pity touched their eyes. Matthew tells us what moved before he tells us what happened. “Pity” (splanchnistheis) is the word for something turning over in a man’s insides: deep compassion, the same word used when Jesus saw the crowds harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd (9:36) and four thousand hungry people (15:32). The healing is not the first event in the verse; the compassion is.

He touched them. He did not have to, and this Gospel has already shown us so. He healed a centurion’s servant from a distance without going near him (8:13), and a Canaanite woman’s daughter by a word (15:28). Power was never the issue. So the touch was not for the miracle; it was for the men. Two beggars who had spent the morning being told by a crowd to be quiet, and the first thing that happens to them is a pair of hands on their faces. Whatever they had been in that town for years, a fixture, a noise, a thing to step round, they were not that to him.

And immediately they recovered their sight. Isaiah’s sign of the messianic age: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened (Isaiah 35:5; see 11:5). The kingdom had come near enough to touch.

And followed him. The last words are the point of putting the story here at all. Followed him where? Up the road he had just described in detail. Their first act as seeing men was to fall in behind somebody walking to a flogging and a cross. These are the last people Jesus heals before Jerusalem, and what they do with their new eyes is use them to follow him into the passion. They are a picture of true disciples: they recognised Jesus, cried for mercy, received sight, and followed.

The contrast. The chapter shows two kinds of request: James and John asked for power and were rebuked; the blind men asked for mercy and were healed. The disciples who could see were spiritually blind to the meaning of the cross. The blind men saw who Jesus was. The Twelve had been told three times where this was going and were arguing about seats. The crowd was going up for a festival. Two beggars, blind an hour earlier, saw exactly who he was and went with him.

The whole chapter in one movement. It opens with a landowner who does not send his foreman but walks down to the market himself before dawn, and goes back at nine, at noon, at three and at five for men nobody had chosen. It closes with the Son of Man stopping a procession on the way to his own execution because two beggars the crowd had silenced were shouting for mercy. The parable said that is what the owner of the vineyard is like. The Jericho road shows him doing it.

Does Jesus still open blind eyes? He still does the greater thing these healings pointed to. Physical healing is in his hands, and he sometimes grants it in answer to prayer, though he does not promise it to every believer in this life. But every Christian is a blind man who has been given sight: the god of this world had blinded our minds, and God shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:4–6). If you can see who Jesus is and want to follow him, that is the miracle of this verse, done in you.

In a sentence. Jesus had compassion and healed the blind men, who immediately followed him.

On a Tuesday. When God opens your eyes, use your sight to follow Jesus, wherever he leads, including up hard roads. Think of one place where following him this week will cost you something, and go there with him. And look for one person whom everyone steps around, and put a hand on his shoulder, the way your Lord put his hands on theirs.

For worship. He is still, at the end of the chapter, going out to the people who were left standing. His heart turned over at the sight of two beggars; his hands touched faces the town had stopped looking at; his road led to a cross where he would be the one left alone, so that the blind could see and the outcast could follow. Once we were blind, and now we see, and what we see is him: the Son of David, full of compassion, walking ahead of us up the road to glory.

20.theology: The atonement as ransom. Matthew 20:28 is Matthew’s clearest statement of substitutionary atonement. The word “ransom” (lytron) carries the weight of a payment that secures release — it is used in the Septuagint for the price paid to redeem a slave or a firstborn. Jesus applies it to his own death: he gives his life as the price that sets the many free from their captivity to sin, death, and judgment. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is primarily objective — it actually accomplishes something in the divine court (the cancellation of debt, the satisfaction of justice) — before it is subjective (inspiring us, moving us, transforming us). The ransom is paid; the captives are free.
20.examples:
Then: James and John wanted the best seats. They had left everything (19:27) and felt entitled to the premium return. Jesus redefines the currency: greatness is measured in service and suffering, not in position and honour. The Twelve would spend the rest of their lives learning this.

Now: The parable of the workers challenges every theology of spiritual merit — the idea that longer service, greater sacrifice, or more faithful obedience earns a greater share of God’s favour. Grace cannot be earned; it can only be received. The workers who grumble are those who have forgotten that any wage at all is mercy. The appropriate response to grace is gratitude, not calculation.

21.title: The King Enters Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, <sup>2</sup>saying to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and he will send them at once.” <sup>4</sup>This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying, <sup>5</sup>“Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’” <sup>6</sup>The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. <sup>7</sup>They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. <sup>8</sup>Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. <sup>9</sup>And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>10</sup>And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?” <sup>11</sup>And the crowds said, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.” <sup>12</sup>And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>13</sup>He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you make it a den of robbers.” <sup>14</sup>And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. <sup>15</sup>But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” they were indignant, <sup>16</sup>and they said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” And Jesus said to them, “Yes; have you never read, “‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise’?” <sup>17</sup>And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. <sup>18</sup>In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. <sup>19</sup>And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, “May no fruit ever come from you again!” And the fig tree withered at once. <sup>20</sup>When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree wither at once?” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen. <sup>22</sup>And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.” <sup>23</sup>And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?” <sup>24</sup>Jesus answered them, “I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>25</sup>The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?” And they discussed it among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>26</sup>But if we say, ‘From man,’ we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet.” <sup>27</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And he said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>28</sup>“What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, ‘Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’ <sup>29</sup>And he answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind and went. <sup>30</sup>And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, ‘I will, sir,’ but did not go. <sup>31</sup>Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. <sup>32</sup>For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him. <sup>33</sup>“Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. <sup>34</sup>When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. <sup>35</sup>And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. <sup>36</sup>Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them. <sup>37</sup>Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>38</sup>But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’ <sup>39</sup>And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. <sup>40</sup>When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” <sup>41</sup>They said to him, “He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons.” <sup>42</sup>Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: “‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’? <sup>43</sup>Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. <sup>44</sup>And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>45</sup>When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. <sup>46</sup>And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the hinge between the Galilean ministry and the Passion Week. Jesus enters Jerusalem not as a military conqueror on a warhorse but as a humble king on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 with deliberate precision. The crowds shout “Hosanna to the Son of David!” — they are celebrating a political liberation that is not coming. Jesus has a different kind of liberation in mind.

The chapter is structured around three confrontational actions: the entry (vv. 1–11), the temple cleansing (vv. 12–17), and the cursing of the fig tree (vv. 18–22), sandwiched around a series of parables and controversies. The fig tree and the temple interpret each other: Israel, like the fig tree, has leaves of religious activity but no fruit. The temple establishment has turned the Father’s house of prayer into a market. Jesus’ authority is challenged (vv. 23–27); he responds with the parable of the two sons (vv. 28–32) and the parable of the tenants (vv. 33–46), both of which declare that the kingdom will be taken from the current tenants and given to a people who produce its fruit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Triumphal Entry, Cleansing of the Temple, and the Withered Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt, enters Jerusalem to the crowd's Hosannas, cleanses the temple of money-changers and dove-sellers, heals the blind and lame in the temple, and returns to Bethany. The next morning he curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit; it withers immediately. He teaches the disciples about faith that moves mountains. In between, children run about the temple courts shouting the same Hosanna, the chief priests object to what they are saying, and Jesus answers them out of Psalm 8 (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The triumphal entry deliberately fulfills Zechariah 9:9: the king who comes humble and mounted on a donkey, not a warhorse. Jesus is not claiming the military kingship Israel wanted; he is claiming the humble-servant kingship Zechariah foresaw. The Hosanna (Hebrew: save now!) from Psalm 118:25-26 is the pilgrims' greeting to the coming king. The crowd who shouts it does not fully understand what they are saying; they are speaking more truly than they know. "Hosanna to the Son of David" is the church's cry from that day to this. Two things the section does that are easily missed. Hosanna is not a cheer but a prayer — hoshia-na, save now — and the crowd prayed it with the wrong emergency in mind, wanting Rome dealt with while he came for something they had not thought to mention. And the psalm they sang is the psalm he quotes back in the temple: the pilgrims shout Psalm 118:26 on the way in (v. 9), and Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, the rejected stone, to the men who run the place (v. 42). Between two verses of one psalm lies the whole week.
verseByVerse.examples: The cleansing of the temple is an act of prophetic judgment: the court of the Gentiles (the only place where non-Jews could pray) has been turned into a market. The money-changers and dove-sellers served legitimate temple functions, but their location in the court of the Gentiles prevented the very prayer the temple was meant to facilitate. Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7 — "a house of prayer for all nations" — and Jeremiah 7:11 — "a den of robbers." He restores the temple to its purpose as a place of prayer and healing, then leaves it to be destroyed (ch. 24). The withered fig tree is a living parable of Israel's fruitlessness: outward leaves of religious activity, no fruit of genuine repentance. Three notes on that sign. It belongs to a recognised prophetic genre — Jeremiah smashing a jar, Ezekiel lying beside a brick, Ahijah tearing a cloak — and it is worth observing that in a ministry of raising the dead and healing all who came, the only thing Jesus ever destroyed was a plant, by a roadside, where nobody was hurt. The charge against the tree is precise: not barrenness but advertising, since a fig in full leaf out of season is making a claim that can be checked from the road. So the guard matters for the anxious reader — this condemns pretence, not weakness, and the same Gospel says a bruised reed he will not break (12:20). The children of vv. 15-16, meanwhile, get Psalm 8 quoted in their defence, and the rest of that verse — to still the enemy and the avenger — tells the chief priests which part of the psalm they are standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples ahead: go into the village in front of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me.

Meaning first. Matthew 21 is the day the King comes to his city and his house. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, deliberately acting out Zechariah’s prophecy of a humble king who brings peace, while pilgrims spread their cloaks and shout Hosanna, save now, to the Son of David. He goes straight to the temple, drives out the traders who had turned the court of the nations into a market, and heals the blind and the lame there while children sing his praise. The next morning he curses a fig tree that is all leaves and no fruit, an acted parable of the judgment coming on a busy, fruitless religion. Then the temple leaders demand to know by what authority he acts, and he answers with a question about John and three parables, two of them in this chapter: two sons, one who says no and goes and one who says yes and does not; and wicked tenants who beat the owner’s servants and kill his son. The rejected stone, he says, will become the cornerstone, and that is the Lord’s doing. The chapter shows who Jesus is: the King, the Lord of the temple, the beloved Son, and the stone on which everything rests, and it asks every reader what he will do with him.

The setting. This is the beginning of the last week of Jesus’ life, often called Holy Week. Matthew devotes eight chapters (21–28) to it: a third of his Gospel. Jesus arrives on Sunday, five days before he is crucified on Friday. Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims for Passover; the city’s population of perhaps 50,000 may have swelled several times over.

Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives is a ridge east of Jerusalem, across the Kidron Valley, looking down on the city and the temple. Bethphage (“house of unripe figs”) was a small village on its slope, near Bethany, and it mattered because it was reckoned the edge of the city: cross that line and you were, for ritual purposes, in Jerusalem. So this is the threshold, and the first thing Jesus does on reaching it is stop the whole party and send two men for an animal. And the hill is not incidental. Zechariah had said that on the day of the LORD his feet would stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4), and Jewish hope had settled on this ridge as the place deliverance would come from. Jesus does not stumble into the fulfilment. He stops at the right hill, sends for the right animal, and then rides down it.

The only journey he would not walk. Here is a fact easy to miss and hard to forget once seen. He had walked everywhere for three years: up and down Galilee, out to Tyre and Sidon, north to Caesarea Philippi, down the Jordan valley, up the long climb from Jericho, hundreds of miles in sandals, and Matthew never once mentions him riding. This is the only journey in the Gospels that Jesus refuses to walk. The one time he lets himself be carried is the mile or so into his own capital, as her king.

Then Jesus sent two disciples. Jesus takes the initiative. He plans his entry deliberately.

Immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Jesus knows exactly what they will find, either by divine knowledge or by prior arrangement with the owner; Matthew does not say, and we should not pretend to know. Either way, he is in control. Nothing about the next five days is happening to Jesus. He is setting it up. Only Matthew mentions the mother donkey as well as the colt. Mark says the colt had never been ridden (Mark 11:2): a sign of an animal set apart for a sacred purpose (Numbers 19:2; 1 Samuel 6:7). Anyone who has been near a young donkey knows what an unbroken animal does in a shouting crowd with cloaks flying under its feet. It carried him.

A royal mount. Guard the donkey against the reading it usually gets. This is not a story about a man too poor for a horse, and the donkey is not merely a symbol of lowliness. In Israel it was a royal mount. When David wanted the succession settled beyond argument he had Solomon set on the king’s own mule and led down to Gihon, and the people came up after him rejoicing until the earth was split by their noise (1 Kings 1:33–40). A king’s son, a borrowed royal beast, a descent from a hill, a shouting crowd: the last coronation procession Israel had seen looked very like this one. The people lining that road knew what they were watching.

Untie them and bring them to me. Genesis 49:11 speaks of the ruler from Judah tying his donkey’s colt to the vine: a messianic image. The sceptre was promised to Judah until the one should come to whom it belongs, and here he is, untying the colt.

Why does it matter that Jesus planned this so carefully? Because it shows that the cross was not an accident that overtook a good man. Jesus chose the day, the hill, the animal and the prophecy, and in doing so he publicly claimed to be Israel’s King, knowing it would bring the authorities down on him within the week. He was not swept along by events. He was laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). That is the comfort of it: the One who arranged this procession is the same One who arranges the days of those who belong to him.

In a sentence. Approaching Jerusalem for the last time, Jesus deliberately arranged to enter on a donkey’s colt.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was in control of every detail of his last week, even as evil closed in. He is in control of yours. Name the part of this week you feel least in control of, and say to him, plainly, that you trust him with it, because he has not lost the thread of a single day.

For worship. The Lord of all creation, who had walked every mile of his ministry, sat down at last on a borrowed colt and rode into the city that would kill him, as her King. He chose the hill of Zechariah’s promise and the beast of Solomon’s coronation, and he rode it not toward a throne of gold but toward a cross. Every detail was his, and every detail was love.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, near Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, 'The Lord needs them,' and he will send them at once." This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone says anything to you, say: the Lord needs them, and he will send them at once. This happened to fulfil what the prophet had said.

The Lord needs them. If anyone says anything to you, you shall say this. Four words to say to a stranger whose animal you are untying, and they are extraordinary in both halves. Take the first. The Lord, ho kyrios, with the article, absolute, no explanation attached. “The Lord” may refer to Jesus himself, as Lord, or to God. Either way, Jesus claims the right to take what he needs, and sends the title ahead of him as the whole of his credentials. No name, no message about who is asking, no promise to return the animal. Everything belongs to him.

Needs. Now the second half, which is stranger. This is a rare moment in the Gospels when Jesus says he has need of anything, and what he needs is the loan of a young donkey. The one through whom all things were made, walking toward the city where he will be crowned and killed, sends two friends to borrow transport. It is the same condescension that runs through the whole story, easy to miss because it is so quiet. He had nowhere to lay his head (8:20). He will borrow an upper room for the supper. He will be laid in a tomb another man had cut for himself (27:60). The only things he owned at the end were the clothes the soldiers gambled for. He owns everything, and he arrives owning nothing and asking for a colt.

And he will send them at once. The owner will give them willingly. Somewhere in that village is a man who lent his donkey for a day and never appears again in the story, and the whole entry into Jerusalem waited on his willingness.

This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet. Zechariah 9:9, with the opening words from Isaiah 62:11.
