Matthew has used this formula a dozen times since chapter 1, and by now the reader should know what he means by it: not merely that a prediction has ticked over, but that a pattern long written has arrived at the thing it was always shaped for (see on 2:15). The words had been on a scroll for five hundred years. Now they are hoofbeats on a road. Jesus deliberately acts out the prophecy. He is presenting himself publicly, for the first time, as the King.

Does the Lord really need anything from me? Not in the sense of lacking anything; God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25). But he chooses to use what his people have, and to give them the honour of lending it. The donkey’s owner was not making up a deficit in God. He was being let in on the coronation. So when you give your home, your time or your skill to Christ, you are not propping him up; you are being given a part in what he is doing, which is a gift to you before it is a gift to him.

In a sentence. Jesus claimed the animals as the Lord, deliberately fulfilling the prophecy of the coming King.

On a Tuesday. The Lord needs it. What do you have that the Lord might ask for: your home, car, time, skill, a spare room, an evening? Hold it loosely, and when he asks through his church or a neighbour in need, give it willingly and at once, the way that unnamed villager did.

For worship. He owns the cattle on a thousand hills, and he asked to borrow a colt. He made the heavens, and had nowhere to lay his head. The Lord of glory became poor so that we, through his poverty, might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and even his royal entry was made on something lent to him. Blessed be the King who emptied himself so completely that he could say, of a donkey, the Lord needs it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.'" The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say to the daughter of Zion: look, your king is coming to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. The disciples went and did as Jesus had told them.

Say to the daughter of Zion. From Isaiah 62:11. “Daughter of Zion” is a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people, addressed tenderly, like a father speaking to his daughter.

Behold, your king is coming to you. Zechariah 9:9. In its context, Zechariah promises a king who will come to Jerusalem, bring peace to the nations, and rule from sea to sea (Zechariah 9:10). He is righteous and having salvation. And notice the little words: your king, coming to you. He is not a foreign ruler imposed on her, and she does not have to go looking for him.

Humble. “Humble” (praus) is the same word as “meek” in the Beatitudes (5:5) and “gentle” in Jesus’ invitation to the weary: I am gentle and lowly in heart (11:29). It does not mean weak. It is the word used of a horse that has been broken in: all the strength still there, and every ounce of it under control. That is the King riding down the hill. Not a proud conqueror, but a gentle king.

And mounted on a donkey. Kings went to war on horses; a king riding a donkey came in peace. Solomon rode David’s mule to his coronation (1 Kings 1:33–40). And Zechariah explains the donkey himself in his very next verse, which is almost never quoted: I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). The animal is not only a note about the king’s humility. It is his policy. He rides the beast you ride when the war horses have been abolished, and the sentence ends with the nations: the same nations whose only court in the temple he is about to clear within the hour. Jesus comes not as a military Messiah to overthrow Rome, but as the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who will bring peace through his death.

Not a Roman triumph. Set it beside what a triumphal entry looked like in that world. A Roman triumph had a fixed shape: the victorious general in a four-horse chariot, the spoils of the campaign carried before him, the captured enemy leaders walking in chains behind, and at the end of the route prisoners executed and bulls sacrificed. Go down the list. This king has no chariot. He has no spoils, having gathered nothing for himself. He drags no prisoners, having spent three years setting them free. And at the end of his route there is indeed a sacrifice, and it is him.

On a colt, the foal of a beast of burden. Hebrew poetry often repeats an idea in parallel: “on a donkey, on a colt” describes one animal. Matthew mentions two animals (vv. 2, 7), because there were two: the colt, with its mother walking alongside, perhaps to keep the unbroken colt calm. Jesus rode the colt (Mark 11:7).

What it does not mean. Not that Matthew misunderstood Hebrew poetry and invented a second animal. He was an eyewitness, and he records that there were two animals, noting how the prophecy’s parallel lines fit.

The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. Obedience. Matthew keeps saying this about them, and it is worth noticing how ordinary the obedience is. They were not asked to understand the Zechariah citation or grasp what was about to happen in the city. They were asked to walk into a village and fetch a donkey, and they did. A great deal of obedience is that size.

Did Jesus accept the crowd’s idea of kingship? He accepted the crown in the one form nobody wanted. The crowd was shouting for a king who would deal with Rome, and the King they were shouting at had come to deal with something they had not asked him to touch: sin, death and the wrath of God. He let them cheer. He did not turn down the volume; he corrected the meaning, and he did it by choosing his transport. So do not be surprised if Christ, coming into your life, does not do first what you most wanted done. He has come to deal with the deeper thing.

In a sentence. Jesus came as the King Zechariah promised: humble, gentle, riding on a donkey, bringing peace.

On a Tuesday. Gentleness is strength under control. Where this week will you be tempted to use your strength, your words, your position, your quick mind, to win rather than to bless? Ride the donkey there: say the quieter thing, make the peace, and trust the King who conquered by gentleness to vindicate you.

For worship. Behold, your King is coming to you: righteous, having salvation, humble, gentle, speaking peace to the nations. He did not come in a chariot to crush his enemies. He came on a donkey to die for them. All his strength was under the control of his love, and the war he ended at the cross was the war between a holy God and his rebellious people, so that we who were enemies might be reconciled and brought home in peace.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse. Matthew mentions both the donkey and her colt.

parallels.desc: your king comes, humble and mounted on a donkey
say to the daughter of Zion

verseByVerse.quote: They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought the donkey and the colt and put their cloaks on them, and he sat on them. Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.

They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks. As a saddle for the King.

And he sat on them. On the cloaks; he rode the colt. This detail has been mocked more than almost any other in Matthew, and it deserves a straight answer. Did Jesus, the scoffers ask, straddle two animals at once? The nearest plural is the cloaks: they threw their garments over both animals, and he sat on the garments of the one he rode. There really were two animals, and Matthew simply notices what the others pass over: the colt had never been ridden, and an unbroken colt is far steadier with its mother walking beside it, exactly the arrangement a careful observer would recall. Far from misreading Zechariah’s doubled wording, Matthew, a Jew steeped in the Scriptures, saw the real scene match even the parallel lines of the prophet and was glad to record it. The eye that notices the mother donkey is not the eye of a careless writer but of a man who was there.

Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road. A gesture of homage to a king. When Jehu was proclaimed king, the people took their garments and put them under him on the bare steps (2 Kings 9:13). It was like laying out a red carpet. And for a poor man a cloak was no small thing: it was his coat by day and his blanket by night, so precious that the law forbade keeping a poor man’s cloak overnight as a pledge (Exodus 22:26–27). They laid in the dust the most valuable thing most of them owned.

And others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. John says they were palm branches (John 12:13), which is why the day is called Palm Sunday. Palm branches were a symbol of victory and national hope. When Simon Maccabeus liberated Jerusalem in 141 BC, the people celebrated with palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51). They also featured in the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40). The crowd was greeting a liberator, and it was large: most of the crowd, Matthew says. The welcome was public and unmistakable. This is the royal entry the whole ministry of chapters 1 to 20 has been moving toward.

Were they right or wrong to welcome him as king? Right in what they did, mistaken in what they expected. He was the King, and homage was exactly what he deserved; Jesus did not stop them. But many wanted a deliverer from Rome, and their welcome would cool when he would not be that. It is possible to honour Christ sincerely with the right gestures and still want him for the wrong reasons. The cure is not to stop the gestures but to learn who he really is, so that the homage stays when the expectations are disappointed.

In a sentence. The crowds welcomed Jesus as King, spreading their cloaks and branches on the road.

On a Tuesday. What would it mean for you to lay your cloak before Jesus: to honour him with what you have, not only with what costs you nothing? Think of the thing you would least like to put in the dust in front of him, your reputation, your evenings, your savings, your plans, and ask whether it is really yours to keep back from the King.

For worship. They spread their cloaks under the feet of the colt, and he went on to give up his own: the soldiers stripped him and cast lots for his garments (27:35). They laid down their coats for a King; the King laid down his life for them. And one day every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10–11), and the honour that a crowd on the Mount of Olives gave him for an afternoon will be given him by all creation, for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, "Who is this?" And the crowds said, "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds going ahead and those following shouted: Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest! When he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred: who is this? The crowds said: this is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.

And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting. A procession of pilgrims, with Jesus in the middle, coming up for the feast.

Hosanna to the Son of David! “Hosanna” is Hebrew for “Save, we pray!” or “Save now!”, from Psalm 118:25. By Jesus’ time it had become a shout of praise and welcome, but it began as a cry for help addressed to God. The crowd on that road was not only applauding. It was praying, at the top of its voice, in the words every pilgrim sang coming up to the feast: save us, we pray, O LORD (Psalm 118:25). “Son of David”: the Messiah (1:1). The crowd openly hails Jesus as the Messiah-King.

The right prayer with the wrong emergency in mind. Ask that crowd what they wanted saving from, and many would have said Rome: the garrison in the fortress by the temple, the taxes, the standards, the humiliation of occupation in the land God gave them. It was a real grievance, and he did nothing about it. He had come to deal with something they had not thought to mention, and the rescue they asked for was smaller than the one he was carrying up that hill. They were more right than they knew and less right than they thought, which is the usual condition of anybody praying.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Psalm 118:26. Psalm 118 was one of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118), sung by pilgrims at Passover. It was a psalm of a king returning in victory, received at the gates of the temple. “He who comes” was a title for the Messiah (11:3). And Matthew is building something with this psalm. The crowd shouts verse 26 on the way into the city. Before the chapter is over Jesus will stand in the temple and quote verse 22 at the men who run it: the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (v. 42). The pilgrims sang the welcome; the Lord supplied the verse about what would be done with him.

Hosanna in the highest! Praise to God in the highest heaven.

And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up. “Stirred” (eseisthē) means shaken, as by an earthquake: the root that gives us seismic. The city was shaken, as it had been at his birth when the magi came (2:3). And Matthew uses that root again: the earth shakes when he dies and the curtain tears (27:51), and again at dawn on the third day when the stone is rolled back (28:2). Three tremors, and the city’s is the only one caused by people.

Who is this? The question of the whole Gospel, and the right one.

This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee. So the crowds answered: a true answer, but incomplete. He is a prophet, the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), but far more. It is the answer the villages had been giving all along (16:14), the honour of a great category that is still the wrong one. Within five days a crowd in the same city would shout, let him be crucified (27:22). Their enthusiasm was for a political deliverer, not a suffering Saviour.

Was it the same crowd that shouted Crucify? Partly, perhaps, but probably not mostly. The crowd on the road was chiefly pilgrims, many of them Galileans who had followed Jesus for months. The crowd at the trial gathered early in the morning inside the city, at the governor’s headquarters, and Matthew says the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas (27:20). So the lesson is less tidy than the usual sermon, and sharper. It was not simply that everyone turned. It was that when it mattered, many who had cheered him were nowhere to be found, and a crowd that had been worked on was. Enthusiasm that is not faith either changes sides or goes quiet.

What it does not mean. Not that the crowd was entirely insincere. Many were genuinely moved. But their understanding was shallow. Popular enthusiasm is not the same as faith.

In a sentence. The crowds hailed Jesus as the Messiah-King with Hosannas from Psalm 118, and the shaken city asked who he was.

On a Tuesday. Who is Jesus to you: a prophet, a great teacher, or the King? Your answer decides how you will stand when the crowd turns. Notice where you are tempted to go quiet about him, at work, among family, online, and decide now that you will not be one of the absent on Friday.

For worship. Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! The crowd cried save now without knowing what it was asking, and he answered the prayer far beyond their asking: not by driving out Rome, but by going up to Golgotha and saving his people from their sins (1:21). Hosanna in the highest: the King who was greeted on a road is enthroned above every name, and every prayer for rescue ever prayed in his name is heard.
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. He said to them, "It is written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer,' but you make it a den of robbers." And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who were selling and buying there. He overturned the money-changers’ tables and the seats of those selling pigeons. He said: it is written, my house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers. And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.

And Jesus entered the temple. The King comes to his Father’s house. Malachi 3:1 promised that the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple, and asked who could endure the day of his coming. The entry and the cleansing are one act: the King takes possession of his city and then of the holy place. Mark tells us that Jesus entered the temple, looked around and went out to Bethany, and cleansed it the next day (Mark 11:11, 15); Matthew tells the story more compactly, as he does with the fig tree. Both are true accounts of the same events.

And drove out all who sold and bought in the temple. The trading took place in the Court of the Gentiles, the large outer courtyard of the temple. Pilgrims needed animals for sacrifice, and buying them in the temple was convenient. But the area meant for Gentiles to pray had become a noisy market.

And he overturned the tables of the money-changers. Every Jewish man had to pay the temple tax (17:24) in a particular silver coin, the Tyrian shekel. Money-changers exchanged foreign coins for a fee, which was often excessive.

And the seats of those who sold pigeons. Pigeons were the sacrifices offered by the poor (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8). Jesus’ own mother offered them at his birth (Luke 2:24). The sellers may have charged exorbitant prices, exploiting the poor.

My house shall be called a house of prayer. From Isaiah 56:7, which continues: for all peoples. God intended the temple to be a place where even foreigners could come and pray. The trading had pushed them out of the one court that was theirs.

But you make it a den of robbers. From Jeremiah 7:11. In Jeremiah’s sermon, the people thought the temple would protect them while they lived wickedly, as robbers hide in a cave between raids. God warned that he would destroy the temple, as he destroyed Shiloh. Jesus’ action is a prophetic sign of judgment: the temple will be destroyed (24:2), as it was in AD 70.

And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. When David captured Jerusalem, a saying arose that the blind and the lame shall not come into the house (2 Samuel 5:8). The Son of David welcomes them in, and heals them. True worship is restored. The tables go over and the sick come in. If a man’s zeal clears a space and nothing tender happens in it, he has done half the scene and the wrong half.

The true temple standing in the court. Ask what the temple was for, and three answers come back: it was where God dwelt among his people, where sacrifice was offered for sin, and through which prayer went up. Now look at the man standing among the overturned tables. He is Immanuel, God with us (1:23), so the dwelling is no longer a building. He is days away from offering the sacrifice that will end the need for every other one. And he is the mediator through whom prayer now reaches the Father (John 14:13–14). John records him saying, after a cleansing like this one, destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, and John adds that he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). This is not a reformer tidying an institution he means to keep. It is the reality walking into the shadow. When the building fell in AD 70, the loss, devastating as it was, took nothing from the people of God that they had not already been given in Christ. The house of prayer for all nations turned out to be a Person, and the Gentiles those traders had crowded out would find room in him.

Did Jesus cleanse the temple once or twice? John places a cleansing at the beginning of the ministry (John 2:13–22), while Matthew, Mark and Luke place it in the last week. Christians who take Scripture with equal seriousness answer in two ways. Some think there was one cleansing and John arranged his Gospel by theme, putting it early. But the simpler answer is that it happened twice, and the details suggest it: in John there are oxen and sheep and a whip of cords, here the dove sellers and money-changers; in John the leaders ask for a sign, here they ask by what authority. And trades grow back. Jesus confronted the temple when he began and when he finished: an opening statement and a closing verdict. Nothing in the meaning hangs on the answer.

Does this passage justify angry confrontation? No passage is quoted more often to excuse the furious post, the walk-out, the scorching email. Notice first who is acting and in whose house: the Lord of the temple, exercising an authority that belongs to him alone, over abuses in his own courts. It is the owner closing a market that had set up in his front room, not a worshipper losing his temper about the church. Notice next what the anger is about. Not a slight to himself; he had been mocked and plotted against without overturning anything. He was moved because the poor were being fleeced and the Gentiles crowded out. His anger ran entirely on behalf of others, the ones with least power in the building. Anger that flares when I am disrespected and stays seated when the weak are exploited is not this anger, whatever it calls itself. (On telling holy anger from the other kind, see on 5:21–22.)

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus approved of violence as a means of reform. His action was a unique prophetic act by the Lord of the temple, not a model for Christians to use force in church disputes. Nor does it forbid churches from selling anything, ever. The point is the corruption of worship by greed and the exclusion of others from God’s presence.

Does this forbid selling things in a church building? A church building is not the temple, which was the unique place of sacrifice, so the comparison must be made carefully. What Jesus condemned was exploitation and the crowding out of prayer, especially for the outsiders who had nowhere else to pray. A bookstall or a coffee table is not wrong in itself. The test is whether anyone is being fleeced, and whether the business is getting in the way of worship or keeping the outsider from finding room.

In a sentence. Jesus drove the traders from the temple, condemning its corruption and announcing its judgment, and healed the blind and lame there.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything in your church, or in your own heart, which God made for prayer, that has become a marketplace? Your body is now a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). Ask what has been set up in its courts that crowds out prayer: the phone by the bed, the background noise, the endless calculation. Overturn one table this week, and put prayer in its place.

For worship. The Lord whom we seek has suddenly come to his temple, and he is the temple. In him God dwells with us; in him the one sacrifice has been offered; through him the poorest outsider may come and pray. He cleared the court of the nations so that the nations might come in, and the blind and the lame walked in behind him. The house of prayer for all peoples is a Person, and his door has never been closed to anyone who comes to him.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples
pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, "Hosanna to the Son of David!" they were indignant, and they said to him, "Do you hear what these are saying?" And Jesus said to them, "Yes; have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things he did, and the children crying out in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”, they were indignant. They asked: do you hear what these are saying? Jesus said: yes; have you never read, “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise”?

But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did. The healings (v. 14). The word, thaumasia, appears only here in the New Testament, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the wonderful works of God. And here is the tragedy of the scene in one sentence: the priests saw the same wonderful things. They watched the blind receive sight in their own courts. The identical evidence produced worship in the children and indignation in the men trained to interpret it.

And the children crying out in the temple. Hosanna to the Son of David! The children had picked up the crowd’s cry. Picture where this is happening: not on the road, where a crowd can be dismissed as over-excited pilgrims, but inside the temple courts, the one place on earth where the chief priests were unquestionably in charge, and the noise is coming from children running about shouting a messianic title at a man who has just overturned the furniture.

They were indignant. The leaders saw the same miracles and heard the same praise, and were angry. They knew what the title meant: the children were calling Jesus the Messiah.

Do you hear what these are saying? Notice precisely what they object to. Not the noise; the content. Children are calling him Son of David in the temple and he is not correcting them, and their indignation is at his silence as much as at the words. They expected Jesus to stop them.

Yes; have you never read, “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise”? Psalm 8:2, in its Greek form; the Hebrew has a word closer to strength, and either way God establishes something formidable out of the smallest voices there are. Psalm 8 is about praise to God; Jesus applies it to praise of himself. The children are praising God by praising Jesus. Once again Jesus claims what belongs to God. The children see what the experts cannot (11:25). And the rest of the line, which he did not need to say aloud to men who knew the psalter by heart, speaks of strength established because of God’s foes, to still the enemy and the avenger. By quotation he has told the chief priests which part of the psalm they are standing in.

Have you never read? The question he keeps putting to the professional readers of Scripture (12:3, 5; 19:4; 21:42; 22:31). It never means they are ignorant of the text. It means they can recite it and have arranged not to be governed by it, which is a condition open to anyone who has owned a Bible for a long time.

Is this a sneer at learning? No. The problem with these men was never that they had studied. It was that their study had become the property of their position, so that a conclusion which would cost them the position had become unthinkable. A child had nothing to lose by saying Son of David out loud. Learning that bows to Christ is a gift to the church; learning that guards its own standing is blindness with a library. Study hard, and stay a child before the text.

In a sentence. The leaders were indignant at children hailing Jesus as Messiah, but he answered that God has ordained praise from the mouths of children.

On a Tuesday. Children can see Jesus more clearly than experts. Teach them to praise him, and learn from their simple faith. Let the children in your church sing loudly, and do not shush the ones who say the right thing at the wrong volume. At home, ask your children what they love about Jesus, and listen; you may hear the truest theology of the week.

For worship. The Lord of heaven and earth has hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children (11:25), and it pleases him. The praise that silenced the enemy in his temple came from children. He who made heaven by his word receives the songs of the smallest, and the King of glory, who will be worshipped by angels for ever, stopped to defend children shouting his name.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus quotes the psalm in its Greek form.

parallels.desc: out of the mouth of babies and infants

verseByVerse.quote: And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left them and went out of the city to Bethany, and spent the night there. In the morning, as he returned to the city, he was hungry.

And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany. It is the evening of the day he entered Jerusalem as her King to a shouting crowd, and the question worth asking is where the King of Israel slept that night. Not in the palace. Not in a room in the temple precincts, though he had spent the afternoon acting as the owner of the place. He walked back over the shoulder of the Mount of Olives to a village. Bethany was about two miles (three kilometres) east of Jerusalem, on the far side of the Mount of Olives. It was the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1), the brother he had raised from the dead. Jesus stayed there each night of his last week, probably with them (26:6). The city that had quaked at his arrival in the morning did not offer him a bed at night.

And lodged there. The city was overcrowded with pilgrims, and Jesus may have avoided staying inside the city at night for his safety until his hour came. A man who sleeps outside the walls is harder to arrest quietly in the dark. But it is more than tactics. He is not living in the city he came to save. He comes in each morning to teach and goes out each evening, and the last night he spends near it he will spend in a garden on that same hillside, awake.

In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. Monday morning. Jesus was truly human, with real hunger. He had walked two miles uphill on an empty stomach, and Matthew tells us so. Do not hurry past it. This is the man who had multiplied loaves for five thousand and again for four thousand, and who had refused to turn stones into bread in the wilderness when he was far hungrier (4:2–4). The power was never absent; it simply was not for himself. He got tired. He slept in the stern of a boat. He wept at a graveside. He was hungry on the way to work. This is the incarnation showing through the narrative at an ordinary hour on an ordinary road.

Why does Matthew mention that Jesus was hungry? Partly to lead into the fig tree: the sign does not begin as a lesson looking for an illustration but with a hungry man walking toward a tree that looked, from the road, as though it had something on it. But it also guards a truth the church has always had to defend: Jesus is truly man as well as truly God, with a real body and real needs. He did not merely appear human. That is why he can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and why his obedience and death count for human beings: he was one of us.

In a sentence. Jesus spent the night at Bethany and returned to Jerusalem hungry in the morning.

On a Tuesday. Jesus needed rest and food like you. He understands your human needs (Hebrews 4:15). Do not be ashamed of being tired, or treat sleep and meals as unspiritual. Bring your ordinary needs to him in prayer as freely as your spiritual ones, and if you have a Bethany, a home where tired servants of Christ are welcomed, keep its door open.

For worship. The King of Israel had no bed in his own capital. He who feeds every living thing walked hungry up a hill. The eternal Son took to himself a true body and a reasonable soul (Westminster 8.2), and in that body he hungered and thirsted and grew weary, so that in that same body he could bear our sins and rise again. There is no ordinary human weakness he did not stoop to share, except sin.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem, home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus.

verseByVerse.quote: And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, "May no fruit ever come from you again!" And the fig tree withered at once. When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, "How did the fig tree wither at once?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing a fig tree by the road, Jesus went to it and found nothing on it but leaves. He said to it: may no fruit ever come from you again. And the fig tree withered at once. The disciples were amazed: how did the fig tree wither so quickly?

And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. Fig trees in Palestine produced small early fruit, called taqsh, along with their leaves in spring, before the main crop. A tree in full leaf normally promised fruit. Mark adds that it was not the season for figs (Mark 11:13), meaning the main crop. But a tree with leaves and no early fruit at all was barren: it advertised fruit and had none. It was not a barren tree quietly failing. It was a tree advertising.

May no fruit ever come from you again! A prophetic sign, an acted parable. In the Old Testament the fig tree was a picture of Israel: when I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree (Jeremiah 8:13; see Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). Everyone on that road had the association ready. The tree was like the temple and its leaders: impressive, full of leaves (religious activity), but without the fruit God looked for (righteousness, justice, mercy, faith). Jesus had just found the temple the same way (vv. 12–13), where the noise and traffic and sacrifices were at full volume while the poor were fleeced in the court of the Gentiles. The tree’s withering pictures God’s judgment on fruitless religion, which fell on the temple in AD 70.

Why curse a tree? It is the only destructive miracle in the Gospels, and anyone who has felt uneasy here is reading attentively: on the face of it, a hungry man does not find breakfast and kills the tree. But this is not a miracle of temper. It is a prophet’s sign-act, a genre Israel had seen for centuries. Jeremiah smashed a clay jar in front of the elders (Jeremiah 19:1–13). Ezekiel lay on his side for months beside a brick with the city drawn on it (Ezekiel 4). Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces and handed ten to Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:30–31). The prophets acted their message when words had stopped landing. And see the mercy in the choice. In a life in which he raised the dead and refused every chance to harm a soul, the only thing he ever destroyed in a sign of his own was a plant. He could have made the point on the temple itself. He made it on a tree by the roadside where nobody was hurt.

And the fig tree withered at once. Mark has Jesus curse it on the way in and the disciples notice it withered the next morning (Mark 11:12–14, 20–21). Matthew tells the fig tree as one complete episode, because his interest is the sign and not the schedule. And the two do not collide: Matthew says when the tree died, Mark says when the disciples saw it. A tree struck at the root is dead from that moment, whatever hour the men walking past look up and notice the leaves have gone. Matthew gives you the event; Mark gives you the discovery.

When the disciples saw it, they marveled. They said, how did the fig tree wither at once? They were amazed at the power, but did they understand the meaning? They asked about the mechanics; the meaning was standing across the valley, on the temple mount.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was acting in a fit of irritation because he was hungry. This was a deliberate prophetic act, like the prophets’ acted parables (Jeremiah 13:1–11; 19:1–13). It is Jesus’ only miracle of judgment in the Gospels. Nor does it mean that God has rejected the Jewish people for ever. The judgment fell on the temple system and the leaders who rejected the Messiah. Paul shows that God has not finished with Israel (Romans 11).

I look at my life and see very little fruit. Is this verse about me? Read what was actually condemned. Not smallness, not slowness, not a poor year. The tree was judged for displaying what it did not have: full leaf and no fruit at all. That is a charge against pretence, not against weakness, and the same Gospel has told you how this Lord handles the genuinely feeble: a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench (12:20). He is severe with advertising and unfailingly gentle with frailty. If you grieve your fruitlessness and long for more, that longing is itself fruit of his Spirit. Abide in him, and fruit comes (John 15:5).

In a sentence. Jesus cursed a fig tree that had leaves but no fruit, a prophetic sign of judgment on Israel’s fruitless temple religion.

On a Tuesday. Is your Christian life all leaves and no fruit: plenty of activity and appearance, but little real love, obedience and faith? A useful test is to ask what would be left of your faith if every visible part of it, attendance, roles, vocabulary, were taken away for a month. Then ask God for the fruit that grows unseen: patience at home, honesty at work, kindness to the person who cannot repay you.

For worship. The Lord comes looking for fruit, and he has every right to. He planted, he watered, he came hungry. And the wonder of the gospel is that the One who withered the fruitless tree was himself hung on a tree and cut off, bearing the curse that fruitless people deserved (Galatians 3:13), so that we might be grafted into him, the true vine, and bear fruit that lasts. The judgment that fell on the fig tree fell, for his people, on him.
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds that “it was not the season for figs”; leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: truly, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, “Be taken up and thrown into the sea”, it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.

Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt. The disciples ask a question about mechanics and get an answer about their own future. They wanted to know how it was done. He tells them what they will be doing. “Doubt” (diakrithēte) means to be divided, to waver between two opinions (James 1:6–8). It is not the honest question of a struggling believer, but a heart split between trusting God and not.

You will not only do what has been done to the fig tree. The disciples could share in Jesus’ power through faith.

But even if you say to this mountain. Probably the Mount of Olives, where they were standing, or the temple mount, visible across the valley. Both are within sight of his outstretched arm, and both carry weight. The Mount of Olives is the hill Zechariah says will be split in two on the day of the LORD (Zechariah 14:4). The temple mount is the thing the withered tree has just been a parable about.

Be taken up and thrown into the sea, it will happen. A vivid picture of doing the impossible (see 17:20). If Jesus pointed to the temple mount, there may be a further meaning: the old temple order would be removed, and God’s people would no longer need it, because they would pray in faith directly to God through Christ.

The mountain that moved. Notice what these men were actually promised authority over. Not fig trees: none of them ever withered anything. Not weather, or their own circumstances arranged to preference. Look at what they actually moved. Within a generation, twelve provincial men with no money, no standing and no army had carried this message into the great cities between Jerusalem and Rome, against the settled opposition of both the Sanhedrin and the empire, and most of them were killed for it, and it did not slow down. That is the mountain. It went into the sea.

And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith. A great promise about prayer, to be read in the light of the rest of Scripture: asking in Jesus’ name, according to God’s will (John 14:13–14; 1 John 5:14–15), and from a heart that forgives (Mark 11:25). Read the clause where Matthew put it: attached to kingdom work, in the temple week, spoken to men about to be sent out. It is the assurance that the work he is about to hand them will never fail for want of supply, and that they may ask accordingly and enormously.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a technique that guarantees whatever we want, or that unanswered prayers prove a lack of faith. Jesus himself prayed in Gethsemane, “If it be possible, let this cup pass from me”, and it did not pass, because it was not the Father’s will (26:39). Faith trusts God and submits to his will. The promise is that God answers the prayer of faith; he answers as a wise Father, not as a vending machine.

Is this a promise that anything I ask with enough faith will be given? No. Prayer is answered according to God’s will (1 John 5:14), not according to wrong motives (James 4:3), and Paul’s own prayer for healing was answered no, with the better gift of grace sufficient for him (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). The mountain is a picture of what seems impossible, not a literal mountain to be moved for show. Faith is trust in God, not confidence in a particular outcome. If a prayer of yours has not been answered as you asked, it does not mean your faith failed; it may mean your Father has something better, or a different time.

What we ask for. The passage turns on the reader with an uncomfortable question, and it is not the one we usually bring. We come asking whether we have enough faith for what we want. The passage asks what we are asking for. Almost nothing in most Christians’ praying would require God to move a mountain; a modest tidying of circumstances would cover it. These men were told to expect the impossible because they had been given something impossible to do: to make disciples of all nations.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that faith without doubt can do the impossible, and that believing prayer will be answered.

On a Tuesday. Pray today with faith, about a specific need, trusting God to answer in his wisdom. And add one prayer that is mountain-sized: for a friend who seems far from God, for your town, for a people group with no church. Ask as though the God who raised Jesus from the dead were listening, because he is.

For worship. Nothing is impossible with God. The One who spoke to the fig tree spoke the worlds into being, and he has bound himself to hear the prayers of his children. Through twelve ordinary men he moved the mountain of a hostile world, and he is still building his church on the rock, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (16:18). Our prayers are small; our Father is not.

parallels.desc: ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Authority Questioned: Three Parables of Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chief priests and elders challenge Jesus's authority: by what authority do you do these things? Jesus answers with a counter-question about John's baptism that they refuse to answer, then tells three parables of judgment: the two sons (the one who refused then obeyed vs. the one who agreed but didn't), the wicked tenants who killed the vineyard owner's son, and the implied parable of the rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118. The parables systematically indict the religious leadership of Israel for rejecting God's messengers and the Son himself. The counter-question is not a diversion: John had already answered the authority question in public, so to ask whether John was from heaven is to hand it back in the one form they cannot answer safely. And the verdict between the parables is the sharpest sentence in the chapter — the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom ahead of them (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The authority question and Jesus's counter-question about John expose the leaders' bad faith: they do not want to know the source of Jesus's authority; they want to discredit him publicly. Their refusal to answer John's question (whether from heaven or from men) reveals that they are governed by crowd opinion rather than truth-seeking. Jesus therefore refuses to answer them directly — but he answers indirectly and devastatingly through the three parables. The wicked tenants is the most explicit: they will kill the son, and the vineyard will be given to others who will produce its fruits. Two details carry the tenants parable. Jesus quotes Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard almost item for item (Isa 5:1-2) and then changes it: in Isaiah the vine is at fault, here the vine is fine and the tenants are the problem — the indictment is narrowed off the nation and onto its leaders. And the tenants do not kill the son by mistake. This is the heir — recognition is the motive, which is why unbelief in this chapter is never a shortage of information. Note also 2 Chr 36:15-16, which is this parable written four centuries early: God sent persistently by his messengers, and they kept mocking them, until there was no remedy.
verseByVerse.examples: The rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118:22 — the same psalm shouted at the triumphal entry — completes the argument. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; what the religious establishment rejects, God establishes as the foundation of his kingdom. The chief priests and Pharisees understood that he was speaking about them — and they wanted to arrest him but feared the crowds. The rejection is comprehensive; the judgment is announced; the crowds are the only restraint preventing its immediate human execution. Two applications. Verse 43's taken away from you is about tenancy, not race — the vineyard is re-let, and the people it was first let to were Jews to a man (see the verse-by-verse on vv. 43-44). And verse 45 is the most sobering sentence here for anyone who reads the Bible well: they perceived that he was speaking about them. The parables landed perfectly, were understood completely, and produced not repentance but an arrest plan. Understanding the text is not the goal, and it is possible to be an excellent reader of Scripture and be destroyed by what you have correctly understood.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, "By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?" Jesus answered them, "I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus entered the temple and was teaching, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to him and asked: by what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority? Jesus answered: I will also ask you one question. If you answer me, I will tell you by what authority I do these things.

And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching. Tuesday of Holy Week. The chief priests and elders were members of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. They controlled the temple. Jesus had just driven out their traders. This is not heckling. It is an official delegation, and the question they put is one that body existed to ask. Israel’s law required anyone who spoke and acted as a prophet to be tested (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22). On the face of it they are doing their job, in the right place, with the right words.

By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority? “These things”: the triumphal entry, the cleansing of the temple, the healings, the teaching. In twenty-four hours he had ridden into the city like a king being crowned, cleared the temple court by force, healed in the sanctuary, and let children call him Messiah without correcting them. Every one is an act of ownership. They were the official authorities over the temple; Jesus had no official position. Who did he think he was? It was a trap. If he said “from God”, they could charge him with blasphemy; if he said “my own”, they could dismiss him.

I also will ask you one question. Rabbis often answered a question with a question. It was ordinary procedure, not a dodge, and he attaches a promise to it.

And if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. Jesus is not evading. His question will reveal the answer to theirs. He is offering them a genuine transaction.

Why answer with a question? Because the question about John is the authority question, handed back in the one form they cannot answer without convicting themselves. John was the one man in Israel who had already answered it publicly. He had pointed to Jesus as the one coming after him, whose sandals he was not worthy to carry; he had baptised him and seen the Spirit descend while the voice from heaven spoke (3:11–17). If John was from heaven, they had their answer already. Christ often does this: he answers not the question we put but the one underneath it, and points us back to the evidence we have already declined to act on.

In a sentence. The temple authorities challenged Jesus’ authority, and he answered with a question of his own.

On a Tuesday. Are you asking questions about Jesus to find the truth, or to avoid it? A man who says he would believe if God only made it clear is often a man with something specific already in view that he has decided not to act on. If that is you, go back to the last thing you know God has shown you, and obey it; the next light usually comes after that.

For worship. They asked who gave him authority, and the answer was standing in front of them: the Father had given all things into his hands (John 3:35). He did not need their licence to cleanse his own house. He is the Lord of the temple, the Son over God’s house, and every authority in heaven and on earth is his (28:18). Blessed are those who bow to it gladly, for his authority is the authority of a Shepherd.

verseByVerse.quote: The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" And they discussed it among themselves, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say to us, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But if we say, 'From man,' we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked: the baptism of John, where did it come from? From heaven or from man? They discussed it among themselves: if we say from heaven, he will ask us why we did not believe him. But if we say from man, we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet.

The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man? “Baptism” stands for John’s whole ministry. “From heaven” means from God. If John was sent by God, then his testimony about Jesus was true: he pointed to Jesus as the Coming One (3:11–17). The answer to Jesus’ question is the answer to theirs: Jesus’ authority comes from the same God who sent John.

And they discussed it among themselves. Matthew takes us inside the huddle. We are given the minutes of a private conversation among the most senior religious men in Israel, standing in the temple, deciding what to say about a prophet of God. They did not ask what was true, but what was safe.

If we say, From heaven, he will say to us, Why then did you not believe him? They had rejected John (21:32; Luke 7:30). Read the minutes and notice what is missing. Two options, each assessed purely for what it will cost. Not one syllable about whether John was in fact from heaven. The question of truth is not raised, not dismissed, not even avoided: it never occurs to anyone to bring it up. That is the difference between a man who is wrong and a man who is corrupt. Being mistaken about John would have been forgivable and correctable. These men are not weighing evidence badly; they have stopped weighing it.

But if we say, From man, we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet. Luke adds that they feared the people would stone them (Luke 20:6). John was popular, and his death at Herod’s hands had made him a martyr. And see what they were afraid of. These men could summon the temple guard, would shortly arrest a man at night and hold a trial before dawn, and had the standing to rouse a Roman governor. They feared the opinion of ordinary people in the street, and the fear governed them. The men in charge of Israel’s conscience were taking their instructions from Israel’s mood.

The test in the huddle. Most of us fail it more quietly than they did. It is not whether you have ever told a lie. It is whether you can recognise the moment when the question in your mind has silently changed from what is true here to what will this cost me to say. It happens in a staffroom when somebody says something about Christians and you decide, in a second and a half, that this is not the moment. It happens when a group is settling on an unfair view of someone you know. The calculation is so fast that it does not feel like a decision at all, and that is exactly what these men would have said.

Is it always wrong to keep quiet? No. Prudence is not cowardice. Jesus told his followers to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves (10:16); there are things not to say yet, and moments badly chosen, and the Lord himself sometimes kept silent. The difference is what sits in the driving seat. Wisdom asks how and when to say the true thing, and plans to say it. What was happening in this huddle was not wisdom deciding the timing; it was safety deciding the content. If you find you never seem to find the right moment, safety may be driving.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether John’s ministry was from God, and the leaders, thinking only of their safety, saw that every answer trapped them.

On a Tuesday. Do you decide what you believe based on what is true, or on what is safe and popular? Before your next hard conversation, ask yourself the honest question first, what is true here?, and only then the second, how can I say it with love?

For worship. In that huddle every man feared the crowd, and only one man in the temple feared nothing but his Father. Jesus never once weighed the cost of the truth against his safety; he spoke it, and went to the cross for it. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and in Christ we see a man wholly free, because he feared God alone. In him we are set free from the tyranny of the crowd.
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And he said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work in the vineyard today.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they answered: we do not know. Jesus said: neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. What do you think? A man had two sons. He went to the first and said: son, go and work in the vineyard today.

We do not know. So they answered Jesus: a lie, or a deliberate refusal to commit. Four words, and everyone present knew they were false. These are the men whose whole office was to know: to rule on clean and unclean, true and false, prophet and fraud. And the subject was not obscure. Jerusalem and all Judea had gone out to John (3:5); half the country had an opinion about him. The official custodians of Israel’s faith, standing in the temple, declared they had not been able to form one. Their refusal to answer showed that they were not seeking truth. What they were really saying was: we have an answer and we cannot afford it. That is more dangerous than ignorance, because ignorance can be cured by information, and this can be cured only by repentance.

Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. Jesus keeps his word exactly. He does not scold and he does not argue; he declines, and the declining is itself a judgment. Jesus will not give further revelation to those who reject what they already have (7:6; 13:12). To a man who will not act on what he has, more light is not a kindness; it is only more to answer for. But his three following parables answer the question indirectly: his authority comes from his Father, who has sent his Son (v. 37).

What do you think? A man had two sons. Without a pause, he begins to tell them a story. They have refused his question; he will not answer theirs. But he has not finished with them. The first of three parables against the leaders (21:28–22:14), each aimed at them, each still giving them a way to see themselves and turn. He is being more patient than they deserve, and far more patient than they will be with him. The father pictures God.

Son, go and work in the vineyard today. A father has the right to his son’s obedience. The vineyard again pictures God’s kingdom (20:1; Isaiah 5:1–7). And notice the word today. The call is not to a vague future willingness but to a day’s work now.

What if I sincerely do not know what I believe about Jesus? Then this passage is not a condemnation but an invitation. The leaders did know and would not say; honest uncertainty is a different thing. Ask God plainly to show you who Jesus is. Read one of the Gospels through, asking at each page, who is this man? Talk with a Christian you trust. But be honest with yourself about one question: if it became clear, what would it cost me? If the answer frightens you, that fear may be the real obstacle, and it can be brought to God too.

In a sentence. When the leaders refused to answer, Jesus refused to answer them, and began a parable about a father and two sons.

On a Tuesday. Refusing to answer God’s questions does not make them go away. Is there a question God has been asking you, through his word, through a friend, through your conscience, that you keep answering with we do not know? Give it an honest answer before him today.

For worship. Even to men lying to his face, the Lord kept speaking. He would not cast pearls before the scornful, yet he did not stop calling: what do you think? The patience of God in Christ is past understanding. He reasoned with his murderers on the way to the cross, and on the cross he prayed for them. There is no heart so hardened that he cannot reach it with a question, and no sinner so far off that he is not still being invited into the vineyard today.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he answered, 'I will not,' but afterward he changed his mind and went. And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, 'I will, sir,' but did not go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first son answered: I will not. But afterward he changed his mind and went. The father went to the other son and said the same. He answered: I go, sir. But he did not go.

And he answered, “I will not,” but afterward he changed his mind and went. A rude refusal, followed by repentance. “Changed his mind” (metamelētheis) means regretted, repented. His first words were wrong, but his actions were right. The first son is not held up as a model of manner: he was insolent, and Jesus does not pretend otherwise. What commends him is not his candour about his reluctance, since plenty of people are candidly disobedient and stay that way, but that he changed his mind and went. The parable has no interest in which son felt better about himself. It asks only who ended up in the field.

And he went to the other son and said the same. The same command.

And he answered, “I go, sir,” but did not go. “Sir” is literally “Lord” (kyrie). A polite, respectful answer, with no obedience. Words without action (7:21). He does not refuse. He is not rude or rebellious. He says the right thing, in the right tone, using the right title, and everyone within earshot would have thought well of him. His failure is entirely invisible until you go and look at the vineyard. That is the shape of a great deal of respectable Christianity: the yes given years ago at a conversion or a confirmation or a moment of dedication, the language still fluent, the vineyard unvisited.

Textual note. Some manuscripts reverse the order of the two sons, and the leaders’ answer in verse 31 then varies. Verdict: the ESV’s order is best supported; the meaning is the same either way.

Which son am I? Most people who read a commentary are in more danger of being the second than the first. So take it as a question with a date on it. Not did I once say yes, but: since the last time I said yes to God about something specific, have I actually gone? There is usually one thing in view: a conversation to have, a debt to repay, a habit to end, a person to forgive, money to give, a reconciliation to attempt. You will know it as you read this, because it is the thing that came to mind before the sentence finished.

I have been the second son for years. Is it too late? No, and the first son’s story is the better news of the two, because it means a bad start is not a settled verdict. Nothing prevents a man who said no this morning from being in the vineyard by the afternoon. And notice that the father in this parable does not require a speech first. He requires a son in the field. If you have been the second son for twenty years, the way out is not despair or a better promise; it is a change of direction today, in one thing, trusting the Father’s welcome. The vineyard gate is still open.

In a sentence. One son refused but then obeyed; the other politely agreed but never went.

On a Tuesday. Are you the second son: saying yes to God in church on Sunday, but not doing his will on Monday? Name the one thing you have said yes to and not done, and do the first step of it before the day is out.

For worship. There was one Son who never said no and never failed to go. The eternal Son said to the Father, I have come to do your will, O God (Hebrews 10:7), and went all the way into the vineyard, into the heat of the day, to the cross. Because of his perfect yes, sons who said no and sons who said yes and did not go can be forgiven and brought in. The Father’s vineyard is full of repentant children, and every one of them is there because of the obedience of the beloved Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the two did the will of his father?" They said, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of the two did his father’s will? They said: the first. Jesus said: truly, the tax collectors and prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God before you. John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and prostitutes believed him. Even when you saw it, you did not change your minds and believe him.

Which of the two did the will of his father? The answer is obvious. Jesus asks the question himself, so it is plainly meant to be answered by every reader and not only by the men in front of him.

They said, The first. They condemn themselves. The parable was too plain to get wrong and too small to feel dangerous. Then he tells them what they have agreed to.

Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. A shocking statement. Tax collectors (see 9:9) and prostitutes were the most despised sinners in Jewish society. Tax collectors were collaborators who bought the right to extract Rome’s money from their own neighbours and kept the surplus. Prostitutes were beyond the edge of respectable society, and many were there because a man had discarded them or hunger had driven them. These are the two groups Jesus names, in the temple, to the highest religious authorities in the nation, and he puts them in front. They had said “no” to God by their lives, but repented when John preached. The religious leaders had said “yes” to God by their words and religious practice, but refused to repent. “Before you” may mean “instead of you”: they are entering, and you are not.

The door is still open. Guard the sentence, because it is more merciful than it is often made to sound. The verb (proagousin) is present tense: they are going in ahead of you. That is a statement about the order of a procession, and a procession is something you can still join. Even at the sharpest moment of the confrontation, the door is not slammed in their faces. It is being held open while they are told, with some force, who is walking through it first. A tax collector who repented at John’s preaching last spring is further into the kingdom of God than the high priest, and there is nothing in the sentence to stop the high priest joining him.

For John came to you in the way of righteousness. John preached and lived righteousness: repentance and a changed life (3:1–12).

And you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. Luke says that tax collectors came to John to be baptised (Luke 3:12; 7:29–30). The charge is precise: not you did not like him, or you disagreed with his methods, but you did not believe him. The issue is never eloquence or manner but whether a man goes to the vineyard.

And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him. They saw sinners changed by John’s preaching, and still did not repent. The same word as the first son (v. 29): he changed his mind; they did not, ou metemelēthēte. He has told a story, made them praise its hero, and handed them the hero’s verb with a not in front of it. And take the last clause slowly, because it names the hardest condition in the chapter: even when you saw it. They watched collaborators pay money back and ruined women come up out of the Jordan new, and it moved them not at all. There is a settled state in which fresh evidence has stopped working as evidence. It is not reached by one bad decision, but by a long series of moments in which the honest answer was known and not acted on.

What it does not mean. Not that being a tax collector or prostitute is a way into the kingdom. It is repentance and faith that bring people in. Nor does it mean that religious people cannot be saved. But they must repent like anyone else, and their religion can make that harder.

Why can religion make repentance harder? Because repentance begins with admitting you are in the wrong, and a respectable life gives a man a great deal to hide behind. The tax collector had nothing to protect; his sin was public, and so his need was obvious to him. The religious man has a reputation, a record of attendance, a vocabulary, and the habit of being the one who is right. Every one of those can become a wall between him and the plain prayer, God, be merciful to me, a sinner (Luke 18:13). The cure is to let God’s word search the respectable sins: pride, coldness, contempt, self-righteousness.

In a sentence. Notorious sinners who repented at John’s preaching are entering the kingdom ahead of the religious leaders who said yes to God but refused to repent.

On a Tuesday. Never think you are better than the obvious sinners. They may be entering the kingdom ahead of the respectable. Think of the kind of person you would least expect to see in heaven, and pray for one such person by name this week. Then ask whether anything in you would be offended to see him there.

For worship. The kingdom of God has a door wide enough for tax collectors and prostitutes, and that is the best news a sinner ever heard. Christ was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (11:19), and he wore the name gladly. He came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance, and the procession into his kingdom is led by people the world wrote off. Glory to the Saviour whose grace goes first to the last.

parallels.desc: the tax collectors baptized, the Pharisees refusing

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told another parable. A landowner planted a vineyard, put a wall around it, dug a winepress in it and built a watchtower. Then he leased it to tenants and went to another country. When harvest time came, he sent his servants to the tenants to collect his fruit.

Hear another parable. The second of the three parables.

There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower. Every man listening recognised it within a few words. The details echo Isaiah 5:1–7, the song of the vineyard, which Jesus’ hearers knew well. In Isaiah, God planted a vineyard, cleared it, built a watchtower and dug a wine vat, and looked for good grapes, but it produced wild grapes. Isaiah explains that the vineyard is the house of Israel. So the chief priests knew the ending before the story had properly begun: Isaiah’s song ends with the hedge removed and the vineyard trampled. The fence protected it from animals; the winepress was a pit cut in rock to crush the grapes; the tower was for watchmen and storage. The owner had provided everything. This is a fully equipped estate, and the labour is all done before the tenants arrive. Every advantage they enjoy came from the hands of the man they are about to rob.

The change Jesus makes. In Isaiah the fault is in the vine: the owner looked for grapes and it yielded wild ones. Here the vine is not blamed at all. The vineyard is fine; the crop is coming; what has gone wrong is the tenants. Jesus has taken the best-known indictment of the nation in the prophets and narrowed it, off the people and onto the men given charge of them. That is a far more dangerous parable to tell in the temple than Isaiah’s, and if you are an ordinary Israelite in that crowd, a more merciful one.

And leased it to tenants, and went into another country. Absentee landlords were common in Galilee. Tenant farmers worked the land and paid part of the harvest as rent. It was a live grievance, and the crowd’s instinctive sympathy was with tenants, right up to the moment these tenants start killing people. It is the same method as the two sons: get the hearers to take a side, then show them which side they took. The tenants are Israel’s leaders, entrusted with God’s people (v. 45).

When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. The owner had a right to his share. God had the right to the fruit of his people: righteousness, justice and faithfulness. The servants are the prophets. And notice what he sends for: not rent in coin, but his fruit, the thing the vineyard exists to produce. He is asking a vineyard to be a vineyard. That is the standing question of this whole chapter, put to the fig tree in full leaf, to the temple full of noise, and to the men in charge of both: not whether the operation is busy, but whether anything is growing.

Who are the tenants today? In the first place, the leaders of Israel who rejected Jesus; Matthew says they knew it (v. 45). But the principle reaches every generation of those entrusted with God’s people: pastors, elders, teachers, parents. The vineyard is never theirs. They are stewards, and the Owner will ask for his fruit. In a wider sense every Christian is a tenant of what God has given: life, gifts, time, family, church. None of it is ours to keep for ourselves, and all of it is meant to bear fruit for him.

In a sentence. A landowner carefully planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and at harvest sent servants to collect his share.

On a Tuesday. Everything you have is God’s vineyard, entrusted to you. What fruit is he looking for from your life? Take one gift he has given you, a skill, a home, a position, a child, and ask, what would it look like for this to give the Owner his share this week?

For worship. Every good thing we have came from the hands of the Owner before we arrived. He planted the vineyard, built the hedge, dug the press, raised the tower, and then trusted it to people like us. What a Lord he is: generous in giving, patient in waiting, and coming at last not to rob his tenants but to receive what is his own, and to give his servants the joy of having fruit to hand him.
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the tenants seized his servants: they beat one, killed another and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they did the same to them.

And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Three verbs and no explanation. The escalation is quick and the parable does not slow for it, because the people listening did not need it explained. They knew what happened to men God sent to Israel. The history of Israel’s treatment of the prophets. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks, and later lowered into a cistern to sink in the mud (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15; 38:6). Uriah fled to Egypt, was brought back and killed with the sword (Jeremiah 26:20–23). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20–22), a killing Jesus will name two chapters later (23:35). Jesus later says Jerusalem kills the prophets and stones those sent to it (23:37). This is not a parable reaching for exaggeration. It is a summary.

Again he sent other servants, more than the first. The owner’s patience is astonishing. A normal landlord would have sent soldiers. A man whose employees are being beaten and killed does not respond by sending a larger party, unarmed. Read it as history and it is the patience of God across centuries: after Elijah, Amos; after Amos, Hosea; then Isaiah, Micah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and on, each sent into a country with a record of what it did to the last. God kept sending prophets, century after century. The Chronicler wrote it in one sentence: the LORD sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people, but they kept mocking the messengers of God, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). That verse is this parable, written centuries before it was told.

And they did the same to them. Persistent rejection.

Both halves are true. Hold them together, because each without the other distorts the text. The patience is real and nearly unbelievable: God keeps sending long after any reasonable owner would have sent soldiers. And the Chronicler’s last clause is real too: until there was no remedy. Patience is not indifference, and it is not permanent. A man who reads the long delay as evidence that nothing will ever be said has misread the one thing the parable is about to do next, because after all the servants there is one more figure standing at the estate gate.

Does God still send messengers today? Not new prophets adding to Scripture; the canon is closed, and God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). But he still sends his word, through faithful preaching, through the Bible open on a table, through a friend who tells you the truth, through a parent’s prayers. Every time Scripture is faithfully explained to you, the Owner is sending to collect his fruit. The question this verse asks is not whether he sends, but what we do with the messenger.

In a sentence. The tenants beat, killed and stoned the owner’s servants, and when he patiently sent more, they did the same.

On a Tuesday. God is astonishingly patient. How many times has he sent his word to you through others? Do not test his patience. Think of the last sermon or friend that told you something you did not want to hear, and instead of resenting the messenger, go back to the message and do what it said.

For worship. The LORD sent persistently, because he had compassion on his people. That is the heart of God laid bare: century after century of rejected messengers, and still he sent. He is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. And his patience was not weakness; it was the long road by which he was bringing the world to the moment when he would send, not another servant, but his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "Finally he sent his son to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally he sent his son to them, saying: they will respect my son. But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves: this is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.

Finally he sent his son to them. The word sits there like a door closing. There is nothing after this; the owner has one more person to send and then the sending is over, and everyone listening could feel the story running out of servants. The last messenger, after all the servants. Mark says a beloved son (Mark 12:6). Jesus is distinguishing himself from all the prophets: they were servants; he is the Son. This is the answer to the question about his authority (v. 23): he comes from the Father, as the Son (Hebrews 1:1–2).

Saying, They will respect my son. The owner’s hope. It shows the depth of God’s patience and love: he sent his own Son.

Did God not know what they would do? He did. Jesus had told his disciples plainly, more than once, that he would be handed over, mocked and crucified (16:21; 20:18–19). But this is a parable, and it speaks the way a father speaks. It is not a report on the limits of God’s foreknowledge; it is a way of making you feel the size of what is about to be done.
