The owner sends his boy to men who have killed his servants, and the sentence lets you hear him hoping. God is not cold in sending his Son. He is not ignorant either. He knew, and sent him anyway, for us.

But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, This is the heir. They recognised who he was. The leaders knew, at some level, that Jesus had a claim on them. Read it twice. They do not kill him because they mistake him for someone else. They kill him because they know exactly who he is. Recognition is the motive. If he had been another servant they would have beaten him and sent him back; it is precisely his being the son that makes the murder worth committing.

Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance. Under the law of the time, if an owner died without an heir, tenants might be able to claim the land. Their reasoning was absurd: the owner was still alive. But it reveals their motive: they wanted to keep control of the vineyard for themselves. The leaders wanted to keep their power over God’s people, and Jesus threatened it (John 11:48). And Matthew will show us the calculation made for real. Within days the chief priests and elders gather in the high priest’s palace and plot together to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him (26:3–4). The parable was not a warning about something that might happen. They walked out of the temple and did it.

Is unbelief just a lack of information? Sometimes. But this parable says the deepest form of it is not confusion at all. It is a clear-eyed calculation that this man’s rightful claim is incompatible with keeping what I have, and a decision to keep it. The tenants’ problem was never that they did not know whose vineyard it was. It was that they did. That is why more arguments rarely convert anyone on their own: what is needed is a new heart that is willing to give up the vineyard. And that is why we pray for unbelievers as well as reason with them.

In a sentence. Finally the owner sent his son, but the tenants recognised him as heir and plotted to kill him to seize the vineyard.

On a Tuesday. What do you want to keep control of, rather than surrender to Christ, the heir? A relationship, a habit, your money, your future, your opinion of yourself? Name it, and give it back to its Owner today. It was never yours, and it is safer in his hands than in yours.

For worship. Last of all he sent his Son. God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (John 3:16), knowing what the tenants would do, and the Son came willingly, walking into the vineyard where the servants had been killed. He is the heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and by his death the inheritance that the tenants tried to steal is given as a gift to those who were once rebels, so that we become heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

parallels.desc: God has spoken by his Son

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him. When the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?

And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Jesus predicts his own death in the parable. Note the order, because it is odd and deliberate. An ordinary account of a murder would have it the other way round: kill the man, then dispose of the body. Here he is put outside first and killed outside. He was crucified outside the city walls of Jerusalem (Hebrews 13:12–13; John 19:17). The writer to the Hebrews makes exactly that point: Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp. The tenants threw the son over the wall to be rid of him, and in doing so put him precisely where the sacrifice belonged.

When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants? Jesus asks his hearers to pronounce the judgment, as Nathan made David pronounce judgment on himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7). It is the second time in a few minutes that he has invited these men to judge a case that is their own. He did it with the two sons, and they answered correctly and were told what they had said. Now he does it again with a heavier case and lets them dictate the sentence.

A mirror, not a snare. Do not mistake what the method is for. It is not a trap set to destroy a man; it is a mirror set where he cannot avoid it. Everything in this chapter has been an attempt to get these men to see themselves while there is still time: a question about John, a parable about two sons, and now a story in which they must say out loud what such tenants deserve. He is not steering them toward the sentence. He is steering them toward recognition, which is the only thing that could have saved them.

How do I avoid reading the Bible like these men? Ask, every time, where am I in this passage? It is entirely possible to read with real attention, form a confident judgment about the people in the story, and never notice that the judgment applies to you. These men were not bad listeners; they understood the parable perfectly (v. 45). They simply assumed, until the last second, that it was about somebody else. So when you find yourself thinking how blind they were, stop and ask where you are blind in the same way, and pray, search me, O God, and know my heart (Psalm 139:23).

In a sentence. The tenants threw out and killed the son, and Jesus asked what the owner would do to them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knew exactly how he would die, and told his killers. He went to death with open eyes. When you read Scripture this week, take one passage that describes a sinner, and before you think of anyone else, apply it to yourself first.

For worship. They threw him out, and in throwing him out they put him where the sin offering belonged: outside the gate, bearing the shame. Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:13). The Son was cast out of the vineyard so that we who were outsiders might be brought in. His rejection was our welcome, his death our life.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus was crucified outside the city walls.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons." Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the Scriptures: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said: he will put those wretches to a miserable death and lease the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruit in their seasons. Jesus said: have you never read in the Scriptures, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes”?

He will put those wretches to a miserable death. They answer without hesitating, and the vehemence gives them away. In Greek it is a hard little play on words, kakous kakōs, bad men badly: the phrase a man produces when he is enjoying his indignation. They condemned themselves. They have no difficulty seeing that such tenants deserve destruction, and it is, almost word for word, the verdict about to be pronounced on them. The judgment came in AD 70, when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, ending the rule of the priestly leaders.

And let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons. The new tenants: those who produce fruit (v. 43). The vineyard itself is not destroyed; it is let to others.

Have you never read in the Scriptures. Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22–23, the same psalm the crowds sang at his entry (v. 9), and asks it of the men who read Scripture for a living (see on v. 16). The pilgrims coming down the hill had been shouting verse 26: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. Now, in the temple, he quotes verse 22. Two verses of one psalm, a few lines apart on the scroll, and between them, in the events of that week, lies everything: the welcome, the refusal, the trial, the cross and the empty tomb.

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The picture changes from a vineyard to a building. The builders (Israel’s leaders) rejected a stone as useless, but God made it the cornerstone (see Ephesians 2:20), the most important stone of the whole building. Jesus, rejected and killed, will be raised and exalted by God to be the foundation of God’s new temple, his people (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8). The image is chosen with precision. Assessing stone was the builders’ whole competence; their standing rested on being the ones who knew what belonged in the building. And the one block they examined and discarded turned out to be the stone the whole structure would rest on. They were experts, they inspected him, and they got it exactly wrong.

This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes. The resurrection and exaltation of Jesus is God’s work, astonishing and wonderful. And notice what is called the Lord’s doing. Not, this happened despite the Lord’s plan. Not, God salvaged something from a disaster. The rejection itself was taken up into his doing. The builders threw the stone off the site and were, in that very act, laying the foundation of a building they did not know was going up. Nothing excuses them; the parable has just shown that they knew what they were doing. Both are true at once, as Peter says at Pentecost: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). The word marvellous (thaumastē) shares its root with the wonderful things the children were shouting about in verse 15. The children had it right. It is a wonder.

What comfort is there here for my own rejections? A real one, but it must be offered carefully. The stone did not become the cornerstone in spite of being thrown away; it became the cornerstone by being thrown away. That cannot be turned into a technique or promised cheaply over every sorrow, to someone still bleeding. But it happened once, publicly, in the most important week in history, and it means that the worst thing men ever did was in the hand of God. If you belong to Christ, your rejections are not outside his hand either. He who brought the cornerstone out of the rubbish heap can bring good out of what was done to you (Romans 8:28), even when you cannot yet see how.

In a sentence. The leaders condemned the wicked tenants, and Jesus quoted Psalm 118: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone by God’s doing.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone, or something about Christ, that you have rejected as useless? The builders’ error was confidence in their own assessment. Ask God to show you where your judgment of people, and of him, has been too quick. And if you have been rejected, bring it to the rejected Stone, who knows exactly what it is to be thrown off the site.

For worship. Praise God for raising the rejected stone to be the cornerstone. It is marvellous in our eyes. The One men threw away, God set at the head of the corner, and on him the whole household of God is being built into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:20–22). This is the Lord’s doing: the wisdom that turned the worst crime of history into the salvation of the world. Let the builders’ rejection be swallowed up in our wonder.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And whoever falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.

Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you. “You” means the leaders and those who follow them in rejecting Jesus. Their privileged position as stewards of God’s people would be taken from them. Look at who is addressed: not a nation in the abstract but the men standing in front of him, and two verses later Matthew says the chief priests and the Pharisees perceived that he was speaking about them (v. 45). These are the tenants, and it is the tenancy that is being revoked.

And given to a people producing its fruits. “People” (ethnei) is singular: a nation, a people. It is the new people of God, the church, made up of believing Jews (beginning with the apostles) and believing Gentiles: the “holy nation” of 1 Peter 2:9. They produce the fruit God wants: repentance, faith, righteousness. And notice who received it first. The people producing its fruit turned out, in the event, to be a community whose first thousands were Jews: the apostles, the three thousand at Pentecost, Paul, and the whole first generation of the church.

And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces. Isaiah 8:14–15: a stone of stumbling, over which many will fall and be broken. Those who stumble over Jesus, rejecting him, are broken.

And when it falls on anyone, it will crush him. Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45: the stone cut without hands that strikes and crushes the kingdoms of the world, and becomes a great mountain filling the earth. At the final judgment, the stone falls on those who reject him. The stone of judgment is the same stone as the stone of salvation: the Christ who is the cornerstone for believers is the crushing stone for those who refuse him. There is no neutral way to stand near this stone.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit verse 44. It may have been added from Luke 20:18. Verdict: the evidence is divided; it is probably original, and Luke confirms that Jesus said it.

What it does not mean. Not that God has rejected the Jewish people as a race and replaced them with Gentiles (a crude form of “replacement theology”). The leaders who rejected Jesus lost their stewardship; the new people includes believing Jews, starting with the Twelve, and Paul hopes for many more (Romans 11:1–2, 11–26). There is one people of God in Christ, the one olive tree, into which Gentiles are grafted and from which unbelieving branches are broken off, and into which Jews who believe will be grafted again (Romans 11:17–24).

Why does this matter so much? Because this verse has been made to carry a weight it will not bear, and across some dark centuries it was used to teach that God had finished with the Jewish people and that Christians were free to despise them. Worse was done in the name of that idea than can be written here. Paul, who knew this saying, asks the question in so many words: has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite (Romans 11:1). Christians differ on exactly what Paul means when he says all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:26), whether a great turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end or the full number of believing Israel gathered through the ages, but no reading of Scripture permits contempt. And Paul turned the warning on the Gentile church at once: do not become proud, but fear (Romans 11:20). A church that keeps the leaves and yields no fruit has been told, in this very chapter, what happens to trees like that.

In a sentence. The kingdom will be taken from those who reject Jesus and given to a people who bear its fruit, and the stone they reject will break and crush them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is either the cornerstone you build on, or the stone you stumble over. Which is he for you? Then look at your church, not just yourself: is it a tenancy giving the Owner his fruit, or a building busy with leaves? Pray for the church you belong to, that it would bear fruit, and do one thing to help it.

For worship. The kingdom of God is his to give, and he gives it to a people he makes fruitful. Out of Jews and Gentiles he has formed one holy nation, a people for his own possession (1 Peter 2:9), built on a stone that cannot be moved. Kingdoms of the world rise and are crushed, but the stone cut without hands becomes a mountain that fills the whole earth, and his kingdom shall never be destroyed.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verse 44.

parallels.desc: the stone that breaks the kingdoms

verseByVerse.quote: When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the chief priests and Pharisees heard his parables, they realised he was speaking about them. They wanted to arrest him, but they were afraid of the crowds, because the people held him to be a prophet.

When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. They understood the meaning clearly: they were the second son, and the wicked tenants. The parables worked. There was no failure of communication anywhere in this chapter: the question about John landed, the two sons landed, the tenants landed, and these men understood every word.

And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds. They understood, and instead of repenting, they wanted to do exactly what the parable described: kill the son. That is the most sobering sentence in the chapter. Perfect understanding produced no repentance whatever. They saw themselves in the story, recognised the verdict, knew who the son was, and went out to arrange his death. These men would have passed any examination on the parable of the tenants. And there is the fear again, the same fear that decided their answer about John (v. 26), and that would keep them from arresting him openly during the feast (26:5). They had the offices, the titles, the temple and the guard, and their diary was set by a crowd.

Because they held him to be a prophet. The crowds’ opinion (v. 11) protected Jesus for now. The leaders would wait until they could arrest him away from the crowds (26:4–5). And the protection was thin. A public opinion that had not yet got him right, prophet and no more, was for the moment the wall around him. A crowd that thinks you a prophet can be persuaded otherwise in a few days by men who work at it, and Matthew tells us it was: the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas (27:20). The restraint was not a reprieve. It was a delay.

What it does not mean. Not that understanding God’s word is enough. They understood perfectly and responded with hostility. Knowledge without repentance hardens.

How do I know whether my Bible knowledge is helping me or hardening me? Ask what it produces. Knowledge that is helping you leads you to confess sin, to love Christ more, to be gentler with others, and to obey in specific things. Knowledge that is hardening you makes you quicker to judge, slower to repent, more confident that the hard passages are about other people, and more irritated when a sermon comes close. The test is not how much you know but whether what you know is bending you toward Christ. If you see signs of hardening, the remedy is the one these men refused: humble yourself before the word, and repent.

In a sentence. The leaders understood that the parables were about them, and instead of repenting, they plotted to arrest Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word convicts you, respond with repentance, not resentment. The next time a passage or a sermon lands on you uncomfortably, do not argue with it or change the subject in your head. Say to God, that is me, and ask him what to do about it.

For worship. The chapter closes where it opened, on the question of who this is: a crowd that half knows, a leadership that fully knows and will not have it, and a King who spends the whole day telling them the truth in stories while the plot is being laid. He did not run, and he did not soften it. He had three days of teaching left, and he spent them in the same courts with the same men listening. He is the faithful Son, the rejected stone, the coming King, and he laid down his life of his own accord. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

21.theology: Christ as the true Temple. The temple cleansing in Matthew 21 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the replacement and fulfilment of the temple. The temple was the place where God dwelt with his people, where sacrifice was made, where prayer ascended. Jesus embodies all three functions: he is Emmanuel — God dwelling with his people; he is the Lamb whose self-offering ends the sacrificial system; he is the mediator through whom prayer reaches the Father (John 14:13–14). John’s Gospel makes this explicit (“the temple he had spoken of was his body”, John 2:21). The destruction of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 was the confirmation that the type had given way to the antitype.
21.examples:
Then: The crowds welcomed Jesus with genuine excitement and completely wrong expectations. They wanted a Maccabean king who would drive out Rome; they got a crucified Servant who would drive out death. The Palm Sunday crowd’s theology is a warning: it is possible to praise Jesus enthusiastically while fundamentally misunderstanding who he is and what he has come to do.

Now: The fig tree is the perennial warning against fruitless religion — maintaining the form of Christian practice without the substance of faith, repentance, love, and transformed life. The church with its worship services, theological conferences, and evangelical brands may be full of leaves. The question Jesus asks of every institution and every individual is the same: where is the fruit?

22.title: The Great Banquet and the Hard Questions
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, <sup>2</sup>“The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son, <sup>3</sup>and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent other servants, saying, ‘Tell those who are invited, “See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.”’ <sup>5</sup>But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, <sup>6</sup>while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. <sup>7</sup>The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. <sup>8</sup>Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. <sup>9</sup>Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find.’ <sup>10</sup>And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests. <sup>11</sup>“But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. <sup>12</sup>And he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?’ And he was speechless. <sup>13</sup>Then the king said to the attendants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ <sup>14</sup>For many are called, but few are chosen.” <sup>15</sup>Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. <sup>16</sup>And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. <sup>17</sup>Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” <sup>18</sup>But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, “Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? <sup>19</sup>Show me the coin for the tax.” And they brought him a denarius. <sup>20</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” <sup>21</sup>They said, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” <sup>22</sup>When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away. <sup>23</sup>The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, <sup>24</sup>saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.’ <sup>25</sup>Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. <sup>26</sup>So too the second and third, down to the seventh. <sup>27</sup>After them all, the woman died. <sup>28</sup>In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her.” <sup>29</sup>But Jesus answered them, “You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. <sup>30</sup>For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>31</sup>And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” <sup>33</sup>And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. <sup>34</sup>But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. <sup>35</sup>And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him. <sup>36</sup>“Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?” <sup>37</sup>And he said to him, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. <sup>38</sup>This is the great and first commandment. <sup>39</sup>And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. <sup>40</sup>On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.” <sup>41</sup>Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, <sup>42</sup>saying, “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “The son of David.” <sup>43</sup>He said to them, “How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, <sup>44</sup>“‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet”’? <sup>45</sup>If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” <sup>46</sup>And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 is a day of public controversy in Jerusalem. The religious establishment sends wave after wave of opponents — Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees — each with a question designed to trap Jesus. He answers all of them and turns the final question back on his attackers, leaving them silenced. Matthew arranges the chapter as a trial in which the judge is the one in the dock: every party that challenges Jesus is exposed by his answers, and the final question — “Whose son is the Christ?” — reveals that the Messiah is not merely David’s descendant but David’s Lord.

The chapter opens with the parable of the wedding banquet, which recapitulates the entire history of Israel’s rejection of God’s invitations and the extension of grace to the Gentile roads and byways. “Many are called, but few are chosen” is not a statement about the inefficacy of the gospel but about the mystery of election: the call goes out wide; the choice of God secures who will respond. The banquet hall will be full — but with those God has chosen, not those who presumed on their invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Parable of the Wedding Banquet and the Question about Taxes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells the parable of the wedding banquet: a king invites guests to his son's wedding, they refuse and some kill his servants, the city is destroyed, and the hall is filled instead with whoever is found at the road junctions, both bad and good. One guest is discovered without a wedding garment and is cast out. Then the Pharisees and Herodians, in an alliance of convenience, try to trap him on the Roman poll tax; he asks for a coin, and answers that what bears Caesar's image goes to Caesar and what bears God's image goes to God. They marvel, and leave him.
verseByVerse.theology: The invitation is free, finished and urgent. Everything is ready is perfect tense throughout — the oxen are already slaughtered, nothing is pending, and the only thing outstanding is attendance. And the guests who refuse had already accepted, since invitations in that world went out twice; they are the second son of 21:30 again, whose word and whose feet have parted company. Grace then reaches the road junctions and gathers both bad and good with no screening at the door, which is the Gentile mission in parabolic form. But grace is not universalism: the king walks the room, and the man without the garment is speechless because nothing had been withheld from him — he had declined what was offered, not failed to manufacture what was required. On the tax, Jesus neither divinises Caesar nor anarchises the gospel. The coin bears Caesar's image and may be returned to him; the image on the man is God's, and that Caesar may never have.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what the first guests were doing instead: one went to his farm, another to his business. Not vice, not blasphemy — a field that needed walking and a shop that needed running. The most effective rival to God in most lives has never been wickedness but respectable occupation, and it works because nobody has to defend it. Indifference and violence end in the same place in this parable, which should sober anyone who has assumed that not being hostile is the same as being safe; nobody here is condemned for opposing the king, only for not turning up. The tax scene has its own sting: asked for a coin, they produced one — in the temple, from men professing scruples about Caesar's tribute, a denarius inscribed Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus and Pontifex Maximus. It is easy to hold a principled objection while living comfortably inside the thing, and be unaware of the gap. The test is not what you would say if asked, but what turns up when somebody says: show me. And verse 22 names the most respectable way of rejecting Christ — they marvelled, and they left him.

verseByVerse.quote: And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told another parable: the kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding feast for his son.

Meaning first. Matthew 22 is Tuesday of the last week, in the temple courts, and it is a day of questions. Jesus first tells the third of three parables against the leaders: a king prepares a wedding feast for his son, the invited guests refuse and even kill his servants, and the king throws the doors open to anyone found at the crossroads, bad and good, until the hall is full. But one man is found inside without a wedding garment and is thrown out, for many are called, but few are chosen. Then his enemies come at him in turn. Pharisees and Herodians ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, and he tells them to give Caesar the coin that bears his image and give God what bears God’s. Sadducees mock the resurrection with a story of seven brothers, and he answers that they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God, for the God of Abraham is the God of the living. A lawyer asks for the greatest commandment, and he gives two: love God with everything you are, and your neighbour as yourself. Finally he asks his own question: how can the Christ be David’s son if David calls him Lord? No one can answer, and no one dares ask him anything more. The whole chapter displays the wisdom and authority of the King’s Son, who is both David’s son and David’s Lord.

And again Jesus spoke to them in parables. The third of three parables against the leaders (21:28–22:14). The first showed their refusal to repent; the second their rejection of the Son; this one their refusal of God’s invitation, and God’s invitation going to others. He is telling it to the men who had asked by what authority he acted, in the temple, days before they killed him. Speaking in parables is mercy and judgment at once: a story gets past defences that an argument would only harden, and the same story leaves a man who will not have it holding nothing but an anecdote about a banquet.

The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son. The king is God; the son is Jesus. Notice first whose wedding it is, because that single fact governs everything that follows. A royal wedding was the greatest celebration in the ancient world, and could last a week. It was the one occasion on which a king put his whole house on display, the herds slaughtered, the stores opened, and the entire point of it the honouring of his son. To decline an invitation of that kind was not a social lapse. It was a public verdict on the son.

A feast, not a courtroom. In Scripture, the age to come is pictured as a great feast (Isaiah 25:6–9), and the relationship between God and his people as a marriage (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus is the bridegroom (9:15; 25:1–13). The final consummation is the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). Isaiah’s picture is worth hearing whole: on this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, and he will swallow up death for ever and wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:6–8). It is worth registering how unlike most people’s picture of the last day that is. The prophet’s word for the end is not a cloud or a silence. It is food, and company, and wine kept a long time for a particular occasion.

Is this the same parable as the great banquet in Luke 14? Most likely not. Luke 14:16–24 has a similar shape, but here it is a king and his son’s wedding, with murdered servants, a burned city and a guest without a garment, and it is told in the temple in the last week rather than at a meal in a Pharisee’s house. Jesus often taught similar themes on different occasions, and a preacher who travelled for three years would naturally use a strong story more than once, shaped for each audience.

In a sentence. In a third parable, Jesus compared the kingdom to a king’s wedding feast for his son.

On a Tuesday. God’s kingdom is a feast, a celebration of joy. Do you think of following Christ as a burden or as an invitation to a wedding? If your faith has become mostly duty, go back to the invitation itself: a King who wants you at his Son’s table. Duties done for such a King are not the price of the feast but the joy of the guests.

For worship. The Father has prepared a wedding for his Son, and the bride is a people gathered from every nation. All of history is moving toward that feast, where death will be swallowed up for ever and God himself will wipe away every tear. The Son, who will be honoured at that table, is the same Son who laid down his life to win his bride. Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).
verseByVerse.note: A royal wedding feast could last a week.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Again he sent other servants, saying, "Tell those who are invited, See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. He sent other servants: tell those who are invited, see, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and fattened calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.

And sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast. In the ancient world, guests were invited in advance, and then summoned again when the feast was ready (Esther 6:14; Luke 14:17). The first invitation is God’s call to Israel through the Old Testament prophets and John; the guests had been told the feast was coming. Now the servants announce that it has come. So the people who refuse are not strangers turning down a stranger. They had already accepted. They had said yes long ago, and the servants at the door are simply calling in a promise. It is the second son of 21:30 again, who said I go, sir, and did not go: a person of good standing whose word and whose feet have quietly parted company.

But they would not come. A deliberate refusal. To refuse a king’s invitation was a grave insult. The Greek is plain: they were not willing (ouk ēthelon). Not they could not, not they were prevented. The obstacle in this parable is never circumstance; it is the will, and Matthew says so before any excuse has been offered.

Again he sent other servants. The king’s patience, as with the tenants (21:36). That is not what a slighted monarch does. He has been publicly snubbed by people who had already accepted, and his response is another delegation with a warmer message.

See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. A lavish feast, with the best meat, which was rarely eaten by ordinary people. Listen to the tenses: prepared, slaughtered, ready. Done, finished, standing complete. Nothing is pending. And in a world without refrigeration the slaughtered oxen carry weight a modern reader misses: meat cannot be put back. Once the animals are killed the king is committed, the cost is already spent, and every hour of delay is waste. He has made himself vulnerable to their refusal before they refuse. Everything is ready: the guests need bring nothing, only come. This is grace. The gospel is the announcement that God has prepared everything in Christ.

Come to the wedding feast. A personal, urgent invitation. The church is not sent to persuade God to be gracious, or to ask people to help him prepare something. It is sent to say that everything is ready, and that the only thing outstanding is attendance. What was still to be done when Jesus told this parable would be done within the week, and his last word from the cross would be the word this message rests on: it is finished (John 19:30).

What am I waiting for? Most people who are not at the feast imagine they are waiting for something: to understand more, to feel differently, to get a part of their life straightened out first, to become the kind of person who belongs at such a table. Read the message again. There is nothing on the list. The oxen are killed, the tables are laid, and the only word left in the invitation is come. You do not tidy yourself before you accept a king’s invitation; you come, and he deals with the clothing (see on vv. 11–12). If you have been meaning to settle this for years, the invitation is not asking you to be ready. It is telling you that he is.

In a sentence. The invited guests refused to come, but the king patiently sent more servants to say that the lavish feast was ready.

On a Tuesday. God’s invitation is still come; everything is ready. Have you accepted it? And if you have, tell someone today that it stands open, in plain words: not try harder, but come, it is ready.

For worship. Everything is ready, because the Son made it ready. The Lamb was slain, the price was paid, the feast was spread at the cost of his own body and blood. The King has committed himself before we ever answered, and he keeps sending, warmly, to people who have already said no. What a Father, whose grace waits at the door with the table laid, and whose only word to sinners is come.
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business. The rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully and killed them.

But they paid no attention. The verb (amelēsantes) means they made light of it, did not care, could not be bothered. Nobody argues. Nobody sends a message explaining. They simply have something on.

And went off, one to his farm, another to his business. Two kinds of rejection. Some were indifferent: they had more important things to do. Look hard at what they had on, because this is where the parable stops being only about Jerusalem. A farm and a shop. Not vice, not blasphemy, not a rival religion: a field that needed walking and a business that needed running. Their farms and businesses were not wrong in themselves, but they put them before the king’s invitation (13:22; Luke 14:18–20). The most effective rival to God in most lives has never been wickedness. It is respectable occupation, and it works because nobody has to defend it. A man who misses the feast for a mistress knows he has done something. A man who misses it for the farm has merely been busy.

Why indifference is so deadly. Hostility at least concedes that the matter is serious. The men who went off to the farm had come to a settled view about a royal invitation without ever once thinking about it, and if you had asked them at the gate they would have said, quite sincerely, that they had nothing against the king. Their diaries had decided it for them years earlier.

While the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. Others were violent, as the tenants were (21:35). God’s messengers, the prophets, John, and later the apostles, were persecuted and killed (23:34; Acts 7:58–60; 12:2). Within a few years Stephen would be stoned in that city and James cut down by Herod’s sword.

The same end for both. Hold the two groups together and notice the verdict. The violent and the busy are dealt with in the same sentence and end in the same place: outside, with the feast going on without them. That should sober anyone who has quietly assumed that not being hostile is the same as being safe. Nobody in this story is condemned merely for opposing the king. They are condemned for not coming.

But I have real responsibilities. Am I supposed to neglect them? No. Farms must be worked and businesses run, and Scripture honours diligent work (Proverbs 6:6–11; 2 Thessalonians 3:10). The fault was not that they had work but that the work came first when the king called. The question is one of order: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (6:33). In practice that means Christ’s claims are not fitted into the gaps the farm leaves. The Lord’s Day, prayer, Scripture and his people are given their place first, and the farm is worked as service to him.

In a sentence. Some guests ignored the invitation for their business, and others murdered the king’s servants.

On a Tuesday. Indifference is as deadly as hostility. What farm or business keeps you from responding wholeheartedly to God? Look at your diary for the coming week and ask what it says you believe about the King’s invitation. Then move one thing to make room for him.

For worship. The King’s feast went on, and still goes on, though men have walked away from it to their fields for two thousand years. His purposes are not stalled by our indifference or overturned by our violence. And the Son, whose servants were mocked and killed, was himself seized, treated shamefully and killed, so that the invitation could go out again, sealed in his blood, to those who had once made light of it.

parallels.desc: the servants in the vineyard beaten and killed

verseByVerse.quote: The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king was angry. He sent his troops, destroyed those murderers and burned their city.

The king was angry. God’s just anger at those who reject his grace and kill his messengers. This is the hardest verse in the parable, and it should not be softened. But read the offence carefully, because read carelessly the verse looks like a monarch burning a town over a declined invitation, and that is not what happened. The men of verse 6 seized the king’s envoys, humiliated them and killed them. In the ancient world the murder of a royal embassy was an act of war, and everyone understood it so.

And he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. An unusual detail in a story about a wedding: a war in the middle of the preparations. It points to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Roman army in AD 70, which burned the city and the temple. Josephus, who watched it, describes the catastrophe in detail: the famine inside the walls, the temple burned, the city levelled. Jesus is speaking prophetically of judgment on the city that rejected him (23:37–38; 24:2). Two chapters later he says it plainly on the Mount of Olives: not one stone will be left here upon another. God can use pagan armies as instruments of his judgment (Isaiah 10:5–6).

What it does not mean. Not that God hates the Jewish people, or that Christians may hate them. The judgment fell on a generation that rejected the Messiah, and Christians have often sinfully misused such passages to justify anti-Semitism. Jesus himself wept over Jerusalem (23:37; Luke 19:41–44).

The guard that matters most. This verse has been quoted with satisfaction by Christians about Jewish people for much of two thousand years, and the satisfaction is itself a sin. Look at who is addressed: the leadership who had the vineyard on lease (21:45), not a race. Look at who wept over the city and longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her brood (23:37): the same speaker, one chapter later, in tears. And remember who the church in Jerusalem was: Jewish believers, warned by Jesus to flee when they saw the armies coming (Luke 21:20–21). There is no reading of this verse in which a Gentile Christian gets to feel superior.

Is it right for God to be angry? Yes, and it would be wrong for him not to be. What the verse says, without apology, is that patience has an end. A God who could be refused for ever with no consequence would not be a God who cared what happened. The anger exists because the invitation was real, the Son was real and the murders were real. God’s anger is not a temper; it is his settled, holy opposition to evil, and it is always just. And it is the measure of the cross: this is the anger that Christ bore for his people, so that it would never fall on them.

In a sentence. The angry king destroyed the murderers and burned their city, a picture of the coming judgment on Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. God’s patience is great, but it has an end. Do not presume on it. If there is a call of God you have been putting off, the time to answer is now, while the servants are still at the door.

For worship. The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and will by no means clear the guilty (Nahum 1:3). His wrath is as holy as his love, and both met at the cross, where the King’s own Son was handed over to the troops and his body broken outside a city that would itself be burned. Whoever is in him has passed from wrath to the wedding. Holy and righteous is the King, and in his anger he remembers mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Many see here a pointer to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to his servants, "The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king said to his servants: the wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go to the main roads and invite to the feast as many as you find.

The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Not worthy because they refused. Worthiness here means willingness to come, not merit (see 10:11). Take the word carefully, because it is about to be turned inside out. The first guests were not disqualified by failing a standard; they were disqualified by not coming. And those who fill the hall in their place are not more deserving in any respect: they are simply willing to walk through a door. In this parable the only unworthiness that matters is refusal, and the only worthiness on offer is an empty stomach.

Go therefore to the main roads. Literally “the partings of the ways”: where a city street leads out into the country roads, where travellers, beggars and all kinds of people gathered. The invitation goes out beyond the original guests. These are not the second tier of the guest list. There was no second tier. The king’s staff are being sent to gather whoever happens to be standing at a road junction on the afternoon of a royal wedding.

And invite to the wedding feast as many as you find. No restrictions. Anyone. This is the gospel going to the Gentiles and to the outcasts of Israel (8:11; 21:31; 28:19). The feast will be full. And the invitation the second group receives is not a lesser one. They are not let in at the back to watch. They are guests at the wedding of the king’s son, with the same food, at the same tables, on the same evening.

You are the person at the junction. Set the two groups side by side. The first had covenant standing, ancestral promise and a reserved place. The second had no pedigree, no claim, no warning and no reason to think a palace had anything to do with them. If you are not Jewish, you are the person at the road junction. You had no claim on the God of Israel, nothing to bring, and no grounds for complaint if the servants had walked past you. Paul writes of Gentiles who were once without hope and without God in the world, and now brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:12–13), and he never quite gets over it. Neither should we.

Who should my church be inviting? The king’s instruction is not invite the people most likely to accept, or the ones who will fit in. It is: go to the junctions and bring in whoever is there. A church whose members all come from one part of one town has not been to the main roads; it has been to the people it already knew. Ask where the junctions are in your area: the estate, the students, the newcomers, the lonely, the people of other languages. Then go there with the invitation, not waiting for them to find the door.

In a sentence. Since the invited guests refused, the king sent his servants to invite everyone they could find.

On a Tuesday. You are one of the servants sent out to the roads. Whom could you invite to the feast this week? Think of one person who would never expect to be asked, and ask: to church, to your table, to hear about Christ.

For worship. The King’s generosity is not exhausted by the refusal of the first guests; it overflows to the roads. He had always intended the nations to come: in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed. And so the Gentile at the crossroads, with nothing to bring, finds himself seated at the wedding of the Son of God. Praise the King whose table is wider than our imagining, and whose servants still go out to the partings of the ways.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.quote: And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servants went out into the roads and gathered all they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.

And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found. The servants obeyed and invited everyone. The instruction was comprehensive, and they obeyed it comprehensively.

Both bad and good. The invitation is not based on moral merit. Notorious sinners and decent people alike are invited. The gospel net catches all kinds (13:47–48). Notice the order. Matthew could have written it the other way round and it would have read more comfortably, but he puts the bad first, and it is not realism apologising for the standard of guest. It is the point. There is no screening in this verse: no pause to establish whether a man at the junction has the sort of history that suits a royal occasion, no discreet enquiry, no probation.

So the wedding hall was filled with guests. God’s purpose will not fail. His house will be full (Luke 14:23). The verb is passive, and the room the original guests left empty did not stay empty. The son’s wedding was not going to be attended by a thin scattering of people who happened to be free. The king had determined that there would be a full house, and there was.

Come as you are, stay as you are? No. The very next verse is about a man who came as he was and was not clothed, and the parable that welcomes the bad without a question at the door also has a king who walks the room. Both halves are in the story: nothing whatever is required to get in, and something is required to be there. The bad are brought in. They are not left as they were found. Grace receives sinners exactly as they are, and then, by the same grace, makes them new.

What this does to a church. If the servants are doing their work, the hall will contain people whose lives are visibly a mess, and it will contain them before they are tidy. A congregation with no such people in it has not been more faithful than the parable; it has been more selective. The early church did this so conspicuously, Jew and Gentile, slave and owner, the respectable and the notorious eating at one table, that the surrounding world could not account for it. That was not a lapse in standards. It was the servants doing what they were told.

In a sentence. The servants gathered everyone, bad and good, and the wedding hall was full.

On a Tuesday. Look around at church on Sunday for the person who does not fit, whose clothes, history or manner mark him as someone gathered from the roads. Sit with him. Learn his name. And remember that in the King’s eyes you were gathered from the roads too.

For worship. Thank God that his invitation reached you, whatever you were. The hall will be full: not one seat that the King has prepared will stand empty on the day of the feast, for all that the Father gives the Son will come to him (John 6:37). Bad and good, gathered from every road, washed and clothed and seated together, the guests will see the face of the Bridegroom, and the joy of that hall will have no end.

parallels.desc: the net gathers fish of every kind

verseByVerse.quote: But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. And he said to him, "Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?" And he was speechless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the king came in to look at the guests, he saw a man who was not wearing a wedding garment. He said: friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment? And the man was speechless.

But when the king came in to look at the guests. The parable turns without warning, and the turn is the reason it is told. The king inspects his guests: a picture of God’s final judgment. He walks the room. Everything up to this point has been about getting people through the door; now the host looks, and one man is found who does not belong at the table where he is sitting.

He is inside. Note where the man is when the trouble begins. He got past the servants, walked the length of the hall, took a place and sat down among the guests, and nothing in the story suggests anybody challenged him. Whatever is wrong here was not detectable at the door. It is detected by the king.

He saw there a man who had no wedding garment. Guests at a wedding wore clean, festive clothing. To come in ordinary, dirty clothes was an insult to the host. Some have suggested that kings provided special garments for their guests, which would make refusing one an act of contempt. There is little firm evidence for this custom. But the point is clear either way: this man came on his own terms, without the clothing the occasion required.

What is the wedding garment? Jesus does not say. So start with the story and with Matthew. In the story, the man accepted the invitation but came as he was, without what the occasion required. In Matthew, righteousness is the life God requires: a righteousness greater than the scribes’ (5:20), fruit in keeping with repentance (3:8), and, in the parable just before, a people producing the kingdom’s fruits (21:43). So the first meaning is clear: the man wanted the feast without the change. He had not repented.

Who provides the garment? The Old Testament background points to God. Isaiah rejoices that God has clothed him with the garments of salvation and covered him with the robe of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). Zechariah saw the high priest’s filthy garments removed and replaced with clean ones, a picture of forgiveness (Zechariah 3:3–5). And the bride of the Lamb is given fine linen to wear, which is the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8). The rest of the New Testament then explains how God clothes sinners: with Christ’s righteousness credited to those who trust him (Philippians 3:9; Galatians 3:27), and with the new life that follows, as they put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:14). Verdict: in the parable, the garment is the repentant, changed life that the kingdom requires. The rest of Scripture shows that this too is God’s gift: forgiveness and righteousness in Christ, and a new life that grows from it. It is not one without the other.

Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment? “Friend” is a cool, polite address (see 20:13). Matthew uses hetairos exactly three times, and this is the middle one: to the labourer grumbling at the pay table (20:13), here to a man about to be thrown out, and in a garden by torchlight to Judas (26:50). Every occurrence is addressed to someone in the wrong, and every one is courteous: the address of a man who has not raised his voice and has stopped pretending. And the question is an enquiry, not a tirade. The king gives him the chance to explain.

And he was speechless. He had no excuse. On the day of judgment, every mouth will be stopped (Romans 3:19). The verb (ephimōthē) means he was muzzled. He is not defiant and not apologetic. If he had been poor he could have said so; if he had been overlooked he could have said that. A man pulled in off a road junction at an hour’s notice could hardly be blamed for his clothes unless something had been open to him that he did not take. He is speechless because he has no grievance. His silence is the admission.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn our place at the feast by our own good works. The invitation is free to all, bad and good (v. 10). But accepting the invitation means coming on the king’s terms: being clothed with the righteousness he provides. Those who claim to belong to the kingdom but have never repented and trusted Christ will be exposed.

Was the man a believer who lost his salvation? Some read it that way. The more likely reading is that he was a professing guest who never truly came on the king’s terms, someone who wanted the feast and not the King, like those who say Lord, Lord, and whom Jesus never knew (7:21–23). Those whom God truly clothes he keeps: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). The warning is not meant to make true believers doubt whether they will be kept. It is meant to make everyone who sits in the hall ask whether he has truly come.

How do I know whether I have the garment? Not by inspecting yourself until you feel worthy; no one does. Ask instead two plain questions. Have you come to Christ, trusting him and not your own record to make you acceptable to God? And is there in you, however weak, a turning from sin and a desire to please him, the repentance the parable looks for? If both are there, even faintly, the King has clothed you, and the new life will grow. If you find that you want the feast but not the change, that is the warning, and the remedy is still open: come to him now, confess it, and ask him to clothe you.

In a sentence. The king found a guest without a wedding garment, a picture of someone who accepts God’s invitation outwardly but has not been clothed with righteousness in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Are you clothed in Christ’s righteousness, or only present at the feast in your own clothes? Being in church, knowing the songs and sitting among the guests is not the same as being clothed. Today, put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:14): trust him again, and put off one specific thing he has shown you is not fit for his wedding.

For worship. I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation (Isaiah 61:10). The King who gathers guests from the roads does not leave them in their rags. He takes off the filthy garments and gives clean ones; he credits his Son’s righteousness to those who trust him, and he works in them a new and holy life. Every guest who stands at the last in the King’s hall will stand there in what the King gave him, and will give the King the glory.
verseByVerse.note: The wedding garment stands for the fitting clothing the host requires — the righteousness God gives and the life that matches it.

parallels.desc: clothed with the garments of salvation
fine linen, the righteous deeds of the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the attendants, "Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." For many are called, but few are chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king told the attendants: bind him hand and foot and throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. For many are called, but few are chosen.

Then the king said to the attendants, Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. Bound so that he cannot return. Thrown out of the brightly lit hall into the darkness outside (see 8:12). The outer darkness is the darkness outside the lit hall, and in Matthew it means final exclusion from the kingdom (8:12; 25:30). Picture the contrast: inside, light, music, food and the face of the King; outside, a dark that does not end.

In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The anguish of final judgment (see 8:12; 13:42): grief, bitter regret and anger, without end. Jesus speaks of it more often than anyone else in Scripture, and he speaks of it with tears in his voice, not with satisfaction. The binding and the darkness come not from dramatic wickedness but from refusing the King’s provision while sitting at his table.

For many are called, but few are chosen. The key saying. “Called” (klētoi) here means invited: the gospel invitation goes out to many, to everyone (v. 9). “Chosen” (eklektoi) means elect: those whom God has chosen, who respond to the invitation with true faith and are clothed in righteousness. Not everyone who hears the invitation responds truly. The gospel call is universal; God’s election is particular.

The two callings. Reformed theology distinguishes the external call of the gospel, which goes to all who hear it, from the effectual or inward call by which the Spirit brings the elect to faith (Romans 8:30; 1 Corinthians 1:23–24; Westminster 10.1, 10.4). Matthew’s word “called” here is the external call. Paul often uses “called” for the effectual call. Both are biblical. That distinction is what makes both evangelism and assurance possible at once: preach to everyone without exception, because the outward call is genuine; and rest, because God secures his own.

What it does not mean. Not that God refuses those who want to come. The invitation is genuine, to all. Those who are not chosen are those who refuse the invitation (vv. 3–6) or come without the garment (v. 12); they are responsible for their response. God’s election does not make anyone a victim; it guarantees that some will come. Nor does “few” give us a number; it means fewer than those invited.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians read “chosen” as those who choose to respond, so that election follows human decision. Reformed theology reads it as God’s prior choice, which produces the response (John 6:44; Ephesians 1:4–5; Acts 13:48). Verdict: unconditional election. But the invitation goes to all, and everyone who comes will be received (11:28; John 6:37).

What if I want to come and I am not one of the chosen? That fear has kept people from Christ for centuries, which is a bitter irony, since the doctrine was given to settle fear and not to create it. Notice first that nobody in Scripture is ever told to establish that he is elect before coming. In this very parable the servants are told to invite as many as they find: no list, no enquiry into anyone’s eternal status. They were not given the names; they were given the invitation. And election is not meant to be looked at from the front. Paul writes about it to people already inside, as an explanation of how they got there and a guarantee that they will be kept. It is the foundation under the house, not the door of it. Calvin’s counsel is still the best: Christ is the mirror in which we see our election. Look at him and come to him, and you are looking at the evidence. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37), and no one has ever found an exception.

Is my wanting to come a sign of anything? Yes, and a hopeful one. No one drags himself toward God unaided; no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). So if you find in yourself a real desire to be at the feast, to be forgiven, to know Christ, you did not manufacture it. That desire is the surest sign that the One who does the choosing has already been at work. Do not sit and analyse it. Act on it: come.

In a sentence. The man without the garment was thrown out, for the gospel invitation goes to many, but only the chosen respond truly.

On a Tuesday. The invitation to you is real. Respond to it fully: come to Christ, and be clothed with him. And because the outward call is God’s means of gathering his chosen, give it out freely this week. You do not know who the chosen are; you only know that the King has told you to invite everyone you find.

For worship. Salvation belongs to the LORD from first to last: he prepared the feast, he sent the invitation, he chose his guests before the foundation of the world, he draws them by his Spirit, he clothes them in his Son, and he will keep them in his hall for ever. Not one of the chosen will be missing. And the call that goes out to all is no pretence; it is the voice of a King who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, saying to every sinner, come.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, "Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to trap Jesus in his words. They sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying: Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances.

Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. Unable to arrest him openly (21:46), they try to trap him into saying something that would turn the crowds against him, or give them grounds to accuse him to the Romans. This begins a series of three test questions (vv. 15–40). The verb (pagideusōsin) comes from the word for a snare, the trap a fowler sets for a bird, hidden, baited and sprung by the creature’s own movement. Matthew tells us the intention before he reports the conversation, so that we cannot mistake what follows for a discussion.

And they sent their disciples to him. They sent their students, perhaps to make the trap look innocent, while the seniors kept their distance from whatever happened.

Along with the Herodians. Supporters of Herod Antipas and his family, who cooperated with Rome. The Pharisees resented Roman rule; the Herodians supported it. They were natural enemies, united against Jesus (Mark 3:6). Whatever Jesus said about taxes, one group would accuse him. On the question they were about to ask, these two parties held opposite views with some passion. They agreed on nothing except that this man had to be finished, and that was enough to put them in the same delegation. Hostility to Christ has always been an efficient organiser of people who cannot otherwise stand to be in a room together.

Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully. Flattery, intended to make him answer boldly. Ironically, everything they say is true. They have described him perfectly, and they do not believe a word of it.

And you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. Literally “you do not look at the face of people”: you are impartial, unafraid of anyone, including Caesar. The purpose is not to please him. It is to build a box out of his own reputation and shut him in it: we have said in public that you fear nobody, so now prove it by answering recklessly. Praise a man loudly enough for his courage and he may do something foolish to keep the compliment. Scripture treats flattery as a form of attack: a flattering mouth works ruin (Proverbs 26:28).

How do I recognise flattery? It usually arrives dressed as respect. You are the only one round here who says what he really thinks. You are not like the others. I knew you would understand; you have always been more open-minded than they are. Each is a door held open in a particular direction, and the compliment is the hinge. The test is simple: notice whether the praise is describing you or steering you, and whether it arrived just before a request. Genuine encouragement leaves you freer to do right; flattery leaves you more obliged to do what the flatterer wants.

In a sentence. The Pharisees and Herodians, normally enemies, joined to trap Jesus, opening with flattery.

On a Tuesday. Beware of flattery. It is often a trap. And watch your own mouth too: when you praise someone, make sure you are not steering him. Give encouragement freely, but never as a lever.

For worship. They told the truth about him in order to destroy him, and the truth stands: he is true, he teaches the way of God truthfully, and he does not bend to anyone’s face. No flattery ever moved him, no threat ever silenced him, and no alliance of enemies ever caught him. The kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:2–4).
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. Their alliance was a trap.

verseByVerse.quote: "Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?

Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? “Lawful” means according to God’s law. The tax was the poll tax (kēnsos, from the Latin census), a yearly tax of one denarius per person paid directly to the Roman emperor. It was bitterly resented as a symbol of foreign rule. It was not the amount that stung so much as what it meant: a census had counted God’s people like Caesar’s cattle, and paying it was a yearly admission of who ruled the land. When it was introduced in AD 6, a revolt led by Judas the Galilean broke out, with the slogan that God alone was Israel’s king (Acts 5:37). The Zealot movement grew from it. Men had died over this question within living memory.

The trap. If Jesus said “Yes, pay”, he would lose the support of the crowds, who hated the tax and hoped the Messiah would end Roman rule. If he said “No”, the Herodians could report him to the Romans as a rebel, and he would be arrested for sedition. Either way, he loses. The delegation had been assembled so that either answer had its own witnesses ready. And they put it as a question of conscience, is it lawful?, so that refusing to answer would look like evading a religious duty. They are not asking him what is wise. They are asking him to rule.

What do I do with questions designed to trap? Almost every generation produces a question shaped so that a Christian must offend one group or another, and the questioner’s interest is not in the answer but in the offence. Do not be rushed into the alternatives you are handed. Ask what the real question underneath is, and answer that, truthfully and with grace. Sometimes the wisest reply is a question back (21:24). Pray for wisdom, which God gives generously (James 1:5), and remember that you do not need to win the exchange; you need to be faithful in it.

In a sentence. They asked whether it was right to pay the hated Roman tax, a question designed to trap Jesus either way.

On a Tuesday. Some questions are designed to trap, not to learn. Ask God for wisdom to answer them. Before your next conversation where you expect such a question, about sexuality, politics, other religions, pray that your answer will be truer and larger than the trap.

For worship. The wisdom of God stood in the temple courts in a human body, and the cleverest men of the nation could not catch him. He is the wisdom of God and the power of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). The snares laid for him he walked through, and the One they tried to trap is the One who, on the cross, sprang the trap of sin and death for us.
verseByVerse.note: This was the poll tax paid directly to Rome, bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, "Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, aware of their malice, said: why are you testing me, you hypocrites? Show me the coin used for the tax. And they brought him a denarius.

But Jesus, aware of their malice. “Malice” (ponērian) means wickedness, evil intent. He sees through the flattery. Matthew does not let the scene proceed as though it were a seminar. They told him he was not swayed by appearances, and discovered that he was not swayed by appearances.

Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? They pretended to seek his opinion; they wanted to destroy him. He names them to their faces before answering a word.

Show me the coin for the tax. The tax had to be paid in Roman coin. And here is the request that wins the argument before it starts. He does not have one. He asks them.

And they brought him a denarius. A silver coin, a day’s wage (20:2). Notice: Jesus did not have one; they did. By producing a Roman coin in the temple courts, they showed that they were already using Caesar’s money and benefiting from his rule. Men presenting themselves as troubled in conscience about paying Caesar’s tax had one in a purse, on the temple mount, and handed it over without a flicker.

The scruple and the purse. That is the quiet accusation, and it lands nearer home than we would like. It is remarkably easy to hold a principled objection to a thing while living comfortably inside it, and to be genuinely unaware of the gap. These men were not necessarily lying about their scruples; they had simply never let the scruple and the purse meet. The test is not what you would say if asked. It is what turns up when somebody says: show me.

In a sentence. Seeing through their trap, Jesus asked for the tax coin, and they produced a denarius.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is never fooled by our pretences. Be honest with him. Think of one conviction you hold firmly, about money, honesty, purity, the poor, and ask what your bank statement, your browser history or your diary would show if he said, show me.

For worship. He knows what is in man (John 2:25). No mask stays on in his presence, and no hypocrisy survives his question. And yet the One who sees through every pretence did not use his knowledge to crush the pretenders on the spot; he answered them, and taught them, and went on to die for sinners whose hearts were open books to him. Blessed is the Lord who sees everything and loves anyway.
verseByVerse.note: The denarius was a silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked them: whose likeness and inscription is this? They said: Caesar’s. He said: then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

Whose likeness and inscription is this? The denarius of that time bore the head of the emperor Tiberius (AD 14–37), with an inscription reading, in Latin abbreviation, “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, Augustus”. On the reverse: “High Priest”. To devout Jews, the image and the claim to divinity were offensive, breaking the second commandment. So the object handed to Jesus in the temple of the living God was a piece of metal announcing that another man was the son of a god and the high priest of the world.

They said, Caesar’s. Their own answer settles it.

Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. “Render” (apodote) means give back, pay what is owed. The coin bears Caesar’s image; it belongs to him. Paying taxes to the government is a legitimate obligation. Governments are established by God and have a right to taxes (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). Even a pagan, oppressive government. Give it back, and do not make a religion of resenting it.

And to God the things that are God’s. The deeper point. The coin bears Caesar’s image; human beings bear God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27). Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, your whole life. Caesar may claim taxes, but not worship. Caesar’s coin called him divine; Jesus quietly denies it. God alone is God. This is more radical than the tidy division of spheres it is often reduced to. Caesar may have your taxes, your obedience in his own sphere, your honour and your prayers. He may never have the thing that bears the other image. That is not a small reservation held back from the state; it is everything, and every tyrant who has tried to take it has found that Christians would give him the coin all day and would not give him that.

What it does not mean. Not that life is divided into two separate areas, religious and secular, with God ruling only the first. Everything belongs to God (Psalm 24:1), including Caesar. Caesar’s authority is under God’s. Nor does it mean that governments must always be obeyed. When the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). The apostles obeyed Caesar in paying taxes and refused him when he demanded worship.

When exactly should a Christian disobey the government? Only when obeying would mean sinning.
