Paul wrote let every person be subject to the governing authorities, and Peter wrote honour the emperor, both under Nero, who would kill them (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:17). So a government being unjust, corrupt or hostile to the faith is not by itself grounds for disobedience. The line is crossed not when the state is wicked but when it requires you to be. Then Scripture is clear: the Hebrew midwives refused Pharaoh’s order to kill the boys (Exodus 1:17), the three young men would not bow to the statue (Daniel 3:16–18), Daniel kept praying at his open window (Daniel 6:10), and Peter told the council, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). And notice the manner: they refused openly, without rebellion or contempt, and accepted the cost. Christian disobedience is the refusal to sin, with the punishment borne.

Where Christians differ: church and state. Some Christians want the state to enforce Christian law (theonomy, or Christian nationalism). Others want complete separation of religion from public life. The Reformed tradition has generally held that the state and the church are distinct institutions, each under God, with different roles: the state bears the sword for justice; the church bears the keys of the kingdom (Romans 13; Matthew 16:19; Westminster 23.1–3). Verdict: Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes, praying for rulers, and seeking justice, while giving ultimate loyalty only to God.

Is it wrong to cut my tax bill, or to complain about how taxes are spent? Arranging your affairs lawfully to pay what is actually owed, and no more, is not wrong; render means pay what is due. Evading what is due, by hiding income or cash-in-hand work, is. And Christians may speak, vote and campaign for wise and just use of public money, since they are citizens as well as believers. What Jesus rules out is treating the tax as a reason to withhold honour from the authorities God has set over us, or making a cause of resentment the centre of our lives.

In a sentence. Give the government what it is owed, since the coin bears Caesar’s image, but give God yourself, since you bear his.

On a Tuesday. Pay your taxes honestly. And ask: have I given God what is his, my whole self? Pray for those in authority by name this week (1 Timothy 2:1–2), including the ones you did not vote for. Then look for one place where you have quietly given Caesar, or your career, or the crowd, something that bears God’s image and belongs only to him.

For worship. Every coin bears some ruler’s face, and every human being bears the face of God. We were made in his image, defaced it by sin, and are being restored to it in Christ, the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). The emperor on the coin claimed to be the son of a god and the high priest of the world. The man holding the coin was the Son of God and the great High Priest, and he gave himself wholly to the Father, that those who bear the image might be given back to God.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

parallels.desc: be subject to the governing authorities

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard it, they were amazed, and they left him and went away.

When they heard it, they marveled. Jesus’ answer escaped their trap completely, and went deeper than their question. The word (ethaumasan) sounds a note Matthew has struck for two chapters. The chief priests saw the wonderful things he did and were indignant (21:15). Jesus called the rejected stone marvellous in our eyes (21:42). Now his opponents stand before an answer they cannot fault and marvel at it. Three marvels in two chapters, and not one of them ends in worship.

And they left him and went away. Defeated, but not converted. They marvelled at his wisdom, but did not submit to it. Not they left the argument, but they left him. They had come with a question, received an answer better than any of them could have produced, were genuinely impressed, and walked away from the person. Whatever had happened in that exchange, nothing had happened to them. And the next time these men are in a room with Jesus they will not be asking questions; they will be looking for witnesses against him (26:59). Admiration that refuses to become allegiance does not stay neutral for long.

Can I admire Jesus and still be lost? Yes, and it is perhaps the most respectable way of rejecting him. It is possible to find Jesus intellectually magnificent, to enjoy the way he handles opponents, to admire the answer about Caesar as a piece of reasoning, to recommend the passage to others, and to have moved not an inch. Admiration costs nothing and flatters the admirer. Faith is different: it bows, trusts and follows. The question is not whether you think highly of Jesus, but whether you have given yourself to him.

In a sentence. Amazed at Jesus’ answer, they left him, defeated but unchanged.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to admire Jesus’ wisdom and still walk away. Do not just marvel; obey. Run the test on the last passage you read: did anything change by Thursday? Not did you agree with it, but did you do anything, stop anything, say anything to anyone, ask anyone’s forgiveness?

For worship. The wisdom that silenced the Pharisees is the wisdom that saves sinners. Let us not be among those who marvel and walk away, but among those who marvel and stay, who fall at his feet and say, my Lord and my God. He is not only the cleverest teacher who ever lived; he is the Lord, worthy of more than admiration, worthy of everything we are.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Resurrection, the Great Commandment, and David's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three delegations in succession, and then Jesus asks a question of his own. The Sadducees construct a levirate-marriage absurdity with seven brothers to make resurrection look ridiculous, and are told they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God — the resurrection proved out of the Torah they accepted, from the present tense of one verb at the burning bush. The crowd is astonished. The Pharisees regroup and send a lawyer to ask which commandment is greatest, and receive the Shema and Leviticus 19:18, on which the whole Law and Prophets hang. Then Jesus asks whose son the Christ is, quotes Psalm 110, and nobody is able to answer him a word or dares question him again.
verseByVerse.theology: Two failures are named in one sentence and almost every serious error in the church lands under one of them: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. The Sadducees had the Torah by heart, which is what makes the first charge devastating — knowing the Scriptures is not the same as having them. And they believed in God while not believing he could do anything, which is a God cut down to the size of arrangements we already understand. The resurrection argument turns on covenant: God binds himself by name to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and says I am, not I was, six hundred years after Abraham died. He does not attach his name to dust. Then the double love command, where the verb is krematai — the Law and Prophets hang on two pegs, so the 613 commandments are not separate obligations but the outworking of two. And Psalm 110 closes the sequence: the Christ is David's son according to the flesh and David's Lord according to his eternal nature, which is Matthew's own first chapter put as a riddle (1:23).
verseByVerse.examples: Like angels in heaven needs its guard: it does not mean we become angels or lose our bodies. The comparison is made in one respect only, and the sentence names it — angels do not marry. On the tender question every widow and every married reader brings here, see the verse-by-verse on vv. 29-30: what ends is the institution, not the love. Notice also the woman in the Sadducees' story, whom nobody in it notices — she has buried seven husbands and appears purely as a question of ownership, and Jesus's answer incidentally gives her back what their question took away. As yourself in v. 39 is a measure, not a recommendation of self-esteem: you never have to be reminded to take an interest in your own toothache, and that automatic attention is the standard. Test it where it bites — when something goes wrong for you the mind supplies context, and when it goes wrong at somebody else's hands the mind supplies character. And v. 33 is a warning laid inside a victory: astonishment is not allegiance, and within three days a crowd in this city would be shouting for Barabbas.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses said, 'If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same day, Sadducees came to Jesus. They say there is no resurrection. They asked him: Teacher, Moses said that if a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up children for his brother.

The same day Sadducees came to him. The second test question. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, wealthy and politically powerful, who controlled the temple (see 3:7). The high priest belonged to them, they controlled the temple and its revenues, and they had made their working arrangement with Rome, which is how a man keeps a position like that under occupation. They accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative, and rejected the oral traditions the Pharisees prized. And they had watched Jesus clear the temple courts two days earlier. The temple was theirs. This is not a theological enquiry; it is the men whose market he overturned, coming back with a clever question.

Who say that there is no resurrection. They denied the resurrection of the body, life after death, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). They believed that the soul perished with the body. They argued that the resurrection was not taught in the books of Moses. And notice how well that fits their position. A party with wealth and office in the present world has the least reason to want a world to come. If this life is where the accounts are settled, men in their position have already won, and a coming judgment can only be a threat. Theology is rarely held in a vacuum: the men the resurrection would cost most were the men who found the arguments against it persuasive.

Teacher, Moses said, If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. The law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–6; compare Genesis 38:8), so called from the Latin levir, a husband’s brother. If a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow, and their first son would carry on the dead man’s name and inherit his property. The purpose was to preserve the family line and land, and to protect the widow, since a widow with no son had no protector or means of support. The story of Ruth and Boaz shows the same family duty at work. A man who refused could be publicly shamed before the elders (Deuteronomy 25:9–10).

Do my desires shape what I believe? More than we like to admit. The Sadducees are a warning that we tend to find persuasive the arguments for what suits us, and weak the arguments for what would cost us. That does not make every conviction suspect, but it does mean we should be most careful where a doctrine is most inconvenient. Ask, when you resist a teaching of Scripture: is my objection really from the text, or from what it would require of me? Let God’s word judge your desires, not the other way round.

In a sentence. The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, came to Jesus with a question based on the law of levirate marriage.

On a Tuesday. Some people use the Bible to argue against what the Bible teaches. Read it whole. When you hear a verse used to overturn a plain teaching of Scripture, ask what the rest of the Bible says, and let the clearer passages explain the harder.

For worship. The God the Sadducees served was too small to raise the dead. The God who confronted them stood before them in flesh, three days from his own grave, and he would walk out of it. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead (1 Peter 1:3).
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and probably held the five books of Moses above the rest of Scripture and denied the resurrection. The law of levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

parallels.desc: Sadducees say there is no resurrection

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. So too the second and third, down to the seventh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no children, left his wife to his brother. The second did the same, and the third, down to the seventh.

Now there were seven brothers among us. A hypothetical story, designed to make the resurrection look absurd. Perhaps it echoes the book of Tobit, where a woman had seven husbands who all died. It is a debating-school construction, and seven is chosen because it is the number of completeness: pile it high enough and the doctrine looks ridiculous.

The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. Following the levirate law.

So too the second and third, down to the seventh. All seven died childless, each having married her in turn.

The logic of the trap. It is worth stating plainly, because it drives many objections that sound more sophisticated than they are. If your doctrine is true, this absurd situation follows; the situation is absurd; so your doctrine is false. Everything depends on the hidden premise. Here the premise is that resurrection means the resumption of this life exactly as it stands, with the same arrangements and the same property law. Jesus will deny the premise rather than the conclusion, which is usually where such arguments break.

The woman nobody sees. Notice her, because nobody in the story does. She is the only person in the scenario who has suffered anything. She has buried seven husbands, been handed on from brother to brother as a legal obligation, borne no children in a society where a childless widow had no protection, and died after a life of accumulated grief. And she appears in the argument purely as a difficulty, an object whose ownership must be decided. The Sadducees have taken a law that existed to protect destitute widows and used it to mock the one hope that would have comforted her. People who use other people as counters in an argument usually do not notice they are doing it.

In a sentence. The Sadducees told of a woman who married seven brothers in turn, all of whom died childless.

On a Tuesday. Clever arguments against God’s truth often rest on false assumptions. Look for them. And watch that you never turn real people into examples in your arguments. Behind every hard case is a person with a name, and Christ sees her.

For worship. The Lord sees the widow the debaters forgot. He is a father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5), and in his answer he gives her back what their question took away: in the resurrection she will not be the property of any brother, but herself, raised and glorified, beloved of God. The God of the resurrection is the God of every forgotten grief.

verseByVerse.quote: "After them all, the woman died. In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Last of all, the woman died. In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven? For they all had her.

## After them all, the woman died.

In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? The trap. If there is a resurrection, she would have seven husbands, which is absurd and against the law. So, they argued, the resurrection must be false. Moses, by giving this law, could not have believed in it.

For they all had her. All seven were married to her. The verb is to have and to hold as one’s own, and the assumption is baked into the whole question: seven men had a claim, the resurrection would produce a dispute, and a doctrine that produces disputes about property cannot be true.

The assumption. The Sadducees assumed that resurrection life would simply continue this life, with marriage and family arrangements carried on. The Pharisees taught the resurrection, and some may have described it in very earthly terms. Jesus will expose the assumption.

This life, improved? The error is not confined to Sadducees. Ask most people, including many Christians, what they expect of heaven, and you hear the present world improved: the same house without the mortgage, the same work without Monday, the same relationships without the friction. It is natural, since this world is the only material we have. But it is an extension, not a transformation, and it is why heaven strikes many people as faintly boring. Paul answers the same confusion with a seed: what you sow is not the body that is to be (1 Corinthians 15:37). The plant is truly continuous with the seed, and not remotely predictable from it. Nobody holding an acorn would guess an oak.

So will my resurrection body be real? Yes: real, physical and recognisable, and also transformed beyond anything we can extrapolate. The risen Christ ate fish in front of his friends and invited Thomas to touch his wounds (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27); his body was truly his. Yet it was raised imperishable, in glory and power (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Both halves must be held. Drop the first and you get a vague spiritual mist that Scripture never promises. Drop the second and you get the Sadducees’ question. We will be ourselves, body and soul, made fit at last for the presence of God.

In a sentence. The Sadducees asked whose wife the woman would be in the resurrection, trying to make the resurrection absurd.

On a Tuesday. Do not imagine heaven as simply this life continued. It is far greater. When you think of the age to come, begin not with what you will keep but with whom you will see: the Lord himself, face to face. Everything else will be good because he is there.

For worship. No eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him (1 Corinthians 2:9). The Sadducees could picture only a copy of the past; our God does new things. He will raise the dead in bodies like the glorious body of his Son, and the new creation will be as far beyond this one as the oak is beyond the acorn, yet it will be truly ours, and truly his.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered them, "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. In the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.

You are wrong. Literally “you are deceived”, “you have gone astray” (planasthe): led off the road. A strong statement to the leading priests, said in public, in front of a crowd. There is no diplomatic opening.

Because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Two errors. They did not understand the Scriptures, which teach the resurrection (vv. 31–32; Daniel 12:2; Isaiah 26:19; Job 19:25–27; Psalm 16:10). And they underestimated God’s power: the God who created life can raise the dead and create a new kind of life, not merely restore the old one (1 Corinthians 15:35–44). Every error about God comes from one of these: ignorance of Scripture or a small view of God’s power. These men had the Torah by heart, which is what makes the first charge so devastating: knowing the words is not the same as knowing what they say. And the second is worse. They believed in God and did not believe he could do anything; their God had been quietly cut down to the size of the arrangements they already understood.

For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage. Men “marry”; women were “given in marriage” by their fathers. Both halves of that world’s arrangements are simply absent. The Sadducees’ question does not get solved; it stops applying. Marriage belongs to this age. Its purposes, companionship, the bearing of children, and picturing Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32), will be fulfilled. In the resurrection, there is no death, so no need for children to continue the family line, which was the whole purpose of levirate marriage. And the marriage that earthly marriage pictured, between Christ and his people, will be complete (Revelation 19:7–9).

But are like angels in heaven. Like angels in not marrying, and in being immortal (Luke 20:36). The Sadducees did not believe in angels either (Acts 23:8), so Jesus is answering two of their denials at once. The comparison is made in one respect, and the sentence names it.

What it does not mean. Not that people become angels in heaven. Believers remain human, with resurrected bodies (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). Nor does it mean that husbands and wives will not know each other or love each other in heaven. Love will be perfected, not erased. But the exclusive bond of marriage will give way to a greater union, in which every relationship is perfected in Christ. Those who grieve a spouse need not fear that heaven will be less than marriage; it will be more.

Will I be with my husband or wife in heaven? If you are both in Christ, yes, and you will know each other better than you ever did here. What ends is the institution: the exclusive covenant of marriage, with its vows until death, which belonged to this age and to the raising of families. Love itself is not abolished; it is perfected. You will not know your beloved less in that day but far more, no longer through the narrow channel of one exclusive bond, but in the open light of a love with nothing in it left to fear or forgive. Marriage was always a signpost, not the destination: a picture of Christ and his church, and when the Bridegroom comes the picture gives way to what it was painting all along. We are not told every detail. It is enough to know that nothing good is lost in that country; it is taken up and made everlasting, with Christ at the centre of it.

What about someone who never married, or whose marriage was unhappy? This verse is good news for you too. The single person is not a lesser guest at the wedding of the Lamb; in the age to come no one is married to anyone but Christ, and his love is wholly theirs. And the one whose marriage brought grief or harm need not fear that it is fastened to them for ever. In the resurrection every relationship is healed or set free, and every believer belongs first and fully to the Bridegroom.

In a sentence. The Sadducees erred because they did not know Scripture or God’s power: in the resurrection there is no marriage, and people are immortal like the angels.

On a Tuesday. Study the Scriptures, and do not limit what God can do. Most errors come from one of those two mistakes. When you face something that seems impossible, a death, a ruined relationship, your own stubborn sin, ask which you are forgetting: what God has said, or what God can do.

For worship. Great is the power of our God, who calls into existence the things that do not exist and gives life to the dead (Romans 4:17). Death cannot hold his people, and the grave is not the end of any love that is in Christ. The Bridegroom is coming, and the marriage supper of the Lamb will gather every husband, wife, widow, single and child who belongs to him into a joy beside which every earthly joy was only a foretaste.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what God said to you: I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob? He is not God of the dead, but of the living.

And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees accepted. He does not reach for Daniel or Isaiah, where the resurrection is plainest; he argues on the only ground they acknowledged. “Said to you”: Scripture is God speaking to every generation, not merely an old record. He tells men in Jerusalem that a sentence spoken at a bush in the desert centuries before was addressed to them. The text is not merely a record of God having spoken but God speaking still.

I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Exodus 3:6, God’s words to Moses at the burning bush, centuries after the patriarchs had died.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living. How does this prove the resurrection? Not from the present tense of the verb, which is not actually in the Hebrew. The argument rests on the covenant. When God says “I am the God of Abraham”, he is naming himself by his covenant relationship with Abraham. That covenant included promises to Abraham himself: a land, a seed, a blessing, and God being his God (Genesis 17:7–8). Abraham died without receiving them (Hebrews 11:13). If death were the end of Abraham, then God would have failed to keep his promises, and his covenant would have been with a corpse. But God does not bind himself in covenant love to people only to abandon them to dust. A God who calls himself “the God of Abraham” must keep Abraham alive to enjoy the promises, and keep him whole, body and soul, since God made him a body-and-soul creature. So the covenant guarantees the resurrection. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are alive to God (Luke 20:38), and their bodies will be raised.

What it does not mean. Not that the patriarchs are already in their resurrection bodies. Their souls are with God now; their bodies await the resurrection at the last day (1 Thessalonians 4:16; Revelation 6:9–11). Nor is the argument a mere play on grammar. It is about who God is: the faithful God of the covenant, whose love outlasts death.

Where are believers who have died now? With the Lord, consciously, in joy. Their souls do not sleep or drift; to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and Paul calls departing to be with Christ far better (Philippians 1:23). The thief went to paradise that very day (Luke 23:43). There is no purgatory in between, for the blood of Christ has already cleansed them. Yet they wait for something more: the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return, when they and we will be raised together, whole (1 Thessalonians 4:14–17; Westminster 32.1).

What God does with names. Stop and consider whose names God chose. He might have named himself to Moses in any terms: maker of heaven and earth, the One who parts seas. What he said at the bush, and was content to be called for the rest of the Bible, is the God of three men. One lied about his wife twice. One was a passive father who loved the wrong son. One cheated his brother, wrestled with God and limped afterwards. God took their names into his own and kept them there, and on the strength of that bond Jesus tells a hostile court that the grave does not get them.

In a sentence. Because God binds himself in covenant to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and calls himself their God, they must live to receive his promises, and so the resurrection is certain.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to God, he is your God, and death cannot break that bond. Let that comfort you in grief and in the face of death. Put your own name where Abraham’s stands: the God of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and you. Say it at a graveside, and say it on the morning you are afraid of dying.

For worship. Praise the God of the living, who keeps his promises beyond the grave. He is not ashamed to be called their God (Hebrews 11:16), and he has prepared for them a city. He ties his eternal name to failing, limping sinners and will not let death have them. And he proved it when he raised his own Son, the firstfruits of all who sleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). Because he lives, they live, and we shall live also.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees held highest.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.

And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. Jesus had silenced the most powerful religious leaders with the Scriptures they claimed to know. Luke adds that some scribes said, Teacher, you have spoken well (Luke 20:39). The word (exeplēssonto) means struck out of themselves, knocked sideways. Matthew uses it of the Sermon on the Mount (7:28), of the synagogue at Nazareth (13:54), of the disciples when he said the rich would struggle to enter the kingdom (19:25), and here. It is not mild interest. These people had been hit by something.

A warning inside a victory. Note who they are: the ordinary crowd in the temple courts, pilgrims, tradesmen, families, many of the people who had lined the road on Sunday. They have watched their teachers comprehensively beaten by a Galilean, and they are delighted. And yet Matthew has shown us where such astonishment can go. Within three days a crowd gathered at the governor’s headquarters, worked on by the men who had just lost this argument, would shout for a murderer to be released instead of him (27:20–23). Astonishment is not allegiance. The difference between the crowd and the disciples in this Gospel is almost never the intensity of the reaction. It is whether anybody follows him out of the building.

Is it wrong to be moved in church? Not at all. God gave us the capacity, and the Psalms are full of it. Being moved by the truth is a good gift. But it is meant to lead somewhere: to repentance, trust, obedience and love. Ask what the last thing was that moved you deeply, and what it changed. If the honest answer is that it was a very good hour and nothing came of it, that is not a reason to despair. It is a reason to ask him for more than astonishment, and to act on the next thing he shows you.

In a sentence. The crowds were astonished at how Jesus answered the Sadducees.

On a Tuesday. Let Jesus’ teaching still astonish you. Read one of his answers slowly this week, and when it strikes you, do not leave it there: ask what it calls you to do, and do it before the feeling fades.

For worship. Never man spoke like this man. The Word made flesh opened the Scriptures in the temple courts, and the dead were declared alive in the God of Abraham. Let the astonishment of the crowd become in us the worship of the disciples, who were also astonished, and stayed, and followed him to the end, and saw him risen.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. One of them, an expert in the law, asked him a question to test him.

But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. “Silenced” literally means muzzled. The Pharisees may have been pleased that their rivals were defeated, but they were still opposed to Jesus. Read it from their side. Their old rivals, the party they had argued with for generations about this very doctrine, had been publicly defeated by a man defending the Pharisees’ own belief in the resurrection out of the Torah. They might have been delighted. Instead they close ranks and send in another questioner. Opposition to Christ is not, at bottom, a set of convictions that a better argument will correct. It is a disposition that survives every argument, including the ones it wins.

They gathered together against his Anointed. They gathered, perhaps echoing Psalm 2:2: the rulers take counsel together against the LORD and his Anointed. The early church saw it at once. After the first arrests the believers prayed that psalm back to God and named the people in it: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered together against your holy servant Jesus (Acts 4:25–27). The men regrouping in the temple court are standing inside a psalm, playing the part the psalm assigned them, and the psalm’s verdict on the whole enterprise is that the One enthroned in heaven laughs.

And one of them, a lawyer. An expert in the law of Moses, a scribe (Mark 12:28), brought forward because the question is technical and they want it asked properly.

Asked him a question to test him. The third test question. The participle (peirazōn) is the word used of the devil in the wilderness (4:1), of the demand for a sign (16:1), and of the Pharisees on divorce (19:3). Matthew has been keeping a quiet list of those who came to test Jesus. Mark presents this scribe more favourably: Jesus told him he was not far from the kingdom of God (Mark 12:34). Perhaps he was more sincere than those who sent him. And what follows is the greatest answer about the law ever given, drawn out by a test. God has never been prevented from saying something glorious by the poor motives of the person who asked.

Should I bother answering people who only want to argue? Usually, yes, with care. You do not know what is happening in the questioner’s heart; this scribe, sent to test, went away not far from the kingdom. Answer the question honestly and kindly, without trying to win, and let the truth do its work. There are times to decline, when someone is only mocking (7:6), but more often a hostile question is an open door. Jesus answered every one of these tests, and he answered them with the deepest truths he had.

In a sentence. After the Sadducees were silenced, the Pharisees gathered, and one of their law experts came to test Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Even a question asked to test can lead someone near the kingdom. Answer questions about your faith with care. Next time a colleague or relative throws a hard question at you, pray silently before you answer, and give him not a debating point but the heart of the matter.

For worship. The rulers take counsel together, and the Lord laughs; the plots of men cannot touch his purpose. He turns the testing questions of his enemies into the occasion for his clearest words, and he will turn every scheme against his Anointed into the triumph of his Son. Blessed are all who take refuge in him (Psalm 2:12).
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?

Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law? The rabbis debated which commandments were “heavy” and which were “light”, and whether one could sum up the law in a single principle. Later rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments in the law of Moses (248 positive and 365 negative). The traditional reckoning matched the positive ones to the bones of the body and the negative ones to the days of the year. Some teachers tried to summarise them all in one. The question may have been a test: would Jesus downplay some commands, or show himself unorthodox?

A trap with three jaws. Name one commandment great and you imply the others are small, a charge to take to the crowd. Name one associated with one party and you offend the rest. Refuse to answer and you are not the teacher you claim to be. And underneath sits a deeper assumption: that the law is an inventory, a list of separate items that a careful man might sort by importance, so that he could work out where to spend his attention. That way of holding God’s commands leaves the man himself untouched. He remains the one doing the sorting; however scrupulous he becomes, he is managing a portfolio.

What is my own list? Almost every Christian has a working list of the things that really matter and the things that are technically commanded, and almost nobody has written it down or would defend it out loud. The list is usually shaped to be keepable. That is the instinct this lawyer brought into the temple. Watch what Jesus does with it in the next verse: he names not one item from the list but the thing every item is made of, and you cannot manage a portfolio of love with all your heart. There is nothing left over to do the managing with.

In a sentence. The law expert asked Jesus which commandment was the greatest.

On a Tuesday. What do you think is the most important thing God asks of you? Compare your answer with Jesus’. If your honest answer is a rule you happen to keep well, or a duty that leaves your heart alone, read the next verse slowly.

For worship. The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul (Psalm 19:7). It is not a heap of 613 regulations but the expression of one holy, loving heart, and the One being questioned is the Lawgiver himself, who knows exactly what he meant by every word of it. He did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it (5:17), and in him the whole of it is kept.
verseByVerse.note: Later rabbis counted 613 commandments in the law; teachers debated which were weightiest.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment.

You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. From Deuteronomy 6:5, part of the Shema (“Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one”, Deuteronomy 6:4), which devout Jews recited twice daily. The command is love, not merely obedience: wholehearted, personal devotion to God. Love for God is not an emotion added on top of religious duty; it is the life without which no commandment is really kept at all.

Heart, soul, mind. Not three separate parts of a person, but a way of saying “with everything you are”. The heart is the centre of the person (will, desires, thoughts). The soul is the life, the self. The mind is the understanding (Deuteronomy says “might”, meaning strength; Mark includes both mind and strength, Mark 12:30). God wants all of you: your thinking, your desires, your will, your energy. Nothing held back.

Why do the Gospels give different lists? Matthew has three terms, Mark and Luke four (Mark 12:30; Luke 10:27), and Deuteronomy its own three: heart, soul and might. The question dissolves once you see what kind of list this is. It is not an inventory dividing a person into drawers; it is a Hebrew way of saying all of you, and the terms deliberately overlap and pile up. Jesus, like any teacher with a text everyone knew by heart, gives its full sense, not a word count. And the sense is the one thing all the versions agree on perfectly: the list has no edge you can stand outside of. Whatever you were about to hold back is named in it somewhere.

This is the great and first commandment. First in importance, and the source of all the others. All other commands flow from love for God. To keep every rule without loving God is to miss the point (15:8).

Why love? Because God first loved us (1 John 4:19; Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Love cannot be commanded into existence by willpower alone; it grows in response to love received. The gospel, showing us God’s love in Christ, is what makes this command possible.

What it does not mean. Not that love for God is only a feeling. In Scripture, love is shown in obedience (John 14:15), trust and worship. Nor does anyone keep this command perfectly except Christ. It shows us our sin and drives us to him, and it is the goal of the new heart he gives (Deuteronomy 30:6).

I do not feel much love for God. What do I do? First, do not measure love by your emotional temperature on a given morning. Biblical love is more than feeling, though never less: the Psalms are full of longing. But it is chiefly the settled direction of the whole person, which is why it can be commanded. Jesus gives a usable test: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15). Obedience is not a substitute for love; it is its most reliable evidence, available on days when feeling is not. Second, do not try to work on the love directly, which is like trying to feel warm by concentrating. Love is a response, and it rises with what is seen. Look longer at what God has done: read Scripture slowly rather than quickly, come to the Lord’s Supper, sing with God’s people, and remember particular mercies rather than mercy in general. And obey in the meantime. Feelings very often follow the feet.

The command no one has kept. See what this commandment does where it stands. A lawyer asks which command is greatest, and Jesus hands him the one nobody in the room has kept for a single hour. The law’s first and greatest word leaves everybody exposed, and the man saying it is on his way to the cross to keep it perfectly on their behalf. You are commanded to love God with all your heart and soul and mind; you have not; and the one who tells you so did exactly that, all the way to a cross, in your place. Start there, and the loving becomes possible, because it is no longer the price of anything.

In a sentence. The greatest commandment is to love God with all your heart, soul and mind: with everything you are.

On a Tuesday. What part of you is not yet given to God in love: your thinking, your desires, your time, your energy? Choose one this week. Give your mind to him by reading a Psalm slowly and thinking about who he is; give your time by setting aside a quiet half hour simply to thank him for specific mercies.

For worship. Only one man ever loved God with all his heart and soul and mind, every hour of his life: Jesus of Nazareth, who could say, I love the Father, and I do as the Father has commanded me (John 14:31). His perfect love is credited to all who trust him, and his Spirit pours the love of God into our hearts (Romans 5:5). We love because he first loved us, and the God who commands our whole love first gave us his whole Son.

parallels.desc: love the LORD your God with all your heart

verseByVerse.quote: "And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second is like it: you shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.

And a second is like it. The questioner asked for one; Jesus gives two, because they belong together. “Like it” (homoia) means of the same nature and importance. He does not say the second is nearly as important, or merely an application of the first. He puts loving your neighbour in the same category as loving God. Love for God shows itself in love for others (1 John 4:20–21).

You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18. Jesus joins two verses that were not usually linked. “Neighbour” includes everyone, even enemies (5:43–44; Luke 10:29–37). “As yourself” assumes that we naturally care for ourselves: we feed, protect and seek good for ourselves. We are to seek others’ good with the same energy.

As yourself. That is a far harder command than being nice, and it is worth testing where it bites. You do not have to remember to take an interest in your own toothache. Nobody sets a reminder to think about his own future, or needs encouragement to notice when he has been treated unfairly. That automatic, ever-present attention to your own case is the standard: give the same to the person next to you. Or take the excuses. When something goes wrong for you, the mind produces context at once: I was tired, it was difficult, anyone would have. When the same goes wrong at someone else’s hands, the mind produces character: he is careless, she is like that. Loving your neighbour as yourself means giving him the same generous supply of excuses you make for yourself, and it would reshape most families and churches within a fortnight.

Who is my neighbour? The command comes from Leviticus 19:18, where it applies first to fellow Israelites, and then in the same chapter to the foreigner: you shall love him as yourself (Leviticus 19:34). When a lawyer asked Jesus this question, he answered with the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37): your neighbour is anyone in need whom you can help. And Jesus has already said it includes enemies (5:43–48). In practice it begins with the people nearest you, your family, the people in your street, your church, your workplace, and reaches out to whoever God puts in your path.

On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets. “Depend” (krematai) literally means “hang”, as a door hangs on its hinges. Everything Moses wrote and everything the prophets thundered is suspended from two pegs; take them out and the whole structure is on the floor. Every command in the Old Testament is an expression of one or both of these. The first four of the Ten Commandments show how to love God; the last six show how to love our neighbour. Paul says love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:8–10). So the 613 items the lawyer wanted ranked are not 613 separate obligations at all. They are the outworking of two.

What it does not mean. Not that the specific commands of the law can be ignored as long as we have loving feelings. Love does not replace God’s law; it fulfils it. Love tells us why we obey; the law tells us how love behaves. Nor does “as yourself” command self-love as a separate duty, as some modern teaching suggests. It assumes the natural care we already have for ourselves.

Can I love God and not my neighbour? No. John puts it as bluntly as it can be put: if anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar (1 John 4:20). Not mistaken, not inconsistent: a liar. The love of God is not a private arrangement between a man and heaven that leaves the people in his house untouched. It comes down the stairs, or it was never on the roof. And the reverse holds too: love of neighbour cut off from love of God soon becomes either sentiment or self-congratulation. The two hinges hold the one door.

In a sentence. The second command is to love your neighbour as yourself, and the whole Old Testament hangs on these two commandments.

On a Tuesday. Who is the neighbour you find hardest to love? How would you treat them today if you loved them as yourself? Next time he fails, give him the explanation you would give yourself, and then do one practical thing for his good.

For worship. The law hangs on love because God is love. And the One who summed up the law in two commandments kept both perfectly: he loved the Father with all his heart, and he loved his neighbours, his enemies included, more than himself, laying down his life for them. In him the Law and the Prophets find their goal. Glory to the Son who did not only teach the great commandments but fulfilled them, and gives his people the Spirit to begin to keep them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, saying, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "The son of David."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question: what do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he? They said: the son of David.

Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question. Jesus has answered three tests; now he asks one himself. All day he has been answering: the wedding feast to the chief priests, the tax to the Pharisees and Herodians, the resurrection to the Sadducees, the great commandment to the lawyer. Now he puts one question of his own, and it is the only question in the chapter that finally matters.

What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he? The question that matters most. It is close to the question at Caesarea Philippi, where he had asked twelve friends, who do you say that I am? (16:15). Here, in the temple, surrounded by the men arranging his death, he asks it in the third person. It is the question this Gospel has been walking toward since the genealogy, and everyone in Matthew ends up answering it: Peter, the high priest, Pilate, the centurion at the cross.

They said to him, The son of David. The standard answer, and a correct one (1:1; 2 Samuel 7:12–16). But was it the whole truth? Most Jews expected the Messiah to be a human descendant of David, a great king who would restore Israel. It was what the blind men on the Jericho road had shouted (20:30). These men are not caught in an error. They are caught in an answer that is true and has stopped short.

Is a correct answer about Jesus enough? No. It is possible to hold an entirely correct doctrinal position about Jesus Christ and to have got no further than the position. These Pharisees could have passed an examination on the Messiah’s lineage. What they could not do was follow their own answer far enough to notice who was asking. A right answer is precious, and we must never despise sound doctrine. But it is meant to lead to the Person: to trust him, worship him and follow him. Jesus does not correct their answer. He asks them to keep reading.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whose son the Messiah is, and the Pharisees answered: David’s.

On a Tuesday. Your answer to what do you think about the Christ? is the most important answer of your life. Write your answer down in one sentence. Then ask whether your life this week looks like the life of someone who believes that sentence.

For worship. He is the son of David, heir of the everlasting throne promised to David’s house: his kingdom will have no end. Every promise God made to David stood in the temple courts that day, asking the question. And the King who asked it would soon wear a crown of thorns under a sign that called him King of the Jews, and would rise to sit on David’s throne for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: how is it then that David, speaking by the Spirit, calls him Lord? For he says: the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.

How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord. “In the Spirit”: inspired by the Holy Spirit. Jesus affirms that David wrote Psalm 110 and that it is God’s word.

The Lord said to my Lord. Psalm 110:1. In Hebrew: “The LORD (Yahweh) said to my Lord (Adonai)”. God speaks to David’s Lord, the Messiah. David, the greatest king of Israel, calls the Messiah his Lord: his superior, his master. No Jewish father would address his own descendant so.

Sit at my right hand. The place of highest honour and authority, beside God himself.

Until I put your enemies under your feet. The Messiah will reign until every enemy is defeated (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). Psalm 110:1 is quoted or alluded to in the New Testament more than any other Old Testament verse (Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13; 10:12–13). It describes Christ’s ascension and present reign.

Did David really write Psalm 110? Everything in the argument hangs on it, and it is widely denied: much modern scholarship assigns the psalm to a later court poet writing about a king, in which case there is no puzzle at all. Three things are worth weighing. The psalm carries its own heading, a Psalm of David, the oldest testimony we have about it. More striking is what happens in the room: these were hostile experts who wanted nothing so much as to catch him in a mistake, and the objection was available to them in a sentence. Nobody made it; no one was able to answer him a word (v. 46). And for a Christian the third consideration settles it. Jesus stakes a public argument about his own identity on David’s authorship, and says David spoke in the Spirit. A Lord who built his case on a premise he knew to be false would not be a Lord to trust on anything else. The authorship is not a detail on the edge of the passage; it is holding it up.

In a sentence. Jesus pointed out that in Psalm 110 David, inspired by the Spirit, calls the Messiah his Lord, enthroned at God’s right hand.

On a Tuesday. Christ is reigning now, at God’s right hand, until every enemy is under his feet. When the news, or your own life, makes it look as though evil is winning, read Psalm 110 and say it out loud: he is seated, and he is reigning, and the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.

For worship. Worship Christ, seated at God’s right hand, reigning until every enemy is under his feet. David bowed to him a thousand years before Bethlehem. The angels bow to him now. And at the name of Jesus every knee will bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth (Philippians 2:10). He is David’s Lord, and ours, and his throne is for ever and ever.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If David calls him Lord, how can he be his son? No one could answer him a word, and from that day no one dared to ask him any more questions.

If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son? In that culture, a father would never call his son “Lord”; a son honoured his father, not the reverse. How can the Messiah be both David’s son (his descendant) and David’s Lord (his superior)? The only answer: the Messiah is more than a human descendant of David. He is a man, born in David’s line (1:1), and he is God’s Son, the eternal Lord (16:16; Romans 1:3–4). Jesus is hinting at his own identity: fully human and fully divine.

One person, truly God and truly man. There is exactly one arrangement in which both halves are true at once, and it took the church centuries of careful argument to state it: the Christ is David’s son according to the flesh and David’s Lord according to his eternal nature, one person, truly God and truly man (Westminster 8.2). The son of Mary who was hungry on the road into Jerusalem is the same person who was with the Father before David was born. Matthew has been saying it since his first chapter, where the child in the genealogy of David is also the one called Immanuel, God with us (1:23). The riddle in the temple is his Gospel’s first chapter, put as a question.

And no one was able to answer him a word. The experts could not answer, because the answer was standing in front of them, and they would not accept it. Not a bad answer, not an evasion, not a counter-question: nothing.

Nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions. The tests are over. Jesus has silenced every group. Now he will speak against them (chapter 23), and then they will act against him (26:3–5). The next time these men open their mouths in his presence they will not be asking; they will be seeking witnesses against him (26:59). When argument has been exhausted, what remains is not always agreement. Sometimes it is the plot.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus denied being the son of David. He accepted the title (20:30–31; 21:9, 15). His point was that it was not enough. The Messiah is David’s son and David’s Lord.

Three kinds of silence. This chapter has shown us more than one. The man without the wedding garment was speechless because he had no defence (v. 12). These men are speechless because they will not say what they can see. And there is a third kind, which the psalm Jesus quoted points to: the silence of a man who stops arguing because he has finally understood who he is talking to. Every knee will bow and every mouth will be quiet in the end. The only question the chapter leaves open is which kind of quiet a person ends in, and the reason Jesus stood in that court all that Tuesday, answering delegation after delegation and then asking one question of his own, was to give the men in front of him time to choose the right one.

Why does it matter that Jesus is both God and man? Because only such a Saviour could save us. As man, he could take our place, obey the law we broke and die the death we deserved. As God, his obedience and death have infinite worth, enough to pay for all the sins of all his people, and he could not be held by death. A Saviour who was only man could not save; a Saviour who was not man could not stand in our place. That is why the answer to Jesus’ riddle is not a puzzle for scholars but the ground of every Christian’s hope.

In a sentence. Jesus showed that the Messiah must be more than David’s son, since David calls him Lord, and no one could answer him.

On a Tuesday. Is Jesus only a great man in history to you, or your Lord? He is both David’s son and David’s Lord, and yours. Let the silence of this verse be the right kind in you: stop arguing with him somewhere you have been resisting, and bow.

For worship. Great is the mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy 3:16). The root and the descendant of David (Revelation 22:16), David’s son and David’s Lord, the child of Bethlehem and the eternal Son enthroned at the Father’s right hand: this is our Saviour. Every question his enemies could ask fell silent before him, and the only fitting answer left is the one Thomas gave: my Lord and my God.

22.theology: Election and the free offer of the gospel. The parable of the wedding banquet and the phrase “many are called, but few are chosen” bring together two truths that Reformed theology has always insisted must be held together. The general call of the gospel goes out to all people without exception — “Go therefore to the main roads and invite as many as you find.” This is the free and genuine offer of the gospel, and it must be preached without restriction. At the same time, the effectual call of God draws the chosen to the feast. Both are real; both are necessary. The preacher does not know who the elect are; he simply opens the banquet doors as wide as the gospel goes and trusts God with the result.
22.examples:
Then: The religious leaders tried to trap Jesus with politics (tribute coin), doctrine (resurrection), law (greatest commandment). He answered all three with Scripture, clarity, and a question they could not answer. The one they thought to judge was the judge.

Now: The same four questions are still asked of Christians today — political, doctrinal, ethical, and Christological. The answers Jesus gives are still sufficient. Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s; God claims your whole self made in his image. The resurrection is secured by the living God who keeps covenant. Love God with everything; love your neighbour as yourself. And the Christ is both Son of David and Lord of David — the God-man who saves.

23.title: Woe to You, Scribes and Pharisees
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, <sup>2</sup>“The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat, <sup>3</sup>so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice. <sup>4</sup>They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. <sup>5</sup>They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, <sup>6</sup>and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues <sup>7</sup>and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. <sup>8</sup>But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers. <sup>9</sup>And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. <sup>10</sup>Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ. <sup>11</sup>The greatest among you shall be your servant. <sup>12</sup>Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. <sup>13</sup>“But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. <sup>15</sup>Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. <sup>16</sup>“Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.’ <sup>17</sup>You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? <sup>18</sup>And you say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.’ <sup>19</sup>You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred? <sup>20</sup>So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. <sup>21</sup>And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. <sup>22</sup>And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. <sup>23</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>24</sup>You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! <sup>25</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. <sup>26</sup>You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. <sup>27</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. <sup>28</sup>So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness. <sup>29</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, <sup>30</sup>saying, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.’ <sup>31</sup>Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. <sup>32</sup>Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. <sup>33</sup>You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? <sup>34</sup>Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town, <sup>35</sup>so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. <sup>36</sup>Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. <sup>37</sup>“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>38</sup>See, your house is left to you desolate. <sup>39</sup>For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”
23.overview:
Chapter 23 opens the fifth and final discourse of Matthew — and the most sorrowful. It begins with a warning to the crowds and disciples about the Pharisees (vv. 1–12), then delivers seven woes against the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 13–36), and closes with a lament over Jerusalem (vv. 37–39) that is one of the most heartbreaking passages in all of Scripture. The woes are not vindictive; they are diagnostic. Jesus names the disease precisely so that it can be seen for what it is: a religion of external performance concealing internal corruption, a leadership that burdens rather than shepherds, a tradition that has become a wall keeping people out of the kingdom.

The lament over Jerusalem (“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem”) reveals the heart behind the woes. Jesus does not pronounce judgment with cold severity; he pronounces it with the grief of a hen who would have gathered her chicks but could not because they would not come. The image is maternal, tender, aching. The holy Judge is also the loving Shepherd who weeps over the city he must judge. Both are true: God is not willing that any should perish, and God judges unrepentant hardness of heart. The cross, which is days away, is where both truths converge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Seven Woes: The Hypocrisy of Scribes and Pharisees (Part One)
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus turns from silencing his opponents to warning the crowds about them, and this is his last public address in Matthew. He concedes the office before he indicts the men: the scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, so what they read from it binds Israel even when their lives do not match it. Then the indictment — burdens tied on other people's shoulders and not lifted with a finger, phylacteries widened and fringes lengthened to be seen, titles and seats and greetings craved — followed by the levelling of the disciples under one Teacher and one Father. The first three woes follow: shutting the kingdom in people's faces, making converts twice as much children of hell, and the whole scribal machinery of binding and non-binding oaths.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter begins with a distinction the church has needed ever since: the authority of a pulpit is borrowed, every word of it. When a man sits on Moses' seat and reads out what God has said, the hearer is bound and the messenger's hypocrisy does not release him; when he steps off that seat, the conscience is free. So do and observe whatever they tell you is not a blank endorsement of Pharisaic teaching, which this same Gospel calls leaven (16:12) and says made void the commandment of God (15:6). On titles, the reason given is Christological rather than merely moral: no disciple is to be called rabbi because the seat is occupied — there is one Teacher, and he names him as the Christ. And the first woe is the head of all seven. The other six describe men damaging themselves; this one describes men standing in a doorway between other people and the kingdom, and it is put first for that reason.
verseByVerse.examples: The burdens are worth making concrete: thirty-nine categories of forbidden Sabbath work, each subdivided, down to whether a chair might be dragged in case dragging scratched a furrow. None of it was invented by wicked men; it was produced by serious people trying to be careful, which is how such systems are always produced. And the same tradition supplied the devices by which those who knew it could live within it — so the men who designed the yoke were the ones least troubled by it. Matthew makes the contrast with the same noun: heavy burdens here (phortia), and my burden is light at 11:30 (phortion). The phylacteries and fringes were both commanded, and Jesus wore the fringes himself (9:20) — the objection is to the width and the length, which is why this woe cannot be legislated against. The test that gets underneath it is not what you do but who is watching: take something genuinely good in your religious life, suppose it were certain nobody would ever know of it, and see what quietly deflates.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples: the scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat.

The setting. Chapter 23 is Jesus’ last public teaching in Matthew, given in the temple on the Tuesday before his death. After silencing his opponents (22:46), he now warns the crowds and his disciples against them, and then speaks directly to the scribes and Pharisees in seven “woes”. The chapter ends with his lament over Jerusalem. It is the most severe speech in the Gospels.

Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples. The warning is for ordinary people and for his followers: do not be like them.

The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. “Moses’ seat” stands for the authority to teach and interpret the law of Moses. Some synagogues had a stone chair at the front for the teacher of the law; one was found at Chorazin. The scribes and Pharisees were the recognised teachers of the law, in Moses’ place. “Sit” may suggest they had taken the seat themselves.

What it does not mean. Not that every scribe and Pharisee was a hypocrite. Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, Gamaliel and Paul came from among them. Jesus speaks of the movement as a whole, and its characteristic sins. Nor is this chapter a licence for Christians to despise Jews. Its warnings apply above all to religious people today, including Christians and church leaders.

In a sentence. Jesus began his warning about the scribes and Pharisees, who held the authority to teach Moses’ law.

On a Tuesday. Read this chapter as a mirror, not a window. The question is not “How bad were the Pharisees?” but “Where am I like them?”
verseByVerse.note: “Moses’ seat” stands for the authority to teach the law; synagogues may have had a stone chair for the teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: "so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do. For they preach, but do not practise.

So do and observe whatever they tell you. In so far as they teach the law of Moses faithfully, it should be obeyed. The word of God does not lose its authority because the teacher is a hypocrite. Jesus has already criticised their traditions (15:1–20), so “whatever they tell you” means whatever they teach from Moses, not their added rules.

But not the works they do. Do not follow their example.

For they preach, but do not practice. The heart of hypocrisy: saying without doing. Paul makes the same charge (Romans 2:21–23): you who teach others, do you not teach yourself?

What it does not mean. Not that we should follow every teaching of a leader simply because of his position. Jesus has warned against blind guides (15:14) and their leaven (16:12). Every teaching must be tested by Scripture. But truth from God’s word is to be obeyed, whoever speaks it.

In a sentence. Obey God’s law when they teach it, but do not follow their example, because they do not practise what they preach.

On a Tuesday. Do you practise what you preach to your children, your colleagues, your friends? Hypocrisy is not only a sin of leaders.

parallels.desc: you who teach others, do you not teach yourself?

verseByVerse.quote: "They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves will not lift a finger to move them.

They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear. The picture is of a load tied up in a bundle and placed on a pack animal or a porter. The burdens were the many rules the Pharisees added to the law: Sabbath regulations, purity rules, tithing details (12:1–14; 15:1–9). They made religion an exhausting load. Peter later called the law, as the Pharisees taught it, a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10).

And lay them on people’s shoulders. They demanded that others carry them.

But they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. Two meanings. Either they did not keep the rules themselves (finding loopholes, as with Corban, 15:5), or they gave no help to those weighed down by them: no compassion, no grace, no assistance. Contrast Jesus: come to me, all who are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; my yoke is easy and my burden is light (11:28–30).

What it does not mean. Not that God’s commands are burdensome in themselves (1 John 5:3). The problem is human rules added to God’s word, and religion without grace.

In a sentence. The Pharisees loaded people with heavy religious rules and would not lift a finger to help them carry them.

On a Tuesday. Are you placing burdens on others that God has not placed: rules, expectations, standards? And are you helping those who are weighed down?

parallels.desc: a yoke our fathers could not bear

verseByVerse.quote: "They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do all their deeds to be seen by others. They make their phylacteries wide and their tassels long, and they love the place of honour at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues.

They do all their deeds to be seen by others. Their religion was a performance (6:1–18). They wanted applause.

For they make their phylacteries broad. Phylacteries (tefillin) were small leather boxes containing tiny scrolls of Scripture passages (Exodus 13:1–16; Deuteronomy 6:4–9; 11:13–21), strapped to the forehead and left arm during prayer. They came from a literal reading of God’s command to bind his words as a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes (Deuteronomy 6:8). Making them broad showed off one’s devotion.

And their fringes long. The tassels on the corners of the outer garment, commanded by God to remind Israel of his commandments (Numbers 15:38–40). Jesus himself wore them (9:20). Making them long drew attention.

And they love the place of honor at feasts. Seats nearest the host, a sign of status (Luke 14:7–11).

And the best seats in the synagogues. The front seats facing the congregation, where everyone could see them.

What it does not mean. Not that religious symbols or clothing are wrong in themselves. The phylacteries and tassels were based on God’s commands. The problem was using them for display. Nor does it forbid honouring leaders appropriately (1 Timothy 5:17). The sin is loving honour.

In a sentence. The Pharisees did their religious acts to be admired, exaggerating their religious dress and loving the best seats.

On a Tuesday. What do you do to be seen as spiritual: by others, or on social media? Do it for God alone.
verseByVerse.note: Phylacteries were small leather boxes holding verses of Scripture, strapped to the forehead and arm. Fringes were the tassels on a garment’s corners.

parallels.desc: bind them on your hand and between your eyes

verseByVerse.quote: "and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They love greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi. But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers.

And greetings in the marketplaces. Respectful public greetings, in which ordinary people would stop and bow to them.

And being called rabbi by others. “Rabbi” means “my great one”, “my master”, a title of respect for a teacher of the law. It was becoming a formal title.

But you are not to be called rabbi. Jesus’ disciples must not seek titles that set them above others.

For you have one teacher. Christ himself (v. 10). Every Christian teacher is a student of the one Teacher, with no independent authority.

And you are all brothers. In Christ’s community, all are equal as brothers and sisters. There is no religious hierarchy of superior and inferior believers.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never use any titles at all, or that there are no teachers in the church. The New Testament speaks of teachers, elders and overseers (Ephesians 4:11; 1 Timothy 3:1–2; James 3:1), and honours them (Hebrews 13:17). Calling someone “pastor” or “doctor” is not forbidden. What is forbidden is the love of titles and status, and the spirit that sets leaders above other believers as masters. The test is the heart: do we want the title for the honour, or do we serve as brothers under one Master?

In a sentence. Jesus forbade his disciples to seek titles of honour, because they have one Teacher and are all brothers.

On a Tuesday. Do you care about titles, position or recognition in the church? Remember that you are a brother or sister, under one Teacher.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabbi” means “my great one,” a title of respect for a teacher.

parallels.desc: not many of you should become teachers

verseByVerse.quote: "And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. And do not be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ.

And call no man your father on earth. “Father” (abba) was used of revered teachers and leaders, the “fathers” of tradition. Jesus forbids giving any human being the kind of spiritual authority that belongs only to God.

For you have one Father, who is in heaven. God alone is our Father in the ultimate sense (6:9).

Neither be called instructors. “Instructor” (kathēgētēs) means a guide, a tutor, a leader.

For you have one instructor, the Christ. Jesus calls himself the Christ, the one instructor. He claims an authority equal to the Father’s.

What it does not mean. Not that we cannot call our natural fathers “father”. Jesus himself honoured father and mother (15:4). Paul called himself a spiritual father to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 4:15) and Timothy his son (1 Timothy 1:2). Jesus speaks against titles that give human leaders a status that belongs to God. Protestants have often applied this verse against the Roman Catholic and Orthodox practice of calling priests “Father”. The real issue is not the word but the attitude: no human leader may stand between the believer and God as an authority over conscience.

In a sentence. No human leader may be given the ultimate authority of a spiritual father or instructor, because God is our one Father and Christ our one instructor.

On a Tuesday. Do you treat any Christian leader as if their word were final? Respect your leaders, but your ultimate authority is Christ.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?
one God, the Father, and one Lord

verseByVerse.quote: "The greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest among you must be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
