The greatest among you shall be your servant. The same teaching as 20:26–28. True greatness is service. The Pharisees sought honour; Jesus’ followers seek to serve.

Whoever exalts himself will be humbled. God brings down the proud (Proverbs 3:34; Luke 1:51–52). Self-exaltation ends in humiliation, if not now, then at the judgment.

And whoever humbles himself will be exalted. God lifts up the humble (James 4:10; 1 Peter 5:6). Jesus himself humbled himself to the cross, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9). The passive “will be exalted” means by God.

What it does not mean. Not that we should humble ourselves as a strategy to get exalted. True humility does not seek a reward. But God does honour it.

In a sentence. The greatest must be servants, for God humbles the proud and exalts the humble.

On a Tuesday. How can you serve someone in your church this week in a way that no one will notice?

verseByVerse.quote: "But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. You neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in.

But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! The first of seven woes. A “woe” (ouai) is a cry of grief and warning, announcing coming judgment, used by the prophets (Isaiah 5:8–23; Habakkuk 2:6–19). It is the opposite of “blessed” (5:3–12). Jesus speaks not with glee but with sorrow; the chapter ends in tears (v. 37). The seven woes may deliberately contrast with the eight Beatitudes.

For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. As teachers of the law, they held the “keys” of knowledge (Luke 11:52). They should have opened the way to God. Instead, by rejecting Jesus and teaching a religion of human merit, they slammed the door shut.

For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. They refused Jesus, and they discouraged others from following him (John 9:22; 12:42). False teaching is doubly destructive: it damns the teacher and those he leads.

In a sentence. The first woe: the scribes and Pharisees shut the kingdom in people’s faces, refusing to enter and stopping others.

On a Tuesday. Is anything in your life or church making it harder for people to come to Christ: legalism, coldness, hypocrisy?
verseByVerse.note: A woe is a solemn lament and warning of judgment, used by the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You travel across sea and land to make a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 14: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows’ houses and for a pretence you make long prayers; therefore you will receive the greater condemnation.” It is missing in the earliest manuscripts and was probably copied from Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. Verdict: not original in Matthew, though Jesus did say it.

For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte. A proselyte was a Gentile who converted fully to Judaism, through circumcision, baptism and sacrifice. Some Pharisees were zealous in seeking converts, though the extent of Jewish missionary activity is debated. They took great effort to win even one.

And when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. “Child of hell” (literally “son of Gehenna”) means someone who belongs to hell, destined for it. Converts often become more zealous than their teachers. The Pharisees taught them a religion of rules without grace, and their converts adopted it with double fervour. They became more legalistic, more proud, and further from God.

What it does not mean. Not that evangelism or zeal for converts is wrong. Jesus commands it (28:19). The problem is converting people to the wrong thing: to a system or a party rather than to God; to rules rather than grace. Christians can fall into the same trap, making converts to a denomination, a culture or a set of rules rather than to Christ.

In a sentence. The second woe: they worked hard to win converts, but made them even worse than themselves.

On a Tuesday. When you share your faith, are you bringing people to Christ, or to your church culture and preferences?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 14, a woe about devouring widows’ houses and long prayers for a pretence. A proselyte was a Gentile convert to Judaism.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, blind guides, who say, 'If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.' You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, blind guides, who say: if anyone swears by the temple, it means nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath. You blind fools! Which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred?

Woe to you, blind guides. The third woe (see 15:14). They claimed to guide the blind, but could not see.

Who say, “If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing.” “Nothing” means it is not binding. They had developed a system of oaths (see 5:33–37). An oath sworn by the temple could be broken; an oath sworn by the temple’s gold, its treasury or golden decorations, was binding.

But if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath. These rules allowed a man to choose in advance which of his oaths he would keep. Someone could swear impressively “by the temple” and know he was not bound. It was a system of legalised lying.

You blind fools! “Fools” (mōroi) means morally foolish, people who reject God’s wisdom. Jesus forbade calling a brother “fool” in contempt (5:22), but here he is not insulting a brother in anger; he is making a judgment about their teaching, as God’s word does (Psalm 14:1).

For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? The gold was holy only because it belonged to the temple, God’s house. The temple was greater. Their priorities were upside down. They valued the gold more than the God it was dedicated to.

In a sentence. The third woe: their oath rules were absurd and dishonest, valuing the temple’s gold above the temple itself.

On a Tuesday. Do you leave yourself loopholes in your promises? Let your yes be yes (5:37).
verseByVerse.note: These rules let a man decide which of his oaths were binding.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you say, 'If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.' You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you say: if anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift on the altar, he is bound by his oath. You blind men! Which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred?

And you say, “If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing.” The same evasion. The altar of burnt offering stood in the temple court, where sacrifices were offered.

But if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath. The gift was the sacrifice placed on the altar.

You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred? The altar made the gift holy (Exodus 29:37). Again, they valued the lesser thing above the greater.

In a sentence. They also taught that oaths by the altar did not bind, but oaths by the gift did, absurdly valuing the gift above the altar that made it holy.

On a Tuesday. Our values can become upside down, valuing the gift above the Giver. What do you value more than God?

parallels.desc: whatever touches the altar shall become holy

verseByVerse.quote: "So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by the one who dwells in it.

So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. You cannot separate the altar from its gifts.

And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. God himself dwells in the temple (1 Kings 8:13; Psalm 26:8). Every oath by the temple is an oath by God. You cannot escape him by swearing by something else.

In a sentence. Every oath by the altar or the temple is really an oath by God who dwells there, so all such oaths bind.

On a Tuesday. Every promise you make is made before God, whether or not you mention his name.

parallels.desc: a place for you to dwell in forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits on it.

And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. Heaven is God’s throne (5:34; Isaiah 66:1). All oaths, however phrased, involve God. Their system of evasions was a lie before the God who sees everything.

In a sentence. An oath by heaven is an oath by God himself, who sits on its throne.

On a Tuesday. Live as one who speaks every word before God’s throne. Be truthful in everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–39 — Seven Woes Concluded and the Lament over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last four woes drive from the outside inward: tithed garden herbs while justice, mercy and faithfulness are neglected; a cup scoured outside and full of plunder within; whitewashed tombs; and monuments built to murdered prophets by men arranging a murder. Then the language hardens further — serpents, brood of vipers, fill up the measure of your fathers — and the blood of the righteous from Abel to Zechariah is laid on that generation. And then the voice breaks: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem… how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing. The chapter ends not on desolation but on a single word: until.
verseByVerse.theology: Woe and lament sit in one chapter and must be held together, because each without the other is a distortion. Woe is ouai, the prophets' cry of grief rather than a curse, and it is aimed with precision: not at sinners — no harsh word in this Gospel ever falls on a prostitute, a tax collector or a dying thief — but at men shutting the door on them. Severity toward a shepherd fleecing the flock is mercy toward the flock. Then the remedy, which is the most important clause here for anyone who reads the seven and wants out: first clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. The order is the whole difference between the gospel and moralism, and the promise is that the outside follows. It is also the one thing no one can do for himself, which is why the honest response is David's after his worst year: create in me a clean heart (Ps 51:10). And the measure of v. 32 explains the patience of God — judgment waited four hundred years for the Amorites' cup to fill (Gen 15:16) — without promising that the delay is permanent.
verseByVerse.examples: Two images repay their background. The gnat and the camel is a joke: straining wine through cloth to catch an unclean insect was ordinary practice, the camel was the largest unclean animal in the country, and in Aramaic the words chime — qalma and gamla. And the whitewashed tombs were limed before Passover not for beauty but as a warning, since touching a grave barred a pilgrim from the feast for seven days (Num 19:16); the mark meant to keep people away was what made them gleam. Which makes the charge worse than inconsistency: such men are contagious, and their respectability is the danger. The seventh woe is the one to watch for while reading this chapter — if we had lived in the days of our fathers is the cheapest sentence in the world, because the sins of a previous age are labelled and ours are still disguised as normal life. Everyone is certain he would have hidden Jews in 1942. The certainty costs nothing and is almost always false. The seven translated into their modern forms, and the guard on whether we may speak as Jesus does here, are set out in the verse-by-verse on vv. 33-34.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You tithe mint, dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!

For you tithe mint and dill and cumin. The fourth woe. A tithe was a tenth of one’s produce, given to God (Leviticus 27:30; Deuteronomy 14:22–23). The law required tithes of grain, wine and oil. The Pharisees extended it to the smallest garden herbs, counting out every tenth leaf of mint.

And have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. “Weightier” means more important. Justice means fairness to others, especially the poor and powerless. Mercy means compassion. Faithfulness means loyalty, both to God and to others. The prophets summed up God’s requirements this way: to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8; Hosea 6:6; Zechariah 7:9–10). The Pharisees were careful about small matters and careless about great ones.

These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. Jesus does not abolish tithing or condemn attention to detail. They should have done both. But the weightier matters come first.

You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! A comic, vivid picture. A gnat was the smallest unclean creature; a camel the largest (Leviticus 11:4, 20–23). Strict Jews strained their wine through cloth to avoid swallowing a gnat and becoming unclean. The Pharisees carefully avoided tiny sins, while swallowing enormous ones: injustice, cruelty, unfaithfulness. In Aramaic there may be a wordplay: gnat (qalma) and camel (gamla).

What it does not mean. Not that small matters of obedience do not matter. Jesus says they ought to tithe. Faithfulness in small things matters (25:21). Nor does it mean that Christians are bound to the Old Testament tithe as law. The New Testament calls for generous, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 8–9), and many Christians rightly use the tithe as a starting point. The point is priority: justice, mercy and faithfulness are the heart of God’s law.

In a sentence. The fourth woe: they carefully tithed tiny herbs while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness, straining out gnats and swallowing camels.

On a Tuesday. Are you careful about small religious duties while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness toward the people around you?
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to kitchen herbs. Both gnats and camels were unclean; wine was strained through cloth to remove insects.

parallels.desc: a tithe of the seed of the land
do justice, love kindness, walk humbly

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, so that the outside also may be clean.

For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate. The fifth woe. The Pharisees had detailed rules about ritually cleaning dishes (Mark 7:4). The picture is of someone who washes the outside of a cup but leaves it dirty inside.

But inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. “Greed” (harpagēs) means robbery, plunder: what they filled their cups with was gained by exploiting others. “Self-indulgence” means lack of self-control. Their outward religion covered inner corruption. The cup represents their lives: clean outside, filthy inside.

You blind Pharisee! Singular: Jesus addresses each one personally.

First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. Inner change must come first. A clean heart produces a clean life (15:18–20). Outward religion without inward cleansing is useless. Only God can cleanse the heart (Psalm 51:10; Ezekiel 36:25–26).

What it does not mean. Not that outward behaviour does not matter. It does: the outside should also be clean. But the order is inside first.

In a sentence. The fifth woe: they cleaned the outside of their lives while the inside was full of greed, when inner cleansing must come first.

On a Tuesday. What is inside your “cup” that no one else sees? Ask God to clean it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness. So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful on the outside but inside are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness.

For you are like whitewashed tombs. The sixth woe. Tombs were whitewashed each spring, before Passover, so that pilgrims could see them clearly and avoid touching them accidentally. Touching a tomb or a dead body made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), which would prevent them from celebrating the Passover. At this very time, just before Passover, the tombs around Jerusalem would have been freshly whitewashed, gleaming in the sun.

Which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. A bright white exterior hiding death and decay. The most unclean thing imaginable to a Jew.

So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness. They looked holy; they were spiritually dead. And worse: as touching a tomb made people unclean, contact with their teaching corrupted others. “Lawlessness” (anomia): for all their law-keeping, inside they were lawless (7:23).

In a sentence. The sixth woe: like freshly whitewashed tombs, they looked beautiful and righteous outside but were full of death and corruption inside.

On a Tuesday. Is your Christian life a whitewash: looking good on Sunday, but dead inside? Ask God for real life within.
verseByVerse.note: Tombs were whitewashed so that passers-by would not touch them by accident and become unclean.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, saying, 'If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, saying: if we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.

For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous. The seventh woe. In Jesus’ time there was a fashion for building elaborate monuments to the prophets and righteous people of the past. Herod the Great built a monument at David’s tomb. These still stand in the Kidron Valley, east of the temple: monuments popularly linked to Absalom, Zechariah and others.

Saying, “If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.” They honoured the dead prophets and claimed they would never have killed them. They felt superior to their ancestors. It is easy to honour prophets who are safely dead.

In a sentence. The seventh woe: they honoured the dead prophets with monuments, claiming they would never have killed them.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to honour past heroes of faith. Would you have stood with them when it was costly? Do you stand with the faithful today?

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who murdered the prophets. Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers.

Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. By calling the murderers “our fathers”, they admitted they were their descendants. And in Hebrew thought, a “son” shares his father’s character. Their claim to be better was false: they were about to kill the greatest prophet of all, the Son (21:38–39).

Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. Irony and judgment. Their ancestors had filled the cup of guilt partly; they would fill it to the brim by killing Jesus. Sin accumulates until judgment falls (Genesis 15:16; 1 Thessalonians 2:16).

In a sentence. By calling the prophets’ murderers their fathers, they confessed their likeness to them, and they would complete their fathers’ guilt.

On a Tuesday. We are not automatically better than those who came before us. Ask God to show you the sins of your own generation.

parallels.desc: which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?

verseByVerse.quote: "You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You snakes, you brood of vipers, how will you escape being sentenced to hell? Therefore I am sending you prophets, wise men and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town.

You serpents, you brood of vipers. John’s words (3:7), and Jesus’ before (12:34). Snakes and the offspring of snakes: children of the serpent, the devil (John 8:44).

How are you to escape being sentenced to hell? “Hell” is Gehenna (5:22). If they continue to reject him, they cannot escape judgment.

Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes. Jesus speaks as God, who sends prophets (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). Luke says: the Wisdom of God said, I will send them prophets and apostles (Luke 11:49). Jesus speaks as God’s Wisdom in person. The “prophets, wise men and scribes” are his apostles and followers, the Christian messengers.

Some of whom you will kill and crucify. Stephen was killed (Acts 7:58–60); James was killed (Acts 12:2); Peter, by tradition, was crucified.

And some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town. Paul himself had done this before his conversion (Acts 22:19; 26:11), and later suffered it (2 Corinthians 11:24).

In a sentence. Jesus warned his opponents that they could not escape judgment, and that they would persecute and kill the messengers he would send.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those today who are flogged and persecuted from town to town for Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna.

verseByVerse.quote: "so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. Truly, all these things will come upon this generation.

So that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth. The guilt of all the murders of God’s servants will come on this generation, because they will complete the pattern by killing the Son, the culmination of all rejection.

From the blood of righteous Abel. The first murder in the Bible: Abel, killed by his brother Cain (Genesis 4:8). His blood cried out from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

To the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. The last murder recorded in the Hebrew Bible, which ends with 2 Chronicles. Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest was stoned in the temple court at the king’s command, and as he died he said, May the LORD see and avenge (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). “From Abel to Zechariah” means “from A to Z”, the first to the last martyr in Scripture. Why “son of Barachiah”? The prophet Zechariah, who wrote the book of Zechariah, was the son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). Possible explanations: Jehoiada may have been Zechariah’s grandfather (with Barachiah his father), as “son” can mean descendant; or the names have been conflated in transmission (Luke 11:51 omits the father’s name); or Jesus combines the two Zechariahs, both prophets, both martyrs by tradition. Verdict: uncertain; the point is clear: from the first to the last martyr.

Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. Within that generation, judgment fell: the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70 (24:34).

What it does not mean. Not that the Jewish people as a whole bear guilt for all time for Jesus’ death. This has been tragically misused to justify persecution of Jews. Jesus is speaking of the generation that rejected him and of the judgment on Jerusalem. All humanity was responsible for the death of Christ, and he died for sinners of every nation, Jew and Gentile (Acts 4:27–28).

In a sentence. The guilt of all the martyrs, from Abel to Zechariah, would fall on the generation that killed the Son.

On a Tuesday. God remembers the blood of every martyr. Their suffering is not forgotten. Pray for persecuted Christians today.
verseByVerse.note: Abel is the first murder in Scripture; Zechariah’s is the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order, which ends with Chronicles. On “son of Barachiah,” see the commentary.

parallels.desc: Zechariah stoned in the temple court
blood that speaks a better word than Abel’s

verseByVerse.quote: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! See, your house is left to you desolate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! See, your house is left to you desolate.

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem. The double name expresses deep emotion, like David crying “O my son Absalom, my son, my son” (2 Samuel 18:33). Jesus’ denunciation turns to lament. Luke says he wept over the city (Luke 19:41).

The city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! Jerusalem, the holy city, had the worst record of rejecting God’s messengers.

How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings. A tender, motherly image. A hen spreads her wings over her chicks to protect them from danger, from a hawk or a fire. God is pictured in the Old Testament as a bird protecting her young (Deuteronomy 32:11; Psalm 91:4; Ruth 2:12). “How often”: Jesus speaks as the God who had sent prophet after prophet, longing to protect his people. He may also mean his own repeated visits to Jerusalem (John 2; 5; 7; 10).

And you were not willing! The tragedy. God was willing; they were not. They refused his protection.

See, your house is left to you desolate. “Your house” is the temple, and perhaps the city. No longer called “my house” (21:13), but “your house”. God’s presence will leave it, as in Ezekiel’s vision when the glory left the temple before its destruction (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Jeremiah 22:5 warned that the king’s house would become a desolation. Immediately after this, Jesus leaves the temple for the last time (24:1).

God’s will and human refusal. How can God be sovereign over salvation and yet grieve that people were not willing? Scripture holds both truths. God sincerely calls people to repent and grieves when they refuse (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11; 2 Peter 3:9). And God sovereignly works all things according to his purpose, including who is saved (Ephesians 1:11; Romans 9:16). Reformed theology distinguishes God’s revealed will (what he commands and desires, in the sense of what pleases him) from his decreed will (what he has determined will happen). Jesus’ tears are real. People who perish do so because they were not willing; those who are saved are saved because God made them willing (Psalm 110:3). We may not fully see how both fit together, but both are taught.

In a sentence. Jesus lamented over Jerusalem, which killed the prophets and refused his tender protection, and announced that its temple would be left desolate.

On a Tuesday. Jesus longs to gather people under his wings. Are you sheltering there? And does your heart break, as his did, for those who refuse him?

For worship. Thank Jesus for his tender, protecting love, like a hen gathering her chicks.

parallels.desc: under his wings you will find refuge
this house shall become a desolation

verseByVerse.quote: "For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I tell you, you will not see me again until you say: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

For I tell you, you will not see me again. Jesus is leaving the temple, and the city’s leaders will not see him again in his public ministry. After his trial and death, they will not see him until he returns.

Until you say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Psalm 118:26, the words the crowds sang at his entry (21:9). This may be a hope: one day Jerusalem will welcome its Messiah. Paul speaks of a future turning of many Jews to Christ (Romans 11:25–27). Or it may be a warning: when he returns in glory, they will have to acknowledge him, willingly or not (Philippians 2:10–11; Zechariah 12:10). Verdict: both. At his return every knee will bow; and there is hope that many in Israel will welcome him with faith, as Romans 11 teaches.

In a sentence. Jerusalem will not see Jesus again until it acknowledges him as the one who comes in the Lord’s name.

On a Tuesday. Pray for Jewish people to come to know Jesus as their Messiah.

For worship. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

23.theology: The danger of religious hypocrisy. Matthew 23 is the most sustained treatment of hypocritical religion in the New Testament. The Reformers used it relentlessly against the medieval Catholic establishment; every subsequent generation has needed to hear it applied to itself. The structural sin of the Pharisees — outward conformity concealing inward corruption, burden-laying without burden-sharing, precision in minor matters and blindness to major ones — is the perennial disease of organized religion. The only cure is genuine regeneration: the new heart of Ezekiel 36 that produces obedience from the inside rather than performance for the outside. The woes are also a mirror: every reader must ask which whitewashed tomb they are decorating.
23.examples:
Then: The Pharisees were the most theologically serious people in first-century Judaism. They memorized Scripture, tithed fastidiously, prayed publicly, and honoured the tradition of the fathers. And Jesus pronounced seven woes over them. Theological seriousness and religious diligence are not equivalent to knowing God.

Now: Every church tradition has its own version of the Pharisaic trap: the evangelical who is doctrinally precise but personally unkind; the liturgical churchgoer who loves the service but not the neighbour; the activist who fights for justice but has no interior life. The woes are not for the obviously wicked but for the outwardly religious. That is why they are so searching. The question is not “Am I religious?” but “Does my religion proceed from a heart that loves God and loves my neighbour?”

24.title: The End of the Age
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Jesus left the temple and was going away, when his disciples came to point out to him the buildings of the temple. <sup>2</sup>But he answered them, “You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>3</sup>As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?” <sup>4</sup>And Jesus answered them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>5</sup>For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will lead many astray. <sup>6</sup>And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>7</sup>For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places. <sup>8</sup>All these are but the beginning of the birth pains. <sup>9</sup>“Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death, and you will be hated by all nations for my name’s sake. <sup>10</sup>And then many will fall away and betray one another and hate one another. <sup>11</sup>And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. <sup>12</sup>And because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold. <sup>13</sup>But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>14</sup>And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come. <sup>15</sup>“So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), <sup>16</sup>then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. <sup>17</sup>Let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take what is in his house, <sup>18</sup>and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. <sup>19</sup>And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! <sup>20</sup>Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath. <sup>21</sup>For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be. <sup>22</sup>And if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short. <sup>23</sup>Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘There he is!’ do not believe it. <sup>24</sup>For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. <sup>25</sup>See, I have told you beforehand. <sup>26</sup>So, if they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out. If they say, ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. <sup>27</sup>For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>28</sup>Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather. <sup>29</sup>“Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. <sup>30</sup>Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. <sup>31</sup>And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. <sup>32</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>33</sup>So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>34</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>35</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>36</sup>“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only. <sup>37</sup>For as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>38</sup>For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, <sup>39</sup>and they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>40</sup>Then two men will be in the field; one will be taken and one left. <sup>41</sup>Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left. <sup>42</sup>Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming. <sup>43</sup>But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what part of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into. <sup>44</sup>Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. <sup>45</sup>“Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his master has set over his household, to give them their food at the proper time? <sup>46</sup>Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>47</sup>Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>48</sup>But if that wicked servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’ <sup>49</sup>and begins to beat his fellow servants and eats and drinks with drunkards, <sup>50</sup>the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know <sup>51</sup>and will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
24.overview:
The Olivet Discourse (chapters 24–25) is Jesus’ extended teaching on the end of the age, delivered on the Mount of Olives overlooking the temple. It is the most complex and debated passage in Matthew, weaving together two horizons: the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 and the final coming of the Son of Man at the end of history. Jesus deliberately leaves the two horizons blurred, because the near event (Jerusalem’s fall) is the type and foretaste of the far event (the final judgment).

The chapter resists every system that charts the future with calendar precision. “No one knows the day or the hour” (v. 36) is not a temporary limitation but a theological statement: the appropriate posture before the end is not calculation but watchfulness, not a schedule but readiness. The gospel of the kingdom must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 14) — the mission is the church’s present calling. The Son of Man will come as lightning, suddenly and unmistakably. Until then: stay awake.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — Signs of the End and the Great Tribulation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus walks out of the temple and tells the disciples that not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives they ask three questions as though they were one: when will this happen, what will be the sign of your coming, and when is the end of the age. His answer runs through false messiahs, wars and famines that are expressly not the end, betrayal inside the church and love growing cold, the promise that endurance marks the saved and the gospel will reach all nations, the abomination of desolation and the order to run for the hills, a tribulation cut short for the elect, and a final warning that his coming will be as unmistakable as lightning.
verseByVerse.theology: The discourse answers a compound question and therefore has a compound shape, in the manner of Old Testament prophecy, which repeatedly sees a near horizon and a far one in one view. Everything to v. 35 is hedged with signs and set inside a generation; from v. 36 there are no signs at all. The judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 is both a real event and a type of the last one. Two doctrinal loads are carried in this half. Endurance to the end is the mark of genuine salvation rather than a feat the anxious must manage, kept by the God who promises to keep. And the days are cut short for the sake of the elect: the duration of the worst years in that nation's history was measured with reference to people whose names appear in no chronicle. History bends around them, not around Titus.
verseByVerse.examples: The most ignored clause in the chapter is the end is not yet (v. 6). Every generation has read its wars into the timetable and every one has been wrong, which is exactly what this verse said would happen. The usable test is not prophetic but personal: when the headlines are bad, does your confidence in God's government move? Two other verses land closer to home than the tribulation does. Verse 12, love growing cold, is the commonest condition in a mature congregation and almost nobody names it: prayer as a duty discharged, Scripture familiar, other people's troubles mildly tiresome. The remedy is the one given to Ephesus: remember, repent, and do the works you did at first, because feeling follows the feet. And the response to the sign in v. 15 is startlingly practical: not gather, not interpret, but leave the district. The Christians of Jerusalem did, and lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus left the temple and was going away, when his disciples came to point out to him the buildings of the temple. But he answered them, "You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus was leaving the temple, his disciples pointed out its magnificent buildings. He said: you see all these? Truly, not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.

The setting. Chapters 24–25 are the fifth and last of Jesus’ great teaching sections in Matthew, often called the Olivet Discourse, because he gave it on the Mount of Olives. It answers two questions: when will the temple be destroyed, and what will be the sign of Christ’s coming and the end of the age (v. 3)? Jesus speaks of both events, and the challenge for readers is to see which he is speaking of at each point. His main purpose is not to satisfy curiosity about dates, but to warn his disciples to be ready and faithful.

Jesus left the temple and was going away. His last departure from the temple, right after announcing that its house would be left desolate (23:38). God’s presence is leaving it (Ezekiel 10:18–19).

When his disciples came to point out to him the buildings of the temple. Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple in 20 BC on a vast scale; the work was still going on, and was finished only in AD 63, seven years before its destruction. It was one of the wonders of the ancient world. Its stones were enormous, some over forty feet (12 metres) long, of white limestone, and parts were covered with gold, so that it shone like a snowy mountain in the sun, according to Josephus. The rabbis said: whoever has not seen Herod’s temple has never seen a beautiful building.

You see all these, do you not? Look carefully.

Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down. An astonishing prophecy. Forty years later, in AD 70, the Roman general Titus besieged and destroyed Jerusalem. The temple was burned, and the stones were thrown down. Josephus describes it in detail. Only parts of the retaining walls of the temple platform remain, including the Western Wall.

In a sentence. When the disciples admired the temple, Jesus foretold that it would be completely destroyed, as it was in AD 70.

On a Tuesday. The most impressive human works will pass away. What are you building your life on?
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt and enlarged the temple on a vast scale; work was still going on. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately: tell us, when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?

As he sat on the Mount of Olives. Facing the temple across the Kidron Valley, with a view of the whole complex. Zechariah 14:4 says the LORD’s feet will stand on the Mount of Olives on the day of the LORD.

The disciples came to him privately. Mark names Peter, James, John and Andrew (Mark 13:3).

Tell us, when will these things be. The destruction of the temple (v. 2).

And what will be the sign of your coming and of the close of the age? “Coming” (parousia) means arrival, presence, and was used for the official visit of a king. It is the word for Christ’s return. “Close of the age” is the end of the present world (13:39–40; 28:20). The disciples probably thought these were all one event: if the temple fell, surely the end of the world would follow. Jesus distinguishes them, while showing that the first is a preview of the second.

How to read the discourse. Interpreters differ. Futurists see most of the chapter as about the end of history. Preterists see most of it as fulfilled in AD 70. Many Reformed interpreters (such as R. T. France and D. A. Carson) see verses 4–35 as mainly about the destruction of Jerusalem within that generation (v. 34), and verses 36 onward as about the final coming of Christ, whose day no one knows. Others see both events throughout, the near event foreshadowing the far. Verdict: verses 4–35 speak mainly of the events leading to AD 70, which also foreshadow the end; verses 36–25:46 speak of Christ’s personal return at the end of the age. This reading takes seriously Jesus’ statement that “this generation will not pass away until all these things take place” (v. 34).

In a sentence. The disciples asked when the temple would fall and what would signal Jesus’ coming and the end of the age.

On a Tuesday. Curiosity about the end times is natural. Jesus’ answer focuses less on dates than on faithfulness. Read this chapter that way.
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: see that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, I am the Christ, and they will lead many astray.

See that no one leads you astray. Jesus’ first concern is not to give a timetable, but to protect his disciples from deception. The greatest danger in times of crisis is not suffering but being misled (vv. 11, 24).

For many will come in my name, saying, “I am the Christ.” False messiahs. In the decades before AD 70, many arose in Judea, promising to deliver Israel from Rome: Theudas (Acts 5:36), “the Egyptian” (Acts 21:38), and others described by Josephus. After AD 70, Simon bar Kokhba led a revolt in AD 132 and was hailed as messiah. Many have arisen since.

And they will lead many astray. Many people followed them, to disaster.

In a sentence. Jesus warned his disciples first not to be deceived by the many false messiahs who would come.

On a Tuesday. In times of crisis, people look for saviours: political, religious or personal. Do not be led astray from Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will hear of wars and rumours of wars. Do not be alarmed, for this must happen, but the end is not yet. Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places.

And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. In the years before AD 70, there were wars and revolts across the Roman Empire, including civil war after Nero’s death in AD 68 (the “year of the four emperors”), and the Jewish revolt from AD 66.

See that you are not alarmed. Do not panic. Do not read every war as a sign that the end is about to happen.

For this must take place. These things are part of God’s plan in a fallen world. They do not mean God has lost control.

But the end is not yet. Wars are not the sign of the end. They are part of normal history between Christ’s comings.

For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. Echoing Isaiah 19:2 and 2 Chronicles 15:6.

And there will be famines and earthquakes in various places. A famine struck in the reign of Claudius (Acts 11:28); earthquakes occurred in Asia Minor, Italy and Jerusalem in the decades before AD 70. Famines and earthquakes have continued throughout history.

What it does not mean. Not that every war, famine or earthquake signals that the end is very near. Jesus says the opposite: the end is not yet. Many have set dates based on world events and been proved wrong. These things characterise the whole time between Christ’s first and second coming.

In a sentence. Wars, famines and earthquakes will come, but disciples must not panic, because they are not the sign of the end.

On a Tuesday. When the news is full of wars and disasters, do not be alarmed. God is still in control. Pray, and keep faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: "All these are but the beginning of the birth pains. Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death, and you will be hated by all nations for my name's sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these are only the beginning of the birth pains. Then they will hand you over to persecution and put you to death, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name.

All these are but the beginning of the birth pains. “Birth pains” was a Jewish image for the sufferings before the coming of the messianic age (Isaiah 26:17–18; Micah 4:9–10). Labour pains are painful, but they lead to new life. The troubles of history are the labour pains of the new creation (Romans 8:22). And they are only the beginning.

Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death. Persecution of the disciples, as Jesus warned in 10:17–22. Within a few decades, James, Peter, Paul and many others were killed. Nero persecuted Christians in Rome in AD 64.

And you will be hated by all nations for my name’s sake. Not only by the Jewish leaders, but by Gentiles. Early Christians were accused of atheism, hatred of the human race, and disloyalty to Caesar.

In a sentence. World troubles are only the beginning of the birth pains, and disciples will be persecuted, killed and hated by all nations for Jesus’ name.

On a Tuesday. Persecution is not a sign that God has abandoned his people. It was foretold. Pray for persecuted believers.
verseByVerse.note: Birth pains are a prophetic image for the troubles before God’s new age.

parallels.desc: the whole creation groans in the pains of childbirth

verseByVerse.quote: "And then many will fall away and betray one another and hate one another. And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then many will fall away and betray one another and hate one another. And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray.

And then many will fall away. “Fall away” (skandalisthēsontai) means stumble, abandon the faith under pressure (13:21). Persecution sifts true faith from false.

And betray one another and hate one another. Betrayal within the community, even in families (10:21). In Nero’s persecution, the historian Tacitus says Christians were arrested on information from others who had been arrested.

And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. Not only false messiahs (v. 5), but false teachers within the church (7:15; Acts 20:29–30; 2 Peter 2:1; 1 John 4:1).

In a sentence. Under pressure, many will fall away and betray one another, and false prophets will lead many astray.

On a Tuesday. Test the teaching you hear by Scripture, and pray for the endurance to stay faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: "And because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because lawlessness will increase, the love of many will grow cold.

And because lawlessness will be increased. “Lawlessness” (anomia) is disregard for God’s law, wickedness (7:23; 23:28). As evil increases around them, believers are affected.

The love of many will grow cold. Love for God and for others cools, like embers left untended. The surrounding wickedness, the pressure of persecution, the disappointment of betrayal, and false teaching all chill love. The church in Ephesus was warned that it had abandoned the love it had at first (Revelation 2:4).

In a sentence. As wickedness increases, the love of many believers will grow cold.

On a Tuesday. Is your love for God and others growing warmer or colder? Ask God to rekindle it, and avoid what chills it.

parallels.desc: you have abandoned the love you had at first

verseByVerse.quote: "But the one who endures to the end will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the one who endures to the end will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.

But the one who endures to the end will be saved. The same words as 10:22. True faith perseveres. Those who endure through persecution, deception and cooling love show that they are truly God’s (see 10:22).

And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world. Despite persecution, the gospel will spread. “The whole world” (oikoumenē) often meant the inhabited world, the Roman Empire. By AD 70, the gospel had spread across the empire: Paul could say it was bearing fruit in the whole world (Colossians 1:6, 23; Romans 1:8; 10:18). It continues to spread to every nation today.

As a testimony to all nations. A witness, both an offer of salvation and evidence for judgment.

And then the end will come. In the immediate context, the end of the temple and the old order in AD 70. In the wider sense, the gospel will reach all nations before the final end (28:19–20; Revelation 7:9).

What it does not mean. Not that we can calculate the end by counting the nations or unreached people groups, or that the church can hasten the end by its strategies. The point is that the gospel will spread irresistibly, whatever opposition it faces.

In a sentence. Those who endure to the end will be saved, and the gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed to all nations before the end comes.

On a Tuesday. The gospel will reach all nations. What part are you playing: praying, giving, going, or sharing it with your neighbour?

verseByVerse.quote: "So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.

So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel. From Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11. An “abomination” is something detestable to God, especially an idol. “Of desolation” means something that causes desolation, or that makes the temple deserted (as God’s people abandon it). In 167 BC, the Greek king Antiochus IV Epiphanes set up an altar to Zeus in the temple and sacrificed a pig on it. Jewish writings called this the abomination of desolation (1 Maccabees 1:54). Jesus says a similar event will happen again.

Standing in the holy place. The temple. Luke’s parallel explains: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near (Luke 21:20). In AD 66–70, Roman armies with their pagan standards, which bore images of the emperor and were worshipped by the soldiers, surrounded Jerusalem. Before that, Jewish Zealots occupied the temple, committed murders in it and installed an unqualified high priest, which Josephus describes as a profanation. When the temple fell, Roman soldiers set up their standards in the temple court and offered sacrifices to them.

(Let the reader understand.) A note to the reader of the Gospel, or to the reader of Daniel: think carefully about what this means.

Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. When this happens, do not stay to defend the city; flee. The early church historian Eusebius records that Christians in Jerusalem, warned by a prophecy, fled before the city’s destruction to Pella, east of the Jordan, and were spared.

What it does not mean. Many dispensationalists see the abomination of desolation as a future Antichrist setting up an image in a rebuilt temple during a seven-year tribulation. But Jesus tells his own disciples, in Judea, to flee when they see it. The instructions are local and practical: Judea, housetops, fields, winter, Sabbath (vv. 16–20). This fits AD 70. Verdict: the abomination of desolation was fulfilled in the Roman desecration and destruction of the temple in AD 66–70. It may also foreshadow the final rebellion against God before Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4).

In a sentence. When the temple was desecrated as Daniel foretold, which happened when Rome destroyed Jerusalem, Jesus’ followers in Judea were to flee.

On a Tuesday. Jesus gave his followers practical warnings to save their lives. Heed his warnings in your own life, and do not cling to what God is judging.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel foresaw an idolatrous desecration of the temple. It was foreshadowed in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there. Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take what is in his house, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the one on the housetop not go down to take things out of his house, and let the one in the field not turn back to take his cloak.

Let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take what is in his house. Roofs in Palestine were flat, used for work and rest, and reached by an outside staircase. A person on the roof should go straight down the outside stairs and flee, without going into the house to gather possessions. Speed is everything.

And let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. Workers left their outer cloaks at the edge of the field. Do not even go back for it. Lot’s wife looked back and was lost (Genesis 19:26; Luke 17:32).

In a sentence. The flight from Judea would need to be so urgent that people should not stop for possessions.

On a Tuesday. What possessions would you go back for? Hold everything loosely enough to leave it when God calls.
verseByVerse.note: Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: "And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
How terrible it will be for pregnant women and nursing mothers in those days! Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath.

And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! “Alas” (ouai, “woe”) here expresses compassion. Fleeing would be hardest for them. Josephus records horrors during the siege of Jerusalem, including famine so severe that a mother ate her own child.

Pray that your flight may not be in winter. Winter in Palestine was the rainy season. The rains made roads muddy and the Jordan flooded, making flight across it difficult.

Or on a Sabbath. On the Sabbath, travel was restricted to a short distance, gates might be shut, and help would be hard to find. Jewish Christians might also have scruples about travelling. This detail shows Jesus was speaking to Jewish believers in first-century Judea.

In a sentence. Jesus showed compassion for the vulnerable in the coming flight and told his disciples to pray that it would not be in winter or on a Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cares about the most vulnerable in times of disaster. So should we. Pray for refugees, especially mothers and children.
verseByVerse.note: Winter rains made roads and river crossings hard; Sabbath rules restricted travel.

verseByVerse.quote: "For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be. And if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, and never will be. If those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, those days will be cut short.

For then there will be great tribulation. “Tribulation” (thlipsis) means distress, affliction, crushing pressure.

Such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be. A common prophetic way of describing an unparalleled disaster (Daniel 12:1; Joel 2:2; Exodus 11:6). The siege of Jerusalem was one of the most horrific in ancient history. Josephus estimated that over a million people died, through famine, disease, civil war within the city and the Roman assault, and tens of thousands were enslaved. “Never will be” shows that history continues after this event: it is not the end of the world.

And if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. “Saved” here means survive physically. If the siege had gone on longer, no one would have survived.

But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short. God limited the time of suffering for the sake of his chosen people. God’s sovereignty extends even over the length of disasters.

What it does not mean. Not necessarily a future “Great Tribulation” of exactly seven years before Christ’s return, as some dispensationalists teach, from which Christians will be removed by a secret rapture beforehand. Jesus speaks to his disciples about a tribulation they would go through, and from which they would flee. Verdict: the great tribulation of these verses was fulfilled in the siege of Jerusalem; the church has suffered tribulation throughout history (John 16:33; Acts 14:22; Revelation 7:14), and there may be intensified tribulation before the end, but there is no secret rapture to remove the church from it.

In a sentence. An unparalleled tribulation would come on Judea, but God would shorten it for the sake of his chosen people.

On a Tuesday. God sets limits on every suffering of his people. He knows exactly how long it will last.

parallels.desc: a time of trouble such as never has been

verseByVerse.quote: "Then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'There he is!' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then if anyone says to you, look, here is the Christ! or, there he is! do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect.

Then if anyone says to you, “Look, here is the Christ!” or “There he is!” do not believe it. During the crisis, many would claim that the Messiah had come to save the city. Do not believe them.

For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders. Signs and wonders do not prove that someone is from God (7:22–23; Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 2 Thessalonians 2:9–10; Revelation 13:13–14). The test is whether their message agrees with God’s word.

So as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. The deception would be powerful. “If possible” implies that it is not possible: God protects his chosen people from final deception (John 10:27–29). But they must be on guard.

What it does not mean. Not that the elect cannot be confused or misled for a time. But God will not let them be finally deceived and lost. His keeping works through their watchfulness and his warnings.

In a sentence. Do not believe claims that the Messiah has appeared, because false christs will perform impressive signs to deceive even the elect, if that were possible.

On a Tuesday. Do not be impressed by miracles, signs or charismatic personalities. Test every claim by Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: "See, I have told you beforehand. So, if they say to you, 'Look, he is in the wilderness,' do not go out. If they say, 'Look, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, I have told you beforehand. So if they say to you, look, he is in the wilderness, do not go out. If they say, look, he is in the inner rooms, do not believe it.

See, I have told you beforehand. Jesus has warned them, so that when it happens they will not be surprised or deceived.

If they say to you, “Look, he is in the wilderness,” do not go out. Several would-be messiahs led crowds into the wilderness, promising signs of deliverance like the exodus (Acts 21:38). The Romans slaughtered them.

If they say, “Look, he is in the inner rooms,” do not believe it. Others claimed the Messiah was secretly hidden somewhere. Christ’s return will not be secret.

In a sentence. Jesus warned in advance that claims of the Messiah appearing in the wilderness or in secret rooms must be ignored.

On a Tuesday. Do not chase rumours about Christ’s return. When he comes, everyone will know.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.

For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west. Lightning is sudden, unmistakable and visible to everyone across the whole sky.

So will be the coming of the Son of Man. Christ’s return will not be hidden in a desert or a secret room, needing anyone to announce it. It will be public, sudden and visible to all (Revelation 1:7). This contrasts with the false messiahs who need advertising.

Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather. A proverb (Job 39:30). Vultures (or eagles, ESV footnote) circling in the sky show where a dead body lies. It is obvious. Two possible meanings: just as vultures inevitably find a corpse, so judgment will inevitably fall on Jerusalem, now spiritually dead; the Roman legions, whose standards bore eagles, would gather there. Or: Christ’s coming will be as obvious as vultures over a carcass. Verdict: probably judgment: where there is spiritual death, judgment will come.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ will come secretly to remove his church, with a later public coming. His coming is like lightning: visible to all.

In a sentence. Christ’s coming will be as sudden and visible as lightning across the sky, and judgment will fall where there is death, as surely as vultures find a corpse.

On a Tuesday. No one will need to tell you when Christ returns. Live ready for that day.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “eagles” for “vultures.”

parallels.desc: where the slain are, there is he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–51 — The Coming of the Son of Man and the Call to Watchfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The discourse turns to the coming itself: the heavens shaken, the Son of Man on the clouds, the tribes of the earth mourning, and angels gathering the elect from one end of heaven to the other. The fig tree teaches the season without the date. This generation will not pass until all these things take place, and then comes the hinge at v. 36, where no one knows the day or the hour, not the angels, not the Son, only the Father. From there the teaching is all readiness: the days of Noah, two in a field and two at a mill, the thief in the night, and two servants left in charge of a household, one of whom decides his master is delayed.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 36 is the seam of the discourse. Before it, signs and a generation; after it, no signs, no timetable, and a coming likened to a burglary and a flood. Signs and no signs cannot describe one event, which is the text's own answer to the charge that Jesus predicted his return within his hearers' lifetime and was wrong. Nor the Son raises the question of how the Son of God can be ignorant of anything, answered from the two natures: according to his deity he knows all things, and the human mind he genuinely took grew and learned. Note that in the same sentence he ranks himself above the whole angelic host and names himself absolutely as the Son. The gathering of the elect from the four winds is the pastoral weight of the section: believers buried at sea, in unmarked ground, under wrong names. Nobody is mislaid.
verseByVerse.examples: Stay awake has been made to mean two things Jesus did not mean. It is not reading the news apocalyptically, since six verses earlier he said no one knows the day; and it is not living in dread, since see that you are not alarmed is a command in this same discourse. Wherever the New Testament describes the church's own attitude to that day the emotion is longing, not terror. What it does mean is testable tonight: is there anything in your week you would need to stop or start if you knew he were coming on Thursday? The picture Jesus himself reaches for is not a watchman scanning the horizon but a steward handing out food at the proper time, which is catering, and which is how the most exalted prophetic discourse in the Gospels chooses to define faithfulness. And the wicked servant's ruin begins in one sentence never said aloud: my master is delayed. He does not deny the master. He postpones him, and the postponement does all the damage the denial would have done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

Immediately after the tribulation of those days. After the great tribulation of verses 15–22.

The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Quoted from Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4. In the prophets, these cosmic images describe the fall of nations and empires under God’s judgment. Isaiah 13 uses them for the fall of Babylon; Isaiah 34 for the judgment of Edom; Ezekiel 32:7–8 for the fall of Egypt. The language is symbolic: the political “heavens” and “lights” of a nation are falling. It is the end of a world order.

Two readings. If verses 4–35 speak of AD 70, this describes the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the old covenant order, in the prophets’ symbolic language. If it speaks of the end of history, it describes literal cosmic upheaval at Christ’s return (2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 6:12–14). Verdict: in context, the fall of Jerusalem described in prophetic imagery, which also foreshadows the final shaking of heaven and earth at Christ’s return (Hebrews 12:26–27).

In a sentence. After the tribulation, the cosmic signs of the prophets will mark a great act of God’s judgment and the end of a world order.

On a Tuesday. Every human empire and world order will fall. Only Christ’s kingdom will remain.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: the stars will not give their light
the host of heaven rotted away

verseByVerse.quote: "Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn. They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. He will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.

Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man. Perhaps the sign is the Son of Man himself in heaven, revealed in glory.

And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn. From Zechariah 12:10–14, where the tribes of Israel mourn when they look on him whom they have pierced. “The land” or “the earth”: the same Greek word. Mourning may be repentance, or grief at judgment.

And they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. From Daniel 7:13–14. In Daniel, the Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days, God, and is given everlasting dominion. It is a coming up to God’s throne, an enthronement, not first a coming down to earth. Jesus used the same words at his trial (26:64): from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven. The fall of Jerusalem would show that Jesus had been vindicated and enthroned. The vision is also fulfilled finally at his return to earth (Acts 1:11; Revelation 1:7).

And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call. Trumpets announced festivals, gathered God’s people, and signalled the day of the LORD (Isaiah 27:13; 1 Thessalonians 4:16; 1 Corinthians 15:52).

And they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. “Angels” (angeloi) can also mean messengers. Some see the gathering of the elect from all nations through the preaching of the gospel after AD 70, as the kingdom passes from the temple to the worldwide church. Others see the final gathering at Christ’s return. Both are true: the gathering has begun through the gospel and will be completed at the end (Isaiah 27:12–13; Deuteronomy 30:4).

What it does not mean. Not a secret rapture. The gathering is public, with a loud trumpet, after the tribulation, not before it. The New Testament knows of one return of Christ, visible to all, at which the dead are raised and believers caught up to meet him (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17), and judgment follows (25:31–46).

In a sentence. The Son of Man will be seen enthroned and coming in glory as Daniel foretold, and his messengers will gather his chosen people from the whole world.

On a Tuesday. Christ is enthroned now, gathering his people from every nation through the gospel. Be part of that gathering.

For worship. Worship the Son of Man, coming with power and great glory.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man with the clouds

verseByVerse.quote: "From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Learn this lesson from the fig tree: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates.

From the fig tree learn its lesson. Most trees in Palestine are evergreen. The fig tree loses its leaves in winter, and its new leaves in spring are a clear sign that summer is coming.

As soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. An obvious sign.

So also, when you see all these things. The signs Jesus has described: false messiahs, wars, persecution, the abomination of desolation, the flight from Judea.

You know that he is near, at the very gates. Or “it is near”: the destruction of Jerusalem. When the disciples saw these signs, they would know the end of the temple was imminent.

In a sentence. As fig leaves signal summer, the signs Jesus described would show that Jerusalem’s judgment was at the door.

On a Tuesday. Learn to read God’s warnings in Scripture and history, and respond in time.
verseByVerse.note: Unlike many trees in Israel, the fig loses its leaves in winter; its new leaves mark the coming of summer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. A key verse. “This generation” in Matthew always means the people living in Jesus’ time (11:16; 12:39–45; 16:4; 17:17; 23:36). “All these things” are the signs and events of verses 4–31, including the destruction of the temple. About forty years later, in AD 70, it happened, within that generation. This is strong evidence that verses 4–35 refer mainly to the fall of Jerusalem. Others take “generation” to mean “race” (the Jewish people will survive until the end) or “the generation that sees the signs”, but these readings are less natural.

Heaven and earth will pass away. The present creation will be renewed (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1).
