verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The council reconvenes at dawn to give the night's verdict a legal form, then takes Jesus to Pilate, because they may condemn but may not execute. Judas returns the silver, is told to see to it himself, and hangs himself; the money buys a burial field for foreigners. Before Pilate the charge is quietly rewritten from blasphemy to kingship. Pilate tries the Passover custom, is warned by his wife, finds no fault, washes his hands, and condemns him anyway. Barabbas goes free. Jesus is scourged, mocked by the cohort, crowned with thorns, and led out to Golgotha, where he is crucified between two brigands and jeered at by passers-by, priests and the dying.
verseByVerse.theology: Substitution is not imposed on this section by later theology; it is the shape of the narrative. One cross and two candidates: a guilty insurrectionist walks free for exactly one reason, which is that the innocent man took his place, and Matthew records both in a single verse (v. 26). The mockery carries the same doctrine inside out. He saved others; he cannot save himself is true in every word and false in every intention: not a failure of power, but a necessity built into substitution, since a substitute who steps out from under the weight has stopped being one. He could have saved himself or saved them. There was never an afternoon in which he did both.
verseByVerse.examples: Pilate is the study in this section, and he is a modern figure. Nobody in the chapter sees more clearly: he is amazed at the prisoner, warned by his wife, told by his own judgement that the charge is driven by envy, and asks what evil he has done and declares himself innocent of his blood. And nobody does less with what he sees. He never once considers simply doing what a judge is for; he looks instead for a procedure that will produce justice at no personal cost — the crowd, the custom, the basin — and when no such route exists he chooses the cost he can bear and lets the innocent man pay the other. Admiration is not allegiance. Pilate was impressed by Jesus in the early morning and signed his death warrant before it was out.

verseByVerse.quote: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. And they bound him and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When morning came, all the chief priests and elders took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. They bound him, led him away and handed him over to Pilate the governor.

When morning came. Friday morning, at dawn. A formal session of the council confirmed the night’s verdict in daylight (Luke 22:66–71), perhaps to give it legal form.

All the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. They had condemned him for blasphemy (26:65–66). But under Roman rule, they could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). They needed the Roman governor, and a charge that Rome would care about.

And they bound him and led him away. Bound like a criminal.

And delivered him over to Pilate the governor. Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect (governor) of Judea from AD 26 to 36. His usual residence was at Caesarea on the coast, but he came to Jerusalem at festivals with troops to keep order. Josephus and Philo describe him as harsh, stubborn and insensitive to Jewish feelings; he had provoked riots by bringing images of Caesar into Jerusalem, and slaughtered Galileans at the temple (Luke 13:1). An inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea in 1961. His name is in the Apostles’ Creed: suffered under Pontius Pilate, anchoring Jesus’ death in real history.

In a sentence. At dawn the council confirmed its decision and handed Jesus over in chains to the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate.

On a Tuesday. The Christian faith rests on real events in real history, under a real governor. You are trusting a fact, not a myth.
verseByVerse.note: The Jewish leaders could not carry out a death sentence under Roman rule. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

parallels.desc: not lawful for us to put anyone to death

verseByVerse.quote: Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood." They said, "What is that to us? See to it yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he was seized with remorse and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: I have sinned by betraying innocent blood. They said: what is that to us? See to it yourself.

Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned. Perhaps Judas had not expected this outcome. Perhaps he thought Jesus would escape, or perform a miracle.

He changed his mind. “Changed his mind” (metamelētheis) means regretted, felt remorse. It is not the word usually used for repentance (metanoeō), though the two overlap (21:29, 32). Judas felt deep regret, but it did not lead him to Christ.

And brought back the thirty pieces of silver. He tried to undo what he had done, by returning the money.

I have sinned by betraying innocent blood. A true confession: Jesus was innocent. Even his betrayer testified to it. But he confessed to the wrong people. The priests could not forgive him.

What is that to us? See to it yourself. Total callousness. The religious leaders, whose job was to care for souls, had no interest in a sinner’s guilt. They had used him and now discarded him.

In a sentence. Judas, overcome with remorse, returned the silver and confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood, but the priests coldly dismissed him.

On a Tuesday. Bring your guilt to Christ, not to those who cannot help you. Regret without turning to Christ leads to despair.

verseByVerse.quote: And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and he went and hanged himself. But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, "It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, Judas left, and he went and hanged himself. The chief priests took the silver and said: it is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money.

And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple. Into the sanctuary itself, perhaps. Zechariah 11:13 foretold the thirty pieces thrown into the house of the LORD.

He departed, and he went and hanged himself. Despair. Acts 1:18 adds that he fell headlong and his body burst open, perhaps when the rope broke or his body was later cut down. The two accounts are complementary. Judas’ end contrasts with Peter’s. Both sinned terribly against Jesus. Peter wept and returned; Judas despaired and died (see 26:75).

But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money.” Astonishing hypocrisy. They had paid the money to have an innocent man killed, and now scrupled over the ceremonial law about where to put it (Deuteronomy 23:18). They strained out a gnat and swallowed a camel (23:24).

What it does not mean. Not that suicide is an unforgivable sin in itself, or that every person who dies by suicide is lost. Judas’ end was the final expression of a life that had rejected Christ. Christians who struggle with suicidal thoughts need care, help and hope, and they can find forgiveness and life in Christ.

In a sentence. Judas threw the silver into the temple and hanged himself, while the priests scrupled over the money they had used to buy a death.

On a Tuesday. If you are in despair over your sin, do not do what Judas did. Come to Jesus. There is no sin too great for his forgiveness. If you are struggling with thoughts of suicide, please talk to someone today.

parallels.desc: the wages of a dog into the house of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: So they took counsel and bought with them the potter's field as a burial place for strangers. Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they took counsel and used the money to buy the potter’s field as a burial place for strangers. That is why that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.

So they took counsel and bought with them the potter’s field. A field probably used by potters for digging clay, and no longer good for farming. Tradition places it in the Hinnom Valley, south of Jerusalem: the same valley that gave Gehenna its name (5:22).

As a burial place for strangers. For foreigners and pilgrims who died in Jerusalem and had no family tomb. The money paid for Jesus’ death bought a burial ground for Gentiles: a quiet picture of his death benefiting outsiders.

Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day. In Aramaic, Akeldama (Acts 1:19). “To this day”: the place was still known when Matthew wrote.

In a sentence. The priests used the blood money to buy a potter’s field to bury strangers, known ever after as the Field of Blood.

On a Tuesday. Even Judas’ betrayal money ended up serving God’s purposes. God can bring good out of the worst evil.
verseByVerse.note: A potter’s field was probably land used for digging clay. Acts calls it Akeldama, “Field of Blood.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.

Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah. The words are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, where the good shepherd of God’s people is paid off with thirty pieces of silver, a contemptuous wage, which he throws to the potter in the house of the LORD. Why does Matthew name Jeremiah? Jeremiah also visited a potter (Jeremiah 18–19), smashed a potter’s jar in the Hinnom Valley as a sign of judgment on Jerusalem, renaming it the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 19:1–13), and bought a field as a sign (Jeremiah 32:6–15). Matthew combines Zechariah’s words with Jeremiah’s themes, and names the more prominent prophet, as Jewish teachers sometimes did (compare Mark 1:2, which combines Malachi and Isaiah under Isaiah’s name). Verdict: not an error, but a combined reference, naming Jeremiah because the themes of the potter, the field, the Hinnom Valley and judgment on Jerusalem come from him.

The price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel. In Zechariah, this is the contemptuous price at which Israel valued God’s shepherd. Israel’s leaders valued Jesus at the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32).

And they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me. God’s plan was being worked out, even through this.

In a sentence. The purchase of the potter’s field fulfilled prophecy, combining Zechariah’s thirty pieces of silver with Jeremiah’s potter and field.

On a Tuesday. What price do you set on Jesus? The leaders valued him as a slave. He is worth everything.
verseByVerse.note: The words are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, but Matthew names Jeremiah, who bought a field and visited the potter.

parallels.desc: thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" Jesus said, "You have said so." But when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him: are you the King of the Jews? Jesus said: you have said so. But when the chief priests and elders accused him, he gave no answer.

Now Jesus stood before the governor. The Judge of all the earth stands before a Roman official. Probably at Herod’s palace on the west side of Jerusalem, or at the Antonia fortress next to the temple.

And the governor asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” The leaders changed the charge. Blasphemy meant nothing to Rome. But claiming to be king, without Caesar’s appointment, was treason. Luke records their accusations: misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and calling himself Christ, a king (Luke 23:2). The magi had asked for the King of the Jews at his birth (2:2).

Jesus said, “You have said so.” Yes, but not in the sense you mean. John records Jesus’ explanation: my kingdom is not of this world (John 18:33–37).

But when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer. Silence before false accusations (26:63; Isaiah 53:7).

In a sentence. Before Pilate, Jesus acknowledged he was the King of the Jews, but was silent before the leaders’ accusations.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is King, though not the kind the world fears or expects. Is he your King?
verseByVerse.note: “King of the Jews” was the political charge that mattered to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate said to him, "Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?" But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Pilate said to him: do you not hear how many things they testify against you? But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.

Do you not hear how many things they testify against you? Pilate expected him to defend himself. Under Roman law, a defendant who did not respond could be convicted.

But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge. Complete silence. Isaiah 53:7: as a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.

So that the governor was greatly amazed. Pilate had never seen a prisoner like this: calm, dignified, unafraid, and not trying to save his life. Isaiah 52:15: kings shall shut their mouths because of him.

In a sentence. Jesus answered none of the charges, and Pilate was astonished at his silence.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ silence was not weakness, but trust in his Father (1 Peter 2:23). You do not always need to defend yourself.

parallels.desc: when he suffered, he did not threaten

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the feast, the governor used to release to the crowd any one prisoner they wanted. They had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas.

Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. A Passover amnesty, apparently a custom to please the crowds. No document outside the Gospels mentions it, but similar amnesties are known in the Roman world. At Passover, which celebrated Israel’s release from slavery, the release of a prisoner was fitting.

And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. Mark and Luke say he had been arrested for insurrection and murder (Mark 15:7; Luke 23:19). John calls him a robber (lēstēs, John 18:40), the word used for violent revolutionaries. He was probably a Zealot, a rebel against Rome: a popular hero to some.

Textual note. Some manuscripts call him “Jesus Barabbas” (ESV footnote), in verses 16 and 17. Jesus was a common name. Scribes may have removed it out of reverence. If original, Pilate’s choice was stark: “Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus called Christ?” “Barabbas” means “son of the father”: another irony, set beside the true Son of the Father.

In a sentence. Pilate had a custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover, and held a notorious rebel named Barabbas.

On a Tuesday. Barabbas was guilty, and was set free because Jesus was condemned. That is your story too.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “Jesus Barabbas.” Barabbas means “son of the father.”

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, "Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?" For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowd gathered, Pilate asked: whom do you want me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ? For he knew it was out of envy that they had handed him over.

So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, “Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” Pilate hoped the crowd would choose Jesus, and he could release him without offending the leaders. A murderer and rebel, or a healer and teacher.

For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up. Pilate saw through the leaders. Their motive was not justice or loyalty to Rome, but envy: jealousy of Jesus’ popularity and authority. Envy is a deadly sin (Proverbs 14:30).

In a sentence. Pilate offered the crowd a choice between Barabbas and Jesus, knowing the leaders had acted out of envy.

On a Tuesday. Envy can lead to terrible acts. Is there anyone whose success you resent? Confess it.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, "Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him: have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream.

Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat. The bēma, the raised platform from which Roman officials gave judgment. Paul would later stand before Gallio’s judgment seat (Acts 18:12).

His wife sent word to him. Only Matthew records this. Later tradition named her Procula.

Have nothing to do with that righteous man. A Gentile woman declares Jesus innocent, “righteous”.

For I have suffered much because of him today in a dream. God spoke through dreams at Jesus’ birth (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), and now at his death. Romans took dreams seriously as omens. This was a warning from God to Pilate. He ignored it.

In a sentence. Pilate’s wife, warned in a dream, urged him to have nothing to do with the righteous Jesus.

On a Tuesday. God gives warnings. Pilate had every reason to release Jesus and did not. Do not ignore God’s warnings in your conscience and in his word.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. Only Matthew records the message from Pilate’s wife.

parallels.desc: the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor again said to them, "Which of the two do you want me to release for you?" And they said, "Barabbas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor asked them again: which of the two do you want me to release? They said: Barabbas.

Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The leaders worked the crowd. This was probably not the same crowd that welcomed Jesus on Palm Sunday, mostly pilgrims from Galilee, but people gathered early at the governor’s palace, perhaps including supporters of Barabbas. Crowds are easily manipulated.

Which of the two do you want me to release for you? Pilate asks again.

And they said, “Barabbas.” They chose the guilty man and rejected the innocent one. The murderer goes free; the giver of life goes to death (Acts 3:14–15). Barabbas is a picture of every sinner: guilty, condemned, and released because Jesus took his place.

In a sentence. Persuaded by the leaders, the crowd chose Barabbas to be released and Jesus to be destroyed.

On a Tuesday. Do not let the crowd decide what you think of Jesus. Crowds can be manipulated; Christ’s word cannot.

For worship. Thank Jesus that, like Barabbas, you go free because he took your place.

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to them, "Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?" They all said, "Let him be crucified!" And he said, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Let him be crucified!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate said: then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ? They all said: let him be crucified! And he said: why? What evil has he done? But they shouted all the more: let him be crucified!

Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ? The question every person must answer.

They all said, “Let him be crucified!” Crucifixion, the Roman punishment for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals (see 20:19). Under the law, a man hanged on a tree was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). They wanted the most shameful death possible.

And he said, “Why? What evil has he done?” Pilate declares Jesus innocent. He could find no crime (Luke 23:4, 14, 22; John 18:38). The judge knew the prisoner was innocent.

But they shouted all the more, “Let him be crucified!” No reason, only shouting. Mob hysteria.

In a sentence. When Pilate asked what to do with Jesus, the crowd shouted for crucifixion, and when he asked what evil Jesus had done, they only shouted louder.

On a Tuesday. What will you do with Jesus who is called Christ? You cannot stay neutral.

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, "I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves." And all the people answered, "His blood be on us and on our children!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Pilate saw that he was getting nowhere, but that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying: I am innocent of this man’s blood; see to it yourselves. And all the people answered: his blood be on us and on our children!

So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning. Pilate feared a riot at Passover, which could cost him his position. John adds that the leaders threatened him: if you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend (John 19:12).

He took water and washed his hands before the crowd. A Jewish ritual to declare innocence of a death (Deuteronomy 21:6–9; Psalm 26:6), which Pilate may have adopted to communicate with the crowd. Only Matthew records it.

I am innocent of this man’s blood; see to it yourselves. The same words the priests used to Judas (v. 4). But Pilate could not wash away his responsibility with water. He had the power to release Jesus and chose not to. He condemned a man he knew was innocent, out of cowardice. The creed remembers him for it.

And all the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!” A formula accepting responsibility for a death (2 Samuel 1:16; Jeremiah 26:15). The crowd accepted the guilt.

What it does not mean. This verse has been terribly misused through history to justify hatred and persecution of Jewish people as “Christ-killers”. That is a grave sin and a grave misreading. First, the crowd that shouted this was a particular crowd, not the whole Jewish people then or since. Second, Jesus prayed for his executioners’ forgiveness (Luke 23:34), and Peter offered forgiveness to the very people of Jerusalem who had demanded his death (Acts 2:36–39; 3:14–19). Third, Jews and Gentiles together were responsible (Acts 4:27), and in the deepest sense, all humanity, including us, put Jesus on the cross by our sins. Fourth, the blood of Christ is not only a blood of guilt but of forgiveness. “His blood be on us” is the prayer of every believer, for cleansing (Hebrews 12:24; 1 John 1:7).

In a sentence. Fearing a riot, Pilate washed his hands to disclaim responsibility, and the crowd accepted the guilt of Jesus’ blood.

On a Tuesday. You cannot wash your hands of Jesus. Neutrality is not possible. And may his blood be on you, not as guilt, but as cleansing.
verseByVerse.note: Washing the hands was a public declaration of innocence in a death.

parallels.desc: the elders wash their hands over the heifer
I wash my hands in innocence
to bring this man’s blood upon us

verseByVerse.quote: Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Pilate released Barabbas to them, and after having Jesus scourged, handed him over to be crucified.

Then he released for them Barabbas. The guilty man walked free.

And having scourged Jesus. Roman scourging (flagellatio) was brutal. The victim was stripped and tied to a post, and beaten with a whip made of leather thongs with pieces of bone or metal tied in. It tore the skin and flesh, sometimes exposing bones and organs. Many died from it. Isaiah 53:5: with his wounds we are healed.

Delivered him to be crucified. Pilate handed him over to the soldiers for execution. The innocent man was condemned; the guilty man released.

In a sentence. Pilate released Barabbas, had Jesus brutally scourged, and handed him over to be crucified.

For worship. By his wounds we are healed. Thank Jesus for the stripes he bore for you.
verseByVerse.note: Roman scourging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it could itself kill.

parallels.desc: with his wounds we are healed

verseByVerse.quote: Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor's headquarters, and they gathered the whole battalion before him. And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the headquarters and gathered the whole battalion around him. They stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him.

Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor’s headquarters. The praetorium, the governor’s official residence in Jerusalem.

And they gathered the whole battalion before him. A “battalion” (speira, cohort) was nominally six hundred soldiers. These were probably auxiliary troops recruited from non-Jewish areas like Samaria and Syria, who despised Jews. A Jewish “king” was an object of mockery to them.

And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him. A soldier’s red cloak, mimicking the purple robe of a king or emperor. Mark and John say purple (Mark 15:17; John 19:2): scarlet and purple were often confused. Stripping a man was a deep humiliation.

In a sentence. The soldiers took Jesus into the governor’s headquarters, gathered the whole cohort, and dressed him in a mock royal robe.

On a Tuesday. The King of kings was stripped and mocked. Nothing you suffer is beyond his understanding.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. The ESV notes that a battalion (cohort) was a tenth of a Roman legion. A soldier’s red cloak served as a mock royal robe.

verseByVerse.quote: and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head, and put a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him: hail, King of the Jews! They spat on him, took the reed and struck him on the head.

And twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head. A mock crown, perhaps from thorny branches used for kindling, imitating the radiant crown of a ruler on coins. It caused real pain. Thorns were a sign of the curse on creation after the fall (Genesis 3:17–18). Jesus wore the curse as a crown.

And put a reed in his right hand. A mock sceptre.

And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” A parody of the greeting to Caesar, “Hail, Caesar!” They did not know they were speaking the truth. One day every knee will bow to him in earnest (Philippians 2:10–11).

And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head. Driving the thorns deeper. Spitting, as at the Jewish trial (26:67). Both Jews and Gentiles mocked him.

In a sentence. The soldiers crowned Jesus with thorns, knelt in mock homage, spat on him and beat him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus wore a crown of thorns so that you might receive a crown of life (James 1:12).

For worship. Bow in true worship before the King who was mocked.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe, put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him.

And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him. The robe would have stuck to his wounds; removing it reopened them.

And led him away to crucify him. Crucifixions took place outside the city walls, on main roads, so that passers-by would see and be warned (Hebrews 13:12).

In a sentence. After mocking him, the soldiers dressed Jesus in his own clothes and led him out to be crucified.

On a Tuesday. Jesus went outside the city, bearing disgrace. Hebrews calls us to go to him there, bearing the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:13).

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. They compelled this man to carry his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, named Simon, and forced him to carry Jesus’ cross.

As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. Cyrene was a city in North Africa (modern Libya), with a large Jewish community. Simon was probably a Jewish pilgrim who had come for the Passover. Mark adds that he was the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21), apparently known to Mark’s readers; a Rufus is greeted in Romans 16:13. Perhaps Simon’s family became believers.

They compelled this man to carry his cross. Roman soldiers could force civilians to carry loads (see 5:41). A condemned man normally carried the crossbeam (patibulum), weighing perhaps 30–50 kilos, to the place of execution. Jesus, weakened by the scourging, could not continue. Simon literally took up the cross and followed Jesus (16:24).

In a sentence. The soldiers forced Simon of Cyrene, a passing pilgrim, to carry Jesus’ cross.

On a Tuesday. Simon carried Christ’s cross unwillingly; you are called to carry yours willingly. Who might you help carry a heavy load this week?
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Mark adds that Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull), they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they came to a place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull, they offered him wine mixed with gall to drink, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it.

And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). “Golgotha” is Aramaic for “skull”; the Latin is Calvaria, from which comes “Calvary”. Perhaps a rocky hill shaped like a skull, or a place of execution. It was outside the city walls but near the city (John 19:20). The traditional site, inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, was outside the walls in Jesus’ day.

They offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall. Mark says wine mixed with myrrh (Mark 15:23), a narcotic to dull the pain. Jewish women of Jerusalem reportedly provided such a drink to the condemned out of mercy (Proverbs 31:6). “Gall” means something bitter. Matthew echoes Psalm 69:21: they gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.

But when he tasted it, he would not drink it. Jesus refused to dull his senses. He would drink the cup his Father had given him fully conscious (26:39), bearing the full weight of suffering for his people.

In a sentence. At Golgotha, Jesus refused the drugged wine offered to dull his pain.

On a Tuesday. Jesus faced his suffering with clear eyes, for you. Do not numb yourself to the reality of what he did.
verseByVerse.note: Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.” The drink was probably a drugged wine to dull pain; Jesus refused it.

parallels.desc: they gave me poison for food

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. Then they sat down and kept watch over him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. Then they sat down and kept watch over him there.

And when they had crucified him. Matthew describes the crucifixion in four Greek words. He does not dwell on the physical horror, which his readers knew well. The victim was nailed or tied through the wrists and feet to a wooden cross, raised upright, and left to die slowly, often over hours or days, from exhaustion, blood loss and suffocation, as he struggled to push himself up to breathe. It was designed to be as painful and shameful as possible. The Roman writer Cicero called it the cruellest and most disgusting punishment.

They divided his garments among them by casting lots. The clothes of the condemned belonged to the execution squad. Psalm 22:18: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (John 19:23–24 quotes it). Jesus was crucified naked, a final humiliation.

Then they sat down and kept watch over him there. To prevent rescue, and to make sure he died.

In a sentence. The soldiers crucified Jesus, divided his clothes by lot as Psalm 22 foretold, and sat down to watch.

For worship. Thank Jesus, who was stripped of everything, so that you could be clothed in his righteousness.
verseByVerse.note: The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: And over his head they put the charge against him, which read: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews." Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over his head they put the charge against him, which read: this is Jesus, the King of the Jews. Two robbers were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.

And over his head they put the charge against him. A board (titulus) stating the crime, carried before the condemned and then nailed to the cross, so that all would know why he died. John says it was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek (John 19:20).

This is Jesus, the King of the Jews. The charge was treason: claiming to be king. Meant as mockery of the Jews, it was the truth. The magi had sought the King of the Jews at his birth (2:2); now he is proclaimed King at his death, in the languages of the world.

Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left. “Robbers” (lēstai), probably revolutionaries like Barabbas. Isaiah 53:12: he was numbered with the transgressors. James and John had asked for the places at his right and left in his kingdom (20:21). Here are the ones at his right and left as he is enthroned as King.

In a sentence. Above Jesus’ head the charge read “King of the Jews”, and he was crucified between two rebels.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was numbered with the guilty so that the guilty could be counted righteous.
verseByVerse.note: The charge was written on a board for all to read. The “robbers” may have been insurgents.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who passed by insulted him, shaking their heads and saying: you who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.

And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads. Psalm 22:7: all who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads. Crucifixions were by the roadside; passers-by joined in the mockery.

You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! The false charge from the trial (26:61). The irony: he was at that moment fulfilling it. His body, the true temple, was being destroyed, and in three days he would rise (John 2:19–21).

If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross. The words of the devil in the wilderness: if you are the Son of God (4:3, 6). The same temptation: prove yourself, save yourself, avoid the cross. Jesus could have come down. He stayed, because he is the Son of God, obedient to the Father. It was not nails that held him there, but love.

In a sentence. Passers-by mocked Jesus to save himself and come down if he was the Son of God, repeating the devil’s temptation.

On a Tuesday. Jesus did not save himself so that he could save you.

parallels.desc: “If you are the Son of God”

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him in the same way: he saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him.

So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him. The highest religious leaders of Israel came to gloat.

He saved others; he cannot save himself. Unknowingly, they spoke the heart of the gospel. Because he was saving others, he could not save himself. If he saved himself, he could not save us. He chose not to save himself.

He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. A false promise. They had already seen many signs and did not believe. Even when he rose from the dead, they did not believe (28:11–15). A greater sign than coming down from the cross was coming: rising from the tomb.

In a sentence. The religious leaders mocked Jesus for saving others but not himself, promising to believe if he came down.

On a Tuesday. He could not save himself and save you. He chose you. Let that move you to love him.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he did not save himself, so that he could save you.

verseByVerse.quote: "He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.'" And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. For he said, I am the Son of God. And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way.

He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. Almost word for word Psalm 22:8: he trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him. The leaders, experts in the Scriptures, unknowingly quoted the psalm that described Jesus’ suffering. Psalm 22 begins with the words Jesus would soon cry out (v. 46), and ends in triumph.

For he said, “I am the Son of God.” They mocked his claim. If God really loved him, surely he would rescue him. They took his suffering as proof that God had rejected him. In a sense, God was forsaking him, but for our sake (v. 46).

And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way. Even the condemned men joined in. Luke records that one later repented and asked Jesus to remember him, and Jesus promised him paradise that day (Luke 23:39–43).

In a sentence. The leaders mocked Jesus with the words of Psalm 22, and even the crucified robbers reviled him.

On a Tuesday. Suffering is not proof that God has rejected you. Jesus was the beloved Son, and he suffered.
verseByVerse.note: Luke records that one of the two later repented.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–66 — The Death, the Burial, and the Guard at the Tomb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Darkness covers the land from noon until three. Jesus cries out the opening line of Psalm 22, is offered sour wine, shouts once more and yields up his spirit. The temple curtain tears from top to bottom, the earth shakes, tombs open, and the centurion who has watched it all confesses him Son of God. The women who had followed from Galilee look on; Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for the body and buries it in his own new tomb; two Marys sit opposite it. On the Sabbath the council persuades Pilate to seal the stone and post a guard.
verseByVerse.theology: The cry of dereliction is the theological centre of the atonement, and two things must be held together or one of them will be lost. He is quoting — the opening line of Psalm 22, which names the whole psalm, a psalm that describes pierced hands and feet and garments divided by lot, and which ends not in darkness but in vindication and a worldwide people and the words he has done it. And he is not merely reciting: the forsakenness is real, for he was made sin for us and became a curse for us. Not the tearing apart of the Trinity — the Father never stopped loving the Son — but the full judicial weight of standing in the place of the guilty. He lost the sight of his Father's face without ever losing his grip on his Father's character, and he still said my God.
verseByVerse.examples: The curtain is the pastoral centre of this section. It hung across the way into the Most Holy Place, and its entire function was distance: one man, once a year, with blood, and no one else ever. At three in the afternoon, with no hand near it, it tore from the top down. So the barrier was not removed by anyone becoming fit to pass it; it was removed by a death, from God's side, downward, before the reader did anything at all. Anyone who has been waiting until he is clean enough to pray has been waiting for something that was dealt with on a Friday afternoon. And note who fills the rest of the section: the women who stayed when every apostle had run, and a member of the condemning council who found his courage on the one evening when there was nothing left to gain by it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?" that is, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
From noon until three in the afternoon there was darkness over all the land. About three o’clock Jesus cried out with a loud voice: Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani? That is, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. From noon to 3 p.m. Not an eclipse, which cannot happen at Passover, when the moon is full. A supernatural darkness. In Scripture, darkness pictures God’s judgment: the plague of darkness in Egypt before the Passover (Exodus 10:21–23); and Amos 8:9: on that day, declares the Lord GOD, I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight. God’s judgment on sin was falling on his Son.

And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice. About 3 p.m., the hour of the afternoon sacrifice in the temple.

“Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The first line of Psalm 22, in Aramaic and Hebrew. The only words from the cross that Matthew records. Not “Father”, as he always prayed, but “My God”. In his agony, Jesus experiences being forsaken by God.

What does it mean? On the cross, Jesus bore the sins of his people and the judgment they deserved (1 Peter 2:24; 2 Corinthians 5:21). The heart of that judgment is separation from God, his face turned away in holy wrath (Isaiah 59:2). Jesus experienced, in his human soul, the God-forsakenness that sinners deserve, so that we would never be forsaken. This is the darkest moment in all of history, and the heart of penal substitution: Christ took the penalty of our sin in our place.

Not despair. Even in being forsaken, Jesus still says “My God”. It is a cry of faith in agony. And he quotes a psalm that moves from abandonment to triumph: Psalm 22 ends with the nations turning to the LORD, and declares that he has done it (Psalm 22:27–31).

What it does not mean. Not that the Trinity was broken, or that the Father stopped loving the Son, or that Jesus stopped being God. The eternal union of the Father and the Son cannot be destroyed. The Father was well pleased with his Son’s obedience even then (Ephesians 5:2; John 10:17). What Jesus lost was the experience of the Father’s comforting presence; what he bore was the Father’s wrath against sin, which he had taken as his own. It is a mystery we can only worship.

In a sentence. In supernatural darkness, Jesus cried out the first words of Psalm 22, experiencing God’s forsaking as he bore the judgment on our sin.

On a Tuesday. If you trust Christ, you will never be forsaken by God, because Jesus was forsaken in your place (Hebrews 13:5).

For worship. Bow in silence before the cross, where the Son was forsaken for you.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders, hearing it, said, "This man is calling Elijah." And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, and put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the bystanders, hearing it, said: this man is calling Elijah. One of them ran at once, took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink.

This man is calling Elijah. They misheard “Eli” (my God) as “Elijah”. Many Jews believed Elijah would come to help the righteous in distress.

And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, and put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink. Sour wine (oxos) was cheap, vinegary wine drunk by soldiers and labourers. Perhaps an act of mercy, or to prolong his life and see if Elijah came. Psalm 69:21: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink. John records that Jesus said “I thirst”, and received the drink (John 19:28–30).

In a sentence. Bystanders thought Jesus was calling Elijah, and one gave him sour wine on a sponge.

On a Tuesday. Jesus thirsted on the cross so that you could drink the water of life (John 7:37).
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: But the others said, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the others said: wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.

But the others said, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him.” Mockery or curiosity. Elijah would not come. John the Baptist, the Elijah who was to come, had already died (17:12). No one would save Jesus from death. But God would save him out of death.

In a sentence. Others mocked, waiting to see whether Elijah would come to save him.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes God does not rescue from suffering, but through it. Trust him in the waiting.

parallels.desc: Elijah before the day of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit.

And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice. Crucifixion victims usually died exhausted, with no strength left to shout. Jesus died with a loud cry, in full control. John records the words: It is finished (John 19:30), one word in Greek, tetelestai, meaning completed, paid in full. Luke records: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46), from Psalm 31:5.

And yielded up his spirit. Literally “released his spirit”. Jesus did not merely die; he gave up his life, deliberately, at the moment he chose. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). His death was an act, the final act of obedience.

In a sentence. Jesus cried out with a loud voice and deliberately gave up his spirit.

For worship. It is finished. Thank Jesus that he paid in full for your sins.

parallels.desc: I lay it down of my own accord

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. The tombs also were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised,
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. The earth shook, and the rocks were split. The tombs also were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised.

And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. The great curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, where God’s presence dwelt (Exodus 26:31–33). Only the high priest could pass through it, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). According to later Jewish tradition it was about sixty feet high and as thick as a man’s hand. “From top to bottom”: torn by God, not by man. Its tearing meant that the way into God’s presence was now open to all, through the death of Christ (Hebrews 10:19–22). It also meant that the temple and its sacrifices were finished: the final sacrifice had been offered.

And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. An earthquake, as at Sinai when God gave the law (Exodus 19:18). Creation itself responded to its Creator’s death. Earthquakes accompany God’s acts of judgment and salvation (Joel 2:10; Haggai 2:6).

The tombs also were opened. The earthquake opened rock tombs around Jerusalem.

And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised. “Saints” here means holy people of the Old Testament, believers who had died. “Fallen asleep” is the Christian way of speaking of believers’ death. Only Matthew records this. It is a sign that Jesus’ death defeats death (Hebrews 2:14–15). Ezekiel 37:12–13: I will open your graves and raise you from your graves, O my people.

In a sentence. At Jesus’ death the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom, an earthquake split the rocks, and tombs were opened as saints were raised.

On a Tuesday. The way into God’s presence is open. Come to him with confidence through Christ (Hebrews 4:16).

For worship. Thank God that through Christ’s death the curtain is torn and you may come near.
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many. When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe and said, "Truly this was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they went into the holy city and appeared to many. When the centurion and those with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe and said: truly this was the Son of God!

And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection. Matthew says they came out after Jesus’ resurrection. Jesus is the firstfruits of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20); they followed. Matthew mentions their raising here, at his death, because his death caused it, but places their appearance after Easter.

They went into the holy city and appeared to many. Jerusalem. Their appearance was a sign. Were they raised to resurrection bodies, or restored to earthly life like Lazarus, to die again? Scripture does not say. Some interpreters take the account as symbolic. Verdict: Matthew presents it as a real event, a sign and foretaste of the resurrection Christ’s death secured. We should not speculate beyond what is written.

When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus. The Roman officer in charge of the execution (see 8:5) and his soldiers.

Saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe. Terrified, filled with fear.

And said, “Truly this was the Son of God!” A pagan soldier, who had just crucified Jesus, confessed what the religious leaders had mocked (v. 43). Gentiles worshipped him at his birth (2:11) and confess him at his death. Whether the centurion understood it fully or not, Matthew’s readers hear the confession of faith that the whole Gospel has been leading to.

In a sentence. The raised saints appeared after Jesus’ resurrection, and the centurion and soldiers, seeing the signs, confessed: truly this was the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. Even a hardened soldier came to see who Jesus was at the cross. No one is too far from God.

For worship. Join the centurion: truly this was the Son of God.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records the raised saints. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him, among whom were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joseph and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many women were there, watching from a distance. They had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

There were also many women there, looking on from a distance. The male disciples had fled (26:56); John alone is recorded at the cross (John 19:26). The women stayed. They could not get close, but they did not leave.

Who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. “Ministering” (diakonousai) means serving, supporting. Luke says they supported him from their own means (Luke 8:1–3).

Among whom were Mary Magdalene. From Magdala, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus had cast seven demons out of her (Luke 8:2). She is not identified in Scripture as a prostitute; that idea comes from later tradition, which confused her with the sinful woman of Luke 7. She became the first witness of the resurrection (28:1–10; John 20:11–18).

And Mary the mother of James and Joseph. Perhaps the wife of Clopas (John 19:25).

And the mother of the sons of Zebedee. The mother of James and John, who had asked for her sons to sit at Jesus’ right and left (20:20–21). Now she saw who was at his right and left.

Women as witnesses. In that culture, women’s testimony was considered less reliable and was often not accepted in court. If the Gospel writers had invented the story, they would not have made women the chief witnesses of the death, burial and resurrection. Their presence is a mark of truthfulness.

In a sentence. While the male disciples had fled, many women who had served Jesus from Galilee watched from a distance.

On a Tuesday. These women stayed when others fled. Faithfulness in the dark hours matters. Stay close to Christ when it is hard.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake.

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.quote: When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was evening, a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who had also become a disciple of Jesus, went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Pilate ordered it to be given to him.

When it was evening. Friday evening, before sunset, when the Sabbath began. Under the law, a body hanged on a tree must not remain there overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). Romans often left bodies on crosses to rot as a warning, or threw them into a common grave.

There came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph. Arimathea was a town in Judea, probably northwest of Jerusalem. Mark and Luke say he was a respected member of the council, who had not consented to their decision, and was looking for the kingdom of God (Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50–51). Isaiah 53:9: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death.

Who also was a disciple of Jesus. John says he was a secret disciple, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). Now he came out into the open, at the moment when it was most dangerous, when the other disciples had fled. Nicodemus joined him (John 19:39).

He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. A bold act, risking his position and reputation.

Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him. Pilate first confirmed that Jesus was dead (Mark 15:44–45). The death was certain: Roman soldiers knew death.

In a sentence. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich council member and secret disciple, boldly asked Pilate for Jesus’ body and received it.

On a Tuesday. Are you a secret disciple? Joseph found courage in the darkest hour. Ask God for courage to be openly Christ’s.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council (Mark, Luke); John adds Nicodemus. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death
not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen shroud and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. He rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away.

And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud. John adds that Nicodemus brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, and they wrapped the body with the spices, as was the Jewish burial custom (John 19:39–40). A royal quantity.

And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. A rock-cut tomb was expensive, a mark of wealth. “New”: no one had been laid in it before (Luke 23:53; John 19:41). This matters: there could be no confusion with another body. John says it was in a garden near the place of crucifixion (John 19:41).

And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb. Tombs were closed with a large stone, sometimes a disc rolled in a groove, to keep out animals and grave-robbers. It would take several men to move.

And went away. The burial was complete. Jesus was truly dead and truly buried. The Apostles’ Creed: crucified, dead and buried. Paul includes the burial in the gospel: that he was buried (1 Corinthians 15:4).

In a sentence. Joseph wrapped Jesus’ body in linen, laid it in his own new rock tomb, and closed it with a great stone.

On a Tuesday. Jesus lay in a tomb so that your grave would not be the end. For the believer, the grave is a resting place, not a prison.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, in wealthier tombs sometimes a disc-shaped stone rolled in a groove.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. They saw where he was buried (Mark 15:47; Luke 23:55). This matters for the resurrection: they knew which tomb, and on Sunday morning they did not go to the wrong one. They are witnesses to the death, the burial and the empty tomb. They watched in grief, perhaps unable to leave.

In a sentence. The two Marys sat watching the tomb, seeing exactly where Jesus was laid.

On a Tuesday. Sit with those who grieve. Faithful presence matters.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate and said, "Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, the day after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate and said: sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, after three days I will rise.

The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation. Saturday, the Sabbath. Friday was called the Day of Preparation because people prepared on it for the Sabbath, when no work could be done. The leaders went to Pilate on the Sabbath itself, breaking their own rules.

The chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate. The Pharisees appear together with the priests for the first time in the passion story.

Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive. “Impostor” (planos) means deceiver. They remembered his predictions better than his disciples did.

After three days I will rise. Jesus had predicted it publicly (12:40) and privately (16:21; 17:23; 20:19). The enemies took it seriously; the disciples did not.

In a sentence. On the Sabbath, the leaders went to Pilate, remembering that Jesus had predicted he would rise after three days.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ enemies remembered his promise when his friends forgot. Remember his promises, especially in the dark.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead,' and the last fraud will be worse than the first." Pilate said to them, "You have a guard of soldiers. Go, make it as secure as you can."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, or his disciples may go and steal him away and tell the people, he has risen from the dead, and the last fraud will be worse than the first. Pilate said to them: you have a guard of soldiers. Go, make it as secure as you can.

Therefore order the tomb to be made secure until the third day. They feared a hoax.

Lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, “He has risen from the dead.” Their fear, and later their explanation (28:13). But the disciples were frightened, scattered, and not expecting a resurrection.

And the last fraud will be worse than the first. The “first fraud” was his claim to be the Messiah; the last would be a fake resurrection.

Pilate said to them, “You have a guard of soldiers.” Or “Take a guard” (ESV footnote). Either their own temple guard, or Roman soldiers. The guards later reported to the chief priests (28:11), but feared the governor (28:14), which suggests Roman soldiers placed under the priests’ authority.

Go, make it as secure as you can. Perhaps sarcastic: do your best. No security could stop what God would do.

In a sentence. The leaders asked Pilate to secure the tomb against theft, and he told them to guard it as securely as they could.

On a Tuesday. No human power can stop God’s purposes. Whatever you face, God’s promises cannot be sealed up.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard.

So they went and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone. A seal was a cord stretched across the stone and fastened with wax or clay at both ends, stamped with an official seal. Breaking it would be a crime against Roman authority, and would show tampering. Compare Daniel 6:17, where the king sealed the stone over the lions’ den.

And setting a guard. Soldiers on watch. Every precaution was taken. Ironically, their precautions only make the evidence for the resurrection stronger: the tomb was sealed, guarded, and still found empty.

In a sentence. They sealed the stone and posted a guard at the tomb.

On a Tuesday. The seal and the guard could not hold Jesus in. Nothing can hold back God’s power to bring life out of death, in history and in your life.
verseByVerse.note: A seal (a cord fixed with wax or clay) would show if the stone had been tampered with.

parallels.desc: the stone sealed over the lions’ den

27.theology: The atonement: the cross as the world’s turning point. Matthew 27 narrates the event that is the hinge of history. Reformed theology has always insisted on the objective reality of what happened at the cross: the wrath of God against sin was exhausted in the person of the Son; the legal debt of humanity was paid; the judgment that was ours was borne by him. This is not one theory among many — it is the heart of the apostolic proclamation. “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Cor 15:3). The tearing of the veil demonstrates it architecturally: the barrier is gone. The centurion’s confession demonstrates it personally: the cross reveals the Son of God. Every subsequent generation is invited to stand at the foot of the cross and make the centurion’s confession their own.
27.examples:
Then: The women who watched from a distance (v. 55), who followed him from Galilee, who served him, who would be the first to the tomb on Sunday morning — they stayed when the disciples fled. Love kept them at the cross when fear drove others away. The crucifixion was not the end of their faith; it was its most costly expression.

Now: The cross is the Christian’s only boast (Gal 6:14). Not our moral achievement, not our spiritual progress, not our theological sophistication — the cross of Christ crucified is the one thing on which salvation rests. Charles Spurgeon preached: “I have a great need for Christ; I have a great Christ for my need.” Matthew 27 is the ground of that confidence. The stone rolled over the tomb is the last attempt of human power to contain what cannot be contained.

28.title: He Is Risen — Go and Make Disciples
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. <sup>2</sup>And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it. <sup>3</sup>His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. <sup>4</sup>And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men. <sup>5</sup>But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. <sup>6</sup>He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay. <sup>7</sup>Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and behold, he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you.” <sup>8</sup>So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples. <sup>9</sup>And behold, Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.” <sup>11</sup>While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. <sup>12</sup>And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers <sup>13</sup>and said, “Tell people, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.’ <sup>14</sup>And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.” <sup>15</sup>So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day. <sup>16</sup>Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. <sup>17</sup>And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted. <sup>18</sup>And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. <sup>19</sup>Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, <sup>20</sup>teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
28.overview:
The Gospel of Matthew ends not with a conclusion but with a commission. The resurrection of Jesus is announced by an angel, confirmed by the empty tomb, and experienced in a personal encounter — the women grasp his feet and worship. Then comes the mountain in Galilee: the eleven, some worshipping and some still doubting, gathered around the risen Lord. And from the mountain — the place where Moses received the law, where Jesus gave the Sermon, where Peter heard “listen to him” — the final and greatest declaration is made: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

The Great Commission is the Matthew bookend that closes the Emmanuel bracket. In chapter 1, an angel announced “they shall call his name Emmanuel — God with us.” In chapter 28, the risen Lord promises “I am with you always, to the end of the age.” Emmanuel is still with us — not in a manger, not on a cross, but in the risen, enthroned, all-authoritative presence of the Son of God who goes with his people to the ends of the earth. The Gospel does not end; it is sent. The reader is commissioned. Every disciple who has read these twenty-eight chapters is addressed by the last three verses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Resurrection and the Great Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At dawn on the first day the two Marys come to the tomb; there is an earthquake, an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it, and the guards collapse. The women are told he is risen as he said, invited to inspect the empty place, and sent to the disciples — and on the way the risen Jesus meets them himself and calls the men who deserted him his brothers. Meanwhile the guards report everything to the chief priests, who convene, pay them, and put out the story that the body was stolen. In Galilee the eleven meet him on a mountain, worship, and some waver; and he sends them to all nations with all authority and an unbroken promise.
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection is the hinge of everything: without it the cross is a tragedy, with it the cross is the decisive act of redemption, declared effective and guaranteed. Note that the angel identifies the risen Lord as Jesus who was crucified — a perfect participle, a standing title. The resurrection does not cancel the cross; it vindicates it, and the marks stay. The commission then rests on a royal decree rather than on human enthusiasm: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me is the ground of therefore go, and it is Daniel 7:14 fulfilled. Baptism is into one name, singular, held by three persons — the clearest Trinitarian sentence in the Synoptics.
verseByVerse.examples: Three things in this chapter are worth carrying away. First, the section Matthew alone records (vv. 11-15): the guards give the chief priests a complete eyewitness account, and the priests neither investigate nor go and look — they buy a story. Nobody pays a large sum to suppress a report he believes is nonsense, and the alibi they purchase destroys itself, since sleeping men cannot testify to what happened while they slept. It closes the thread opened at 12:39 — they demanded a sign, were promised the sign of Jonah, received it on the day he specified, and paid to have it denied. Evidence has never been the problem. Second, the word my brothers (v. 10), spoken over deserters before one of them had apologised. Third, the clause Matthew could have tidied away and did not: some doubted (v. 17). He commissioned waverers, and went with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. And there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, rolled back the stone and sat on it.

Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week. Sunday morning, at first light. Jesus had been in the tomb from Friday afternoon, through Saturday, to early Sunday: “three days” by Jewish counting (12:40). From then on, Christians gathered for worship on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, in honour of the resurrection (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10).

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. The same women who watched him die and saw where he was buried (27:56, 61). Mark and Luke say they brought spices to anoint the body (Mark 16:1; Luke 24:1). They came to mourn and to honour a dead body. They did not expect a resurrection.

And behold, there was a great earthquake. As at his death (27:51). God’s mighty acts shake the earth.

For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone and sat on it. The angel did not roll away the stone to let Jesus out; the risen Jesus could pass through closed doors (John 20:19, 26). He rolled it away to let the witnesses in, so they could see the tomb was empty. Then he sat on it: a sign of victory. The great stone that sealed the grave became a seat.

In a sentence. At dawn on Sunday the two Marys came to the tomb, and an angel, descending in an earthquake, rolled back the stone and sat on it.

On a Tuesday. Every Sunday is a weekly celebration of the resurrection. Gather with God’s people to worship the risen Lord.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men.

His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. The brightness of heaven. Like the angel in Daniel 10:6, and like Jesus at the transfiguration (17:2).

And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men. The irony: the guards set to watch the dead man became like dead men themselves, while the dead man was alive. The guards “trembled” (eseisthēsan), the same root as the earthquake: they shook as the earth shook. They were witnesses to the angel and the empty tomb, which is why the leaders later had to bribe them (vv. 11–15).

In a sentence. The angel shone like lightning, and the guards shook with fear and fell like dead men.

On a Tuesday. Human power is helpless before God. The soldiers who guarded Jesus’ tomb were powerless to keep him in.

parallels.desc: his face like the appearance of lightning

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to the women, "Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel said to the women: do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay.

But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid.” The guards are terrified; the women are comforted. “Do not be afraid” is God’s word to his people at his great acts of salvation (1:20; Luke 2:10).

For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. “Who was crucified”: the perfect tense in Greek suggests “who has been crucified and remains the crucified one”. The risen Lord is the crucified Lord; he bears the marks of the nails (John 20:27). The cross is not forgotten in the resurrection.

He is not here, for he has risen. The central announcement of the Christian faith. “He has risen” (ēgerthē) is passive: he has been raised, by God (Acts 2:24; Romans 6:4). The tomb is empty because Jesus is alive. Not a spirit, not a vision, not a memory: raised bodily from the dead.

As he said. Exactly as he had predicted (16:21; 17:23; 20:19). Every word he spoke is true.

Come, see the place where he lay. The empty tomb is evidence. The women can see for themselves. Christianity rests on events that were seen and tested (1 Corinthians 15:3–8; 1 John 1:1–3).

The evidence. The empty tomb was never disputed in the first century: even the authorities explained it, rather than producing the body (vv. 11–15). The women, whose testimony was socially discounted, were the first witnesses, which no one inventing a story would have chosen. The disciples, who had fled in fear, were transformed into bold witnesses willing to die. Paul lists over five hundred people who saw the risen Jesus, most still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:6).

What it does not mean. Not that the resurrection was spiritual only, or that Jesus “lived on” in his disciples’ hearts, as some modern theologians have suggested. The tomb was empty. His body was raised, transformed and glorified (Luke 24:39; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17).

In a sentence. The angel told the women not to fear: Jesus, the crucified one, has been raised from the dead as he said, and they could see the empty tomb.

On a Tuesday. He has risen. Every promise Jesus made is true, because his most impossible promise came true.

For worship. He is not here; he has risen! Praise the living Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and behold, he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you." So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead, and that he is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him. See, I have told you. So they left the tomb quickly with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.

Then go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead. The women become the first messengers of the resurrection. “His disciples”: the same men who had fled and denied him. He still calls them his.

And behold, he is going before you to Galilee. As he had promised (26:32). Like a shepherd going ahead of his flock, he will regather his scattered sheep (26:31).

There you will see him. A promise.

See, I have told you. The angel’s message is complete.

So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy. Fear and joy together: awe at God’s power, and overwhelming gladness that Jesus was alive.

And ran to tell his disciples. They ran. Good news this great cannot be told slowly.

In a sentence. The angel sent the women to tell the disciples that Jesus was risen and would meet them in Galilee, and they ran with fear and great joy.

On a Tuesday. You know the same news the women carried. Who could you tell, with joy, today?

parallels.desc: I will go before you to Galilee
