verseByVerse.quote: And behold, Jesus met them and said, "Greetings!" And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. Then Jesus said to them, "Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly Jesus met them and said: greetings! They came up, took hold of his feet and worshipped him. Then Jesus said to them: do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.

And behold, Jesus met them. The risen Lord himself meets them on the road. The first resurrection appearance in Matthew. John records that he appeared first to Mary Magdalene (John 20:11–18).

And said, “Greetings!” “Greetings” (chairete), literally “rejoice”. An ordinary greeting, in an extraordinary moment.

And they came up and took hold of his feet. They touched him: he was physically real, not a ghost or a vision (Luke 24:39).

And worshiped him. They bowed down before him (prosekynēsan). Jesus accepts their worship, as only God may (4:10).

Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers. “My brothers”: after their desertion and denial, Jesus calls the disciples his brothers. Not “those cowards” or “those failures”. Forgiveness and restoration are already in his words (Hebrews 2:11–12).

To go to Galilee, and there they will see me. He repeats the angel’s message.

In a sentence. The risen Jesus met the women, who held his feet and worshipped him, and he sent them to tell his brothers to meet him in Galilee.

On a Tuesday. If you have failed Jesus, he still calls you his brother or sister. Come back to him.

For worship. Worship the risen Jesus, who calls you his brother or sister.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.quote: While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were going, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests everything that had happened. When the chief priests had met with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers.

While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place. Two reports go into the city at the same time: the women with the good news, the guards with the same facts. The guards were the first to tell the chief priests about the resurrection: the earthquake, the angel, the empty tomb.

And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel. Another council meeting (26:3–4; 27:1). They were faced with the evidence of the resurrection.

They gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers. Not repentance, but a bribe. They paid Judas to betray Jesus (26:15), and now they pay soldiers to deny his resurrection. Those who reject the truth must keep paying to hide it.

In a sentence. The guards reported everything to the chief priests, who met and responded by bribing the soldiers.

On a Tuesday. Faced with the evidence, the leaders chose to cover it up. How do you respond when the truth about Jesus confronts you?

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Tell people, 'His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.' And if this comes to the governor's ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They told them: say, his disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep. And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.

Tell people, “His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.” The story they had feared (27:64), now used as their explanation. It is absurd. If the soldiers were asleep, how could they know who took the body? Could frightened, scattered disciples have overcome armed soldiers, broken the Roman seal, and rolled away a great stone without waking anyone? And why would the disciples then suffer and die for a lie they knew to be false?

And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble. Sleeping on watch could be punished by death for Roman soldiers (Acts 12:19; 16:27). The priests promised to protect them, by persuasion or bribery.

What it does not mean. Not that there are no other explanations offered for the empty tomb. Others include: the women went to the wrong tomb (but they had seen it, 27:61); Jesus did not really die but revived (but Roman soldiers knew death, 27:50; John 19:33–34); the disciples hallucinated (but hallucinations do not empty tombs or come to hundreds at once). None explains the evidence as well as the resurrection itself.

In a sentence. The priests told the soldiers to say that the disciples stole the body while they slept, promising to protect them from the governor.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection has been explained away since the first morning. The evidence remains. Examine it honestly, and believe.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman soldier who slept on watch could be punished with death.

parallels.desc: the guards executed after Peter’s escape

verseByVerse.quote: So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they took the money and did as they were told. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day.

So they took the money and did as they were directed. They sold the truth for money, as Judas sold Jesus.

And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day. “To this day”: when Matthew wrote, perhaps thirty years later, the story was still being told. The second-century Christian writer Justin Martyr records that it was still in circulation in his day. The very existence of the story confirms that the tomb was empty: no one claimed the body was still there.

In a sentence. The soldiers took the bribe and spread the lie, which was still being told when Matthew wrote.

On a Tuesday. Lies about Jesus have been spread from the beginning. Be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. When they saw him they worshipped him, but some doubted.

Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee. Eleven, not twelve: Judas was gone. The number itself is a reminder of the betrayal.

To the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. Mountains are places of revelation in Matthew: the temptation (4:8), the Sermon on the Mount (5:1), the transfiguration (17:1). Now the final mountain.

And when they saw him they worshiped him. They bowed before him, as the women had (v. 9), and as they had in the boat (14:33).

But some doubted. Remarkable honesty. Even then, some hesitated. “Doubted” (edistasan) means wavered, were uncertain (the same word as 14:31, of Peter sinking). It may mean some of the eleven, or others with them. Perhaps they could hardly believe what they saw; perhaps they were unsure how to respond. The Gospel does not hide the disciples’ weakness. And Jesus does not reject them; he comes to them (v. 18) and commissions them all.

What it does not mean. Not that doubt is a virtue, or that the resurrection was uncertain. But it shows that Jesus can use people whose faith is still weak and mixed with questions. Faith grows.

In a sentence. The eleven met Jesus on the mountain in Galilee and worshipped him, though some still wavered.

On a Tuesday. If you worship Jesus and still have doubts, you are not alone. Bring your doubts to him and keep following.

parallels.desc: more than five hundred at one time

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus came and said to them, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came and said to them: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

And Jesus came and said to them. He came near to them, including the doubters.

All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. The fulfilment of Daniel 7:13–14, where the Son of Man is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples should serve him. The devil offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world if he would worship him (4:8–9); Jesus refused, went the way of the cross, and now receives all authority from the Father. “All”: over everything, everywhere, in heaven and on earth. There is no area of life, no nation, no power, outside his rule. This is the foundation of the commission that follows.

Go therefore. “Therefore”: because Jesus has all authority, the disciples can go everywhere. The mission rests on his authority, not theirs.

And make disciples. The main command. Not just converts or church attenders, but disciples: learners and followers of Jesus, who trust and obey him for life.

Of all nations. All peoples, every ethnic group, Gentiles as well as Jews. The mission that began with the lost sheep of Israel (10:5–6; 15:24) now goes to the whole world. The promise to Abraham, that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), is fulfilled. Matthew’s Gospel began with the son of Abraham (1:1), and ends here.

Baptizing them. Baptism is the sign of entry into Christ’s people, union with him, and the washing away of sin (Acts 2:38; Romans 6:3–4).

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. “Name” is singular: one name, one God, in three persons. This is one of the clearest statements of the Trinity in the New Testament. To be baptised into the name is to be brought into belonging to the triune God. The Son is named alongside the Father and the Spirit as equal.

Where Christians differ: baptism. Paedobaptists baptise the children of believers, seeing them as part of the covenant community to be discipled. Credobaptists baptise those who are made disciples, by profession of faith (Acts 2:41; 8:12, 36–38). Verdict: credobaptist, held charitably: those who are discipled and profess faith are baptised. Christians who differ on this are still brothers and sisters, under the same commission.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that all authority has been given to him, and commanded his disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptising them into the name of the triune God.

On a Tuesday. Jesus has all authority, including over the people in your street and your workplace. How can you help one person become his disciple this year?
verseByVerse.note: Disciples of every nation are to be baptized into the one name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

parallels.desc: to the end of the earth
all peoples, nations and languages should serve him

verseByVerse.quote: "teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.

Teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. Making disciples includes teaching. Not only teaching them to know, but to observe: to obey. “All”: the whole of Jesus’ teaching, including the hard parts. Matthew’s Gospel is organised around five great blocks of Jesus’ teaching (chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18, 24–25). Now the disciples are to pass it on. Discipleship is a lifelong process of learning and obeying.

And behold, I am with you always. Literally “all the days”. The promise that makes the mission possible. Jesus is not leaving his disciples alone. He is present with them by his Spirit (John 14:16–18). The Gospel began with the promise of Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23); it ends with the risen Lord’s promise: I am with you. The whole Gospel is framed by God’s presence.

To the end of the age. Until he returns (13:39–40; 24:3). For every generation of disciples, in every nation, in every hardship. No missionary, no persecuted believer, no lonely Christian is ever alone.

The end of Matthew. The Gospel ends not with an ascension scene or a farewell, but with a promise of presence and a mission still going on. The story is not finished. The reader is included: the commission is now ours.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded his disciples to teach all nations to obey everything he commanded, and promised to be with them always, to the end of the age.

On a Tuesday. Whatever you face today, Jesus is with you. Go in his authority, teach his words, and rest in his presence.

For worship. Thank Jesus, Immanuel, who is with you always, to the end of the age.

parallels.desc: I will not leave you as orphans

28.theology: The resurrection as the foundation of everything. Matthew 28 establishes the resurrection as the ground of mission, authority, and presence. Without the resurrection, the Great Commission has no basis (no authority), no confidence (no living Lord accompanying the missionaries), and no goal (no risen Christ to present to the nations). Reformed theology has always insisted that the resurrection is not a supplement to the cross but its necessary vindication: the cross without the resurrection is a tragedy; the resurrection without the cross is a mystery. Together they are the gospel: he died for our sins and was raised for our justification (Rom 4:25). The risen Christ on the Galilean mountain, commissioning doubting disciples with unlimited authority, is the culmination of the new genesis that began in Matthew 1:1. The biblos geneseos — the book of the new beginning — ends with the world opened to the word of the King.
28.examples:
Then: Eleven ordinary men — fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot — were commissioned to disciple all nations. They had no army, no empire, no money, no social status. They had a risen Lord with all authority and a promise of presence. Within a generation the gospel had reached Rome. Within three centuries the Roman Empire had been transformed. The mustard seed had become the tree.

Now: The Great Commission has not been rescinded or transferred. Every church, every believer, every generation stands in the Galilean company — some worshipping, some doubting, all commissioned. The command is threefold: go, baptize, teach. The ground is unchanging: all authority belongs to the risen Christ. The promise is absolute: I am with you always. This is enough. It has always been enough. Go.
